This is a solid space shooter with a lot of diablo/roguelike elements to it. The star sectors are randomly generated, and the various alien races play out their own real-time game of 'Galactic Civlization' while you run around choosing sides and playing kingmaker - or just explore and fight the various rogue vessels and space monsters that threaten the galaxy.
The combat pacing is moderate, it's neither a twitch oriented bullet-hell game, nor is it slow paced. The strongest aspect of it from what I've seen so far is its very deep itemization system, with a vast array of different technologies and upgrades for your ship. Likewise its catalog of enemy factions and vessels is quite large as well, with new types and abilities being regularly introduced as you proceed through the game.

Being an somewhat of a fan of the Souls franchise, I've heard a lot of things about this game, most of them, as I've found out, untrue. Lords of The Fallen (further only as LoTF) gets a lot and I mean a LOT of flak for, copying dark souls, being way too hard/way too easy/way too clunky. Well I went into it expecting what it is, clunky souls and boy was I surprised. So let's get a few things straight.
Combat - It's slow, really slow, even one handed weapons take longer than your average two-hander in dark souls, that's not even mentioning the really big stuff, this game loves its big and metal things, so much so that some weapons are so heavy in fact, you can't even use them one handed, not even with proper stats, now that's a weapon. So for you guys out there who breezed through dark souls via R1 spams, you are not going to have a lot of fun here. Certain enemies demand certain tactics, hell there is an enemy that will smash you into the ground over and over again until you learn how to parry, really loved that one. Speaking of which, yes, your usual suspects of light/heavy attacks are here with your backstabs and parries, giving the combat a nice depth, really forcing you to learn how to fight your enemies and see the openings.
Theme - As mentioned above, this game goes in big, hard and metal. You can wear outrageous amounts of armour and you will be moving at the speed of snails and fat roll everywhere, BUT, you can clear the game just as well doing that as if you go for light armor and dodge everything. I've really felt powerful being able to shake off big hits as minor bother. So unlike in any other souls-like game, here, heavy armor is actually a legitimate choice and a welcome one at that, I've had unbelievable amounts of fun crushing through enemies with a 2 handed axe, effectively making some of them into a wet spot on the floor.
Story - Honestly, not the strongest point, you can take it or leave it, there is plenty to know about the world and how it came to be if you choose to hunt for audio bits and bops or you can ignore them and skip through most of it, so unfortunately this one might be one of the weaknesses. It doesn't have that "I wanna know more" pull to it, but is still enjoyable enough as short as it is.
Performance - Oh yeah, this one...yeah... clunky is the best I could put it, frame rate drops on a fairly powerful rig for today's standards, texture pop-in, few enemies joining the space program and rocketing off into space, oddly stiff and stood upright weapons, leading to more than a few morning wood jokes, you get the idea, it's not gamebreaking, but it's not quite what it should be.
Overall, I'd say this game is definitely worth 20 bucks, it's difficult, but fun as it is meant to be. I can see myself clearing it a few more times to see all the secrets and find all the armor sets and challenges. So if you enjoy yourself a bit of challenge yourself, but not so much of it to be overwhelming and want to feel like a buldozer let loose in a cardboard box this might just be the game you might enjoy.

It has an open survival story mode; as well as individual challenge arenas. The pieces are designed exceptionally well, and are easy to snap together with no instructions. The availability of pieces in the challenge modes is self-explanatory and doesn’t require a manual for players to jump right in and begin building.
Currently Terratech is enjoying a boom in interest for the crowd that plays Minecraft. (There are a lot of Minecraft wannabes out there like Elvis impersonators.) Terratech is not Minecraft. But, like a similar sandbox mechanic game called Scrap Mechanic, or even Kerbal Space Program, Terratech expands on a niche component from Minecraft and goes where no miner has gone before. After playing Terratech, I found them to be very different games. Scrap Mechanic is more of a tool-based construction game, also in an open world. Like many people, I love Minecraft, and many of the newer games are learning from that game. While Terratech and SM both deliver aspects that Minecraft stopped short of, each one veers in a different direction.
For Terratech, that direction is automotive mechanics. It does have open world exploration, but that's not what the kids (& adults) are there for. Most Terratechies are there for the Combat aspect. They build cars to race, planes & rockets to out thrust, & mechs to shove other mechs around. Yes, it is extremely fun and exciting to build and then trash a design in a competition. It is similar to Besiege, but it improves on the idea by providing platforms and arenas for you to pit creations against each other.
I explored the story mode, and like many others, I found the survival aspect of the open world to be counterintuitive to my efforts at actually constructing a vehicle while trying to defend my base. So I ended up in the challenges mode, where I discovered the sharing options.
The camera icon on-screen is not just for screenshots as it appeared at first glance. It actually saves a copy of the tech you've built to reload after crashing and trashing in competitions. It also allows you to share the tech via Twitter, a feature that I found cumbersome and unwieldy. You are unable to share techs without connecting to Twitter every time you log in to the game’s server. Then, you have the game search all Tweets for techs built and shared by the public. I most often came up with nothing. In the Mechs mode I found about 9 techs, while only 2 in ground vehicles, and none in wings or rockets.
Personally, I don’t believe too many kids playing Terratech have Twitter accounts. I hope they plan to expand sharing and connection options, as in being able to play with Steam friends. On the other hand, Scrap Mechanics has no options for sharing creations, while you can invite other friends to join you in game. But, one advantage perhaps to the current Terratech system is that while kids may not always be able to share techs, at least they will be inspired to build their own creations, which is a big part of this game.
After exploring the racing, wings, rockets, and sumo mechs challenges, I was sucked into the world of the R&D dlc, and I was very glad I got that. It turns out the R&D mode is where not only many more fun building pieces are, along with the more colorful cosmetic pieces; but it is the only open sandbox/ lab in the game thus far. There is talk of such a sandbox to come.
Some have complained about “day one dlc,” but the official word is that the dlc is for experimental users who want to try pieces out before they are actually put into the game. It does seem that techs designed within this R&D Lab are not available in the menu to access while in other modes. Likewise, techs designed in story mode are not accessible in one of the challenges. Each mode houses its own techs.
Terratech is extremely playable with minimum demands from your pc, where Scrap Mechanic is not so friendly with high demands. SM also not only will take a learning curve, but places a manual in the hotbar for reference. That is cumbersome. And, in KSP of course, I’m sure that will take a learning curve for younger kids. I think not needing a handbook is great in Terratech, meaning the game is more accessible from the start, for a wider range of gamers. (They are all very well-designed games. Each game has its positives.)
Terratech is early access, and anyone considering buying the game needs to keep that in mind. The developers are open to suggestions, and even include an email address for contacting them with ideas. The game is being updated regularly with patches, and you can expect a lot of big changes over time.
Easy snap-type building blocks
Clear linear directed goals with arenas and modes
Bright, colorful art and graphics with a western style of music
Active and energetic playstyle
Streamlined interface with no reading required, but the parts are labeled for reference
No parent ever stepped on a Terratech tech with barefeet (unlike legos)

Twitter sharing feature is not designed with young children in mind.
Very early access
It is a game that is enjoying popular status for a very good reason, and I can only imagine what the future holds for kids who grow up learning to use mechanics from games like Terratech.

I love this game, and I was certain I was going to hate it.
I passed this up on release day due to all the negative reviews. Then, months later, I bought it on Steam summer sale and gave it a try. It's an amazingly fun Fallout game. Is it different from its predecessors? Sure, but that doesn't diminish the fun-factor. It has issues, but like all Bethesda games on PC most, if not all of those issues can be addressed
.
And those are my two biggest gripes.
Everything else.
Power Armor is now handled in a really neat way that makes it worthwhile to own and a small burden to maintain (as one would expect). Gone is the requirement of past games to "train" to use it (I always thought that was a stupid, artificial mechanic). Fusion Cores are a great mechanic for managing the use of the Power Armor in the early stages of the game. I love everything about this.
Weapon and Armor customizing is awesome. Special, unique effects for weapons are absolutely wonderful.
Perks are well done. I know, there's some folks who complain about it, but I actually love the implementaton. Level-up in Fallout 4 is so much fun because of the way Perks and Stats are done now. And I like how the various abilties are grouped under logical stats.
The ability to create different character "builds" in this game is pretty good. Much like Skyrim. You can be a Power Armor junky who wades into battle, or a VATS sniper with sneaky armor... Up to you how you want to build out your character. I like the flexibility.
The setting is great. Boston makes for a really neat environment.
The various factions are interesting and the story is well done. The factions lack that ambiguity of those in New Vegas, but that's okay. I wish it were possible to get more of the "good" factions to play nice together and perform some joint operations, but it all works out fine.
Settlement building is fun and addicting. I didn't think it was going to be anything I wanted to spend any time on, but they actually did a great job with it and I end up spending more time than I planned making settlements cool.
The DLC's are okay. Nothing may ever be as cool as "Old World Blues" in New Vegas, but oh well. "Far Harbor" is the better of the two with a great atmosphere and a storyline that allows for multiple paths. "Nuka-World" is geared for those players who have an evil gene (I do not). For "good" style players, it's a big disappointment with the exception of the 7.62 rifle... which is the bomb.
: I have put easly as many hours into this game as I did in New Vegas, which I loved. I think it's a better game that Fallout 3, but not by much. They're all great games IMO. I've been playing since Fallout 1 & 2 and in my eyes this is simply one of the best franchises to ever grace the gaming world.
Fallout 4 is quite simply: fun. Loads of it.

Starbound is a phenomenal Early Access game (something people apparently forget) that has a vast amount of potential. It already is home to countless alien worlds with even more innumerable lifeforms, both friendly and aggressive. Its quirky atmosphere and building mechanics are simply amazing. You can simply get lost in this game for hours on end. In a very, very good way. I highly encourage people to go read the devblog and official forums quite frequently. It is there where you will see the progress being made on the game.
There are three builds to the game: Stable, Nightly, and Unstable. Stable is the default build for the game. Nightly and Unstable both are builds where players can test features before they make their way to Stable. These two builds are updated frequently so as to make sure the content, you guessed it, is stable. And as such, can be moved to the Stable build. Chucklefish likes packing in tons of content into Stable updates. Meaning Stable is updated much less frequently. Most negative reviews fail to mention the game is being updated frequently, just not on the Stable build. As I said above, just go check out the official forums and devblogs and you will see just how active and frequently Chucklefish is actually working on Starbound. Don't be deceived by people lacking the wherewithal to see truth.
The game is insane amounts of fun and is only getting better. Want to know how to check out Nightly or Unstable? That's excessively easy. Right click Starbound in your Library and go to Properties. See that Beta drop-down box? Click that and choose Nightly or Unstable. It is that easy.
So go check out Starbound. But always keep in mind it is an early access title and is being supported by those who purchase it. This isn't a Gold release. So don't treat it as such. See you out there in the great beyond!

Basically a extension of Lovecraft's "The Rats In The Walls" if you are into Lovecraft, his canon and mythos, lore, or cosmic horror this will be at least an interesting game. However it reminds me much of a hybrid of Ogre Battle(or/insert turn-based strategy game title) and Castlevania. Basically a large map with locations that can be revisited. Narrated by Wayne June whom performs a plethora of dark themed voice overs and narrations (including several quintessential Lovecraft stories) and adds an authentic and exciting atmosphere as you torment your hired thugs to delve deep into the Darkest Dungeon and the depths of their own fragile minds. The game offers copious amounts customization and intricacies so that each mercenary has a personality different from their peers. Both flaws and perks to keep your party members unique. The best part in my mind - to make the game truly Lovecraft inspired, is the breaking of moral and sanity due to the emotional torment that each adventurer endures. Certain ailments and psychoses can be lifted, however if a adventurer dies they will never return. Tragic for those gamers privy to developing emotional attachments to characters. All in all a personal favorite. Yet not for everybody.

I'm a sucker for games that are both relaxing and challenging, like Zen Bound, Darwinia, even Bejeweled.
Osmos falls into this category as well. Just a beautifully done game, both in its visuals, atmospheric ambient music (my favourite genre!) and simple concept and controls.
You are a mote - a speck, particle or cell. You can propel yourself in a direction by ejecting some of your mass, which makes you smaller. You can absorb smaller motes upon touching them and enlarge yourself, but larger motes will eat you.
And that's about it really. Level goals vary from "become the biggest" to "hunt this specific mote", but don't be fooled - there are intricacies that will emerge as you progress.
But why take my word for it? Give the demo a try. I have this game on Steam and Android, that's how much I like it.

Fractured Space is a 5 v 5, MOBA style game, set in space. You pilot massive ships fighting for control over 2 lanes which, when captured by your team, allow you access to the enemy base so you and/or your team can sieze it for victory.
There are ships with different "roles", ranging from: light attack, to heavy defense, to stealth utility ships.
Compared to most games with in-game transactions you can buy a lot. with $10 you can buy 2 - 5 ships. And these ships aren't any stronger than your ability to pilot them. This game is not a pay-to-win game.
The "grind" is easy and not horrible to do. While you are learning to play you will earn credits towards buying a ship or unlocking new weapon types for the ships you own. Which is the way games are supposed to work.

TLDR
Tactical and cinematic spaceship fights; some grinding required to unlock new ships
It's not pay-to-win, more expensive ships have different abilities and are likely flown by more experienced players but all have their own strengths and weaknesses.
Do you need to grind to get new ships?
Yes.
Does it take long?
No.
By the time you've played enough games to benefit from having a more niche ship than the all-rounder starter ships, you should have enough credits (in-game currency) to buy yourself some of the cheaper ships.
Credits are awarded for kills/support/captures and even just inflicting damage, essentially if you are helping your team in any way you get credits for it. So even if you lose because your team was bad, or you got matched badly for some reason, you can still move towards a new ship.
Phase 3 - There's a lot of hate about making the maps smaller and other Phase 3 changes, I have a ridiculous amount of hours in the game and I can say all the changes were good things.

Update 25/11/2016: Nominated for my “Just 5 More Minutes” Award.
I saw some footage of this game in January 2013 which was enough to tempt me into trying the free demo. My curiosity was piqued but I wasn't expecting much - just a bit of a time killer to tap away at and fill up a bit of the afternoon. I came away several hours later with the music stuck in my head, feeling as if very little time had passed, then went on to have a dream about Drox Operative that same night. I bought the game from Soldak's site the next day and have been playing Drox on and off since then without ever having cause to regret the puchase.
It's a hugely addictive little loot-focused ARPG with a beguiling amount of depth. As most reviews have mentioned, the most compelling feature is the sense of a living galaxy going about its business in the background while you perform the basic functions of clicking, killing, looting, equipping and selling. Essentially the alien AI races play a 4X style strategy game against eachother (albeit in real-time) while you fly about attempting to affect the outcome, with the goal of satisfying the win conditions set by the Drox guild (such as uniting the AI races, or allying with the winner of an all-out war, or victory via exploration and volume of quests completed, etc.). After triumph in one sector, you move onto the next one - presumably a harder one, although the player can set the parameters for each randomly generated sector, including difficulty. Coop online play is possible, as well as 'Hardcore' (permadeath) mode which unlocks once you get a ship to level 25.
Everything the player does affects the game universe in some way. Destroy a named boss monster and the planets in that system will become more prosperous for the alien races who hold them, giving those races more resources to build ships and advance their technology faster. Leave that monster to its own devices and he may form a fleet with other tough mobs, create malicious devices in space or perform acts of sabotage against the AI and their planets - which in turn leaves them crying for help from you, the Drox Operative, to solve all their newfound problems in the form of new quests.
Performing a fetch quest to prevent a planetary famine may solve that planet's problem - or it might produce another fetch quest from that planet, as they ask you to help destroy their rampant 'super weed' created by the fertiliser you delivered. Failing to solve fetch quests involving riots and civil war may even result in the creation of new races, who splinter off from their parent race and colonise planets of their own, becoming a new force in the sector. Alternatively you might intentionally foment discord and quest for rebel ships in order to fulfil precisely that goal. Much of this sense of life and variety comes only through the flavour text of the quests, but it is all very cleverly conceived and the quests do all have real consequences for the calculations under the hood, for the prosperity and the military fortunes of the AI. If you get tired of questing and manipulating, then you can simply explore and leave the AI to tear eachother to shreds (albeit hopefully without triggering any of the Drox guild's failure conditions).
My current ship, which I've been running a long time, is level 92, it's in a sector with 10 AI races all with their own grudges and friendships and problems, half of whom are at war with me and half of whom love me (and some of those that like me are at war with me anyway). The sector is so busy with catastrophes and weird developments that the events windows scrolls too fast for me to digest. I know I could fire this game up right now and easily lose several hours enjoyably.
To be honest, I don't know enough about the ARPG genre itself to make a judgement on the game loot balance, the min-maxing potential, or the diversity of builds available in Drox compared to other games. It feels very deep in this regard - you have stats, racial specialisations, plus a great variety of shield modules, armour modules, instant hit weapons, aimed weapons, minions (drones), buffs, debuffs, hulls and miscellanous doodads (installed in modular fashion). However I don't play enough of this type of game to know whether Drox is really deep or my understanding of ARPG systems is really shallow. I'll leave that aspect for other commenters to examine. All I know is I'm still having a great time with the unpredictable outcomes and three- or four-way battles that Drox Operative sometimes throws up, over a full year since purchase.
A special mention should be made of Soldak's excellent post-release support. The game has been patched regularly throughout this last year or so, while Soldak (creator of
and
) has also responded promptly and effectively to community feedback and bug reports. Drox was a fully formed game long before its recent emergence from Greenlight onto Steam. Now it has the benefit of this wider exposure it deserves to be played by as many people as possible, because it's an unsung gem. Clever, addictive and great fun.

A short little platformer, worth the very modest asking price despite the lack of polish it displays in a few ways.
I wouldn't really call it a Metroidvania though.  Most of the upgrades you can find are weapons, and all the "get to a new place" items are passive in nature, so your character's mobility is basically as good as it's going to get from the beginning of the game. As such, there's basically no backtracking needed for optional upgrades -- aside from when the plot requires to to re-visit an area, if you can get something, you can grab it the first time through.
Pros:
- excellent price for ~5 hours of content
- music, graphics, and gameplay all hold their own
Cons:
- limited gamepad support (no bindings by default, no D-pad support, need to use mouse in menus)
- unnecessary interstitial launcher offering a download of some other game
- marketed as a Metroidvania, but (IMHO, at least) doesn't really feel like one

This review is based on 12 hours of gameplay, mostly My Career, and a tiny bit of My Park and Pro AM. I wrote this review between the pre-release and the release of the game, so some of the problems might have already been solved when you'll read these lines.
Quite a lot of things improved this year, but the game is riddled with bugs, crashes and exploits at the moment.
PROS:
- Graphics (more details, better skins, shoes, etc.)
- Animations don't lock you so much any more. It's easier to place yourself accurately on the court for these previously hard-to-reach play positions.
- The My Career mode has more things to do, such as drills on off days. You have access to a real court filled with your team mates, where you can take part in different drills or just shoot around with your mates.
- You can also manage how you want to spend the rest of your off-time to gain VC or fans with endorsements and connections with influential people in the NBA.
- You have a customizable court where you can play or just chill out with friends
- The game is a bit harder than last year, at least in My Career, which is a good thing
- The reworked controls are easier to grasp and work better for me
- a bunch of bugs from last year have been fixed
- less lag in My Park
- Maybe the Pro AM mode, when it works? (see below)
CONTROVERSIAL:
- The Spike Lee story takes you from High School (3x8 minute games) to college (4x10 minute games) to your rookie year (8 normal-length games). It ends at the end of your rookie year, so it's not very long. After that, you get your usual but improved My Career experience
- Some people don't like it, but I think that the story is pretty good. It immerses you in the life of (your) an NBA player and serves as a big tutorial, starting with easy games. I put brackets around "your", because you answer by the stupid nickname of Frequency Vibrations (Freq in-game, sounding like Freak). You can change it when the story ends, but they still continue calling you Freq sometimes when they refer to what happened in the story.
- It's a non-interactive story, apart from the choice of high-school and college, which has no incidence on the story.
- Even though you create a white character, you'll still have the same black parents and sister. It doesn't bother me though, because it's only apparent during the (not so long) story. Also, their skin is more mixed than really black, so it didn't really break immersion with my white character.
CONS
- new year = new bugs (nothing game breaking so far, apart from the lines below)
- frequent crashes to desktop when navigating through specific menus
- less frequent CTDs when loading a game
- Some players could exploit the VC store and now have rating 88+ characters in My Park. So no point in going there until they are banned, reset, or you can catch up with their characters.
- The Pro AM mode just doesn't work at the moment, you can see your player entering and leaving the court endlessly
CONCLUSION:
It's a much improved version this year, adding plenty of major and minor things which improve the gameplay and immersion. You might want to wait for a few patches though, especially if you plan on playing online.

My friend. Let me tell you about space. Space is out to kill you. Space has rewards in it. Space will turn on you in a moment's notice acting on the guise that it is your friend.
Friend have I ever told you about interracial intergalactic relations? Space simulates sci-fiction stereotypes with 86% accuracy. You better get used to them as they represent the entire charm of this game other than our star pupil, diabloesque loot system. It does not care what you think. It will brag to all your friends even though it acts like a real load. I hope you're organized friend because space is not.
Do not take zero gravity lightly. Random events send you hurling into farther reaches of space or even more in space then you currently are. A pseudo-space that is not space.
You can't just win or lose space. Space is not some battle to be won or a prize to be earned. Space is a multi-faceted space chimera that chokes on such concepts such as linear gameplay and sandbox freedom. Space will move on without you unless you pause to take a look at it's glory. The glorious space.
Stay in space my friends.

Starbound.
A game that has been followed, that people threw money at, that released a beta. That got a lot of flack.
I got this game back when, well, before it was even released. Pre-orders opened up; we signed up to get access to the early beta, along with (I assume) hundreds of thousands of other people.
We went in understanding that the game would be released in a year. We went in knowing it would be a beta, not a stable project, and that it wouldn't be perfect from the start. We paid 15 dollars to play this experience.
And you know what?
I don't regret any of it. 124 hours into the game at this point. That's more that I've put into some triple A titles out there. That's more than I've put into games that cost 40 dollars, for the love of god.
So why do I see it differently than other people? WELL.
For one, I went in knowing it was early access. That means, buggy, glitchy, probably prone to wipes, prone to bugs. Do you all remember the first wipe? I do.
It wiped out everyone's character. And what did we all do? Most of us ♥♥♥♥♥ed. 'Why did you do that', 'Why is it not stable', 'Why are wipes necessary'? Give me my money back, this is horrid and disgusting, how could you release something so incomplete under the guise of early access - Oh, wait.
It's early access.
They didn't have to set it up so there was a stable version at all. 'Thick and fast' would ahve meant 'constant wipes, constant restarts, constant exposure to more unstable product'. The alternative was what they did now; they released a stable version, they set it to that. Anyone who wanted to experience the thick and fast updates? Opt for the nightlies.
And it WORKS.
The nightlies? Buggy as♥♥♥♥♥♥ You still have to wipe characters. You still have to deal with sometimes game-breaking bugs or imbalances. But you can see the love, the attention, the soul that the developers are pouring into this game almost every single night. You can see how much they want this product to succeed.
Yes, they made some mistakes. They pushed the launch date forward. There was that debacle with 'what is release', and all that. But how would YOU react to a sudden knee-jerk when everyone got what they wanted, then released it WASN'T the perfect space-cupcake hamsterball?
Rant over. Onwards to my real review.
The gameplay is fun. Each race has its own story and unique asthetic; the new novakids even start out with GUNS (which is weird, since nobody else does, but refreshing!). The music is tasteful and enjoyable, peaceful, explorative, creepy, awesome. You really feel the atmosphere that they're trying to get across.
Combat in the newest nightly is MUCH improved. No longer do you get hurt from touching a monster; instead, you get hurt if htey use an ability and land it on you. You can walk through mobs with no trouble.
Lighting, weather, and other minor effects like that are awesome. Rainstorms can actually drown out your crops if they aren't properly irrogated, or flood your house! It's neat and I've never seen something like that before. Not to mention, on some planets, fire will LITERALLY rain down from the sky.
The random monsters and planets also add to that feeling of adventure that I know -I- wanted in a game that was, essentially, Terraria meets Star Trek. Everything is weird, neat, and new. An entirep lanet of trees that are made of flesh and brains? Weird and gross! .... But awesome.
Environment hazards are also pretty sweet. It adds to the realism if you need OXYGEN to survive in space, as well as to stay warm (it's ♥♥♥♥ing cold out there, bro).
The new missions and quests that you can access? Also pretty darn awesome. They add a bit more that I felt the game was missing; narrative.
Bosses are fun, loot is rewarding, dungeons are challenging..
I don't know. TL:DR, The game is fun, people have issues with it that I personally do not understand, and you should really try the nightly builds.

Edit: 01/29/15
Although I didn't have time to try it out yet the trailer for the "Winter Update" looks promising. It mentions several of my issues with the game that appear to have been heavily changed from what it once was. In case a few or all of the issues I had with the game are now "fixed" consider the review below a relic from the past when it was indeed a lot less fun than it could've been.
Before Starbound came out it was hyped as Terraria's spiritual successor.
It isn't.
Think of the things that made Terraria fun. They're pretty much all missing or done in a totally different (and, in my opinion, bad) way in Starbound. This wouldn't be a bad thing if they replaced it with original ideas and content of their own... but they didn't.
There's also less purpose in everything. Building a base is utterly useless besides looks. Let that one sink in, especially if you know how important/convenient a good base was in Terraria.
a base is useless because the ship not only has
but is also more convenient than having to warp to your "home" planet (with the warp point being non-changeable from its original position!) Also, there's no NPCs that you have to build a home for. There's no need to build any kind of farm either because the "food meter" is a joke because food costs close to nothing, can be stacked and you only need to eat like once every (real) hour. There's also no kind of "alchemy" so besides useless food you can't plant anything.
The "random" aspects of the game were hyped all the way to eleven but in the end it's a dull experience.
are hardly different from each other besides their visuals and the type of blocks they're made of. The shape of the surface is similiar, there's no reason at all to dig further than a few feet deep to get materials because the best materials can be found anywhere. Going underground is boring, doesn't yield better or more ressources and it always feels the same with
to discover. Also, every planet of the same tier has the same ores. Talk about obsolete variety.
, while randomized, all feel similiar: You have a nearly infinite amount of enemies that look different, behave only slightly different and can be fought in exactly the same way: With the help of the clunky combat system. Combat is nothing more than "left-click to strike/shoot". It feels unresponsive and is far from fluid, let alone balanced (one-shotting monsters way above your current equipment tier with an 8-second cooldown hammer... balance.)
aren't anything revolutionary either but more importantly they're buggy and exploitable. The dragon boss misses his fire breath attack as long as you keep standing in the same place. Poke him with arrows for a few minutes to win. Other bosses can be exploited by building around them and then activating them or by standing behind a wall with a little hole to shoot through. Even when fighting them without using any "trick" there's hardly any strategy involved except "keep hitting until it dies".
On a last note, just google how Chucklefish handles their customers nowadays to see that this isn't a poor but hard-working indie company trying its best but instead a bunch of people taking the money for their half-finished mess and then making a run for it.
If you expected a Terraria 2.0, this isn't it. Wait for the real sequel that got announced recently.

Bethesda should be ashamed of what they've become. I love the Fallout and Elder Scrolls series but I cannot condone their recent actions regarding the creation club. As a huge fan of the Assassin's Creed franchise, this game was really disappointing.
The weird thing about AC Unity is that it's an excellent game ruined by horrible business decisions.
Finally, stealth is fixed: there's a crouch button, combat is harder, and there are more options for stealth. Parkour is easier and more fluid. Combat is the best it's been since AC2, at least. Customization is finally here, and you can completely customize your outfit based on your playstyle. Different weapons with different stats are back for the first time since the Ezio trilogy. Paris is beautiful, massive, and feels alive with all the enterable interiors and all the people in the streets, and the graphics are the best I've ever seen in a video game (including Crysis 3, Dragon Age Inquisition, Far Cry 3, GTA V, etc).
These things all sound great, right? They are. Which is why it's so sad that the game got ruined.
Horrible optimization means almost unplayably awful performance. On both low and max settings I usually get the same FPS, and I've never gotten a constant 60 (for reference, I have an i7-3770k, a GTX 680 SC, and 16GB of RAM).
Beyond performance in gameplay, performance in cutscenes is usually around 15 FPS.
A lot of the chests you find in the world require you to log in to a separate companion app on your phone to unlock them, which is completely immersion breaking and really sucks.
For some reason, everyone in Paris speaks with a British accent (which is more annoying than it sounds).
You're required to go through Uplay, a separate client, to play the game.
The co-op often doesn't work because the game can't connect to Uplay.
The second thing that shows up when you pause the game, right below "resume," is an option to go pay real money for in game stuff. This ♥♥♥♥ing sucks for a $60 game when micotransactions up to $100 are shoved in your face.
The best armor and weapons in the game are locked behind either a real-money paywall or a requirement to use some stupid external companion app.
The mini-map is stuffed with so many options that it's almost impossible to find anything useful.
Overall, this game is incredibly disappointing, not only because it follows the amazing Black Flag, but also because it could have been the best AC game ever if it wasn't completely ruined by awful business decisions.
Don't buy this game.

TLDR first: Read the negative reviews carefully, a lot of them are just bad gamers. This game is great if you know how to make conscious decisions and are aware of gameplay elements. Plus, amazing art and unique, humanizing gameplay elements.
I usually don't play RPG games because I don't like how grindy they are, especially considering how conservatively I tend to play (I usually let higher level players play easier campaigns until level restrictions stop them). But people complaining about RNG don't seem to realize that a LOT of games rely on RNG, and there really are way too many guides and strategies out there to help mitigate this thing. Sure, I spent a lot of battles praying every turn for my dodge boost to work. But sometimes it doesn't and you just have to understand and move on. The "abandon quest/battle" option is there for your characters to live another day. The whole point is so that you feel connected to them and don't just use them like pawns like you would in other RPGs because they're human as well.
Honestly it doesn't really take that many quests to get new characters back up (which is why it's so important to upgrade your stagecoach, too), and for someone used to FPS games with the attention span of a dog, it was just fine.
A lot of the complaints here are unfounded--glitches and not working on different operating systems, I get. The game relying on a lot of RNG? I get. But "I can't tell when my turn is" and "stress is unrealistic" don't realize that GAMES ARE UNREALISTIC. You have to adapt to their style of gameplay and learn that stress is more important than health most of the time. In The Evil Within the main character perfectly healthy-looking Sebastian can only sprint for 2 seconds before he keels over like a cancer-ridden chain smoking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Who cares? Adapt and move on. By the way, if you have eyes you'll realize that there's little tallies next to their stress bars that tell who's going and how many turns they get. By the WAY, if you've read a SINGLE piece of advice on the internet, you'd know that character SPEED determines WHO GOES FIRST. SO UP THEIR SPEED WITH TRINKETS.
Don't know what the hell the Antiquarian is for? LOOK IT UP. Hate the RNG but have no clue how to improve your chances (because you CAN)? LOOK IT UP. I usually try not to play games while reading up on guides because I feel like it ruins the difficulty of the gameplay, but GUYS, this is a TEN SECOND SEARCH.
Anyway, this game features an amazing art style and so many cool discoveries. Lovecraftian horror and a great soundtrack and all that.
There are always ways to regroup, recover, and, most importantly, up your chances. Once you stop seeing yourself as the victim of a "bad" game and start playing according to the game's rules you might realize that it's not even that difficult of a game. And this coming from someone who put down Dark Souls after ten minutes.

I paid roughly 3 dollars for this and used a 360 controller for Windows.
I think this is Telltale's best game that isn't Sam and Max.  It might be less of a game than Sam and Max though, it's more of an experience.  Experiences aren't really why I play games though.  I like it when I make the experience rather than the experience be something set when it comes to video games.  If I want a set experience, I'll go to a movie or visit an art gallery or ready a book which are all things I do semi-reguarly anyway.
I have not read the comics, I have only watched 3 seasons of the television show, and I have currently played 2 seasons and a DLC of this series of games.  It's better than the tv show by a country mile for having superior writing, characters, and pacing.   The dialogue is great and I did like most of the story.
There were *some* puzzles.  None of them required any thought or skill.  All stealth sections are on-rails with no improvisation needed.  Combat, if any, is mostly Quick-Time-Events.  There's a cover-based shooting segment, but it's over before you know it.  If you are in this for a typical Point and Click Adventure game or something with more meat to the gameplay, you will be disappointed.
I mentioned that I liked most of the story.  Without spoiling it, I do but my choices factored into very little of the whole experience.  I've seen and played games where my choices changed the game and the flow of time itself.  Not here.  This is Telltale's story and you have a little say in it, but not much.  I'm barely comfortable with that, but as long as the story works I'm ok with it.
I suppose this was worth the 3 dollars that I paid for it, but perhaps this series isn't really for me.  I'll get into why in my DLC and Season 2 review.

Here is my review for Spaceport Hope:
(Do not mind my ingame time,  since I often left the game open when I went to work.)
Spaceport Hope is an interesting sci-fi themed indie game. For me the nostalgia factor was big on this one,  for I am a big MetroidVania fan since ever. Basically you jump in the role of a soldier, who defends his planetary system against an invasion of another intergalactic race.
The story:
Definitely one of the big downsides.  No depth or real plot-twists and very rare use of humor or surprise moments. I don't really want to talk about the plot in detail, because I don't want to spoil anything, but then again there is not much to spoil anyway.  Pretty flat characters, linear story-telling. But I don't really feel like the plot is a very important thing in platformers and MetroidVanias after all,  so this doesn't hurt us all too much.
The gameplay:
This is where SH shines. The movement and physics just feel right. And although the storyline is linear,  the levels are not. You will find yourself in underground, sea and skyplatforming maps that are lovely designed and matching the sound themes. From time to time you have to solve puzzles to progress which are not complicated but do increase the diversity of the gameplay. Lots of planets to discover, 13 unique bosses and 12 weapons, that you can buy,  find or one that you have to forge out of different parts. The game surely doesn't fail to entertain us for a short time at least (and that's what an indie is for). There are a handful of frustrating situations though in which you really won't know how to progress e.g. Opening the councils door.
Achievements:
Since I myself am an achievement hunter I want to lose a sentence or two to that topic. They're easy. All beside of one. The 'pro' achievement is kinda a pain for quite some reasons: First of all it is indeed challenging unless you play on easy difficulty but even then it might take you a couple of tries. The larger problem is that if you miss it there is no chance to repeat the fight so you would have to start from scratch.  In fear of that I fought the last 3-4 boss fights with the beginning weapon never knowing which one is the last boss. Quite annoying . I found out though,  that if you missed that achievement you can send your safe file to the dev team and they will reset it to the moment before the fight.  Big shoutouts to them for the support and great work they are doing for such a low priced game.
Conclusion:
Definitely recommended. It's not the best MetroidVania for sure. But considering the low price there is not much of regret for purchasing it. Couldn't even buy a beer for it and I had some hours of good fun.

Spaceport hope is a decent platforming game with puzzle and shoot-em-up aspects. Definitely not a story-rich game, but it has some sort of a plot to progress the game. There are some sentences that can be touched up, but if you aren't paying attention, you won't catch them.
The tutorial at the beginning of the game will teach all you need to know to play the game. Whatever you learn from the tutorial is all you need to know for navigating through the game. After the tutorial, you will start the free navigation of the world as the main character - Cole. While the game has the mission status available, for a player playing it around the first time, it can be confusing as to which direction were you suppose to go first. So basically, explore everything and remember where things are for the future. Perhaps some more direction or instructions would've been better to tell the player where to go instead of talking to all the NPCs/going to locations to figure out that is where the lab is or that is where the mines are. So as the game progress, you get to enjoy the platofmring aspects as well as the shoot-em-up parts of the game. Killing every moving object isn't mandatory, but helps as they drop gold. Another aspect that some playeres may not like is that when gold pieces are dropped into spikes or certain niches (not pitfalls), Cole can't reach them. That kind of sucked, but it isn't that big of a deal since you can easily kill other enemies for the lost gold. After that, you just progress along the game's story plot and you will find yourself finishing up the game in no time. There are unlockables throughout the game where it requires some puzzle-ing and mass exploration on your own part. I wished there were some more puzzle aspects into the game to off set the mass exploration and shoot-em-up aspects of the game.
In terms of game design, the game is fairly decent for pixel art. Definitely better than other pixel art games I've played.
Game mechanics, as described earlier, are easy to pick up and I don't think they are as tight or hard to master in the game. One annoyance in the game design is the enemy hit boxes. For hitboxes are exceedingly large and the only two enemies with such large hitboxes are the spiked balls on Derelict and the guard bots (4 legged guard bots). Based on the pixel art, I am not touching the enemy, but I still get hit. Next, the bosses are interesting to fight. The game is very forgiving where they always provide a save point before a boss so you don't have to keep trying to get back to the same spot if you die. After a death or two, you will start to know the boss' pattern and how to beat it. Nothing impossible and you can even use the first gun to defeat all the bosses. You don't really need the wide variety of guns available in the game. Although, it may help for some players and offers variability into the game. Along the lines of the weapon variability, each gun has its own pros and cons. I honestly just used the 1st gun and the bazooka one the most. All the other weapons I found to be less effective compared to those two. Even the ultimate weapon wasn't as good as the first gun imo. Last thing about the weapons is the shared ammo pool. Nice concept, but I kind of wished the ammo capacities were separated from each other instead of linked together.
Two negatives from me. Because the character just walks and jumps, it can get boring when you are exploring a world and you can't go any faster than walking speed. Especially when you killed all the monsters in a stage (monsters don't respawn unless you die) and you are backtracking to see if you missed anything in the stage. From the first playthrough, I did wish the character can tumble or dash to progress faster throughout a stage. Last negative is the water mechanics. During the water stage, everything is managable, but annoying since you may have to double-jump to progress through the platforms. Next, getting out of the water can be a struggle. Also, there is one stage in the game where you see a pitfall, but it's filled with water. You think you can just land in there and swim across, but it acts just like a pitfall and you will die if you drop into it.
Overall, decent game. Had to play the game twice to get all of the achievements. Forgot about beating the final boss with the 1st gun only, so I had to play the whole game again to reach that point :(. Kind of annoyed from that since you can continue playing from the save slot from when you beat the game to collect unlockables, but you can't play that last boss fight again. I believe I got this game in a bundle so I do think I got my money's worth from playing this. One playthrough without unlockables would probably be just 2-3 hours, but if you want to take your time, that can get extended to 5+ hours. 7.5/10 from me.

Unless you have loads of free time - don't buy it because it's pretty good.  It's been a fun game so far, although now that I'm getting farther along it is losing some of its lustre.  The only down side I've run into was spawning into a new sector and being completely surrounded and outgunned by a plethora of enemies.  I died over and over until the horde was drawn away by other things to shoot.  Then I limped around in a broken ship until I lost the sector.  Yep, you can lose a sector but keep going with the same ship and items.
Even though the diplomacy system is a bit weak it works better than most space sims with a similar system - becuase sometimes it actually WORKS.  I guess my only complaint is that once you get beyond level 10 or so the items you find beceome so varied and you find so many that you can waste a lot of time reading what each item does and trying to decide what to use, save for later or sell.  I'm sure with time I'll be come used to the item variety and know, much faster, what to keep and what to toss.  You can even put stuff in a shared "stash" so other ships you create can pick it up.
There are five ways to win a sector, four ways to lose and when the loss conditions are met you get a 10 minuite timer to rectify the situation - if you can - or just zip around and blow up more stuff for xp and loot before the time expires.
You can often BUY your way to a win if you have enough credits - but not always and it's not always necessary.  So far each sector has felt different in the way things play out.  I even had one sector with all the races in the same star system - let me tell you that was a fast game because they didn't get along.  I had to spend about 30,000 credits (over half of what I had) to convince the last race to ally with me in the last 3 seconds so I wouldn't lose.  Overall this is probably around 8 out of ten.

I've been insane for this game since I tried it and realized what was going on: At first it just looks like Diablo in space; a solid space-spaced ARPG with enough stat-building and ship-customizing (with the random components from blown up ships, or scenario rewards) to keep you blasting for a bit. Fans of games like EV Nova might enjoy this game just for that.
But there's more. Instead of being story-driven, the game randomly generates new quests and events as you play. An elite space monster shows up, starts gathering a fleet, and if you don't react, he might take over a star system. Then the monster starts sowing chaos on nearby colonies; they might contract a plague, get computer virus, etc. These events can also escalate if unchecked. I've seen empires lose planets to open rebellion. I've HELPED rebels escalate, and contributed to the creation of offshoot races!
Also the various species - and your guild, the Drox - all have dynamic relationships. Help a race, they like you more. Attack them, they like you less. Help their allies, and they like you. Attack their allies, and you might earn more enemies than you intended. You can carefully nursemaid a sector-spanning alliance of friendly races for a diplomatic win... or watch the network of alliances fail like a house of cards if you bungle your relationship with one of the races. That might be a good time to switch tactics and go for another type of win.
The various systems interact in what looks like a well-tuned, balanced way - no surprise because the game has been out for some time. The interactions give this game a nice emergent-gameplay edge that keeps things interesting, and there's nothing more hilarious than being a few planets away from a military victory and having the Drox Guild tell you that you MUST, due to Circumstances Beyond Your Control, ally with the race you've just been eradicating colony by colony from this area of known space.
Highly recommend for fun ARPG-in-space with a sandboxy twist.
Edit: There is an expansion out, which is not on Steam at the time of this writing. You can purchase the expansion from Soldak and apply it to the Steam version of the game to gain access to additional features. He's also said that he's working on getting it into steam. He's been providing Steam codes for anybody who purchases directly, and we can expect this to continue for the expansion.

Lords Of The Fallen is a third person action RPG bearing many similarities to the Souls series. The main differences lie in the persistence and reuse of the world, the loading screens between certain areas, and the fact that this game does not support multiplayer of any kind.
So right off the bat the gameplay is golden. This is the only game of this type in which I was capable of using a keyboard and mouse to play. The movement of the camera (which seems meant for a controller) is a little off-putting every time I start up the game, but as I actually begin playing I get used to it very quickly so it’s not that big of a con. The actual action and fighting of this game is very fluid and very fun. The lock on mechanic for me sometimes seemed to mess up and I couldn’t scroll between enemies. I don’t know if that was my fault or if the game had some sort of issue with that.
What story there is in Lords of the fallen is sparse but refreshing. This game allows for far more story than any of the Souls games have. This helps to give you motivation to keep trudging onwards against the increasing difficulty the game throws at you. It allows you to make some choices as well and gives you dialogue options in a very RPG like manner that I did not expect, coming from the Souls series. Definitely a plus. And this game can be difficult when you’re first learning the enemies. There were a few regular enemies I found that kept killing me, and finally being able to kill them was a huge turning point and always gave me a sense of accomplishment. This game is also packed full with lore you can find spread throughout the world in the form of audio recordings which is always a nice touch.
The boss fights in this game are intense, difficult, and long-lasting depending on your playstyle and whether or not you research the bosses beforehand online, which I did not do. Some of the bosses have some pretty nasty tricks that you will not be prepared for in this case though. Either way, I haven’t played a game with such engaging boss fights in quite a while. This game can really surprise you too. You can be walking through an area where you already killed one boss and then BOOM, another one jumps out at you. And this game has a LOT of bosses in it. In fact it even reuses the first boss as a regular enemy. The first time I saw that I was completely not expecting it and got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. Of course once you realize what you’re up against you can face it again and win, but that’s part of the fun of this game is learning and adapting. Getting better with every attempt.
This game also has a very intricate level design that I really enjoyed too. Everything is connected. My favorite part was how in the first fifteen minutes you get to watch someone go flying through a door just before a boss fight, and then 7 hours later you unknowingly walk through the same doors from the other side to face a mini boss.
The graphics of this game are absolutely gorgeous for 2014 and still damn good for today. My only complaint in this department is in the animations. Some of the ways characters move around as they talk to you is extremely silly and when you pair it with the extreme fail that is lip syncing, then watching someone talk can be the most entertaining part of the first 10 minutes of the game.
Unfortunately this game has a lot of glaring issues that stop it from being game of the year material in my opinion. The biggest issue? Bugs. Visual bugs. Skills not doing what they say they’re supposed to. For example, this one rogue skill that lets you go invisible, but unless you use it before combat starts the enemies still know where you are. Hitbox bugs which cause your attacks or your skill attacks to miss. Strange unexplainable bugs. And finally the worst of them all...crashes. All of this may have at most made me rage for a bit and refuse to play for the rest of the day, but the game was just so damn good I had to come back the following day.
Then there’s the fact that just like the Souls game this one refuses to even slightly guide you. Just got 5 new side quests after fighting a boss? All you have to go on is the very vague directions the npcs gave you. I had to search on google how to solve most of these quests. The game also doesn’t let you keep track of side quests so make sure you are paying attention to the dialogue. But then again there are some sidequests that are as simple as finding a flint and using it to light a fire, no dialogue included. Seriously. That’s a side quest. I don’t know where I got the flint, but I got like 1000xp for completing a side quest once I lit a fire with it. And then I got attacked.
The lack of any form of competitive or cooperative play in Lords of the fallen kind of fits with the design of the levels which can sometimes be very narrow, but combined with the lack of any friendly npc companions to help you in fights? This game’s world can feel very lonely. This does help to put you in a very survivalist mindset though; knowing that everything you find is against you. I wish that they gave you something to make the world feel less empty. Even the generic NPCs you find standing around that are supposed to be friendly REFUSE to fight enemies that are right next to them!
Overall though I really did like Lords of the fallen despite the issues it did have. But to have so many bugs rampant in your game 2 and a half years after your release is laughable. Lords of the fallen gets a 7/10. It’s a good game, but far from perfect. It is buggy, it requires many google searches to make sure you don’t miss anything, but it is still fun and new game+ and the following mode add plenty of new things to the game to give it two more playthroughs of replayability. I definitely recommend this game at full price if you enjoy these kinds of games and enjoy doing new game plus. A half price sale is good enough if you just want it for one playthrough. But do make sure you can be tolerant of this game’s flaws.

Starbound is a phenomenal Early Access game (something people apparently forget) that has a vast amount of potential. It already is home to countless alien worlds with even more innumerable lifeforms, both friendly and aggressive. Its quirky atmosphere and building mechanics are simply amazing. You can simply get lost in this game for hours on end. In a very, very good way. I highly encourage people to go read the devblog and official forums quite frequently. It is there where you will see the progress being made on the game.
There are three builds to the game: Stable, Nightly, and Unstable. Stable is the default build for the game. Nightly and Unstable both are builds where players can test features before they make their way to Stable. These two builds are updated frequently so as to make sure the content, you guessed it, is stable. And as such, can be moved to the Stable build. Chucklefish likes packing in tons of content into Stable updates. Meaning Stable is updated much less frequently. Most negative reviews fail to mention the game is being updated frequently, just not on the Stable build. As I said above, just go check out the official forums and devblogs and you will see just how active and frequently Chucklefish is actually working on Starbound. Don't be deceived by people lacking the wherewithal to see truth.
The game is insane amounts of fun and is only getting better. Want to know how to check out Nightly or Unstable? That's excessively easy. Right click Starbound in your Library and go to Properties. See that Beta drop-down box? Click that and choose Nightly or Unstable. It is that easy.
So go check out Starbound. But always keep in mind it is an early access title and is being supported by those who purchase it. This isn't a Gold release. So don't treat it as such. See you out there in the great beyond!

This review is mainly slated towards MyCareer.
It's really upsetting, I played a lot of NBA 2K15 and after spending a majority of time finishing MyCareer and MyGM/MyLeague, I definitely got my money's worth after 300+ hrs. NBA 2K16, however, got pretty overhyped when regards to their MyCareer, which seemingly got worse.
I think most people were under the impression that after all the positive feedback 2K14 and 2k15 got in regards to MyCareer, and how they enjoy a story around your character, 2k would finally go all out with one this year by hiring Spike Lee to direct it.
Somehow, they went backwards. Even though 2k never had a white voice actor, hiring Spike Lee to be a ghetto visionary and make your family black and growing up in Harlem sort of ruins any illusion that most of the white players could relate to, which btw, alot of your audience is.
As for the customization people were hoping for, it some how becomes even more linear with Spike Lee making a strict storyline with choices you can not choose. Literally, the only choices you can make in MyCareer is Choosing a High School (1 of 3), choosing a college (1 of 9), and at the end of 8 games played (of 82) you get to become a free agent. Meaning if you wanted to play the 2015-2016 league, you only are playing 8 games against the legitimate rosters, and then enter free agency.
How did this happen? Outside of actual games, MyCareer lasted a total of maybe an hour. After completeing college and moving into the draft, Im finally in the NBA, next to top draft picks that have overalls of 78 and 77, meanwhile I have 55 overall and am somehow considered a top 10 pick. Where's summer league? Training camp? Where is anything that can allow me to actually progress without having to spend VC on attributes ?
Most people do NOT want to start the NBA with 55 overall and don't want to have to spend money on VC to stay competitive.
As for what they did right, High School and College felt legitimately realistic. You're a high school phenom, and as such your character is seriously OP. You can steal and run the ball and shoot better than everyone, and as you progress towards the NBA, games get harder in college. Unfortunately there was no real culture to talk about with colleges, the only differences is the uniform and logo, and High School + College combined are over very quickly.
Edit: More time put into MyCareer and gameplay is still solid, and now that the mediocre story is over, the grind for getting badges and practicing in the gym is actually enjoyable. Connections would be more interesting if they were more indepth and you weren't able to exploit them, but overall a nice addition. Still disappointing overall.
Another annoying thing to point out is the fact that during creating MyPlayer, while height and wingspan actually matter in this version of 2k ( which is a good thing ), the fact that choosing inside/outside/balanced position when creating your character limits your possibility as a player, and can't be changed. As a balanced 6'6 SF with maxed shooting, my 3 pt is below average that of another SF in the league.

5) Working through the rare lull in narrative excitement is instantly rewarded with action and fast-paced plot progression.
6) The multi-faceted gameplay is expansive and immersive, and intrinsically rewarding.
7) The game is gorgeous.
8) The parkour mechanics are superbly streamlined and intuitive, more than ever before - thus, just inter-mission exploring is thrilling and addictive.
9) As always, I wish there was more than the default difficulty level to choose from.
10) I strongly recommend using a gamepad. Keyboard and mouse controls are a veritable nightmare and interfere with the supple free-running mechanics that are central to all aspects of AC gameplay.
11) The system for learning and accessing Assassin abilities, tools, and weapons adds anticipation and a sense of accomplishment that lasts from beginning to end.

I've thoroughly played all of the Assassin's Creed games from the beginning and this one is by far the most visually stunning. That I'm afraid is about all the good I've got to say about it so far.  I'm 25 hours in at this point and I'm ready for it to be over. All of the games have had their frustrating moments with mechanics while free running but Unity takes it to a whole new level. From the first game to Brotherhood I spent as much time as possible on buildings running across rooftops because it was damned fun to parkour across the cities. In Unity I spend as much time as humanly possible on the ground because climbing anything will inevitably end up in a fit of keyboard punching while Arno is stuck to a wall/window/overhang making jerking motions in all directions going nowhere. The change to pressing Space to go up and E to go down might have been a good plan if it adhered to that and Arno reliably moved in the directions I press. If you find yourself having to choose between taking on 20 soldiers or going down one ladder to reach a target you'll want to take on the soldiers, believe me. Combat has changed significantly from previous games and while many people seem to enjoy the increased difficulty I'm not a fan. Were characters a little overpowered in the previous games, maybe, but combat was far more satisfying when you got the timing down and the characters are master assassins after all. Even after 25 hours I cannot find any sort of rhythm to combat sequences and it always ends up as a cross your fingers and key smash situation. I especially love when Arno decides to stop responding to attack/block keys and just stand there while being slashed to death, over, and over, and over again.  I've desynced more times in this game than all of the previous combined and it is 99% due to bugs.
Beyond the core mechanics problems lie some core issues that also significantly set Unity apart from the rest of the franchise. I've enjoyed spending many hours at a time in Assassin's Creed games because of the great feeling of immersion in historical settings. Sure they've had plenty of repetitive events, missions, etc but overall I still had a decent feeling of being there. Despite the amazing visuals Unity has little to no immersion, it feels like I'm just playing a game and it reminds me of that constantly. Chests that can only be opened by a companion app, chests that are opened by some kind of online events, co-op popups in the middle of missions, etc. At this point I'm just grinding through the main missions. The diversity of the side missions is definitely appreciated and I'd love to see all the side story content but I have no interest in subjecting myself to more miserable parkour and combat bugs. In truth I would have stopped the game all together by now if it were not for the fleeting hope that there may be some continuation of the background story that has spanned all of the Assassin's Creed games. However, thus far no time at all has been spent outside the Animus and there have been no tidbits at all about the Assassin and Templar struggle, locating artifacts, or what any of the artifacts we've been playing through six games worth of genetic memories to locate are even for.
Update: I have now completed the game so I can report that there are no updates to the overall Assassin's Creed story line so there was really no point in playing this game at all.  I now have over 40GB more free disk space at least.

Well, I was fooled by the glowing reviews and promptly disappointed after only a few hours of play.
Early progression is utterly boring. Every ship available to you moves slightly faster than a beached whale, relative to the size of the combat areas.
Mouse sensitivity at maximum does not even begin to keep up with camera speed and prevents you from properly engaging ships when they pass above or below you. If  a ship suddenly appears behind you, you're essentially space scrap in most situations.
The tutorial offers some free rewards, like 60 platinum. Then you find that the cheapest store item costs 84 platinum. On the bright side, most of the microtransactions are cosmetic, albeit expensive.
As far as modifications to your ships, abilities can be modified in extremely limited ways and you must platinum for these modifications. You start with a default space crew that gives percentage based improvements to various apects of your ship but I have not seen any way to acquire new crew members short of buying them in the store.
Now the primary reason this game is not worth playing to me is that matches consist of only 5 players on each team, which leads to too much meandering around the arena, maybe capturing a mine for some reason and not too much combat. I only played 4 matches, to keep things in perspective here but in all of them, they were nearly snooze-fests.
Important to mention, as well, one of the teams was already guaranteed victory because a higher class ship manned by an active player was able to single-handedly take out 2 ships on the other team, then take time to repair, upgrade, assess movement of their remaining opponents and return to combat.

The game has its charm:
Very intersting soundtrack - dynamic, but not interruptive. Perfect for the pace of the game.
Interesting weapon: Imagine demolition of buildings with mace attached to a plane. That kinda describes the gameplay.
It is not that kind of game where enemies sidescrolling with speed of light to test your patience. This is good combination of abstract visuals with physical dynamic of The Weapon(named 'Particle Mace') which makes it into unique tactical arcade game where challenge is proportional to how dangerously you plan to play it. Due to unique weapon it is possible to discover different tactics on how to manipulate it effectively, especially considering different unlockable 'ships' with their own down- and upsides with special abilities.
Missions mode deserves its own prize: you are granted with 3 tasks each round. When you complete them all you get a new set, but if you die new ones will replace the completed ones leaving the unfinished tasks to the next round and as some modify the enviroment(like do A in a black hole or smash 50 asteroids in asteroid field) the old one can become a challenge(Hiker(reach spots without hurting asteroids) mission along with asteroid field or yellow space) which opens new tactical opportunities on to how approach them to make problematic tasks easier by shifting others. Priorities matter!
The only downside I have managed to discover is absence of network multiplayer.

I would give Drox Operative an 8 -8.5/10, Pick it up, you will not be disappointed.

I love this Space ARPG! I've been playing it when it was available on Soldak's website, but now it has finally arrived on Steam. Off the top of my head there is:
-Diplomacy
-Co-op multiplayer
-Ship & character upgrades
-Loot!
-Exploration
-Multiple win & lose conditions
-Quest generation
-Hardcore mode
-Random galaxies
-Races trade and declare war on each other
-Open-ended and dynamic gameplay
-Pew pew lasers
You are a surviving member of the Drox race; former masters of the universe that are now extinct except for an elite guild called the Drox Operatives. The only goal is to achieve victory through any means such as Military (allied w/ the strongest race left standing), Diplomatic (convince the remaining races to ally with each other), Economic, Fear (destroy everyone) and Legend (explore all the systems, kill named monsters and never attack a race). It's up to you to back the winning horse in a galactic struggle, exploit their weaknesses towards your own gain or play as an altruist.
It may not have the greatest graphics in the ARPG genre, but I promise it has great gameplay if you're a fan of isometric dungeon crawl-monster stomps like Diablo, Path of Exile or Torchlight, only with a 4X space twist!

Wow, what do I NOT have to say about this game? Honestly, I am a huge fan of Minecraft and Terraria and their "make your own adventure, your own story" gameplay. I even own both on my PC, Console, Tablet, and other "smart" devices. Saying this, I do have somewhat of a knowledge of how these games work: you are given the bare minimum you need to survive, obtain some wood, make some tools, mine and chop for resources, make better tools so you can mine and chop faster and longer... this goes on. Now where most games would only have this aspect to create your little "home" or rather forward operating base, and upgrade till your heart stops, Starbound goes that one step further. The setting of the game usually puts you in a senario where you are a speciese known to the universe and you are now alone, and while I would perfer a little more detail or action to take place based off of this info, I was overall satisifed, I got to decide what happened in greater detail, and may  the Lord never forbid, I had a desire to know more! All I knew was that I am a Glitch (a self-aware robot) who was exiled from his land due to the fact that he did not follow the Hive and its Hierarchy. From there on, it was my tale to make it.
You start off in YOUR own ship, that acts as your transportation around many galaxies throughout the game, by far trumping Terrarria on the environment. With each new planet you go to, you can find a new atmosphere and population. for example I started on an acidic Planet where most all of the water would harm me, and there were violent storms that would destroy my home on more than one instance, forcing me to rebuild time after time. On top of that, I felt entirely alone... there was not a single other race on the planet.
Eventually, I was able to upgrade my tools and weapons enough to face the first boss of the game, and just like in comparison of Terrarria, Chucklefish gets the boss fights down as well, adding a new element, and new summoning recipe that gave challenge and a reason to adventure in search of materials. And with time, I was able to defeat every boss.
Admittedly, I will say that I did not conquer all of them on my own, but I had another friend playing with me as well. He and I spent HOURS one night playing this game, acting as if our goal were the same as the starship enterprise from star trek. Interaction with each player if fun, however I will state that getting the multiplayer set up can be a bit tricky, due to the fact that you are required to run off of a server. Unfortunatley if you are running on a, dare I say it... cough... Apple Computer... cough... you have to know how to access certain libraries and folders in order to launch it in the first place, let alone if your computer can run both the server and game at the same time.
On top of that concern though, and I know it is difficult to figure out a happy medium of singlular accomplishment and co-op cohesiveness, there was a bit of a "catch up to me" concept at play. My first friend and I went through and defeated every boss in the game (so much fun!) however, I had another friend who also started playing, he defeated the first boss and constructed the second, but my selfishness kicked in and I was not about to start a whole new character and go through the start of the game, in order to possibly not even  get to play with my comrade after all that night. My character was extremely Over Powered and I just reverted back to trying to find cool new stuff rather than killing enemies. I even beat the bosses a second time through that night with him.
One good thing did come from playing with my other friend is that I found books on different planets that describes all of the different races in this universe, and I get to learn more about my race that I chose, further making exploration for civilizations all the more important.
What they Do right:
they are creating a new lore for their universe
The technological setting and the game concept fit really well together and transistions smoothly
In my opinion, this games traits out performs Terrarria
Mulitplayer is fun
Things That They Can Work On:
More bosses
More upgrades for the ship
More lore and races
better multiplayer system
