This is how Early Access should be done. Take note, other developers.
If you are reading reviews you already know what kind of game this is.  If you don't then watch the videos or check out others on YouTube.  This review is more about the developers, the state of the alpha, and the general experience of TerraTech.
Early Access is a crapshoot.  Every developer makes promises of awesome features, steady updates, listening to player feedback, etc.  Most of them fall short of these goals, some fall far shorter than others.  In my experience there are three types of Early Access developer:
Group 1: The Real Deal.  These people make promises that they know they can keep, or have a very reasonable, educated expectation that they can keep them.  These are the developers who know what they are doing, have a plan, and know how to make it all work.  They have the drive and motivation to get their game out there and they look forward to feedback from the community.  They are skilled game designers and passionate gamers and they exemplify what Early Access is meant to be. This is like the big holiday dinner at your grandmother's house when you were a kid.  The food is great, its prepared with care and skill, and you feel welcomed and wanted.
Group 2: MEDIOCRE. This group of Early Access developer has some skill, but no soul.  They usually fail to meet some of the stated goals and they almost never involve the community in the decision making process.  They might end up with a playable game or they might not, but the process is often painful for everyone involved.  Updates come slowly and fans don't really feel involved in the process in any meaningful way. Sometimes they make sweeping changes to the structure of the game that result in an experience very different from what the fans paid for. This is like cheap fast food.  It was made by someone who doesn't care about the food, doesn't care about you, and will almost certainly "forget" the extra pickles you asked for.
Group 3: The Snake Oil Salesmen. These developers are one step above criminals.  They are the bottom of the barrel, the worst that Early Access has to offer.  They grossly oversell their game often with little or no idea how to live up to the promises.  They gladly collect the money, release a few half-hearted updates, then disappear into the night.  They often treat upset fans with unwarranted hostility and they usually leave the game totally unfinished. These developers can be criminal or incompetent...or more likely, a lot of both. This is like a street vendor in a shady part of town.  They are selling burritos filled with meat of indeterminate origin and they only take small bills. You might get a decent meal, or you might spend the next 12 hours doing a reenactment of "The Exorcist," but from both ends. Either way, when you return to the spot where you found the food cart you will see only a deserted lot.
TerraTech is at the top of Group 1.  The developers are active in the community, they listen to public opinion and let it gently guide their decision making process, and they are very, very active with updating the game.  When I first started playing this game I found the tutorials a little hard to follow and the world was a little too harsh.  Within a day or two an update was released that clarified the starting quests and made starting out a touch easier.  After getting a feel for the game I found that over time the game slows down due to an excessive amount of spare parts floating around the map.  The very day I went to the forums to complain I see that a new update was released that adds a new block that sucks up all the spare bits and keeps the map clean.  Today I get on and see that they released yet another update that fixes some other minor issues the community has been complaining about.
If you browse the discussions you will see the developers out there talking to people, answering questions, taking suggestions, and engaging the public.  They don't just shake hands and kiss babies, they are there to work with the fans to make the game better.

This game could have been one o' the greats, but NOPE. The load times are atrocious, most everything is at *least* slightly clunky, and there is no polite way to describe the workshop construction. The story is bland, but passable, and the RPG elements feel watered down in comparison to past titles. In addition, I am occasionally forced to restart the game, due to a variety of annoying, glitches.
On top of that, the game was shared with me by a relative. I encountered so much trouble with Steam's Sharing system that I was forced to (very angrily) purchase it for myself.
There are a few points I think are worth mentioning as positive: the array of special weapon and armor traits as well as the ability to customize and name weapons and armor, the changes to power armor (which I think adds a bit of flavor to combat, depending on how it's customized), and the addition of workshops (even if building onto them can be a hellish experience). I also enjoy the perk system (though some of the choices, so far as I can tell, are useless). Also, while I am aware of a few, I have never personally encountered any game-breaking glitches, which I find to be especially infuriating,
As I hate to end on a positive note, I shall mention the money-grubbing tragedy that is the "creation club."
Overall, I begrudgingly recommend this title, which can be downright fun on occasion, if only to those with a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of patience to spare.

TLDR first: Read the negative reviews carefully, a lot of them are just bad gamers. This game is great if you know how to make conscious decisions and are aware of gameplay elements. Plus, amazing art and unique, humanizing gameplay elements.
I usually don't play RPG games because I don't like how grindy they are, especially considering how conservatively I tend to play (I usually let higher level players play easier campaigns until level restrictions stop them). But people complaining about RNG don't seem to realize that a LOT of games rely on RNG, and there really are way too many guides and strategies out there to help mitigate this thing. Sure, I spent a lot of battles praying every turn for my dodge boost to work. But sometimes it doesn't and you just have to understand and move on. The "abandon quest/battle" option is there for your characters to live another day. The whole point is so that you feel connected to them and don't just use them like pawns like you would in other RPGs because they're human as well.
Honestly it doesn't really take that many quests to get new characters back up (which is why it's so important to upgrade your stagecoach, too), and for someone used to FPS games with the attention span of a dog, it was just fine.
A lot of the complaints here are unfounded--glitches and not working on different operating systems, I get. The game relying on a lot of RNG? I get. But "I can't tell when my turn is" and "stress is unrealistic" don't realize that GAMES ARE UNREALISTIC. You have to adapt to their style of gameplay and learn that stress is more important than health most of the time. In The Evil Within the main character perfectly healthy-looking Sebastian can only sprint for 2 seconds before he keels over like a cancer-ridden chain smoking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Who cares? Adapt and move on. By the way, if you have eyes you'll realize that there's little tallies next to their stress bars that tell who's going and how many turns they get. By the WAY, if you've read a SINGLE piece of advice on the internet, you'd know that character SPEED determines WHO GOES FIRST. SO UP THEIR SPEED WITH TRINKETS.
Don't know what the hell the Antiquarian is for? LOOK IT UP. Hate the RNG but have no clue how to improve your chances (because you CAN)? LOOK IT UP. I usually try not to play games while reading up on guides because I feel like it ruins the difficulty of the gameplay, but GUYS, this is a TEN SECOND SEARCH.
Anyway, this game features an amazing art style and so many cool discoveries. Lovecraftian horror and a great soundtrack and all that.
There are always ways to regroup, recover, and, most importantly, up your chances. Once you stop seeing yourself as the victim of a "bad" game and start playing according to the game's rules you might realize that it's not even that difficult of a game. And this coming from someone who put down Dark Souls after ten minutes.

This will be a very subjective and quite long review about most apsects of Darkest Dungeon. I play this game since the begenning of Early Access and it is the first game I'm ever reviewing, because I think the devs deserves it for their exemplary behaviour.
I. THE GAME
1. Combat balance
The Game is RNG heavy but knowing how to deal with each trap and monster makes it largely doable despite bad luck streak : it makes the game hard but rewarding and never frustrating to the point of rage-quitting. The balance between frustration and reward for decision making is amazing. After all, what is a lovecraftian world without terrible forces awaiting in darkess to wipe you without letting you any chance? To all Cthulhu RPG players, sorry for your loss :)
2. Aesthetic
The aesthetic is GOLDEN. One of the most coherent and immersive dark fantasy game alongside the Dark Souls serie. The characters fit into the universe, the monsters ar amazingly designed, the backgrounds and curios are perfect and the Narrator spices everything with spicy comments that wont get repetitive until at least 10 hours into the game.
As for the musical aesthetics, I am in two minds : on one hand the sound design and narrator are AMAZING and help greatly the oppressing atmosphere of the game, but on the other hand, the soundtrack is nothing special. It's not bad, I just don't think it's innovative or rememberable like for example the one of FTL.
The characters all have their little quirks in what they say when they are happy, mad or dying. It makes you like them, and makes you even sadder when they die. Which is what you want, don't you? Suffering. Anyway, you can also rename them, if you want to create a party composed of you, Bob, Billy and Emily, your closest frinds, so you can watch them suffer, going mad and die. Or if you are weird like me, name they all like the philosophs you studied in college and imagine their interactions. Oh, and don't put Hobbes the Leper and Locke the antiquarian in the same team. Anyway, that's just me, but the ability to create your own story, given by the very limited amount of explanation the game gives is a good plus. I love roleplay and stories.
3. Classes balance and variety
The classes are all more or less equilibrated, and every single one has it's pros, cons and felling. Some dungeon will NEED you to have a certain class on your team for it to be doable without having to sacrifiate a lamb to REGesus, but these are the exception. Some composition are optimal, but once you become used to the mechanics and monsters, you can mindle with them, try wacky things and make them work... or die horribly. Spoiler alert : 4 grave robber is the funniest and most powerful group ever in easy and veteran dungeons if you know how to make it work. But then, it won't carry you through the hard bits of the game nor help you complete achievements so... good balance, game.
4. About grind
The biggest downside people complain about is grind, and to be honest, the game IS grindy. Like, really grindy. But the devs added the "Radiant mode" in an update, which is NOT an easy mode. Radiant is just less grindy : you gain more rewards, you can use heroes with less restrictions and they level faster, BUT the monsters stay as strong, your heroes do the same and will die just as hard. If you don't like grind, go for it, and don't be ashamed.
That's it for the game in itself, now let's talk about the devs.
II. The devs
Red Hook have made an amazing job on Darkest Dungeon. The game was Kickstarted, went through early access with a strong following and regular update, and the dev kept communicating about the advancement of the early access. And then came the release...... AND THEY KEPT THE SAME ATTITUDE !
The game sold a lot for it was complete and good and the dev took the opportunity to mak it even BETTER. They kept communicating, they did many bug fixes, bakance patches and even free updates. Yes, FREE UPDATES in 2017. They added content for free multiples times after release while preparing their first dlc. Monster, difficulty/anti-grind modes, heroes, trinkets among other things.
And then came the DLC. And as always it was amazing. It kept th atmosphere, it added new mechanics and was overall a nive addition. And even for those who didn't buy it, they put all the new mechanics in the core game! I mean, how cool is that? One very fair DLC for 10 quids, and if you don't want it, you still get the QoL changes!
Red Hook, good job, keep it up, I'm waiting for your next DLC on this amazing game.
III. The community
Be it on their website, on steam or on the nexus, the community is present, hard-working and helpful. This is true of a lot of games, but worth mentionning. As I said, the game is great in itself. But modders are starting to make more and more amazing work as time passes. Before, it was only reskins or twisting certain classes or moves. Now you have so much diversity in new classes, new trinkets, new monsters etc. And that's again partly due to Red Hook, who helped modders decrypt their codes and given them advice on modding. And that is, again, amazing from them.
Also, you can activate or desactivate mods at any point during a game, and even choose on which of your games you want them WITHOUT EVEN HAVING TO QUIT THE GAME. Thanks for the free QoL update, devs. I realise how I thank them for anything but god, have they been fair with their community.
So, mods. Skyrim would have been an average game, but it still shines 6 years after it's launch and everybody played it for at least 150 hours. Why? Because mods. Mods, mods, mods. A community and the ability to mod the game is what makes solo-player games last. And I believe that with Red Hook being in love with their game and the community being very present and hardworking, Darkest Dungeon will last.
You want a brand new class? Oh, god, pick your poison. Lore frindly or not, OP or weak, rich in new mechanics or vanilla-like. Pick and chose, don't be shy.
You want new monsters? I only tried "Army of Bones", it's good, and lore friendly.
You want skins? "Palette Expansion" adds 10 for each class, and many other mods add more refined or specialized ones.
You want winter on the Hamlet? Done. Harder game? Done. Easier game? Deal. God, even nude mods are starting to bloom, and oh, god why would you do that, modders! I love you guys.
IV. Conclusion
Buy it. Love it. Farm it. Stop to pee. Farm it. Stop to eat. Farm it. Stop to sleep (no, actually, one more run). Finish it. Uninstal it. Wait two weeks. Reinstal it. Mod it. Love it even more. Uninstal it. Get hyped by a new update comming. Reinstal it. Love it.
Anyway, that's all for me. The game is amazing, the balance is okay, the tension is well kept, updates are regular, the devs keep in touch, the modders are on fire and the price is MORE. THAN. FAIR.
Also, for the most shy of you. Buy it, put a timer, test it for 1h30 and get a refund if you don't like it. The only risk is to waste 2 hours of your time, and you have that time. Yes, you do, facebook user, WoW player or youtube cat-video fan. You do have time. You can get a feel of the game without playing much, but it grows more and more interesting with time and emotional investment.
20/20, well desrved.

Fractured Space is a competitive 5v5 arena based space game. Built around battling people and AI with behemoth ships in space, this game shines a ray of uniqueness to the library of MOBAs already out there. If you're looking for super fast paced, mindless shooty-shooty guns blazing type gameplay, then you probably won't enjoy this game. This game relies heavily around coordination and teamplay. It takes tactic and strategy to effectively counter the enemy fleet. Jumping headlong into a group of enemy ships alone will get you nowhere. Learn how to support your teammate(s) and let them support you as you work your way down the two-laned arena to get yourself to the enemy base.
The game gives a pretty large array of ship variety, all of which (except for the starter ships) require ingame currency to unlock, which you can acquire finishing rounds. The developers have done a respectable job keeping all of the ships balanced, as well as making the short grind to get credits as enjoyable as possible. Here, free players won't get stomped by paying players in this F2P game. The devs have given bonuses to buying DLC, but not enough to make anything gamebreakingly lopsided. A free player has just as much chance to win as a paying player, as long as they work as a team with their teammates.  There is absolutely no P2W aspect to this game, unfortunately, a very rare thing when it comes to free games in this day and age.
Most ships have unlockable upgrades to your main systems, like missiles, cannons, and other assortments of tools each ship is uniquely equipped with. These "upgrades" aren't direct upgrades, mind you, merely even more options to truly find the ship that perfectly matches your playstyle or specific scenarios. Ship picks are just as important as other teamwork oriented things in rounds. And the more ships you have, the more situations you can fill for the perfect team build.
Control wise this game is pretty straight forward, in my opinion. Main controls include WASD+Ctrl+Space for maneuvering, with LM, RM, and buttons 1-6 to use abilities. I know some people that find that the controls are too complex or too roundabout almost to the point of being gamebreaking. I simply cannot agree. The controls are rather simple to my eyes, and I had no problem getting used to them when I first started playing. I'd say this game has a learning curve to it, but not a very large one. More of an Easy to Learn, Not Really Hard to Master.
Visually this game is a beauty. The graphics alongside the gigantic ship battles makes this one of the prettiest games in my library. The eye candy is truly magnificent. The sheer detail the developers put into the ship models is truly commendable. Optimization wise this game isn't bad, but it could be better. It can be a little laggy at times but you should find that most gaming rigs these days will be able to run this smoothly.
Overall, this game is a solid game that I enjoy playing the only true downside that I can see right now is that it can take a while to find a match, but that's not the game's fault. That's just the results of a small community. But since it's a free game, there's really no reason to at the very least try this game. If it isn't your kind of game, then uninstall. The only thing you want to know is if it's worth the time. And the answer to that question is a solid Yes. I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys Sci-Fi, competitive matches oriented around teamplay and coordination.

- Summary of the game's aspects [Remember that this is a indie game!] :
Scroll down for the expanded review!
Graphics: Fine.
Sound: Fine.
Music: You'll mute it after the first half hour.
Gameplay: Fun and you can fine tune the difficulty extremely well, however, the game is extremely repetitive and really lacks depth.
- Review:
Drox Operative is great fun if you're not looking for great depth or hardcore experience.
The only problem with this game is that you should NOT BUY this for any other reason than a nice little past time.
It's VERY addictive for those who like the theme and genre, however it is EXTREMELY repetitive and has no depth at all, failing to satisfy any kind of gamer that isn't looking for a casual experience or a pastime.
It's very fun to play with others, specially when everything goes to hell, but eventually the repetition gets to everyone.
There's also an expansion pack for the game, which includes some content but does nothing to address the repetitive gameplay and lack of depth and lack of persistance.
If you are looking for hardcore space games, or something in the lines of EV Nova, Transcendence and other amazing classics of the Top-Down and Isometric space RPGs, this WILL dissapoint you greatly - you have been warned!
Past that, the game can be very fun.
I must say it's amazing to see things go to hell if you don't manage your sector's threats.
Have fun! :)
- Conclusion:
Nice, fun little game, that you should definetly try the demo before buying.

Steam can sometimes go weeks without a bringing a quality title to the store; but I have to say they made a great addition with Drox Operative. I knew nothing about this game when I picked it up, and I will say that I have been disappointed by the Steam impulse buy before. Not this time though.
There are some downsides of course; the games production value feels quite low. The graphics are dated, and the game is sorely in need of a basic tutorial. If you can see past the graphics however, and its moderate learning curve; you'll see it is an excellent action RPG in its own right. It is remarkably deep; easily scales to be as difficult as you want it to be, and delivers on every feature the store page promises.
I'll be honest; I really fell in love with the novelty of the concept. Instead of playing as just another 4x empire; you are a very small player in each randomly generated sector's galatic politics. You cannot take on any one of these empires by your lonesome; but through clever gameplay you can manipulate the entire galaxy and forge its destiny over time. With 5 different ways to win; this concept is awesome and incredibly addicting.
Now it just needs more exposure so that cooperative games are easier to find/put together. I look forward to picking up the expansion, and maybe trying out Din's Curse as well.

Basically, the game is Din's Curse..IN SPACE! with some heavy focus on diplomacy and politics.  The idea is that you are part of a group called the Drox Guild, with the goal of maintaining the presence of the Guild in the sector (the game world).  There are several ways one can win or lose, giving YOU the player the ability to choose how to win/fail.  Like the other Soldak games, this features the living world around you aproach to the hack and slash.  Quests have time limits.  Success or failure will cause changes to the game world.  That radiation leak on the planet won't fix itself, and if you leave it for long enough the planet can suffer more woes that you can solve.  But should you buy this game?
Yes.  Yes you should.  Here is why:
+You are a space mobster.  Really the game should be called Drox Moberative.
+Technically infinite gameplay, just because you beat the sector doesn't mean you can't keep playing in particular in HOW you won the sector.  I got a "fear" victory while at war with two races and battled them for a good two hours to make little head way.
+Decent gameplay.  Its a hack and slash, but it is tuned to make sense and it plays pretty well.  The battles are engaging and enjoyable, if not overwhelming at points.
+VERY diverse worlds.  It is improbable that you will get the same sector twice.  In addition to simply having a random lay out, each system and sector have different moddifiers (more enemies, more agressive behavior, more traps) so you never know what you are going to get with your new sector.  On top of that, Mods Mods Mods.  Add more mayhame with mods
+Easy to lose track of time with.  Not sure why that is a plus but what ever.
That said there are some things to be desired such as stat point distribution, but most if not all can be fixed with mods.  Give the demo a try if you are still not sure.  It is much more engaging than one would think.

People mention that this game is not Dark Souls and should not be reviewed as if it were a Dark Souls title. That being said, a game creates an experience for the player, and if they made a game influenced by Dark Souls then that relationship will be inherent in the experience because that is how it was designed.
The Good: Exploring the level is enticing and bound to create some interesting experiences. The "bonfire" mechanic where you can opt out of a character refresh for higher experience points is an interesting take on the checkpoint system for a harcore ARPG.
The Okay: The combat is really sluggish and clunky. You need to get used to slower dodge mechanics and a slight input delay if you are coming fresh off of a Souls experience. Once you get used to it, the game is definitely doable and offers a unique challenge. The feeling it provides the player is less of a nimble assassin, or powerful warrior, and more of an old man doing his best not to die. Not bad necessarily, just different.
The Bad: Boss Battles and Crashes. The boss battles are very drawn out. This would be fine if there was multiple phases, or that gameplay led to a high paced action battle. As mentioned earlier, the combat is slow. A long slow battle becomes boring. Even when you have been trying over and over again and finally succeed, you don't let out a victory cry, you just feel like you came off a slow day of work and are finally done. This game loves to crash in the second half of boss battles, as if it wasn't tedious enough.
This game is a different experience that is not super terrible. They tainted the experience by drawing a lot of influence from Dark Souls and missing the boat on some of the significant elements that created such a strong community. If they modified the bonfire and souls aspects to make it less like dark souls and more like its own game, the experience may have stood out and been judged by its own merit.

Absolutely recommended!
Bad > 1-10 < Good
These are not in any particular order of importance:
1. Fun factor: 10 (nothing better than destroying your opponent then using his pieces to strengthen yourself)
2. Creative factor: 9 (it becomes a 10 with the R&D pack as you can save your creations then purchase them in story mode)
3. Challenge factor: 7 (fights can be challenging but once you learn the nuances of certain techs and the corporations that they are using you can adapt relatively easily.  It can be heartbreaking losing your tech that you've spent hours on building, especially if you didn't save it and is the reason I didn't rate this aspect of the game lower)
4. Graphics factor: 8 (this is a personal preference I'm sure, but I like the sort of cartoonish graphics and the bright color range that is present.  Also, the nights are dark, and sort of longish... and winter may be coming... though the lights make everything look pretty!)
5. Music factor: 7 (I enjoy the couple of tracks that are present in the game.  I enjoy the calming strum of the track that plays during peaceful times, and I like the battle track decently enough as well.  I hold music as a very important aspect to experiencing a game)
6. Cinematics factor: 5 (the only cinematic sequence is in the very beginning when you witness your pod crash landing to the planet, though it looks great!)
7. Story factor: 6 (there are story aspects that are in the game right now through the item descriptions on the various blocks/weapons that are available.  Could end up being pretty good for this type of game however)
8. Content factor: 8 (4 biomes, 5 corporations with more to be added I believe, and tons of blocks per corporation)
9. Control factor: 8 (the only issue I've had was reversing a tech.  There is an option to switch the direction you must press in order to move that way.  e.g. moving forward and turning to the right, to reverse you can have it set to either moving backwards and turning to the left OR remain turning to the right.  I keep the latter option on as it feels more natural to this game, but is opposite of what most other games do with their turning while moving forward or reverse)
10. Gameplay factor: 10 (its pure fun from the outset, with the possibility of soul crushing loss if you lose your giant tech you've spent hours on building.  That feeling goes away quickly however as you begin building up your tech from scratch again.  Chicago wouldn't be as great of a city as it is if not for the fire)
Issues:
1. Some crashing still though not nearly as much as I experienced from early builds.  Mechanically speaking I've witnessed great improvements in the last few updates.  The game handles large vehicles and lots of blocks admirably at this point.
2. Story quests still need more fleshing out.  Some still hang up and will not complete but the system itself is working great.
3.  Flying techs, while fun, don't really mesh too well with the game right now.  Sure you can make them but they are really only useful for exploration purposes.
Speaking of flight I have made a smaller fighter type flying tech that is propelled upwards by mini guns.  The only issue with this is when I get close enough to another tech to attack it, the mini guns auto aim and throw off the vertical thrust needed to maintain level flight.  It also isn't capable of sustained fire on a single target.  I have yet to see a combat worthy flying tech.  This is a very minor gripe however.
It is easy to lose hours upon hours tinkering in the R&D section.  It is equally as easy to lose that much and more to the story mode.  I like having to explore for new parts and each part augments what you can do by quite a bit.  There is little redundancy amongst the block types available.  Speaking to this as well is the fact that I really don't mind starting new games and each patch has refined the starting process more and more.
TerraTech is a great example of a fun sandbox game where you're left to your own devices.  Though I wish there were more purpose in designing some of your techs with the available corporations, there is still time for all that to be fleshed out at a later date and the present amount of content is absolutely worth the money, especially with the R&D DLC.
I give TerraTech in its current state a 7.8/10 rating and it gets better with every patch.  The dev team is passionate and great at communication, and the community is very helpful as well.

December eleventh, 2014.
Starbound, hoo boy where do I begin. The touted king of indie, the toppler of terraria and saviour of the games industry.
How foolish we were to buy into Chucklefish's sensationalism. It's been a year since those "Thick and Fast" came to a screeching halt, leaving your fanbase to sit in stunned silence as you turn to abuse them when they ask where all the progress has gone. This review will indeed be heavily influenced by the Devs' interactions with their playerbase.
Now for the actual game, this game had a ridiculous launch, multi millions of copies for an indie game sold rather quickly to feed the community's growing need for it. Launch day, the game was broken. Monsters were nearly unkillable, i.e. birds would kill you in one shot with a lightning bolt or a fart cloud on your first planet with no real way to combat it. That was promptly fixed and the game became playable, hallelujah! It was a truly wonderful experience for several months, those promised thick and fast updates proving to be satiating and truly jam packed with content. Angry Koala comes along and Chucklefish stops updating stable patches. Perhaps six months without word from the developer outside of vague deflections and often times outright BANNING their consumers for their simple question. We were promised things as simply as The Novakid, a new race which was decided would be added as a kickstarter milestone. It would take two weeks to create. That was pushed aside it seems, for more pressing matters such as... Well, the nightly updates of course! Wonderful, nightly beta alpha builds which will more likely than not crash on launch for no reason, or leave you scratching your head wondering what they added. As it stands, do not buy this game. In fact, you may want to hold back from buying anything from this developer. A boycott may indeed open Chucklefish's eyes when we all stand up for our sixty dollars' worth of lies.
-=Update=-
As of late, Chucklefish have increased performance and finally added the Novakid as a playable race. I am glad to see these changes but still feel it is a little too late and am soured by their detestable business practices. However, the game itself is still fairly stale and now receives a lukewarm rating from me instead of the burning disdain I felt before. They are working on it at a snails pace but I am glad to see them working on it at all. Though I'm still sore about them removing the heat system they had in an early alpha build. So much wasted code.

Darkest dungeon is a game that is not about winning, its not about being a hero, like they say in the title screen, its about making the best of a bad situation.
From the instant you press play you have entered a world of eldritch horrors, savage men and cosmic creatures. You must drag the living corpses of your men and women to the most decrepit dungeons to die for the honor of your family.
Knowing this you must understand that the game is about suffering, and if you go unprepared you must know that the game will destroy you and your men, if you go prepared be aware that the game will still have chance to destroy you with a random crit, encounter or boss fight.
But you must also understand that all of that is the spirit of the game, it is made so you can never relax because that what it means to be a mere human, crawling on a hall filled with horrific abominations, with barely a torch to light the way.
The atmosphere of the game is absolutely briliant, the narrator is amazing and will make the game for everyone, especially anyone that enjoys lovecraftian horror.
The game is briliant and you will be able to enjoy it if you are prepared. The infamous Darkest Dungeons are quests that you are not expected to survive, so that makes the moment you do survive that much triumphant.
Beware that if you are that kind of hardcore gamer that want to speed run the whole game in 12 hours than DO NOT GO NEAR this game.
But if you are the kind of guy that likes to play the game for 1 or 2 hours, just to grind a little bit and then stop than i HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game.

Eyo! This is my first review, but I'll try to be as informative as I can to try and help you make your decision of either to buy or not buy this game. :D
To buy or not to buy... that is the question.
FYI: I'm writing this only after having the game for one day... I actually just purchased it today.
Pros/Cons:
Pros:
-Cheap!
-Not a shooting game! (not sure if that's considered a pro, but just letting you know)
-The pro above this one rhymed
-Addicting
-150 missions
-Arcade-style (which I'm guessing you must like if you're even considering this game. :P)
-Many different unlockable ships with their own unique traits, try to collect 'em all!
Cons:
-Not really a multiplayer game (you can play in multiplayer but then you'd all have to be sitting in front of the same computer, and don't quote me on this but I'm 99% sure multiplayer requires a controller)
-No way to get rid of the border around the area where you're allowed to travel, meaning that you are always stuck in that little space.  There's no option for an unlimited world, so you are always stuck within the restraints of that border.  Just something that bugs me a little.  Just a little.
-The soundtrack isn't included with the game.  You have to purchase it separately.  This is my first time encountering this so I'm not sure if it's common practice, but something I didn't like.
-Graphics are well... arcade-like.  But it's an arcade style game, so...
----------
Overview
----------
You're a small, tiny ship stuck in the middle of space.  You have no weapons except some orange trash particles attached by strings to your ship.  You must maneuver your ship around to get the trash particles to hit the asteroids and other enemies.  Your enemies are the red shapes, which, unlike the asteroids, will actually aim for you.  In mission mode, you can try and complete various challenges.  In arcade mode, there are no preset challenges, so you just try to top your previous high score.  There are 3 different difficulties, 4 if you count tutorial mode: Easy, Hard, and Asteroid.  Easy and hard are pretty self-explanatory, while asteroids has no enemies in it, only asteroids.  There's also 2 different multiplayer modes, but I can't say much for those because I'm unable to play them due to a lack of controllers.  Overall, I would definitely reccomend this game to anyone with time to spare and prefers a strategy, arcade style game over a violent shooting game.  If what you've been reading sounds like your cup of tea, then I'd definitely reccomend you pick this game up.  It's worth the money, although I did get mine for 53 cents as it is on a 92% discount as of this moment (39 cents for the game, 14 cents for the soundtrack).
Thanks for reading my first ever game review! :D Hope I helped you with your decision.  If you have any questions, just let me know.

The Walking Dead is an episodic interactive story adventure developed and published by Telltale Games based on The Walking Dead comic book series.  The game consist of five separate chapters which we released spread out across 2012.
The game takes place shortly after the start of a zombie apocalypse in the US state of Georgia. Most of the characters are all unique to the game. You play the role of a university professor, who is also a convicted murderer. You rescue and care for a little called called Clementine.
Very much unlike other adventure games, there is hardly any puzzle solving to be found in The Walking Dead; it focuses mainly on the story and character development and relationships. The story is heavily effected by dialogue choices and actions taken during quick time events - these choices will often lead to game altering changes such as a character being killed off etc.  All of the choices and events from one episode are carried over onto the next. I have also leaned since completing the game; that Telltale actually tracked the choices made too, and helped them to influence their writing in later episodes in the story.
You play the game mainly in a third person perspective and the camera changes depending on the scenery and objects around the player. You are constantly in communication with the rest of your group of survivors; you will build friendships, enemies and you will bond with most of the characters in someway. You will be emotionally attached to them, especially the young child, Clementine. While most of the game is also based around the dialogue, there are a number of quick time events throughout the series, normally I am not a huge fan of QTEs, but these are required in the story in order to get their point across and to at least keep you conscious of your surroundings when playing.
Graphics do not play a huge role in this game; it is by far the least important aspect to be seen. Saying that; the art style is nice and many developers should learn from this that having top of the range graphics isn't always the be all and end all for when creating a game.
The story is probably the best I have ever seen/heard in a video game; you will be drawn in from the minute you start interacting with different characters, learning about their backstory, building bonds. There are so many twists and turns in the story to keep you guessing too. By the end, if you are like me, you'll be a complete and utter emotional wreck with that the cast have gone through. This is one of the only games that has almost brought me to tears.
Since the game doesn't resolve around fast paced action other than the QTEs, there isn't any real difficulty; there is no "wrong" choice when it comes to dialogue, you are free to let the story develop however you choose.
Each of the chapters level design are so well thought out; there are tons of objects to interact with, pick up and use with you in future situations. If it is of any interest; then you will be able to do something with it. The art style really gets across how doomed the civilized world is in the ruined remains of cities and towns.
I have run through The Walking Dead two times now; my first play through was back when it originally came out during the sporadic release of the episodes, and just recently when I played through them all in a big binge. It is very rare that I want to play through a game again a second time; and The Walking Dead offers exactly the same excitement the second time around; you make different choices allowing the story to change and adapt to them. The whole game takes about fourteen hours to get through all of the chapters; so you are looking at a really good length game/story too.
The game can be played using a controller too - which is a nice touch given that this is the perfect sort you could play while sitting back on the sofa and soaking up the story.  I also had no other technical problems while playing.
Most people already have The Walking Dead; and most will probably have already played it given it's age now. But this is a genre defining game that has brought the adventure games right back to the forefront of PC gaming. You need to experience this heart wrenching tale. Even if zombies aren't your thing; you will get emotionally hooked from the get go. Do your self a favor and play this masterpiece.

An epic sci-fi themed MetroidVania. A huge hand-crafted world packed with 13 unique bosses, a gripping story, and tons of enemies, Spaceport Hope is the ultimate test of gaming prowess.
None of this matters, you are here to run, jump, and blow [expletive] up - and, oh lords, can you! You can control quite a bit of where you go, both on the ground and in the air, the jumps feel good, and while some jumps are a little tricky, none of them are frustrating (the game tends to fall on the "too easy" side of things in it's platforming). Biggest difficulty is keeping yourself under control while firing (all your guns have kickback that will move you a little. When using a rapid gun, like your main one, this can add up if you don't pay attention). Also, you input gets cut when you move from screen to screen. For example, you may cross a screen, stop dead, fire at an enemy, and be knocked back into the previous screen - this can get frustrating. Also kicks in after cut scenes - holding the firing button as the boss loads won't let you start firing the minute you get control, you have to re-press the button.
On the "blow things up" measure, you do have a lot of options, some of which are very fun...but you probably won't use them. Firstly, you can win without ever switching out the main weapon to fight. It's hard, but do-able. There were only a few bosses that even made me think of switching up. Further, there are 3 types of ammo, so you don't really want to use all of the guns you are given. Ammo isn't exactly hard to find, but it can be a big deal if you run out of one type (and it isn't hard to do so, with certain weapons). For example, you get a rocket launcher, a "frag" gun, and a grenade launcher - all use "red" ammo. You will almost never use the frag gun - it's half as powerful as the rocket launcher, and there just aren't that many times when you want to put out a massed number of weak shots.
The Pulsar is twice as powerful as your main gun, but you'll mostly use your main to conserve ammo. If you want more oomph, you'll go to a better gun that doesn't suck ammo like a kid at a soda shop - the rocket launcher, for example, or the Ultimate Destroyer. Same problem with the Wave Gun and the Laser - too much ammo eaten for the damage dealt.
Don't get me wrong, a lot of the guns are fun - a lot of fun - but you just aren't going to have the ammo to play around with most of them a lot of the time, and when you Need a special weapon, the rocket launcher is almost always the best bet, unless you have side case - using the Hydro gun to shoot through a wall, for example, the Grenade launcher for indirect fire and traps, or the flame thrower to burn a bone pile.

This game I seriously wanted to like. The backgrounds and music felt very nice and i enjoyed the aspect of exploration involved, but there is too much wrong with this game to defend it. From the numerous weapons you find in the game, I found myself using only the default one(infinite ammo and didnt even need to be reloaded) or the explosive weapon for the bosses.
The enemies could be described as frustrating. Many of the random mobs have abilities that make them invunerable for a time, forcing you to wait still and hope you can kill then in the next cycle. This invunerability in a lot of enemies cuts up so much of the gameplay and makes comnbat feel frustrating, especially if you're backtracking or farming money for the shop. The bosses fall into an extremely similar vein to regular mobs. You either have a ridiculously easy boss you just have to hold down fire to kill, or you have an invincible enemy that has a frustrating gimmick to deal with (the first boss on the spaceport needs you to time a switch perfectly to open up the weak spot, and you had to do it ~3 times). The expansive areas also feel really empty or confusing. At one time, i thought a seemingly innocuous pool of what I thought was water turned out to be deadly chemicals that killed my character.
The plot at times feels contrived or frustrating, such as the scene where the two guys in shades just up and walk past you after a quick boss fight, regardless of the fact that you could have shot them at any time. The sudden "aliens" twist felt obtuse as well, having not heard anything about them until then.
It's relaitively cheap price makes me not dislike the game as much as I feel I should, since I did manage to squeeze some enjoyment out of the game. If the game goes on sale, or if the developers fix it up some, I'd recommend it.

The game is already a marvel in itself when it first came out, given its sense of nostalgia to the older 16-bit farming simulator. People nowadays might associate farming simulators as free-to-play casual mobile games that took inspiration from this genre. With Stardew Valley, that association might return to what it should have been: an open-ended farm simulator with depth of character, stories to tell, and the most important of all, fun. It might be a hassle for those who prefer a simpler game, but for me, Stardew Valley will always take me on a nostalgic trip, and to let me forget everything for a while.

I've been playing this game for a few years now, but it has only just become available on Steam.
Don't let the rather unattractive visuals fool you (admittedly the screenshots look just terrible): this is the best action RPG out there.  Period.
Drox Operative is actually and ARPG set inside a 4X game being played out by AI's.  You can influence events in a myriad of ways.  You create a ship, generate a galaxy which will have some number of races playing in it, and you can win by allying yourself with the victors, or if you are particularly bloodthirsty you can just♥♥♥♥♥♥everything in sight until you accumulate the points for a "Fear" victory.  Afterwards you can retain your ship in a newly generated galaxy.  It is so satisfying to play an RPG in a "living" universe rather than mindlessly grinding through the same old dungeon with randomly spawning enemies until you reach some boss.
One of the great innovations is that the modules with which you fit your ship do not go into specific slots, but instead there are "hi, mid, low" slots (much like in EVE).  So, if you want 4 lasers, you can do it.  If you want 5 reactors to give you very rapid cap recharge, you can do it.  You want 5 engines so your ship zips around the map?  You can do it.  Are you a Romulan who fantasizes about redundant cloaking devices?  Well, you get the idea.
There certainly seem to be no other RPG's out there like Drox, so if you like space and you like RPG's it's a must-buy, but there is some room for improvement:  In my opinion the visual appeal of the game is non-existant, and staring at it for hours gets rather drab, but rest assured the great gameplay will keep you doing just that.  Though there is large array of loot you will find, I certainly feel that they could add many more modules which do a much wider variety of different things.
Anyway, for $10 or $20, you certainly shouldn't regret this buy.

Starbound.
A game that has been followed, that people threw money at, that released a beta. That got a lot of flack.
I got this game back when, well, before it was even released. Pre-orders opened up; we signed up to get access to the early beta, along with (I assume) hundreds of thousands of other people.
We went in understanding that the game would be released in a year. We went in knowing it would be a beta, not a stable project, and that it wouldn't be perfect from the start. We paid 15 dollars to play this experience.
And you know what?
I don't regret any of it. 124 hours into the game at this point. That's more that I've put into some triple A titles out there. That's more than I've put into games that cost 40 dollars, for the love of god.
So why do I see it differently than other people? WELL.
For one, I went in knowing it was early access. That means, buggy, glitchy, probably prone to wipes, prone to bugs. Do you all remember the first wipe? I do.
It wiped out everyone's character. And what did we all do? Most of us ♥♥♥♥♥ed. 'Why did you do that', 'Why is it not stable', 'Why are wipes necessary'? Give me my money back, this is horrid and disgusting, how could you release something so incomplete under the guise of early access - Oh, wait.
It's early access.
They didn't have to set it up so there was a stable version at all. 'Thick and fast' would ahve meant 'constant wipes, constant restarts, constant exposure to more unstable product'. The alternative was what they did now; they released a stable version, they set it to that. Anyone who wanted to experience the thick and fast updates? Opt for the nightlies.
And it WORKS.
The nightlies? Buggy as♥♥♥♥♥♥ You still have to wipe characters. You still have to deal with sometimes game-breaking bugs or imbalances. But you can see the love, the attention, the soul that the developers are pouring into this game almost every single night. You can see how much they want this product to succeed.
Yes, they made some mistakes. They pushed the launch date forward. There was that debacle with 'what is release', and all that. But how would YOU react to a sudden knee-jerk when everyone got what they wanted, then released it WASN'T the perfect space-cupcake hamsterball?
Rant over. Onwards to my real review.
The gameplay is fun. Each race has its own story and unique asthetic; the new novakids even start out with GUNS (which is weird, since nobody else does, but refreshing!). The music is tasteful and enjoyable, peaceful, explorative, creepy, awesome. You really feel the atmosphere that they're trying to get across.
Combat in the newest nightly is MUCH improved. No longer do you get hurt from touching a monster; instead, you get hurt if htey use an ability and land it on you. You can walk through mobs with no trouble.
Lighting, weather, and other minor effects like that are awesome. Rainstorms can actually drown out your crops if they aren't properly irrogated, or flood your house! It's neat and I've never seen something like that before. Not to mention, on some planets, fire will LITERALLY rain down from the sky.
The random monsters and planets also add to that feeling of adventure that I know -I- wanted in a game that was, essentially, Terraria meets Star Trek. Everything is weird, neat, and new. An entirep lanet of trees that are made of flesh and brains? Weird and gross! .... But awesome.
Environment hazards are also pretty sweet. It adds to the realism if you need OXYGEN to survive in space, as well as to stay warm (it's ♥♥♥♥ing cold out there, bro).
The new missions and quests that you can access? Also pretty darn awesome. They add a bit more that I felt the game was missing; narrative.
Bosses are fun, loot is rewarding, dungeons are challenging..
I don't know. TL:DR, The game is fun, people have issues with it that I personally do not understand, and you should really try the nightly builds.

Although I didn't have time to try it out yet the trailer for the "Winter Update" looks promising. In case a few or all of the issues I had with the game are now "fixed" consider the review below a relic from the past when it was indeed a lot less fun than it could've been.
Before Starbound came out it was hyped as Terraria's spiritual successor.
It isn't.
Think of the things that made Terraria fun. They're pretty much all missing or done in a totally different (and, in my opinion, bad) way in Starbound. This wouldn't be a bad thing if they replaced it with original ideas and content of their own... but they didn't.
There's also less purpose in everything. Building a base is utterly useless besides looks. Let that one sink in, especially if you know how important/convenient a good base was in Terraria.
a base is useless because the ship not only has
but is also more convenient than having to warp to your "home" planet (with the warp point being non-changeable from its original position!) Also, there's no NPCs that you have to build a home for. There's no need to build any kind of farm either because the "food meter" is a joke because food costs close to nothing, can be stacked and you only need to eat like once every (real) hour. There's also no kind of "alchemy" so besides useless food you can't plant anything.
The "random" aspects of the game were hyped all the way to eleven but in the end it's a dull experience.
are hardly different from each other besides their visuals and the type of blocks they're made of. The shape of the surface is similiar, there's no reason at all to dig further than a few feet deep to get materials because the best materials can be found anywhere. Going underground is boring, doesn't yield better or more ressources and it always feels the same with
to discover. Also, every planet of the same tier has the same ores. Talk about obsolete variety.
, while randomized, all feel similiar: You have a nearly infinite amount of enemies that look different, behave only slightly different and can be fought in exactly the same way: With the help of the clunky combat system. Combat is nothing more than "left-click to strike/shoot". It feels unresponsive and is far from fluid, let alone balanced (one-shotting monsters way above your current equipment tier with an 8-second cooldown hammer... balance.)
aren't anything revolutionary either but more importantly they're buggy and exploitable. The dragon boss misses his fire breath attack as long as you keep standing in the same place. Poke him with arrows for a few minutes to win. Other bosses can be exploited by building around them and then activating them or by standing behind a wall with a little hole to shoot through. Even when fighting them without using any "trick" there's hardly any strategy involved except "keep hitting until it dies".
On a last note, just google how Chucklefish handles their customers nowadays to see that this isn't a poor but hard-working indie company trying its best but instead a bunch of people taking the money for their half-finished mess and then making a run for it.

Darkest dungeon is a game that is not about winning, its not about being a hero, like they say in the title screen, its about making the best of a bad situation.
From the instant you press play you have entered a world of eldritch horrors, savage men and cosmic creatures. You must drag the living corpses of your men and women to the most decrepit dungeons to die for the honor of your family.
Knowing this you must understand that the game is about suffering, and if you go unprepared you must know that the game will destroy you and your men, if you go prepared be aware that the game will still have chance to destroy you with a random crit, encounter or boss fight.
But you must also understand that all of that is the spirit of the game, it is made so you can never relax because that what it means to be a mere human, crawling on a hall filled with horrific abominations, with barely a torch to light the way.
The atmosphere of the game is absolutely briliant, the narrator is amazing and will make the game for everyone, especially anyone that enjoys lovecraftian horror.
The game is briliant and you will be able to enjoy it if you are prepared. The infamous Darkest Dungeons are quests that you are not expected to survive, so that makes the moment you do survive that much triumphant.
Beware that if you are that kind of hardcore gamer that want to speed run the whole game in 12 hours than DO NOT GO NEAR this game.
But if you are the kind of guy that likes to play the game for 1 or 2 hours, just to grind a little bit and then stop than i HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game.

The mechanics & gameplay are generally simple; you propel yourself by shooting out blobs of your own to move around the map in order to avoid or eat other blobs. The level select screen is split into three parts with each part having their own unique mechanics, but the main objective for every one of them is that you pretty much want to be the biggest blob in the map by eating other, smaller blobs. If others are even a smidge bigger than you, they eat you instead. Many mechanics for the levels are more simpler than others to get the hang of whereas some levels like the ones that involve the science of gravity & orbit can get more complicated.
The later levels start to become much harder, turning into a game of strategy, skill, and most of all, patience. The patience aspect may be a serious deal-breaker since most situations in those later levels absolutely require you to wait to succeed or else you get severely punished. You can speed the game up & slow it down, restart the level, and even randomize the current level on restart. Regardless, patience is still a huge factor in those later levels.
Beating the game just means that you cleared all the base levels. After doing so, all that happens is that you unlock "forever" levels that supposedly get harder & harder the more you clear them.
The visuals & audio, the overall ambience, are pretty fitting for the early levels as it's still a relaxing, simple game from there unless you decide to push on to the more difficult parts, then the ambience is pretty much non-existant.
It's a fun & simple little game overall where it doesn't actually take very long to beat all the base levels. $9.99 may be far too much for something like this.

I see a lot of reviews not recommending this game because they say it's "pay to win". I don't agree with this at all. I've played this game quite a bit, not only through steam but through the website itself as well. I think the reason people believe it's pay to win is because of the starting area, where the new developer put the option, right where you spawn, to purchase very high tiered gear with coins, which can only be bought with real money. I don't think this is the best idea, because it imbalances the economy some and also encourages people who don't know what their doing to spend money on this equipment, only to lose it soon after by dying in this PERMADEATH game. That said though, this DOES NOT make the game pay to win. All of this equipment is obtainable through looting or trading with other players for other loot. There aren't many things that can ONLY be bought with real money, and these things are mostly clothing dyes, alt skins, food items to grow your pet faster then normal, and things like character slots or inventory space. Not having these things won't really detract from your experience playing this game, and it is definitely not pay to win. Maybe pay to get ahead slightly faster, but not pay to win.
With that out of the way, I can definitely recommend this game. Like I said above, I've put many hours into this game because, put simply, it is a lot of fun. It's a fast paced bullet-hell permadeath shooter mmo that also just happens to be free, and there's no risk in trying it out.

There are a great many positive things to be said about this game. Wayne June voice acting, fantastic art design, fun combat. Unfortunately, some fundamental design flaws ruin this game. It's really almost tragic.
This is a difficult game, but most of the difficulty stems from an unrelentingly brutal random number generator. Yes, there are things you can do to maximize and minimize the impact of randomness, but a series of multiple bad rolls can place you in a failure state. It's possible to recover from this through grinding. However, situations all too frequently arise where a player who makes proper and intelligent tactical choices is still forced to compensate for a failed state which is almost entirely caused by bad dice rolls. These failed states make you more vulnerable to strings of poor dice rolls. Conversely, a string of good luck makes you far less vulnerable to a later string of bad luck. This is a game which is won or lost within the first hour of the game, yet the game takes many, many hours to actually complete. This leads to multiple restarts, and eventually results in a feeling that the progress of the game isn't going to be determined by the player, but by the results of a random number generator.
Many games are heavily influenced by randomness, but the degree to which a player feels that they can or cannot control the impact of this randomness can greatly affect the play experience. Poker is a great example of a game which, though it is inherently random, introduces enough player agency to make it more absorbing then a game where simply drawing the high card wins. Darkest Dungeon often reduces the impact of player agency so far below the impact of randomness that it begins to feel as though flipping a coin might be as fun as actually playing the game. This is not ideal.
The developer should note that there is a difference between difficulty and a string of bad luck. In particular, the "sanity" mechanism (which is essentially a hit point pool which persists between dungeon runs) as implemented can lead to runaway fail states which are out of the control of the player and have no correlation with the decisions which the player has made. When failure occurs despite whatever actions the player has made, failure and success become irrecvocably divorced from player decisions. The direct impact of this is that player decsions have no impact on failure or success. Thus, one might as well bet on the outcome of a coin toss. This isn't fun. At least, it isn't worth paying money for.

I stumbled over Bastion by accident during the Christmas Holiday Sale 2011. The game had a discount of 66% at the time and I bought it, because the description was pretty interesting: a constant narrator commenting your actions? Hand-drawn game graphics? You don't see that all day! And the artworks looked pretty nice indeed.
Still, my expectations where pretty low, as the game was an Indie title and I didn't expect a great game for only 4,50€.
God, I'd kill myself right now, if I would not have made this deal! For me, Bastion is one of the best games of 2011 and probably the best Indie game out there.
The artstyle is incredibly detailed and you can see that a lot of love and work was put into it. The soundtrack is so cool that I spent another 4 bucks to buy it and the gameplay itself is an action-RPG which can easily be described as "easy to learn, hard to master". But the best thing of it all is the narrator: excellent voicework and a decent story create one hell of an atmosphere!

A pretty solid game for the price tag. Kind of shallow, but it scratches the Metroidvania itch. (Reported play time is basically doubled from having left this alt-tabbed while doing other things; I'd say 7-9 hours.)
Pros:
- Some unexpectedly charming worldbuilding. Games that look/play like this often eschew a story entirely, but this had a little heart to it.
- Fun areas to explore that seem massive and daunting at first. Very satisfying to realize that you know your way around them.
- Good diversity of enemy behavior!
Cons:
- Like I said, the actual gameplay is kind of shallow. Enemies have small hit boxes and high HP. You'll spend a lot of time dodging bullets and getting off a single shot on a stationary enemy or else running away so you can spam attacks from a safe distance until everything falls down. You don't really aim so much as hope that an enemy crosses your field of fire.
- Lots of little things that are more like helpful notes I'd give to a developer than complaints.
So yeah, I'd go for it if you're into this kind of thing.

Look, Trove can be a hell of a lot of fun and it would be one of my favorite games if it were singleplayer. However, it's obviously not; you're at the mercy of the servers' latency. For most games this is a non-issue, as the developers actually invest in decent server capacity. For a frenetic Action RPG where pinpoint accuracy and constant movement is always a factor, latency means everything.
While you're out and about adventuring and getting addicted to this game, you're going to experience countless bugs, rubberbanding, lag, lag, and more lag. If an enemy is strafing you, you can hit them directly with a ranged attack MULTIPLE times and they won't take damage because of client/server desync. The same issue happens when clearing a dungeon; after finishing the quest a chest appears that you destroy to get gear. Usually this takes 3-5 attacks, however due to lag and desync you can be attacking a dozen times before the damn thing finally pops. Speaking of attacking, spamming skills can cause your character to be stuck autoattacking on some classes, which may or may not actually do damage. And there are no real options to resize the chat window or filter "local" chat or club (guild) chat. Spam ahoy, and you have to install a mod to be able to get rid of the chat window. Brilliant.
But wait, there's more! Literally EVERY SINGLE major patch this year the developers have consistently made the game WORSE for new players. That's right, they are actively DISCOURAGING people from playing their game. Classes used to be purchasable with an in-game currency from daily rewards, and now you have to pay money or grind out tens of thousands of the equivalent of gold (flux in this game) and purchase a cash shop item from other players to unlock new classes. This most recent patch made it far more difficult for a new player to upgrade their gear to endgame level. And they always give a different BS reason when in reailty they're just trying to make more money by being scumbags. This is about on par with every other game published by Trion, and it doesn't look like they're going to get better any day soon. Absolutely friggin pathetic.
The game is incredibly fun and plays great... when it works. Then it gets pretty damn frustrating. If you're not prepared to be frequently frustrated by rubberbanding, desync, bugs, and consistently regressive updates that make the game harder for new players, this is definitely not the game for you. If some of those issues finally were addressed after however many years they've existed, Trove would be an instant recommend. Buuut looks like that's not gonna happen.

Very interesting game. Gameplay is arcadey, more so in my opinion than World of Tanks or Armored Warfare, and I have next to nothing to say about the graphics because I'm running the game on a potato.
Premium tanks in this game all have distinct roles and are very usable unlike in other games. Premium ammo for gold only is a thing (Of course, the developer has to make money somehow and frankly with the small amount of players the game has at the moment I doubt premium tanks are selling that much).
There is an in-depth crafting/rewards system that gives you crates after a battle based on whether you won/lost, while the level of the crate depends on how well you did. Usually level 15 and higher crates contain crafting components for the higher tier craftable tanks, while 14 and below contain materials for the lower tier ones.
Helicopters add verticality to the game, and prevent camping if their target is not careful. Most MBTs have mounted machine guns or anti-air guided missiles though, so helis can't just have an endless reign of terror.
Artillery in IStorm seems to be fairly well balanced compared to other games. It doesn't one-shot same-tier vehicles like in World of Tanks, nor is it almost entirely useless like in War Thunder.
The aiming system has far less RNG (at least from what I've experienced) than World of Tanks, but aiming is a bit slow.
Lastly, this is a minor issue, but the T58 premium tier 2 MBT seems to be bugged. While viewing it in garage, it is invisible and while in a match the camera glitches far below the map and stays there. While in this state, the tank cannot be moved, but apparently I can still fire.
All in all, IStorm is pretty fun. There are a few bugs, but I have faith that the devs can fix them.

DARKEST DUNGEON IS ABSOLUTELY NOT A GAME FOR EVERYONE.
It requires a lot of time dedication, learning and mental resilience.
It's as much an art piece as it is a game, and like any good art, it often takes you to places you'd maybe rather not go.
-If you are a casual gamer, you should probably avoid this. Unless you know for sure you are able and willing to love this game for it's virtues, and to shrug off some of it's imperfections.
-If you are a hardcore gamer who rejoices in difficult games, you might enjoy this very much. Do what you always do- study and understand all the stats, quirks, functions, interactions and synergies, until you dominate the game.
-If you are a pretentious gamer gourmet (like me) who prowls the depths of Steam for only the most unique of experiences, let me just repeat: this game is ART, and a unique piece indeed. You'll never regret and never forget.
Still wanna play this? OK, I'll try to dissect the game a bit more.
---------------------------------------------------------------
THE DUNGEON CRAWLING AND COMBAT is severe, but it can always be overcome; you just need to provision well, build a group of heroes that is functional together and at least roughly adapted to the dungeon and goal, make a battle plan A, make a battle plan B (and plan C doesn't hurt either). In the dungeon, just do what works and don't do anything rushed and stupid.
Many people complain about the combat being to unpredictable and unfair. They should GIT GUD. It's true that the Champion and Darkest difficulty (=3rd & 4th level of dungeons) get pretty brutal, so be extra careful and cautious and exploit every ability and oportunity to the extreme. Just shamelessly cheese it. In the most extreme of circumstances, survival is not about heroism ;)
Some people complain that the stress mechanic is excessive. They have a point, but they should've probably expect that, since the game vocally advertises it as it's core mechanic. After all, we're talking an anachronistic dark fantasy gothic horror with a crusader who murders guys by showing them a scroll, so don't expect 100% lifelike realism.
So I'll give you a tip. Not unlike Dark Souls, this game has a rather brutal learning curve if you go into it blind. Darkest Dungeon has very helpfull stats, tooltips and tutorial panels, but the amount of information, percentages, values, stats, interactions, combinations and synergies will still be dazzling to a beginner. Thus, unless you are the most zealous kind of hardcore gaming masochist who only accepts the complete and unadulterated challenge, don't be ashamed to do a bit of prior research. And even if you really want to explore the game all by yourself, which is commendable, you still HAVE to at least watch a little bit of playthrough and make sure you really like the combat system. THIS IS INCREDIBLY IMPORTANT, BECAUSE YOU ARE GOING TO BE DOING A HUNDRED METRIC ♥♥♥♥-TONS OF FIGHTING AND IT WILL GET TEDIOUS UNLESS YOU ARE REALLY REALLY INTO IT.
The final bit of intel you need about combat is the trinkets, which alter the stats of your heroes. The trinket system is well done and enjoyable. Trinkets allow your heroes to be more effective, more persistent, or to serve more diverse roles, but they often handicap them in other ways, so they never feel overpowered and cheap. Just be warned that trinkets are more important in this game than it first seems. You should choose missions based on how good the trinket reward is.
THE TOWN BUILDING, ECONOMY AND HERO MANAGEMENT is crucial, and while I enjoy it, I'll admit that most people probably won't. The amount of micromanagement is towering. You have to plan cautiously and only spend money if you have to and if it will benefit you immediately. You have to make sure to always bring back enough cash from dungeons, but make room for heirlooms too... maybe I'm overstressing this, but the thing is that if you do run out of money, you're kinda ♥♥♥♥ed and you practically lose your save. So just saying.
And finally, THE ATMOSPHERE. The visual style, character design and artwork, the sound design, the music by Stuart Chatwood(!), the writing, the unforgettable narration of Wayne June(!!!), the simple but powerful story. IT'S ALL ABSOLUTELY ♥♥♥♥ING GLORIOUS. Altogether, it creates a gorgeous and unparalelled atmosphere. And that's kinda the main reason to play the Darkest Dungeon.
---------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR: Make sure you really like it before you buy it.
Oh, and I can not really speak for the DLC, since I haven't played it. However, it feels to me like a redundant addition to a story that was already good enough, well-rounded and complete. And the new hero, while functionally interesting, defeats some core principles of the game and seems rather overpowered to me (and he is objectively overused as a result). So that's a nope on the DLC from me.

I will get into detail, but I start with that the game is absolutely well done.
The design of the game, the setting and the visual aspects (such as the design level of the character faces, design of enemies, and so on) have created a fundamental role in this game- the art and visual aspects are what makes this game unique. The characters themselves feel alive, the enemies- real and dangerous, and the bosses- grotesque abominations created with regards to the iconic Lovecraftian style. This is why I think this game stands out- the atmosphere and the visual aspects fit beautifully in this roleplaying game where death is the main enemy.
I have not talked about the sounds and soundtrack yet, but here I am. I include it in because sound is side to side to the visual aspects, and plays a large part of what the gameplay would feel like to the player.
The music itself is unique. It has the feeling of the constant dread within the Hamlet, while adventuring.

If it gets switched up with other tracks while a battle is commencing, maybe that would be a good idea after all.
The sounds implemented are really good- the darker it gets (note!) the scarier the sounds in the dungeons become, which stresses out the characters even more. Very well done.
Gameplay is perfectly executed for this type of game. The stress bar plays a huge role of character development, as well as the trinket system fits to the class of the characters. The game causes you to feel that you can lose your characters at any times, be it from the enemies, the bleeding/blight effects, or succumbing to a random mini-boss battle-

Overall, I say perfectly executed.

Offensive or not, all snowflakes of all shapes and sizes must accept that this game is meant to be hard.

The overall attention this game has from dev's is sometimes unseen from other games like this one.

This game is a must have to your steam library.The atmosphere makes it unique for its genre, making it a one-of-a-kind. It is a fantastic game worth your time.

In this game, you're a little blob of matter that must absorb smaller blobs to grow while avoiding larger blobs. To change your velocity, you shoot out little pellets of matter, meaning that your "fuel" is tied to your body size. This is a pretty simple game mechanic, but in Osmos, there are many different scenario types which play out like physics puzzles. In some scenarios, you're like an asteroid orbiting a star, and must absorb the rest of the "solar system" by manipulating your orbit; in another scenario, all other blobs are motionless but tightly packed together around you, meaning that you need to plan very carefully to figure out the right sequence of events to escape without getting swallowed. It's hard to describe, but it's a good indie game.

MOBA in Space.
I was hesitant to try it out but luckily it was free2play. So I went for the download knowing I would uninstall it anyway. Then I started to play...
Alright, its really not like a typical MOBA. You just cant jumping lanes blind, you have to use your jump drive which will increase received damage by 400%. You are in a middle of a fight focused by the enemy, forget to jump (classic beginners mistake).
The classic jungle is moved into the lanes with different asteroid types that are not static from match to match.
No NPCs to push through the lanes and hide, you going straight into the fight against the opponent. You do have mining ships you can protect or destroy but that alone wont do smth.
It's all more direct than a classic MOBA and at the same time much more structured and also slower as you command a capital ship and not a fighter. It gives more in depth strategical planning, less hectic reactions.
Pay2Win? No! The starter ships are very well balanced into the endgame, heck 2 out of 3 of those are easily "upper tier" and the tiers are so close to each other its barely noteworthy. A ship that cost much more credits than another does not mean its better, just not so long in the game. There is quite a few ships for the lowest credits that excel in top tier MMR games on very high levels (in the right hand ofc). And any review that cries its grindy is a typical "gimme everything now" player. I played actual grindy games, Fractured Space is so far away from grind that even mentioning it is stupid.
Play the Tutorial, jump into Quick Play to get a feel for the Conquest mode (keep an eye on the minimap, spread out on lanes proper, get into gamma when announced and not in combat, capture mines until reaching lvl 9).
Go check it out, you might be surprised :-)
