Spaceport Hope has an above average musical score for a pixelated side-scroller. This brings back memories of Commander Keen with some elements of Metroid. Spaceport Hope is an effective "old school" arcade platformer. There is a large array of weapons, though I found the initial gun to be more than sufficient for most fights--with the rocket launcher being the second most useful.
Some boss fights are keyed to make certain weapons more viable, however, once you see the patterning, as with all games of this sort, any weapon would be a contender.
My greatest critisism with the game relates to the final boss fight--you have no idea it is the final boss fight. This, for me, made it somewhat of a "meh" situation. I had been expecting, as I followed the story, that there would be "more to come". In reality, one does not need to fully explore all areas of the game to complete the primary story itself. This made for a final fight which was "unexpected" less in the difficulty and more in the realm of "hmmm was that the end of the game"?
I like the partially open ended exploration which is possible, however, I would have also prefered a greater emphasis on the final fight--to make it more memorable.
A secondary critisism would be the large array of weapons--rather the lack of necessity of their use. I played through this game to full completion using 3 weapons(as alluded to above), and of those, 2 were vs. secondary bosses with the starter gun my main gun the entire game. Although the starter gun is supposed to overheat, and there is a bar indicating such, I never noticed any real "cool down" required. Its dps was more than adequate for almost all encounters. The overheating aspect of the starter gun should be increased to afford more utility to other weapons.
Overall I enjoyed this title and would recommend it anytime you find it on sale.

I was driving around last night wondering what game to review next when I realized that it had been staring me right in the face the whole time: Spaceport Hope. I had purchased it fairly recently and there was so much I felt had to be said about this game while I was playing it but by the time I was done, stowing it away in the deepest, darkest recesses of my Steam library seemed the best thing to do. Here I am, though, having dusted it off to share with you all the adventure I had with this one. So, let's see here. What can I say about Spaceport Hope? Let me break this down for you, so we can all scrutinize it together, hmm?
The good: There is some good to this game but honestly, the positives are far outweighed by the negative. The soundtracks are probably my favorite thing about this particular 2-D adventure and I have to credit the developer here because I found myself paying more attention to the music than I did the game. I don't mind telling you either, that such an occurrence is very unusual for me because I have a tendency to be far more visual. While this is a step in the right direction, it's also not what you want because the music should go hand in hand with the rest of the game to create a completely immersive experience for the player but failed to do so. To be honest with you, the music was so much better than the gameplay by comparison that I would have considered purchasing the soundtrack separately if I hadn't already gotten it with a bundle.
The graphics in Spaceport Hope are another one of the bright spots that are so few and far between and deserves a gold star for effort at the very least. The handcrafted pixel art is actually pretty good and a nice reminder of so many pleasantly nostalgic moments that I would recommend it on that basis alone, for all the fans of these 8-bit style throwbacks like myself.
The bad: No controller support for an action/adventure game? That's a hefty blunder right from the start. It claims to have "Partial Controller Support" but fails to deliver on this feature, which happens to be one of the most important in the genre. I have a Razer Sabertooth Elite and could not for the life of me get it to work with this game. I've read a lot of other reviews and done some research and those who actually were able to play with a gamepad are an extreme minority. This was almost a deal-breaker for me before I even started, but I like to support indie creators of all kinds so decided to push through, hoping the rest would make up for this rather dubious mark against itself. I'm sorry to say that it did not and was forced to use irksome, counter-intuitive controls on my keyboard in order to play a sub-par game.
Although the story is by no means the most important feature of a game, especially one of this type, the narrative itself was poorly delivered. The NPC's seem nearly impossible to differentiate because their dialogue is limited to dim one-liners that are far from memorable. Even the key characters only provide tidbits of information about what's actually going on in a handful of brief snippets. If you want to get right down to it, there isn't much of a story at all, just a very dry, quick and dirty plot that seems primarily to be used as filler more than anything else.
The ugly: As I said before, the plot if not lackluster is direct and to the point but the problem arises when there is so much extra content that is in no way tied into the main story arch. It comes off as an afterthought that becomes tedious when you realize that you're about to fight the last boss and you still have five, six, even seven guns left to find, heart containers and some quests to boot, so if you're looking to 100% this game then sadly, this is what will happen. Just to clarify and show you what I mean: there are ten worlds to explore in order to find all the items and achievements but for people who just want to enjoy the game and beat it, only five of those worlds are absolutely necessary, one of which includes the planet used as the starting area.
As soon as you start a new game file and commit, plunging in head first with eyes wide and hopes high, looking forward to an exciting action adventure, the disappointment starts almost immediately. You begin squinting as you plummet towards the reality of what you've gotten yourself into. The double jump, something that should and is usually an upgrade of some sort that offers a smidgen of satisfaction when you finally acquire it, is handed to you. I hate to say it but that isn't even the worst part because the already floaty controls make the much-coveted double jump unwieldy and difficult to use.
Putting that aside for the moment, this sweet skill also comes along with a starter weapon that has unlimited ammo. Before you start thinking to yourself "well that's not so bad, it is a starter after all," let me stop you right there and just say that the balance is non-existent. It is all too possible to go through the entire game armed with nothing but your first gun with relative ease because that's exactly what I did. The fire rate is insane and because there's no need to reload your weapon you can stand on one side of the screen, hold down the fire button and simply walk forward with minimal resistance. Even the achievement for beating the final boss with nothing but the first weapon wasn't that hard and I certainly did not feel like I 'achieved' anything.
This takes me to my next point. The enemy AI seems a little flat and more than a touch boring. I became increasingly zoned out while playing until finally, a switch flicked on in my brain and broached the threshold of full-on zombie mode. Which is kind of funny when I think about it because this was my experience on "Normal" difficulty; after I beat the game and was taken back to the main menu, I was scrolling past all the settings and saw "Expert" mode that listed its associated alterations.
--> Enemy life is increased by 40%.
--> The player takes an additional 30% damage.
--> Fire rate for all weapons is decreased by 40%.
There's nothing wrong with this in theory but in practice, I think there's just not enough creativity put into programming the AI to warrant such a drastic increase in difficulty. The only result I can imagine is nothing short of mind numbing.
Spaceport Hope sporting thirteen unique bosses, however, sounded incredibly appealing and was definitely a selling point for me, but the novelty quickly wore off after the first few encounters as they appear to be strongly choreographed and obvious. I also thought the point of having so many different guns was an indication that each boss had a corresponding weakness and some of them do but for the most part the rocket launcher will do the job quite efficiently. There's no real need and (speaking for myself here) very little desire to even bother looking for the rest of the weapons, even though I eventually did so anyway.
My final thoughts are thus... Spaceport Hope is by no means a lost cause and is a half-decent time waster if you've got a couple of hours to kill. The frustrating thing about this game is being able to see all the squandered potential because by all rights it could have been an excellent side-scrolling shooter but subsequently lost its footing and fell flat on its face.
Here at the end, after it's all said and done, you might ask if I would even recommend the game that could have been? The truth is... I'm torn. Yes, I would recommend Spaceport Hope because it's not all bad and there were moments where I genuinely enjoyed myself. The catch is that I would only give it the go-ahead to a small, niche fan base that can forgive or look past its failings and wouldn't mind adding this indie title to their collection.

Once upon a time, there was a game called Trove. Trove was a wonderous game, filled with a community who loved to build and work together to clear even the hardest of bosses. Everyone worked to help everyone out, and all was well. Sure, the grind for classes and better gear was sometimes tedious, and we had our fair share of trolls, but in the end everyone had fun.
Then came that fateful day in February. There was talk of Trove moving towards a Pay-2-Win model, and the community had protested it. We didn't want to spend real money to get items that were, in the past, available to us for free. With the increase of prices in the shop, classes no longer being purchasable with cubits (a free currency obtained daily), and the class coins being scalped in the market, Trove lost it's allure. Other players felt the same, and many of us quit. The magic of being able to play a MMO without having P2W features shoved down our throat was amazing, and being able to  pick up and play any class with free currency was great. No real-time crafting costs, no money needed to be spent. Now, Patron (the "membership" status) was being advertized everywhere, as it got you double cubits, which were now worthless to new players because of their limited uses, among other bonuses. Now I hear of a PAID expansion to Trove? Trove was a wonderful free to play game, with purchases being entirely optional. I even ended up buying Patron before the update that pushed a lot of people away because I loved the game and wanted to support the devs. Now, with the new pay to win structure, a paid expansion for features players have been asking for for ages, and the game becoming more grindy and less fun for new players, Trove has fallen off the ranks of great games.
TL;DR Trove used to be good, now it's garbage. Don't waste your time with it.

Another attempt at a "Minecraft mixed with Call of Duty" game. The game is listed as a Free to Play game, so if you'd like to try it by all means try it, but it's nothing great.
Overall, this is a decent Minecraft shooter game. You have a set number of blocks you can use, a weapon that can either be used to melee enemies or to break certain blocks, a primary weapon, a pistol, and once you level up, a medkit, grenade, rocket launcher, etc. This game is pretty much a pay to win if you are to solely use the Assault and Support classes, as I feel the weapons available to free players are far inferior to weapons you can buy for those classes. However, the sniper class in the base game is already extremely overpowered. If you were to buy a scope for the sniper, as it does not come with one, you would really be degrading the weapon. You can use it at really any range and it seems to be a one shot headshot from just about anywhere.
On the topic of weapon balancing, the pistol is absolutely atrocious. The point of a pistol in a shooter game is usually to be a back up in case you somehow run out of ammo for your primary weapon and need a gun immediately. Honestly, in this game, you'd be better off taking the time to reload your primary weapon. I haven't done any testing on this but it seems as though the pistol takes five to six headshots to kill and a lot more body shots. It's honestly one of the worst weapons I've used in any game ever, although I have gotten a few kills with it. The default assault rifle isn't my favorite either, but it doesn't seem too underpowered.
My favorite gamemode of the bunch was the Capture gamemode, which is like territories. Your team gets points by having a bunch of territories and you just walk into it with no enemies there to take it. It's very simple. One of the worst developed games I have ever had to endure. If this game succeeded at one thing, it succeeding at setting a standard for how similar games should [not] be made.
There is a glaring disconnect between the visual designers and the team that planned the gameplay progression. Clearly there are areas that the player is not supposed to venture into early on, but there is literally nothing that blocks the player from accidentally venturing in to those areas.
Playing through this game, I constantly found myself fighting NPCs and bosses that I was not supposed to fight until later on. I wondered why those NPCs and bosses seemed arbitrarily difficult, at least until after the story took me to them after the fact.
The mechanics of the game are poorly thought out. There is excessively bad logic in the way weapons, armor, and equipment escalate in power. No clear definition exists, whatsoever, between power and speed. Innocently, players will be led to presume that the latest weapon they acquire is the most powerful, but that is never the case at all in this game.
Under my good conscience, I cannot recommend this horridly broken product to anybody. Fanboys who have grown complacent with the mechanics have no doubt beaten the game and reached the highest level, but they still very likely struggled early on.

Having pre-ordered NBA 2K16 (following the hype train, woot-woot!), I got the opportunity to play already, and I was able to quickly form an opinion on the in my eyes most important mode of the game, the MyCareer mode. I’m one of those who basically bought the game for this mode alone, where you take control of a new player in the NBA and lead him to greatness.
By now, I’ve played three quarters of my rookie season, after leading my player through high school and first year of college. I’m blown away by how much of a blowout this game is. “Hold it right there for a second,” you might say, “the game isn’t out long enough for you to have played so far ahead!” If I didn’t know better, I would agree with you on that. The problem is, however, your “rookie season” is 8 (eight!) games long.
Yes, you’ve read right. I was shocked when I got to the “gym menu” and read that it was the first of eight games I would get to play in my rookie season. It’s frustrating. The game doesn’t give you any option to change this. This is not a basketball simulation anymore, it’s a farce.
I want to lead my player through all 82 games of a season (plus even more in post-season, if possible), and in full-length at that. Maybe I don’t get much further than my rookie season until the next game comes out, but I’m with my player all the way until then. When the commentators praise my last game, I want to have been there for that. Why should I give a damn about what the AI made my player do?
I don’t get any credits for that to spend on my abilities, I don’t get any chance to rise to starhood early on, and I don’t get any sort of information how I’m doing outside of the commentary for the next game I’m playing, or at least I haven’t found it in the cryptic menu structure.
“Featuring a Spike Lee joint” is the worst thing they could’ve done. You’re forced to suffer through one of the most annoying stories I’ve ever played. And I’ve been through all of “Dying Light”. They praise it in the trailers with “Be The Story”. Guess what, that’s all you get to do, because you can’t make one on your own.
I didn’t know what to expect, so my player is pretty much me. Every NBA 2K game I’ve played before gave me the opportunity to “be myself”, which mostly meant, a white guy with a similar name (so the commentators don’t just call me by my nickname) and “College” Germany (and a different height, depending on the position). In 2K16, that means a 7ft tall (Center) white guy has a black twin sister that seems at least a foot smaller, has no similarities in their looks whatsoever, and stays bland throughout the story, a problem all characters have in this. You don’t get to choose anything about yourself beside the appearance and some on-court details. Everything but the teams you play for is pretty much set in stone; and the teams you play for do not change the story a bit.
You follow a story of some random dude, instead of forming him yourself. There are some major crossroads he just barrels through without you being consulted. But hey, you can choose to go to UCLA instead of UConn. Congratulations.
Even when you think you can choose something important (what a heated discussion in a cut scene about staying another year in College or agreeing to enter the Draft builds up to), he just says, “here’s what I’m going to do…”, cut to black screen, and whoop-de-do, welcome to the NBA Draft 2016!
I feel no connection to Harlem. I feel no connection to the family. Suddenly I have a girlfriend, and I have no idea why she’s here (when I first saw her, I was like “Hey, who’s that? Oh, she looks nice, and she’s in an important meeting… she might be my girlfriend. Oh her name’s Yvette? Cool.”). My so-called best friend is always up to no good and I spend six-figure sums in lawyers and settlements to keep everything quiet about him and his escapades. My agent (who I obviously don’t get to choose, either) is a New Yorker, a self-proclaimed “Shark” with italian roots, where every “Mobster cliche” bell in my head starts ringing like a shot clock. I have no say in this at all.
The story tries very hard to create drama (to the point where it’s hard for me to suspend my disbelief), but it fails miserably at making me care, because it lacks decisions where my actions would have any sort of impactful consequences. If this was a movie, I wouldn’t see it in theatres, I wouldn’t rent it, and wouldn’t even waste my time on it would it be on Netflix.
Technically, the game is up to snuff concerning the simulation part, even though I despise getting fouled out in the third quarter because of the mechanics for setting picks (and for calling illegal screens). Otherwise, it’s ridiculously bad. The menu structure is horrible, you don’t find anything quickly. A training option where you get to train the moves one by one is completely missing, instead you get four instructional videos with instructions read by NBA stars who can muster about as much enthusiasm as if they were reading a recipe for sour cream cheesecake - or dubbing a 70s sex ed video.
In the few hours I’ve played, I’ve had about half a dozen Back-To-Desktop crashes, without the game freezing (it just closed the window). Other than that, the servers aren’t the most reliable, but that might be because the game isn’t even officially released yet. Oh god, I dread what it will be like in the week following the official release...
Graphically, it looks very good, but that’s to be expected. There isn’t much more to improve graphically, anyway. Last year’s NBA 2K looked great, too. My PC isn’t the best out there, but it manages to give a decent image.
UPDATE: As one of the comments so helpfully pointed out, the game "reverses back to normal" in the second season. The so-called "story" only ruins your rookie year, but oh boy is it bad, and cheesy, tacky, and all sorts of wrong. I write fanfiction for a hobby and I would've been able to write a better story on a tipsy saturday evening.
After now going strong in my second season, the game does get better; but I still can't bring myself to recommend it, most of all not at full price. You lose the probably most important season of your career to a joke of a story.
Bugwise, it's playable, although for me there's one recurring thing: it has a kinda useful feature telling you things about your opponent when you come into the game (at tipoff or from the bench), but sometimes it fails to load that overview (only showing the player in idle animation), and the game takes about 20 sec to skip that screen and go back into the game.
TL;DR: It’s not a bad game, per say, and perhaps you’ll find joy in it if you don’t care about the MyCareer mode, but in that mode, it dumps all its negative points right in my face early on although I usually like the NBA 2K franchise. I will continue playing it at least until after my rookie season, and maybe pick it up again once they bring me a patch that fixes this abomination called “Featuring A Spike Lee Joint”. Until then, keep away from this because no way this is worth the full price.
TL;DR: UPDATE: Got to second season. Story over, so game got better. Rookie season still ruined. Don't buy at full price.

DARKEST DUNGEON IS ABSOLUTELY NOT A GAME FOR EVERYONE.
It requires a lot of time dedication, learning and mental resilience.
It's as much an art piece as it is a game, and like any good art, it often takes you to places you'd maybe rather not go.
-If you are a casual gamer, you should probably avoid this. Unless you know for sure you are able and willing to love this game for it's virtues, and to shrug off some of it's imperfections.
-If you are a hardcore gamer who rejoices in difficult games, you might enjoy this very much. Do what you always do- study and understand all the stats, quirks, functions, interactions and synergies, until you dominate the game.
-If you are a pretentious gamer gourmet (like me) who prowls the depths of Steam for only the most unique of experiences, let me just repeat: this game is ART, and a unique piece indeed. You'll never regret and never forget.
Still wanna play this? OK, I'll try to dissect the game a bit more.
---------------------------------------------------------------
THE DUNGEON CRAWLING AND COMBAT is severe, but it can always be overcome; you just need to provision well, build a group of heroes that is functional together and at least roughly adapted to the dungeon and goal, make a battle plan A, make a battle plan B (and plan C doesn't hurt either). In the dungeon, just do what works and don't do anything rushed and stupid.
Many people complain about the combat being to unpredictable and unfair. They should GIT GUD. It's true that the Champion and Darkest difficulty (=3rd & 4th level of dungeons) get pretty brutal, so be extra careful and cautious and exploit every ability and oportunity to the extreme. Just shamelessly cheese it. In the most extreme of circumstances, survival is not about heroism ;)
Some people complain that the stress mechanic is excessive. They have a point, but they should've probably expect that, since the game vocally advertises it as it's core mechanic. After all, we're talking an anachronistic dark fantasy gothic horror with a crusader who murders guys by showing them a scroll, so don't expect 100% lifelike realism.
So I'll give you a tip. Not unlike Dark Souls, this game has a rather brutal learning curve if you go into it blind. Darkest Dungeon has very helpfull stats, tooltips and tutorial panels, but the amount of information, percentages, values, stats, interactions, combinations and synergies will still be dazzling to a beginner. Thus, unless you are the most zealous kind of hardcore gaming masochist who only accepts the complete and unadulterated challenge, don't be ashamed to do a bit of prior research. And even if you really want to explore the game all by yourself, which is commendable, you still HAVE to at least watch a little bit of playthrough and make sure you really like the combat system. THIS IS INCREDIBLY IMPORTANT, BECAUSE YOU ARE GOING TO BE DOING A HUNDRED METRIC ♥♥♥♥-TONS OF FIGHTING AND IT WILL GET TEDIOUS UNLESS YOU ARE REALLY REALLY INTO IT.
The final bit of intel you need about combat is the trinkets, which alter the stats of your heroes. The trinket system is well done and enjoyable. Trinkets allow your heroes to be more effective, more persistent, or to serve more diverse roles, but they often handicap them in other ways, so they never feel overpowered and cheap. Just be warned that trinkets are more important in this game than it first seems. You should choose missions based on how good the trinket reward is.
THE TOWN BUILDING, ECONOMY AND HERO MANAGEMENT is crucial, and while I enjoy it, I'll admit that most people probably won't. The amount of micromanagement is towering. You have to plan cautiously and only spend money if you have to and if it will benefit you immediately. You have to make sure to always bring back enough cash from dungeons, but make room for heirlooms too... maybe I'm overstressing this, but the thing is that if you do run out of money, you're kinda ♥♥♥♥ed and you practically lose your save. So just saying.
And finally, THE ATMOSPHERE. The visual style, character design and artwork, the sound design, the music by Stuart Chatwood(!), the writing, the unforgettable narration of Wayne June(!!!), the simple but powerful story. IT'S ALL ABSOLUTELY ♥♥♥♥ING GLORIOUS. Altogether, it creates a gorgeous and unparalelled atmosphere. And that's kinda the main reason to play the Darkest Dungeon.
---------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR: Make sure you really like it before you buy it.
Oh, and I can not really speak for the DLC, since I haven't played it. However, it feels to me like a redundant addition to a story that was already good enough, well-rounded and complete. And the new hero, while functionally interesting, defeats some core principles of the game and seems rather overpowered to me (and he is objectively overused as a result). So that's a nope on the DLC from me.

I will get into detail, but I start with that the game is absolutely well done.
The design of the game, the setting and the visual aspects (such as the design level of the character faces, design of enemies, and so on) have created a fundamental role in this game- the art and visual aspects are what makes this game unique. The characters themselves feel alive, the enemies- real and dangerous, and the bosses- grotesque abominations created with regards to the iconic Lovecraftian style. This is why I think this game stands out- the atmosphere and the visual aspects fit beautifully in this roleplaying game where death is the main enemy.
I have not talked about the sounds and soundtrack yet, but here I am. I include it in because sound is side to side to the visual aspects, and plays a large part of what the gameplay would feel like to the player.
The music itself is unique. It has the feeling of the constant dread within the Hamlet, while adventuring.

If it gets switched up with other tracks while a battle is commencing, maybe that would be a good idea after all.
The sounds implemented are really good- the darker it gets (note!) the scarier the sounds in the dungeons become, which stresses out the characters even more. Very well done.
Gameplay is perfectly executed for this type of game. The stress bar plays a huge role of character development, as well as the trinket system fits to the class of the characters. The game causes you to feel that you can lose your characters at any times, be it from the enemies, the bleeding/blight effects, or succumbing to a random mini-boss battle-

Overall, I say perfectly executed.

Terraria is a fascinating 2-dimensional, block-based, multiplayer experience, and is fun accessible to all ages.
Often referred to as a 2-dimensional version of Minecraft, especially earlier on, Terraria is more-or-less the first of its kind, so with that comes some downfalls. Namely:
○ Performance isn't as good as you might expect from a 2-dimensional game.
○ Not available on Mac OS or Linux without using Wine or a similar compatibility layer.
○ Insecure and buggy netcode.
○ Somewhat disjointed gameplay.
While most of those points sound major, it's important to note that they are not incredibly apparent in the majority of cases. Also, point #2 is thought to be rectified soon, as the developers of Terraria have mentioned that a Linux and Mac OS version of Terraria is in the works.
Some good points this game has:
○ Moderately easy to pick up and play
○ Somewhat challenging to master (as it should be!)
○ Countless enemies, bosses, items, collectables, etc
○ Several area types to explore - Jungles, dark caves, giant trees, deep oceans, arid deserts, floating islands, and even HELL, all complete with their own enemy sets.
○ Challenging-but-fun gameplay.
○ Simple online multiplayer, to make co-operative gameplay easy to jump into.
With all that said, I highly recommend this game to anybody out there who thinks they might have an autism-spectrum disorder.

Osmos starts off as a relaxing physics puzzler with strategy behind every move. Just a few sections later, the pace speeds up and competing AI complicate everything, becoming notoriously difficult. I can understand challenges, but a lot of the frustration comes from awkwards controls and gameplay that punishes single mistakes. Later levels require speed to outpace the AI growth, and the relaxing style quickly disappears.
I made a push to finish off the game, and there is the potential for unlimited levels. These Forever levels continue to ramp up in difficulty, and it really seems like the game is intended to be more challenging than relaxing. After finishing off the requirements, I've have my fill. The Ambient Impasse levels were the most enjoyable in the end, as they have no rushing elements. Strategy and planning is key in Impasse, instead of urgency and random luck.
I'd recommend trying the demo and checking out videos. Gameplay is solid, but is probably a bit dated compared to the mobile market options. It's not as bad as I remember, but fails to shine or impress anymore. Definitely not worth $10 USD.

AoE 3 is the third installment in the series, offers an intriguing main single player story as various characters search for the fountain of youth. The single player skirmishes, custom made games, and multiplayer is the bread and butter of the game. In single player skirmishes, enemies are further apart, giving your base time to upgrade and build your army to your specifications before attacking enemy camps. You receive experience points when in battle, building, working, etc. Combat is much better than in AoE2, but unless you are playing on harder difficulties, the AI isn't as good as in AoE2.  This time around you  get wars dogs as well as cannons, and other weapons. You can build decks of cards for the shipments to your colony, forge alliances with natives or other allies to take over the new world.  There are a few things in the game that is annoying. 1. You can't put your soldiers in patrolling mode, you have to manually put them where you want them to be. 2. The npcs are dumber than a bag of rocks. Workers will just stand there while being attack instead of fighting back, soldiers will ignore enemies attack them while they are attacking buildings. 3.They have taken out most of the different matches from AoE2 like King of the Hill, Capture the Relic, Wonder Race, Deathmatch (where you start with supplies), and other matches that made AoE2 great making this game a dumb down version of AoE2. It is still a very good game in the series it just lacks depth. The music is okay and the graphics are beautiful I just wish it had more to offer. 8/10. A good strategy game to own.

This game didn't recieve great reviews (mainly due to removing several features players loved from AOEII), but in spite of some things I miss, overall I consider this to be the best of the Age of Empires Franchise. Just make sure you pretty much ALWAYS launch the Asian Dynasties DLC to get all content and improvements (such as the ability to use all maps/factions and the ability to view unit/building health by holding ALT). It's the best looking of the franchise, and features a really nice new system where you can build 'hands' of shipments to send in from your Home City (you're colonising, so you can call in reinforcements!).
This system adds in a new level of progression on top of that which already exists in strategy games, greatly increasing replayability and gives you a range of ways to play. This Complete Collection features a massive amount of maps, as well as a custom map creator and decent randomisation of attributes. All in all there are 8 Vanilla Factions (British, Spanish, German, Ottoman, Russian, French, Portugeuse and Dutch) Plus 6 Expansion Pack Factions (Sioux, Aztec, Iroquois and Japan, China, India) totally for a respectable 14 factions total, each plays differently and encourages a variety of unique tactics.
Migrating from AOEII you will notice the lack of the diplomacy feature, instead just relying on FFA or a Two Team system to work (you can still request/send resources to each other, as well as help each other out with TEAM Cards or sharing certain buildings). Whilst I do miss these two features, AOEIII adds enough content to keep you contentwithout it, and there is a joy in fighting through Skirmish maps on different sizes and with different factions, as well as levelling up and unlocking more powerful cards for use in your next battle.
All in all AOEIII is a great game, a must for RTS fans, and my overall favourite of the franchise. It's also pretty easy to mod the SXML files to fix up some of the odd balancing (Culverins and Ranged Calvary being U.P.) which also can be fun.

The most important thing I need to say, before anything is that I am generally not a big fan of Dark Souls. It is a nice game, but too hard core for me... Also, I have played a game for about 2 hours, before quitting.
So, Lords of the Fallen... It is definitely heavily influenced by Dark Souls (in terms of Gameplay) so some comparisons are inevitable. The game looks really nice, atmosphere is great and what I liked much more here than in DS series is that story is more aproachable.
Music and sounds are nice, but voice acting is hit and miss, but nothing horrific.
So, the thing I really didn't like here is probably the most important part of this type of game, and that is combat. Dark Souls is hard, really, really hard, and it was the main reason I never actually ended up playing it to the end, but it was a fair game. You need time to learn how to fight! Here, situation is different, the game is still really hard, but I don't feel it's fair: Hitboxes are strange, few times I missed enemy I was sure I was going to hit, but many times enemy would hit me, although my character was half a metre away from the his weapon. Other than that, my character is locked in animation when I go for a hit or dodge, but enemy characters easily turn around in their animations... These things are both unrealistic looking, and totally unfair towards a player.
Other than that the game looked and felt nice, but this thing is too important to ignore, so I need to leave a thumbs down...

This game could have been one o' the greats, but NOPE. The load times are atrocious, most everything is at *least* slightly clunky, and there is no polite way to describe the workshop construction. The story is bland, but passable, and the RPG elements feel watered down in comparison to past titles. In addition, I am occasionally forced to restart the game, due to a variety of annoying, glitches.
On top of that, the game was shared with me by a relative. I encountered so much trouble with Steam's Sharing system that I was forced to (very angrily) purchase it for myself.
There are a few points I think are worth mentioning as positive: the array of special weapon and armor traits as well as the ability to customize and name weapons and armor, the changes to power armor (which I think adds a bit of flavor to combat, depending on how it's customized), and the addition of workshops (even if building onto them can be a hellish experience). I also enjoy the perk system (though some of the choices, so far as I can tell, are useless). Also, while I am aware of a few, I have never personally encountered any game-breaking glitches, which I find to be especially infuriating,
As I hate to end on a positive note, I shall mention the money-grubbing tragedy that is the "creation club."
Overall, I begrudgingly recommend this title, which can be downright fun on occasion, if only to those with a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of patience to spare.

TL;DR: journal pages are good, Lepers are bad. Buy this game unless you’re fussy.
General: Darkest Dungeon is a unique,ambitious game about exploring dungeons, killing monsters, finding treasure, and subsequently discarding that treasure to pick up journal entries.
Also, your journal-finders sometimes contract diseases, develop psychological dysfunctions, get renamed after co-workers you dislike, and get kicked out of your town (by you) when their baggage outpaces their usefulness.
In many ways it’s the ultimate example of an indie title that can be so impressive that it cements a studio in the gaming landscape, while simultaneously teaching a generation the importance of personal reflection over material wealth. If it has a real problem, it’s that the game is so good in some ways that it raises expectations that are almost impossible for it to continuously meet. For instance, statistically you should find all of the journal entries available after only about 25% of the campaign.
Difficulty/DLC: This review is written from the perspective of the default difficulty (Darkest), with the Crimson Court DLC installed, on build 20343. I also used an inventory stacking mod so that I could discard more treasure when I found journal entries. I find I just don’t appreciate the cryptic verse if I don’t toss at least eight emeralds to make room for each page.
Strengths: If you’ve played Darkest Dungeon, or are considering purchasing it, I’m willing to bet that art style is what first caught your eye. The ‘crowquill,’ ink-and-more-ink aesthetic is excellent, and I expect to see it imitated by many developers in the years to come. Combined with the excellent voice narration, Darkest Dungeon makes for one of the most immersive experiences in modern journal collection simulation.
Beyond that, the turn-based combat is fun and resonant; you cheer when you crit, you cringe when you miss, and you scream in fury when the journal-hoarding crabman crits your healer for 150% of her total health and leaves her bleeding out. Then you scream louder when he does the same thing to your Plague Doctor on the next turn. Then you have to decide between carrying home the rare ancestral trinkets they had equipped, or holding on to the journal entries you found. There is only one correct option.
Boss fights are generally good, though a few are lamely gimmicky, and a lot of times the fight seems to be in the balance right up until the end. One of the best feelings is losing a character or two and still being able to bring the boss down via a crucial crit, clutch dodge, secret weakness found in a journal page (drag a torch onto Vvulf, see what happens).
Weaknesses: As I see it, Darkest Dungeon has two major weaknesses, and unfortunately, they kind of work in tandem to make each other worse than they would be on their own.
The first is the amount of RNG. I think I have a little less tolerance for RNG than most gamers, and DD infuriated me more than once. You can be cruising along, clearing a dungeon with no problem, then have 2-3 bad rolls that completely derail your run. Whiners will argue, but these critical failures are often not down to something you did wrong. At endgame, journal-searchers can and will be reduced to zero on a freak crit, and they will bleed/blight out before you have any chance to recover them. In my most recent campaign, I lost seven Champion level heros on their first death’s door check. FML.
Unpopular opinion: Some people think this is challenge, and this game is super hardcore, but they’re utterly wrong; Darkest Dungeon isn’t a deeply skill-intensive game. It’s a series of coin flips where good preparation can give you a boost of 10-15% and poor preparation means your time is probably better spent playing No Man’s Sky.
Some in the community hide behind the disclaimer ‘making the most of a bad situation’ but I don’t think that covers all manner of design shortcomings. Making the most of a bad situation is sending two Lepers, the diseased Arbalest with bad quirks, and the occultist you just don’t like the look of on a suicide run into the courtyard, and only pulling out once both Lepers are dead and you’ve learned your lesson not to waste roster slots on recruiting them.
The second major weakness of Darkest Dungeon is the repetitive encounters. Over the course of a campaign you’ll fight close to 1000 (or more) single battles, and there just aren’t enough mechanics to sustain so many. Fights are always 4v1-4, and there are really only half a dozen enemy archetypes with slight skill and appearance variants. It’s a fine system for a couple 100 battles, but the final stretch of the game feels painfully redundant. The seams really start to show on a game with such a long campaign.
Unfortunately, the punishment for failing RNG is more missions to replace what was lost...more missions aka the same encounters you’ve been fighting for dozens of hours. See how those things work together to hinder an otherwise excellent game?
I haven’t played the new Radiant mode, but my understanding is that it considerably mitigates both of these flaws. Too bad it’s for filthy casuals who recruit Lepers and waste inventory slots on treasure.
It’s a really good game, and I think most people will enjoy it more than I did. There are some deeply flawed mechanics, but they don’t overwhelm the genuinely high quality of the game.

Darkest Dungeon offers an appealing aesthetic with it's grim tone, which extends to it's gameplay. The game has incredible music and artwork, and the theme is appealing, but I cannot suggest this game due to it's aggrevating RNG based gameplay. While RNG does have a place in keeping things interesting, and in this game, the idea being that there is no perfect strategy (The community begs to differ, see 4 Man-at-Arms builds), this game relies so much on it that it barely has to think for itself. The Speed mechanic is typically out of your favour, where a med speed enemy is scarier than a high speed enemy, due to the fact they can go from being last on one turn to first on the next, resulting in a two hit combo that can be bring a party memeber down immediately. This would be fine, if it weren't so cumbersome to recover from this by week 50.
This can also get aggrevating when you have a particular string of bad luck and lose core characters, such as healers. In one such run, the only characters I lost were vestals, and they were lost in quick succession due to poor fortune (in one case, as mentioned above, due to two consecutive hits from the same enemy). The game ramps up it's difficulty at champion to a degree that is almost masochistic, where you have to find strategies to abuse the game or be at it's mercy, where enemies scale significantly faster than you do, in terms of crit, dodge, HP, and damage.
The issue with the game isn't even in it's mechanics, but the scaling of it. Stress is easily managed and abused with a crusader or bard, and light is no different. It's the crit RNG that seems to always be out of your favour, in that one crit fo you can kill an enemy, but their crit costs you weeks in game to recover that character (Which can interfere with your time limit, and after a few choice deaths, ruin the run altogeher). An occurance of this type basically ends your previous 20 hours and forces you to start again, and often having learned nothing. You can abuse gimmicky group compositions to get 100% dodge, or complete damage immunity, but at that point you have had to break the game to be able to contest the unforgiving punishments for simply playing. When everything comes to a dice roll, you aren't really playing anymore
While I think this game is enjoyable to play up until champion, I feel like the game as a whole is what should be judged, and as champion & darkest are considered a part of the game, I cannot reccommend this game at the price it is. The over-reliance on RNG could easily be handled in other ways to instill hopelessness in the player as is the theme. The creator's past comments, however, have shown there is explicit intent for this.
This game is thus built for a masochistic player, one who enjoys chanced failure, and putting the pieces back together. Over several hours.
YOU SHALL NOT BUY this crap, do not make the same mistake I've made.

SSTD is held back by a failure to focus on the backbone behind the gameplay. The window doesn't let you resize. This means the cutesy pixel graphics scale horribly and all the pixels become different sizes. The options in general for this game seem pathetic. Anti Aliasing, hotkeys, and music choice seem to be the extent. They do use the default windows combination for fullscreen rather than set it as an option. There's no choice to lock the mouse to the game either, which means you can overdo a movement and your camera flies off the screen. The actual gameplay is pretty okay, if a bit vague at times (For example, trying to upgrade a tower with insufficient funds only states that the tower is not a "valid target") and the idea of particpating in the attack phase has been applied here as well. I was pleasantly surprised by this indie game, to the point I wanted to reach the end, which is rare nowadays.
Spaceport Hope is a platformer shooter, some kind of Megaman in a very simple way. The music is really nice, the art is somehow personal (I almost felt a different tone in it, like some eastern country look or something?) and the world/narration/setting are all very nice and interesting to dive in.
Now hear me out, this game is far from perfect, it has a few flaws:
- no map (though it has some metroidish wannabe vibe)
- loose physics (the jump option is not sensitive)
- repetitive gameplay: contrarily to Megaman you only jump and shoot with no dash or powers, just different guns
- and an overall "rough" feel to it, as if the game had been rushed. Some characters undeveloped, some dialogues which could have been deeper, some level design which feels too approximate...
When you play and finish it, you could think it was intentionally made from A to W without any plan for X, Y or Z in the beginning. Or maybe it is just a first indie game by a couple of young devs with some inevitable amateurish finishing taste to it? if so it is good news! as it is a good start and I will be on the lookout for this studio's next works.
All in all, if you forgive its rough looks and its imperfections, Spaceport Hope is pleasant to play and only promises of potential great other games to come.

Alright, beat the game and unlocked all achievements - so that allows for a qualified review, here goes.
Spaceport Hope is a space-themed platformer, where you go to different planets (stages) to solve a case after a trade goes wrong.
On each planet there are different kinds of enemies, hidden weapons to unlock, different level design etc., though some planets are rather small compared to others.
It's a standard platformer, where you fight enemies, dodge traps, collect coins, buy items, unlock new weapons, fight bosses and so on. It's a well done platformer, with great variety in enemies, and a fine variety in platform/trap design. The graphics are also pretty good for a retro/pixel-style IMO.
It's a relaxing game, with a mediocre difficulty, however stages don't seem to get much harder, besides the bosses which overall are harder the further you progress. There are a total of 13 bosses, which are all unique and fun to fight. Sound effects are decent, and the music is actually pretty good and fitting for the stages.
Even though there are a lot of different guns you can play around with, you can still do fine with the default gun the entire game if you are skilled at dodging and learning enemy patterns, expect if there are several enemies at once, where other weapons will a better choice. Even so, in most situation there will be a weapon choice that makes the situation easier: beam is good for enemies that can't jump or shoot back, rockets are good for stationary enemies, the homing gun is good for flying etc., but you can also jump around while dodging and just spam the default gun.
There are some puzzles also, which needs to solved to unlock hidden items or sometimes progess the game, but the puzzles are quite simple so you should never get stuck on those.
The only slightly annoying things in the game are the inventory/shop system and finding the objectives. The shop items don't explain what they are for, and while the game tells you what your current objective is, it doesn't always tell you which direction to go, or which planet to look, which sometimes will require you to explore a bit, although you will be very likely to to find some items and collect coins in the meantime, so effort will never be wasted.
Overall it's a very well done platformer, admittedly nothing too special, but what's most important is that it's FUN and relaxing, not too easy and not too boring either, and for the very low prices I will definetely recommend this game if you want to play a  short relaxed platformer.

Spaceport Hope is a fine little Metroidvania with a retro style. Not perfect, but satisfying. It's around a 7-7.5/10: if you enjoy Metroidvania platformers, the $2 price tag is quite fair and it's worth a look, but it's far from a must-play game. Gave me a bit over 4 hours of enjoyment. I chose not to grind out the last few achievements.
PROS:
+ Nice pixel art visuals. Each location has distinct visuals and its own colour palette. Visuals, not writing, are what gives this game a sense of charm.
+ Solid controls. Main character is responsive so platforming and dodging projectiles never feels unfair.
+ Good weapon variety. You'll be collecting different weapons up until the last level. Each of the 16 weapons has a unique feel. Ammo limits prevent you from relying on one gun, but ammo drop frequency feels fair. This is not a game where you should conserve ammo.
+ Level design, enemy encounters, and boss fights are mildly challenging: enough to be fun, never discouraging. You may have to redo a couple of long platforming sections if you die between save points, but don't expect to be stuck on boss fights for more than a couple of tries. This is a game made to be completed.
+ Good sound effects.
+ Nice music. Lots of variety. A couple of tracks felt out of place in certain levels where a peaceful soundtrack was matched with tense action. Most were good. A couple really stood out, like the Spaceport Hope level's piano theme.
CONS:
- Requires Java. I didn't have it installed, and uninstalled it right after completing SPH.
- Occasional obtuse design may leave you wondering where the hell you're supposed to be going or why a door won't open. (eg. To open the first door you need to switch weapons, by opening the gun menu, by pressing the G key, to 'activate' the gun you just picked up, so it enters the weapon rotation you cycle through by pressing the switch weapon key, so you can blow up the door.)
- I experienced minor, temporary stuttering/frame drops after loading the game, and after gaining new weapons. This went away after a few seconds and never really interfered with gameplay.
- Writing is forgettable, but doesn't get in the way. Don't expect smart dialogue, memorable characters, or a story that will make you think.
- Metroidvania die-hards may not find it challenging enough to satisfy.

I will admit it. I'll come out at say it. The finale had me in tears. Before The Walking Dead, I only cried during one video game- "The Last of Us". Now it's two. But that doesn't mean I've still felt a variety of emotions- shock, desperation, mistrust- through playing other games, but this one seems to do especially well at it. The gameplay of TWD is incredibly minimalist. It's a point-and-click game. And normally I despise this genre (except for anything made by Humongous Entertainmen, because they knew what they were doing), but Telltale has not only made me excited to play their second season, they've made me excited to play their entired library of games, because they understand the concept of good story... and good mechanics for a point-and-click game.
Unlike the last of this type of game I played, Ankh 2, you don't have convoluted answers to very simple puzzles. There are no bags of rasberries that attract ants where you have to utlize some fish bones and make the ants carry the bones so a cat will chase down the bones, in this game. A+B=C in this game, which can make people argue, "Well, where's the challenge in THAT!?". Personally, I like games that make sense other than the average point-and-click where A1+A2xB+C(D-E)=F. And also, the real challenge of this game is the decisions you make. A lot of these choices can really make you think and are very morally grey, which I absolutely loved. It's not like other moral-choice systems in games where there are very obviously good and evil choices that make your personality starkly different, but little choices and big ones that effect you, the people around you, and the circumstances you find yourselves in. And these choices have lasting effects in the future episodes. If someone dies, they're dead. If you killed that person, Clementine will see it and it WILL have consequences.
And that's what it all boils down to- the choices are linked together by a wonderful story with a cast of well-written characters. It keeps you emotionally invested and hungry for more, every time you finish an episode. And I wasn't disappointed with the ending, either. The Walking Dead is a must-play for anyone who's tired of games that put gameplay and graphics over the most important aspect in any medium... story.

Lords of the fallen is often accused of being just a dark souls rip-off, to be honest it doesn't rip-off dark souls because this is not dark souls, the game is extremely linear, barerly to no exploration and the level design just can't compete with dark souls 1.
Does this mean that the game is bad? well no, it's not awful, it does a lot of thing right but it has a lot of issues.
Issue 1: The game performance is extremely inconsistent.
My pc is not stellar in any way but i think that most pc users will not enjoy this port's perfomance, my frame-rate varies to 40fps to 8fps, sometimes even when there is nothing on the screen it drops to 15 or even 10 fps.
The graphics look incredible at max settings, but at low they look horrible, i know that low settings the game does not have to look spectacular but the thing i don't understand is why my fps gain is 5 or 10 compared to max settings, even lowering the resolution does not help me at all.
Issue 2: Combat:
Combat in lords of the fallen is somewhat of a mixed bag, it starts just like a dark souls game but then it becomes extremely unfair and boring with bosses.
It's unfair because most enemies will practically do massive damage to you while knoking you to the ground, just so you will get up and then KILL YOU BECAUSE THEY SOMEHOW FORGOT TO MAKE YOU INVINCIBLE WHILE YOU GET UP (you can't dodge while getting up on the ground), or you could equip a weapon that attacks faster but does little to no damage to those enemies, and to make it worse those types of enemies always go in packs of 3 or more.
The boss-fights are complete and utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ this is another huge complaint i have, they only have like 3 or 4 attacks max,
one when they are close to you, another one when you are far and one special attack. They are extremely predictable but worse of all is that it makes battles boring, it's just attack, dodge, attack, dodge... you get the idea.
Issue 3: Exploration and the landscape.
For a game that it's said to be based on dark souls is very suprising to find that they didn't implement one of the best things in the dark souls games, the exploration. It's an extremely linear game with barerly any exlploration at al and when it does offer you a chance to explore, it ends with a room whitout nothing in there or an item, it never goes beyond this and it's extremely frustating.
The places you go in the game are not very inspiring either, they look like they just look at hellish monsters and places, while they at first look inspiring, it quickly becomes clear that it's the only theme you will see with the monsters.
Issue 4: Challenge
One of the most nerving things about this game is that unlike other games that provide a hard challange, but are fair is that they give you enough room to prepare and learn from your mistakes, this game does not, it's not a challenge to be thrown in a room where you will get constantly killed by a monster that takes 100 hits to kill while it kills you in 1 or 2 hits, and to make it worst he has other monsters that chase you and want you dead, just so can drive you ♥♥♥♥ing insane, if this was, you know optional i would say, meh it's not worth it, but when the game does this 3 or 5 times it gets really on my nerves, so no this is not a challenge it's ♥♥♥♥ing unfair.
So no, i will just continue to play dark souls, which is what i should be doing in the first place.
It's becoming better, much better.

Half-life is regarded as one of the greatest games of all time.
The story is you are Gordon freeman, who is a character with zero personality at all with a bad case of silent protagonist, and you’re on your way to work at the black mesa facility. Not long after you cause a disaster unleashing aliens inside the base going around killing everyone and the military is sent in to “clean things up”. The story is nothing special and a lot is left in the dark since you don’t really know all that much in the game, but what was special for the time was how it was told, since you never leave Gordon’s perspective.
The gameplay is a mix between solving puzzles, exploration and the standard late 90s shooter gameplay. This game also added a bit of realism to shooters compared to the previous games of the 90s, no more floating guns, a more realistic progression rather than level by level and hunting for keys to open doors. The gameplay also shifts and changes throughout the game, at the beginning you only have a crowbar and a handgun and you’ll mostly be fighting monsters in a horror-ish style, later you get your hands on more weapons being; a shotgun, a machinegun, a magnum and some grenades as the game becomes more action oriented as the soldiers show up, and the game changes again as the alien soldiers show up and you get your hands on more weapons; a rocket launcher, and some original weapons in the game (being energy weapons)  it changes yet again as you go onto the alien planet. The game also changes pace quite a fair bit since the game will sometimes throw a platforming section or a puzzle at you after gunfights.
Though being a so called great game of all time Half-life does have a number of issues:
The melee combat: all gold source engine games have terrible melee combat since you have to be so close to hit anything but this is a shooter so this isn’t a big deal unlike some other gold source engine games.
The shooting isn't very good since enemies don't react to getting shot at all, so there's no stunning them when shooting at them, and you can also peek around coners so you can see the enemy's hands, and then just shoot their hands until they die, which is pretty stupid and just cheating. To me this is kind of weird, since the gold source engine is basically the quake 1 engine, and in quake 1, all of the enemies get stunned when shot apart from the wampa/yeti things which are meant to be bullet sponges.
Also the fall damage is very over exaggerated and this is really annoying during some of the platforming sections, and the ladders, the ladders in this game are very clunky, because you feel like a magnet stuck to them and you usually detach from them and fall right down to the bottom.
The game does also get boring for two reasons:
Reason no1: there is no music for the most part which was to add to the emersion, however it does get boring after while listening to nothing but your own footsteps.
Reason no2: Some of the sections in this game drag on, and on, and on.
There are also some game breaking bugs, thank god for the existance of NOCLIP.
At the time this was groundbreaking but today it's an ok game but it just hasn't aged very well, to the point where I sometimes call it half-S H I T E. Still better than half life 2 though.

First of all, I played this game on my netbook at 1024x600 resolution and it worked perfectly (which is handy to know because most developers never specify the minimum resolution for their games). I also used a mouse rather than a gamepad. I suspect a gamepad might be better, but the mouse is perfectly usable too.
I initially didn't like this game. I started in the arcade mode and found it
too difficult to reliably control the swinging action of the trash particles that you use to smash the astroids and ships (especially without swinging myself into something else). Unlike the classic
game where you generally have plenty of space to move, it's a very crowded universe and it just made it frustrating to be able to build up momentum.
However, the lure of trading cards made me persevere and I tried the missions. These were much more accessible than the arcade mode since it gave me just three small goals to try at a time. Rather than just keep swinging around wildly in a vain attempt to clear the level (impossible), I had to use some finesse to complete a mission and this really improved my experience. Sometimes I had to go racing around to get to certain points within a time limit so that rather than smashing the asteroids I just weaved around them like Han Solo. Other times I had to only destroy a certain number of the enemy, which can be tricky when they all group together. I learnt to let them chase me and trick them into ramming my trash. Other missions have you staying within a small area for a certain time, or destroying a particulary fast enemy ship.
I still have a fair way to go in the missions, but I know that I will keep this game around once I have finished it just to have quick sessions when I find myself with a bit of spare time. Just for the sake of this review, I tried playing the arcade mode again to see how I fare this time. It was much better than my first attempt. The skills I had learnt in the missions really paid off in the arcade mode. Rather than spinning around wildly, I could do surgical strikes on any asteroid or ship that took my fancy. I am so glad I spent the time building the skills to be able to find this game such a blast!
Now if you don't mind, I have just unlocked a new ship so I have to go run it through its paces.

Spaceport Hope is a short but competent indie developed Metroidvania game with MegaMan flavored combat that has a surprisingly deep bag of tricks.
Pros:
+Interesting locations with lots to explore, plenty of secrets and exploration is usually well rewarded
+Most of the pixel art is rather good
+Responsive controls*
+Nice variety of weapons with a well balanced ammo system
+Some really cool boss fights and other interesting looking enemies
+Not crazy difficult to get 100% achievements in a single play through (about 5 hours)
Cons:
-Some of the art is very bad (character portraits)
-*Controller support is wonky. Dev states controller support is in beta and while it didn’t cause me to die it was annoying when my character got stuck moving in a direction I didn’t want to go
-Some technical limitations. Game actually runs in Java (!) and I hit a moment of lag every time a new sprite got loaded into the game. The first time I fired each gun, the first time I faced a certain type of enemy, the screen froze for a second
-WAY too many enemies that hunker into an invincible defensive mode that you must either wait out to finish killing, or bypass them entirely and miss out on dropped money. Small pink turrets, green cannons, flying death orbs, tripod robots, plus half a dozen bosses…
-There is a gun you can get from some pirates in the game but it involves trekking down a long level, coming back, going down another long level, coming back from that, then through the first level again and back. Rather annoying and obvious padding. And the gun’s not even that good!
Meh:
=Music is hit or miss but never bad
=Generic story but it has some fun bits
=There are like 2 puzzles that don’t add much to the game
=Early on it’s hard to tell what is background art and what are platforms or interactive objects. You tend to get a feel for it further into the game but some better differentiation would be nice
=It’s sometimes unclear where you should go next. If you love exploring or don’t mind checking a guide from time to time it’s not that big of a deal
Overall this is a quite serviceable Metroidvania style game that rewards exploration and allows for a variety of playstyles in combat. Minor technical hiccups, a few poorly designed enemies, and some unnecessary back-tracking are annoying, but these aren’t enough to dismiss the game. It’s also quite impressive considering the game was made with a very small team of like 4 people. It won’t redefine the genre and doesn’t really push the boundaries but I had a good time playing; it's well worth checking out.

Kind of like a hybrid of Spore and Robocraft
So you start off with jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ a tiny little robot with none of the essentials. Wheels, one gun, one drill.
As you kill enemies and do some of the starter quests you get parts from the actual robots you fight, they explode into bits and you put the bits... well on yourself! The starter quests get you some essentials like a battery ( for powering up shields, and heal bubbles ) and the game leads you through with a basic quest system on refining ores in a refinery, and selling items.
Could use a little more in-game info on the crafting of blocks seeing as its a "wiki game" when it comes to crafting things.
Combat is great, you blast away at robots firing all your guns at once, then steal the parts either to take them away to sell - or use them on your bot. The area where you build your base becomes a wasteland of parts from dead robots and there are ways to break down items ( the scrapping module ) and ways to make money other than selling parts at the stores.... by mining / taking down trees. There are various blocks that allow you to pick up items, make your own basic conveyor systems to either break down weapons/armor, or refine ores/wood to have them automatically sell things... power up generators ( which power batteries )
Its very fun playing this game fresh from the start again because as a small bot the real challenge is there, you think "OH WHAT IS THAT!" at every part you can't recognize.
Eventually you snowball out of control either into a fortress of death with shield/heal bubbles, or into a mining maniac.
You can even man things you build with AI modules that mine or fight in combat, but the AI is very derpy.
The one thing I'll say is a con is performance is very bad in the later game when you have 50+ weapons firing all at once. GPU usage drops to 0, the game locks up when your bot fires and it makes it a bit troubling to play at that point.
Its early access so pricing of parts needs to be adjusted for sure. I've seen earlier videos where things were priced higher, but as for now things are so cheap it lets you build ANYTHING you want with a blanket price of 100 for most higher end parts.
This is one of the better early access games worth playing and putting feedback on. I really have enjoyed the bit I have played, I hope for more parts - and performance tweaks so that the game doesn't lock up on super-mega-huge builds!
There is also a non-mandatory twitter integration feature I used with a dummy twitter account. It allows you to upload your bots as a tweet so they appear in other peoples games ( at the expense of losing that robot once its sent out as an "invader" ) which I think was well done and amazing.
I look forward to this games completion! For a 20$ price point I'll say if you like vehicle based combat, open ended games ( this game is procedurally generated in its maps/store locations ) then its a shoe in. Just needs the rest of its content and some polish - the core gameplay is great!

This is a hidden object and not a logic puzzle game. The problem arises due to the fact that it is a terrible hidden object game where instead of hiding objects everything is just so dark you can't see them instead. Even though it is free it is simply not worth the time.

For newcomers to the puzzle or specifically hidden object genre it just gives a poor impression and the veterans will just find it to be a game of waiting for the apple creature to move. Performance wise it is terrible as well, although that does not really matter in this game. I ran this game at 3840x2160 (although I have no idea if I rendered it in 3840x2160 or just scaled it as there is no options panel.) with a beefy Hawaii XT GPU yet I got stuck at 27FPS even though it is a 2D sprite game with no intense effects. It could be so that the game is locked at 27FPS due to animation but that is still a negative as one can solve that in other ways even with lower than refreshrate animations. Although I am wondering why they picked 27 over 30 which would remove screen tearing. If they have V-Sync enabled (no options panel) 27 FPS means that most people with 60Hz monitors and no active sync will be stuck at 15FPS while 30 FPS animations would mean people would get stuck at 30FPS.
I did however like the artstyle in the light parts of the game, the only parts where you can actually see it too badly.
Conclusion:
Not worth your time even though it is free.

This game has received lots of bad press, and while some of it is deserved I think that the vast majority of it is uncalled for.  Let me start by saying that I am a fan of the Assassin's  Creed games as a whole and that I  have been since the first one was released.  I have, for the most part, played the series on the PC.  It seems like every year there are a ton of people that come out to complain about how porely optomized the newest entry in the series is, and quiet frankly it gets old.  These games are open world games that push the entirety of a computers resources.
The rig that I am playing on is: i7-2600, 16GB DDR3-1600, and an R9 280X.  I play the game at 1920x1080 with the ingame ultra graphics preset.  I have V-Sync turned on and I get a rock solid 30 frames per second in the game other than the occasional hiccup when the game is loading lots of data off of the hard drive.  I have the game installed on a Western Digital Black 4 TB harddrive, so I imagine that these hiccups would not occur for someone using an SSD.  I have only experienced one crash of the game   in the entire time I have played it, and I have not encountered any of the glitches others caim to have in single player.  I have also had no problems with the co-op missions that others have had.  I do have an ADSL2+ 20Mbs/1.5Mbs internet connection, so I have a constant strong connection to the UPlay servers.  In the end this is the best looking game I have yet played for the PC.
Now with the technical aspects of the game taken  care of lets look at the game for it's content.  The story ius fairly standard for the Assassin's Creed series.  The main story is a fairly simple trope revolving around love and revenge.  Like the other games in the series what makes the plot interesting are all of the surrounding interesting characters that are synonymous with the setting of the game.  As is par for the course in this series the mainplot is used as a staging area to introduce the more interesting aspects of the setting.  This game makes the information about the surrounding places and people more accessible in the form of a companion app, that you can either install on your computer, or preferably have on a portable device next to you so that you can read about things that interest you.  The companion app also provides an ingame map that controls like a GPS app would on touch screen devices.  I have this app on my tablet and it works well with the main game to create an immersive experience.  I found myself reading about in game places on the go when I was not playign the game.  It honestly feels like the best realization of the concepts that were introduced into video games with the Wii U controler.
This app does have a slightly sinister side to it.  There are in-game chest that require you to play a side game on the companion app to unlock.  These are not only numerous in the main game but the app requires huge amounts of time to do the side quest.  The times are fairly similar to the fleet sidequest in the previos game Black Flag, but they feel far more intrusive the way they are implemented in this game.  Similar in annoyance are the other ingame chaest that are unlocked using the
system.  They are less obtrusive than the first set of chest, but innexplicably the ingame daily quest have not been implemented into the game yet even though they were working for Black Flag at launch last year.  Luckily, you can still level up on the site simply by playing the game.  There is no extra effort needed, outside the game, other than connecting your uplay account to the ACinitiates server which requires all of about 2 minutes since the web siter uses the same login as the uplay servers.  In this sense it serves as a replacement to the content that was unlocked via ingame progress achievements in the previous games.  I hope that Ubisoft's goal with this is to allow long time fans of the series to unlock content more quickly in future installments of the series, but this is unclear at the moment.
The gameplay is fairly standard for the series.  THey have added the ability to control wether you are climbing up or down, which feels like a natural evolution to the parkour system in the series.  The combat in the game has received some criticism from other reviewers, in that it is much more difficult than the looser swashbuckling combat systems in more recent entries in the series.  It harkens back to the weighty counter heavy combat of the original game in the series.  Also, enemies with guns will force you to retreat for cover before re-engaging melee enemies.  I like this weigthy feeling combat, though I can see why it would be a hinderance for people that are looking for a more action oriented affair.  The game forces you to pick and choose when to enter open combat in order to be succesful.  No longer can you run headlong into each situation.  Because, of this the game rewards silent kills in a much more tangible way than more recent entries in the series, and in the end it reminds you of why these games were called "Assassin's Creed," in the first place.
I hope that this review has given you a good idea of what to expect when considering purchaisng this game.  I personally love the game and I recommend the game to anyone who is a fan of the series and has a beefy enough rig to run it.  The minum specs on the store page are, for once, actually a good guideline for the minum system needed to run the game with good performance and in-game high settings.  With this in mind, it really is one of the first true next gen games.

I'll start with what little positives there are with this 'next-gen' AAA title.
As far as AC games go the free running is vastly improved. Much more smooth with the ability to free run up or down and it works much better when trying to climb things diagonally. The graphics are an improvement but not enough to really warrant praise. I like the added customisation to armours however the bonus stats it parades aren't really special, AC has never really been a hard game to play, you could probably finish it in the starting gear.
Negatives. Oh boy.
The combat is a step backwards. Things have been taken away from previous titles and not really much more added. A new 'feature' is that more than one guard can attack you at once. The kill animations are so long though that sometimes you have to cancel the kill to defend against other guards. It's not satisfying and makes the game harder for the wrong reasons.
The main character is boring and blah blah blah. Content is mediocre but hardly the worst thing about the game.
PERFORMANCE. My pc maybe a little old, probably 5 or so years with a GPU upgrade about 2-3 years ago. But I have to run this game at 720p on the lowest settings and still have poor framerate. I realise how open the game is and many pointless npcs are wandering/rioting but it's ridiculous. I can run DA:I on medium settings with a stable framerate even with my old hardware. The latest patch (4) meant to address performance issues has done nothing at all.
Performance aside there is one last issue. Uplay. I understand it's not Valve's fault that I have to run both Steam and Uplay to play this game but it's honestly unacceptable. I have to open Steam, click to play AC:U, wait for Uplay to launch, probably wait for a pointless update, wait for syncing, then the game will launch. Yes I could have just bought the game through Uplay but frankly it's an inferior program and I have no wish to use 3 of these prgrams (Origin included).
AC:U syncs everything to Uplay, that's your save file. ONE SAVE FILE. I have no idea why I can't have multiple (for other users or multiple play thoughs) and it's a pretty poor 'addition'. If Uplay crashes (which it does) I can't save until I open it again, it's just ♥♥♥♥ing stupid.
The companion app. Cool idea. Say I'm out, wanna do some missions on it to get some♥♥♥♥♥♥when I get home and play Unity. Nah. You have to be playing Unity and sync up your app. WHY THE ♥♥♥♥ WOULD I WANT TO USE THE APP WHILE I'M PLAYING THE GAME. Not to mention it constantly loses connection. It wouldn't be much of a problem but you gain extra content, which I assume I paid for, by using it. Whoever thought the idea up to make you connect to both at once should be buried alive.
TL;DR
Some cool new mechanics with free running and some new customisation.
Terrible performance, intrusive Uplay, useless ♥♥♥♥ing Companion App.
Just another steaming pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥that Ubisoft it getting notorious for releasing.
♥♥♥♥ Ubisoft, ♥♥♥♥ Uplay, ♥♥♥♥ Unity.
