This game follows the trend of being an indie-game with way too hard gameplay. This game is like the quintessential "rogue-like" where literally everything in the game is random. EVERYTHING. Enemy spawns, map-layouts, combat and in the end it is waay too much so. This is a game where in the end-game you can't expect any sort of consistency with success and failure and it always feels like the deck is stacked against you, even when, like me, you've played for 48 hours and is sort of able to take everything into account. Is your attack a hit or miss? About 50%. Will this stun succeed or fail? 50%. Will this debuff succeed or fail? 50%. Will I get stunned? 70%. Will I get hit? 70%. This is what it feels like. Add to that all of the other factors that play into whether you succeed or fail, it's waay too much.
When it's impossible to actually master the game, I feel like asking, well then for what am I playing? This is a tiny indiegame with so little diverse gameplay, it shouldn't take more than 20 hours to complete and even that is too much. Other games that sort of committed this sin: Binding of Isaac, Risk of Rain, Super Meat Boy - the difference is, these games have the added value of having a learning curve that actually flattens at some point and there are successes along the way. Darkest Dungeon doesn't have that and you can't blame yourself for it, because of the sheer randomness.

Note: This will be a review of both Darkest Dungeon and Crimson Court - the main game review is first, with thoughts on the expansion later.
Darkest Dungeon kept popping up in my queues but easily got dismissed - I do love turn based, as well as RPG Rougelikes, but it seemed to me to be like the bajillion other retro/pixel graphic games that showed up in my "Discovery Queues". However, I eneded up getting it on a whim since it was on sale for dirt cheap.
Oh my goodness, how wrong I was.
Darkest Dungeon is nothing like the plethora of other hack and slash RPGs you see floating around (and no disservice to those; they're just not my thing). It is, in fact, a very deep, engaging, beautifully created strategy game that challenges you on multiple levels. Not only that, but this thing is so polished you could use it as a mirror in a telescope - every part of the game is so perfectly crafted with love and care that you forget you're playing a game and do really feel like you're trying to take on the world all by yourself.
The atmosphere of the game is wonderful - even the "tutorial" is part of the story. The omnipresent narrator is nothing short of brilliant, and the writer of the dialogue should win an award. Even after playing for many dozens of hours, I'm still excited to hear the narrator say, "Desroy. Them. All." after a hard battle, or to bemoan his prior life's faults.
And don't take "roguelike" to literal. While there is permadeath it's your hereo's that die. Unless you're playing on the hardest difficulty (which imposes a time and death limit) then you can always bounce back. Even if your entire roster is wiped out you can recruit 4 new people and go at it again. So while you're often down, you're never out.
The action is done in a turn-based fashion that emulates a pen and paper type initiative system. I.e., each of your heroes has a "speed" stat, but there's still a roll involved - so someone with a higher speed will not always necessarily go before someone with a lower speed (though you do end up seeing it happen more often than not). One interesting thing here is that turn order is hidden from you.  So while you know who has YET to go, you don't know in what order it will happen (either you or the monsters). Some may not like this but I find it gives the battle, especially "routine" ones, a bit more excitment.
It's hard to say what makes Darkest Dungeon so special. Perhaps it's the unique approach to combat, the simple-yet-complex array of skills and heroes, or the cleverness of the presentation. Whatever it is, it's done to damn near perfect. You can see it in every art asset and every name of a quirk - this game was made with attention to absolutely every detail and by god does it show.
In short, Darkest Dungeon is an absolute joy to play.
For those that may be tricked by the video that auto-plays on Steam's page (like I was), I'll describe the game in more detail. If you've already got a handle on what the game is, scroll down for the Expansion info.
In Darkest Dungeon, you inherit a family estate that is crawling with demonic enemieis. Your goal is to get to the bottom of it (literally) by exploring the various dungeon and killing the baddies within. To do this you recruit a handful of heroes and send them on their quests, with the hope that they live and level up, and become even better heroes. But be careful if they die - they're gone for good.
Your have several classes of heroes to choose from, all with unique skills. Skills are generally aligned into "physical", "bleed", "blight", "buff", and "debuff" and they act exactly how you'd expect. Your heroes, as well as enemies, have certain stats that can both increase the chance of an effect (such as causing an enemy to bleed, resulting in damage over time) as well as provide a resistence to having that effect happen to them, or simply reducing physical damage.
The "Dungeons" are divided into 5 key areas: The Ruins (of your estate) where bad, but mostly humans, dudes dwell. The Cove where evisl fish monsters do their evil fish monster things, the Warrens where malformed pig demons have a taste for more than just slop, and The Weald where a corrupted forest produces all the things you'd expect a corrupted forest to produce. Finally, you have the "Darkest Dungeon" which is, in fact, the darkest and dungeon-ist of them all. Each of these areas has a unique profile, both in enemies and strategy. Each of these dungeons also have bosses in them that proceed the plot (along with various mini-bosses that can show up in any dungeon).
While you're adventuring you'll also have to deal with stress - which comes from simply being in a dungeon filled with hell beasts, enemy attacks, traps, etc.  Stress can cause your heroes to temporarily go insane and even... well, other bad things can happen. The first time it cascades on you, you will actually enjoy watching it happen even though it means you probably just lost a party. Stress is managed from the main estate, where your hereos can drink, screw, pray, or flaggelate their stress away.
If this all sounds like a lot it is - but don't worry! Everything is seamless and intuitive (though it may take you a few clicks to figure out where everything is). The main screen shows your estate and you simply click on the building you want to utilize, drop your hero in, and pay the cost. This brings me to my only critique - the interface. Apparently this started as a console game and so the interface is prettty segregated, meaning it's easy to miss doing something important, like changing your hereo's skills, before you adventure into the dungeon. While a minor annoyance, its is one nonetheless.
EXPANSION:
The Expansion, "The Crimson Court" offers a new class, new enemies, and a new dungeon. The Crimson Court shares the same polish and wit of the original. The art is amazing, the music and sound is amazing, and the narrator still rules. It also introduces new diseases, afflictions, etc. as well as a new resource (blood) you must manage. It certainly enhances the game.
While I am glad I purchased the Crimson Court, it does lack the seamlessness of the original. Perhaps it's simply because I played the original first, but it's easy to tell that Crimson Court is an ADD ON. I.e., it was "dropped into" an existing game that was already 100% whole, so it seems a bit out of place.
Don't take this to mean it isn't fun - it is. It simply highlights how tight the game was before. I've started a new game with it and am enjoying the new class immensely, as well as the added challenge the expansion brings through its new disease/curse.
If you're already a fan of Darkest Dungeon it's worth it, especially on sale. However, if you're unsure of whether this game is your cup of tea, you will not miss anything by simply purchasing the core game. Crimson Court is more ideal for a second play through, in my opinion.

Particle Mace has a bullet hell shooter vibe, but also has a much stronger feeling of flow / getting into a groove than shooters typically do. The game feels great and is very satisfying to play. The controls are polished and intuitive, the physics of the mace weapon are easy to learn, but there's clearly a high skill ceiling for tricks and techniques. Enemies, obstables, and level have simple and easy to read designs, very well done.
In spite of how easy the game is to learn the missions (meta objectives) add a surpising amount of depth. For instance, some require you to limit movement or avoid killing things for a period of time. This challenges you to alter your style of play to complete a goal and think tactically rather than turn off your brain.
I can't say how the game feels over a longer period time but the core mechanics are very well polished. You can pick this up and play it for just a few minutes and get quite a bit of enjoyment out of it. I feel like the psychological rewards in the core game loop are capable of making longer play sessions enjoyable too. I definitely recommended this if you like physics-based gameplay and/or bullet hell shooter types, and don't suffer from epilepsy.

Super Sanctum TD (SSTD) is a 2-D retro-styled tower defense (td) game developed and published by the company Coffee Stain Studios, who are also responsible for ‘Sanctum’ and ‘Sanctum 2’.
+ Broad spectrum of abilities, skills and towers allow for various loadouts.
+ 14 maps with increasing level of difficulty will put your strategical abilities to the test.
o Repetitive musical background with limited sound support.
SSTD makes sure to keep the player involved from the beginning to the end, and I was positively surprised by the level of complexity the game has to offer. It profits from the experience of a veteran td publisher like Coffee Stain Studios, which can be seen as a quality label.
Recommended for achievement hunters and hardcore td freaks.
Estimated time for 100% completion: +20 hours
Singleplayer achievements: 27
Multiplayer achievements: none

For example, at the start of the game, it wanted you to go to the factory, however, it didn't say that the factory was to the left, and ended up spending about 10 minutes trying every door in the village, only to realize that I had to keep going right to exit the village.
A map or an arrow pointng in the general direction of where I needed to go would be a perfect addition as it'll make navigation of the game world easier. Alternatively, adding a sense of direction into the dialog (i.e. "The factory is to the left of the village") would've made things less confusing.

Bias: I did the sounds for this game (not the music), and I'm friends with Andy (the dev). While my clocked hours may not seem significant, trust me when I say I've played this game A LOT outside of steam.
PARTICLE MACE is an arcade game that you can pick up and play in seconds. The only input is movement. That's it. You only press buttons in the menu. This makes for an easy to learn, difficult to master experience... gamer or not. It's great to play alone, and even better to play with friends.
Part of why I love this game is how refined the movement is. PM doesn't try to be anything other than a rad arcade game. It doesn't stretch itself too thin, choosing instead to be a surgical strike of awesome. You want to top the charts on the high score list, or you want to destroy your friends by elegantly weaving through every obstacle and hitting that PERFECT swing of the mace into lesser players. You won't find branching dialogue, super crazy 3D graphics, or dozens of intricate maps. What you will find is an environment you think you've mastered, only to realize (either by high scores or deathmatch) that you aren't anywhere near as great as you thought you were. Killed by a stray asteroid? You failed. Dodge it next time. This is what PARTICLE MACE is.
The ships all change the way you move / play in a meaningful and drastic way, which really made me eager to unlock and try them all. The music is amazing (again, friends with the composer), and the game is really nice to look at. The background is awesome to look at. While it can be played on damn near everything, I prefer the controller. If you live in the NYC area, track down the actual arcade cabinet for the best experience.

PARTICLE MACE is a frantic blast of space trash smash'emup action where you will spin it to win it. The elegant movements of your ship are like a ballet of geometrical anarchy. In the same way that games like Nidhogg bring the local multiplayer insanity to the platforming brawler genres, PARTICLE MACE brings the same level of abstract and chaotic couch co-op to the action arcade genre.
The controls and the physics revolving around your cluster of tethered space garbage really hit the nail on the head. There's a serious feeling of weight to the mace you're swinging around as you swerve to each side trying to get it's momentum going, and when you do it feels very natural. There are different ships of different speeds to accommodate each and every play style, ranging from the super slow ship with a large and effective particle mace to the extremely fast and speedy ship with a longer and harder to control mace.
Getting into the groove of the game is a very zen-like experience, becoming lost in the motions of your ship weaving in and out of clusters of asteroids. The movement of your chosen ship feels incredibly fluid and responsive, giving you the edge you need to navigate through the narrowest of passages in-between asteroids and your intimidating red foes.
The multiplayer co-op is where PARTICLE MACE really shines as it isn't just the simple addition of new players on the screen, but features some discoverable techniques like the combining of Maces or the revival of fallen teammates floating by helplessly which will require the full coordination of each participating player.
Even in it's early stages there's already a whole slew of really great modes and options you would expect from a polished full release, including the progressive mission mode which dishes out a series of unique and increasingly harder tasks to take on  that will earn you new ships, à la Luftrausers. Although seemingly simple on the surface, PARTICLE MACE is a huge game with incredible polish and an almost infinite learning curve, making this one hell of an addictive ride to pick up and play for the shortest bursts of play to the longest couch co-op jam sessions.

I will admit it. I'll come out at say it. The finale had me in tears. Before The Walking Dead, I only cried during one video game- "The Last of Us". Now it's two. But that doesn't mean I've still felt a variety of emotions- shock, desperation, mistrust- through playing other games, but this one seems to do especially well at it. The gameplay of TWD is incredibly minimalist. It's a point-and-click game. And normally I despise this genre (except for anything made by Humongous Entertainmen, because they knew what they were doing), but Telltale has not only made me excited to play their second season, they've made me excited to play their entired library of games, because they understand the concept of good story... and good mechanics for a point-and-click game.
Unlike the last of this type of game I played, Ankh 2, you don't have convoluted answers to very simple puzzles. There are no bags of rasberries that attract ants where you have to utlize some fish bones and make the ants carry the bones so a cat will chase down the bones, in this game. A+B=C in this game, which can make people argue, "Well, where's the challenge in THAT!?". Personally, I like games that make sense other than the average point-and-click where A1+A2xB+C(D-E)=F. And also, the real challenge of this game is the decisions you make. A lot of these choices can really make you think and are very morally grey, which I absolutely loved. It's not like other moral-choice systems in games where there are very obviously good and evil choices that make your personality starkly different, but little choices and big ones that effect you, the people around you, and the circumstances you find yourselves in. And these choices have lasting effects in the future episodes. If someone dies, they're dead. If you killed that person, Clementine will see it and it WILL have consequences.
And that's what it all boils down to- the choices are linked together by a wonderful story with a cast of well-written characters. It keeps you emotionally invested and hungry for more, every time you finish an episode. And I wasn't disappointed with the ending, either. The Walking Dead is a must-play for anyone who's tired of games that put gameplay and graphics over the most important aspect in any medium... story.

This is a surprisingly fun little platformer that was a lot deeper than just going from left to right.  At first I was almost put off by the keyboard-only controls, but I used Controller Companion (also on Steam), and bound keys to my Xbox360 gamepad that felt very intuitive to me (stated below), and then the game was fun.  It is so easy to map to a controller, I'm not sure why the dev didn't.  But the game itself is a platformer, has varying difficulty, and decent controls.  I died a number of times early on until I got the hang of it.  At first you probably will not know what you are supposed to do, but just walk around and soon enough you'll be on your way.
It ran well full screen on my Windows 10 Alienware Alpha on a large TV.  It starts in window mode, but you can set it to full screen and restart it.  It is also the first Steam game I have played that runs on Java, so it prompted me to download & install Java.  As such, Controller Companion only sees it as Java when you set up a profile for the bindings, so it cannot have a workshop profile for this game specifically.  But I started the game in windowed mode, opened to the option > bindings, and then had the profile editor up, and set everything.
The bindings I preferred were: A=a (jump), B=b (shoot), X=e (interact), LB=q (prev weapon), RB=w (next weapon), Down=h (mission info), Right=w (next weapon), Left=q (prev weapon), Up=g (gun menu), RT=s (shoot), Start=Esc (menu), Left Stick=Nothing (avoid issue if you click it).
UPDATE: Even though I was playing on easy, I still got stuck on an early boss fight where you had to do some jumping platforming to avoid rising lava while avoiding getting hurt by the boss shooting at you, until you reach the top where the fight begins.  I always ended up with too little life at the top.  It just wasn't fun to keep replaying that part.

I think the main problem people have with this game is they compare it a little too much to and hold it up to the standards of multimillion masterpieces like those that From Software makes. Sure, this game has similar systems to Dark Souls and may remind you of it from time to time, but this is its own game and should be reviewed as such, not how it holds up to the game of another developer.
On its own, the game is moderately entertaining in how it approaches the combat system (which does feel very different than that of a Souls game), but in the end suffers to its lack of enemy variety and formulaic liniarity. After all, I was a little dissapointed to see that the first 2 bosses were guys with shields and swords, a standard knight archetype, and how you will see the same 5-6 enemy variants most of the time in the opening hours. This may or may not improve in the late game, and ill push through to the end to find out, but the goal of a game should be to grab the player's attention early on and maintain that interest, building on its systems and mechanics. Lords of the Fallen fails in this aspect.
Some commendable early-game attractions would be the combat and loot systems. The combat feels much more Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning esque than Dark Souls, be that good or bad is up to you. It feels slightly more fast paced and less methodical than Dark Souls too, giving the impression that this game is a little less about careful life or death combat choices than its counterpart. Though don't take this the wrong way, Lords of the Fallen is still a difficult game and at times, especially during boss fights, you will feel closer to the Dark Souls style of calculated blows and dodges. The loot early on feels a little like a Diablo game. There is plenty of loot (armor, weapons, such) in the first couple levels allowing great customizability in playstyle, especially when it comes to the weapon variants and the variety they give to your approach to combat.

This game follows the trend of being an indie-game with way too hard gameplay. This game is like the quintessential "rogue-like" where literally everything in the game is random. EVERYTHING. Enemy spawns, map-layouts, combat and in the end it is waay too much so. This is a game where in the end-game you can't expect any sort of consistency with success and failure and it always feels like the deck is stacked against you, even when, like me, you've played for 48 hours and is sort of able to take everything into account. Is your attack a hit or miss? About 50%. Will this stun succeed or fail? 50%. Will this debuff succeed or fail? 50%. Will I get stunned? 70%. Will I get hit? 70%. This is what it feels like. Add to that all of the other factors that play into whether you succeed or fail, it's waay too much.
When it's impossible to actually master the game, I feel like asking, well then for what am I playing? This is a tiny indiegame with so little diverse gameplay, it shouldn't take more than 20 hours to complete and even that is too much. Other games that sort of committed this sin: Binding of Isaac, Risk of Rain, Super Meat Boy - the difference is, these games have the added value of having a learning curve that actually flattens at some point and there are successes along the way. Darkest Dungeon doesn't have that and you can't blame yourself for it, because of the sheer randomness.

I honestly tried my best to like this game, but it went out of its way to disgust me.  To begin with, this is perhaps the most poorly optimized game I've ever seen.  The game is massive in terms of data, even more so with the texture pack.  The graphics are fairly dated, but you can still get wild framerate drops on a 1080Ti and a Skylake i7.  The worst part however are the load times.  Even with an SSD, there were times I thought the game had froze because I was getting load times of 90 seconds and up simply walking through doors.
Now lets get to the game itself.  RPG elements are stripped down in favor of FPS gunplay mechanics, which is already straying away from what a Fallout game is about.  The protagonist is no longer silent, which is odd, but it doesn't matter because the story is bland and frankly pretty stupid.  Enemy scaling is all over the place.  It isn't common to start a quest and fight through an area full of snoozefest enemies that die in one shot, only to run into something near the end that is a legendary enemy double your level that can one shot you depending on your build.  And yes, the game will punish you early on if you try for a more interesting build ouside of just trying to Rambo your way through the game.
There is a town building mechanic that is clunky, boring, and completely pointless.  The devs clearly wasted a lot of time and effort on that, and I think it is one of the reasons the rest of the game is a mess.
Oh, and on top of it all paid mods are now a thing, and enabled via a 2GB update.
I got this game during a steam sale, and I deeply regret it.  Go play any other Fallout game instead.

PARTICLE MACE is a frantic blast of space trash smash'emup action where you will spin it to win it. The elegant movements of your ship are like a ballet of geometrical anarchy. In the same way that games like Nidhogg bring the local multiplayer insanity to the platforming brawler genres, PARTICLE MACE brings the same level of abstract and chaotic couch co-op to the action arcade genre.
The controls and the physics revolving around your cluster of tethered space garbage really hit the nail on the head. There's a serious feeling of weight to the mace you're swinging around as you swerve to each side trying to get it's momentum going, and when you do it feels very natural. There are different ships of different speeds to accommodate each and every play style, ranging from the super slow ship with a large and effective particle mace to the extremely fast and speedy ship with a longer and harder to control mace.
Getting into the groove of the game is a very zen-like experience, becoming lost in the motions of your ship weaving in and out of clusters of asteroids. The movement of your chosen ship feels incredibly fluid and responsive, giving you the edge you need to navigate through the narrowest of passages in-between asteroids and your intimidating red foes.
The multiplayer co-op is where PARTICLE MACE really shines as it isn't just the simple addition of new players on the screen, but features some discoverable techniques like the combining of Maces or the revival of fallen teammates floating by helplessly which will require the full coordination of each participating player.
Even in it's early stages there's already a whole slew of really great modes and options you would expect from a polished full release, including the progressive mission mode which dishes out a series of unique and increasingly harder tasks to take on  that will earn you new ships, à la Luftrausers. Although seemingly simple on the surface, PARTICLE MACE is a huge game with incredible polish and an almost infinite learning curve, making this one hell of an addictive ride to pick up and play for the shortest bursts of play to the longest couch co-op jam sessions.

Note: This will be a review of both Darkest Dungeon and Crimson Court - the main game review is first, with thoughts on the expansion later.
Darkest Dungeon kept popping up in my queues but easily got dismissed - I do love turn based, as well as RPG Rougelikes, but it seemed to me to be like the bajillion other retro/pixel graphic games that showed up in my "Discovery Queues". However, I eneded up getting it on a whim since it was on sale for dirt cheap.
Oh my goodness, how wrong I was.
Darkest Dungeon is nothing like the plethora of other hack and slash RPGs you see floating around (and no disservice to those; they're just not my thing). It is, in fact, a very deep, engaging, beautifully created strategy game that challenges you on multiple levels. Not only that, but this thing is so polished you could use it as a mirror in a telescope - every part of the game is so perfectly crafted with love and care that you forget you're playing a game and do really feel like you're trying to take on the world all by yourself.
The atmosphere of the game is wonderful - even the "tutorial" is part of the story. The omnipresent narrator is nothing short of brilliant, and the writer of the dialogue should win an award. Even after playing for many dozens of hours, I'm still excited to hear the narrator say, "Desroy. Them. All." after a hard battle, or to bemoan his prior life's faults.
And don't take "roguelike" to literal. While there is permadeath it's your hereo's that die. Unless you're playing on the hardest difficulty (which imposes a time and death limit) then you can always bounce back. Even if your entire roster is wiped out you can recruit 4 new people and go at it again. So while you're often down, you're never out.
The action is done in a turn-based fashion that emulates a pen and paper type initiative system. I.e., each of your heroes has a "speed" stat, but there's still a roll involved - so someone with a higher speed will not always necessarily go before someone with a lower speed (though you do end up seeing it happen more often than not). One interesting thing here is that turn order is hidden from you.  So while you know who has YET to go, you don't know in what order it will happen (either you or the monsters). Some may not like this but I find it gives the battle, especially "routine" ones, a bit more excitment.
It's hard to say what makes Darkest Dungeon so special. Perhaps it's the unique approach to combat, the simple-yet-complex array of skills and heroes, or the cleverness of the presentation. Whatever it is, it's done to damn near perfect. You can see it in every art asset and every name of a quirk - this game was made with attention to absolutely every detail and by god does it show.
In short, Darkest Dungeon is an absolute joy to play.
For those that may be tricked by the video that auto-plays on Steam's page (like I was), I'll describe the game in more detail. If you've already got a handle on what the game is, scroll down for the Expansion info.
In Darkest Dungeon, you inherit a family estate that is crawling with demonic enemieis. Your goal is to get to the bottom of it (literally) by exploring the various dungeon and killing the baddies within. To do this you recruit a handful of heroes and send them on their quests, with the hope that they live and level up, and become even better heroes. But be careful if they die - they're gone for good.
Your have several classes of heroes to choose from, all with unique skills. Skills are generally aligned into "physical", "bleed", "blight", "buff", and "debuff" and they act exactly how you'd expect. Your heroes, as well as enemies, have certain stats that can both increase the chance of an effect (such as causing an enemy to bleed, resulting in damage over time) as well as provide a resistence to having that effect happen to them, or simply reducing physical damage.
The "Dungeons" are divided into 5 key areas: The Ruins (of your estate) where bad, but mostly humans, dudes dwell. The Cove where evisl fish monsters do their evil fish monster things, the Warrens where malformed pig demons have a taste for more than just slop, and The Weald where a corrupted forest produces all the things you'd expect a corrupted forest to produce. Finally, you have the "Darkest Dungeon" which is, in fact, the darkest and dungeon-ist of them all. Each of these areas has a unique profile, both in enemies and strategy. Each of these dungeons also have bosses in them that proceed the plot (along with various mini-bosses that can show up in any dungeon).
While you're adventuring you'll also have to deal with stress - which comes from simply being in a dungeon filled with hell beasts, enemy attacks, traps, etc.  Stress can cause your heroes to temporarily go insane and even... well, other bad things can happen. The first time it cascades on you, you will actually enjoy watching it happen even though it means you probably just lost a party. Stress is managed from the main estate, where your hereos can drink, screw, pray, or flaggelate their stress away.
If this all sounds like a lot it is - but don't worry! Everything is seamless and intuitive (though it may take you a few clicks to figure out where everything is). The main screen shows your estate and you simply click on the building you want to utilize, drop your hero in, and pay the cost. This brings me to my only critique - the interface. Apparently this started as a console game and so the interface is prettty segregated, meaning it's easy to miss doing something important, like changing your hereo's skills, before you adventure into the dungeon. While a minor annoyance, its is one nonetheless.
EXPANSION:
The Expansion, "The Crimson Court" offers a new class, new enemies, and a new dungeon. The Crimson Court shares the same polish and wit of the original. The art is amazing, the music and sound is amazing, and the narrator still rules. It also introduces new diseases, afflictions, etc. as well as a new resource (blood) you must manage. It certainly enhances the game.
While I am glad I purchased the Crimson Court, it does lack the seamlessness of the original. Perhaps it's simply because I played the original first, but it's easy to tell that Crimson Court is an ADD ON. I.e., it was "dropped into" an existing game that was already 100% whole, so it seems a bit out of place.
Don't take this to mean it isn't fun - it is. It simply highlights how tight the game was before. I've started a new game with it and am enjoying the new class immensely, as well as the added challenge the expansion brings through its new disease/curse.
If you're already a fan of Darkest Dungeon it's worth it, especially on sale. However, if you're unsure of whether this game is your cup of tea, you will not miss anything by simply purchasing the core game. Crimson Court is more ideal for a second play through, in my opinion.

This means that no matter how perfect your strategy is... when you enter
a dungeon there will always be a chance that you'll lose your favorite heroes.
The fear of this happening is always present, and that's what keeps you immersed
at all times.
Pray that lady luck is on your side, and if misfortune does strike you down, it's your job
to get back up and rebuild your team.
Remember not to spread yourself too thin when caring for your heroes. If you don't wish to
go broke you'll have to sacrifice those not worth having their afflictions or diseases cured,
in order to upgrade your favorite heroes and prepare yourself for a risky dungeon.
In short; this game is not for quitters nor dummies. If you're neither of those two, I'm
sure you'll enjoy this game just as much as I did.

But that doesn't mean I've still felt a variety of emotions- shock, desperation, mistrust- through playing other games, but this one seems to do especially well at it. The gameplay of TWD is incredibly minimalist. It's a point-and-click game. And normally I despise this genre (except for anything made by Humongous Entertainmen, because they knew what they were doing), but Telltale has not only made me excited to play their second season, they've made me excited to play their entired library of games, because they understand the concept of good story... and good mechanics for a point-and-click game.
Unlike the last of this type of game I played, Ankh 2, you don't have convoluted answers to very simple puzzles. There are no bags of rasberries that attract ants where you have to utlize some fish bones and make the ants carry the bones so a cat will chase down the bones, in this game. A+B=C in this game, which can make people argue, "Well, where's the challenge in THAT!?". Personally, I like games that make sense other than the average point-and-click where A1+A2xB+C(D-E)=F. And also, the real challenge of this game is the decisions you make. A lot of these choices can really make you think and are very morally grey, which I absolutely loved. It's not like other moral-choice systems in games where there are very obviously good and evil choices that make your personality starkly different, but little choices and big ones that effect you, the people around you, and the circumstances you find yourselves in. And these choices have lasting effects in the future episodes. If someone dies, they're dead. If you killed that person, Clementine will see it and it WILL have consequences.
And that's what it all boils down to- the choices are linked together by a wonderful story with a cast of well-written characters. It keeps you emotionally invested and hungry for more, every time you finish an episode. And I wasn't disappointed with the ending, either. The Walking Dead is a must-play for anyone who's tired of games that put gameplay and graphics over the most important aspect in any medium... story.

Osmos is a puzzle game where you control an orb that absorbs smaller orbs, usually with the goal of becoming large, but movement makes you smaller. It's a good concept with a lot of applications, but it falls flat in execution.
I'll get this out of the way first: the music is ambient background noise. Nothing stunning or impressive as claimed. It's boring.
The controls are simple: click to fire in a direction, propelling you the other way. Firing and propelling are both important, and this is well-explored. However, most of the game's obstacles are exercises in patience. You'll often be left waiting for collisions to happen or for obstacles to move, and you'll wait for a long time, even on maximum speed. But if you wait too long, the level sometimes becomes unwinnable. Most levels are randomly generated, and I think the fun factor suffers as a result.
I got this with Humble Indie Bundle 3, and it's not a bad add-in. I couldn't recommend it at anything over $1 on its own, though.

"The Walking Dead" is, by far, the best choose your own adventure style game that I have played since "Heavy Rain" was released. This comparison is fairly accurate, as both games allow the player to make major decisions that completely change the course of events in the narrative. Who lives and dies? That's up to the player. Who gets to join your group? Again, a choice which is left largely up to the player. It's worth noting that, while many key decisions in the game are left up to the player, no decision is without consequences. The game does a great job of making you feel like your choices are important, because they are.
Additionally, "The Walking Dead" tells a fantastic story! Its the kind of story that keeps you going forward to find out what happens next. The writers have done a great job of making you feel for every character you meet. You'll hate some, love others, even be annoyed by a select few. However, the choice of how you react to them and deal with them is largely up to you, the player. I can not stress enough how much I enjoyed the storyline and the personalities which populated it.
The only thing that may put a few people off is the scare factor. The game is by no means a horror movie, but it does have it's share of jump scares and the overall tone of the game is one of danger around every corner. Although, if you are looking into a zombie game, you're probably fine with that. The game holds about the same scare factor as "Resident Evil" on the Playstation 1, but with far better storyline. Additionally, these scenes all make sense within the narrative and don't feel like a cheap scare tactic. If you have ever seen "The Walking Dead" television series, you should know what I'm referring to. The game can also be a very dark in certain spots, as it deals with desperate people trying to survive. However, the player is allowed to take the moral highroad in nearly all situations if they so desire.
Overall, "The Walking Dead" is a fantastic gaming experiance! If you find yourself on the fence about playing this game, play it!

The music was fairly good, the controls were solid, and the art design is servicable - you'll never get lost in the stage (visually) and all but 1 danger are clear and easily seen (one enemy shot is very small, and fades into the last stage's background fairly easily, especially if you've upgraded your main gun). At $.50, the game is well worth it. At $5, it's much more iffy. Catch it on a sale. 8/10
The Full: The plot is an excuse - early on, you run afoul of The Man and go to jail - never comes up again. Medical supplies are tampered with, but no one mentions it outside of The Plot, and the planetary government doesn't seem to care. There are 2 dudes who mess with you regularly, and you aren't ever sure why (Odds are good they work for the big bad, but that doesn't really get confirmed one way or another)
None of this matters, you are here to run, jump, and blow [expletive] up - and, oh lords, can you! You can control quite a bit of where you go, both on the ground and in the air, the jumps feel good, and while some jumps are a little tricky, none of them are frustrating (the game tends to fall on the "too easy" side of things in it's platforming). Biggest difficulty is keeping yourself under control while firing (all your guns have kickback that will move you a little. When using a rapid gun, like your main one, this can add up if you don't pay attention). Also, you input gets cut when you move from screen to screen. For example, you may cross a screen, stop dead, fire at an enemy, and be knocked back into the previous screen - this can get frustrating. Also kicks in after cut scenes - holding the firing button as the boss loads won't let you start firing the minute you get control, you have to re-press the button.
On the "blow things up" measure, you do have a lot of options, some of which are very fun...but you probably won't use them. Firstly, you can win without ever switching out the main weapon to fight. It's hard, but do-able. There were only a few bosses that even made me think of switching up. Further, there are 3 types of ammo, so you don't really want to use all of the guns you are given. Ammo isn't exactly hard to find, but it can be a big deal if you run out of one type (and it isn't hard to do so, with certain weapons). For example, you get a rocket launcher, a "frag" gun, and a grenade launcher - all use "red" ammo. You will almost never use the frag gun - it's half as powerful as the rocket launcher, and there just aren't that many times when you want to put out a massed number of weak shots.
The Pulsar is twice as powerful as your main gun, but you'll mostly use your main to conserve ammo. If you want more oomph, you'll go to a better gun that doesn't suck ammo like a kid at a soda shop - the rocket launcher, for example, or the Ultimate Destroyer. Same problem with the Wave Gun and the Laser - too much ammo eaten for the damage dealt.
Don't get me wrong, a lot of the guns are fun - a lot of fun - but you just aren't going to have the ammo to play around with most of them a lot of the time, and when you Need a special weapon, the rocket launcher is almost always the best bet, unless you have side case - using the Hydro gun to shoot through a wall, for example, the Grenade launcher for indirect fire and traps, or the flame thrower to burn a bone pile.
Musically, half the stages are merely meh, while one or two are pretty nice, and the rest fall in-between. Nothing is particularly painful, and everything is servicable. I consider the sound effects to be fairly good, if a little loud.
Replay-wise, this game doesn't have a lot going for it - there isn't enough challenge to make a replay satisfying, there aren't enough secrets to make a completionist re-run it (without really trying, I cleared 95% of the game's hidden/side bits. Just have to figure out what to do with one item).
Time to cost, the game is probably worth $5 bucks, but I do recommend taking it on a sale - there wasn't anything really spectacular about the experience, and 4 hours to clear the main game just isn't a great return. Definitely better than a movie ticket, though.

I received the game key for free from the designer on Reddit and I'd like to offer my impressions on this game. After playing for a bit under an hour here is what I have to say: the game is visually appealing and it's easy to understand/read what is on the playing field even in the most crowded scenes. The color palette and the mostly black background really help with that. Because of this, all the obstacles are clearly visible and that can be very helpful when pulling off more complicated moves. Players can learn a bunch of things from experimenting with the mechanics: how to move between planets, how to use a planet's gravity to propel yourself, how to fall/land with some grace and so on. Actually, I'm quite fond of physics-based games (Besiege, Poly Bridge, Turbo Dismount, Kerbal Space Program and etc) and SLI-FI features nice use of gravity/orbit in a platforming environment. Considering it is still in beta, there's a lot of potential to grow the game in different directions. I don't know if this is in the plans, but adding mutators (in the style of Unreal Tournament, like altered gravity, doubled movement speed, explosive objects and so on) and user-created levels/skins/challenges would be an awesome addition. The music is nice and there's a subtle touch I love: when you're out of orbit between planets the percussion fades and comes back only when you reach a planet. That amplifies the suspense of "will I make that jump or will I float away into space?". The game features co-op, but I have yet to try it. TL;DR - Cool game with room to grow, physics-based gameplay, easy to understand and very accessible.

Hacknet is a great gem of a game. Its primary function is to be a portable 'hacker simulator' and to that extent, it does that quite well. A genre naturally suited for the typing and point-clicking games, hacking inside hacknet, is devoid of large explosions or the rejoice of having brought the world to its knees. It seeks to measure achievement in a world, where humans speak through machines and asking the right question open doors.
The games' mechanics work on using time and resource allocation, as well relying on the curiosity of the player; who with his magical key, is capable of accessing anyone's cyberspace and playing god, to that extent. Despite this rather dramatic description, the game is mostly that, drama, as it exists between people, mediated through technology. The player is the central arbitrator. Good Story line, would be nice if it was extended, as the gamut of technology topics covered is not really as broad as could be.
In sum: not a bad way to spend a weekend at home.

Black Squad is one of the better fps games you'll find and one of the best fps that's free to play. There isn't too much pay to win (the pay to win part is just for buying cases like in CS:GO). All weapons are accessible by playing the game and not paying but paying makes it easier for you to get weapons. Black Squad is also fair with their reward system. The controls on the game are mostly familiar from other fps games but some of the controls aren't similar or the most comfortable to use like the sensitivity. The third way is a clan match where your clan goes against another. The last way hasn't been played by me so I can't say much about it. Black Squad is better than most people think and I recommend that you play it if you are into playing fps for free.

This was an incredible game, and I highly recommend it to everyone, especially if you're familiar with or want to learn the UNIX command line (bash).
Hacknet is very well-paced, slowing down and allowing you to "explore" at times while keeping a sense of urgency throughout. At times there will be a ticking clock on screen depending on what you're hacking into, but this is my first gripe with the game: the seconds are never consistent from machine to machine. Sometimes it's 3 seconds per on-screen second, sometimes it's a millisecond per on-screen second. I wish there had been a little more consistency here, because it does take time to figure out exactly how long you have before something bad happens.
Other than the timers, this game really was well-thought-out. And after one playthrough, you can go back and do it again, because
. It's also a great puzzle game. I was initially frustrated by how vague some of the instructions were, but I quickly realized that's by design. You're given an endgoal, but you have to figure out exactly what steps to take to make it there. It also helps that many of your missions can be picked from a list, allowing you to either take an easy or hard case, depending on how you feel, without affecting the story.
I really can't recommend this game enough, and I can't wait for the DLC that's about to come out!

A very introspective look at UNIX commands and the general actions of hacking - which is basically accurate, but taking out the time required to accomplish these things (for example, you can solve port protocols within a few seconds, but IRL this might take hours).
Basically, if you want the "reality" where you are the hacker in one of these movies (you're not playing the hacker, but ARE the hacker), then this is pretty spot-on. It just removes most of the tedium of the acitivites. This is not to say that the game isn't repetitive; it is, and remains true to its roots as a simulator. By nature, most simulators run off of repetitive actions which require muscle memory and timing in order to complete.
In actual fact, this is more of a puzzle-solving game. However, combined with some funny easter eggs (IRC chats can get hilarious) and honest-to-god methodology on the principles of hacking, this actually becomes enjoyable unless you just want to shoot things in the face (in which case, this is NOT the game for you).
Anyone who wants to work in software QA should be able to play this game comfortably, figure out most of the puzzles, and genuinely enjoy the experience. If you can't, don't take QA as a career. Because this in almost any form is what you do - all day, every day. I know this from 14 years of experience at that job in everything from game development to SAS or security software.
There are a few points I wish there were more of, or more developed. As game, it's pretty linear. There are nice little things like finding additional information on a server which gives you another terminal to hack, or a phone to break into, but these are too few and far between. It could be far more sandboxy if there were a freeform mode for points, which had sets of systems and connected devices which would allow you to randonly investigate things you found on another system. In this, you'd need a points system or something to gain (money, cred, whatever) - which would be a welcome addition to the game. I think another fun mode would be to actually use the system specs for the computer it was running on for memory, etc. as well as randonly generating in-game groups to become involved with, do missions for (from forums, etc.)
I recommend this game, just due to the simulation nature being captured very well. That being said, this game won't be for everyone. Much of the game is tedium and random investigation - which is exactly what hacking is about. One of the best missions which represents this is the "Project Junebug" mission. You're basically let loose to figure out how to accomlish the task, you have a lot of reading to do to catch up on how to accomplish it, and there isn't any handholding. YOU have to do the tasks, to the best of your understanding, and figure out indeed, what those tasks are, and it involves multiple servers, and different methods of having the same outcome.

Darkest Dungeon has a warning before the main title screen of the game. In essence it says "The game has been balanced around the idea that the odds are always stacked against you, and the aim is to figure out how you're going to get around that trial to succeed." So it does warn you, "hey,♥♥♥♥♥♥s not gonna be easy yo, make sure you have your big boy pants on."
I like this game, well, I liked it until about five minutes ago where I had yet another expierience that has finally convinced me to write a review.
Darkest Dungeon succeeds in breeding an atmosphere that affects you in the real world. I've had two panic attacks palying this game. I've gotten as salty- no actully MORE salty about the mechanics in this game than I ever did playing League of Legends and I've QUIT that game indefinitely after almost 5 years of play.
The odds are so stacked against you that even when you KNOW how the game works, you still get ♥♥♥♥ed by RNG. For instance today, after prepping for a long scout mission I closed the game. It saved all my selections EXCEPT what dungeon I had picked. I close the game to go eat lunch, jumped back on, ran through provisioning and hit go... ONLY TO REALIZE IT RESET MY DUNGEON PICK AND AUTOSELECTED A BOSS DUNGEON.
I've dropped 5k on supplies, I have a super tanky, low DPS team becasue it was supposed to be a scout mission I was using as a money run! So now I'm loaded into a prophet fight with no chance of beating him and I'm confronted with the option of "Back out now, lose 5k in supplies, another 3k in stress treatment, and be down 4 party members a week" OR "Stick it out and try."
I say ♥♥♥♥ it, lets try. Dungeon is going fine, not that hard a run. Until, after camping and walking down the hall the boss, I get ambushed and proceed to be crit 6 TIMES IN A ROW by two different arbalests. Two of my guys are half health, one is at 70 stress, I'm ♥♥♥♥ed. Might as well try to tank the boss fight, its not a hard one, I have the tanks needed.
Prophet Fulminates twice, and Rubbles once. All three attacks are crits. I lose 4 people in the span of two rounds of combat to♥♥♥♥♥♥deathblow resist rolls. Queue my second panic attack. I'm done. I'm done with this game.
For people that like being mildly rewarded for high stakes combat with mechanics that either love you or hate you depending on the day, this game is for you. For anyone else that isn't into that, don't bother. (PS this was on the easiest difficulty setting, Radiant, which doesn't actually affect the actual combat at all. ♥♥♥♥ this game.)

Ask yourself which of these two things is more dangerous:
1.) Four skeletons wielding rusty swords
2.) Four skeletons who are trying very hard to spook you
Now ask yourself which of these two parties sounds more effective in combat:
1.) A healer, a crossbowman, a berserker, and a tank
2.) A healer, a jester, and two crusaders spamming stress relief spells in combat
If you answered #1 to either of these questions, you will be frustrated by this game, which firmly believes that stress is the most powerful force in the universe, and that human beings have to go to incredible lengths to avoid having heart attacks during tasks that they have performed dozens of times in the past.
The "Stress" mechanic in Darkest Dungeon is like a secondary health bar for each party member, except it's infinitely more important than health and really you can just ignore health altogether if you have a single healer and a couple sturdy frontline types.
Just about everything in the game causes unmitigateable Stress to your party. Triggered a trap? Take 20 stress. Spend too long in a dungeon? 2-3 stress every minute or so. Get hit by a crit? Haha, 15 stress for you. This is all on top of the many, many enemies that eschew damage completely in favor of dealing Stress damage directly to your party. These are the high priority targets in combat, because stress is more dangerous in the short AND long term than stab wounds.
The difference between gaining Stress and losing health is that when your character reaches 100 Stress, he/she will gain a random insanity trait for the foreseeable future, and will be a massive liability until he/she is mercifully killed. They will spend every one of their turns in combat causing even more unpreventable Stress damage to their allies, they will refuse to do what you tell them, and they will spout hundreds of lines of custom "insane" dialogue to let you know that this game is edgy and acknowledges that people can be crazy sometimes, or something.
If you make the mistake of not loading your party with crusaders and jesters (who have the only stress relief abilities in the game) you can also abandon a quest at any time and send the whole party back to camp, but this will severely stress them (because they didn't want to be in the dungeon, but they also didn't want to leave?)
At 200 Stress, your useless party member will have a heart attack. This is the best option, since treating their mental illness is far, far, FAR more tedious and expensive than recruiting a new party member.
No, you can't just send a single insane party member home. That's unrealistic, apparently.
Speaking of realism, it's very immersive that there is no turn order indicator in combat. This way, you never know who's going to get a turn. It's probably going to be the one enemy with the super powerful Stress attack, and he'll probably get two consecutive turns for some reason even though his Speed stat is pitiful, but that's your fault for not knowing he could do that. This game is revolutionary; a masterpiece of mechanics.
Nevermind that all the characters' stats and mission rewards are listed clearly in every menu; turn order is where the line apparently HAS to be drawn for realism. If you know what's going on, you're just not going to have fun, so the game keeps you in the immersive fog of not knowing whose turn it is, or if turns are maybe just randomized every time or something.
And it's even more immersive that your strong party members will refuse to go on low-level missions. So, despite the game being so proud of its disregard for party member progression, it harshly punishes you for getting new party members, since your experienced veterans will outright REFUSE to help your rookies get acclimated, because this game is a revolutionary edgy dark realistic fantasy experience for adults.
There are a lot of other fun and fair mechanics you should know about, but this review is too long.

Coming from a longtime 2K Sports fan, I have mixed feelings on this entry of NBA2K. However, just because I have it not recommended I suggest you read the entire review to see if you would like it.
I am not going to get into day one issues like crashes, bugs, and server issues because frankly basing a review off that this early before they can fix things is stupid. But there are issues I PERSONALLY have with the game. But I'll say a few things this game offers over 2K15 first.
These were a few off the top of my head I was pleased with.
However, as I mentioned before I had a huge gripe with this game. In my personal opinion they seem to have taken a step back when it comes to MyCareer. Others apperently like it but I was extremely disappointed by the fact the "story" was stereotypical, thoughtless and not enjoyable. I expected more from Spike Lee & 2K. So with giving us an actual story (if you want to call it that) they severely limited how we can play. This isn't OUR story. It is Freq's story. Yes the protagonist has a name and even if you had a simple name like Joe Johnson they will still say Freq regardless. You do not have a choice to be called something else like in previous MyCareers (my personal choice was "Silky" Johnson) If you want to play a white, asian, hispanic or really any race that isn't black you have to suspend your disbelief that your family is black and you are not. To make matters worse you have a fraternal twin sister so you really cant think your mom cheated on your dad either. You can't win Rookie of the Year because you can only play a few games in your rookie season. The "story" is insanely short, badly written, predictable, pointless and a waste of time. They took away more of our choices and options so they could waste our time with that?
You may be saying, but wait! Didn't they let you play through high school and college? That sounds fun. At first yes it was interesting to just destroy the high school competition and finally see some college basketball, but its exactly the same as a normal game just reskinned. You only play a few games of high school and a few of college then you get drafted. And after a handful of years MyCareer has been out, THEY STILL HAVENT ADDED A REACTIVE DRAFT. Meaning if you get drafted first, guess what? The Timberwolves get two number one picks. You and Karl Anthony-Towns. So the draft is basically pointless because it's always the same even though you are in it no matter what your position is. Sucks for you if you play PF and you get drafted first because you're gonna share minutes with a guy who shouldn't even be on the team. Teams won't draft based on needs either apparently, in fact its hard to say for sure what they'll draft on. But if you're a center for example expect Detroit, Utah, Sactown, and Orlando to want to draft you even if they have a franchise center because why not. Same for playing any other position, they will draft you regardless. They should have just placed the MyGM/MyFranchise draft AI into MyCareer so we could get SOME chance of being surprised even if they arent that great as well.
Once the story ends, its basically MyCareer as last year.
I feel so ashamed of 2K and Spike to have made this game mode such a huge selling point of the game. If you are considering getting the game because of MyCareer, do not get the game.
The other gamemodes are solid, if you can can see past the cheesers, hackers, etc in online modes you'll have a lot of fun in ProAm, MyTeam and other game modes. Personally I play mostly MyLeague/MyGM and I enjoy it throughly even though I was hyped to play MyCareer. The relocation aspect of MyLeague/GM was sorely needed in previous entries and they finally added it and its actually good and not bare bones. You can upload images to use as the team's logo, court logo, advertisements, arena name. You can edit the court exactly how you want it, all black if you want to. You can also do this in online modes, create your own team and court which is what it needed. The animations are fluid and smooth. They changed the passing mechanics a bit and a few of the controls so it's an adjustment. Still slightly disappointed that 2K still hasnt revamped the draft prospect aspect of League/GM because its still extremely generic. They could at least pull a Madden and give the prospects a storyline and allow us to actually grow attached or get hyped for a prospect. I was also going to say they could give the random generated prospects faces but they still use the team jersey portraits (say if you trade Damian Lillard it changes from showing his real life counterpart to some nasty ultra low settings doppelganger) so there goes that.
Overall however, aside from MyCareer its what you can expect from a yearly sports game release.

I should start by saying that I enjoyed this game. It is very short, it only took me 13 minutes to complete, but still worth your time, if only to get an idea for how this developer would make a full length game.
There isn't any story explaination at all. All you know is you are guiding a small, white, grape-shaped creature through a strange environment that appears to be a combination of the inside of a tree and, what appears to be, a hotel for insects and small robots.
Graphically speaking, this game has some interesting and beautiful visuals. It started with a sense of awe that I couldn't shake until the game was finished.
You do not directly control the character, but rather you manipulate the enviroment to help its progression through the game. Your charge seems to know exactly where to stop and wait for you and where to go next, as if by instinct or memory.
A lot is implied, or perhaps I assumed, about the character and the story. It's a shame there wasn't more to it, but for a free game, I don't feel like my time was wasted. If anything, it just made me seek out the developer to see what they would do next.
By the way, the same developer is actually realeasing a full length game called
It follows Purseus the Dog and Professor Gagayev (a monkey) as they explore the universe. Given how this game turned out, I'd say it's worth the time checking out their demo.

Wallet over gameplay like so many other games today means this will be a temporary game that will dwindle away.

It is obvious that Trove has become too greedy in its shop changes and terrible in its implemented game design.
-This is surprisingly not the biggest problem with Trove right now.-
Ever since Live, you can see the gap of meaningful content production correlates to your player numbers dropping. Meaningful content defined as adventure world updates (combat, quests and dungeons), crafting, and building.
[MONEY]
I also fear that any game that you can spend hundreds ($300+ personally) on isn't enough to get everything. While somehow the devs claim that there isn't any incentive to develop and update a system unless a price tag is directly on that feature.
But Trove does have incentive to update content and classes. That's what everything else in the cash shop was for. The devs clearly don't understand that though.
[CLASS COST CHANGE]
Classes didn't need to be pay for only. There was plenty in the store and $20 packs people were buying including myself to keep the game going strong. And those packs are filled with items players made giving devs the free time to make content. The devs didn't even hold up their end.
[FORCED GAME PLAY]
Another problem is that Mantle of Power essentially divides the community. Not because of power or even RNG, but because of Shadow Tower itself. We thought Shadow Tower was going to do that before until the community found out how to avoid it entirely since it had nothing to do with the adventure world. But MoP was designed to force it to be an integral part of the game to advance. Its promises of adding more abilities and content is just a cosmetic paint job for both with no real substance.
We waited a year for the same worlds only with gaps in between dungeons and a gear RNG that makes no sense but to put lucky/rich players in a different league from everyone else.
[SAYING ONE THING, DOING THE OPPOSITE]
This leads to the biggest problems which is the devs' two-faced policy. That may be a cruel thing to say but it is an honest criticism that the devs must face. "We don't want too much RNG into the game." Gems. "We want to feel like players are progressing." Nerf then add new stuff to farm to regain that lost power. Actions entirely money driven. Ever since the game went live the team has done an about-face to meaningful content production.
It has stopped growing and instead added money dependent systems without doing anything substantial as thanks. Remember the content added thanks to dragon caches in the shop? What about making classes credit only? MoP is a result of that, asking you to spend more money not for cosmetics but for numbers that mean nothing.
They didn't lose money because of these decisions, but because of the lack of decisions to advance adventure world and building content. The things this game was founded on.
[LEFTOVER POPULATION DEPENDENCY]
You are losing players from such greedy decisions in every system you add to Trove. To think where we would be if the number of players that Live and Steam added to the game stayed. This would have come to be if the dev team kept their Alpha and Beta momentum and kept advancing the content rather than pack in cash grab only systems. You would have had a large enough population to keep your pockets full while providing more content that is fun to play and not grind intensive. Including new classes and more abilities to former ones.
[RETURN TO A FORM OF RESPECT]
Despite that gap that dropped your population to a petty fraction, you still have a chance to return to the team that your were in Beta. You have enough money systems to make this game last a lifetime, so cut out the gem RNG and stick back to making money on the $20 packs and cosmetics (that players are making for you) and focus on actual content from here on out. Content development that people were brought into the game for in the first place.
[[TL ; DR]]
Think about how big Trove was in its first Live month and why. Its because of everything up to that point and none of anything that followed. Make your players happy as a priority, because that was how you were making your money.
And kill extreme RNG.

I've read a lot of stories about how "broken" this game is and to be honest, with how polished previous games were, I just couldn’t believe that this would be any different, regardless of the news stories. However after several hours of play time of both co-op and single player, I can handily say that this game is unfinished.
While not "broken" anymore, this game is far from finished. The most noticeable would be the free running. In the most recent AC games, free running felt fluid and extremely responsive and each game was progressively more polished. However AC: Unity is a leap in the opposite direction. I felt like I was back to AC 1, and perhaps the beta of AC 1. I would go in opposite directions I wanted, I would jump off ledges when I didn’t, and when I wanted to jump of ledges (even when I knew I would take damage) the game just wouldn’t let me for a good two or three seconds. While that’s not a lot, while free running its excruciating and a real game breaker in a game revolving around free running.
The controls are obviously made for the console and this feels like a mediocre port at best, while the constant advertisements to spend extra money really kept the emersion into the game to a minimum.
Onto the graphics! The game really shows how it is rushed in this respect. With everything set to ultra-high, the game looks like it was made in 2009. Hands, body parts, and weapons blatantly go through clothing, time was obviously not taken when it came to hair on any characters main or not. And it is easy to see the seams in between two physical objects (showing the sky underneath). The draw distance is horrid, you can easily see characters clothing change right in front of you as the computer renders them into a higher resolution.
I must say, that the story line so far has been intriguing, though not ground breaking. This game just feels like you need to use a bulldozer to get through when free running requires a delicate touch. Assassins Creed: Unity should still be in beta for another good three months before they should think about releasing it. I would gladly wait longer to get a polished game. Wait a half year before buying. I have lost a lot of respect for UbiSoft. I dont blame the developers for making this game so horrid, I blame the company for not giving the developers enough time to do their damn jobs.

I don't like to give poor reviews, especially for one of my favorite game genres, but I'm afraid I really can't recommend this one. Havn't played long but don't think I'll play more so I'm leaving my thoughts, feel free to take that in to consideration.
cons:
-Wants to use the keyboard, cannot access to manu with a controller, controller support is poor; forces you to use the analogue stick for movement making it really sloppy to control and since it's not made for a controller there is one set jump height(we've had better since nintendo..).
-Can only fire in the four cardinal directions with your basic gun.
-The story setup is just amateurish. I'm ok with next to no story in a game but this one, at least at the start, is just silly; I'd have rather just been dropped in the field with a memo of whatever's happening. You're also given poor direction; only when you exhaust your places to go do you come to the conclusion your ship is not parked in town but instead all by itself on the other end of a monster-infested cave, because, your character is as indifferent to that kind of thing as he is to being set up and imprisoned.
-No map I could find, at least at the start.
-No way of knowing what pits you can jump down and which insta-kill you; I'm not really used to instant death environmental hazzards in metroidvanias either.
-I don't mind pixel graphics but these were rather rough; I suppose that's a matter of personal preference, though.
pros:
-Nice looking and laid out environments.
-Really good music.
-Looks like a nice big inventory of guns to find.
Hopefully they work out some of these shortcomings and streamline things because I think it's got potential; if and when that happens I'll be the first one back to give it another try.

Many of you are looking for a new place to call home right? You've seen Black Squad and you're skeptical about leaving your main game to come and shoot some melons here aren't you. I'm here to completely reassure you and to let you know that when you join Black Squad, you will not be wasting your time, not at all.
I was highly skeptical upon hearing about the game and I immedaitely put on my detective outfit and jumped straight onto youtube to look at videos of it. "Hm, yeah, doesn't look too bad, yeah, yeah.." And so the game was downloaded.
Upon arrival in the game I was slightly overwhelmed with the UI as I found the inbox system where you receive mail/rewards was made much more difficult than it really needed to be. The UI in general was a bit meh but after an hour you get used to it and think nothing of it, so don't worry. As a strict F2P player I scouted around the regular shop which contains bits and bobs that you buy with the currency you obtain through just playing the game. I then hopped into the 'Medal Shop' where the donator items are. I compared the same gun models from the regular shop to the gun of the same name/type etc to the medal shop. It's comforting to know that the guns you get from donating(BS/BULLETS) are
the same as the ones in the regular shop.
. But of course it is obvious that if you for example didn't have an AK47 in your inventory, and you bought the AK47 Legendary with 10k BS coins then you will get the gun with the skin.
I was very pleased when I hopped into my very first match and I loved the simplistic look the UI has, apart from the character you've equipped in the bottom right, that's very pointless and shouldn't be there whatsoever. I ran around copped a few kills and noticed the recoil on guns are actually fun. I was using the ARX and absolutely hated it because I can't control the damn thing with this horrible £10 office mouse.
I played for some hours and managed to rack up enough medals (you get them through leveling up and opening crates which you also get from leveling up) so I bought an AK47, of course. I thought it'd be easier to use the AK47 as I thought it was the OP gun (it somewhat is) however it does require skill.
guns require some level of skill to use and not every gun will be for you. Everything feels fluid all the way from the satisfying crunching sounds of when you get a headshot, to standing on a claymore and flopping out like a dead fish.
In conclusion, I strongly recommend that you put this game on download and investing a good few levels into it (at least SGT R4) so you can get a feel for the game properly with all modes etc. I haven't seen any PW2 aspects whatsoever in my hours played because donating money into the game will only give you cosmetic rewards such as skins, characters etc. I currently have had no problems with lag in the EU servers as I live in the UK and my ping has always comfortably sat at 38-45.

Lords of the Fallen is a weird one. It’s obvious that devs ware targeting fans of Souls games as their main demographic. While in reality the only people who could possibly fully enjoy this game are those who have played none of the Dark Souls games(yes, even DS2).
I think this because, LotF copies almost every single gameplay mechanic from Souls games, which in itself isn’t bad, but unfortunately whenever a new mechanic was introduced all I was able to think about was “Hmmm, Dark Souls did this much better”.
The only positive thing I can say about this game is that it made me appreciate how well designed the original Souls games actually are.
For the first half of the game combat felt very clunky and slow. Some of it is because every weapon is slower than its equivalent in Dark Souls, probably because devs wanted every attack feel heavier and meatier, but I think that they overshot their goal and made it too slow. It just feels bad.
Later on I adapted to LotF speed, but it still wasn’t a great gaming experience.
LotF is also a perfect example that graphics aren’t everything. On the technical side this game has top notch visuals. All the effects are there - lighting, physics etc. The only place where it fails is the esthetic. It’s just soooooooooooo generic. Every piece of armor is covered spikes and random fantasy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Same goes for weapons. Devs probably just wanted every piece of gear look crazy and “cool”, but if there is no progression “boring” regular weapons to fantasy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t(and I don’t mean that in a negative way), then the “cool” stuff doesn't feel special. If everything is special nothing is.
All enemies are forgettable as ♥♥♥♥, both visually and how they interact with you. So are the bosses. I will forget each and every one of them really quick.
There’s no nuance to anything.

As a fan of fallout games, it really is unfortunate that I have to write this review. I have hundereds of hours in this series, 590 in Fallout 4 and roughly 800 hours in Fallout New Vegas (with tale of two wastelands, to play Fallout New Vegas and 3 in the same game) and can say that it is one that while Fallout 4 was not a bad game, the practices of Bethesda in regard to the Creation Club and their audacity to release microtransactions into a game with a surpringly lacking Season's Pass truly displays Bethesda's opinion of their user base. The entire reason that many PC gamers, myself included, moved to this platform is for the ability to use mods to improve the overall experience of the game. I know that Bethesda recognizes the impact that modding has had on their games, they stated that the giveaway of Skyrim: Enhanced Edition on PC was a gesture of appreciation to the modding community that kept Skyrim, a game released in 2011, fresh and interesting with a mix of graphics, story, and mechanics mods. The Creation Club is an example of unoriginal, cash grab style content that contradicts Bethesda's statements about not enacting paid mods, a scandal that originally occured when they attempted to impliment a similar style program on Skyrim's modding community. Furthermore, even if the Creation club offered anything more that reskins of pip boys and worse versions of already free content, the attempt to charge users for mods is a dangerous trend that, if not entirely rejected in the fullest form here, may spill over into the habits of other gaming companies following Bethesda's example. I refuse to ever support a company that acts in such a way. Prey looks like an interesting game, but I won't touch it with a 10 foot pole because of the implimentatoin of the Creation club. I won't ever be able to get excited for a new Elder Scrolls or Fallout title again.
