What can I say about Lords of the Fallen? Well if you like Dark Souls you'll probably like this and if you don't like Dark Souls? You'll still probably like it.
Graphically this game is wonderful. The setting is beautiful, the environments are well rendered. Enemy design is pretty unique (Especially the bosses) and whoever designed the armour and weapons deserves some kind of trophy because the gear in this game looks absoloutely amazing.
Speaking of gear, it's very important in this game. Unlike Dark Souls where you pile your souls in to your stats and gear gives you a minimal boost at best, the gear in LoTF is essential to completing whatever build you feel like going for. That brings me to the first negative of the game, build flexibility. There isn't much in the way of build flexibility here, You'll either go Faith (Magic) Strength (Heavy user) or Agility (Rogue-like) With not much room for creating hybrids. Hybrid builds don't really become a viable or worthwhile option until new game plus.
The game has a story but it is barely there to be honest with you. It's interesting and I'd love to know more about it but if you focus solely on that side of the game you'll find yourself feeling a bit dissapointed by the end. Though while the story seems to be a bit lack-luster, the characters themselves are pretty damn good though some of the interactions between your character (Harkin) And others will leave you scratching your head and feeling like you missed something (You didn't miss something, it's just that Harkin and some characters seem to have a history that's never explained)
Combat. Combat is very, very similar to Dark souls with stamina management being a huge part of the game. While the combat doesn't feel as deep as Dark Souls combat it's still very entertaining if not an easier version of what a souls fan would be used to. The main takeaway in combat is the bosses. In souls-like games those are the fights that give a true test of the combat system.
It's good, but no great. Even in light armour everything feels very clumbsy and slow but it's not an overall bad thing. If you're coming from the souls games then it's going to take a bit of getting used to when it comes to the face of these boss fights (Some can take a while due to the clunky nature of movement and combat) But if you're coming in fresh having not played a game of this type before you likely won't notice it like I did.
Though I will say I enjoyed the game thoroughly and can't wait to see what the developers do next (Hopefully more souls-like games) I highly recommend picking this up as you'll get plenty of hours of playtime from it and speedrunning (If you're in to that) Can be a very viable option, just not as flexible as the soulsborne games.

XCOM 2 is a great leap forward, bringing a classic franchise to par with all the new AAA titles coming out in 2016. Everything that was annoying in the first "new" XCOM was fixed or removed, and anything that was awesome was improved even further. From basic combat mechanics, through incredible character customisation (which made me actually care for my soldiers) and great range of both familiar and new enemies.
The game is a gem to every turn-based strategy lover, and its graphical fidelity surpasses many mainstream first person shooters (and every console game in existence). With interesting (but not too deep) plot, and immersive gameplay XCOM drags you into a world dominated by so-called "Elders" - an acient alien race wandering through the galaxy, conquering countless worlds in pursuit of new spiecies to "cure".
You ever get this "one more turn" feeling?
Then prepare for the new "one more mission" complusive disorder, cause XCOM won't just let you leave.
XCOM 2 is a must-have for any strategy fans, and DLCs add a little bit of content (not a huge lot, by no means neccessary to fully enjoy the game itself, but provide some re-play value).

OK, lot of negitive reviews recently, so I want to set the record straight; Darkest Dungeon is a great game; it might not be to your tastes, you might be completely unlucky and get an unplayable buggy mess, but it is objectively a great game, for the following reasons:
First, it went above and beyond with it's polish; many other reviewers state that it's starts off great, and that's because is sucks you in with it's premise, with little to distract you from the game or take you out of the story. It's 2D hand-drawn sprites are of high quality, the music is varied and compelling, and the mechanics, from the combat to the base management, are all done with a attentiveness to detail that elevate Darkest Dungeon into a top tier steam game.
Second, its difficulty is harsh, but fair. Comparable to Dark Souls, this game will whip you into shape pretty sharpish. Enemies are plentiful, but are consistent in their actions and can be dealt with in a variety of ways. The tutorial is clear, the hints and warnings descriptive enough to explain the rules early and make trips to a Wiki un-necessary. Spikes in difficulty are telegraphed and dare you to rise up to the challenge, from bosses to harder tiers of dungeons.
Third, Darkest Dungeon knows what it wants to be, and executes it brilliantly. You really feel the grimdark, c'thulu-esque nature of the premise in every facet of the game. You start rooting for your hapless dungeoneers, each with a shady background, and a whirlwind of pain and suffering ahead of them. The decrepit hamlet that doubles as your base nails home the tragegy of it all, and the slow onset of hope as you steadily rebuild it. And the icing on top? A narrator on par with Bastion's, that will remind you constantly, with dulcet tones, how hopeless it all is (seriously, that voice sells the game on it's own).
And finally, it's ups and downs will keep you invested. The developers themselves stated (paraphrased somewhat) that they want the players to feel crushing despiar, so as to make triumphs taste all the sweeter. The RNG nature means the game's most memorable moments are when it swings heavily to your favor, and when it swings against it. Heros die a lot, and it will hurt, but just as often they will carry you to victory on a a wing and a prayer. If you play it, I predict at least one boss fight will start poorly and yet be won by the skin of your teeth, and it's worth it just for that.
This game's critics do make poignant points though. If you want to complete every side opjective (and they don't feel like side objectives) the game will drag out. Even with perfect form, you cannot guarrantee a perfect run; the cost of allowing swings of RNG. Frustation will set in, and the game will feel contrived or impossible at particurally bad parts of your playthrough. The only thing I can say to these are; they are part of the experience, they are the negatives that accentuate the many positives, and that despite them, this game is worth playing.

I think the scariest moment for me was fighting that huge boss from afar, I cant recall his name but the whole experience with Half life was haunting. Only 2 games did I play as a kid where I was literally walking step by step. One was Silent Hill 2, the other was Half Life. By today you should already know what Half Life represents and what it influenced. If you haven't played it, I don't need to tell you what you need to do.

Is Half-Life truly the greatest game of all time? I can answer that question with one word.
No.
My friend had been pestering me for months to play this game. I had heard so many wonderful things about it, “It’s the greatest game of all time”, “It has an amazing story” are just two of the many great claims I’ve heard about this game. I’ve got to say, I’m extremely disappointed.
After launching the game, I’m greeted by some pretty abysmal graphics. The original game was released sometime around 1996, so poor graphics are to be expected in the original version of the game. What’s not to be expected is for there to be poor graphics in the remake/remaster of the game (Half-Life Source). If the graphics are this bad, I might have well just played the original version.
At first I put this aside; a game with bad graphics doesn’t always equal a bad game. I decided proceed through the “tutorial” area until I actually reach the real part of the game (in which you get your first weapon). I was quite frustrated to find out that I had to use a crowbar as a weapon, which in my opinion is quite a bad design decision. You are going to get a gun later in the game anyway, so why not just provide a gun earlier in the game? Another thing I can't work out is why did they put glasses on the main character? It doesn't seem very badass for the main character to wear glasses.
I then struggle to play though the game due to the dry story and boring combat mechanics. I honestly don’t know why everyone thinks the story to this game is so amazing. A science laboratory gets filled with aliens and you need to escape that laboratory. The story doesn’t get any more complicated or in-depth than that.
You also see a man in a suit from time to time. I don’t see the point in this since you never get the chance to fight him. He is clearly the bad guy in the game, but instead of fighting him at the end of the game, you just speak to him instead. What a disappointment.
Take my advice. Save your money and spend it elsewhere.
(This is from my Half-Life source review. They are pretty much the same game. If you HAVE to buy this game, just buy whichever is cheaper)

I play this on my Dell Latitude E6500 laptop which has no graphics card and just 1gig of ram. It starts up fine and doesn't lag at all. Each tower can be upgraded three times. Some towers attack just ground, some just air, and some ground and air. All levels have a survival mode, and every level has a leaderboard.
There are upgrades that carry from level to level in the form of commander upgrades which can be reset at any time without penalty which lets you experiment with different tower specs and loadouts. There are also special spell-like abilities that you can employ such as a bomb that resets every 20seconds, croud control effects such as freezing, and temporary tower boosts.
There are strategy elements to how towers are placed, how abilities are used, and what your spec is, and how they compliment each other. There are lots of options to play with, and it is fun to experiment. It is not as deep of strategy as a larger game, but this is not meant to be that kind of game. A basic level can be completed in 10 minutes. In survival mode a level can last an hour easily. This game is very very accesible and easy to drop in and out of.
The difficulty escallates rather slowly, but with survival modes and leader boards you are ensured a challenge. That said I am past the first half of the game, and did so casually from my baby's hospital room. I got this title on sale for under $1, and it has been well worth it. Very happy with this game and purchase, and replayability is awesome.
For the price, depth of strategy, and replayability I give this a solid 7/10, and if you like tower defense it is a no-brainer to pick it up I believe.

Super Sanctum TD is the first tower defense game I've played all the way through. I've always enjoyed the genre, but I guess its never been able to keep my interest. However, Super Sanctum TD has opened a door for me, and beyond it is a genre I want to fully experience.
The difficult thing about reviewing Super Sanctum TD is that I have no other experience to compare it to. That being said, I really, really enjoyed it. As a beginner to the genre I found the pacing to be on point, as the waves steadily grew in difficulty. I'll admit that I became stuck on a level for a few hours--trying and trying again to survive the onslaught. My mistake was thinking that it was your level (and in turn what items and weapons you've unlocked) that mattered when in reality it was a matter of strategy. Strategy plays a huge part in this genre, and when I realized that it wasn't my level but how I had set up my paths that was the problem, I beat the level with a perfect rating. Super Sanctum TD was teaching me that brains beats brawn in its playground.
You have access to a wealth of different towers and perks to unlock as you progressively beat levels of the game. There are countless combinations to try out, and I have no doubt to each item's viability. There's also a lot of variety here, that lets you figure out your own playstyle. I for one leaned towards slowing enemies down while they got pummeled by towers that used AOE attacks. You also have access to a skill tree that grants bonuses to your towers and other areas. I haven't played much more after beating the campaign, so I haven't fully explored the tree. I did like the ability to regain all your points for redistribution whenever I wanted. It was helpful when I realized I had no idea what I was doing.
In the end, all I can really say that I found Super Santcum TD an awesome experience. It certainly makes me want to play more of the genre. I definitely recommend this one for those times when you just want to sit down and play something for a few minutes without having to go too indepth.

This game really isn't as bad as most people say it is, it brings new innovative, although small, changes to the sneaking part of being an assassins, with an attempt to take off the restrictions, letting you have extra, optional objectives, these are called opportunities, which may vary from changing the environment, making it easier to escape the area, or fight in, or even receive aid from other people while in combat. The AI is not yet perfect, but is actually a challenge when it comes to combat, each having varying classes as in the previous games, but also with specific levels, showing how difficult they are to fight. Sneaking is as well improved, as you can finally crouch, and stick to cover by pressing a single button. Character Customization is there, giving different outfits each being suited to a certain playstyle, and having different stats on them. France itself is definitely alive, having hundreds of npcs everywhere, as they may aid you in a fight, call for even more enemies to attack, or are even easier for use to escape from an enemies line of sight, which is a borrowed feature from Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Blacklist. Graphics alone are only a small improvement over Black Flag, and Rogue, Honestly I understand if Ubisoft made a new engine for a more diverse and active environment, but I really thought there was no need to improve the graphics over the other game that was released this year. This is why the specs for this game are so demanding. Boss Battles are my main issue with this game, the Bosses alone are really tough, and I actually like that, this time around, Assassin's Creed forces you to use the varied skills and tools you have earned to battle against each boss, each of them actually having a tough ai, of course this is not to the extent of other games, like Batman: Arkham City, but in Ubisoft's Case, it is in an improvement, unfortunately, there is an involvement of highly annoying quick-time events, not even varying in the button you use, but also making you mash the button, although this is a disappointing feature for a boss battle, it would've been acceptable, if it wasn't broken. I don't know if it's a bug or not, but I think the game's qte system is actually trying to make you take a long time to kill your opponent. This isn't a bad game, but it cannot even compete with Assassin's Creed Rogue, or Black Flag. I don't recommend this game to anyone, unless you are a desperate, die-hard Assassin's Creed Fan. Otherwise, I give this game a 5.5/10.

Mayhem Intergalactic is a fun update to a classic game type. To win, a player must eliminate all enemy starships and planets. Planets produce starships, which can be sent to other planets to conquer or bolster defenses. The tricky part is that space travel can take multiple turns. Two fleets might pass one another on long voyages, leaving an undefended planet for attackers to conquer while the planet that fleet departed from gets demolished by the enemy fleet that just left the planet they attacked. If it sounds confusing, it can be odd to try to outthink your opponents to attack them but defend your own holdings, but there's no tech tree or micromanagement to handle. This is one of those simple yet complex fun to play games. The graphics are decent, the music and sound are good, and its mechanics, controls, and help are solid. Mayhem Intergalactic's well worth a few bucks for a bit of mental exercise.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is back, and the aliens have beaten you. Instead of winning the previous game, you lose the base assault mission, and the game picks up twenty years later. In subjugated Earth, fight on tightly gripped territory for the lives of the brainwashed masses that worship their captors.
XCOM 2 delivers more of the same, wonderful XCOM formula, but with key refinements. New and restructured classes shake up the dynamic, adding new character abilities and making some of the obvious choices non blocking (*cough cough*
*cough cough*) The story is as good as ever, and keeps you emotionally invested in kicking some Xray♥♥♥♥♥
The only thing that holds this game back is the engine, which is sadly buggier and far less optimised than the previous installments. While beautiful, the game just doesn't perform well, going from 80+ frames per second to a paltry 20+ in some dynamic moments.
The SteamOS support is laudable, and I wish more games would give it a try, but whatever wrapping technology Feral uses sadly imposes an unecessary 20-40% performance drain. :< Come on Feral, we love that you're doing this, but we need you to do better.
All in all, this game comes highly recommended, and I could not have enjoyed it more, save for the performance issues. Well done Firaxis and Feral!
(Tested on a 780 Ti, 32 GB of DDR3-1866 RAM, and a i7 4930k. Seriously, this should be way overkill, but the engine bogs down when the camera switches and during explosions. This is exacerbated on Linux, but still a problem on Windows 10.)

The first time I reviewed this game, I was infuriated at it and becuase of that I feel as if I didn't review it to it's full potential, and have come back to make a review that I feel isnt trash talking the game, or just me being "mad", now keep in mind I still stand by my dislike of the game, but I'll be going in depth as to why I can't find the game "fun" anymore. (The original review will be at the bottom as I feel this version will be much better than the first.)
So here goes my actual review of Darkest Dungeon.
Darkest Dungeon is a 2D side scrolling dungeon crawler developed by red hook studios which has a heavy emphasis on hero management. And it is also by far one of the most annoying games I have ever played due to it's RNG elements.
While games such as Dark Souls, The Binding of Issac, Nuclear Throne, and Enter the Gungeon are hard, they are all fair in their difficulty, as in you won't be given a challenge you can't surmount through your own skills at the game, but in Darkest Dungeons case you can't just solely win through skill as every action performed has some aspect of RNG tied to it. To extrapolate on this, imagine XCOM, any time you moved there was a chance enemies will appear or you get hurt, or if you get shot at and instead of being unable to control your person due to stress for one turn it would just happen when ever it wants to, which can cause other people to be unable to be controled becuase they got stressed out from them.
What I briefly described at the end of the last paragraph was the games poor implication of a stress feature, while good on paper it was done terribly in the game and I understand it wants to emphasize what the actual effect of dungeon crawling is and what it does to a person, but what the feature did wasnt add a new interesting thing "Oh carp how will I deal with this?" moment, it just had me going "OH BOY, my guys are suicidal again yaaay!" and then wanting to throw all the characters off a cliff when they all refused healing and died or killed themselves through their own stress. Keep in mind theres Perma-Death meaning your characters are never coming back when dead which I dont mind the feature by it self if the game allows me to learn from my mistakes and move on with the game, as the games I mentioned at the beginning do  but when you die in Darkest Dungeon you now have to grind characters to get them up to the level the last ones were at.
The main aspect I dislike in Darkest Dungeon is the massive amount of RNG the game has, but the second is the grind that the game has. each mission can take around 10 minutes to an hour of your time, and the longer ones do give more RESOLVE (EXP) as do the harder dungeons but as you need to complete about 7-12 dungeons for a party to be max level it's going to take a while to get to the end game content, but wait when you finally finish a expidtion to the darkest dungeon and come back the game will inform you that you can't send those people back to it, causing you to have to grind three more parties at a minimum to beat  the game. Now the reson I said at a minimum was becuase the final few missions are hard as hell, with every enemy sporting tons of health and even more damage, so if you want to win prepare to grind for hours upon hours just making back progress you will lose due to over inflated numbers.

Darkest Dungeon. No light, no hope, no end. Or is there? This is a game that practically and psychologically really depends on you, the player.
They say this game is about RNG. And that's true, When a hero strikes a monster, RNG reigns supreme. But everything before and after is up to you. Few dangers can be avoided entirely and few are guaranteed, most of the events are in the murky soup of 'possible but unlikely'. You will hate the game when that spider dodges a finishing blow over and over and you lose a teammate in a supposedly easy fight. But you will never, ever forget the moment when your suddenly Courageous Vestal pulls your undereqipped and exhausted team from the brink again, and again, and again, and you succeed without losses where by all accounts it should've been a wipe with no options. Fear not the darkness, I am your Light!
They say you can't do anything about RNG. And this is also true, but only technically. You can't prepare for every hit of yours missing and every enemy hit critting. What you can do is significantly widen the gap between 'bad/unfortunate' and 'terrible/disasterous'. 'The cost of preparedness, now measured in gold, later - in blood'. Damage and speed is king, the forums say. Then the spiders happen. And then it dawns upon you that, you know what, without that -20% hp item everyone so adores your teammate would still be alive! It's the little things like that, being prepared, thinking at least a little bit ahead and leaving a safety net for those 'not quite like I wanted it to go' times goes a very, very long way.
And when things go sour and the safety net breaks, run away. That is the primary comeback mechanic for this game, probably one hardest to use, because overconfidence and all that. Your heroes bend, but never break. With a little bit of attention they invariably will be ready to fight again. And while the dead don't usually come back, new faces can take the veterans' places when need arises. There is no rush. Evil is timeless, after all.
They say the world's dark. That everything is useless, that the heroes march blindly to the oblivion, that your every action feeds the horror below. 'Victory, such as it is', Or is it? The Hamlet, once a mess of ruins and desolation, now a bustling town, a regional center and a fortress. The products of the Ancestor's work, once roaming the countryside, now under siege in their own dwellings, it is they who feel fear (those that are capable of something that complex anyway). The heroes, once misfits and outcasts, now with a home, a purpose... and profit, should they desire it. They fight and sometimes die, but their goals are within their reach. Reynauld and Dismas WILL find their redemption on the Old Road.
Even the horror below - maybe we need bigger guns to kill it for good. But right now we postponed it's awakening, and that is all that was needed at the moment. There's a lot the game doesn't explicitly tell you about the world, and pretty few of those things are actually bad.
They say the story's amazing. That's absolutely false. The setting is great, but the story, told by Narrator and Ancestor's writings, visibly changes with develpment iterations. The opening fits the ending, but doesn't fit anything in-between. The Crimson Court doesn't fit anything at all, not that it nessesarily needed to, but it's self-contained and completely alien to the rest of the story. It's generally impossible to build a timeline for it. Granted, not everything the Ancestor would write down would nessesarily be true, but, eh. This really could have been handled better.
And there is the game. Be prepared, be cautious. Have a plan B, don't be greedy and don't be afraid to run. Don't read too hard into the story told, it has gaps a train could drive through. This is a world of heroes, even if it's up to you to decide if those under your care will be heroes or fodder. In the end, however, you will prevail.

Fallout 4 is one of my favorite games. While I understand people who felt that it was too great a departure from the RPG elements that the series started with (and were still more present in 3 and New Vegas), I still felt like I was embarking on another great adventure, and if the lack of attention to RPG elements made the story weaker than usual, well, just wander off and make your own fun and stories, like most in the series. Modding, of course, serves to extend its replay value just about indefinitely.
Let me just clarify that again: I LOVE Fallout 4. I sunk countless hours in and enjoyed literally all of them. So when I say that the inclusion of Bethesda's Creation Club makes the game no longer worth it, please believe me. Aside from the fact that the paid mod model is a transparent cash-grab, it actually hurts the game.
"So what?" you may ask. "Isn't the Vanilla game good enough to be worth the price?" I'd say yes. I've always said yes, defending it through the backlash when tons of gamers didn't get what they expected. I'd still defend the content of the game itself, though I'd think twice before supporting Bethesda with the sale anymore. That's because the game no longer works on my computer. Bethesda games are (or used to be) known for being great despite a lot of quirky bugs, but fortunately it was no problem to find a mod real quick to allow me to play on my system.
Well, that mod is incompatible with Creation Club. It added no content except for support for something Bethesda neglected. I can either have the game crash on start up, or be unable to even interact with the main menu for the broken display. While this problem may be very specific to me, there could be no more perfect example of how they now place quick profits ahead of player satisfaction. If they took the time one modder did to fix a display issue, I could still play their game, but instead they ignore the problem and disable non-propietary solutions.
I would love to still be able to recommend Fallout 4, but I just can't. It was a great game, despite what haters said, but now I can't play it, and don't think I'd enjoy it anymore even if I could. I used to consider Bethesda's name a seal of quality, but I have to admit that I'll need to reconsider buying any future games from them unless they roll back on this CC fiasco. I don't want to buy another game with an invisible expiration date, when Bethesda might decide any day to break its playability in exchange for $4.99 golden Pip Boy sales.

Lords of the Fallen is a third-person action role-playing game containing a slow tactical approach to close-quarters combat gameplay, with difficult enemies and locations to overcome, while learning from their encounters. The player takes the role of Harkyn, who, from the beginning, can be tailored towards the player's preferred combat styles from a range of different classes, each with their own specializations in certain weapons, armours, spells, and abilities. A class is determined based on two major choices of three kinds of magic; brawling, deception, and solace, followed by the second choice of three different armour sets; warrior, rogue, and cleric. Different combinations of both choices allow the player to choose how to play Harkyn from the start. With sets, the warrior uses heavy yet strong armor and weapons, the rogue is much lighter and quicker, and the cleric utilizes staffs and armour that supports spell use. Magic adds to the variability of each class. For example, a warrior set combined with brawling magic creates a pure warrior with high strength and vitality, while a warrior set can also be combined with solace magic to create a paladin class that is not as strong but can specialize in spell usage early in the game. As the player progresses through the game and defeats enemies, experience can be gained and spent to upgrade Harkyn's skills and unlock new spells to use in combat.
The game is divided into acts with hubs and nonlinear gameplay progression through a main central story, with new areas continuously opened as the player progresses while also being allowed to return to previously completed areas. However, each new area has multiple paths, hidden locations, and potential shortcuts and secrets to uncover. Along the way, the player will also encounter non-player characters who offer further information, lore, and in many cases, grant additional tasks to the player for more rewards. In dialogue, the player can also make choices with certain characters and their quests. The game utilizes a checkpoints system that the player must locate and can choose to use to save, replenish consumable items, such as healing potions, and upgrade their character.
Lords of the Fallen uses a "risk and reward" system when it comes to upgrading Harkyn. The amount of experience the player can gain for use can be increased through a multiplier that builds up the longer the player mixes up combo attacks or avoids using checkpoints and spending their experiences. If a checkpoint is used, the multiplier will reset. If a player dies during combat, they will appear at the last checkpoint they used but with previously defeated non-boss enemies respawning back in the original location across the in-game world and losing any unspent experience they have gained since they last spent any. At this point a timer will begin, requiring the player to return to the spot they last died in order to regain what they previously lost. However, if the timer runs out or if the player dies again before reaching this point, the unspent experience they had lost before will be lost for good.

Everyone's first look at this is going to be: "Oh... this is just like Dark Souls" . Indeed, this game takes alot from Dark Souls. The slow but steady combat system, dodging, stamina and eventually mana, but it mixes it with an interesting story and beautiful graphics. Most Dark Souls fans are immediately going to dislike this game only because it copies much from their favourite game, and that's apparently sacriliege or something, but if you give it a try, you will enjoy it.
Without trying to spoil much, the premise is that you're somebody trying to take down these powerful creatures coming from god knows where
. You're much stronger than your usual man, able destroy these creatures, but some things you can just see coming. When I got to the mid game, I immediately knew one of the characters wasn't who he seemed and I was correct. It follows a kinda usual fantasy trope with a generic twist, but everything else is still enjoyable. The characters are interesting with their motives and goals.
Gameplay is very similar to Dark Souls, as you can imagine. You have a health bar, stamina bar and a magics bar. Each bar depletes depending on your actions and what the enemies do. Stamina drains while you attack or dodge, magic bar drains whenever you use a magical attack and health depletes whenever you take damage. Simple. There are multiple equipment pieces that you can mix and match to create a proper defense against every enemy. There are multiple classes you can create at the beggining of the game depending on your starting magic and set. For begginer's I reccomend the Warrior, while for more skillful players take the Cleric or Rogue, or you can mix and match inbetween to create inbetween classes that mix some strengths of one class and the other. You can level up by collecting experience and spending it to increase statistics or ability levels. Basic RPG tropes. Every enemy has their patterns that you can easily remember and counter. Some enemies will charge at you, and you can roll or block to stop their strike. Some enemies circle you and you can counter their strikes. You have a light and heavy strike with each having their properties. There's a combo system for saving Stamina and leap attacks. It's fun to leap attack with a heavy weapon and watch as the enemy tries to flee, yet he can't.
One thing CI Games is consistent with... is their Graphics. They settle you in with fitting visuals and music... or lack there of. During boss fights, the music gets you prepeared to fight a powerful foe, and the terrain is beautiful. Characters look very detailed and have their medival fantasy mood. The main character especialy has so much detail put into him, for storyline reasons. Dungeons and Crypts have an old and rotten atmosphere, as if anything could suddenly suprise and attack you. Every character has their personality, and special interactions depending on your current status or what you said, and it all mixes together into one beautiful landscape.
I enjoyed this game, and played it for hours. It's simple yet still difficult. If you really want to, you could play the whole game with a keyboard, and you wouldn't mind it. I'd reccomend it to fans of the Souls series, and Action RPG fans around the world. Some might find it hard or easy, but that doesn't take away from your enjoyment of the game. Afterall... if you find it hard, you can practice patterns in old areas, while if you find it easy, you can challenge yourself with a self-made challenge like never switching your equipment from your starters.

Before coming across Hacknet I first played Uplink. A hacking game quite like this one. I thoroughly enjoyed it, and when I came across Hacknet on the store page when it was released I loved the idea of a newer version. Little did I know I was stumbling across potentially one of the best games I have ever played!
Unlike other games, Hacknet's beautiful story is woven into dialogue and .txt files. Some of these are hidden so you feel like the story is being slowly unveiled to you until you finally discover what is happening.
The gameplay is one of the things I quite enjoy about this game. You begin with simple tools allowing you to access lightly secured systems. As the game progresses, you gain more tools and skills until you are hacking your way into complex and difficult systems. This feels quite satisfying to grow from a beginner into a skilled hacker. As you explore the systems in Hacknet, you are encouraged to dig deeply into the systems, often uncovering interesting parts of the story and some rather comical dialogue. The game also puts you on edge, as when you begin you are told you are being tracked and are encouraged to always remember to cover your tracks. This feeling becomes quite exhilarating as you are hacking into secure systems and deleting your tracks with seconds to spare for your own safety.
Overall, this game is unlike Uplink, the game I expected it to be like. And is an amazing gem of a game in it's own way. If you're looking for a game that gives you the experience of hacking, being constantly under threat with great gameplay and a beautiful story. I highly recommend this game.

I have many other problems with the game, including glitched story chains that stopped me from beating it (even today I've gotten to the end game 3 times and never been able to beat the game because of glitches that Bethesda has known about for a year and never fixed) and atrocious level design.  The game doesn't really add anything and almost feels like a graphical upgrade (and in almost every other way minor downgrade) from New Vegas.  Hugely disappointing even before paid mods, but paid mods are just too much to take for me.  Don't buy this, don't support it.  If you do, you are part of the problem with gaming and you will get more of what you pay for (unfinished, mediocre products that sell you things that used to be free).

The tension in the game is superb, especially if you make a mistake or are racing against the clock, and this is perfectly reflected in the music.
I also love the semi-realistic way that the game uses ports (with real port numbers and protocols), firewalls and proxies rather than the Hollywood *presses all the buttons without showing you what happens.* The way you then have to browse through files to find / work out passwords or discover systems to work through is very gripping and makes you feel very good when you solve a big complex puzzle. When the game actually functions properly, this is the best Assassin's Creed game to come out in a long time, at least machanically.
You have more control over your movement (still needs work though), the combat is actually a challenge at times, and you're not the overpowered demigod that you were in previous iterations of the series. It's the only Assassin's Creed game I actually enjoyed since Brotherhood. If everything went right, it would have been a step in the right direction.
However, as everyone knows, it didn't. The game has performance issues across almost everyone's machines for no discernable reason, and it's filled with bugs at every turn.
I was lucky. Maybe my computer runs on black magic or something, but at 1080p, almost max settings, I was able to get about 45-60 fps for the vast majority of the game. My computer however is likely just a fluke, as people with even stronger machines struggle to get that speed in the same conditions. I was also lucky enough to actually not encounter a single game breaking bug during my playthrough, the only bug I found was one time a NPC was running down the street, arms and legs stretched, flailing them like a necromorph.
Based -solely- on my experience with this game and not the experience others have had, I have to recommend it, but it is the most cautious recommendation of all time. I know that for most of the people reading this, your experience will not reflect mine. Honestly? Wait a few years until a new generation or two of video hardware comes out before picking this up. By then, maybe you'll be able to just throw enough hardware at the game where the performance issues won't matter as much.

TLDR; Superb, methodical, Free-to-play, capital ship MOBA which has recently seen many changes that make the new player experience very good!
I have enjoyed this game immensely throughout development, in particular I like the more methodical pace of game play and the ability to have a plan of attack and execute it, it's not just about your reaction speed.
The release of the game on the 22nd September brings some pretty significant features that push the game from good to great;
- Solo + Co-Op play versus AI.
This is so important as it allows you as a player to really get to grips with your purchased ships before commiting to trying them versus other players (I should note all ships are free to try in the "shooting range first"). It also gives a nice way to casually enjoy the game if you so choose.
- Improved matchmaking and team play.
Prior to this update teams were limited in size (whilst matchmaker was worked on) now you are able to make full teams of 5 and you can even set up custom games if you have more friends so you can play against each other easily. While the matchmaker is an ever evolving system it appears to do a far better job at matching similar skill players against eachother than previous iterations.
- Armada Pack DLC
While the ships are balanced around each other (i.e. there's no artficial "tiers" to the ships) many are situational, and it could be annoying to not have the "right ship" for the job (or maybe you just want to shoot huge cannons/lasers at things).
Those of us who have been playing some time have had a chance to unlock the current 31 ships in game, but for new players this could take some time. For those less patient you can unlock all the ships for what is a pretty cheap price (purchasing them all seperately for money would cost a lot more). Whilst not as good as say the deal available in SMITE it does bring players up to the number ships available at release and I would recommend it to players who don't mind spending the cash.
Again just a warning if you decide to grab them all; play against some AI with your new toys, as some of the ships are highly specialised!

After the not-so-smashing effect the first Runaway game had on me, I was a bit wary of the second. Unfortunately, I was more than right.
To make it simple, the second game is like the first one in almost every aspect, only more so. That means the visuals are even better, the music... well, it's not quite as good but still superb - and that's where the positives end. The characters are either a-holes or idiots, our protagonist being the prime example of the former class. And he's not even funny, because that, according to Handsome Jack, would make it OK. But no such luck. The story is... when you look at it, it's almost non-existent. You spend huge amounts of game time achieving trivial feats (via non-sensical puzzles half the time), while the story stands utterly still. You click through diarrheic dialogs which advance neither story nor character. You try to figure out what to do next when what you have to do is click through all discussion with a character
. And to top it all off, the game finishes without any solution - we get another idiotic rant by Brian (our supposed hero) and a half-a**ed attempt at team spirit. I wonder who has any mind playing the third game after this - for me it would feel like a burden.
I love small studios who try to achieve big things, so it hurts me to downvote Runaway #2, but I was so far from enjoying this game that it can't go any other way. Sorry.

This was...pretty much a disappointment for me. Not a huge one, more like a big meh feeling. I think the only upsides were the new environments/backgrounds and that they finally cured the game of pixel hunting-itis. The items you can interact with and pick up were a lot more visible and obvious now.
But then, everything else seemed to have rolled downhill from there. I brushed it off initially from the first game since I was convinced it was a one time thing, but sadly, they kept the glaringly racist caricature of a character (Joshua) and made him part of this game's main story. And the main plot itself was just so disappointing in comparison to the first. Joshua's mission from the first game should have been kept as just a silly joke to help Brian with his main goal, how did it escalate to become the second game's plot? Just...no. I thought it could be as fun of a mystery as the Broken Sword series, but it just got too ridiculous as soon as chapter 3 to 4 rolled in.
And ultimately, I feel like taking back what I said in the previous game's review about Brian. In the first game, he was sweet, nerdy and polite but here he had finally transformed into the generic douchey protag I said I was glad I didn't experience. I also have gripes about how in Chapter 2, you had to loop the conversation with Flowerpot (and the guard) to get to Kordsmeier over and over again. I don't want to have to deal with that more than once. And Sushi's VA sounded really robotic and slowly that it was pretty aggravating.

Second part of the "Runaway" trilogy.
In my opinion this is the most difficult episode, it took me about 25 hours to finish it and I got really stuck in a couple of occasions. Let me be clear, the difficulty level still has nothing to do with the Monkey Island series, but for someone who is not an expert of Point & Click (like me) you can definitely see the difference with the first Runaway episode, and even more with the third.
The graphics is excellent like the first episode, the plot more complex. The ending is not really an ending, this didn't bother me at all because I already had the third episode to finish the story. But maybe it could have frustrated players at the time.
Just like for the first episode, the gameplay has some differences with most of Point & Click Adventures: you can look in the same place and not find something the first time but finding it the second, depending on what your characters know. Same thing for some actions. This is not very common in these kinds of games, I was a bit suprised at the beginning, but still, it makes sense, so you get used to it quite easily.
There were a couple of crashes, but they were easily solvable looking for a solution on the net.
In the whole, a fun and enjoyable adventure! I advise you to buy it if you like the genre.

I'm actually kind of baffled that this game has mixed reviews. Maybe I was one of the lucky ones, but I've never experienced any crashes, glitches, or game breaking bugs. I also don't understand some of the people who say, I had fun playing this, but still give it a thumbs down. If you have fun then isn't the game doing it's job?
Most people that want to try this game out are probably familiar with the Dark Souls series. This is essentinal a DS-Lite game. Same combat system but not as cryptic, and more straight forward. Another complaint I see is the main character is slugglish. I do admit in the beginning this is true. It's like you start off with a slow swing greatsword, but there are better weapons later on and you'll eventually get used to it. Another thing is the lack of enemy variation. This really didn't bother me because, as a DS veteran, the combat system was enough to keep me highly entertained. Graphics are pretty good and story is ok, but like I mentioned, the main appeal to me is the Dark Souls combat mechanics. I also want to note that I finished this game in a little over 20 hours, even though it says 2 hrs on my playtime. I played the game 'elsewhere' but enjoyed it so much I wanted to show support and officially purchase it. Bottome line, if you like Dark Souls and don't try and critique the comparisons too much, you might actaully enjoy this game as much as I did. Hopefully we can expect a sequel with some improvements.

While not incredibly long, this game was a lot of fun. As a programmer, the fact that *NIX-like commands are used was both a good and a bad thing. While driving the game purely from the terminal was straightforward, I often found myself typing variants of the comands that the game does not recognize (i.e. 'cd -', 'ls -la', 'rm -rf dir\*.*').
I found that the puzzles were not too hard, but I think if the game were longer it would get quite repetitive. Many have asked if this is like 'real' hacking or that they feel like the are in Mr. Robot. In my experience, 'real' hacking isn't nearly as easy, nor predictable. That said, even though I deal with these kinds of systems professionally, this game was very fun and I think it will give you a taste of the command line.
Bottom Line: Worth $10
One note for the author, include man pages and make them a requirement. One of the most fun aspects of the game is learning how to use the programs and what they do. It would be great to have to read man pages and pipe commands together.

Graphicwise Runaway: The Dream of the Turtle follows in the footsteps of the first game Runaway: A Road Trip. It is partially hand-drawn and partially 3D rendered considerably smoothly animated graphics. The outcome works out very nicely.
On the sound department the game balances between good an corky. The melody of the theme song is rather catchy and personally I liked it. In overall the sound effects are mostly on point but some sound a bit low-res. Voice acting... well, some is good, some is over exaggerated and misses the target but nothing really stands out in a bad way. On the positive side everything is well enough articulated that the game can be played without subtitles and even one characted who speaks in heavy French accent can be understood.
Gameplay drags along the positives and the negatives of the first game; Long-winded dialogs, pixel hunting objects hidden in plain sight within the beautiful hand drawn graphics, running back and forth in the same locations... Despite the fact that this is common in adventure games, Runaway brings in one annoyance that LucasArts and Daedalic fans are not used to. Brian is not "loot all" kind'a guy. He only takes what he needs at the moment so whenever you feel that you're stuck, if there is a box or a room where you found an object earlier, go look again, and there might be more where it came from. The availability is triggered by some other game event (often either a dialog option or trying out something that doesn't work out). Or it could be that you need to mix up inventory items. Use everything on everything is sometimes the only (il)logical way to go -- the usual annoyance.
As the first game, towards the end of the game (6 chapters) the emphasis moves from playing the game to more and more watching pre-rendered story clips. And even though personally I prefer to figure out solutions by myself, both of the first two Runaway games had their moments when I was more than happy to get a hint from a walkthrough. I just felt that to get ahead with the story I had probably missed something relevant, and often it was some "hidden" item in a place I already plundered... Oh, how I missed the Deponia hotspot key sometimes.
Despite all the negatives, the game is actually good. It's not Daedalic or LucasArts good but here are worse adventures to spend your time on. Just bare with often over excited monologs of our main character and you may find enjoyment in this game. Playing A Road Trip is recommended before this as it will explain some characters, and a few joke references. However, it is not mandatory to be able to enjoy this game.

The first time I reviewed this game, I was infuriated at it and becuase of that I feel as if I didn't review it to it's full potential, and have come back to make a review that I feel isnt trash talking the game, or just me being "mad", now keep in mind I still stand by my dislike of the game, but I'll be going in depth as to why I can't find the game "fun" anymore. (The original review will be at the bottom as I feel this version will be much better than the first.)
So here goes my actual review of Darkest Dungeon.
Darkest Dungeon is a 2D side scrolling dungeon crawler developed by red hook studios which has a heavy emphasis on hero management. And it is also by far one of the most annoying games I have ever played due to it's RNG elements.
While games such as Dark Souls, The Binding of Issac, Nuclear Throne, and Enter the Gungeon are hard, they are all fair in their difficulty, as in you won't be given a challenge you can't surmount through your own skills at the game, but in Darkest Dungeons case you can't just solely win through skill as every action performed has some aspect of RNG tied to it. To extrapolate on this, imagine XCOM, any time you moved there was a chance enemies will appear or you get hurt, or if you get shot at and instead of being unable to control your person due to stress for one turn it would just happen when ever it wants to, which can cause other people to be unable to be controled becuase they got stressed out from them.
What I briefly described at the end of the last paragraph was the games poor implication of a stress feature, while good on paper it was done terribly in the game and I understand it wants to emphasize what the actual effect of dungeon crawling is and what it does to a person, but what the feature did wasnt add a new interesting thing "Oh carp how will I deal with this?" moment, it just had me going "OH BOY, my guys are suicidal again yaaay!" and then wanting to throw all the characters off a cliff when they all refused healing and died or killed themselves through their own stress. Keep in mind theres Perma-Death meaning your characters are never coming back when dead which I dont mind the feature by it self if the game allows me to learn from my mistakes and move on with the game, as the games I mentioned at the beginning do  but when you die in Darkest Dungeon you now have to grind characters to get them up to the level the last ones were at.
The main aspect I dislike in Darkest Dungeon is the massive amount of RNG the game has, but the second is the grind that the game has. each mission can take around 10 minutes to an hour of your time, and the longer ones do give more RESOLVE (EXP) as do the harder dungeons but as you need to complete about 7-12 dungeons for a party to be max level it's going to take a while to get to the end game content, but wait when you finally finish a expidtion to the darkest dungeon and come back the game will inform you that you can't send those people back to it, causing you to have to grind three more parties at a minimum to beat  the game. Now the reson I said at a minimum was becuase the final few missions are hard as hell, with every enemy sporting tons of health and even more damage, so if you want to win prepare to grind for hours upon hours just making back progress you will lose due to over inflated numbers.

Gotta say, I'm a fan. This is gonna be my MOBA of choice over League of Legends or Dota.
Well, let me see why...graphics are excellent and the sound design is great as well.
Gameplay-wise, the ships (aka the "heroes") are very well balanced to each other for the most part. The default ships are pretty decent, but there is no progression tree, so the next ship you get is literally whatever ship you want. There is a firing range for you to practice with a ship before you buy it.
You unlock the ships through either in-game currency by playing games, or through premium currency. There is no benefit to unlocking them through premium currency, so there's no pay-to-win.
What you can buy with premium are skins, specifically Ultimate Skins which increase your credits earning.
Once you've bought a ship, you can take it into a 5v5 battle, or you can play PvE - 5 human teammates on one side and 5 AI enemies on the other.
Either way, you're tasked with defending a home base that is heavily armed with automated turrets from the other team, who have the same. There are two lanes with a forward base on either end and three mining stations between them. Players must capture the mining stations to increase the rate at which resources are gained; gain enough resources, your ship levels up and gains various stat bonuses. The stat bonuses are necessary because the base is heavily armed and you cannot survive its fire without upgrades.
Capturing the forward base on the other side of the lane unlocks jump access to the enemy's home base, where you must contend with the base's turrets and any defenders in order to capture the base and win the game.
Every few minutes, however, there is a single large mining station in the middle that becomes available to capture. It is only available every 2-5 minutes and cannot be captured outside that window. It provides a huge bonus when captured, so you're guaranteed to get a huge fight at least every 2-5 minutes at the middle of the map.
Well, this game ticks all the boxes I look for in a good game. Good graphics, good sound, good gameplay, a fair payment model, and PvE options in addition to PvP. So, if you're looking for a game which sends teams of five huge spaceships against each other, then this is the game for you. And if not, just try it. It's free to play, after all.

Runaway: The Dream of The Turtle feels like 6 separate poorly designed point and click adventure games strung loosely together by extremely dated racism and sexual "humor" that culminates to a cringe worthy cliff hanger that was clearly intended to hype the next game but fails miserably.
First, the game suffers from some critical design flaws. Namely performing tasks requires flags to be triggered. Say you search a trunk and find nothing. Go fish some goggles out of a puddle and suddenly that trunk has everything you need in it.  Sometimes talking to other characters will suddenly allow you to see the random item that will be useful later on.
The game was also buggy, Snow fall halted the game to a near standstill, I had to use a DirectDraw wrapper to get the game running at full speed.
There is also some unusual cut scenes that add nothing.  Near the end, we see main character Brian go scuba diving about 6 times in 1 cut scene, repeatedly getting in the water, getting out, talking to another character then repeating the process with slight variation in the animation.  It doesn't make any sense WHY the extra-long animations were included when so many have nothing to do with the main story or are just inflated for no reason.  Worse yet, the game has a tendency to crash during these cut scenes, so hopefully you saved before they started.
But all of that is just design, I haven't gotten to the story. Story is nonsensical.  I feel like it is trying REALLY hard to be Secret of Monkey Island and portray Brian as the second coming of Guybrush Threepwood, but he is not.  He's an extremely unlikable and unfunny character that I tried to click of a cliff more than a few times.  The game takes place in 6 locales, and with every shift in location the grip on the main story lines slips further away.  At the start of the game you are searching for your girlfriend you kicked out of a plane, and by the end you are a mighty pirate. In between all that, you cheat on your girlfriend, get a man♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and finish that off by getting drunk.
Yeah this is some real frat boy humor. It is filled with stuff that might have flown in an 80s sexcapade movie, but here it is just painful to sit through now.
Like I said in the start to this review, the game ends on a cliff hanger.  You go through each stage of the game looking for the next McGuffin, only to be rewarded with a To Be Continued.
Racism is just annoying in this game. They have a 1950s Japanese stereotype running around being annoying. He was in the last game but only for a few scenes, now he is a major character.
The game doesn’t seem to know what it is trying to be. Whether it’s an Animal House parody, a Spy like Us parody, Indiana Jones parody, or Secret of Monkey Island parody, it just fails at all of them. None of the little throw backs amused me. With that in mind I can’t recommend.  I played the Runaway game that came before this, it had a ton of issues too, but it benefitted from a more humble character and more diluted sexism and racism.

To start off, since I've seen people mostly complaining about constant crashes, I've not experienced any problems with that. I don't know what I've done right, but I'm happy I didn't have to put up with it.
Secondly, a lot of people are comparing this game to Dark Souls and the game really is inspired by the Dark Souls series. The thing is, if you played through Dark Souls series first, Lords of the Fallen will be incredibly dull, mostly easy, empty and boring to you. But if you're playing Lords of the Fallen first it probably would be pretty hard, but it would be just a tutorial for Dark Souls and you would simply be amazed by Dark Souls.
Story:
To be honest, I didn't really follow the story through, so I can't say much. But if you visit LotF wiki you'll see everything. I'm sure the devs tried to make the story interesting, but I just didn't want to keep track of what's going on. Probably because the game doesn't explain from where Harkyn (protagonist) comes from, what he's done, you only know he's a convicted criminal who now has a chance for redemption to kill some gods or whatever. I don't think wiki's got more than that.
Combat:
In the beginning you get to choose between 3 Magic types and 3 starting equipment. Rogue (light), Warrior (heavy), Cleric (medium). There are stats: Strenght, Agility, Faith which scale with weapons (meaning you have more damage with an agility weapon the more agility you have) and other stats like Vitality, Endurance, etc.
In the game, it doesn't really matter with what you start with because you can build your character differently later. I usually play with light armor and fast weapons so when I did go as Warrior on my second playthrough I just ended up with agility weapons because I don't like being slow.
The 3 Magic types give you different magic abilities which you have to unlock with experience and they sometime do appear useful, but I didn't use them that much because I wasn't going for Magic stat.
And also you get The Gauntlet, which is a big gun, basically. It uses Magic to shoot.
Most effective fighting technique is to do combos. With combos Energy (read "stamina") depletes less with each attack. Agility weapons like fists, daggers and shortswords have a special combo move on the 3rd and 4th attack, which can stagger opponents and deal fair amount of damage.
Weapons:
As I said, weapons scale with stats. Hammers are the only weapons scaling with Faith, so there's no point in going for too much Faith for damage because I find hammers awfully slow, but Faith also gives you Magic.
The problem is, weapons, for example swords, all have the same animation and same attack speed. Meaning when you get a new weapon, you don't care what kind of animation it has, you just look at the damage you output. Again, if you look at Dark Souls, almost every weapon has it's own move set. And that's what the game is missing.
There are also different damage types, like physical, magic, fire, lightning to be extra spicy and you acquire those from runes. When you find a blacksmith he can put runes in to your equipment.
Armor:
Nothing much to say about this. There are light, medium and heavy armor, depends on your playstyle. There is a weight load so if you put too much armor you'll move and roll slower.
Armors are nicely designed, I really liked that.
Enemies:
There are not a lot of enemies, around 15-20 coming at you throughout the whole game. Enemies with shields are really annoying because they don't do anything besides sitting behind a shield and maybe attacking you one or twice before you manage to somehow kill them.
Generally, they are all easy and... Basic.
Locations you have to go through get recycled.
Bosses:
Every boss is nothing special, they all have some basic attacks and they are all extremely boring, because they have too much health and the fight doesn't progress at all. So it's just the same moves for 5-10 minutes straight.
Music:
Not bad when there is something in the background. It's quiet mostly.
Love the theme song though.
Overall, it's a good game to play, but I didn't find much worth in it. The devs tried at least.
Just go play Dark Souls.

Darkest Dungeon. No light, no hope, no end. Or is there? This is a game that practically and psychologically really depends on you, the player.
They say this game is about RNG. And that's true, When a hero strikes a monster, RNG reigns supreme. But everything before and after is up to you. Few dangers can be avoided entirely and few are guaranteed, most of the events are in the murky soup of 'possible but unlikely'. You will hate the game when that spider dodges a finishing blow over and over and you lose a teammate in a supposedly easy fight. But you will never, ever forget the moment when your suddenly Courageous Vestal pulls your undereqipped and exhausted team from the brink again, and again, and again, and you succeed without losses where by all accounts it should've been a wipe with no options. Fear not the darkness, I am your Light!
They say you can't do anything about RNG. And this is also true, but only technically. You can't prepare for every hit of yours missing and every enemy hit critting. What you can do is significantly widen the gap between 'bad/unfortunate' and 'terrible/disasterous'. 'The cost of preparedness, now measured in gold, later - in blood'. Damage and speed is king, the forums say. Then the spiders happen. And then it dawns upon you that, you know what, without that -20% hp item everyone so adores your teammate would still be alive! It's the little things like that, being prepared, thinking at least a little bit ahead and leaving a safety net for those 'not quite like I wanted it to go' times goes a very, very long way.
And when things go sour and the safety net breaks, run away. That is the primary comeback mechanic for this game, probably one hardest to use, because overconfidence and all that. Your heroes bend, but never break. With a little bit of attention they invariably will be ready to fight again. And while the dead don't usually come back, new faces can take the veterans' places when need arises. There is no rush. Evil is timeless, after all.
They say the world's dark. That everything is useless, that the heroes march blindly to the oblivion, that your every action feeds the horror below. 'Victory, such as it is', Or is it? The Hamlet, once a mess of ruins and desolation, now a bustling town, a regional center and a fortress. The products of the Ancestor's work, once roaming the countryside, now under siege in their own dwellings, it is they who feel fear (those that are capable of something that complex anyway). The heroes, once misfits and outcasts, now with a home, a purpose... and profit, should they desire it. They fight and sometimes die, but their goals are within their reach. Reynauld and Dismas WILL find their redemption on the Old Road.
Even the horror below - maybe we need bigger guns to kill it for good. But right now we postponed it's awakening, and that is all that was needed at the moment. There's a lot the game doesn't explicitly tell you about the world, and pretty few of those things are actually bad.
They say the story's amazing. That's absolutely false. The setting is great, but the story, told by Narrator and Ancestor's writings, visibly changes with develpment iterations. The opening fits the ending, but doesn't fit anything in-between. The Crimson Court doesn't fit anything at all, not that it nessesarily needed to, but it's self-contained and completely alien to the rest of the story. It's generally impossible to build a timeline for it. Granted, not everything the Ancestor would write down would nessesarily be true, but, eh. This really could have been handled better.
And there is the game. Be prepared, be cautious. Have a plan B, don't be greedy and don't be afraid to run. Don't read too hard into the story told, it has gaps a train could drive through. This is a world of heroes, even if it's up to you to decide if those under your care will be heroes or fodder. In the end, however, you will prevail.

This a great step up from the first installment in the Runaway series in many ways. The improvements are enough for me to say that I would recommend this game to a friend. Before I talk about what really worked for this game, let me say the big issues I experienced.
I broke the game in Act 2 by using the butter on Joshua while worked on the bull, before I greased up the chain and untied it. This made it so I was unable to progress and it wound up taking me about an hour to finally consult the walkthrough and find out that it was impossible to continue. This is a really unfortunate thing to happen so early in the game, but I wish that was the worst thing I experienced. All of Act 4 was laggy beyond playability. I had to go through it with a walkthrough next to me, because every action took double the amount of time it should. If I did this legitimately, it probably would have taken a day just to play this one Act. Also, Joshua felt a little too much like the racially charged Mickey Rooney character in Breakfast at Tiffany's, which got overbearing at times.
The story is pretty good, and it definitely keeps you guessing with the inclusion of military and alien things. There are some great characters that you'll remember like Knife, O'Connor, and Archibald. I didn't understand that I was playing through a "To Be Continued" game though, which can be upsetting when you see it. I feel like Pendulo could have stated that better in the description on Steam, because after 20+ hours of figuring out puzzles, I want to see Brian save Gina!
All around, it's a great game, and I enjoyed all of the parts that played well. The logic through the game made sense, and it was fun to get the rewarding moments of successfully solving a puzzle. The cutscenes were also fun to watch, and it felt like they greatly added to the player having empathy to the characters.

Okay, so where to begin.
Assassin's Creed Unity takes the game back to its original roots. Is that a bad thing no, not really, but it also doesn't bring much "new" and revolutionary additions to the table.
Beautiful buildings, wonderful architectural designs of famous places, I mean the team did an excellent job at sculpting this eye-candy pieces of art. The scope is beyond impressive, the technology behind it, top-notch, but the price is performance and other issues that I'll note below.
Interiors look amazing, polished, glossy, it's like they spend more time fixing the inside than the outside, because once you set foot on the cruddy looking outside streets of France you'll probably gag.
Fighting is terrible. The animations are a step backwards, they've had what SEVEN games to get the battle system down, and I seriously felt it was unpolished, the worst from ANY of the previous games. This is NEXT GEN? No, it's more like a rush job to get money from the Holiday crowds.
The world itself is somewhat bland, boring, and lifeless. It's sad that they attempted to bring it to life with all those pointless NPCs that glitch left and right, do random things, get in your way, see crowds upon crowds revolting, but honestly, I couldn't care less... WHY? Because I had NO part in the situation at hand.
Things to do: So there's tons of stuff to do, collectables, tons of side missions, but guess what, I didn't really care to complete them. See the game doesn't really give you reasons to care about these side quests, I never felt the need to do them. There's no consequence, your efforts don't change anything. It's sad, and I love Assassin's Creed games, this review is coming from someone who grew up playing ALL the AC games.
The French Revolution setting didn't make sense to me. And the story, SPOILER, about vengeance loses itself somehow to the point where I was killing these paper trail targets solely to get to the final guy who was apparently some Sage?
They could have done so much with the story. The whole time warping thing didn't make sense to me (Cool and awesome) because I am trying to figure out who is trying to find me! At least in Desmond's case from AC 1~3 I understood what was going on, I knew the background story! It's like this is a sequel to some game I've never played before!
And then the ending comes along. SPOILER: So I recall the Apples of Eden in the previous games, and now my character has the Sword of Eden. But there's no logical explanation to ANYTHING! How did the sword come to be?
Who created the sword?
Was it crafted from the Apples of Eden?
Wasn't this SWORD what that woman telling me what to do, wanted?
The woman wanted to know where that guy was buried, WHY?
I wanted to know more about this mysterious woman telling me what to do.
I wanted to know more about this Sword of Eden.

So I wanted to update my Phase One “Beta Release” review. A lot has changed, and since you are browsing the reviews, I assume that you have seen that several members of the community dislike the changes. Although I don’t like everything that has changed, I can say that I am actually enjoying the game more than I was before.
So what happened since my last review?
-Implants added in, allows you to specialize crew for each ship similar to Runes in LoL. You can have up to 5 of a type of implant, and 15 total. They range from base hull strength to utility cooldowns to attack damage, ect... When these first game in, defense implants were incredibly overpowered. Since then, they have been brought down to a more balanced state.
-Crew leveling. You can now level crew members up to legendary status, which only really lets you use whatever type of implant you feel like in their slots. (Normally they are tied to attack/defense/utility.) They also get small animations. Used to be the only way to get them was from RNG drop pods.
-3 new ships added. All of them were pretty strong at first, then they were brought down balance wise. (The Paragon “carrier” did get a few buffs, if you read my previous review.)
-Lots of improvement on the art and optimization side. There is now a “low performance” mode for those of you who don’t have the time or money to build a supercomputer. I don’t have experience using this mode, but apparently it’s helped a lot.
-Quite a bit of balancing, bug fixes, and other stuff that I have probably forgotten about.
-And last and least according to who you ask, the map changes to Conquest mode:
As per usual, the devs introduce radical changes then scale them back. (Like the implant example above) At first, we had significantly reduced lane sizes and respawn durations. These changes have since been partially reverted, but their impact on the game is still there.
That being said, I have not had as much fun as I am currently since they reverted some of their previous changes. The matches are faster paced, yet still retain their strategic side from before the changes.
Don’t get me wrong, there are still many things that I feel need to be changed and/or improved upon (like the tutorial, which is forced by the way, you have been warned XD), but I actually like where the lane sizes are now.
Before I wrap this up, I just wanted to say the tutorial forces you to play a game type called Frontline. Most people play Conquest, so the queue times will probably be longer. Have patience. No, the game is not "dead".
So in conclusion, did the recent patches change the game? Yes.
Is this game now “Call of Duty in space” like some of the reviews say? No.
Since the game is free to play, I suggest you try it. Not everyone likes space games, and not everyone likes MOBAs. I happen to really like both.

So I am updating my review after just over a year for the upcoming Phase 1 launch. (Original is below if you are interested)
Here’s my attempt at a TL; DNR:
Fractured Space is a 5v5 team based space ship MOBA with two game modes. Both require objective control (and coordination) to win. (Conquest is the main mode though) There are currently 31 ships in game, each fitting loosely into tank, dps and support roles. Each ship comes with a primary weapon and 4 other abilities. (EG: Missiles, fighters/drones/bombers, teleports, cloak, shields, heals, ect…) These abilities vary greatly depending on what the ship is designed to do. (EG: a Brawler can use a harpoon torpedo to grab enemies and pull them into its close ranged weaponry.) Ships have 6 sides of armor (front, left, bottom, ect) that reduce damage taken from that direction, and can be broken to remove this damage reduction.
Ships can only rotate on a 2d plane (Left and right), but can move in a 3d plane. Some people hate this, but the lack of 3d rotation adds a great deal of importance on positioning and playstyle variation depending on both your target and your ship. (For instance, some ships have powerful frontal weaponry, but are vulnerable to top/bottom/side attacks as a result.)
I recommend Fractured Space because:
-It’s free to play.
-It’s not pay to win. (No, not at all. Everything can be obtained in game for free save for skins.)
-It’s actually pretty balanced. (With some ships hard countering others.) As a newer player, you may run into teams filled with cloaking, heavy or even sniping ships, but you will learn how to deal with them eventually if you stick with it. To expand upon this, the starter ships are great at their intended roles if you take the time to learn them! (They are less specialized than their more expensive counterparts.)
-It is a deep game with a high skill cap that requires both knowledge of your ship’s capabilities as well as your enemy’s. (It’s good to note the game is generally balanced around mid-high skill level, so some ships will feel underpowered until you learn how to use them.)
-It has 31 ships each with separate abilities and unique playstyles. Some ships overlap others, but still play very different from each other thanks to their ability kits. (EG there are 3 sniper ships in the game that play fairly different from each other.)
-It can get pretty competitive.
-It doesn’t have a skill tree, meaning you can unlock any ship once you have the credits with no exponentially growing “ship tree” like Star Conflict. Additionally, more expensive ships are generally more specialized and harder to play, but not always better depending on the situation. (Good for new players)
-It has a neat little crew system. Crew members will give status notifications (Jumping, armor destroyed on x face, ect), enemy spotted notifications, and even taunt players that you kill. You can have a max of 5 crew members, each with slightly varying stats. (And none being outright better than others)
-Pretty good graphics.
Cons:
-I’ve heard some people have trouble running the game on lower end rigs. I don’t have any issues with a 980TI/i7-6700k. (I have crashed 0 times within the last 30 hours of gameplay.) If you have a low end rig, you may not be able to play this game very well even with the graphics turned down.
-Heavily skill reliant? Some people may find this frustrating, especially after they win a few games and get put up against more experienced players.
-The recently reintroduced Paragon (A heavy carrier ship) feels fairly useless, especially in higher skill games. It’s a polarizing ship that if over buffed could be overpowered, so it is a difficult ship to balance.
Neutral/Misc facts:
-Pick/Ban phase is currently in the works. Will be nice for higher level play.
-Voice Communication is also in the works.
-Not too grindy. Just enough playtime required in order to unlock new ships IMO.
-Legendary skins for ships provide slightly more credit income, and look pretty cool/have different animations. (These are purchased with real money.)
-A basic competitive league.
-Some ships have loadouts with slightly varying modules to choose from. These choices aren’t always impactful/meaningful. Newer ships generally don’t have loadouts yet. I’m assuming this will improve with time.
-Some PVE, though I haven’t played it since they’ve added it, and as a result cannot review that feature.
Conclusion:
All in all, as of last week this game is now my most played game on Steam. I have thoroughly enjoyed it thus far, and I am glad that I have been able to watch this game develop over the last year and a half.
If you like space games, or you like competitive games, I think you should at least try this game.
