Well... Here is the continuation to Runaway series,
, made in 2006. Aside that little bit of factual definition, there is not a single good thing to say about this game. If you've played the first game and declared it a tasteless, tacky and overcomplicated little adventure full of character stereotypes as I did, be warned: This is way worse than the first game. At least, the first game was working properly!
Adventures of self-acclaimed genius Ken doll Brian Basco continue from where we left him: on a vacation in Hawaii with the oversexualized bimbo stereotype Gina who he ended up as lovers beforehand. Thanks to a series of unfortunate - and mindlessly obvious - wrong choices, Brian ends up surviving a plane crash to only get stranded on an island invaded by military forces, missing Gina without a clue to her whereabouts. How...very...convenient. As before, his story will start with a destined accident and progress to become ridiculous, fast pacing and needlessly complicated over a short period of time. Buckle your seats, and be ready for alien conspiracy theories.
First and foremost, I really have a problem about the story execution in this game. In the first game, we went through a series of absurd events and got blessed with miraculous luck so random strangers with extraordinary talents and means ended up helping us regularly to get a happy ending. Brilliant. Here in this continuation, the same dynamic applies - but the game is needlessly extended to present the illusion for the presence of a game time. The first 3 chapters that take place in Mala Island are somewhat consistent with the main story if not harbored with annoyingly superficial humor and aroused teenage level sexual remarks. The rest of the game is an unbearable story anchor for situational comedy purposes mostly. The whole chapter 4 is only there to serve as a situational comedy during a supposed intergalactic emergency! Look, I can appreciate absurd humor, I loved every single moment of
series, but there is nothing funny about deliberately feeding a complete stranger to a polar bear's sexual frustration, just because Brian decided to icefish at the spot the bear's standing! It's plain disgusting.
Aside a slight improvement on graphics and in-game animations, the game uses the same character design, 2D environments and a combination of 3D modeled cut scenes alongside 2D dialogue sequences among characters. Gosh, even the design choice is over complicated here! Fair warning: 3D cut scenes where Brian talks to Sushi, beginning from the start of the game, are spastically slow for some reason. Speaking of bugs, first 3 chapters of the game work fine, but the game gets unbelievably slow when you reach 4th Chapter. It takes a couple seconds to even move the mouse from one point to another. I think it's a problem with the snowing animation. I tried everything in my ability but couldn't find a way to mend it so I ended up closing the game and finding a YouTube playthrough to watch the rest to learn the story. This bug occurs with both Windows 7 Pro and 8.1 Pro. Be warned.
As before, game logic is flawed - not letting you go for the obvious solution before trying everything else to be rejected properly is our main thing. But ask yourself this: what kind of dimwit of a protagonist gets snow shoes to his inventory in a tropical island and leaves first aid kit behind, after a plane crash??? Such is our game logic. Puzzles are somewhat simple, but story progression and dialogues are a pain to go through. I'd vote for "nope, surely there is something better to do".
If you enjoy crass humor and are fond of "It was aliens!" skets - and able to forgive not being able to play half the game - sure, go for it. Otherwise, avoid it. Yeah, I will still play the last part of the series to get done with it and write a review. I know, I know. I love my community...

The second Runaway game is more beautiful and even stupider than the first one. If you like immature sex jokes and rampant racism, and don’t mind horrific plot dump dialogues, you may have some fun, but otherwise just skip it. (It’s not even needed for the third game.)
Runaway: A Road Adventure was a beautiful, but overcomplicated point ‘n’ click with ridiculous puzzles, terrible voice acting, and a story that eventually turned out to be quite nice in the very end. The Dream of the Turtle has no redeeming factors other than better graphics; everything else is worse.
Much, much worse.
The voice acting will make you cringe, especially after you meet Joshua, who is the most offensively racist stereotype you will ever see in a commercial video game, ever. And, again, this is the
issue.
The larger problem is the plot, which is beyond stupid. Not because it is about unravelling a government conspiracy about aliens– real, actual, tinfoil suit wearing, bug-eyed aliens–, but because it has no direction or story structure: things just happen out of nowhere without rhyme or reason. Also, the humour is mostly sex jokes. Very childish sex jokes.
The insane, but entertaining characters are also replaced by one-dimensional clichés. Brian is now a goatee-wearing muscular douc
hebag who cheats on his girlfriend while she is being held in captivity. One of the antagonists is a military operative dominatrix with spider fetish. And don’t we ever forget Joshua, whose entire role is to extend all puzzles by ruining your initial solutions.
On the topic of puzzles: get a guide. Don’t even attempt to play this game by yourself. None of them make any sense, and they are so overcomplicated even walkthroughs can get entangled in their stupidity.
Is there anything good in this game besides the graphics? No, but the final Runaway title will redeem the series, if you manage to stay on board…

While I do recomend this game, be sure you know what you're getting before you do. It has the potential for hours of fun if you like this sort of game, but at the moment there is still a lot they can do with it.  It has quite a learning curve and is very difficult if you do not know what you are doing. While this means that, with patience, players can eventually build giant flying death machines to rain terror on their enemies, it also means that the lack of a proper tutorial level will severely hurt progress.You do have the R&D pack, but that costs extra money and is still a little overwhelming if you don't know what you are doing.
Another problem is that every time you die, you are back to a very weak, tiny tank and have to either go back and miraculusly defeat the enemy that killed you or start over from scratch, and neither option is a good one. This can lead to and endless cycle where you can never get to the point where the game really shines: when you already have all the parts you could ever need and get to create anything that comes to mind. There could be a solution to this: have an option to buy your old designs from the trade station. This would allow you to quickly get back to where you were, while still providing a punishment for death (having to pay for all the parts.) Speaking of which, another good addition would be the ability to sell off excess parts.
I personally requested a refund for my copy, but if this game ends up meeting its potential I would happily buy it back.
All in all, it has the potential for being a great game, but at the moment only people willing to risk it never panning out should get it. After all, that is what early access means, right?

XCOM 2 is bigger, better, and more fleshed out than XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within in every way (not including the Long War mod).
Almost everything has been improved upon to create a truly incredible sequel. The combat, or tactical view, has been improved, rebalanced, and is now much faster with the addition of Zip Mode. Managing your base, or strategic view, has also been improved, though less so than tactical view.
Tactical view is a turn based mode where you pit your squad of 4-6, depending on upgrades and you can raise the max with mods, against hordes of aliens while trying to reach an objective. Most missions will start out with your squad in concealment, at which point the aliens won't know where you are and you have to move as fast as possible towards the objective as most missions are timed. You can be seen while in concealment, though the game will notify you if an action will break concealment. An excellent strategy any player can use in concealment is, when you find a group (or 'pod', as they're called) of enemies, to set all but one of your soldiers to 'overwatch', a mode where they fire on any enemies they see move (though they only get one shot - improvable with upgrades), and using that last soldier to shoot, or launch a grenade, or use some sort of heavy weapon to break concealment. Nine times out of ten this will kill the entire pod in a single turn.
After concealment has been broken, you must use your available supplies and abilities to survive the alien onslaught while also completing your objective, be it extracting something, protecting something, or taking out a specific enemy. Sometimes the game will also force you to extract from the mission site, causing you to have to place an extraction zone and manually extract all of your soldiers one by one, often while fighting off more aliens.
As I said about the strategic view, it has been changed substantially less so. You no longer have to worry about aliens shooting down satellites, and you can no longer shoot down UFOs. Otherwise it is mostly the same, except for the part that your base moves around the world instead of staying in one place.
A new feature is the Character Pool, which allows you to create custom characters (AKA your friends and family) that can be encountered in any and all save files you may have. You can even set it so the game will only use characters from the Character Pool until it runs out, at which point it will create random characters to use, like how it was in EU/EW (though these characters are also fully customizable).
XCOM 2 is also one of the few games I would recommend getting the Digital Deluxe Edition, as two of the three (and rumored fourth) DLCs adds something new and truly unique to the experience that is XCOM 2. Getting both noteworthy DLCs (Alien Hunters and Shen's Last Gift) + the base game would cost more than the DDE itself, so there's that to consider.
Lastly, this game is almost completely moddable, so it has that over the first.
All in all, everything I love about the first has either been redone, improved, or both, and even more has been added. In a time of remasters, cashgrabs, and yearly releases that barely change a thing, this is a game worthy of the $60 price tag.

I've sunk hundreds of hours into this game and I don't regret any of them, not even the ones I spent when I could've been doing something more "productive." Stardew Valley has lovable characters, a relaxing atmosphere, and great music among other great aspects. It takes some time to understand how the world and mechanics work, but once you figure it out, you'll be arguing with yourself whether to plant Ancient Fruit because it's profitable or cranberries because you love the popping sound they make when you harvest them. You'll plan to spend the morning fishing and then realize it's 1:30 in the morning and you're about to pass out with dozens of squids in your inventory. Before you know it, you'll be married with kids and be best friends with the homeless man who lives in a tent in the mountains and gives you life advice. It's easy to lose track of time while playing this, and the time I've spent on this proves it. As a person with anxiety, this game relieves so much stress and gives me some soothing, non-stressful goals to focus on instead of school or work. My only complaints are a few minor, non-game-breaking glitches and the lack of things to do after completing both Mr. Qi's challenges and the community center. However, this didn't happen until I'd already poured about 200 hours into this game. If you need a quiet game to decompress with that's still fun and rewarding to play, Stardew Valley is definitely for you.

Buy the original instead of Black Mesa. Black Mesa's team did a fantastic job of recreating the world of Half Life with truly awe inspiring graphics and detail, but then they decided they could improve it by quadrupling the number of monsters and making all of them twice as deadly and treating the player like a moron. Given how much praise they're getting for it, I guess most of the people who paid money for it must be just that. Or maybe they just want a game about brainlessly shooting aliens, not being trapped alone and desperate in the once familiar crumbling remains of a now completely hostile underground laboratory, bombarded from all sides by insanity and chaos as reality itself unravels around you, sneaking and fighting from one end to the other in a mad attempt to just survive another hour.
Half Life has bad graphics because it's from 1998, but the pacing, atmosphere, narrative, and triple headed gameplay of exploration/puzzle solving/platforming shooty action outclass every other first person game from its day and just about all of them today as well. The primary brilliance of Half Life is immersion, kept intact by no cutscenes and peerless storytelling that leads the player along without revealing itself. Bad linear games keep players on track through force, making them do what the designers intended regardless of what the player thinks would be a good idea. Good linear games keep the player on track by designing the world to make the player want to do exactly what they need to to progress, and nobody does it better than Valve.

Runaway, Dream of the Turtle is the second installation after Runaway , Road adventure which I also played. Those games are made in the typical point and click adventure styles which was made famous by classics like Monkey Island or day of the tentacles in the 90s. Those games with some others made in the 90's are seen as the pinacle of adventure games, with their smart puzzles, great stories and humour, a golden age which is gone. Although adventure games are not as numerous or famous as they  once were, they are still around in the new millineum with various grades of quality and enjoyment.
Runaway , Dream of the Turtle, developped in 2006 is made in this spirit, a new take on adventure games with better graphics and newer functionality . I liked Road adventure , the first Runaway, well enough and it seemed Pendulo which developped the game had even more ressources to make this game, with better graphics (2,5 D animations some places) , nice, cartoony and longer cutscenes, more characters and longer story than before.
But I rather think this game is inferior to the first for several reasons:
The characters:
Where to start? the main character, Brian Basco, which was sympathic if not very interesting in the first installement, has become a arrogant douchey prancing in eurotrash cargo pants with a goatee on top of being boring and annoying. As a main character, he is also not a very nice person. During the game he basically two-times his girlfriend (who he is supposed to save) with the local bimbo on an island, then he litteraly pimps out his newfound lover in order to advance the plot, very classy. On another instance he  throw a character who actually wanted to help him litterally into the arms of an lustful polar bear, for an unclear destiny of either being maimed or violently violated. He might have gone away with it if the scene was funny, but it wasn't , my reaction was of pity and discuss mainly...
He get a little less annoying by the end of the game, but it's too little too late...
The other characters which help or counter our "hero" are not much better,it's a mixed bunch of annoying and forgettable clichè characters , some of them are bearable. in a few instances they might bring a smile on your lips, but don't expect much. The ones that are really annoying like Joshua will make you cringe, just think of something nice while they are in a scene...
The Graphics:
Honestly for a game from 2006, they're pretty good, the backgrounds are colourful and diverse and save the whole game from being a complete chore. The characters if you look away from their personality are cartoony and nicely done, my main critic is how frozen they look and how unnatural they're moving around. You could get away with it in 1994 when everything was pizelated, but I kind of expected better animations from the 2000's. The sounds and music are forgettable but ok.
The puzzle.
Nothing revolutionnary here, the normal point and click routine. While some of the puzzles are ok both in complexity and logic, some others are really hard and arcane, and you end up trying all kind of combination or to save time and your nerves, check a walkthrough.
In few instances I manage to solve a puzzle by luck , I couldn't help but feel bewildered by the unlogic solution. Other times , the whole setting didn't make sence, like when you have to solve a rather complex chains of events to get a measly notebook from another character while roaming in a huge and expensive multimillions dollars yacht full of expensive stuff.
To be honest the puzzles in the game are no worse than in many other middle of the road adventure games, but they're not better either, if you put on top of that a rather unlikable main character and annoying surroundings, it just makes thing worse.
The story and dialogs
The story is rather forgettable and not especially intersesting, which would have been ok with good characters and nice and witty dialogues, but Runaway , The Dream of the Turtle has none of that. It could have been if the writers had put more time in designing their characters to be more interessting and put some humour in the game through the dialogues. But instead we've get one liners that aren't even remotely funny and strange situations that don't make sence, since they were intended to be humourous but weren't.
The creative minds behind this game this put some effort in putting most of the poor female characters in vaguely sexy skimpy outfit , probably to appeal to the more juvenile segment of the player with a bit of softcore . But it end up giving the game an almost mysoginistic feel since most female characters end up being just eyecandies at some level.
Conclution:
It's definitively not the worse adventure game out there, but it's really not among the best, it's barely mediocre. I didn't hate playing it, but I definitively won't repeat the feat. The sad thing is that it could have been a lot better if they had put better writers to bring up more interesting characters with better and humourous dialogues.

Half Life is a First Person Shooter that takes place in a hidden laboratory that experiments with teleportation. As you can guess things quickly go wrong and our protagonist Gordon Freeman must fight to survive. Gordon is an engineer but he is proficient with firearms and has no qualms about killing. He is a generic mute character with no personality and very little back-story. As is pretty much everyone you meet throughout this adventure. There are only three character models of scientists and one character model of the security guard rehashed throughout the game. It quickly makes you stop caring if they survive an encounter since you will surely meet the same exact guy again. I know it is from 1998 but it would have been better to make those three scientist models count and have actual characters in the game instead of meeting an endless clone of scientists throughout.
The story is told during gameplay and there are no cutscenes which is nice. If you don't care about story you can just as easily whack the character talking instead of listening to them. There is no consequence for killing allies but sometimes they do lead to some extra loot or simply help you fight off aliens. It feels like a grand adventure since all the missions are seamless and connect together perfectly. Most of the areas early on are bland and gray but it is impressive how much variety there is in the actual objectives to get through them. It is never as simple as running and gunning, if something can go wrong it always does for poor Gordon.
Which leads to my main problem with the game. The amount of platforming is kind of ridiculous and it  feels pretty awkward. They also demand too much precision as well as that annoying need to crouch jump to reach just a tiny bit higher so you can jump over certain objects. Another similar problem is that ladders are extremely unreliable and you never know if Gordon will hold on to it causing you to have to try over and over again. Luckily missing it is very rarely fatal although trying to go down one can be fatal as Gordon decides he has no need for ladders and that he can land a 30 ft fall. Quick saving is a godsend and makes these situations much more tolerable. The puzzles are never too complicated though the game can be inconsistent at times such as certain identical objects are not destructible but suddenly one is. Or just plain odd like them expecting you to figure out you can change tracks by shooting a sign during the railcart level.
Actual gameplay fairs a lot better. You start off with a crowbar and quickly get a pistol which I used throughout the whole game since it has decent damage and is very accurate.  Most of the weapons are pretty standard like an assault rifle, shotgun and revolver but there are some pretty unique weapons late game. Some do share certain types of ammo like the assault rifle and the pistol. The assault rifle and shotgun are pretty inaccurate which makes sense considering Gordon is an engineer.  Gordon's main source of survival is some kind of special suit that takes the impact out of most damage and allows navigation through toxic hazards. For a while at least, Gordon does not wear a helmet for some reason and the toxicity will kill him eventually. The suit works pretty much the same as armor from any other FPS of the time and can be recharged by finding small glowing vials or through a wall mounted H.E.V center. The same goes for health, both first aid kits laying around and wall mounted health centers will heal you.
Enemies in this game each have their own unique attack patterns and have pretty good AI. Most of the time humans will be your greatest foe since bullets are way too fast to dodge in this and they pull off impressive maneuvers at times such as when you chase them they drop a grenade behind them allowing them to regroup. The security guards yo can have follow you around are completely useless on the other hand. Most of the times they don't react until they get struck first and are only useful to distract the enemies. The game does steadily introduce new powerful enemies but you will be fighting mostly the same group of enemies from beginning to end. Aliens do look very weird and are not simply just humanoid enemies. Some enemies have weird death animations that play whenever they are dying so make sure to recognize them and not waste any ammo even though they are still moving.
Overall Half Life is a pretty good game but don't let all the praise make you expect something amazing. There is no gripping story here nor is there even any characters aside from one mysterious man. Platforming in a FPS very rarely works and it sure as heck doesn't here. Still it is a solid title when it is not trying to be an Adventure game instead of a FPS. Half Life continue to be supported after all these years so it features modern controls and modern resolutions which is always nice. The physics like boxes floating on water and some puzzles solved by it are pretty fun to watch and neat. This is definitely a thinking mans shooter, you will be fighting your surroundings as much as shooting guns. If you can stomach all the forced platforming and want more in your FPS than shooting hordes of bad guys this is the game for you.

Like Runaway 1, it's not the best adventure game out there. However, I still liked it even more than the first. It's true that there are many annoying parts, such as not being able to skip animations, or having to repeat the same action many times. In this way, The Dream of the Turtle is perhaps worse than the first game. Despite these potentially major problems however, I think it's still possible to fully enjoy this game. The story and characters make you want to keep playing, even if you have to use a walkthrough for a significant percentage of the puzzles like I did. Besides, there is a lot of humor and crazy situations to keep things interesting.
To get the best experience, I would play Runaway: A Road Adventure first. That way you'll be more invested in the world of Runaway, which will make it easier and more enjoyable.  Overall a very good adventure game with many laughs and references that really got me pumped for Runaway 3 (which was truly amazing by the way).

PREFACE! This is not another negative review about broken game or complaining about the actual genre of game this is (That being an interactive miniseries show.) It worked fine for me, and The Wolf Among Us is one of my favorite games (It's also made by Telltale.)
Don't get me wrong, it's a pretty decent game, good in fact. But 2 episodes in and i'm bored. It's just a chore. Personally The Wolf Among Us does a supremely better job of hooking the player and keeping interest. This game is far too slowed down by it's "free-roam" segments. It teases puzzle action, but they aren't very interesting puzzles.
And during action scenes any single failure of the QTE results in failure, forcing you to start the QTE segment over again. While this makes it "more of a game", it also makes it less enjoyable. In the Wolf Among Us, i never had a lose game state because i would only occasionally fail an unexpected QTE, so it made my character seem less invincible, but didn't penalize you, it made the narrative feel more interactive if anything.
Overall, if you want a good Telltale game, I recommend The Wolf Among Us (also tip for that game, read the fairy tale entries occasionally as they often provide new information to characters.)

I can highly recommend this game with one caveat - you have to have a system that can run it.
This game shipped with a lot of problems, but the worst of the problems was the system requirements. A lot of players were rightly upset when the game performed poorly on their systems which met the game's requirements. Other players with beefy systems, expecting smooth 60 FPS gameplay like they see in other modern games, were frustrated by 30 FPS frame rates in Unity. Still others, thinking they could squeak by on an older system, were frustrated by crashes, glitches and all manner of problems.
The bottom line is: ignore the minimum specs for this game. They are not accurate. If your system meets the *recommended* specs or better, you can play the game. Players with SLI setups may still have graphical issues, but I suspect that players with SLI setups are used to having graphical issues in various games.
The biggest reason that I can recommend this game now is due to the latest video drivers from AMD and Nvidia. The latest (beta in Nvidia's case) drivers significantly improve performance and go a long way towards making the game more enjoyable. Still, if your system just meets the required specs and you use high graphics settings, expect to see 30 FPS framerates. If you're playing the game with a controller, as it was meant to be played, that's not really a problem. It's still quite playable. Using a mouse to look around, 30 FPS can be a drag.
I played all the way through the game with 30 FPS frame rates, and I still had a lot of fun with it. The combat is much improved, no more counter-to-win. The Paris Stories and murder mystery missions are outstanding. The voice acting and music are superb. I really enjoyed the story, too, though opinions differ on that one. I didn't run into any crashing bugs or glitches at all, and I am not alone in that. The only thing that really gave me trouble was the companion app, but since its latest update it is working well, too.
I'm just starting my 3rd playthrough of the game, and I wouldn't be doing that if I wasn't having fun with it. If your system can handle the frankly poorly optimized graphics of this game, I say go for it.

Runaway, The Dream of The Turtle is game 2 of the Runaway trilogy and while it has it's faults (I'll get to them) overall it was a pretty fun adventure point-and-click that reminds me a lot of the later Kings Quest adventures.
The story has 5 chapters which vary in difficulty with the first chapter being surprisingly difficult in that you have to somewhat aimlessly move your pointer around the screen to see what lights up to move forward (hint: look up). The second and third chapter pick up steam and you're much more easily able to figure out what to do while the fourth chapter has one puzzle that is not intuitive at all (at least...to me). The fifth chapter has a really fun math puzzle that I greatly enjoyed figuring out on a piece of paper. With regards to the "not so intuitive" puzzles you can sometimes find yourself clicking and re-clicking objects to see if they interact or give you clues as to what to do next when you get stuck. As with the first game you sometimes have to research an area or talk to a person AGAIN to move the story forward but the game is pretty good at letting you know when to do that.
Overall, though, I had a lot of fun playing. The story is fun and there are quite a few throwbacks to the first Runaway game which made me laugh. The different chapters were varied enough that I never got bored with the scenary and the dialogue almost always drives the story forward. LOVED the "dumb" soldier who kept helping out and the beach chapter was probably one of best puzzles I've played in awhile.
If you like point-and-click adventures I definitely recommend you try this one out. It's on par with the Sierra adventure games we all remember and love. You may have to check out a walk-thru once of twice but it's definitely a "recommend".

I know I don't have a load of playtime in this game so far, but despite my short playtime, I already love this game to pieces. And I honestly want to play more, I just haven't been able to find time to. But I'm pretty sure, like everyone else, my playtime will get a definite boost when the multiplayer comes out. So without further ado, let's get onto my review of Stardew Valley
Stardew Valley is such an amazing game, it's a great experience for people who love the farming simulators that we used to have in the form of Harvest Moon. It was well loved by it's developer, and made to damn near perfection. Despite the game being in Terraria and Starbound graphics, the game's visuals still manage to catch your attention and make you happy, you feel content just looking at this game even though it's not in the HD standard that most gaming companies go for today. Stardew Valley just gets it's visuals right with all the colors it provides, and no object is taken for granted in it. You're fully content with all the game contains in a visual sense
Stardew Valley also has some astounding music that fits the theme of the game like no other, it's a calming and relaxing, like you'd expect from a game based around a farming simulator. The music is just beautiful, Chucklefish has made another game that contains music that just fits, you feel calm listening to the music of Stardew Valley while your managing your crops and tending to your animals. There is no sudden spikes in mood, this game just keeps you in a relaxed state and it's music is a great help in keeping you in that mood. Additionally, the sounds in Stardew Valley are also amazing, listening to the ocean on the beach in this game gives you a feeling of serenity. Stardew Valley's sounds and music are just things you can just fully relax to, these combined together forms just a beautiful soundtrack, that I'd highly recommend you listen to, especially in moments where you simply need to keep yourself calm, the soundtrack is definetly one you can take a nap to.
The characters in this game are all well loved and very diverse. You can just see these characters as real people, with their own real struggles, struggles that I believe some people can definetly identify with. Every person in Stardew Valley leaves an impression on you, good or bad, and you can't help but love the atmosphere they all create together. No character in this game, much like it's visuals, are taken for granted here, you simply just don't meet anybody who's a cardboard cutout of a character, who simply exists to take up space. Everyone in here is a different individual, with their own likes and dislikes. From the children in the game, all the way to the mayor himself, these people are just that, people. And throughout this game you can interact with every single one of them, and slowly learn who they are as you cement your place in this new home you found in Stardew Valley. But, you have to play the game and interact with everyone to get to who they are underneath the surface of their inital character, everyone leaves a starting impression on you when you first meet and that tends to make you judge them before really interacting with them. But as you play this game, you can develop friendships and relationships with all these characters and as you develop these, their real personallity begins to unravel. As you become friendly with these characters, they show you just who they are on the inside, instead of the inital impression you get at the start, and with time you truly being to understand them. The characters in this game are simply amazing, and that's all there is to it.
You'd think that since Stardew Valley is mainly a farming simulator, that it wouldn't have any form of a good plot or story, but you would be absolutely wrong. Stardew Valley contains a really great story, and easily surpases all other farming simulators in this right. In the very beginning of the game, you're introduced to the conflict that is between the community of Stardew Valley vs JoJaMart. JojaMart wants to take over the small town of Stardew Valley for their own profit, while the community of said town want to remain as they are without JoJaMart interfering. You have the choice to decide what side of the conflict you want to take, you can either take the easy way out of the conflict by siding with JoJaMart which has it's consequences, OR you can side with the community of Stardew Valley and help them in their struggle against this large company that wants to ruin the home they has spent all up to now making. As you can develop relationships with the Stardew Valley's people, and become close friends with them all, you can also develop a romantic relationship with a special someone within this game.
*NOTE: This game allows you to go for same-sex relationships without having to mod the game, unlike most games today where you can still only have straight relationships. And I personally believe that that's a beautiful little detail for ConcernedApe to include*
The story of Stardew Valley is most definetly superior to any other game like it, and it makes this game all the more replayable, just so you can see the different outcomes of different ways you can progress this story.
I'm... not the best at explaining mechanics of a game, so you're gonna have to take a look at other reviews for a more in-depth review of those, but I can honestly say that Stardew Valley is an amazingly crafted game, and the control of the game just feels completely right, you are very clearly in control of what you do here, from where you plant your crops, to down you defend yourself while dungeon crawling. Stardew Valley is a game that just feels good to play, if you're a fan of games like it.
Stardew Valley is just a beautiful game, with atmospheric music, amazing visuals, diverse characters, and an outstanding story. It's definetly a game I'd highly recommend people pick up, and I say it's most assuredly worth the money I paid for it. I think other people believe that Stardew Valley was developed to be a kind of successor of the ever-popular series Harvest Moon, myself included for a time. But I can assure you that Stardew Valley is so much more than that, if it was developed to be that way, then the people at ConcernedApe did far more than make a successor, they absolutely made a game that surpases the old Harvest Moon, and has become it's own game outright, and they're still developing new things for the game today. Soon enough we're going to be getting a Co-op function for the game that I am excited for, and it will probably boost the playtime I have on it.
Stardew Valley is an amazing game, and I would really recommend you pick it up if you ever get the chance.

It is not as good as Dark Souls, but still has one or two features that I really liked about it.
I would decribe it as mix between Dark Souls 2 (where everything was a bit slower) and Darksiders (from the design).
The story was a 7/10 for me but I liked that you could change your path here and there.
I seems kinda dull. You find a random weapon with a socket on it, where you can put in a number of runes (random drop) you have to decipher. If you want a better chance for a better rune you can "bet" up to 1.000 EXP on a big rune and I think up to 500 on a small one... you see I didn't even decipher the small runes from some point on.
I just put 1.000 EXP in all the big runes and got the good runes where I only needed 3 max for a weapon and I got 3 at the beginning. My sword/axe only needed the lucky runes... lucky runes = more scaling.
For me the runes on armor where total useless. No big difference. I used mostly heavy armor and strength weapon.
You're not as agile as in Dark Souls 3 for example. If you wear heavy armor. You feel that you use heavy armor. There is no fast, medium or slow roll. There was only slow roll for me when I was wearing heavy armor and still got 20 units of equipment left.
The same with great weapons... you can't even swing a polesword or greataxe with one hand. You have to use 2hand.
This was a cool idea at first but later on I only found great weapons and so I only used my normal axe/sword, because I used a towershield and didn't like the slow swings of great weapons.
I felt like I was Arthas from Warcraft with my dark themed heavy armor you can find. The medium armor design was cool either but I can't say anything about the light armor. (didn't wore it)
I used the defensiv magic skill tree, Solace. I got myself the skill Shelter which gives you massiv boost to defense and thorn damage, plus you heal yourself over time. I didn't even used my healing potions because I didn't needed it with my HOT spell.
Every skill tree has the standard spell "Prayer", which is simply a decoy, and 3 skill tree specific spells. Like I said I only needed one. They could have added a bit more magic and spells for my taste.
OH I almost forgot. At the beginning you find a gauntlet which is like a refilling magic cannon. You can add runes to it to change the damage type or complety change the function. Like a stun gun for example.
I used mostly heavy armor with normal sized weapons and I started as a cleric with the defensiv magic, Solace. Paid 10€ on a key website and played for 10 hours. Worth my money.

Degree of Difficulty 4/10 (sadly it was way to easy for me... but I'm used to Souls so)

Half Life is a First Person Shooter that takes place in a hidden laboratory that experiments with teleportation. As you can guess things quickly go wrong and our protagonist Gordon Freeman must fight to survive. Gordon is an engineer but he is proficient with firearms and has no qualms about killing. He is a generic mute character with no personality and very little back-story. As is pretty much everyone you meet throughout this adventure. There are only three character models of scientists and one character model of the security guard rehashed throughout the game. It quickly makes you stop caring if they survive an encounter since you will surely meet the same exact guy again. I know it is from 1998 but it would have been better to make those three scientist models count and have actual characters in the game instead of meeting an endless clone of scientists throughout.
The story is told during gameplay and there are no cutscenes which is nice. If you don't care about story you can just as easily whack the character talking instead of listening to them. There is no consequence for killing allies but sometimes they do lead to some extra loot or simply help you fight off aliens. It feels like a grand adventure since all the missions are seamless and connect together perfectly. Most of the areas early on are bland and gray but it is impressive how much variety there is in the actual objectives to get through them. It is never as simple as running and gunning, if something can go wrong it always does for poor Gordon.
Which leads to my main problem with the game. The amount of platforming is kind of ridiculous and it  feels pretty awkward. They also demand too much precision as well as that annoying need to crouch jump to reach just a tiny bit higher so you can jump over certain objects. Another similar problem is that ladders are extremely unreliable and you never know if Gordon will hold on to it causing you to have to try over and over again. Luckily missing it is very rarely fatal although trying to go down one can be fatal as Gordon decides he has no need for ladders and that he can land a 30 ft fall. Quick saving is a godsend and makes these situations much more tolerable. The puzzles are never too complicated though the game can be inconsistent at times such as certain identical objects are not destructible but suddenly one is. Or just plain odd like them expecting you to figure out you can change tracks by shooting a sign during the railcart level.
Actual gameplay fairs a lot better. You start off with a crowbar and quickly get a pistol which I used throughout the whole game since it has decent damage and is very accurate.  Most of the weapons are pretty standard like an assault rifle, shotgun and revolver but there are some pretty unique weapons late game. Some do share certain types of ammo like the assault rifle and the pistol. The assault rifle and shotgun are pretty inaccurate which makes sense considering Gordon is an engineer.  Gordon's main source of survival is some kind of special suit that takes the impact out of most damage and allows navigation through toxic hazards. For a while at least, Gordon does not wear a helmet for some reason and the toxicity will kill him eventually. The suit works pretty much the same as armor from any other FPS of the time and can be recharged by finding small glowing vials or through a wall mounted H.E.V center. The same goes for health, both first aid kits laying around and wall mounted health centers will heal you.
Enemies in this game each have their own unique attack patterns and have pretty good AI. Most of the time humans will be your greatest foe since bullets are way too fast to dodge in this and they pull off impressive maneuvers at times such as when you chase them they drop a grenade behind them allowing them to regroup. The security guards yo can have follow you around are completely useless on the other hand. Most of the times they don't react until they get struck first and are only useful to distract the enemies. The game does steadily introduce new powerful enemies but you will be fighting mostly the same group of enemies from beginning to end. Aliens do look very weird and are not simply just humanoid enemies. Some enemies have weird death animations that play whenever they are dying so make sure to recognize them and not waste any ammo even though they are still moving.
Overall Half Life is a pretty good game but don't let all the praise make you expect something amazing. There is no gripping story here nor is there even any characters aside from one mysterious man. Platforming in a FPS very rarely works and it sure as heck doesn't here. Still it is a solid title when it is not trying to be an Adventure game instead of a FPS. Half Life continue to be supported after all these years so it features modern controls and modern resolutions which is always nice. The physics like boxes floating on water and some puzzles solved by it are pretty fun to watch and neat. This is definitely a thinking mans shooter, you will be fighting your surroundings as much as shooting guns. If you can stomach all the forced platforming and want more in your FPS than shooting hordes of bad guys this is the game for you.

People say DD is RNG based. Maybe. Maybe. In that same logic, Darksouls is RNG based. No that does not sound right.  Well it is. There is under the hud systems that is not clearly pointed out to players. Here I'm going to spoil the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of those systems but nothing story based.
-Hit chance always caps out at 90% chance, this counts for blights and status effect. For both you and the monsters.
-There is phases to the fight, first the rush of you trying to kill the monster's dps and stress casters which tend to hang out in row 3-4. Then after that you want high chance stunners like the hound master or the bounty hunter to stun either the first 2 rows or 1 monster that is left over. You have 2 turns of a single monster hanging around before your heros take stress damage if its an single row monster.
-If your smart, you will almost always take 1 healer, 1 stunner, 1 stress healer and 1 dps.  It's ok to have 2 dps that can stun, you just want to spec just one for stunning though. The best healer is the vestel.
-If there is a shrine wanting you to but a torch into it, don't. You will die, you will cry.
-Having at lest one scout chance item is a party is a must have.
-Nearly everything can be 'turned off' with an item. Some things like a sack of books or a book self will give you stress and nasty stuff most of the time and should be avoided. On that note don't touch dead things unless you either have herbs or bandages. Back packs are never trapped.
-Remove kleptomaniac as fast as possible or flat out disband people with this. There is other lesser things that will force your person to interact with things. Remove this as fast as possible. He does not know where that body has been!
-If your still having issues like hitting things. Use the Jester and run buff and destress. You can ignore his other skills other then the 2-3 bleed he does which is ok but not perfect.
-Always disband a Leaper. He can't rush the 3-4 row, destress others or even stun the front row. Crusader is 110% better then the Leaper at everything since he can stress heal which is the main use I have him for. When he can stun his low hit chance, speed and over all low stun chance makes me rather use the Hunter or Hound for this role every single time.
-The first hit into death door can't kill someone and it takes 1 hp heal to get them out of it. Having at lest one other person with a low heal other then your main healer is always nice. Blights and bleeds will trigger death's door roll, on that hero's turn.
-Never bring a bleeder to the ruins or cove. With that said don't bring blighters to the other 2 places.
-Always remove trinkets from heros after every run. Also always try to get them to pray. Never use places like the Tavern unless you have to.

Keep this issues in mind when choosing whether to purchase this game.
Runaway, the Dream of the Turtle is a point and click adventure game by Pendulo. It is the sequel to Runaway, a Road Adventure, and the second in the Runaway trilogy. In this adventure, Brian and Gina are continuing their island vacation shown at the end of the previous game. Things go awry, however, and Brian must become the hero once again.
Mechanics in this game are exactly the same as the previous entry in the series. You can switch between looking at and interacting with objects using the right mouse click. Double click on scene transitions to switch quickly to the next scene.
I did not notice much of a change from the graphics of Runaway, a Road Adventure, so my same critiques apply. Backgrounds look great once again. There are more of a variety in backgrounds as well this time, which is a nice addition. Character models could use some improvement. The voice acting is mostly similar, so serviceable without any major complaints.
There are some story concerns this time around. Once again, almost zero interaction is had with Gina through the majority of the game, so it's hard to feel an attachment to her. Brian must feel this way too, since he jumps at the first new girl he finds on his adventure. I do have some issues with one of the characters, Joshua. He feels a little too much like a stereotype for my liking. The man character also dabbles in some light racism through the use of blackface while in disguise. The main character, Brian, comes off as very punchable during the first half of the game is in island attire. I believe it is the combination of soul patch and spiky hair that does it. The humor overall is funny at times, corny at others. There are some problems with pacing, with some areas done in a flash and others taking a very long time.
The puzzles are very similar in style to the previous game in the series. You will have to spend some time trying to pick up everything in the scene to see what works. There is a fair bit of combining objects to complete puzzles. Some use the dreaded adventure game logic, but there are no unwinnable scenarios or deaths so you really just need to keep plugging away.
Overall, I see Runaway, the Dream of the Turtle as on par with Runaway, a Road Adventure. There are some positive developments, such as variety, and some negatives. I would have given it the same score and my recommendation if there had not been a problem running the game. Since performance is spotty for AMD video cards, and I even had some crashes with my Nvidia based laptop that caused me to lose a good deal of progress, I cannot recommend this game.
Score: C-

This review is written by someone who has played every AC game with the exception of Rogue. In each installment, I have achieved 98%+ synch with 100% in Black Flag, Liberation, and Brotherhood. I have completed the AC:Unity main storyline and am leaving the game at 62% synch. I just cannot continue navigating around the map doing all of the side quests and gathering the collectibles.
The beauty of the older AC games is the ability to enter a new zone and clear the map. This is nearly impossible in AC:U. Aside from the Nomad chests littering the map (of which I have been playing the Companion App since release and am about 70% done) completed Rift and Co-op quests still remain on the map. This makes it harder to prioritize what stil needs to be completed, etc. The older version had a map filter, so does AC:U. However, the filter does not allow for customization like the older versions and you cannot filter "Collectibles."
Graphically the game is amazing. The story is ok. There is not real-world connection outside of the Animus like Black Flag had. You're just locked in there the entire game. This creates a lack of depth which made the other games so involving. From an AC fan with over 300 hours invested into the series, I am fairly disappointed with this installment.

This is absolutely one of my favorite game series, so if I'm a little biased take what I say with a grain of salt.
The Walking Dead is a heavily story-driven series. In this first season, you play as Lee Everett, a character you'll definitely get attached to along the way. As TWD is heavily story-driven and choice-based, the choices you make impact how other characters will view or act towards Lee. Nearly every choice is timed, so if you don't think quick a choice will be made for you. The only choices that cannot be made for you are some life/death decisions when forced to save one character over another/over not saving them. Overall, the actual action gameplay isn't really there, so if you're looking for just another zombie game, then this probably isn't for you. While there is some zombie killing, your goal is usually stealth-killing them, so this definitely isn't a shooter, though that's not to say you never see a gun in this game.
However, as stated before, the story is heavily based on choices and the game's plot. The great thing abut this is, you WILL get emotionally attached to characters. I don't remember how long episodes are in this season, but they are fairly long and will take over an hour to play through.
I don't want to spoil this game as telling much more than basic expectations might spoil the plot, so here are some pros and cons of the game:
Pros:
-Great plot
-Plot doesn't conflict/bring over spoilers for the TWD comics or TV Series
-One character in the game has made appearances in both the comic and TV series though, if you've seen/read either you will recognise him and probably be happy about it
-You can make really sassy choices and become sass-master Lee
-The art style is amazing and unique
-The game is easy to play through in the sense that you won't get "stuck" at a point over and over, the flow of the game makes things pretty obvious and if you do get stuck it won't be forever
-I said it before but the characters are really easy to get attached to, you get a pretty good depth of who they are and what their morals are.
Cons:
-Story isn't too largely effected by your choices. Choices make more of a plot impact in Season 2.
-Point and click aspects to it, so sometimes figuring things out takes some time/gets annoying
-Some of the characters are nasty pieces of crap and you just want to kill them
-You can't expect the outcomes of some decisions, especially with Kenny
-Not a lot of "action"
-The ending (not that it's bad per se, but you'll know what I mean when you play it.)
The cons really aren't that bad, honestly. Overall, TWD is definitely for a specific audience. I'd say if you love the storylines in games and you are interested in zombies/post-apocolyptic situations, this game is for you.

First off, let me say this: on sale, this is a fun PAC-MAN spin-off, especially if you're playing it casually and on short bursts. That alone deserves my recommendation.
However, for someone who played and 100% the original Championship Edition DX+, this sequel is very disappointing. Most mechanics were changed, and that means that this feels like a different game, instead of a cheap expansion, but for me it was much worse. There's only one change that i liked: in the original, to have the best scores you needed to almost always follow a certain path, and in here you have a bit more freedom. Now for the things i didn't liked: The ghosts are more harmless, and most of the time you just run straight into them, and only then you can die if you touch them; Eating ghosts is frustrating and less satisfying. You can get better at it, but sometimes it feels like a lottery; Most of the new songs aren't that great, but thankfully you can choose the original ones, however you have to unlock them first; The game is freaking hard to master, and a completionist nightmare; Ranks are tied to scores, instead of your position in the leaderboards; You only have access to the top 50 replays; There isn't a global score, which was neat; And worst of all, the lack of modes. Not counting the tutorial, there's the classic score attack mode, with 10 courses each with 3 difficulty settings, and adventure mode. But adventure mode is mostly the same, to collect a set amount of fruit in a set amount of time. And the boss battles are terribly disappointing. They're essentially a harder main stage. Looking at the trailer, you may think that the big ghost can actually hurt you. Nope! It's just part of the background! There's no 10-minute stages, apart from practice. You can't practice a certain part of a stage or a certain ghost killing section. And the controls feel less responsive. When you start the game, the mouse icon doesn't even hide, so you need to push it to a corner! WTF? And there's no Steam Cloud! I also experienced some lag a few times.
So, if you want to play it casually, get it on sale. If you want to master it, you're better off sticking to the original Championship Edition DX+. It's a much better experience.

Somewhere during my first playthrough of Bastion, I forced myself to pause the game and wipe the tears from my eyes.
Bastion is by no means a depressing game.  Maybe my emotions acted the way they would normally react if I had been placed in "the Kid's" shoes.  Maybe, as I listened to a tale of struggle to piece together the fragments of a shattered reality, I felt sympathy towards the protagonist.  But there are plenty of games or movies or stories where there is suffering and struggle.  Just because suffering exists, we don't automatically feel suffering as well.  Yet something about Bastion was making me care about the world and the few people that remained in it.
This immersion, as I'll call it, can't stem from one specific aspect of Supergiant's game.  It's the occasional quip and endearing voice of the narrator as he tells the tale of a young boy who took on a burden many times the size of himself.  It’s the lush scenery, brightly colored and lovingly crafted as it pieces together paths and hallways ahead of you, only to tumble away into the abyss as the world falls apart. I'm kinda torn about this game. Overall, I really liked my time with it, but there are some BIG problems with it.
The game is beautifully thematic. The Lovecraftian plot and dreary art style are very enjoyable. The stress system is, to me, genius. It fits the games theme and forces the player into changing up their party after every run. My first ~20 hours with this game were some of my favorite in my recent gaming history, but after that the game slowly starts to drag. The new DLC helped me out at this stage, as it released when I got around 20 hours into my first run and gave a breath of fresh air to my experience. Without it I may have put it down at this point.
There is a big issue in the mid game. There isn't a tonne of variety in mission types, and there are only 8 bosses in the base game, each of which is repeated three times at different difficulties. This has two effects; it both allows you to understand how each mission, region and boss functions to plan your mission better, but also makes the mid game feel very repetitive. I think there 'grinding' becomes problematic here. You just do the same few missions over and over again to level characters up and unlock subsequent bosses.
Towards the end of the game, things started to get more interesting for me. As you enter the 'Champion' stages your roster should be filled with lots of level 6 characters and you should understand how the games mechanics work. The game becomes genuinely tense at the higher levels, and your favorite heros can easily die if you slip up. I found the game, for the most part, fair. Only one character died for a reason I felt wasn't my fault in some way. Some might say that is still too much but hey, I didn't mind. It's a game based off of percent chances, so there's always going to be a degree of randomness. The end game boss in the Crimson Courtyard DLC took me a couple tries. (Full disclosure, I lost a whole team to that boss. Twice). I think I learnt about the boss in each of those attempts, and had fun, but this difficulty can emphasise the 'grinding' issue if you lose critical team members and need to train new ones.
At the end of the game, when you assault the eponymous dungeon, the game becomes fresh once more. New level designs for each stage and interesting mechanics on each attempt. However, another massive problem rears its head here. For almost no discernable reason, you can't send the same hero into the Darkest Dungeon twice. Guess what that means? MORE GRINDING. Yay.
I'm divided. I really loved my time with the game. The story was interesting, the atmosphere captivating and the gameplay fun, but the issue with repetition and grinding in the midgame tarnishes my love for this game. I am sure I will remember my experience with this game fondly.
If the setting of the game is interesting of you and you believe you would enjoy the mechanics, I would recommend you pick the game up. It's fun. Even if you don't push past the grind of a mid game, the first few dozen hours of your time with the game will probably be worth it.

I started a drunken bar brawl and lost my favorite pocket watch.  Instead of learning from my lesson and that the pocket watch was the price paid I killed three to four dozen guys to get the watch back.  Setting me up for lifelong success.
UPDATE: Now that I've finished the main story line, some thoughts.
I still recommend the game *if* you have the system to run it and like the series, however it's one of the weakest in the series.
For reference I ran the game at 1920x1080 with graphics max'd and rarely had a performance issue (i7-3770, 16GB RAM, GTX 970 4GB RAM, 64GB SDD as a cache on top of a 1TB drive).  Was this top notch FPS?  No it wasn't, I think every Assassin's Creed is a bit of a slog, but the performance wasn't bad at all, it was consistently good enough to pretty much never distract from the experience.
Anyways onto the game itself:
- City itself is incredible visually, it's a shame the main story line doesn't take you to the southern areas to help break up the visuals.
- You never really get into the character, as such I developed my own thoughts about who and what the character believed in.  Only to then get into scripted sequences where my character would act out of line with my perception of who I've developed him to be.  This makes for a bad experience.  Why does this happen?  There are three reasons I think:
1) Not enough time is spent developing the character into an assassin.  Just one day you are one, and you can do some pretty crazy stuff right from day one.  Missed opportunity to grow the character here.
2) All your equipment upgrades and skill upgrades are simply a function of hitting ESC and purchasing them from a menu when you have the resources.  Huge missed opportunity here to force interactions between the character and his peers here help flesh him out as well as the backstory.
3) Some of the main story available to help fill in who the character is and why he's doing what he's doing come in the form of letters delivered to your home.  However there is no notification when a letter arrives.  It was only at the conclusion of the game that I became aware that there were a stack of letters to read because the area they're placed in you have little reason to visit.
These are all things Black Flag does MUCH MUCH better, it's a shame to see such a step back.
- Ignore the folks complaining about MTX, the MTX in this game can be completely ignored.  First upgrade your base in Paris as fast as possible, between the income you generate with it and by simply collecting chests, cockades, and completing crowd events while you travel to story missions you'll quickly have almost top tier equipment.  This is another area of game imbalance.  Within ~4-6 hours of playing the game I had gear that was so much better than the content I was being provided that it made combat largely a joke until the very end of the game.  It also made weapon and armor rewards from most quests totally irrelevant and made the benefit of doing the quests seem nil.  Gear progression is very poorly thought out and the game experience suffers for it (Disclaimer: I did come into the game with some level of rewards already from playing previous games in the series, I'm not sure how much this impacted the experience).
- Locked Chests, Initiate Chests, Nomad Chests - all of these make for a horrible experience. Two reasons:
1) Right off the bat they're visible on your minimap, so you're inclined to go and try to collect them.  What happened to buying maps that add this info to your ingame map? This AC standard is nowhere to be seen and would help gate map clutter.
2) Once you find a chest and realize you're not able to open it there's nothing added to your information that allows you to note that it can't be opened currently.
- Once you approach a locked chest it should be noted on your map in some fashion what level the chest is.
- Initiate Chests should only become available/visible once you've reached the appropriate initiate level.
- There should be an option to hide Nomad Chests or some sort of filtering if you don't want to play the companion mobile app (it's unclear if these chests count towards % complete or not)
- Normal chests behind locked doors, these are really dickish.  Shouldn't be done, or the level of the locked door should be added to your map information.
- High level chests on low level story missions, you spend 3/4th of the game doing story quests and while on them generally at some point passing by chests you can't unlock.  Very frustrating, locked chests encountered on story missions should be at a skill level you could open at that point in the story.  I eventually conditioned myself to never approach a locked chest until I had max'd my lockpick level.
- Climbing - all the new moves/animations when climbing are awesome.  However there are many times Arno found hand holds where none appear to be present and many more times I saw places that looked like obvious hand holds that I couldn't get Arno to use.
- BUG: There appears to be a bug that if you ledge kill someone you then can't climb up onto said ledge until you move somewhere else then move back, then attempt to climb up onto the ledge.  This made many 'badass entrances' into a room a lot less so as Arno fumbles around.
- Disconnect: Sometimes Arno will leap incredible distances from one roof top to another, very inhuman distances covered, yet he'll not do the same when trying to air assassinate someone.  Frustrating.
- Double Air Assassinations are too hard to pull off.  There are times it appears obvious you will get one to instead only get one guy.
- Crowd Events - I liked these, but they are too frequent.  Many times they crop up when they shouldn't, these should be suppressed when on a story mission. There's no ingame way to preview the rewards for completing the crowd events.  Also sometimes these come off silly - ex: a thug is literally killing a citizen in front of some guards and the guards only react once the citizen is dead, not at the point the thug starts attacking.
- AI - The AI is horrible, you can make a mockery of just about any mission.  Fighting piles of guards while others not too far away don't even recognize a fight has occurred.  Enemy NPCs are able to identify you entirely too easy sometimes.  Sometimes it'd be just the top of my head visible over a rooftop or through two sets of windows and it'd set a guard off.  Guards not aware of or responding to crowds of citizens fleeing the scene of a murder.
(SPOILER) Perhaps my favorite of all was an early mission where a bonus objective was to kill a guy in a confessional booth.  I killed three of his guards literally right outside the confessional booth.  He inspected each one, thought nothing of it and stepped into the confessional booth.  These are the Templar that have somehow almost taken over France?
(SPOILER) Second favorite was when I was to assassinate La Touché while he was at the Gallows.  There were a ton of guards and a very large crowd about.  In the course of removing all the perimeter guards I managed to scare away almost all of the crowds.  However the guards and La Touché up on the guillotine platform were none the wiser.  People were running to and fro to avoid the massacre.  Eventually cleared enough of the crowd out that thugs assaulting citizens and pickpockets stealing women’s purses started to spawn right in the middle of the mission area.  The whole thing was a giant circus.
(SPOILER) The Disguise skill is such a copout.  You can disguise yourself as the final boss and walk right up to his face and stab him - _RIDICULOUS_!
In general through a combination of the poor AI, spotty mission design and my impatience with AC:U's rough edges the game was less Assassin's Creed and more Murder Everyone Creed, more so than any previous AC. Was still largely entertaining however and looked fantastic.

Welcome to Paris circa 1789 and meet a ♥♥♥♥♥torm that is the french revolution.
You're some cliche obnoxious male model with a ponytail minus father.
You're in the wrong place at the wrong time and eventually end up as an assassin in the Brotherhood of Paris, an organisation of assassins.
Your merry group of hooded model citizens is fighting an ancient war against another, evil organisation of Templars who seek to gain control of the world and make everyone wake up at 4 in the morning (true story).
Oh and there is a sword that shoots lightning, yay!
Before I flame the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this piece of crap, I've just got to say that I love(d?) Assassins Creed games.
Overall for me, Unity is the new low point in the long line of Assassins Creed games. Here is why.
Time to vent about dirty money. You're offered packages of in-game currency up to worth of nearly 100 euros to buy items which make the game easier for you. The game is already relatively easy and you don't need any of the bling provided by the cha-ching. Besides, you're rewarded with in-game items as you progress in the game and I found those items to be just enough help. Now I do realize that mtx-business is the current trend and its understandable for them to try and make money out of their product but it just feels wrong, like dirty money. Not like Valve's business model which doesn't make the game any easier. Cheats used to be there to make the game easy for scrubs but I guess that time is long gone.
The story of the game is not entirely "flat" but it lacks that something which made the original Assassins Creed game have such an impact on me. Perhaps its the fact that the AC games used to have a "real life"-side to their storyline as opposed to Unity where all the action happens in-game. The main story in the series that (without going too much into detail) had to do with a certain ancient civilization and their relics, the happy fun times that is the impending demise of the world etc.  seems to have lost much of its importance and role in the game. Now Templars are just some chumps looking to make money at others expense and the really sinister world-domination is not that prominent a theme anymore.
Luckily the storyline conscists of traditional AC themes such as betrayal, romance and "fight the power"-mentality which is all good there and definitely a big plus but overall still lacking.
Now, some good things to say about the game.
Graphics are fantastic. The level of detail and architecture (thats a plus for architects of Paris of the time though) in the various castles, churches, palaces and whatnot is of very high quality and really just a sight for sore eyes.
The gameplay of AC conscists of freerunning and combat as usual and it feels fairly smooth (albeit for some incredibly silly controlling flaws and bugs, much of which were fixed on the first patches), except for the combat mechanics: the "skills" are bought with yet another currency and to me it feels ridicilous that you just can't do anything to an enemy on the ground before you "buy" ground execution (which btw. can't be used in multiplayer, no idea why).
Shooting mechanics are allright but the phantom blade addition just feels silly (much less than blowgun used in the black flag).
Perhaps the biggest and the best addition Unity has tried to give us are the multiplayer missions. A nice idea truly, but the lack of communication makes coordinating a 4-man assassin team a ludicrous job. Multiplayer bit has a lot of improving to do and I hope future patches do just that.
The Unity companion app is allright but the rewards it gives are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥. 250 credits from a single blue "nomad chest" makes me just think "yes mad". Not worth my time doing the ridicilous puzzle♥♥♥♥♥♥ mission bit and then having to fetch it myself or wait for 24 hours. Right.
Unity app feels like its just something they took out of the actual game for the sake of taking it out. Playing it on your mobile or tablet is okay I guess but what if someone doesn't have said devices at their disposal? Surely, they're living after their time but I'm just saying they should've added an option to do that♥♥♥♥♥♥in-game.
The game, with all its flaws, works as a fantastic time-sink even after completing the main story.
Running around the city, collecting the collectibles and doing mini-quests, multiplayer missions and stuff can give many hours of enjoyment if you wish to call it that.

Okay...I admit I've read some reviews beforehand, so sorta knew what to expect, but it was one buck on humble bundle, so decided to check for myself. Unfortunately, the other reviews were right... :-(
I initially made a wrong assumption: that a pac-man game would run well on any machine (like...my gpd win). It didn't: this game is fully 3D (despite it only even noticeable in level switches), and thus ran slower than it should. Video options are pretty much none, so in that field it's not the best first impression. This gets upped when the tutorials are obligated - despite them being both long and blatantly boring - and the game doesn't have any cloud save system. Meaning: by the time I noticed the slow speed wasn't intentional and ran it on my high end pc, I had to do the tutorials AGAIN!
Unfortunately, it isn't forgiven by the game itself. It has some fancy music, but everything else just isn't impressive. The game is as fast as its predecessor, but because it has more things going on (now you can bump into other ghosts but not kill them, there's these little ghosts that become part of the conga, there's a "go back to the starting point" button, there's an end goal and...some ghosts that just get in the way ???), you have to divide focus where you should really focus on your pac-man.
I get what the developers tried to do (except for the tutorial obligation part). It has more going on but stays true to its roots. The problem is that it's also less engaging when not in said roots. The first championship edition understood that. Pac man 256 understood that. Here...it just isn't there for me.
For one buck, I really can't complain. Because there is nothing wrong with it on a technical level. It's just a bunch of choices I personally disagree with. I would pick the first version and (especially) 256 over this version. Any time.

Pac-Man Championship Edition 2 takes the tried-and-tested formula of the original few Pac-Man games and flips it on its head by allowing the player to bump into ghosts a few times before they become aggressive, as well as by adding several game modes to the mix.
There are three modes: tutorial, score attack, and adventure. In tutorial mode, you learn the ropes; in score attack mode, you complete levels of varying difficulty in hopes of landing a high score; and in adventure mode, you complete various challenges—some easy, some incredibly difficult—to unlock stars that grant you access to additional challenges and even a few boss fights.
This game is addictive. I can not tell you how many times I have told myself "one more round" before looking at the clock again and realizing three whole hours have passed since I told myself that. You will definitely have fun playing this game.
A word of warning for anyone hoping to complete 100% of what this game has to offer: it is incredibly difficult. Notice how I have 27 hours of play time? Well, most of that was from completing the adventure mode. The mode starts off well enough, but to actually complete the final area, you have to complete every single challenge on "pro" difficulty—a feat easier said than done.
In conclusion, this is a fun game. I enjoyed its various modes and addicting game-play. I found the adventure mode to be frustrating toward the end, but was ultimately satisfied upon completing it. Perhaps the only thing that would make this even better would be the inclusion of a level editor. Maybe the next entry will have something like that.

The Walking Dead (Season 1) is a masterpiece of story- and character-centric video games. It's consistently well written, with completely believable three-dimensional characters; each with their own desires, motivations, and unique interpersonal relationships. This makes the deaths of certain characters throughout the game that much more affecting. Excellent voice acting really makes these well written characters that much more believable. And the music and sound design is pretty great too.
Gameplay mechanics also work very well, with a point-and-click style as well as a heavy focus on multi-branching dialogue with the game's large cast of characters. However, my only complaint about the game really is to do with the multi-branching dialogue. As the central character, Lee, is highly mysterious at the beginning at the game, one can find oneself lying to certain characters who one wants to be honest with, and vice-versa.
The DLC episode, 400 Days, is also a nice change away from the group-focus of the main storyline, though some parts of the episode were clearly much more interesting than others.
All in all, The Walking Dead is a solid experience for both fans of the comic books/TV show, and for general gamers. I can't wait to pick up Season 2!

I was quite looking forward to this game, right up until i played it. The game in of itself is fine in theory, its as youd expect, being similar to other MMO team v team games out there, however the game is clunky at best, and i would personally name if Fractured Time than anything else.
In the past 3 days, ive had 3 games, today, ive had 1 game in two hours, because players are either dropped from the queue thanks to ping, quit because they themselves are sick of waiting, both forcing you to wait to go back to dock, then repeat the process which usually takes around 4/5 minutes, or the game freezes while preparing to start the match, which happened to myself, forcing a PC restart.
Another problem i have, is the whole quitting game system thats in place. While, yes, having team mates that quit is annoying in itself, they already have a penalizing system in place, denying you any credits or XP for a game you quit. You are literally paying for it. However, theyve gone a step further, you are forced to either sit in dock until that game is finished, stop playing theg ame, or re join the match you just quit. In my case, we were barely holding onto the Alpha/Beta stations, but the enemy had broken through once already. Their team were ALL above 20 kills each, and we barely even broke the double digits. That was nothing but a frustrating match, and not fun for anyone on my team. So, of course i quit. I wasnt going to stick around fighting a losing battle where it honestly felt like they were just toying with us, lo and behold however, i had only those three options above. Wait, exit, or rejoin. I was already going to get penalized for quitting, so why should i have to be penalized further by denying me to do aything else?
The game is far too clunky and wastes FAR too much time searching/joining/aborting/searching/joining/aborting matches to be enjoyed at this point. I hope the game improves by its proper release, and that there are more players drawn to it to drop the ridiculous 13 average minute wait time, but right now, i dont recommend this to anyone.
