Somewhere during my first playthrough of Bastion, I forced myself to pause the game and wipe the tears from my eyes.
Bastion is by no means a depressing game.  Maybe my emotions acted the way they would normally react if I had been placed in "the Kid's" shoes.  Maybe, as I listened to a tale of struggle to piece together the fragments of a shattered reality, I felt sympathy towards the protagonist.  But there are plenty of games or movies or stories where there is suffering and struggle.  Just because suffering exists, we don't automatically feel suffering as well.  Yet something about Bastion was making me care about the world and the few people that remained in it.
This immersion, as I'll call it, can't stem from one specific aspect of Supergiant's game.  It's the occasional quip and endearing voice of the narrator as he tells the tale of a young boy who took on a burden many times the size of himself.  It’s the lush scenery, brightly colored and lovingly crafted as it pieces together paths and hallways ahead of you, only to tumble away into the abyss as the world falls apart.  It’s the gentle singing of a girl, notes reverberating on the breeze across complete emptiness, making you hope for a way to bring the world back to what it once was.  It’s “the Kid,” as he tumbles and slashes and shoots to fix what is devastatingly broken, because if there is anyone that can do it, its him.

Darkest Dungeon is probably one of the most polished roguelikes on Steam.
It's an unforgiving turn-based RPG where every single dungeon trip is a grind to the end. In order to beat any mission, you have to manage your roster very heavily beforehand; for example, bringing in a ton of damage dealers and healers sounds good on paper, but will usually have to attack last. Having lots of quick-attackers but no healers will have your entire party bleeding out after only a few lucky critical strikes.
Aside from RPG dungeon crawling, the metagame of Darkest Dungeon requires a lot of pre-planning as well. You bring back all your rewards from dungeons to your town, which has buildings that can be upgraded in order to help you progress through the game easier. Choosing whether or not to upgrade your Blacksmith or Sanitarium affects how quickly you're able to rehabilitate your broken allies or how well they'll perform in combat.
The best part of this game is probably the voicework. The game's narrative is revealed only through a disembodied ancestor, who narrates through combat and gameplay; He provides backstory and auditory cues after almost any action.
I'd recommend Darkest Dungeon to anyone who is looking for a roguelike to occupy a few hours at a time, but play for a LONG time. There's so much content in here, I can't imagine how many hours it's going to take me to see the end of this game.

First Assassin's Creed game i've ever played, and overall i've had a lot of fun with it.
+Large, open map and free roam
+Great detail in buildings and structures
+Complex and interesting story
+Fun parkour controls that aren't difficult to get the hang of
+Fun muliplayer missions and free roam
-Somewhat short story
-Need a mid to high-end gaming PC to even run this game on low settings
-Certain parts of the game can only be unlocked by using apps/other accounts outside the game
-Needs Uplay and Steam to play
-Story can be somewhat hard to follow/need to play the mission twice to fully understand how the story progressed in that mission
Lost my save data once, but luckily I was only a few hours in when it happened and i was able to prevent it from happening again by simply disable sync with Uplay's cloud storage. Despite what everyone else has said, i have only experienced minor bugs about 2-3 times that were fixed by simply restarting the mission.
As for the framerate issues, I have a mid-end gaming PC that does not meet the minimum system requirements for this game and before patch 4 i was averaging about 20-30 FPS on low settings and lag spikes consistently about every 30 seconds. After patch 4, the game runs MUCH smoother and i'm getting about 30-45 FPS with a full 60 FPS in certain parts of the map.
Before patch 4, i probably would have not recommended this game. After patch 4, every problem that i have personally experienced with the game has been resolved and at its core this is a very fun game.

On a personnal I would compare to a precursor, uplink.
Hacknet as uplink :
- Keep hacking feeling
- Are beautiful in their style and release period
Hacknet is mostly keyboard (terminal) directed (it would be great if it could be completely with the option do do stuff by mouse) while Uplink is completely mouse directed.
Uplink goes far in the concept of wan and man/lan, teach us more about security, that hardware are part of the hacking process, active and passive trace and the importance of clearing logs.
Hacknet goes more in the command line branch, familiarize you with typing with the possibility to see and compare the effects in the terminal and the graphic interface, It goes more in the concept of taking control by getting access of more services of the target system. Most of the command can be used and looks like regular linux command.
Uplink is CPU driven, programs are slower the more you start them but doesn't consider RAM usage, your filesytem has a size limit and all file (including all programs) need to fit it, you also need to consider free blocks of storage memory.
Hacknet is RAM driven, the limit of programs depends of your memory but doesn't consider CPU usage, you have a directory based filesystem using a tree similar to unix/linux (/home /bin /sys).
I never finished Uplink because of the lack of command line interface, and so I liked Hacknet for that point, but I feel now I need a game that puts me to the next level, one that combine the two parts ...
Final thought : I use linux since 2007 so nearly a decade, I do most things in terminals, for me the game was disapointing when a repetitive task was done by the mouse (sending mails)

If you go into this game expecting it to be a continuation of CE DX+ or better, you will be severely disappointed because compared to CE DX+, it's inferior in just about every aspect. That said, if you go into this game blindly/not expecting the same treatment as CE DX+ (which is hard), it's okay. It had potential, but a lot of the things this game brings to the table are a bit underutilized, lazy, or just frustrating.
The biggest change to this game is the ghost train mechanic, and this could've been cool if done right, but it's more annoying to deal with. Why can't I eat whatever ghost I want when I eat a power pellet? Why do I have to eat the front of the train to be able to eat the whole train? Why do I keep getting knocked back by the sides of the train and having to waste several seconds in a game that's supposed to be fast-paced to figure out where the hell the front of the train is going to go to be able to eat it?
This leads into two other issues... controls and scoring. The controls feel a lot more slippery than the first game, and even compared to other arcade-esque games I've played they feel too loose at first. It's hard to explain in a review. As for the scoring, well, compared to the first game I think it's better that the ranks have fixed point-values instead of basing your rank off how other people play, especially when outliers such as hackers and people who score super low on purpose can influence your rank as a player. That said, it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get S-ranks because you have to play near-perfect. It's difficult when dealing with the ghost trains because you spend several seconds trying to eat them in the first place. Plus, the game focuses more on nifty transitions which (no pun intended) eat up more of your time. I wouldn't mind it so much if I didn't lose 3 seconds every time it happened. I know it sounds like such a small gripe, but it's worth mentioning in a score attack game. Not to mention, aside from three achievements there's no real benefit to getting S ranks.
There's also an "adventure" mode that you unlock by doing enough score attack boards. I thought maybe this would've been pretty cool, especially since the original CE DX+ didn't have one, but it's not really expanded upon. It's just "eat enough fruit in a certain amount of time" for the most part. You don't even unlock anything from doing it (that I know of, I'm still working on it) aside from a few achievements. The "boss fights" are more of the same... just eat fruit, gather lives, and eat the power pellet at the end. It's a bit lackluster.
EDIT: Turns out there are score-esque missions, but of course they're at the last world. So have fun.
I will praise the unlockables that you get from scoring B or higher on score attack maps. You get lots of board, character, background and music unlockables to customize your scoring experience. It's really nice that a lot of the stuff that was DLC in CE DX+ can be unlocked in this game freely, especially the music. The music in CE2 isn't bad, it's just not as exciting as the first game.
All that said and done, I can't recommend this game if you're expecting something better than the first game, or a good follow-up to it. If you're just looking for a modern arcade-y game to kill some time and you're not super serious about getting S-ranks on everything, then this may be up your alley. Just don't pay full price for it.

Gone is the tense slowdown when you nearly run into a ghost, because now ghosts don't harm you unless they are angry, and they are made angry once you hit them, knocking them into the air for a few seconds to allow you time to pass or avoid them.
Now Ghost Trains are only "edible" when you eat the first ghost and the Ghost Train gobbling turns into a cutscene of Pac-Man eating a swervy line of ghosts which looks pretty cool, but is a passive, less interesting way of eating ghosts.
While the game is designed around these new mechanics, there were many times where it was difficult for me to gobble up ghost trains since I had to chase them into a trap and this often caused me to fail many levels because I took too much time to eat all the ghosts.
No longer does the other half of the maze transform when you eat all the pellets on one side, but instead the whole maze will change when you fill a fruit meter after eating a certain amount of pellets. Eating a train of ghosts in the original was satisfying because you maintained control of Pac-Man during the "attack" and you could start by eating any ghost in the train.  It does at least provide a new challenge of trying to get to the ghosts, which are thankfully restricted to a "track" that only covers a specific path in the maze (instead of giving the train access to the whole maze and making it hard to catch them at all). This "track" could be considered another "annoying casualization concession" but I think it is necessary change for the speed of this game - I miss turns more of than I should because this game is so fast and busy.
There's a new mechanic with jump pads that jump Pac-Man to alternate tracks in the maze, which can be confusing during fast gameplay, especially for the pads that are "intentionally misaligned". There's an entire Map for this mechanic.
The music in Championship Edition/DX was excellent. The music in the sequel is just good.
There is an adventure mode which requires you to earn enough stars from a path of selectable levels (the stars you gain are based on the difficulty you choose) which are used to unlock boss levels. They're a decent addition on their own, but isn't to compelling as it simply requires you to collect enough pellets to eat enough fruit to finally attack the giant ghost that is floating above the maze (at least this is the case in the tutorial boss - I haven't reached an actual boss yet)

I finally played the entire game and the entire DLC and now I can finally make a review. I will be separating my review, focusing first on the game itself, and then the DLC.
MY THOUGHTS ON THE GAME
I was introduced to Telltale by a friend on mine, who loved zombies and had also played Law & Order: Legacies. We both thought the games looked cool and the idea of being responsible for your own choices sounded amazing.
The Walking Dead was a game I also wanted to play because of the TV show and let me tell you right here that there are no connections between the two. Sure, the creators thought it would be cool to add Glenn in the first episode, but excluding the zombie plot, the show and this game are two different things (and that is actually a pro).
The Walking dead has a specific look that in a sense reminds me of comics, however they are still appealing. And when it comes to gore, the comic-looking design still works, which is an amazing plus. Although it doesn't have, in my opinion, the best design/graphics I've ever seen, it's still quite atractive to look at.
In terms of how the game works itself, as you can easily see in any review of this game, if you're hoping for a game where you can get some guns and blow some heads while you walk around Georgia, then you are wrong. Although there are some fighting scenes and the interaction exists in the entire game (you move characters, make them click stuff, etc.), this is a story-driven game, where the plot moves according to your choices. More than playing a game, you're watching a story. And for those who watch the show and like it's heavy/depressed tone, this game has it too.
But how are the choices? Do you REALLY choose? Well, I haven't played many other games where your choices define the story so I dare say you do REALLY choose. But I must also advise you this is a game and being such, it has limitations. Meaning sometimes you might choose the words or other paths but some destinations are the same. This isn't necessarily bad, it still influences on the relations between characters and it still changes situations, so I wouldn't get too worked up about it. Even if it's not perfect, it's still a good game.
PROS
- nice and easy interface. If you've used a computer before, you can play this.
- interesting design/graphics
- strong plot that will very likely make you look for your tissues
- the story is REALLY interesting - I almost felt like I was watching a tv show while still making decisions about it.
CONS
- some episodes are more stronger than others (altough this is highly subjective)
- although you make choices, sometimes you will still be led to the same path
MY THOUGHTS ABOUT THE DLC
When the DLC was announced my first thought was: "oh my god, I have to play it because otherwise I won't understand a thing about season two!". Then a friend of mine actually told me the DLC was totally irrelevant to the story and I wasn't sure what to do. Eventually, I bought the DLC and decided to play it after finishing season 1. The review for The Walking Dead applies here in almost everything, so I will resume this:
PROS
- same graphics/design
- same decision making
- introduces small stories about new characters that are in some ways connected
- some references to season 1
CONS
- the references to season 1 are funny but that's about it. You hear about the fate of one or two characters, you recognise some places or faces, but that's about it.
- introduces a few characters from season 2, giving you an idea of what happened to them before the season itself, but if you don't play it... they will explain it on season 2
- although fun, makes no difference whatsoever, meaning you can just ignore it and start season 2.
Overall, both the game and DLC are a nice addition to your games library and I would recommend it to anyone interested in a good plot while still interacting. And if you are new to games, don't worry - this is a very "noob" friendly game. There is no need for you to be an amazing player to succeed at this. Just play the game, enjoy the story and choose some paths - I assure you: it will be a bumpy, yet awesome, ride.

An excellent little tower defense game that would serve as a good introduction to the genre to those unfamiliar with it.
What it does exceptionally well is mazing- adding a feature where you place foundations for the towers before the towers themselves, thus allowing you to build a maze without committing towers.  Also predicts the path(s) that the creeps will travel along (although not always correctly).
Another positive: powers.  There are many of them and (when fully leveled) you get to pick 4 of them.
Enjoyable retro soundtrack and lovely pixel art.
One small technical note: there does not need to be a toggle for survival mode as one can simply enter it after playing through identical campaign levels.  I once accidentally played through 9 levels of survival while trying to up my star rating on a level.  This was annoying and unnecessary.
No plot except what you bring to it.  Sort of a Catcher in The Rye kind of thing; the monsters exist so that you can stop them instead of the cliff existing so that you can save the lives of small baseball players.
Finally, since no review of a tower defense game would be complete without a comparison to Defense Grid: this game is unlikely to make you realize that sometimes the portion of our lives that we are not simply an intelligence ported into a computer for tactical reasons and that we must take time every day to enjoy whatever berries may be in season.
In my opinion: worth about $2.99.

It's not actually a good game. I mean, it could've been, but it feels like a conscious decision was made to ensure that it wasn't one. Fundamentally the issues are threefold: Too much randomness, lacking information and too much repetition.
For instance, most combat comes down to luck as much as skill. Init order is random, debuffs sticking is random, heal and damage amounts are random, hitting is random, what skills enemies use is random, what enemies you encounter is random, crit attacks that can one-shot you are random. And you're given essentially no ways to dealing with the randomness. You can't, for instance, make a slower or less damaging attack that's guaranteed to hit, while having faster, harder-hitting, chance-to-miss attacks as intentional gambles.
The lack of information is in part some mechanics that aren't explained, for instance, how is init actually rolled? I have a SPD(speed) score, but what's the ACTUAL difference between SPD 6 and SPD 8? Secondly, what IS the init order? You don't KNOW. It gets rerolled at the start of every turn, and not knowing the init order(so you have no idea what enemies to prioritize, for instance, or what skills to use since some skills have bonus effects/greater efficiency if an enemy is stuck with Stun, but Stun clears once that enemy acts or is meant to act, so whether you could stick the Stun, then get an action in before it clears...? You have no idea.). And sometimes just odds you're completely uninformed of. I could poke at a stack of books, which could have a positive or negative effect... but what odds am I gambling with? Does the class I'm using affect it? (you might think that the more scholarly classes would be better at it, if you didn't know any better) The game never tells you.
EDIT: As an addition to the lack of information, you have no idea what enemy skills do before they're used. You have no option to look up enemy stats and go, "oh, this skill has thos effects at those percentages and strengths." so you can gauge which enemies are particularly dangerous until they've already hit you. Another bad design decision.
Lastly, repetition. Any given dungeon crawl is most likely going to involve the same two or three encounters repeating ten or more times. Considering that combat isn't exactly blazingly fast either, it means that fights tend to drag out quite a lot, and you're going to get very tired of the voice-acted lines once you've heard them twelve times in the same expedition.
And you're going to be doing a LOT of expeditions. Because progress is agonizingly slow, in part due to the very strict limits on how much loot you can carry home.
It just feels like lazy game design, in a lot of ways, rather than incompetent game design. Pad out the game with repetition rather than varied content, pile up randomness rather than actually designing stuff so people have to think.

I'm kinda torn about this game. Overall, I really liked my time with it, but there are some BIG problems with it.
The game is beautifully thematic. The Lovecraftian plot and dreary art style are very enjoyable. The stress system is, to me, genius. It fits the games theme and forces the player into changing up their party after every run. My first ~20 hours with this game were some of my favorite in my recent gaming history, but after that the game slowly starts to drag. The new DLC helped me out at this stage, as it released when I got around 20 hours into my first run and gave a breath of fresh air to my experience. Without it I may have put it down at this point.
There is a big issue in the mid game. There isn't a tonne of variety in mission types, and there are only 8 bosses in the base game, each of which is repeated three times at different difficulties. This has two effects; it both allows you to understand how each mission, region and boss functions to plan your mission better, but also makes the mid game feel very repetitive. I think there 'grinding' becomes problematic here. You just do the same few missions over and over again to level characters up and unlock subsequent bosses.
Towards the end of the game, things started to get more interesting for me. As you enter the 'Champion' stages your roster should be filled with lots of level 6 characters and you should understand how the games mechanics work. The game becomes genuinely tense at the higher levels, and your favorite heros can easily die if you slip up. I found the game, for the most part, fair. Only one character died for a reason I felt wasn't my fault in some way. Some might say that is still too much but hey, I didn't mind. It's a game based off of percent chances, so there's always going to be a degree of randomness. The end game boss in the Crimson Courtyard DLC took me a couple tries. (Full disclosure, I lost a whole team to that boss. Twice). I think I learnt about the boss in each of those attempts, and had fun, but this difficulty can emphasise the 'grinding' issue if you lose critical team members and need to train new ones.
At the end of the game, when you assault the eponymous dungeon, the game becomes fresh once more. New level designs for each stage and interesting mechanics on each attempt. However, another massive problem rears its head here. For almost no discernable reason, you can't send the same hero into the Darkest Dungeon twice. Guess what that means? MORE GRINDING. Yay.
I'm divided. I really loved my time with the game. The story was interesting, the atmosphere captivating and the gameplay fun, but the issue with repetition and grinding in the midgame tarnishes my love for this game. I am sure I will remember my experience with this game fondly.
If the setting of the game is interesting of you and you believe you would enjoy the mechanics, I would recommend you pick the game up. It's fun. Even if you don't push past the grind of a mid game, the first few dozen hours of your time with the game will probably be worth it.

New and improved PAC-MAN? Not Really.
Like the first game in the series, this is also a flashy version of the classic PAC-MAN - with some new twists.
- You can bump into ghosts a couple of times without taking damage. Doing so will make them angry, and hitting an angry ghost will cost you a life.
- New features such as bombs that let you teleport to the center of the screen when used, and jump tiles that let you jump from one part of the screen to another.
- Mission objectives and boss fights (mainly in Adventure Mode). Mission objectives include such things as collecting all the bonus lives dropped, or collecting all the fruit/getting 5,000,000 points within the time limit. The "boss fights" just feel like a gimmick, since they are not very different from the regular mission stages.
As a result of the new features mentioned above, this game does not really feel like a traditional PAC-MAN game, which I guess is the main reason why it has received such a fair amount of hate.  I also encountered the same bug (scared ghosts are suppose to follow a visible path, which they often do not) several times, which should have been fixed as it can often be game losing.
If these points are deal-breakers for you, then you should probably avoid this game and get the first one instead. As for me, although I enjoyed the first one more, I thought this game was pretty fun and addictive as well, and I don't regret playing it.

The Walking Dead is an emotional journey that takes place in a zombie appocalypse. Our main protagonist is a guy named Lee, who runs into an abbandoned girl named Clementine, who he has to take care of through the appocalypse, and teach her how to survive in this cruel world.
Gameplay

The Walking Dead is an interactive story, which means there won't be a lot of gameplay. Throughout the game you will mostly be talking to people and when you get to speak, you will get a few sentences which will be your options for what you will say. Those conversations will affect how the story unfolds, who will hate you, who will like you, who will die ? It's all up to you. The gameplay is mostly searching for supplies and some puzzles that don't happen very often and are rather easy. One more aspect in the gameplay and Telltale games overall is the decision making which is really intense and requires quick thinking, or you can just pause the game and think about what you're going to do. Basically if you're looking for a game action packed with zombie shooting and smashing, this game isn't for you.
Graphics
Telltale games has its own artstyle which is really unique, you can either really like it or really hate it, it's really about preference. It has a comic-book / cartooney artstyle, everything is outlined with a black marker. Even though the artstyle is as it is, the zombies, guts, and everything else is really well done. You will notice a lot of details, for example when walking through the forest. Honestly, without the artstyle, I think I would have a completely different view on this game.
Story
This is where The Walking Dead, and every Telltale game really excells at. You create the story, as previously mentioned in the gameplay bit. Who will you save ? Will you regret your decision ? How will the story unfold after your decision ? Everything's up to you! There will be characters who will irritate you to no end, and there will be characters which you will fall in love to. Telltale really makes a bond between the characters and the players, they make you care for them. You might grow an interest in a specific character and make the wrong choice. One more time. Everything is up to you!
Soundtrack
Throughout the game there won't be a lot of music. You will most likely be enjoying the sounds of nature, wind, water, and of course, zombies making fascinating noises. Music will start at the intense, scary, sad moments, which is what makes these scenes sad and/or intense. Overall, soundtrack is enjoyable and makes the game alive.
Overall experience
Personally this game was really enjoyable for me. It had its funny, sad, scary moments. If you're looking for an emotionall journey, and if you are a Telltale games fan, this game is a must buy.

The Old Tree is a short puzzle-solving game made by Red Dwarf Games, I'll start out by saying I enjoyed this game a lot, and have replayed it so many times Ive lost count, the game is pretty short but if you can forgive it for that its a great little play.
So you play as some sort of small alien recently hatched from an egg and you must help it on its way, the puzzles are in the vain of the old point and click games that I played growing up so that was a nice bit of nostalgia for me.
There is no story exactly, more or less you are just trying to help your little friend get to his / her destination
The art style I must say is incredible, its varies through the different areas and really helps each location define itself, the art has a certain charm to it.
The sound is somewhat simple but well used to help draw you into the game and the journey that you are undertaking.
I'll leave you with this, The Old Tree is a great little game and will no doubt keep you interested throughout its duration, and its absolutely free if that's not a good reason to check it out I don't know what is....so Why not give it a try.

This game is beyond anything that I expected. It has such a great attention to detail that you can become absorbed into it within minutes. The entire game is polished to near perfection. There is very few things I dislike about the game, and they are such minor complaints that I still consider this game practically perfect. To start, here is a list of all the great mechanics and details in this game.
-It oozes personality. The game has an incredible style and feeling that you will constantly feel while playing this, which is contributed to by the music. There is humor everywhere, everyone in the game is so unique and fun that you will not get bored with them (with a few exceptions, which will be mentioned soon.)

Your spouse does almost nothing except go outside sometimes or visit town every once in a while. Your kids never grow older than a toddler, which makes them essentially walking furniture. If this was polished and made more interesting and interactive instead of just watching your kids and spouse wander around, I would love this part of the game.
Buy this game.

I've played almost 8 hours of the game with no bugs and only a couple crashes, but the latter was only because I was working on a lower-end machine.  I will attribute this to having only begun playing the game after the 3rd patch was released.
PROS:
Environment: The environment of the game is incredible.  Sometimes I climb buildings just for a good view of the skyline of Revolutionary Paris.  Part of the reason I play AC is simply because I want to see the amazing world they've built.  I have fortunately not experienced any FPS drops, so the quality and color vibrance is stunning.
Great gameplay.  I like the addition of taking cover, and having to actively parry incoming attacks.  This was an element missing in the older games that made battles kinda boring, because all you had to do was hold down the right trigger on the controller to keep up your guard, and wait for the perfect moment to counterstrike.  I almost never lost health when playing AC2.  Adding the requirement of parry makes the conflicts more interactive, and requires fast reaction.  Free running is smooth, combat is smooth.
Customization: I like the outfit customization and weapon options.  They have got some really great clothing and weapon designs.  Right now, I'm running around Paris with an upgraded heavy axe and enjoying the heck out of it.
Multiplayer is really fun, but only under certain circumstances (more on that in Cons).
CONS:
Multiplayer: It sometimes doesn't work too well.  I encountered this when trying to enter a four-player co-op mission.  I got sent into someone else's "world" as the game termed it, but either the mission never started, or I joined too late  and it was already over.  I want to be able to join at the beginning of a mission, not get thrown into someone else's game and not have anything to do.
Color Customization: My only complaint here is that you can only chose from a number of preset color options.  There is no real "customization" here, besides deciding which color combo you prefer.  Plus you have to buy them, which is a negative.  I liked the Halo games in this respect, where the color customization was completely open, any color combination you could think of was at your fingertips.
Outfit Customization: I liked this, except for the fact that they're directly tied to stats.  I liked the look of some of the "armor", but chose not to use it because the stats weren't what I wanted.  Personally, I think the stat upgrades should be separate from the customization options.

Darkest Dungeon is probably one of the most polished roguelikes on Steam.
It's an unforgiving turn-based RPG where every single dungeon trip is a grind to the end. In order to beat any mission, you have to manage your roster very heavily beforehand; for example, bringing in a ton of damage dealers and healers sounds good on paper, but will usually have to attack last. Having lots of quick-attackers but no healers will have your entire party bleeding out after only a few lucky critical strikes.
Aside from RPG dungeon crawling, the metagame of Darkest Dungeon requires a lot of pre-planning as well. You bring back all your rewards from dungeons to your town, which has buildings that can be upgraded in order to help you progress through the game easier. Choosing whether or not to upgrade your Blacksmith or Sanitarium affects how quickly you're able to rehabilitate your broken allies or how well they'll perform in combat.
The best part of this game is probably the voicework. The game's narrative is revealed only through a disembodied ancestor, who narrates through combat and gameplay; He provides backstory and auditory cues after almost any action.
I'd recommend Darkest Dungeon to anyone who is looking for a roguelike to occupy a few hours at a time, but play for a LONG time. There's so much content in here, I can't imagine how many hours it's going to take me to see the end of this game.

It is in fact so addictive to play - that I've many times thought to myself, why doesn't this have multiplayer already? Because it has got that much potential to have multiplayer features in it - and lo and behold, the game creator Concerned Ape (how can anyone name themselves a concerned ape? Shame on you mom for giving your kid that name - I'm kidding of course, it's just a nick the developer has called himself/herself to be nameless I guess), nevertheless - the concerned ape involved has made a game that is insanely addictive to me and my friends, we play it so much I sometimes wonder what's wrong with me.
It's a perfectly relaxed game to come home to after work, here's the story plot if you didn't know it already:
You're a bored worker at a large corporation that delivers stuff to all over the world (yes, you know what company I am refering to) and you inherit a farm from your now late grandfather or perhaps father? I'm not sure on the details here, what I am sure of though - is that it takes me forever to care for this run down farm, and scare crows away, not to mention chasing cavemonsters, OR chasing the same monsters in MY YARD at nighttime.
If some coworker of the JoJa corporation don't drag me away because I fell asleep tired 2 meters away from my home and charge me 1000g for it, I'm sure the good doctor of Stardew Valley will empty my pockets for his services.
Don't be fooled, this isn't a game you'll play for a couple of hours, if you want to achieve anything - expect to play for hundreds of hours, yes - it's a grindy grindy game, you'll need to start small - have a TON of patience, but one thing is for sure, once you're past the first few hours - you're stuck in total addiction for the next few months, possibly  years.
It's a peaceful relaxing game that you can play before you go to bed, but beware - those hours before bed moves on fast, so before you know it - your plan to play it for just 1-2 hours ended up in 5-6 hours instead, and now you're possibly late for work IRL.
And for you moms & dads out there, thinking that this is a perfect game to purchase for your kiddies, don't be fooled by the Nintendo-ish graphics, this is an Adult game, it contains the possibility to purchase alcoholic beverages in the local pub - all the elements of getting drunk. Super Sanctum TD was a game I picked up for the combination of ridiculous sale price ($0.79) with trading cards. When I saw a game that looked to be similar to the original Sanctum games with the fast-paced FPS action taken out, I expected it to be a sloggy, boring grindfest - my standard opinion when it comes to the majority of tower defense games.
Much to my surprise, Super Sanctum TD manages to dodge the most common gripes I have about the TD genre. Most levels have an open-ended "create-your-own-maze" approach, allowing for a lot of freedom and creativity in level solutions. SSTD also does away with long streaks of easy early-game snore-inducing levels - strong planning, resource management, and intelligent skill usage are all needed as soon as you complete the two training levels. The difficulty remains fairly consistent throughout, giving what seems like a paltry 14 stages a pretty beefy amount of playtime, as you'll likely need a few tries to figure out a suitable plan for much of the levels. On the other hand, if you find yourself breezing through the game, there's plenty of replay value in the form of an optional Hard difficulty, as well as infinite survival modes for every stage.
SSTD isn't without its flaws, however - most glaringly is the game's fondness for crashing. Thankfully, the game does a fairly good job of autosaving, letting you continue right at the start of the wave you were left hanging on. The high difficulty I praised earlier can also be a bit of a double-edged sword - with a completely linear level structure, getting stuck on a stage will bring any semblance of progression to a screeching halt. An optional easy difficulty setting may have been a good idea for this reason.
Super Sanctum TD may not be the most innovative game in the world, but what it does, it does very well. If you're a big fan of tower defense games, then this game is an absolute steal.

You know Walking Dead, right? Rick, Carl, Darryl, Michonne, and the rest of them, yeah? Well this game has nothing to do with them, so even if you've seen the show or read the comics, this will still be a fresh experience for you. You play as Lee Everett, a former professor at University of Georgia. After discovering that the world is being overrun by zombies, Lee happens to meet a girl named Clementine who was left with a babysitter while her parents are on vacation. The rest of the game follows Lee and Clementine as they travel through Georgia, find friends, make enemies, and struggle for survival.
For those who aren't familiar with Telltale Games (I myself have only played Walking Dead, but I've seen some gameplay of Wolf Among Us and Tales From the Borderlands), it's more like an interactive narrative experience than a "video game" in the tradtional sense. If you value a game's story and its characters more than its gameplay mechanics, Telltale's Walking Dead should be at the top of your wishlist. If point-and-click adventures filled with dialogue choices and QTEs sound utterly boring to you, then this probably won't be your cup of tea. The story and character development are shaped by your decisions and dialogue choices (or lack thereof). While the overall arc and direction of the story is the same no matter what you do, the way it all unfolds is up to you.
Good stuff:
+ The story is divided into episodes and chapters, and the game autosaves at the end of each chapter. You also have the option to rewind to a certain chapter to make different choices.
+ Both controller support and keyboard+mouse support, and you can switch between the two on the fly whenever you want.
+ The score is awesome and sets the mood perfectly.
+ The voice acting is top notch.
+ The direction of the game feels like a television drama (if only such a thing existed!), shifting between moving and fixed camera angles, each episode begins with a "Previously on the Walking Dead..." segment, etc., which is a rather unique way to present the narrative and sets it apart from other story-focused games like, say, visual novels.
+ Your emotions will not be prepared.
Complaints:
- Some of the animations look a little awkward and unpolished.
- Sometimes there are dialogues with time limits that are too short and/or choices that are too long to read...or maybe I just need to learn to read faster.
- The walking speed is too slow for me during the point-and-click segments of the game. In most other video games, the default movement speed is usually jog/run, but I know that nobody in real life by default runs everywhere they go.
- Kenny pls

I find this to be an excellent game, even if it's in Early Access (it just went to Beta yesterday, as of writing this). The gameplay is simply awesome and fun. There are tons of ships to choose from and each one plays different and feels different. Even certain ships that serve the same purpose but are built by different manufacturers still manage to be different to each other. There's so much variety that each match feels different and fresh.
The game puts a heavy emphasis on teamwork, coordination and tactics. If you have friends and are looking for something to play together, this is the one.
It claims to be a MOBA, and while on principle it is, it still manages to be so much different from other MOBAs, which mostly feel to be a reskin of each other. It's a very different experience, and what makes it so different is largely the immersion it offers you, aside from the fact that it takes place in space with capital ships doing battle with each other.
The world feels fleshed out. Each ship has its own background and how it was developed and why. Each ship has specifications like how many thousands of crew it takes to man, how large it is, special characteristics etc. Then you can choose crew members to put in your ship. Each crew member has their own bonuses they confer to your ships, but they also have their own backstories that explain why those bonuses are there. And then each crew member has their own voice acting, and they will talk to you during the game. Instead of the generic female voice telling you "Warning: Armor 50%", you will hear the frantic screams of your crew as they are rushing to fix the damage before they get flushed out into the void. Even better, the crews of ally and enemy ships will periodically contact you. For exaple, an ally captain will give the order to defend a location, or an enemy weapons officer will taunt you when they manage to bring your ship down in a close fight. All this adds so much to the atmosphere and lets you get immersed.
The atmosphere of the game is amazing. Visually it's a masterpiece, and a well-optimized masterpiece at that (considering it's Early Access, it's very impressive). The sound design is also extremely good. You still get the feeling you are in space and sound doesn't carry, but it feels like each weapon you use, each explosion that happens, each collision that occurs, they are real.
Best of all is that this title is not "pay to win". Yeah, you need to grind a bit if you want to get all ships without actually paying for them, and extra crew members are a bit too hard to acquire without paying real money, but still. About a third of the ships are very easy to get. You need 110 000 credits for the cheaper ones, and you can get about 10-20 000 credits per match. Plus another 10-15000 from daily rewards. In a day (4 hours) you can easily get the credits to buy one such ship. Personally, I've played 20 hours and I've unlocked 4 ships so far. And all of them are pretty good. I don't feel disadvantaged against the more expensive ones. The more expensive ships are actually a lot harder to learn and to play and a lot more specialized. You shouldn't mess with them until you are comfortable with the easier ships. And you get another 3 starter ships, that are also quite good. They are not so specialized, but they are still quite powerful at what they do.
There's no ship that's wildly overpowered. All ships have their roles, weaknesses and strengths. All ships are fairly easy to acquire. The only thing you need to pay actual money for is skins and boosters. All in all, a very good monetization model that doesn't get in your face every second and doesn't give an unfair edge to those willing to pay money. Over time the game has won me over that I am considering giving them money in the form of buying some skins. It's just that good. Oh, skins can also be acquired through daily rewards for PARTICIPATING in matches (not winning, just completing games).
Another rarity is that the devs listen and participate in the forums. You can even find them playing the game and they are always willing to get feedback and act on it. These people love what they do and they want to make the best game they can. And it really shows.
The only negative thing for me right now, is that matchmaking takes a while, but that's because there's a small player-base. As the players increase, the problem will fix itself.
All in all, this is a very fun game, it's free-to-play and it's not pay-to-win. In its current state it can easily pass for a full game, don't be misled by the "Early Access" label it gets. And it just keeps getting better and better. I highly recommend it.

So I'm sure you've seen some of the other more recent reviews of Starbound. I'm going to tell you this: Just because everyone else is hating on it doesn't mean you have to(Of course, if you don't like Starbound then go ahead and hate it, I won't stop you). I think that Starbound is a perfectly fine game. I wouldn't play it all the time, of course. That's just crazy. But when I do play Starbound, I enjoy it.
The controls are simple enough to master, and building is easy to get the hang of. WASD to move, mouse to aim and perform different actions depending on what you're holding. When digging or building, left click to place or break blocks in the foreground and right click for background blocks. Fuel your ship to explore different planets. No two planets are alike as far as I am aware.
There's not a lot in terms of a story, all you get to know is that you ran away or escaped from your home world only to find yourself stranded (convenitly) over an unknown planet. That story varies slightly from race to race, which there are six to choose from (seven if you use the unstable updates). After a few tutorial quests, you're free to do whatever you feel like. Want to explore and visit other planets? Go ahead. Want to dig to the center of the planet you got stranded on? Sure, do it.
I can't speak highly of the multiplayer because of where I live making lag a real issue, but some of the servers have a friendly community. Modding is a thing in Starbound as well. Some servers even have mods working when you log onto them. Like any other game that supports modding, mods add, improve, or change how you play the game.
Now I'm not saying you should buy Starbound, that's your choice. I'm just saying I have fun when I play. Would I recommend it? Perhaps. If you're interested, buy it, and try it out. If you like it, good. You won't be wasting money. Otherwise, too bad and I'm sorry you wasted all that money for something you didn't like.

I decided to write a review of this game because most of the recent reviews are from people who have barely played the game (some haven't even completed the game) with very little achievement progress. I have spent almost 200 hours playing this game, and have earned every achievement. This may go without "saying", but I'll "say" it anyway: I'm going to attempt to chronicle my way through this game and the process I used to learn about the mechanics and what I found frustrating. I used an XBox 1 controller, so button references will be made accordingly.
Firstly, the game crashes. A lot. I did some research and the general consensus seems to be that one must disable "NVIDIA Turbulence". That didn't work for me, so I also disabled "Volumetric Lighting" and "Postprocessing" and that seemed to have worked.
My first playthrough was with the rogue class, whose weapons are governed by the agility trait, which, in my opinion, is disgustingly OP. Part of a rogue's special ability is having a weapon in each hand, which can be strung together into a combo. I used LB, RB, LB, RT, LT a lot. By the end of the game (level 67) I was doing around 1k damage with "claw" weapons, at 28 agility, per combo. The other ability, which the rogue can do from the start, and which other classes can do later, is parry.
There are 3 shield types, Tower, Kite, and Buckler. Bucklers are used to parry, Kite shields can stun enemies, and Tower shields can reinforce blocking. I've come to the conclusion that tower shields are useless. I began by spending the first few hours learning to parry, which can be overwhelming because I was getting hit. A lot. Which became frustrating. I stuck with it and realized the timing window for parrying is quite large. Gauging an enemy's attack is quite intuitive, which made parrying a lot easier. Definitely a plus for this game. If you decide to get this game, parrying is worth investing the time to learn. Be aware, however, that while every class can use the starting buckler, you have to invest in the agility trait to use the other bucklers, which are much better, found later in the game.
The trade-off for a large parry window, at least as far as game mechanics are concerned, is a very small and awkward back-stab activation hit-box. Every enemy has a different hit-box zone and keeping track can become tedious. The other issue with backstabbing is, if you miss the back-stab and are using larger, heavier weapon, you won't recover in-time to block or evade the enemy's attack. This, by itself, isn't a problem, as the rewards with backstabbing is great, and so too must be the risk, but because of the awkward back-stab hit-box, the risk is artificially inflated.
My second playthrough was with the cleric class, whose weapons are governed by the faith trait. I had a lot of fun with this class because most of the weapons available to this class are "hammers" and they're so fun to use in this game because of the move list. Two-handed power moves and rolling away was the strategy I employed for most of the end-game, especially the final boss. I didn't use the kite shield that often because I spent so much time learning to parry, so as soon I found the buckler, I switched to that. I found that fighting most enemies without the ability to parry their attacks became tedious; it was really difficult to fight around their shields or deal with their attacks. One of the major downsides of this game is that enemy attacks track you through the full attack animation, so the only option with rolling is to roll backward. If you try to roll to either side, the camera glitches out and you end up rolling around the enemy, directly into the attack. Another "interesting" mechanic is that enemies, especially bosses, will teleport in the direction of their attack, giving them added range, which, to me, is sloppy programming.
My third playthrough was with the warrior class, whose weapons are governed by the strength trait. This was the most difficult playthrough for me. The warrior class uses heavy armor and sits at about 95% of his encumbrance which means your character will be "fat rolling". Of course, rolling isn't necessary, because, with heavy armor, your character will just poise through attacks without interruption. This didn't happen as often as I would have liked, since most attacks will interrupt your attacks, even from weaker enemies. The weapons were the most frustrating, as the start-up and recovery frames from attacks are extremely long. I found myself unable to recovery in-time to avoid enemy attacks, so I had to use smaller weapons to keep from depleting my potions (you can refill your potions at anytime at checkpoint crystals and you can add to the total amount of potions you have, but this resets your experience multiplier, which caps at x2), which, to me, defeated the purpose of the warrior class entirely. I couldn't "roll" out of the way or block because, with these heavier weapons, the majority of your energy (stamina) is used, especially if you do a power move (RT).
The story is quite vapid. Without spoiling anything, the player isn't told why the protagonist is doing what he is doing. The protagonist doesn't seem to buy into the story and we're left wondering if we ought to ourselves. Dialogue choices are also frustrating as some options will advance the story but we don't know which. My first playthrough was riddled with accidental story advancement when I wanted to learn more about what was going on around me and why. No take backs in this game.
There isn't a quest selection option either. All secondary quests are done when you remember to do them. You won't know when or how to trigger each side quest either. For this, I highly recommend browsing the wiki:
Some enemy's attacks, I would argue all enemies, don't have recovery frames, something I've noticed with western studios. This means that there isn't a buffer between the end of one attack and the beginning of another. An enemy can go right into another attack as soon as the previous attack frames end. Your character, on the other hand, has recovery frames. Which means there will be a pause between attack animations. This is a personal pet-peeve.

A bit of a letdown in comparison to the first, but it didn't hamper my enthusiasm to play it too much. Although it's considered a sequel thanks to recurring characters, it felt like a completely different story. I agree with some reviewers that the Magic Mirror was not initially a villain, he'd only punished the children because I assume they had broken him. To see him with a different personality was...kinda disappointing.
It would have worked much better if Tommy wanted to go into the worlds his mother spoke about so he'd have foolishly broken the mirror again or threatened it and the mirror retaliated by doing what he says although not promising that he'd be safe when he gets to the other worlds.
The main character this time has zero personality and zero dialogue; only descriptive narration to explain what you need to do and what things do.
They did up the ante with the hidden object scenes by rotating the items all over, in comparison to the first game which claimed that the object is exactly in the same position as on your list. They removed the 'place elsewhere' system which was what I felt made Mirror Mysteries a little more unique, and replaced it with your standard 'get one item to help you move on to the next place' reward that most HOGs contain.
There were also significantly less worlds (only 4) and the time you spend on the last two hardly qualifies as a 'world'. It felt like they invested all their energy into Sky World and none into the rest. Which is sad since you hardly stayed in any world to be honest. The voice actors for the NPCs all sounded like they had to go really bad so they rushed everything they needed to say.
There weren't a lot of puzzles and if there were, they were so simple you'd have finished in a minute or less. Some of the puzzles were entertaining though.
Overall, I still really liked the first one more. I wouldn't call this horrible, but it is a little bland and I do kinda wish it was a more standalone game now rather than a continuation. I hope that if they do make a third installment that they go back into the first game's formula and build it better instead of passing off the series as just another typical HOG. It's just as short as the first game with significantly less entertainment value so I don't think it's particularly worth the full price.

I think of Hacknet as a spiritual successor to Uplink, it has a good blend of fresh ideas and features borrowed from Uplink. When I compare the two, I view Hacknet as the more realistic game, whereas Uplink is more Hollywood styled.
Hacknet features real Linux/UNIX commands, as well as real port numbers, Port 21 for FTP, Port 22 for SSH, 1433 for SQL etc. Now playing this won't teach you how to hack but it kind of gives you an idea of how it works, each system has a set number of ports that have to be open before you an crack it. Some of the later game systems have Proxy servers and Firewalls. Proxies can be overcome by opening a shell on 3-4 computers and telling them to spam it with junk traffic and data, meaning that it will allow unchecked traffic through, whereas Firewalls take a bit more time, you have to analyse it and doing so will reveal some characters, once you think you've got it you type SOLVE [FIREWALL SOLUTION] and it will check to see if it matches.
Some tools can be run while a Proxy is up, but not while a Firewall is active and some can't be run with a Proxy active but they work while a Firewall is up.
Each tool has it's own visual effect while it works and they're all beautifly done. My favorites being PortHack and SQL_Mem_Corrupt.
The game is a bit more linear compared to Uplink, in Hacknet you're forced into the story as soon as the game begins, whereas with Uplink the story kicks in a couple of weeks into the game after some freelance work.
Hacknet has some intresting things to search for though, certain documents such as IRC logs are pretty funny.
Overall though I'd say it's worth the buy, espiecally due to it getting a free multiplayer and some DLC content later in the year. And the soundtrack fits the game extremely well.

I've been a huge fan of this series from the very first game.  After extreme satisfaction from Black Flag, I couldn't wait to get my hands on this game, especially since it's set during the French Revolution.  However, I am extremely disappointed in this game.  I don't even think this was optimized, as I am well above the recommended specs but I cannot play on normal graphics settings without my fps dipping well below 30 FPS.
Melee combat has been nerfed on an extrodinary scale.  This can be a good thing or bad thing depending how you liked the melee in the past games.  I for one am not a fan of dying to 4 enemies.  Oh, they also got rid of using people as a body shield when enemies are about to fire, lovely isn't it?
I'm not a fan of how co-op was forced upon us.  You are forced to play co-op missions in order to get 5 star armor.  Most people playing co-op have absolutely no care for stealth and will just run into the mission guns ablazing.  I could expect this, but co-op should not be forced on us.
The parkour in this series has always frustrated me, no matter what.  I thought they were getting better with it in Black Flag, but this game has taken 2 steps backwards.  It seems like they've tried to get too cute with the parkour and now it's no longer flowing.  There's countless times where Arno will just stay hanging from a ledge because I do not press the "free run up" button.  Entering through windows is extremely buggy.  Most of the time Arno will climb around the open window instead of actually climbing in it.
On top of all this, Ubisoft has decided to add microtransactions in game.  This utterly disgusts me, and the fact that there are 3 different currencies in this game is just plain ridiculous.
Overall, this game feels like an Alpha release, and I cannot recommend this game whatsoever.

Roguelikes are a dime a dozen these days. It's very easy to create a lot of unstructured, randomised content without putting much thought into how the game should be presented. If anything, this is a big issue with games with roguelike features. That's why you need a bit of structure and polish to make the experience immersive.
Darkest Dungeon is a RPG roguelike with dungeon crawling and base management elements. It is one of those games with polish. It also has a good structure that prevents the randomiser fatigue I get from playing roguelikes. Here's why, in listed form:
1. Feel - This word is passed around a lot in faux gaming intellectual circles, but this game has great game feel and personality. The art style, sound design and pacing of gameplay elements are near perfect. A game should always have impact when you play it and it should be in accordance with its proposed theme.
DD achieves this; it is dark, it is foreboding, it is stressful to play and it makes you feel powerful when you achieve your goals. Red Hook fundamentally got this right. Special mention goes to the casting and performance of Wayne June as the narrator/ancestor, who perfectly bookends player choices and actions with weighty, wordy dialogue.
2. Gameplay - to compliment game feel and the themes, you have gameplay that fits. Characters share their time in the hamlet and the surrounding 'dungeons' with eldritch and unholy entities, gruesome bosses and opportunistic bandits. Everything is trying to kill your characters while making life worse for them. As a setting, few games properly convey the bleak atmosphere without coming across as hammy or silly. DD achieves this.
-An example-
A lynchpin element to this is via the mechanic of stress. Characters actively accrue stress as they play through the dungeon, caused by your actions and the actions of the environment and creatures. When characters reach a milestone in amount of accrued stress, they either start to exhibit negative behaviours such as Hopelessness or Abusiveness, or they power through the mental pain and gain positive traits like Powerful and Stalwart. These last for the dungeon, and they completely change the experience of dungeon crawling.
For this reason, stress and psychological managment are core features of the game. Things such as light level while dungeoneering, giving your characters opportunities to rest while they're back in the hamlet or camping in the dungeons and gearing your skills and inventory to help manage this stress are seemlessly integrated into the entire experience. It is extremely engaging, which leads me to...
3. Difficulty - difficulty is so frequently abused as a term. Good difficulty design in a game makes you aware of consequences of any actions you will take in the future. Bad difficulty is arbitrary and can't communicate consequences through the medium and context its based in.
Darkest dungeon has good difficulty. It punctuates this from the beginning when you boot up the game with a disclaimer; characters will die, autosaves are near constant, nothing short of doctoring your save games are going to bring back those you lose. And you will lose characters, you will fail dungeon crawls, fail to kill bosses. At worst, if you are foolhardy enough to fight to the bitter end, you'll lose everything and everyone you've sent and earned on that expedition.
The most important message that DD has for its players is that you must embrace the finality of your decisions and choices. This is why it autosaves. The game obviously has a bad rep for being ridiculously hard for new players and this sudden shock, this introduction of 'Why can't I reload before I did this?' is hard for players to deal with. But its fundamental to the experience. Otherwise, the previous points in the list would be totally invalid.
Overall, if there's a roguelike I could recommend above all others, this would be it. You should buy this.

So I'm sure you've seen some of the other more recent reviews of Starbound. I'm going to tell you this: Just because everyone else is hating on it doesn't mean you have to(Of course, if you don't like Starbound then go ahead and hate it, I won't stop you). I think that Starbound is a perfectly fine game. I wouldn't play it all the time, of course. That's just crazy. But when I do play Starbound, I enjoy it.
The controls are simple enough to master, and building is easy to get the hang of. WASD to move, mouse to aim and perform different actions depending on what you're holding. When digging or building, left click to place or break blocks in the foreground and right click for background blocks. Fuel your ship to explore different planets. No two planets are alike as far as I am aware.
There's not a lot in terms of a story, all you get to know is that you ran away or escaped from your home world only to find yourself stranded (convenitly) over an unknown planet. That story varies slightly from race to race, which there are six to choose from (seven if you use the unstable updates). After a few tutorial quests, you're free to do whatever you feel like. Want to explore and visit other planets? Go ahead. Want to dig to the center of the planet you got stranded on? Sure, do it.
I can't speak highly of the multiplayer because of where I live making lag a real issue, but some of the servers have a friendly community. Modding is a thing in Starbound as well. Some servers even have mods working when you log onto them. Like any other game that supports modding, mods add, improve, or change how you play the game.
Now I'm not saying you should buy Starbound, that's your choice. I'm just saying I have fun when I play. Would I recommend it? Perhaps. If you're interested, buy it, and try it out. If you like it, good. You won't be wasting money. Otherwise, too bad and I'm sorry you wasted all that money for something you didn't like.

As of Patch 4:
Overall: The Performance of the game runs a little smoother. That is noticeable. Yet, alas... I can still only run on "Low Quality". Minor issue, more less personal taste. At least it runs better while roaming around for goodies or being able to sneak about.
However, If I am attacked by 4+ hostiles the game freezes and lags up still. Making defending (Parry) next to impossible. Using smoke bombs then only amplifies the lag.
In larger area's where the crowd is more dominate I will have issues with "locking-up". Even more so if being chased and shot at.
Speaking of which, please do something about enemy targeting with their guns. I mean, I'll sit there and watch a cutscene in story mode. Those guys couldn't hit anything if it were right in front of them. Yet, gameplay wise, these guys have DEAD ON accuracy. Dodging does not help. Sometimes dropping smoke does not help because they can magically see through it. For the love of god, please make them miss here and there. /end rant.
I've also noted missions that have you "Defend" a target are not working properly and had to restart the memory. What happens is that they get "stuck" and no longer follow you. I don't know if this was an issue or not seeing as I only reached those stories as Patch 4 dropped.
Playing Multiplayer, Every other mission causes my game to crash if I play online, searching for people or playing with a friend. BUT, If I play Locally, being on the same internet network, the game runs smooth and I never crash. Few glitches here and there. Having a target see me through a wall as an example. Other wise, aside from the expected lag (after searching or non local) I haven't stumbled upon any other issues.
The customize menu (Gear/equipment load out) is still rather laggy and is not enjoyable at all.
That's all I was able to notice so far. Still, a very sad panda. Since this was supposed to fix a lot of issues. Which, in a sense it did. But, I'm still locking up and crashing (multiplayer, non-local). I still cannot recommend this game.

I played the first one last weekend, so I figured I might as well wrap up the second while I'm here.
Apart from general bad temper, I'm not sure I get the vocal-minority hatred here for Mirror Mysteries 2: Forgotten Kingdoms. It's true that it commits the scarlet sin of not being exactly the same as the first game in the series, although it's actually pretty close. It's a short, easy, slightly silly excursion into a few realms in the lands the malevolent Magic Mirror, which once again has no sense of humor and intends to take over the world and destroy everyone muahaha. If that sounds a little like the original, well, yeah.
The first had an easier forward-pressing pace, which this one trades for vaguer goals set in more fantastical worlds. The core mechanic of assembling sets of hidden-object items to move from one location to the next is pretty much the same, as is the enraged mirror that taunts you through the settings. This time, instead of playing Tommy and Charlotte's hero mom, you're a detective sent by adult Charlotte to track her grown-up brother Tommy, who has disappeared after chasing down an unusual mirror, because he has dim memories of another mirror when he was a child, and so forth, la la la.
Artwork here is more ambitious - I especially liked the future city in the clouds, which is a little bit steampunk, a little bit Rapture, and a little bit Syberia. Gameplay doesn't throw any unexpected curves, and once again I ran the game in two and a half hours, so mere mortals should get through it in around two. As you put together the pieces to resolve each environment you'll collect mirror shards along the way to get the next portal working, and these are pretty clearly indicated.
Voicing is minimal and not quite as good as the first, but the art is much more interesting, though sometimes the goals aren't as clear as they could be. This time, playing as a detective and not a mother, there isn't any call to tidy up, sew, or do any of the household tasks that plagued the original: here it's all putting machines under power, making the train run, restoring water and flowers to the peaceful glade. Hmph.

I liked the original Mirror Mysteries quite a lot, but this sequel was clearly written by a different developer, and it shows. Gone is the brave and pretty heroine from the first game, only to be replaced by her extremely annoying kid who has grown up and apparently gone insane while searching for the magical mirror his mother talked about. You play a private investigator who travels to the mirror worlds to find him. (Is that really necessary -- we can't just leave the little bugger to his fate?)
Speaking of the mirror, they completely ruined his personality. The original mirror wasn't exactly evil, he was just a curmudgeon who was annoyed at some unruly kids for breaking his mirrors. His sardonic commentary was very entertaining, and he actually helped the heroine in her quest. This new mirror has gone completely off the deep end into deranged villainy. The new voice actor plays him as a one-note bad guy, and there is nothing interesting or entertaining about him at all.
On top of all that, the hidden object scenes are much harder (but not in a good way), tbe puzzles are boring, and the mirror worlds are just derivative copies of worlds we've already seen a hundred times before in other, better games.
Ultimately I cannot recommend this game, even on sale. If you like hidden object games play the original, or search for one of the many superior titles developed by Artifex Mundi or Silverback Games.

Highly recommended...with some reservations. Surprisingly deep storyline for a casually simple "hacking game". Still hellalot buggy though so expect to restart at least a few times.
THE GOOD
I came into this game fresh - I knew it was a "hacking game" and that's pretty much it.
The main storyline is surprisingly deep for something that I thought was a simple hacking game. There's a bit of a mystery over what happened to Bit and it's actually a bit of a heartwrencher at the end even though (minor spoilers)
.
The game starts you off with easy, low-risk missions just to ease you into it. Once you get further along, it gets more interesting because there's a time crunch to do what you need to do before someone tracks you and your computer shuts down.
Just like real life, the game allows for multiple ways for you to do something. For example, instead of hacking into XXX's PC to get something, you can also get it by doing other things, or by hacking into another person's PC. It keeps it surprisingly fresh through multiple playthroughs. And you get to satisfy voyeuristic tendencies by snooping through people's  private files while you're in the system...or just delete everything and imagine the crash and burn.
NEUTRAL
Also like real life, if you accidentally delete everything from your (fake) computer, the (fake) system crashes and you might have to restart your whole game. Or if you accidentally deleted that super important file that has the info that your client wanted...yep, it's gone now. You gonna have to abort your contract. If it's from the main story line, there's no way that I found that will trigger the next sequence.  I hope you saved before doing that...or you gotta have to Google it.
And there's other pretty great stuff too...I'll let you explore those.
The game doesn't offer much of a challenge. Yes, there's that time crunch factor for the harder missions but there are certain features in the game that makes it surprisingly easy. Not sure whether it's a bug or not but (minor spoilers)
.
THE BAD
It's still pretty buggy. In some cases, unless you follow the instructions exactly, it might not trigger the next sequence of the game (e.g. if you skipped ahead and hacked some terminals before you're supposed to or if you've deleted some crucial files that you weren't supposed to delete). It doesn't always happen so it's a bit of a hit and miss. So expect at least a few restarts (I had to do it twice).

TerraTech is a simplistic arcade-sandbox type of game where you control a single vehicle and then upgrade it by adding new parts directly onto itself. The building is awkward but fun to do and quite easy since it is just drag and drop and play. The fighting elements are unique, you choose how to approach your enemy, from the air, from a flank attack or even just blast them out of history using 20 cannons. There's tons of parts to make an excellent plane or car out of (really, I mean alot. I dare to you to use all of them) which can make for some spectacular designs instead of the ag-old♥♥♥♥♥♥plane! There's resource farming which is quite tedious but dangerous since you can run into enemies
, but is worth the risk if you have found something work 70 or more
(BB is the games' currency, it can be used to buy new parts) to obliterate your foes with unless you realize you have just bought one terrible wheel worth 2K BB which you could've simply got off an enemy. That being said, you can destroy enemies and then use all of their parts onto your bot! This makes the game feel more balanced but also a ton easier for players so we don't have to sell all of the enemies' drops to buy our own parts. The texturing is quite basic, however the SFX are the opposite. There's more content to come and I can't wait!
Textures are basic and feel out of date because of that. This is something to be expected since the game is only Early Access and will most likely improve. Otherwise, the SFX are a ton better. The lens flares look as if they would be out of a AAA game, the lazer beams look awesome and aren't just 100% sprites, the building blocks look as if they wouldn't break in 0.5 nano-seconds. But there's not too much to be said other than this, I'll probably update this section once TerraTech becomes a nicer-to-look-at game.
The gameplay is awesomely fun! It reminds me of some older arcade games, there was one 2D game that you had to kill enemy planes to place onto your ship. This game reminds me of that classic. There's just too much parts to even try and find, so you will not get bored with having too much BB, oh no. There's many activities to do too, from simply mining for resources and selling them for fortune , to upgrading your warmachine, to making new ideas for you killer, to working out how certain parts work, to anything else. I could go on making a few paragraphs explaining why you should buy this game soon or on release, but I'm just going to sum it up quickly in the:
Pros:
Low hardware requirements
Tons of parts to use
Arcadish genre game
Simplistic graphics improve FPS
Tons of FPS
Fast paced battles
Farming for resources (if you like it)
Different vehicle combinations
Low price
Replayability
Action-packed game
Cons:
Other than building and resource gathering, the game is a little bit shallow

Darkest Dungeon is a punishing turn-based strategy game about sacrificing brave but stupid soldiers to the darkness. When you build a bond with characters and see them eviscerated it hurts, at first. Eventually you become desensitized and are grimly sending units to what you know is most likely their funeral. It's like This War of Mine in that way - in large part it is about the feeling the hardship of the units you control. They fall apart physically and mentally, and there is nothing you can do.
Some have complained that Darkest Dungeon is repetitive. If you play this game, I hope you like turn-based combat (like you'd find in Final Fantasy games) because there is a lot of that. I enjoy it.

One of the better games released this year.
Xcom 2 pretty much improves on every aspect that made Xcom: Enemy Unknown great. Im not a huge fan of turn based Strategy games, but i instantly fell in love with this series since minute 1.
The thing that makes Xcom games so good in my opinion is how high the stakes constantly are. you have a handfull of soldiers (that you ideally desing and name yourself using the improved character creator), wich you send on missions around the earth to fight the overpowering alien invasion. Meanwhile between missions you upgrade your base and research new weapons, tech and armor. If a soldier dies, thats it, they are gone for good. this combined with the fact that your soldiers level up and gain new skills forces you to think every single decicion you make, since they may have horrible snowballing concequences.
As far as the gameplay goes, its the same great gameplay from Enemy Unknown, but way better balanced and tweaked. There are new classes, skills and weapons to add new layers of strategy on top of a fantastic core. The enemies are also a bigger threat than ever, with a standout being a weird snake...thing. Every mission usually means death is an everpresent possibility and usually more closer than you think. Achieving a close victory gives you a great sense of accomplishment only comparable to taking down a Dark Souls boss with no estus left
Xcom 2 pushes you to make hard choices every minute of the game.
For example: Will i aid this country against the aliens while the other ones panic level rises but the other country is offering resources that i need for help?
Or will i build armor for my soldiers for the cost of not having as effective weaponry? or vice versa.
Or even will i leave one soldier from the squad to draw fire while risking him/her dying and give my squad a chance to evacuate? or will i try to evacuate the entire squad with a risk of multiple people getting hurt.
Unlike a ton of other games, these moment to moment choices, no matter how small will actually effect how you play the game, and the smallest mistake can escalate into a disaster if you are not paying attention. Its truly beautifull when it all clicks together.
The game also attemps to make the pacing of missions faster by having some missions having a turn limit. No longer having snipers wait out everything makes you steamroll through the game like you could in the previous game. While i do like this change in a way, as it fits the concept of you being this guerilla warfare unit, i really dont like the change. I feel it limits the tactical otions you have and forces pressure on the player in what is already a hard game. Luckily The game has been openly moddable from the start, and the community has been creating some amazing stuff for the game.
Overral, I'd totally recommend this game any day, even if you are not a fan of strategy games. It can be kinda unforgiving at first, and your first playthrough will most likely end in a total defeat, but before you know it you'll be playing this till the early hours of the morning. Game's really addictive you guys.
