Mirror Mysteries 2 offers roughly the same short fragmented object hunt its predecessor did, but somewhere along the way lost the charm that made the first instalment a fun game to play.
Mirror Mysteries 2: The Forgotten Kingdom is like a direct-to-video sequel of a moderately successful movie: feels similar, yet doesn’t work that well.
The plot introduces the adult daughter of the first game’s protagonist who has to rescue his brother from the clutches of the same mirror that trapped them years ago. Only this time the mirror is a very cheesy cartoon villain, and not even the charm of the more detailed worlds can save us from his ridiculous monologues.
Game mechanics were left mostly untouched: you still construct items from small parts and use them within the scenes to progress. The magnifying glass is gone, so the scenes require more patience or the use of the hint button. There are a few conventional puzzles, but they hardly worth any notice. Essentially, like most lower-rated sequels, it’s recommended for those who liked the first game and don’t mind the lower overall quality.

TL;DR: This is a very simple, casual version of Sanctum without coop mode and without the 3D visuals.  The level of dificulty will scare some away almost immediately, but tower defense veterans may enjoy some of the subtle gameplay mechanics which allow for deep strategic thought.  The problem is this is not like other Sanctum games.
Rest of the review:
Sanctum was great, and I loved Sanctum 2.  I didn't get the Super Sanctum spin-off game until the 2014 winter sale, because I wasn't really fond enough of the 2D graphical style to part with much money for the game.  Well, the game finally dropped to an absurdly low price, so I took the bait and began playing.
The first thing I noticed was that the combat was almost entirely about the towers and wall placement.  This is not Sanctum-like.  I was expecting a player character, but I got instead a god-like view with generic tower defense fare.  I was disappointed but did not let that sway me from giving the game a fair try.
The tower options were very bare to begin with, but after a few completed levels, I unlocked a lot of towers.  You start with the gatling gun tower and eventually unlock more towers as you beat levels.  You can go back and replay levels using your new towers and new abilities in survival mode.
The abilities are the closest thing you can get to player interaction with the game world, but I found that the best abilities were the ones you didn't actually get to use manually.  For example, you could have abilities which add to tower strength for a limited time when used, but you're better off unlocking the abilities which enhance towers indefinitely.  None of the upgrades are ever permanent, so there's little reason to replay the game from the beginning, but achievement hunters will enjoy the grind, I guess.
The story is non-existent.
Overall, I liked the game in a casual time-wasting way, but I cannot recommend it unless you're looking for something extremely simple, something intended for the most casual of gamers.  Considering the game's intended audience was Sanctum players, I doubt many will be satisfied with this game's more generic approach to tower defense.

What I mean is: This is probably the most overrated game of the last millenia.
Released in 1998, this was probably the coolest thing that was ever created, and I get that. But since I never played this game before a couple years ago, the rose-tinted glasses were sold out. Hence I will review this game from an objective standpoint.
This game's story is interesting enough, the enemies and environments are okay.
But this game has aged. Badly. Like Bruce Jenner. There are some older games that still look good in my opinion (like Unreal, Age of Empires II, Deus Ex) and play relatively well, but this game does neither. The combat is very clunky, and fails to implement any intersting mechanics like those that make Unreal or Deus Ex special. In short, this game is a long hallway, with enemies jumping out at you, and you shoot them. Unreal is the same way, but they at least introduce some scenery changes every once in a while.
The blandness of gameplay elements is accented by a complete lack of instruction or exposition. Gordon Freeman puts the crystal into the laser thing and all goes to hell and aliens pop out of everywhere. That's about as in-depth an explanation that you are given.
The worst part: This game allowed for the existence of Counter-Strike a.k.a one of the most overrated multiplayer games of the last century. I once saw someone say Counter-Strike was as fast-paced as Unreal Tournament...
If you like riding bandwagons, this is definitely the game for you.

Pros:

I would heartely recommend this game to anyone who likes a game that doesnt hold your hand, has a great atmosphere and interesting gameplay.

So the game is an FPS/RPG hybrid. As an FPS, it's pretty terrible. None of the guns feel great to use and the movement feels sticky and unresponsive. Fights consist of either peeking out of cover and taking pot shots at enemies, or running backwards from some ugly♥♥♥♥♥bug chansing you down.
The RPG part they got right though. The levelling up/healing and inventory management makes sense, for the most part. The story is extremely stupid and makes no sense. You just lost your child, I don't think the first thing on my mind is collecting potato plants for some farmer. Much like CoD, the story is just an excuse for the game to exist. With that said, the quests are interesting and fun to go through. Just don't think about it too much.
Overall, this feels more like a DLC for Fallout 3. Nothing is significantly improved and it just feels like another Fallout game. Which isn't a bad thing, but isn't a good thing either. I'd recommend it because I did have some fun and actually finished it, but it's nothing to boast about. Great game, great dev team, great community.
There is clearly a lot of work put into ensuring balance in the game.
Teamwork and tactics are greatly rewarded, promoting a healthy synergy in the matchmaking.
There's a level of depth to be appreciated in the game. Your various crew members have his/her/its own story and personality. They also give you various alerts and advice that can help a rookie get a quick hang on things, and remind seasoned players how to stay alive.
The crew notifies you of various important information. For example, they can tell you if a stealth ship just appeared on radar, or if a section of your target's hull has been breached.
Each ship (any of which can be unlocked without pouring money into the game) has its unique concept, loadout and strategy (a rear echelon stealth ship loaded with missiles to hinder/destroy the enemy team, a light attack craft armed to harass enemy ships and detect cloaked vessels, a heavy ship designed to entrench itself to secure an objective/provide cover for teammates).
The countless ways to compose a team brings countless methods for a team to obtain victory. The tide of battle can be turned in a split second with a team united.
There's nothing more satisfying than using some cunning to pull your self from the jaws of defeat and emerge victorious.
The game is also free; just give it a shot, and I'm positive you'll enjoy it!

If you've played Dark Souls you'll find the setting and some of the combat mechanics familiar and kind of enjoyable. At first.
However, any Souls veteran (or any Hack n' Slash veteran for that matter) will eventually see where this game falls short, as soon as he fights a few enemies:
The combat (at least for Rogues) is bad.
It's not immediately obvious, but to those of us used to the polished combat of games like Dark Souls or DMC, this kind of combat is unacceptable.
The easiest way I can describe  the issue is that the combat is not "tight". It's basically many little failures in the combat system that make it a huge pile of trash when combined. TERRIBLE enemy AI, with enemies who have absolutely random recovery times when they perform an attack, turtling enemies whose shields don't drop with one kick but need many, and their attacks are as quick as a dagger, unreliable dodge/sprint, and the tracking, MY GOD the tracking. Enemies don't pivot with the movement, but they spin on an axis. Combined with their ridiculous recovery times they're just not fun.
Maybe a sword & shield works better, but the Rogue I played with daggers/fists was just frustrating. And not in a challenging sort of way, but in a why-won't-you-follow-my-inputs kind of way.

I was a little late to the party when it came to Telltale's The Walking Dead game. I'll be honest, I didn't think it'd be my kind of game. I'd actually watched someone play it a few years back, and thought that was all I needed. Boy oh boy, I was wrong. It's not until you're in the hot seat, making the tough choices and living with the consequences, that you get the true experience I imagine Telltale were going for.
Now, some people have griped that the choices you make often lead to the same outcome. In a way, that is true. Don't sit down with The Walking Dead expecting to create your own story, that isn't what it's about. Your choices influence how other characters treat you, their loyalties and determine future choices. You can change how the story plays out, but you don't get to change the major events.
I'd definitely recommend The Walking Dead to anyone looking to experience a really emotional, human story. You're not going to change the world, save the day or slay hordes of zombies. You're going on a journey with interesting characters, just trying to find a way to a better life for their families and friends. It's my favourite kind of story, and I'm glad I finally gave it a play!

One of the best RTS games of all time.  It is certainly well ahead of its time.  This classic caters to many different playstyles (aggro, turtle, boom) and has a great unit counter system.  It still has an online community and many informational resources including guides and a well-developed wikia are available online.
The major downsides are lag if playing treaty game mode (e.g. no rush 20 mins/40 mins/55 mins) with many players (3v3 or 4v4) and server reliability (games occasionally don't count for ranking because the servers went offline while you were in a game).  The game is NOT being maintained by Microsoft anymore.  All patches from now on come in the form of fan patches (which are excellent, mind you).
For me, the game is definitely good enough to overcome these major pitfalls.  Everyone that hangs around puts up with it for the love of the game.  I think that says enough.

The second Mirror Mysteries are slighty different than the first one. The graphics are a bit better and the locations more interesting (for example the first world which I liked the most is nicely inspired by art deco and maybe even by the Bioshock). The story again revolves around the same bad character as the previous game but this time it's much better (but still nothing deep). The voice acting sounds more professional and the cheesiness from the first game is gone (that's a shame I liked it :D). There are also more and much better puzzles (but they're skippable if you don't want to solve them). Also the gameplay is slightly different this time. Besides the standard hidden object finding there are also some point'n'click adventure elements  blended in. So all in all if you like hidden objects finding you are on a good address.
Pros:
-More interesting puzzles
-Better story
-Less cheaply hidden objects
-Longer than the first game
Cons:
-Sometimes it's hard to find where to put a completed object
-Still a little bit short
-Puzzles are too easy to solve

Super Sanctum TD is a short and sweet, simple flash-TD equivalent. I got this on sale for under $1, and it delivered everything that it promised.
Tower balance is reasonable, though obviously positioning them properly is always crucial. The in-game skills/unlocks present several different ways to tackle most levels, be it ability-heavy or tower-heavy. I rather liked the 100% sell value unlock, as then I could move max upgraded towers around to kite slow moving bosses, or explore strategies like powering up one lightning tower until it 1-shots everything. The game has just enough cheese in its strategies to keep you amused, as you plow through all 14 levels.
The achievements have good diversity - you'll unlock most of them just by playing. 1 or 2 are puzzle achievements, that require you to think about how to structure your maze and how to use tower synergies to unlock them. If you go for them, they force you to understand the game mechanics a little bit more, making you a better player.
The normal and hardmode achievements are well thought out (play every level on hard and win; play every level on normal and don't lose health) - easy for any TD veteran to accomplish.
There is one grindy achievement - kill 10,000 walkers - I groaned when I finished the game with only ~2700 of them defeated, as I thought it was going to take forever to get. It's actually not that bad... one playthrough of lvl 3 on survival with chargers and splash towers (like ACPs; take your pick) will get you most of the way there.
Overall it was quite fun. I didn't notice any severe engine glitches that didn't work in my favour, but there were a few minor ones. Comboing time-rewind and teleport abilities has some odd/ineffective effects... Saving/loading is bugged, messing up tower stats and sell values, so be careful resuming a previous match. The game is also very likely to crash if you spam hundreds of mines at the end of your maze. I did have two crashes early on that were unrelated to cheese, but they happened on the first levels, which take only minutes to get through.
Overall this TD feels like a 7/10 or 7.5/10. Priced right, with just enough polish and cheese. I enjoyed it.
-BikeHelmet

I really enjoy Pac-Man Championship Edition 2. The new additions to the Pac-Man gameplay strike the right balance between preserving what it means to be a Pac-Man game, and offering the players something new and exciting. The graphics and sound are perfect. That said, I can see why others down this game for its controls. There's no denying, as far as I can tell, that the controls in CE2 are worse than CEDX. The reason this is the case is that in Pac-Man CEDX, you could reliably buffer a turn in advance, pressing the direction you'd like to move while still within a straightaway, and you'd turn that direction at the next opportunity. In Pac-Man CE2, the window to make movement decisions seems to be more like the original Pac-Man games of the 80s, and your window is pretty much a split second in advance of the turn. I miss the turn-buffering, for lack of a better term, as it allowed me to better plan ahead. I could be on a straightaway, having buffered my next turn, and be looking ahead on Pac-Man's route to plan my next and better keep on top of the ghost situation. In CE2, because I'm forced to keep my eye on Pac-Man at all times, keeping a plan for everything else is daunting to say the least, because the controls are so much less reliable. Unlike CEDX, I, like other reviewers, have even lost track of where Pac-Man himself is, and I can't recall that ever happening in any other game with his name on it. I think allowing movement buffering would go a long way to making Pac-Man CE2 pretty much perfect, along with CEDX which already is. All that said, I'd recommend CE2 to anyone who likes Pac-Man.

What I mean is: This is probably the most overrated game of the last millenia.
Released in 1998, this was probably the coolest thing that was ever created, and I get that. But since I never played this game before a couple years ago, the rose-tinted glasses were sold out. Hence I will review this game from an objective standpoint.
This game's story is interesting enough, the enemies and environments are okay.
But this game has aged. Badly. Like Bruce Jenner. There are some older games that still look good in my opinion (like Unreal, Age of Empires II, Deus Ex) and play relatively well, but this game does neither. The combat is very clunky, and fails to implement any intersting mechanics like those that make Unreal or Deus Ex special. In short, this game is a long hallway, with enemies jumping out at you, and you shoot them. Unreal is the same way, but they at least introduce some scenery changes every once in a while.
The blandness of gameplay elements is accented by a complete lack of instruction or exposition. Gordon Freeman puts the crystal into the laser thing and all goes to hell and aliens pop out of everywhere. That's about as in-depth an explanation that you are given.
The worst part: This game allowed for the existence of Counter-Strike a.k.a one of the most overrated multiplayer games of the last century. I once saw someone say Counter-Strike was as fast-paced as Unreal Tournament...

I have about 48 hours into version 1.0 so far. I played the stable Beta before this for over 200 hours. I'm keeping my recommendation as "no" due to the VERY bad storyline mechanics and missing techs.
tl;dr: Get this game if you want to play Terraria in space. Don't get this game if you want a storyline or hate fetch quests.
Full Review:
You get a space ship and fly around the universe exploring random planets, towns, and areas. Think Terraria in space but with infinite worlds.
I spent a lot of my time building colonies with the insanely responsive and customizable building system. It blows Terraria and vanilla Minecraft out of the water with block customization and the smoothness of the building process.
That said, it's not without A LOT of flaws. The thing that sticks out right away is the loss of over 20 unique "techs" that really gave this game immense flavour in the beta. Instead we're forced to use *yawn* basic techs that are the same vanilla flavour that all games of this type have. Seriously. There is 4 flavours of a morphball from Metroid. there is 4 favours of double jumping. There are 4 flavors of dash. All of the work exactly the same, but with a slight twist. Look up the ones that were lost on the wiki and see what you're missing. You'll cry:
We also lost unique storytelling for the individual races during the translation from beta to release. You have races that WOULD NOT become a space cop for earth now suddenly space cops for earth. So say "bye bye" to any sort of fun background story you had in the beta.
Finally, the main quest is just simply bad. Not redeemable bad. AVGN: "What were they THINKING?" bad.
You need to get these dragonball like keys to defeat evil. How do you do it? You scan the furniture of the 5 different races then battle a boss. NO JOKE. You scan a race's FURNATURE in order to find keys to an ancient evil. WHAT. THE. HELL?
ANY other trope-filled storyline would have been better. Mario Brothers 1 had a more interesting storyline. The Matrix 2 had a better storyline. X-Men 3 had a better storyline. This is an unforgivable fail on the part of Chucklefish.
The kicker? The specific furniture pieces are randomly placed in a LARGE infinite universe and you're given VERY vague instructions on where to look. You could look at 30 LARGE planets and find maybe one chair out of 35+ items to scan. It took me 6 hours of boring searching per race. I hated myself for wasting that time. I could have been productive or learned a foreign language. Nope... gotta scan a candle holder on Jupiter.
Pros:
- Procedurally generated worlds makes exploration feel fresh.
- The controls are spot on. All damage you receive is on you.
- Building things is incredibly fun an easy.
- Infinite worlds in infinite combinations
- The weapons and guns are fun to discover and play with
Cons:
- Storyline. Its mechanics is the worst I've EVER seen in a sandbox game.
- Having to scan everything and then scan it again.
- Reward bags do not scale with level so quest rewards rewards are just bad
- Questing, in general, is unimaginative.
- Flavourless "special" locomotion and move sets
- The fans on reddit who think Chucklefish can do no wrong.
Once again: Get this game if you want to play Terraria in space. Don't get this game if you want a storyline or hate fetch quests.
Was this game worth the three year wait for it to get into a stable "finished form?" NO. Terraria made itself 10x more stable and more fun to play in 1/3 the time with less people.
I'll NEVER buy another Chucklefish game while its in beta again because I don't hate myself.

One of the better games released this year.
Xcom 2 pretty much improves on every aspect that made Xcom: Enemy Unknown great. Im not a huge fan of turn based Strategy games, but i instantly fell in love with this series since minute 1.
The thing that makes Xcom games so good in my opinion is how high the stakes constantly are. you have a handfull of soldiers (that you ideally desing and name yourself using the improved character creator), wich you send on missions around the earth to fight the overpowering alien invasion. Meanwhile between missions you upgrade your base and research new weapons, tech and armor. If a soldier dies, thats it, they are gone for good. this combined with the fact that your soldiers level up and gain new skills forces you to think every single decicion you make, since they may have horrible snowballing concequences.
As far as the gameplay goes, its the same great gameplay from Enemy Unknown, but way better balanced and tweaked. There are new classes, skills and weapons to add new layers of strategy on top of a fantastic core. The enemies are also a bigger threat than ever, with a standout being a weird snake...thing. Every mission usually means death is an everpresent possibility and usually more closer than you think. Achieving a close victory gives you a great sense of accomplishment only comparable to taking down a Dark Souls boss with no estus left
Xcom 2 pushes you to make hard choices every minute of the game.
For example: Will i aid this country against the aliens while the other ones panic level rises but the other country is offering resources that i need for help?
Or will i build armor for my soldiers for the cost of not having as effective weaponry? or vice versa.
Or even will i leave one soldier from the squad to draw fire while risking him/her dying and give my squad a chance to evacuate? or will i try to evacuate the entire squad with a risk of multiple people getting hurt.
Unlike a ton of other games, these moment to moment choices, no matter how small will actually effect how you play the game, and the smallest mistake can escalate into a disaster if you are not paying attention. Its truly beautifull when it all clicks together.
The game also attemps to make the pacing of missions faster by having some missions having a turn limit. No longer having snipers wait out everything makes you steamroll through the game like you could in the previous game. While i do like this change in a way, as it fits the concept of you being this guerilla warfare unit, i really dont like the change. I feel it limits the tactical otions you have and forces pressure on the player in what is already a hard game. Luckily The game has been openly moddable from the start, and the community has been creating some amazing stuff for the game.
Overral, I'd totally recommend this game any day, even if you are not a fan of strategy games. It can be kinda unforgiving at first, and your first playthrough will most likely end in a total defeat, but before you know it you'll be playing this till the early hours of the morning. Game's really addictive you guys.

This game is an unfinished masterpiece.
Even with it's many flaws, it's still fun. I recommend it for anyone who enjoys RPG's like Dark Souls, especially people who find Souls to be a bit too challenging.
Despite what fans will try to say, this game is basically a Dark Souls clone. But so what? Is it bad that so many shooters have drawn inspiration from Halo and Counter Strike? Is it bad that so many MMO's have copied Warcraft? Is it bad that League of Legends turned a WC3 mod into an entirely new genre called MOBA? No. This is what the gaming industry does. One game hits it big, and everyone improves on its model.
When I first started playing Lords of the Fallen I was blown away.  In my first few hours of playing it, I was convinced that it was actually BETTER than the Dark Souls series. I liked that the art style was dark fantasy, instead of a miserable nightmare. I liked that it was difficult, but not impossibly hard. I liked how the spells feel complimentary to melee combat, rather than entirely different class skill set. I liked that the longer you go without dieing the more experience you get, encouraging you to gamble with your life.
But the longer I played the more I realized how incomplete this game is. It needs a lot more fine tuning, and it feels like its still in beta. Firstly, the combat gets a little wonky the further you progress. Yes it's hard to kill stuff, but in a weird way. Either you are surrounded by far too many enemies who are spinning your camera around in circles and there's no room to move, or you have come face to face with a wall of shields in a narrow hall way. Most of the difficult fights are hard simply because they are awkard. There isn't the same surgical feeling of precision in this game that there is in Dark Souls.
The longer I played, the more cheese mechanics I learned to just kind of cheat my way through. For example, I was constantly shield bashing people to the ground, and then smacking them, letting them get up, and repeating. But the problem is that you have to do this. When there are huge guys hiding behind shields, thats kind of the only way you can kill them. Alternatively, you can use your big spells, and then hide for several minutes while you wait for the cooldown to end and your mana regenerate.
These problems become even more pronounced when you get to the boss fights. Basically every boss has a trick or two that allows you to sneak in some damage, and then you back off, and repeat. The worst part is that these bosses have far too much health and it takes like 10-20 minutes of cheesing them to slowly work them down. Sadly, all of the bosses themselves look, act and sound really epic, but they just aren't that fun.
The second major problem in this game is navigation. The whole story recycles the same world and zones. As the story progresses, you realize that you have to backtrack to the same areas that you have already been in several times. The only variety is that there happens to be different, bigger enemies in those places. The biggest cause for annoyance in this is that the game never gives you any hints or clues about where to go. You just have to kind of walk around in circles until you figure out where the game's story continues. (Or go watch youtube guides.) What's most frustrating in all of this, is that most of the environments look very similar. It's quite easy to get lost in this game while you wonder around in circles, trying to find some awkwardly hidden door or passage.
Unfortunately, I think the problems with the combat and the world probably only exist because the company that made it is small and couldn't afford to keep working on it.
I had fun playing this game, and I actually played it through to completion. That's more than I can say for 90% of the games in my Library.
I think this game franchise has a ton of potential and I really hope the sequel comes out some time soon. Moreover, I hope they have a budget and team large enough to make a game that lives up to that potential.

With so many moving parts to learn and a seemingly infinite breadth of options to explore, diving into any new MMO is a major investment of time and energy. It's exhausting, really, which is why I appreciate a game like the free-to-play Realm of the Mad God. This fantasy-themed, co-operative bullet hell MMORPG is beautifully simple, yet deep enough to keep you chained to your PC for days on end. It takes only a minute or so to get right into the action, and, once you get a taste for running around with a gaggle of your fellow pixelated-warriors raising hell and slaying beasts across the online realm, it's hard to stop.
Like any of the other thousands of players populating the bustling game world, you've been summoned by Oryx the Mad God to serve as dinner for his hungry minions. Of course, you've got other plans. Venturing out beyond the safety of the hub nexus, your mission is to blast beasties, collect loot, grow more powerful, and then stick it to the evil deity. Spraying magic projectiles around the screen while dodging incoming fire from blocky sumo wrestlers, dragons, goblin wizards, and stranger creatures you encounter takes on a classic, arcade-like quality. The straightforwardness is appealing – move, shoot, collect – and when you weave in exploration, obsessive loot hunting, RPG character growth and the camaraderie of smiting evil alongside other adventurers, sessions grow intensely hypnotic. Even if you never survive long enough get reach Oryx's doom lair, there's a ton of fun to be found in collaborating with other players in battle and unlocking cool new classes to play.
Each of Realm of the Mad God's 13 unique character classes are accessed by reaching certain level benchmarks in other classes. Above all, this is what kept me glued to my keyboard playing for hours at a time. You start as a mewling wizard who can fire blasts of magic in any direction, but as you play longer and level-up, you eventually open-up more interesting classes like the necromancer, huntress, mystic, and assassin. Every class has its own set of weapons and items, magic powers, special abilities, and perks. They all play differently, and I got a thrill every time I unlocked a new one to try out. This adds tremendous replay potential too, since unlocking the coolest characters requires you to spend some serious time with each class.
Perma-death layers-on an intense roguelike element to the already zany large-scale bullet hell RPG slugfest unfolding on any given server, and it seriously ups the challenge and risk factor. Getting careless will get you killed and force you to re-start your current character over from level 1. As frustrating as it can be, death is sometimes a welcome opportunity to try out another class, since you can only have one character at a time without using microtransactions to purchase additional slots. But when you're committed to keeping your favorite character alive, the threat of losing all your hard-earned experience and loot gently nudges you into working together with other players and forming impromptu gang of warriors to tackle the tougher swarms of foes as a group.
Realm of the Mad God's streamlined approach to MMO gaming also changes up player interaction in good ways. Since there's no PvP, everyone in the realm is after the same goals – slay, loot, and level-up. As you come across other players, the desire to tag along and pitch in for tougher fights comes intuitively. You share the experienced gained from defeating foes as long as you hit them once, and there's generally plenty of loot to go around. Typing in chat text makes a speech bubble appear over your hero, and communicating in short bursts is effective for concocting plans outside of the heat of battle. When you do find other comrades you want to stick with, you can highlight nearby players and lock their names to your menu bar, allowing you to teleport to their location instantly if you get separated. It's a simple and easy-to-use system that works well.
The realm itself is surprisingly vast, with a diverse landscape that holds more dangerous and inventive foes the further you venture away from your spawn point. Weaker baddies, like scorpions and pirates, populate the sunny beachside. But push through the thick forests, crumbling ruins, and mountains beyond, and you'll find powerful god-like foes capable of slaying low-level adventurers with a single strike. It's these formidable opponents you have to defeat in order to reach Oryx. Thankfully, when you need a break from battle or a quick getaway, tapping the insert key warps you back to the safety of the nexus where you can trade, use fame points or in-game cash to purchase special items, form a guild, and heal-up.
When so much of the MMO experience is pared down for ease of access and quick play, it's a shame that the controls aren't as tight as they should be for the arcade-style shooter gameplay. Movement with the WASD keys sometimes gets gummed up if you're clicking around to shoot a lot while changing direction. Holding the firing button down or toggling auto-fire smoothes this out a bit, but it's frustrating to die because you get stuck walking in the wrong direction for a few seconds longer than you meant to and wind up charging into the middle of a rampaging horde of angry elves. Fortunately, it's not a game-breaker. While the control wonkiness is a pain, the absorbing gameplay drowns out the irritation it causes.
It may be vastly different from its big-league brethren, but this stylish indie MMO has loads of staying power to match its unique concept. Realm of the Mad God’s accessible arcade-style bullet hell action blends with RPG nerdiness in some truly potent ways, and the lovely pixilated world holds an abundance of adventure that’s ripe for the taking. Easy to jump into and damn near impossible to quit, this unusual free-to-play MMO hybrid is worth every second of your spare time.

First of all I have not played any of the Dark Souls games, so the closest game I played that I can compare LOTF with is Blade of Darkness, which I played way back in the day.
That being said, the game was a mixed bag for me.
The gameplay for starters is not for everyone. You either love it or hate it. So you cannot judge the game by it. I personally enjoyed it. It requires a certain degree of patience that many simply do not possess.
For the good parts:
The graphics are nice, the level design, artwork, animations, all very good.
I finished the game in about 26 hours, which in my opinion is pretty balanced. It's not short enough to consider it a bad investment, but it's not long enough to get you annoyed along the way and not finish it.
Now for the less then good parts:
The voice and lip-sync animations are less then mediocre. The soundtrack is fine I guess, but it did not impress or remain in memory.
The story is pretty simple. You do not get enough information about any character in order to have any sort of emotion invested.
For me personally, at least 75% of the weapons i found were just collectibles. I never once used them. even those that were specific for my class. They do not seem to be properly balanced for the moment that you find them. I think i used a total of 4 weapons the entire game. I mean i used the same staff for 4 bosses in a row. The armor pieces are much better balanced however.
The game allows you to ignore the class selection and use any equipment, as long as you have the stats. That is how i got to be a Rogue that uses heavy armor. The side effect of this is that you will naturally gravitate towards certain weapon classes and others you will never ever touch.
The game has a design choice evident from the start, specifically if you want to uncover certain loot, you have to backtrack a lot. This, coupled with the fact that all enemies respawn if you either die or switch zones, has two effects, neither which I am a fan of. It's either a chore to go run around to open that one door/chest that you couldn't before, which makes the game feel empty, either you have to kill every single monster all over again, which in some cases was annoying as all hell because of the positioning of the monsters.
The game crashed a few times for me. 4 times during boss fights, which was really annoying, and once during normal play. I however did not lose more that 10-15 minutes of playtime.
 
In the end for me that whole experience sums it up to a high 6/10.
The good features outweigh the bad ones for me, but not enough for a second playthrough anytime soon.
The price for me is more than fair (15-20 euro). I do not consider it a waste and for what it's worth, I would recommend it to friends.
 
If a sequel would improve on some of the bad points, it could become a decent franchise.

I highly reccommend this game to anyone who is good with quick reactions, a whole lot of patience, and those who love PAC-MAN. Seriously, though, this game is INSANE. There are a few changes from PAC-MAN Championship Edition DX+, such as each ghost on the screen being able to have its own train. Also, they follow certain routes when you get that Power Pellet. You also don't die the instant you bump into a ghost this time, but instead it takes a few bumps to get them angry. When that happens, the ghost jumps into the air and you can travel under it, but as soon as you bump into an angry ghost, you die and they all go back to the center. Also, now the Fruits / Bell / Key... things... now appear in a set spot which varies slightly from map to map. Speaking of maps, they're no longer split into two halves AND you don't need to collect all the Pac-Dots to move on. (This doesn't apply when you get far into a Score Attack map, though.) Collecting all Pac-Dots rewards you with Bombs, which now send you back to the center instead of sending the Ghosts back to the center.
PROS: This game is flat-out addicting and fun. It's also fast-paced as HECK, especially in the Extreme mode for each map. The graphics are also pretty sweet, and... OH MY GOD THE MUSIC. The music, to me, is hands down the BEST part of this game. There's also an adventure-like mode with giant Ghosts as bosses (coupled with the BEST song in all of the game), and you even get a special prize for completing the adventure mode all the way! Also, for those who REALLY liked the Championship DX+ music, all of that returns in this game as well, except for the two non-PAC-MAN songs (the Dig Dug and the Rally X songs, to be exact). There's also much more customization, with many more mazes, some new skins, much more music, and even the camera angle and the background used while playing! I find this to be a nice 5-minute-burner if I'm REALLY bored, too. There's also a tutorial mode for the beginners.
CONS: Let me start with this: THIS GAME IS DIFFICULT. Like I said earlier, it's incredibly fast paced, namely in Score Attack's Extreme mode, and it can be incredibly hard to control if your reactions are slow. Also, the amount of lives and Bombs you have now count towards your final score as well, so dying is MUCH more problematic than it was in PAC-MAN Championship Edition DX+. Each life / bomb is worth ten / one thousand points (respectively), stacking with more lives. (I.E. the first life counted is 10000 points, the second is 20000, and so on. It may cap out at 100000 points per life if you somehow get 10+ lives in Score Attack, but I haven't done that yet. Bombs work similarly, just the first Bomb is 1000, the next is 2000, until it caps out after 10 bombs at 10000 per Bomb.) If you die, not only do you lose out on a lot of points, but the value of Pac-Dots instantly resets to 1. (If you don't collect all Pac-Dots in a stage, the value only goes down by a maximum of 99, but this isn't too big of a deal if you know what you're doing.) Also, bumping into ghosts pushes you back a bit, which may cause you to mess up. Then, when you Power Up, sometimes the Ghosts can be VERY difficult to catch depending on the map. You also cannot eat multiple Ghost Trains at one time, which, TRUST ME, THIS WILL HAPPEN A LOT. Also, the camera changes when you start eating a ghost, which can throw you off-guard when the camera returns to normal. Plus, this is more of a minor issue, but if you prepare to enter a turn too early and there's an opening, you'll slingshot into that opening. This can cut a lot of points off if you're not careful.
All in all, this game is very fun for those who actually give it a try. I mean, who doesn't love competetive, fast-paced PAC-MAN? WITH ONLINE LEADERBOARDS?

As someone who has put tons of time into Pac-Man Championship Edition and Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ on both XBOX 360 and PC, I was totally excited for this. Sadly, I was promptly thrown in to a world of disappointment and regret once I started playing. I gave this game a good honest try, I did. I thought, "Maybe it will just take some getting used to," but alas, it was not to be. Instead of expanding on the great formulat that they had in the first two Championship Editions, they decided to throw that out the window including many of the basics of Pac-Man itself.
First of all, ghosts (for the most part) don't hurt any more. Pac-Man just bounces off them, which seems stupid (and it is) until you realize that it's neccessary as you can't always tell you're going to run into a ghost because of the games flighty controls. The controls in this game (which were flawless in the previous two) are beyond sensative. All too often will Pac-Man go up when I try to go down, or crash into a barage of ghosts because Pac-Man will suddenly turn left when I was trying to continue straight. Combine this with the warp speeds Pac-Man seems to acheive in no time at all, and sometimes you'll completely lose track of him, only to find Pac-Man in a section of the maze you had no intention of travelling to.
This is to say nothing of the jump pads which springboard you over a wall into another section of the map. Those can be disorienting enough without a warp speed Pac-Man bouncing off a ghost onto one of thse pads.
I wanted to like this game, I really did, but it's just not fun. Honestly, I could've probably dealt with the ghost bouncing if the controls weren't absolute garbage. There's plenty to be annoyed about in this game, but if the controls were great like the previous ones, then there is a chance I would've really enjoyed this one too.

A tower defense game is all about control. Knowing and guiding what's going on. Using your analytical skills to overcome chaos. Outthinking a superior enemy and defeating it in spite of its superior numbers.
And what's the #1 thing you need in order to analyze? INFORMATION.
Where are the tooltips? I got a new tower, but when I started the next fight, I didn't remember exactly how it worked. I just had to plant it and see what happened. That is the opposite of fun.
It begs me to open the encyclopedia so I can see info on the enemies, but the special attributes are not explained. "Squishy", eh? What is that? I guess it makes them die more quickly, but if you're not going to tell me how to take advantage of their squishiness, why not just give them fewer hit points? Thanks for wasting my time.
After I finished a level, a picture of something and a name came on the screen. What is that- an achievement I unlocked? A skill? Where do I find out about it?
And on and on. There's a difference between challenging and frustrating. This one was the latter. Maybe if I'd played it more, it would have gotten better...but why? I can go play better TD games on Kongregate for free, and most of them are fun and informative right from the first level. I think I only paid like a dollar for this game, but I still want my money back.

In the interest of disclosure, I really do not like the developer of this game on a personal level. However, this has nothing to do with anything, as I am also capable of seperating the Art from the Artist, and there are a great many things that I have enjoyed over the years, knowing full well that a jerk made them.
With that said... Oh dear. Oh dear indeed. Fleetcomm is a bit of a mess, to understate the situation completely. From the very first menu's inconsistent (but piercing) audio, to the realization that the ONLY graphical option is 'Fullscreen on/off', we're looking at an incredibly bare-bones game here. Content-wise, this really shouldn't be carrying the 'V1.0' label, as it currently contains justt seven disconnected tutorial stages (plus one survival arena), with the first chapter of the planned story not due until later this month.
Okay, the gameplay - the game claims to be a tactical shooter experience, but what that really means is that it's Asteroids + Gradius' Options with hideously convoluted controls and almost impossible to read graphics. The background (in this version at least) is a near solid black field with occasional dark red haze, and almost all enemies are the EXACT SAME COLOUR with no clearly visible highlights, so in order to clearly see what you're shooting at, you need to hold your Scan button (Tab by default) to draw obnoxious yellow lines to every enemy in the arena.
This is also somehow worse than early alpha builds of the game, which were still pretty confusing to watch, but the background provided at least SOME contrast against the enemies. Basic readability and usability were clearly not the focus of development during this game's many delays.
Besides that, the game feels twitchy and hard to control in the worst of ways. What should be an intuitive arcade shooter is made convoluted beyond reason by drowning every simple and accessible element in a haze of noise, both visual and auditory. The soundscape of the game is a hellacious mess. A cacophony of piercing wails and beeps that never really seem to indicate anything of use.
The engine is also a mess. Just by firing missiles I've managed to drop the game - in windowed mode, to boot - to single-digit framerates, which never recover even after the missiles explode. Music tracks play on top of each other. Physics seem to be a suggestion rather than a rule, with enemies drifting in random directions contrary to what their sprite might suggest. There's also no indication from the starfield to tell you which way you're drifting.
Somehow, despite the framerate tanking, my GPU is still running cool. However, on the totally static mission selection menu, the fans rev up, as if it's rendering some impossibly complex scene that I can't see because there's a couple blue box-buttons in the way.
There's really only one thing I can say in this games favour, and it's that the music isn't too bad, although I gather that was produced by a third party too. In short, this is an ugly, painful, messy experience, and woefully unfinished. Despite this, it's being sold as a full product, with no indication on the storefront itself (you need to check the Recent Updates page) that there's nothing but the tutorial here at present.
Four years of development and multiple crowdfunding campaigns, and this is the 'final' product released. Even with more content planned for release, somehow I doubt adding more of this is going to make the game any better. Avoid. This game is bad. I've written so many words here, but I still cannot really describe how broken this feels on even the most basic conceptual level.

The Darkest Dungeon is 1/3 managing a base like xcom where you must decide what upgrades you need now and what can wait, and 2/3 turn based dungeon crawling. The dungeon crawling aspect is well balanced and at no point in the game so far have I felt that one class is a must bring on any mission. This opens the game up to have a lot of variety as you can mix up team comp to your hearts content. The combat is very responsive and while the animations are simple they are rather satisfying. One thing that you must be aware of thow is the game does have a very real element of RNG to it. Similar to XCOM the game may have to make several checks a turn based of your stats and enemy stats. And again, like XCOM things can seem to go horribly wrong in the blink of an eye. On the other side of the coin the game could give you the rolls you need when it really matters.  Instead of seeing the RNG as a criticism I feel it keeps the game suspenseful, never at any point do I think nothing can go wrong, and that feeling keeps makes it so that the very last mission is just as suspenseful as the first. But also like XCOM with some proper planning and strategies you can minimize these chances for failer to a good degree. The game also has a fun risk reward feeling as you gamble how many supplies you should bring for the next mission or should I just go to one last room before leaving the dungeon. To all those people who can’t stand RNG playing a noticeable part in your game Darkest Dungeon is not for you, but if you like that feeling of unknowing and suspense and those moments of triumph then The Darkest Dungeon is for you.

With so many moving parts to learn and a seemingly infinite breadth of options to explore, diving into any new MMO is a major investment of time and energy. It's exhausting, really, which is why I appreciate a game like the free-to-play Realm of the Mad God. This fantasy-themed, co-operative bullet hell MMORPG is beautifully simple, yet deep enough to keep you chained to your PC for days on end. It takes only a minute or so to get right into the action, and, once you get a taste for running around with a gaggle of your fellow pixelated-warriors raising hell and slaying beasts across the online realm, it's hard to stop.
Like any of the other thousands of players populating the bustling game world, you've been summoned by Oryx the Mad God to serve as dinner for his hungry minions. Of course, you've got other plans. Venturing out beyond the safety of the hub nexus, your mission is to blast beasties, collect loot, grow more powerful, and then stick it to the evil deity. Spraying magic projectiles around the screen while dodging incoming fire from blocky sumo wrestlers, dragons, goblin wizards, and stranger creatures you encounter takes on a classic, arcade-like quality. The straightforwardness is appealing – move, shoot, collect – and when you weave in exploration, obsessive loot hunting, RPG character growth and the camaraderie of smiting evil alongside other adventurers, sessions grow intensely hypnotic. Even if you never survive long enough get reach Oryx's doom lair, there's a ton of fun to be found in collaborating with other players in battle and unlocking cool new classes to play.
Each of Realm of the Mad God's 13 unique character classes are accessed by reaching certain level benchmarks in other classes. Above all, this is what kept me glued to my keyboard playing for hours at a time. You start as a mewling wizard who can fire blasts of magic in any direction, but as you play longer and level-up, you eventually open-up more interesting classes like the necromancer, huntress, mystic, and assassin. Every class has its own set of weapons and items, magic powers, special abilities, and perks. They all play differently, and I got a thrill every time I unlocked a new one to try out. This adds tremendous replay potential too, since unlocking the coolest characters requires you to spend some serious time with each class.
Perma-death layers-on an intense roguelike element to the already zany large-scale bullet hell RPG slugfest unfolding on any given server, and it seriously ups the challenge and risk factor. Getting careless will get you killed and force you to re-start your current character over from level 1. As frustrating as it can be, death is sometimes a welcome opportunity to try out another class, since you can only have one character at a time without using microtransactions to purchase additional slots. But when you're committed to keeping your favorite character alive, the threat of losing all your hard-earned experience and loot gently nudges you into working together with other players and forming impromptu gang of warriors to tackle the tougher swarms of foes as a group.
Realm of the Mad God's streamlined approach to MMO gaming also changes up player interaction in good ways. Since there's no PvP, everyone in the realm is after the same goals – slay, loot, and level-up. As you come across other players, the desire to tag along and pitch in for tougher fights comes intuitively. You share the experienced gained from defeating foes as long as you hit them once, and there's generally plenty of loot to go around. Typing in chat text makes a speech bubble appear over your hero, and communicating in short bursts is effective for concocting plans outside of the heat of battle. When you do find other comrades you want to stick with, you can highlight nearby players and lock their names to your menu bar, allowing you to teleport to their location instantly if you get separated. It's a simple and easy-to-use system that works well.
The realm itself is surprisingly vast, with a diverse landscape that holds more dangerous and inventive foes the further you venture away from your spawn point. Weaker baddies, like scorpions and pirates, populate the sunny beachside. But push through the thick forests, crumbling ruins, and mountains beyond, and you'll find powerful god-like foes capable of slaying low-level adventurers with a single strike. It's these formidable opponents you have to defeat in order to reach Oryx. Thankfully, when you need a break from battle or a quick getaway, tapping the insert key warps you back to the safety of the nexus where you can trade, use fame points or in-game cash to purchase special items, form a guild, and heal-up.
When so much of the MMO experience is pared down for ease of access and quick play, it's a shame that the controls aren't as tight as they should be for the arcade-style shooter gameplay. Movement with the WASD keys sometimes gets gummed up if you're clicking around to shoot a lot while changing direction. Holding the firing button down or toggling auto-fire smoothes this out a bit, but it's frustrating to die because you get stuck walking in the wrong direction for a few seconds longer than you meant to and wind up charging into the middle of a rampaging horde of angry elves. Fortunately, it's not a game-breaker. While the control wonkiness is a pain, the absorbing gameplay drowns out the irritation it causes.
It may be vastly different from its big-league brethren, but this stylish indie MMO has loads of staying power to match its unique concept. Realm of the Mad God’s accessible arcade-style bullet hell action blends with RPG nerdiness in some truly potent ways, and the lovely pixilated world holds an abundance of adventure that’s ripe for the taking. Easy to jump into and damn near impossible to quit, this unusual free-to-play MMO hybrid is worth every second of your spare time.

FleetCOMM is a generic SHMUP clone of asteroids. Okay. Clone may be a bit of a misnomer, because Asteroids was fun.
After four years in development hell, where the developer regularly railed against the game industry, women, and his own backers, the game was finally released last night. Okay. Released may be a bit of a misnomer, as there are tutorial missions and the "promise" of a first episode soon. I wouldn't hold my breath.
Pros: The music is "okay" if you are into testosterone-fueled electronica; the graphics might encourage people suffering from glaucoma to scratch at their eyes until they have relieved the pressure and avoided an expensive surgery.
Cons: High risk of blindness and infection from scratching at your eyes. Supporting an angry boy. Everything else.
Gameplay mechanics - meh. Nothing new here. Perhaps I didn't play it long enough to get a feel for the game, but... It seriously reminded me of the 1979 release of asteroids. Sure, it has more colors, enough to make me want to claw my eyes out, but... ugh.
Playable code - well, it loaded. Then it crashed. Then it reloaded, and I started playing a tutorial mission, and it crashed.
If the dev was a nice person, I might give him the benefit of the doubt and say 'oh, things will be improved.' But honestly, FleetCOMM was written by an angry boy who thinks that the world doesn't like him because he 'speaks truth to power.' When in actually: the world doesn't care about him; the people who have interacted with him don't like him because he is annoying, angry, and alliterative; and his game is a tech demo from 1998 (at best) that I plan on uninstalling and hope to never hear about again.

I will start off by saying that Shadowgate(2014) was the main reason I even opened up a Steam account. I played Shadowgate on NES back in the mid-2000s decade, as I had never played it as a kid. As far as point and click adventures go, it's certainly one of the best ever, and this remake does not disappoint. The atmosphere, enhanced graphics, well told story, remixed music, different difficulty modes, and varied puzzles and paths make this one outshine the original version even. With various customization options, anyone who enjoys point and click adventure titles will feel right at home with Shadowgate.
For the best experience during gameplay, I like to set the music to retro 8-bit style and play that way. That music when the torch is about to run out always puts me on edge, and heightens the foreboding mood that a game like this is supposed to have. Some of the puzzles are the same as the original- such as needing to grab a shield to block the dragon's flame in the treasure room- but others require slightly different approaches than the original game, especially on Master difficulty. If you don't use a walkthrough, it will take quite some time to get through the game. Beyond that, I am certainly not going to spoil anything, so try it and find out for yourself.
Overall, I highly recommend Shadowgate(2014). It truly is one of the definitive point and click adventure games around.

It takes a special game to give you life-long memories - and even more special game to both give you childhood traumas and make you remember it with fondness.
Shadowgate's remake is, in my opinion, a good mixture of old and new. Some puzzles are very similar to the ones in the classic version, yet there are plenty of new ones and some which look a lot like the old ones but might surprise old-timers. The option to switch between remixed music and NES tracks, as well as other retro elements, was also a nice plus.
Some of the puzzles were slightly frustrating and I admit that I resorted to using a walkthrough when I got stuck in a certain point with the curse, but all in all, I would recommend Shadowgate to anyone who likes point-and-click adventures and dark fantasy (which doesn't take it too seriously, though). I liked the art, the music and the general 'feel' of the game, and though the story is relatively simple, it serves its purpose in this tribute to the old MacVenture classic.
Maybe it was worth it to fear the dark and Grim Reaper for 20 years or so.

Pro:
Cons:
To see the rise and fall of your soldiers (as well as the countless hours customizing there individual style) while playing through the story is the real gem for XCOM 2 to me and the sole reason to continually keep replaying through the campaign.
Although not without pitfalls in terms of optimization (minor pauses between actions, long loading between missions, some graphical glitches and fps drops at times) and majority of missions with timers (although more logical for the guerrilla warfare aspect this time around) it does force a more aggressive playstyle to get used to, but it does add a level of tension especially earlier in the game with everything from clutch shots landing to crucial enemy shots missing and extracting out just in time or hacking the device on the last turn while dealing with an enemy pod or two due to said aggressive actions to just get to the objective.

With all that being said its also where XCOM 2 shines in my opinion, with every mission regardless of success or failure, its about a story that develops outside of what Firaxis put in; its about how certain individuals in your squad will become all-stars and how others become a bane to your existence.
To aid in immersing yourself into the game's world, character customization allows you to change your soldiers appearance to express the envisioned personality along with multiple standard voice overs for a few different national ethnic dialects (Aus/UK/US English, French, German, Italian and Spanish base game), naming and creating backstories if you feel imaginative. And with Firaxis allowing for a robust modding community to exist you can download new cosmetics, voice packs, weapon packs, classes or change the pace of the game with community balance changes to ease or increase the difficulty to your liking.
Although optional to buy and play the DLC Alien Hunters and Shen's Last Gift did introduce some interesting content, but I feel that there could've been more story missions unique for both
and
.
All in all I would recommend XCOM 2 wholeheartedly if you're a fan of turn-based tactical games, but anyone with any hesitation I would check out some let's plays or wait for a good sale (already been a few 50% off sales).

Do not let my hours on game fool you, as I do not play through Steam.  I've been playing since Open Beta release.  The game looked VERY promising, and I was instantly addicted to the feel and abilities of my players.  When I first started, there were 4 classes available: Knight, Gunner, Fae Trickster, and Neon Ninja.  I was fortunate enough to unlock all the new classes they have released since then, especially now that - while possible to get the classes without paying, you'll be waiting a long time for a server patch big enough to reward you with a "class coin" to unlock a class.  I currently have 4 saved from different times.
Once this game went out of Beta and released on Steam, there have been major improvements server-side.  There were queues to get into the game for 60+ minutes at times, and now they're rebuilding the infrastructure to include better gameplay/graphic abilities.
Overall, if you're a collector this game is for you.  Unfortunately(much to my despise) they instituted a PvP Arena(which is fairly balanced by all measures) that awards items that a collector such as myself are forced to endure a part of play that I do not enjoy in order to attain these items.
The game is very fast-paced once you go into the adventure realms.  You go from dungeon to dungeon killing bosses for chests that contain loot, and more and more rare items to be found.  The amount of collecting in this game took me 8 months just to finish all the different weapon styles available(and made by players).
The movable house (Cornerstone) is a good idea, and now you can have multiples.  In the harder Adventure worlds the cornerstones are less and less available, making healing/loot collecting a might bit harder.
However:
I am noting that this is more Trionworld's fault than it is the Developers, but the game has become increasingly P2P.  The bonuses players receive by purchasing a subscription are sickening to me.  What took me 6 months to do, they can do in 2 now.
The marketplace is already inflated, and is going to get even more so.  There is only 1 in-game-currency sink in the game, and it only inflates prices even further than before.
People are allowed to play on multiple instances in the game to exploit collecting different types of items so long as they're not automated... but come on- we all know it happens.
The community can be a bit trying at times.  There are many rude people, a lot of younger people, and some salty people.  Overall most just like to have fun and spammers are quickly dealt with.
Trading is pretty much flawless. You can't get ripped off unless you allow yourself to be.
Fishing is arduous, but the collection is pretty nifty.  You can get different trophies for different size fish, as well as trophies for every mob in the game (some are unavailable now and fetch a steep price).
8.5 / 10
I still play, I will continue to play until I am forced to pay out of pocket to enjoy my experience.

Welp, the FleetCOMM steam account hasn't logged on in 2 weeks, the fleetCOMM discussion boards have gone from tightly moderated to nothing, many backers never got their keys, the steam trading cards that are promised on the front page still don't drop and chapter 1 still hasn't been released. What a world, what a world.
Music is decently intense, and easily attainable as decent quality ogg files. There's a game somewhere in here that's playable that I look forward to seeing in the coming months. Squadrons and formations appear to be fully customizable, which may prove to be interesting if the program can handle it.
Poorly optimized, it cannot decide if it wants to play at 10fps or 80fps and eats through CPU. No resolution options. Nearly no environmental feedback whatsoever. Program can't execute a proper close without crashing. Interface feels like a clumsy interactive Flash circa 2006, making preview videos misleading, at best. Spammed input can freeze the game up; Not an great asset for a shmup. The tutorial area is a confusing mess-- It introduces concepts slowly, but with absolutely no explanation. Whether you succeed or fail, each mission boots you back to the title screen. Slow, floaty gameplay does not fit the camera-shaking, no-holds-barred style it portrays itself as and is very slow. Balance issues are present in Chapter 0, where you can die within a couple seconds of starting a level, or not take damage for 15 minutes before knowing how to even properly pilot the ship. (If the ship loads. Sometimes it does not, and you are piloting just the directional circle around it.)
It may be worth testing out, but I'd question keeping it even at this massively discounted price. This game had been delayed well over five times with a complete disregard towards dates set, so updates for future missions feel extremely bleak. Whether or not this is true, we will find out on May 30th. But as a consumer, it would be foolish to not have major trust issues with such promises being treated so flippantly before. Hopefully the dates set from here on-out will be abided by.
I would like to return on May 30th to see what Chapter 1 has to offer, and alter my review to reflect the changes made. I am a big fan of this genre of games and have anticipated this title for a long while.

Fleetcomm in its current state consists of only 8 "tutorial" missions designed to get you acquainted with the game's controls. The actual game chapters are going to be released at a later date (hopefully for free), with the first scheduled for May 30, if it isn't delayed.
UPDATE: Chapter One of Fleetcomm has been indefinitely delayed. If you buy this game you will only receive the tutorial missions and the developer has not set a release date for the actual game itself.
KEEP IN MIND THAT YOU ARE PAYING FOR TUTORIAL MISSIONS WITH NO GUARANTEE OF RECEIVING A FULL GAME.
So what's it like? It's a slightly more "tactical" variation on games like geometry wars and asteroids. It has a fairly typical loadout of shmup-like weapons, a shield, a weak laser with infinite ammo, a stronger "railgun" with limited ammo, a temporary cloaking mode and a bomb (which doesn't seem to actually do anything). The gameplay mostly consists of trying to fulfill simple mission objectives such as "destroy all of X". You'll be given a small ship to navigate around a 2D plane (think asteroids but with freedom of movement) and you'll have to dodge/reflect numerous projectiles and enemy ships, while trying to shoot down as many enemies as you can.
Sounds great in theory, so how does it play? Kind of like a steaming pile of garbage. The controls are really awkward. You use the mouse to steer the ship but the mouse buttons aren't utilized at all, requiring you to engage in some pretty awkward fingerwork on the keyboard.  Enemy design consists mostly of amorphous blob like enemies, which gives you the impression that you're fighting amoebas rather than a menacing alien fleet. The game is certainly colorful and your screen will often be filled with flashing green lights and various bright artifacts but you're more likely to get a migraine than enjoyment out of it.
To be fair, the game is definitely playable and there's a kind of logic to the gameplay, but it's just not fun. Even the original Asteroids feels like a much smoother and more intuitive experience.  I'd also go as far as to say that Asteroid's 4 bit sound effects were a lot better than Fleetcomm's bizarre mixture of hums, drones and blips that make the shooting feel very unsatisfying. Some of the weapons, including your primary gun, don't even make a sound and it's hard to hear the very quiet buzz of exploding enemy units over the deafening dubstep soundtrack. There's just no weight to it at all and you just don't get that feeling of "mass destruction" that you should get from playing a shmup.
As for the deafening dubstep soundtrack? It's as I described. Repetive, distracting, unpleasant, and it consists of one single track that plays over and over again. Just terrible!
I would rate my 30 minutes in Fleetcomm lower than coming down from an ecstasy binge in a really bad nightclub. Really not a very good experience, and nowhere close to a "complete" one. This is essentially an early access game without the early access label, and a bad one at that. Don't spend your money on this rubbish.
And the worst part of it all? It's the result of 4 years of "work" and over $37,000 in public donations. What an absolute joke.
EDIT: ONCE THE PRICE OF THIS GAME INEVITABLY DROPS TO A DOLLAR, IT MIGHT BE WORTH BUYING AS A KUSOGE OR A GAG GIFT, BUT ONLY IF YOU FEEL COMFORTABLE GIVING THE DEVELOPER YOUR POCKET CHANGE.

Lords Of The Fallen is a soulslike game set in a dark fantasy universe very similar to the one seen in Warhammer. Sounds good on paper, however I can't really recommend this game. Let's start with what's good.
- Beautiful art style, lots of interesting details in the environment and in the gear.
- Decent graphics with volumetric lighting. Sometimes the picture on the screen gets borderline gorgeous with all the ashes and sparks from hits flying around. Breathtaking.
- Good combat system. Similar to the one seen in Dark Souls, yet with it's own twist (the addition of the Gauntlet is a nice touch). I love the timing-based combos — no more angry button smashing, you have to be careful with when you attack.
- The Sound in this game is fantastic. Love the clenching of metal and heavy footsteps of the character.
- Good God, camera gets atrocious sometimes. You're supposed to fight mobs, instead you're fighting game's camera.
- Some mobs and bosses auto-aim on you. Meaning that while you're dodging their attack - they will follow you.
- Speaking of Bosses. What was that? They all look the same! And why are they so easy? Beating the final boss in my second try is not good.
- Story? What story? That plot-twist was borderline ludacris.
- Mundane voice acting
- Game's world navigation is frustrating. I've been cycling some areas over and over again, just because a narrow path was hidden between two bigger objects. Not really a good design decision. I personally think this happened because the image lacks depth.
- Speaking of Game's World. It's really small. Loading screens between some areas are extremely frustrating and why are they there anyway? Damn.
- There's only, like, 10 variations of enemies.
- Game finale doesn't feel satisfying at all.
- While Risk-Rewarding Check Point system is a great idea, there's really no risk to it. You can put all of your experience points into stats straight away without saving.
All and all, this game is not hopelesly bad. It has lots of potential, yet somehow, at this moment, the developer didn't seem to push it hard enough. I can't recommend this game, however, I'll keep my ear to the ground for The Surge, see if Deck 13 will work on their mistakes.

-Note: this reveiw is around a week after "eclipse" was released.
Trove is (100% my opinion) a great game.
It most certainly has its fair share of flaws but also a lot of stengths.
-Okay, Trove is a MMO run by the company "Trion", a small MMO maker. Trove is their less serious addition to their MMO list and I feel they can think they can get away with these horrid servers yet it's all you hear about in the global chat. Not sure what they could do about this, they aren't a huge company so I'm sure better servers may be out of their price range.
-As for the Pay2Win stands "eclipse" hasn't helped. They just want you to pay your way to the top. I know a few of the highest players in the game and some of them are Free2play players and that's great and some of them aren't. It's okay to give some $ to comanies and games you love. I'll admit I have put money towards Trove and I bought their "extra life" packs for charity and a couple others and I've bought the "premium" membership. They don't really paywall anything but they just make the grind in Free2play look like a bad choice.
-Razers mice users I'm sorry if you've gone through what I have. Trove hates razer for no reason and there is a bug that makes your camera jump randomly if you're using razer devices (I use a Naga). Don't know why and in the 2 years I've played this and sent tickets about it, it's yet to be fixed.
- Trove has a lot of veriety in it's game from things to do, to how you look to where you can go. It's colourful, it's cheerflu and can be relaxing. You can fish, quest, build, raid, grind, chat to new people, PVP, gain mastery (material level, like how many mounts and fishing rods you own) and you never feel constricted in anyway, the game feels like it's yours to explore.
-The community is quite wholesome for the most part. I've gotten plenty of help in global chat and club chats even about the most bizzare topics and what should be common knowledge to the average player, if you ask it someone will kindly answer, obviously I can't speak for everyone but most are nice. I accidently gave a player 2.2million flux instead of 22k one trade at 3am and they gave back my flux.
-A lot of content means that the players with 1000s of hours still have something to do, but it also means new players get swamped with useless information. The game is so open and free but that means at 1 mastery and 1 Power Rank you are shoved into the world of Trove, standing right next to my character with near 20k PR and almost 600 mastery. It's a little daunting to say the least. But it's a positive once you're into the game and you find you're never out of things to do.

Trove is a fun and relaxing MMO and there's so much a haven't spoken about like the over amount of RNG and the weekly reset raids lag, but all in all I find Trove a fun and enjoyable experience where I've met new life long friends, found new hobbies from people, made structures I'm truely proud of and goals I want to achieve. If you're wanting to get into an MMO this is a great starting MMO to sink your teeth (and life) into. I will say if you're a WoW, BDO or GW2 player you may find this game a little on the simple side, but it's still fantasic to me. I hope you come join me in game \o/

Unfortunately I've removed my previous postive review from back in Feb to write this one.
This gameplay itself is very fun, well-balanced, and engaging, but the matchmaking is just awful. There is a relatively small-ish playerbase, which is not unworkable in and of itself, except the game wants to force this "competitive" style MMR on you, and so this small group of players is split up between a bunch of matchmaking brackets and so it's often impossible to get a match. I've been sitting here from about 15m now and still haven't gotten one.
And to add insult to injury, 1 or 2 people will usually bail mid-match (and sometimes right at the start) and the game has no system for replacing lost teammates. And because of how the game is balanced, once you're down 1 player, you've basically lost (unless the enemy team is wholly and completely incompetant and/or playing with their toes).
So 20+ minutes to get a match, and then when you finally do, expect it to be ♥♥♥♥♥♥ because someone quits on one side or the other, turning it into an unsatisfying steamroll.
Oh, and they still haven't fixed the "match was aborted" bug from 8 months ago. And there's several weird "error" messages that will boot you from the damn matchmaking with no sound notification, so if you think you can alt-tab to find a match (which you will obviously need to, because nobody is going to sit there for 20 minutes looking at nothing), you'll need to check back every 30s or so to make sure it didn't just silently boot you from the matchmaking entirely. How ♥♥♥♥ing stupid is that? The matchmaking had all these issue back in god damn January! And they're still not fixed! Nearly 9 months later, same basic bugs.
Let me stress here that this game has great and well-designed/balanced gameplay, but it's a shame the awful/buggy matchmaking and unpunished quitters mean you'll rarely get to experience it properly.

You haven't played Half- Life yet? I'm disappointed in you.
Half- Life is a linear first person shooter where you play as the legendary Gordon Freeman. Your goal is to escape the Black Mesa science facility after a routine experiment goes horribly wrong and releases countless alien beings into the facility.
The gameplay is fast, like many classic FPS games. You take a lot of damage, but so do enemies. The experience is very well paced, all the "action" setpiece moments are memorable and fun and the parts inbetween will test your skills and punish you harshly if you fail. You will need to be quick and accurate to beat the soldiers and you'll need to be smart to out- maneuver the alien enemies. The difficulty curve is smooth and the gameplay is satisfying. This is easily one of the most enjoyable FPS games there is, even today.
Some people dislike the minor platforming elements, but they aren't too bad.
