Summary: Adventure game with dead-ends
Multiplayer: No
Completion: 6 hrs
Cards: Yes
Cloud: No
I remember seeing Shadowgate for NES in magazines as a kid, and always wanted to try it out, but they never had it at my rental store. Now I get to have that chance, with much nicer eye candy. And... I must say it didn't disappoint, but it clearly is not a game for everybody.
You take on the role of Jair. You want to beat the Warlock Lord. From there the story doesn't really get more complicated that that. It's pretty much your standard good-vs-evil tale. I would have liked some character development through dialogue. For example, there's a lady in a tower who would have been a good choice to converse with, but, well, that becomes moot pretty fast. Sure you become more powerful throughout the course of the game, but Jair never says anything short of grunts and tricks or treats.
Shadowgate comes from an era where dead-ends are both possible and common. I'm still against this design philosophy, but I can't totally blame them for wanting to keep the spirit of the original. Just be forewarned that it's quite possible to screw yourself over, so save often and in different slots. Speaking of which, I would have much liked the ability to name my save files. It gets kind of hard to tell which save is which..
Shadowgate boasts some very nice artwork, and is easy on the eyes. There's a fair amount of clutter in each scene, but I didn't have much difficulty picking out interactable objects, even without the use of F2. Retro graphics on the other hand is very harsh on the eyes. I recommend against using that, as it makes everything difficult to discern. I thought it would replicate the NES look, but instead it's like they took a mosaic filter and applied it to the screen. The music is pleasant, and fits the game quite nicely. It's never out of place and never obtrusive. Even better, the retro music works pretty well.
The interface is a tad on the clunky side. The inventory menu has a brief delay before you can interact with it, which is problematic when you need to access it so frequently. Thankfully you can set bindings, but that's more of a band-aid fix than a proper solution. The ability to use scroll wheel to go through items would have been nice. I suggest learning the keyboard shortcuts, as they will help speed up your progress in subsequent playthroughs. If you play the game entirely with the mouse, certain things feel remarkably slow.
There's 4 difficulty levels as of the time of this writing - Normal, Apprentice, Journeyman, and Master. I ended up playing through all of them in order, and I will say there's a pretty good progression. What worked once before might work differently in a higher difficulty.  I had the most fun with Journeyman difficulty which provides a generous time frame, but lacks puzzles exclusive to Master, which hampered the enjoyment a bit. Master difficulty on the other hand is overkill. I nearly failed both curing myself and beating it by less than 20 turns each. I thought I had a firm grasp on what I needed to do to win, but apparently not!
From Apprentice difficulty and higher (all the "Classic" modes), the game starts to institute hard time limits, primarily in the way of torches. You only have so many turns before your torch flickers out and die. Torches aren't too difficult to find, even on Master difficulty. In all liklihood, you will probably die to the other natural time limits set by the game, especially on Master difficulty.
Compounding the time limit problem is the abundance of items that do absolutely nothing. At least in Bethesda games you can sell all that junk you acquire. In here, the items serve to waste your time and nothing more. Unused items just makes the game feel unfinished. Yes I know they're red herrings, but they feel like an oversight, especially for the adventure game genre.
The game tries its darnedest to be as cryptic as possible sometimes. Most obvious case is in regard to spells. There's no way anyone would know what the spells do, as the game provides vague descriptions when you examine and cast them. And on Master difficulty you really can't spend turns casting spells willy-nilly.
Most of the puzzles in the game make... some amount of sense. The early difficulties are easy enough to figure out on your own, at least with the help of Yorick. The later difficulties I admit to using a guide. Many altered puzzles have solutions I didn't see clues for. When have I ever needed to make a green fire or get a wet cloak?
Overall I found Shadowgate to be enjoyable enough to sit through it through all difficulties. While I can't fault it for trying to be faithful to the original, I can fault the original for its curious design choices. If there's one thing I would have liked, it's the ability to play on Master mode without time limits, because I enjoyed the sheer number of things to see in there, but had no time to see all of it. I think Shadowgate falls into a 7/10.
EDIT: Bunch of spelling errors and grammar.

Ah, Stardew Valley... What can I say that hasn't already been said by countless others?
I was gifted this game last year by a friend who continuously raved and raved about it, insisting that I play it. Let's be clear, Harvest Moon and reality sim type games aren't my cup of tea. I don't hate on em but I know what I like and I like what I like (Action, adventure, RPG, immersive and engaging type stuff, etc).
So when he gifted it to me last Christmas, I did the responsible thing and said thanks and gave it a try. It was a pretty rocky start. The game has a very simple premise -- you're a city born who ultimately tires of the daily grind and does a complete 180 once you find out you've inherited your grandfather's old, run down farm. Graphically, the game looked pretty enough and is fairly easy to pick up. After playing the first day or two, getting my bearings, learning some of the ropes, I remember saying to myself "Meh... it's okay. I'm still not sure how I feel about this" and making stupid mistakes like boxing myself into the center of a 3x3 grid as I built trellis type crops around me going "well damn, I should probably never take up farming."
Time moves VERY quickly in Stardew Valley. I think it's like every 20 minutes or so is a full day in game. And as I understand it, even seasoned players often find that there just aren't enough hours in the day to do everything you intend to. So I kept playing, slowly learning from my mistakes and trial and error teaching me what to do and how to do it better the next time.
Somewhere in that time, the game really grew on me. I was putting aside the games I knew I loved already because I was so engrossed in my fictitious farm life. Now I have 157 hours logged and still don't have everything "done" (still missing a few elusive artifacts for the museum and some of the ultra expensive things for the farm I can't afford yet) but that doesn't bother me as much as it normally does. I still load the game up every now and then when I need to relax or take my mind off of things.
PROS:
- Versatile gameplay with multiple different landscapes to develop your farm (basic, riverland, overrun with monsters that you continually fight off as you farm) based on how you prefer your gameplay difficulty. No two farms will be exactly the same.
- Simple, intuitive controls. Game is easy to learn with a very low curve.
- Strangely engrossing on many levels. I've never cared about interior design or exterior appearances in real life as much as I have about how my farm and my cabin looks.
- Game is very LGBT friendly. I may be a straight, heterosexual man, but I believe in individual rights and freedoms and to see a game like this honor those kinds of choices is deserving of respect.
- Online multiplayer support is coming soon!
CONS:
- Strangely engrossing. This is a double edged sword. Because of how fast the game days pass (and your progress only saves at the start of every morning) it is very easy to say "just one more day..." and completely blow off real life responsibility.
- Lacks some very simple mechanics (that user created mods fix btw) that make you wonder why they aren't a part of the game. Case in point, the ability to harvest everything with your scythe. Unless you don't mind rapid clicking to harvest crops, until you gain access to the Junimo hut where the lil guys will do the work for you, be prepared to do a LOT of clicking on individual plants.
- Plenty of options to earn money, but in order to afford the most expensive stuff without cheating, the "best" way seems to be making and aging wine in the cellar, which takes a long, long time since no matter what star level you put the wine into the cask, it starts at base rarity and takes 30+ days to age to top quality with no way of interrupting the process until it is fully done.
Bottom line, I do not regret playing this game and expect to sink many more hours into it once the multiplayer patch comes out early 2018.

Shadowgate is a point and click/adventure puzzle game developed by Zojoi and published by Reverb Triple XP. Until recently, I had never heard of this title but apparently Shadowgate is one of the most well known point and click adventure titles in history. It was one of the original titles in the popular MacVenture series that went on to be celebrated on the NES, GBC, and Nintendo 64 so this game has alot of history behind it. This version of Shadowgate has been completely remastered by the original developement team from the ground up adding tons of new content to the game. The title thrusts you into the role of "The Seed Of Prophecy", a somewhat novice but "chosen" mage tasked with traveling to the living castle Shadowgate in hopes of defeating the evil that dwells within...the dreaded warlock lord.
Gameplay-wise, the title is presented in the first person perspective with a very minimal heads up display. Your character moves throughout the bowels of castle Shadowgate room by room searching for clues to aid you in your quest while also collecting items and trying to avoid death at the hands of traps, creatures and just plain stupidity. The various puzzles that you have to solve during your questing are the true high point of this game. You have to be keen to figure out many of these puzzles in order to advance the story and some of them will have you wanting to toss your keyboard through the nearest plate glass window. Beware as there will be some frustrating moments to be had in this game but that just makes the reward of solving the puzzles that much more enjoyable once you finally figure them out. Remember that sense of accomplishment that you felt in Dark Souls when you finally defeated that boss after the 103rd try? Kinda like that...kinda.
Graphically, this game is very beautiful. As I stated earlier, this is a remastered version with all new stunningly gorgeous handpainted artwork from beggining to end. The game interface is easy to use and highly customizable. The sound effects are extremely well done, very crisp and fit the title perfectly. The musical score is amazing. It changes depending on the situation and the place that you are inside of castle Shadowgate and does a wonderful job of immersing you within the title.
I was able to complete the game in just under 14 hours but of course I like to explore and backtrack so the typical gamer should be able to finish it in 10-12 hours. It's a short title but very enjoyable especially if you like this genre of games. This was my first dive into this category of gaming and it was a terrific experience that has me looking forward to playing more titles like this one. In fact, there is an available option that let's you turn on the retro version of the game so I definitely plan to go back and replay it in it's original form as soon as possible. When the next game, Beyond Shadowgate due in 2016, comes out I plan to be first in line to get my copy. This title is highly recommended to the puzzle solving adventure gamer or even someone just looking for a different gaming experience. Give it a try I don't think you'll be dissapointed.

Hard to rate this game in a world in which Dark Souls exists. I'd say it's not a bad game, but if you've played DS and loved it, this will simply not do. At all. If you just wanna have some fun or get an easy initiation into "souls" games, you can get this one instead and see if it's anything you like at all. Maybe wait for a discount. So, my review will be heavily flavored by Dark Souls references. Bear that in mind. This game wants to emulate this certain type of game play, so it must also be judged against it. Why a "no recommend" then? Too many bugs. Quest NPCs stopped working suddenly for example. Or simply disappeared completely...or never showed up. So annoying.
Step by step
Story:
Meh. Forgettable. Uninspiring. Despite having voice acting and cutscenes and audio logs, it's just not gripping. The characters are extremely shallow, the dialogue boring. In DS you don't have any of the polish here, no one really tells you about the lore, you have to find out most of it for yourself. And yet, the world is way more interesting somehow.
Graphics:
Pretty decent, especially nice lighting effects. Armore looks badass. YOU look and move like a badass. Animation quality is good. This is probably the biggest plus vs. DS. It doesn't look dated.
Sound:
Same thing. Sound is heavy and good. Voice acting is ok.
Combat:
You can choose between 3 classes to start with (Warrior, Cleric or Rogue) and choose 1 school of "magic" in your first playthrough. Magic is rather bland. Each school has 4 spells, which you gradually unlock via leveling up (i.e. killing stuff...over and over). Casting them, however, takes quite a while. For example, my Warrior was a "Brawler". He has 1 spell that amplifies his damage. This sounds particularly interesting in boss fights. The problem is that it's very risky to even cast the spell, unless the boss is currently incapacitated or whatever. And then you may miss your opening to actually DO damage, and when the next opportunity arises your "buff" has already worn off again. Meh.
Regular combat is "fine, it's weighty, it's heavy or it's stabby stabby. There are you usual weapon types in the game, from swords, axes, maces and daggers to staves, great swords, great axes, great hammers and poleswords. Unlike in DS you will rarely find any non-special weapons, most are named. You will require either strength, faith or agility to wield them. Starting out as a rogue when you're a newbie is also perhaps not recommended. Warriors rely on strength and big weapons and shields. However, I found that most "big" weapons either need to be wielded in 2 hands (the game even tells you so) or are way too slow to begin with. In DS you didn't wield Ultra Greatswords until late in the game, here it is actually possibly, but just not feasible. The first of these weapons I got and actually liked was almost at the end of the game. Unlike in DS these big weapons often don't stagger an enemy as easily. Especially since SO many enemies wield shields and can pretty much block all your attacks. Most slower 1 handed weapons also have the nasty habit of taking too long to recover after a swing. I often found myself hitting a boss or enemy once after an opening, but not being able to block or roll away from the return strike.
I've never tested staves, but daggers are really fun. You can dual wield them and then alternatively attack with left and right for massive damage and staggering effects even (which is funny that my cheap daggers go through an enemy's poise with ease while a greataxe has almost no effect. The real issue are shields though. The game differentiates between 3 classes of shields: Tower, Kite and Buckler. Tower Shields are massive and heavy and you can hide behind them to avoid damage...niche feature. However, they seem to be the only shields that can't easily be staggered. Kite Shields are smaller, but can also block 100% of the damage in theory. You also have a shield bash to try and stagger enemies. Meh. Best use I found is just run at an enemy, raise your shield and then knock him on the ground...Usually works on most enemies. Bucklers on the other hand are the only shield that can be used to actually "parry" enemies. Parrying seems to work pretty well on some enemies and not at all on others. After a parry you can counter strike for massive damage...You can also backstab enemies.
Combat roll is also the same as in DS...fast, mid or heavy roll depending on your equipment burden. You never wanna be "fat rolling" though. Rolling is the best way to avoid damage, since it makes you temporarily invincible if you time it right.
World:
The world in this game is really small. It took me about 15 hours to get through, but I did lots of research as well, guess you can easily get through in half of the time, if you never back track and don't care about side quests or what have you. I'd say the "citadel" you play in is perhaps as big as the entire Undead Burg (without the catacombs) of Dark Souls, just a lot more rooms, since almost everything takes place inside. Very disappointing.
Enemies:
Not all that many, to be honest. You have some kind of wildly slashing tombie, a standard shield bearer, a big 2 handed guy and a sort of rogue with a buckler. Then these get upgraded later on. Later on there are a few more enemies like a mage, a ghost, and a few beasts. Maybe a dozen really different enemies. None of them are particularly flashy though. In Dark Souls every enemy had "soul", character. These here are just meh. They also have the annoying habit of continually trying to shield bash you, which leaves you open to a ton of damage.
Consumables:
Healing potions that get more and better later on, resistance potions and energy regen potions. That's pretty much it.
Crafting:
Non-existant. You get access to a crafter about halfway through the game, but all you can do is slot runes into armor and weapons...
Stats:
Only 3 main stats (strength, faith and agility) of which you only ever need to raise your main weapon stat and perhaps faith if you want to cast a bit, but it's definitely not necessary. Other than that only Vitality, Energy (for attacks etc) and luck, a stat you won't be levelling at all in your first playthrough (if you can stomach playing NG+ or NG++ after you beat the game).
Bosses:
Perhaps the most disappinting aspect of the game. The bosses just lack soul. They have great names such as "Warrior", "Commander", "Worshipper", "Annihilator", "Champion", etc. Almost all of the bosses are larger than life humanoids, but they are just interchangeable and boring and usually not challenging either. Some have small gimmicks you need to pay attention to, but most are just lackluster.
Other stuff, the good and the bad:
- Side quests are terribly, since they apparently bug out somethimes, and you have no way of keeping track of them
- Some areas get cleared out due to story reasons, which is neat. Adds some persistence to the game world
- Boss fights do NOT require you to run through the level again for 1 minute, the save portals are usually right in front of them.
- Inventory is a bit of a mess, however, you can equip a whole set with 1 button press if you own all pieces of the gear.
- Gear is uninspiring. Some have resistances, however, you can't really tell, how much better "1" resistance vs. "0" resistance is...
- You can "bank" experience to level up later, meaning it's not all lost if you die, but if you do die, you only have a certain amoount of time until your lost xp starts to decay and eventually vanishes. On the other hand there are items that will let you immediately recover them.
- No special items that in any way change the game
- A weapon simply disappeared and was never seen again after a relog...
- Only ranged weapon requires mana

Bastion is one of those rare action-RPG gems.
It is a beautiful thing to just observe, given the lovingly designed environments, enemies, and characters, but it's also a beautiful thing to hear. Given that most of you will already be aware of the somber beauty of Ruck's voice, it's unnecessary for me to point out, but I can only describe that voice with the word 'sexual', in literally uncompromising seriousness.
The game itself can be unforgiving, and given how great the story is, I recommend just running through it once just to fully appreciate what's going on, and only after that running through it again to really experience the full-fledged difficulty of the combat system with all the Gods activated. That and it offers up an achievement if you do so.
The story is profoundly good, and really raises quite a few questions about determinism. It's like Bioshock Infinite lite, insofar as it doesn't hit you over the head with these concepts, only presents them to you to think of them as you will.
I would like to recommend this game to everyone I know, but I'm afraid I simply can't recommend it enough.

Championship Edition 2 is one that fans of the original and DX will take some time getting used to, but will find another pretty fun modernisation of the classic Pac-Man gameplay, yet one that is also pretty flawed.
The main gameplay is largely the same; collect pellets, eat power pellet, eat a ton of ghosts. There are small difference though, the main one being that ghosts don't instantly kill you on impact. Instead, you bump into them. While this changes your strategy, it more often than not throws you off course. However, the game's pace is slightly faster than that of the previous CE games, so getting back on track isn't too bad, unless you're in mad "score-attack" mode.
Most of the maps are pretty good with some exceptions personally (I hate Jumping quite a lot as there's no indication where the pads will take you, not even a subtle one, so to do well in this map, it's a lot of trial and error). The range of difficulties are nice, but I wish that there was the option to play a 10-minute version without it being a practise mode. Hopefully this gets added in.
Luckily, while I don't understand why the requirements are so high for Pac Man (and apparently you need them), if you can run it, it generally runs smoothly with no real hic-cups, which is vital for a twitchy game like this. Though the controls seem a bit off for me. Might be getting used to the pace, might be the game itself, not sure.
Overall though, I'd easily say that Championship Edition 2 is one to get if you love score-attack games, retro reimaginings done right and a great soundtrack to dance along to. If you want the best CE game though, I'd still have to point in the direction of DX. CE 2 isn't a bad choice though, not by a long shot.

CE2 is a winner!
Disclaimer: I've been playing Pac Man titles since the original. Yes, I was an arcade kid in the 80's.
In the past, Namco has gotten foxed by people who knew how to take Pac Man to the next level. Bally did it to them frequently. Just look at Ms. PacMan and Baby PacMan. (which was a hybrid pinball/video game)
When CE, CE DX and CE DX+ came out, it was clear that Namco was beginning to realize it's okay to experiment with different formulas for how one eats dots and ghosts.

If you enjoyed Dark Souls, there is some chance that you will enjoy Lords of the Fallen as well, although you might find them too easy and shallow when compared to any part of DS.
If you like the concept of Dark Souls but are also a casual scrub and cannot make it past the asylum demon, Lords of the Fallen is the game for you.
In short, it is much easier, much less demanding, much less complex version of Dark Souls. These games share similarities such as storyline which makes absolutely no sense, or the combat system, which is actually very good in LotF, although when compared to DS it might seem a bit more clumsy - you will often fight enemies in small rooms or narrow corridors, your character is a bit less mobile than in DS, the animations are usually longer and there are less enemies that you will have to face simultaneously, which in my opinion is the exact thing that makes thsis game easier than Souls. The bosses are also well developed and varied - some of them are just a challenge for your combat skills, while the others require you to use some special mechanics in order to defeat them.
So, if you read it all and made it this far, it probably means that you are really interested in getting that game. Just do it. You're not going to regret.

There is a lot of narrative in this game. Since there is no character creation, you just play as Harkyn. Harkyn has conversations with people. Overall I highly recommend. It's a fun and challenging experience.

Pac-Man Championship Edition 2 is ok, but well short of great. Your mileage may very, but I just didn't have much fun with this game, especially as compared to the first one - Championship Edition DX+. I will be requesting a refund.
Note: I didn't have any problems at all with performance, but I did notice my overclocked 980Ti sitting around a pretty steep 35-40% usage to maintain 60fps at 1080p. So I can definitely understand where a lot of the complaints I've read about performance may be coming from.
For me this didn't quite feel like Pac-Man. Mainly in that the speed has been absolutely cranked up, and along with it the game allows for a certain amount of "tolerance" to compensate for the inevitable fidgityness. You can 'bounce' off of the ghosts. Repeatly doing so makes them 'angry' and only then do they become activated and come to kill you. Traditionally, I expect a Pac-Man game to have 0 tolerance for error. You hit a ghost, you lose a life. That way the game is fast, testing the exact limits of control. This one just goes deliberately beyond those limits, and success is determined by your level of sloppiness in how you handle being out of control. Catching ghost streaks seems to be more about making educated guesses and trying to set yourself up to get lucky more often in catching them, rather than just straight up twitch execution. You don't even need to eat all of the pellets before moving onto the next stage; just most of them-ish. This game isn't about hiting the nail squarely on the head.
It is very telling PM:CE 2 is listed on steam under "Casual Games", while the original PM:CE DX+ is listed under "Action Games".
The graphics are certainly colourful, exciting, and fresh, but occasionally a little too much. The wild animations for ghost streaks I found disorienting in that they pulled me completely out of the map and it took me a second to reorient when dropped back in. Pretty graphics are fun, but ultimately they don't always serve the gameplay.
One obnoxious little bug I found when running with Big Picture and a steam controller, the game has a  cursor that just kinda sits there on the screen. I have to actually go over to the computer and use an actual mouse to move the cursor off the edge of the screen.
The first PM Championship Edition DX+ game was great, and I highly recommend it... but no this one.
p.s. Kudos to the publisher for setting a very reasonable price.

This game has had me hooked for the last 3 or so weeks. Even though it is rng heavy, and can sometimes really suck (like when your A team gets demolished), it is quite addicting and an enjoyable experience. The art style is great, the music decent, and Wayne June, the narrator, deserves an award. Gameplay-wise, this game is all about rng and yet somehow it is hardly ever frustrating. Every element of this game, from attacking, to dungeons, to afflictions, to even your own heroes are randomly generated, allowing for a unique experience. Now this being said, some parts of the game do get repetetive, and are hardly note-worthy. (such as blood runs or low-level grinding.) But these still are not at all easy, and never were really boring. Combat is turn-based, reminding me a bit of pokemon. But unlike pokemon, combat in darkest dungeon feels much faster and much more fluent, as heroes don't spend 5 minutes announcing what they are doing. All in all, the game is hard, yet hardly felt unfair, and even through it's difficulty it is enjoyable.
Now the Crimison Courtyard is a whole different can of worms. I would probably recommend purchasing after playing through the vanilla game at least to the late/end game. Why? Well, the Crimison Courtyard pumps the difficulty up waaay early in the game, making the whole DLC seem impossible for less experienced minds. For example, I could push through the early game without much difficulty, and I had quite the fun time. My friend, who hasn't played Darkest dungeon ever, had a much harder time, and as a result had a much less positive take on this dlc. Content-wise, this dlc adds quite a bit of good stuff, and is worth $10. Now you will probably hear people say the Crimison Curse, a new and very unique disease introduced in the dlc, is "too strong," and "makes the game to hard." Yes, the curse is detrimental. Yes, it cannot be outright cured until the late game. Even so, the curse can be held off with the blood, and even aid the heroes through bloodlust. In fact, I've had times where I'm happy my hero has the crimison curse, as when they're in bloodlust they get +25% damage, a very useful buff. To summarize, Crimison Courtyard is hard for new players, but much more managable for the experienced. It adds good content and if you like the game it is worth the $10.
Oh yeah, modding support on this game is great. You can add skins, trinkets, and balance your heroes, or just add new ones. There are mods that change everything, from dungeon backgrounds to loading screens, even adding new dungeons.

Fractured Space has a great deal of depth and tactical complexity. A new player can pick up the basic mouse-and-keyboard commands after a few matches and yet a 100+ hour veteran can still find new tricks and tactics.
The recent change for ship acquisition makes the grind for new ships very manageable.  New players can quickly pick up a decent cross section of ships, while leaving a few more expenive (and newer) ships as goals to pursue.  The only purchaseable elements are purely cosmetic or means to bypass some of the unlock grind.  Despite some reviews here this game is absolutely NOT pay-to-win.
The design team is very active in releasing new updates to the game.  While some bugs and significant ship balance issues remain, as is typical for an alpha-stage game, the updates have largely been incrementally improving the game for the past year-and-a-half.
Key Features:
-Deep tactially spaceship combat
-Beautiful visuals (esp. for an alpha)
-Manageable unlock rate
-No PTW elements
-Active development team
Weaknesses:
-Some server lag and stability issues
-Growing, but currently limited, player base
-Ship balance still a work-in-progress
Verdict: Try it today!  Fractured Space boasts massive spaceships, looks great, and it's FREE!  There's nothing to lose and the game continues to grow, improve and evolve with every update.

I'm really enjoying this game. If you were ever a Lego person, this is the game for you!
Pros:
1) Huge amounts of customization. You can build pretty much anything you can dream up given the pieces currently available. Seeing as it's early access, I'm sure they'll have more toys for us to play with eventually; at the moment there are still plenty of fun things you can build. The only thing that lacks much variety, in my opinion, are the weapons. Again, this is likely just a symptom of early access, and the weapons are still fun to use!
2) Core gameplay is enjoyable. Basically, you start out with almost nothing and you need to gather resources to sell so that you can earn enough money to upgrade your tech. Along the way, you'll randomly encounter tons of different enemy AI techs that will attempt to destroy you. Trying to avoid them to gather safely, or all out engaging them for the hopeful returns of scavenging their parts is something you have to consider. My playstyle has me going in for the kill more often, but as I've continued playing and have more valuable tech that I don't want to lose, I've ended up taking more time to consider my actions. If you run out of power for your shields, you run the risk of losing your tech in a bad engagement.
3) Combat. This can be pretty stressfull. As you see your enemies come into view, you'll probably come to a full stop. Many of these enemies can be behemoths compared to you with dozens of guns ready to blow you to bits (literally). Taking a moment to figure out your enemies capabilities is a good strategy. Maybe you'll have better luck if you come up quickly behind them. Maybe their broadside is weak, so you should focus your positioning there. Eventually, as you earn enough money and scavenge pieces off of your victims you'll end up as one of these behemoths yourself! Come this time, you may want to make sure you have countermeasures for the smaller, faster enemies as they'll tear you apart from your weak points that lack firepower.
4) Destruction. All tech is built from smaller pieces. You place cubes together, just like with legos, and then put wheels, guns, and harvesting equipment on top of that (around, under, inside, whatever you want!). Enemies are made up just the same. When you fight in this game, you and your opponent will be trying to blow the blocks and weapons off of each other to reveal the cockpit; once the cockpit is destroyed, you win (or lose, if it's yours!). Many pieces also just explode if you do enough damage, causing damage to other parts around it; this also translates to blocks that are blown off and then explode later on the ground, so you have to be careful of what debri you roll over as it may turn into a kind of IED!
Cons:
1) Optimization. First off, if you're expecting it to be optimized in early access, you may need to reconsider your viewpoint on early access games. For the most part this game runs pretty good right now; it's definitely playable. The worst part comes when you build large techs with lots of weapons. Firing all of those weapons at once TANKS your framerate to be nearly unplayable, and since typically you're firing to destroy other techs, their bullets just add on to that frame rate drop. Build lots of shields for complete protections, and have 360 degree weapon coverage because you'll need it. I'd expect this to get better later on in development.
(Note: I'm running a very powerful PC and it still can't handle it. SLI 980s, 6-core Intel i7 5930k, 16GB DDR4 3000 Ripjaws, Asus x99 Deluxe MB. Haven't tried CPU or GPU overclocking to test performance there, but I doubt any OC I can achieve will fix the current amount of framerate drop).
2) Unlocking new tech. It appears the developer has plans to change how this works, but at the time of this writing it's kind of a pain to unlock new tech to build with. Right now, you mostly rely on finding enemies, blowing them up, and scavenging their parts. Once you scavenge a part, you unlock it in the shop. There are also "levels" of a sort that you can achieve based on some beginning missions, and those unlock a few items for you. Again, I'm pretty sure the dev plans on cleaning this up. The hardest part is the fact that so many of the items explode very easily, so when you end up defeating an enemy you won't be able to salvage any of the parts that detonated early on (batteries, boosters, etc). Sometimes you'll get lucky, and that's mostly what you have to hope for. Again, I'll chalk this up to the progression system being new and since the game is in early access, I can't expect them to have finished it yet.
3) Flying. It's possible to make flying tech in this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. pretty early on you can encounter and "abandoned" flying tech that the game will instruct you to reclaim, You'd assume that this thing will work well since it's pre-built by the dev, but it really doesn't. Maybe it's just bugs that need worked out, but I'm not sure. The controls are HORRIBLE for flying. You have to hold the SHIFT key and that keeps your engines at maximum; there needs to be a way to set your speed (add a throttle mechanism to the game please!). Also, the pilot must be drunk because if I do nothing but hold the SHIFT key, the aircraft continues to climb (as if it wants to do a loop). Not sure what that's all about. Additionally, turning is huge pain. As soon as start banking, your aircraft pretty much starts to plummet out of the sky. At the moment, the most you can really do with a flying tech is scout around for resources or nearby enemy bases to raid.
Additionally, it either needs to be made clearer through at tutorial or some kind of in-game mechanic whether or not a tech you're building will be capable of flight. Unlike land techs that can be in most any configuration, trying to build a flying tech is a chore. I've yet to be able to make my own flight-capable tech, and only the one given to me seems to be operable. Maybe I'm just incompetent, but my attempt at making a large-scale bomber type tech ended with a really fast land unit with weapons that shot the ground below it and no ability to turn (this thing have 5 props on it and still couldn't take off; I think it may just be that you can't get a large enough wing span to achieve the appropriate amount of lift.
Tl;dr: This game is super fun! I'm not a real reviewer or journalist or anything, but I'd give it a 9/10 as-is (for what that's worth). I can see this game being top-notch assuming the fix the things above, and add in more blocks/weapons/items to build with.
Also:
Adding in multiplayer capabilties so you can play legos...I mean TerraTech...with your friends would be awesome, but by no means do I think it's required. You can't deny that it'd be fun to set up a private server and enjoy this game with your friends, though.
Thanks for reading!

Visually this game is breathtaking--Paris is a joy to behold, expecially if you know the city, and  the character designs are suavely dressed, badass, and interesting. (I am very much reminded of the Brotherhood of The Wolf  movie.)  If you stop to look around you will notice little imaginative vignettes everywhere and even the newspapers are full of interesting historical tidbits. backed up by painstaking historical research. Of course, if you are running as fast as you can from task to task you may never notice the thought and artistry that went into this game. Kudos to Ubisoft for picking such an interesting and unexpected back drop.
This alone makes the game worth playing for me but there's more. Combat is fun and  for me smooth after 9 hours of play. I have never run into any technical issues so far. I've only played this game post patch 3 , but it runs pretty well hovering around 27-30fps nearly all the time, which may not be butter but is on par with many other games and smooth enough not to be distracting. There is occasional stutter but once again not enough to be an issue.
I have also never really played an AC game for more than an hour or two before, so I am somewhat objective and can look at trhe game in and of itself. The story so far is good enough to keep me interested and no worse than the average action movie these days. I mean how many mediocre action movies have you sat though because you loved the visuals. I also don't really expect a literary masterpiece from a video game. Neither do I have any expectations that the combat be different form the last few games, so for me it is not boring but  a new challenge and fun. I suppose if there has to be some radical innovation from the last game to catch one's attention then there might be an issue, but no prob for me.
My impression is that most of the negativity around this game is from people who had technical problems with the launch and /or who are longtime fans and have played every game in the franchise and are therefore unable to apprecaite the game in and of itself. So far as I can tell the technical problems have been largely fixed, and the game has a lot to offer. I am happy with my purchase and will be playing for a long time. It may even motivate me to go and play Black Flag which I purchased but never really got into.
Overall reccomendation for me is quite positive with the caveat that I am a new AC fan and have no expectations or baggage based on playing the game previously.

The comparison of LOTF vs DS (Darksouls) is a fair one.
There are many differences, but game control is similar.
LOTF is less time consuming to play through. I made it through the game in less than 6 hours, something I couldn't have come close to doing with out many more hours of practice on DS games.
LOTF is not nearly as difficult, nor is it as re-playable as DS.
However, I had fun with the game and the story. I just couldn't buy into it as deep as I would have had if I played LOTF before DS.
LOTF is a good alternative for people who like the melee/spell caster games with a medium-ish difficulty (at the harder settings). It has a decent story and some reasons to explore, but not a lot of reward to do the exploration.
I would still say that if you have some time and the money, it wouldn't be a bad experience. Likely, you would enjoy it.

Much like Telltale Games' Back to the Future, The Walking Dead is more interactive story than it is a game. The main difference is that this one has quicktime events and you can actually die if you don't do them right.

You just have to understand this is not a game you play for challenge or even to tax your brain, despite having a few puzzles. Just put enough time into it and you can complete about one chapter a night (with five total and some DLC content).
Since the game's plot is based so heavily around picking different lines of dialogue, it might've been nice if your choices could have had a bigger impact. The minor details may change depending on what you do, but the end results are ultimately the same.
If you want a creepy, brutally unforgiving zombie survivalist story with great characterizations that'll make you reach for a box of tissues by the end, you probably can't do better than this.

DD is great, fine game. I can only wish all kickstarters were anywhere near this calibre. DD is original, innovativa and immensely enjoyable, everything indie should be. Seriously, what more could you ask for? One often hears that DD is too grindy. True, the grind is strong. But that's like saying Super Mario is too jumpy. Calculated risk and profit is the name of the game and there are thousands of little things designed to keep things fresh. Try different team combinations and surprise yourself. Seriously, once you learn the basics combat becomes both enjoyable and rewarding, head and shoulders above non-delivering disappointements like that game with banners and sagas (no names, right?)
So throw that tank with healer with a hitter with a jester. Why not a dog included? Why not two dogs? The dog is strong, after all. Maybe try healer in front rank? Things you might not expect to work play just fine once you stop to think about hows and whys.
DD is tough at first, admittedly, but it is also fair. Combat never feels as lethal and unfair as, let us say, X-COM. You will not and cannot lose people to that infamous one bad roll. In my 260 hours I have lost dozens of heroes. Every time was was because I pushed them too far in my sweaty-palmed grabby greed or send them to a mission above their level, or let them down with rubbish support. To think of it, it was usually all of those reasons. Keep teams solid and support up and don't aim too high, and your heroes will deliver.
The strategic part, town and hero management, is the same story. You are expected to learn all kinds of lessons, either from your mistakes or youtube. There are no ways to lose the game and to keep things fair you will always receive fresh recruits, and there will always be easy dungeons for them. You simply cannot break anything that you couldn't fix.
So DD is not really a hard or unfair, it's just unusual and very clever, and maybe that puts many people off. If you just buy the biggest sword and try to bash things diablo style it will be like playing mario without jump button. Tactics and planning are essential. Use the jump button and those koopas will be that much easier.
Also, graphics and music are wonderful. Especially graphics. Did I mention graphis? The wacky atmoshpere also deserves a medal. If you don't mind little thinking grab this one and don't let the naysayers pull you down.

So.... I'm writing this right after finishing the game. Only barely started season 2, don't know what's going to happen in there yet, but I know it won't be anything fun.
I think of myself as quite emotional. I easily get emotionally attached to fictional characters, be it in books, films or video games. When I was younger, I often got big emotional outbursts over stories. I cried at the end of Final Fantasy IX when I thought that ***DEDACTED:::SPOILERS***, and there were plenty of books that did the same to me. It went the other way too, I would cheer for characters, I would giggle like a demented maniac when something bad happened to a bad guy, I often had to stand up and pace around the room for ten minutes to calm myself down again. However, over the years, all of that kind of faded away. Sure, there's still a couple of books that I really enjoy and that get me involved, but I haven't gotten really emotional about any story in years. Same goes thricefold for video game stories. I've come to realize that games really don't do the straightforward storytelling very well. Sure, there are a handful of exceptions that are decent or even good, but I don't think I have encountered anything that would get 19-year-old me even close to as worked up as 12-year-old me could have been. There are plenty of games that do a great job at building an interesting world, building amazing atmosphere, way better than I think any other media is capable of, but an actual storyline focused around a set of characters rarely gets done well. But, as always in this world, there are exceptions. And Telltale's adventure games are as massive of an exception as it can get.
When I came to the end of the Walking Dead season 1, I didn't cry. But I think there were some tears trying to force their way out. I did play the two Tales from the Borderlands episodes before I played this game, so I knew already that they were great at telling a story and building up interesting and impactful characters. What I didn't know was how heartbreaking they could be. I won't spoil anything, but... damn. I'm 19 years old, I know nothing about life, or family, or responsibility. I'm an autistic basement dweller (or, well, first floor dweller if we want to be completely correct) and I don't see myself ever raising a kid. I guess Clementine is as close to being a dad as I'll ever get. And boy, how everso bad I felt whenever I accidentaly did something that could hurt the poor little girl. And that warm tingly feeling when she was cuddling me or, well, my player character, but you know what I mean) on that RV ride. I'll never deal with this level of responsibility in real life, I wouldn't be able to. But now I think I have some vague understanding what my parents must have gone through dealing with me for 18 years. Okay, it does help that Clem is an overwhelmingly nice kid. Some of the brats I have to deal with at my work place, jeez...
Yeah, this is just a giant wall of randomly splurted out thoughts coming from an underdeveloped mind. Basically the internet in a nutshell, eh? All this rambling aside, I haven't had this touching and influencial of an experience with any other game I ever played. I recommend this game wholeheartedly, to anyone ever. I'll probably take a day or two of a break before tackling season 2. Or maybe I'll continue playing it in two hours. I don't know. The Walking Dead, or any other of Telltale's adventure games, are some of the most well written pieces of media I have ever come across. And it also ripped my heart out and ate it. Bloody zombies.

I read hundreds of reviews here before I decided to give this game a try during the steam summer sales.
So, I want to make clear, that from my point of view most negative reviews are from 2 types of players:
Type A was mistaken that this is a kind of RPG! It is not! So for them it's repetitive, without a real story, no huge world to explore, all those things they would have expected from a RPG are missing.
But it's a strategy game about resource management. It is 10 times more like x-com (or XCOM, The Long War mod) than like, for example, a Baldur's Gate or Elder Scroll.
For a strategy game it has quite a lot of story and something often missed: A very cool atmosphere.
There are a lot of mechanics, tweeks and tricks to learn or discover. You will just get better by playing and experience.
Therefore I would recommend to NOT watch a tutorial video before playing! I played until my first lvl 6 character died, and restarted the campaign, full of ideas how to do it better with all the knowledge I had got.
Type B  complains about unfair RNG and/or difficulty in the game.
Personally, I'm very glad that this one of the rare games that are not so boringly easy, like so many new releases.
But the truth is also, that many cliffs can be sailed around by proper preperation, like change of skills used and/or characters and trinkets. By the knowledge of what kind of monster will await you in the different locations, which quirks to avoid and which to 'lock'. So, for an experienced player that 'evil' RNG and the randomness is much smaller.
I waited for the summer sale, because 10 bucks are not nothing for me, and saving them makes me happy:-)
I did not regret the purchase at all! I played almost 150h by now, so that's like 6 cent per hour, and I had more fun with DD than with most AAA titles.
9/10 for 10 bucks
Edit: I had 3 crashes in 150h playtime, nothing was lost after restarting the program! I entered at exactly the same point before the crash. I wish all programs would be like this!
I have no idea why some reviewers complained about bugs. Maybe that was an earlier version?!
And don't trust any reviews from players with 20 h playtime or less, they scratched only the surface of the game. Especially, if they complain about the randomness. In my last campaign I lost 3 heroes about the course of the whole game( and another one during a retreat from DD's 2nd level), while in my first campaign I lost more than 15 heroes before even entering DD for the first time.
It is definitely no casual game, in the sense, that you can play it for an hour, and then come back next week for another hour, like FTL. There are too many details, mechanisms and tricks to be discovered or learned that you will need to survive in the 'end game', aka the Darkest Dungeon itself. And I can only repeat myself, it is a strategy game!! So, if you completely fail, it's not the RNG or bad luck, it is very likely the wrong strategy or mis-use of your resources that lead to it.
Just do not expect to win the game on the first try, even if you are used to win your other games as easy like taking a candy from a baby.

Evolution Planet: Gold Edition - Win 10 64bit - no problems
Another "pocket picker" - like Fallout Shelter, it's designed to drive you to purchase something to complete levels.
It's a little clumsier than Fallout Shelter in it's approach. But both use "pusher" tactics whereby the player is given aids, at first. [gems in the case of Evolution Planet; Nuka Cola in Fallout Shelter] They learn to play the game, depending on aids to complete. Suddenly, the difficulty spikes and one cannot continue without additional aid.
The first few levels play like a tutorial written for 3rd graders. It continues to hold the player's hand through the intermediate levels, as if written for a child player. Wham! Level 15. You must complete this level or you cannot continue.
The game claims 2 styles of play; Campaign and Survival, but Survival is locked away behind level 15. Where the difficulty to this point has been at a child's level, level 15 requires the strategies of a chess champion. Even then, the random placement of enemies will destroy any strategy.
Everything about this level is intended to thwart you so you'll be forced to buy gems to complete it and have access to the other half of the game.
If you can get it in a bundle or pay .49 cents, it's good for about 4 hours entertainment for an adult and a child together.
Edit: I had to add this analogy. Evolution Planet is like driving onto a toll road. The road is smooth and wide; not much traffic. You're going along pretty good and suddenly have to choose between a toll booth or an exit.  Either you pay the toll to continue or your trip is finished.

All right after so many hours I write this. There are 2 things I want to mention.
1)This game is HARD! Seriously even on Easy you will get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked a lot! I suggest you remove all breakable items and don't play around your pets or your significant other too because you will have the need to punch something.
2)The RNG(random number generator)will screw you! You will get hit by multiple criticals on a row, you will miss several times on a row and such. What can you do?
This game is a turn based RPG on the heart. You control 4 Heroes at once and you venture into dungeons completing quests, gathering items, gold, etc. But there are so many more things too.
You have to manage the Town by upgrading buildings and the most important is to manage the Heroes. There is no main Hero here. You constantly gain new Heroes. And if things go bad you can sacrifice some of them to gto to a quest to gather a little more gold to upgrade something. And you will do that. And you will feel bad too. But it has to be done.
Another thing is that Heroes gain Stress as you battle. Guess in real life if you would battle demons you would be stressed too. And if they get stressed enought usually they refuse to listen to you and they sometimes do various bad things too. They can even die if they get stressed enough! When that happens just retreat I suggest and try again.
So yeah you have to manage heroes, the town, the items, the gold, the stress and other things.
All right so after all these? I will still recommend this game but barely. The difficulty is brutal and unfair most of the times. Obviously it can be beaten, duh. And people have beaten the game on Hard too! I suggest of course Easy mode for the 1st time. Currently according to Steam Achievements less than 2% of the people have beaten the game! Seriously! If they make a sequel or something I would suggest to make the game somewhat easier. Yeah I know it breaks the spirit of the game too! Better prepare to be fully committed if you want to have any chance of success. And don't quit when you will lose your best heroes and your good items because it WILL happen!
But of course not all are bad. If you persevere you will be able to do it. You will lose characters, you will lose items but you constantly gain new characters and items. And when you finally beat a really tough mission you will feel so good!

This game should be right up my street, and indeed there is much I do like about it - the art style for example - is fantastic.  The concept is also a simple but solid one: build up your roster of adventurers by exploring various procedurally-generated dungeons while gathering loot and fighting enemies.
What's not to like?
Well, the main problems I have with the game are not the same as most other negative reviewers.  I see a lot of RNG-bashing in the other reviews, and as someone who has over 600 hours in Battle Brothers, I can tell you that RNG does not bother me in the slightest.  What does bother me however - and this is where I think this game fails next to the aforementioned Battle Brothers - is that I never develop any attachment to my characters.
The reasons for this are simple.  There is nothing to differentiate one character of a given class from another.  They might start with a slightly different set of skills, but all the skills can be unlocked anyway with a little money.  Other than the name and a slightly different colour palette, absolutely nothing distinguishes one bounty hunter (for example) from another.  Yes, there is a trait/quirk system but for me that's not enough.
And worse than that, there is zero sense of progression.  Sure, characters 'level up' and gain access to higher level gear and abilities, but since they refuse (for some utterly bizarre game-logic reason) to take on quests that are 'beneath' them you only - at best - keep pace with the enemies you'll be facing and as a result level advancement is entirely relative.
Utlimately I just don't come away from a session of DD feeling that I enjoyed myself.  It's more of a chore - and that can't be right.

granted, using them is optional, or it should be, and I tried not to move units too much or use undo too often and only bought a few creatures/items towards the end, after 600 failed attempts, but I'm pretty sure 3-starring some levels is impossible without gems. if they adjusted gem costs, undo for 1 or even free, moving units also drastically reduced, etc. or at least made gem levels replayable, it'd be a 'buy on sale because it's kinda fun' recommendation, but as it is, don't bother, level completion is often dependent on using gems.
and even more so on pure luck, which is the second thing I dislike about the game. units randomly appearing on levels can ruin everything at the last minute - or after two moves. it can take many (many!) tries just to finish a level and move on, which is really frustrating because it's not your fault. you can use gems to cheat, but sometimes even that won't help. some levels towards the end are beyond ridiculous, then after many attempts you suddenly pass with flying colors.
bottom line, I can't recommend the game, just stay away until the developer gets rid of mobile shenanigans and look for other match-3 titles in the meantime.

TL;DR - Evolution Planet is an inferior clone of Triple Town, with a vastly larger and oxymoronic emphasis on random elements and pre-designed levels. Several levels in the game cannot reasonably be completed without purchasing creatures, likely a holdover from pay-to-win mobile game elements.
I'll be blunt - in every instance where the developer experimented with the game design instead of merely copying Triple Town, they failed. Enemy creatures that destroy yours (or in later levels, infect and convert yours), an AI that places creatures on your behalf and slaps down multiple creatures per turn, and 84 levels with their own sets of goals and score targets - all of these interfere with each other or with the core gameplay.
When the RNG decides to place multiple creatures at several critical points on the grid that completely wreck your plans, it's not fun. Doubly so when they're high-level creatures that destroy or convert your own creatures and reverse the past 20 moves of progress. That same RNG decides whether you can actually complete a level, which makes you wonder - why even have designed levels? Though, even "designed" is debateable. Several levels in the game - particularly later boss levels - cannot be reasonably completed without spending gems to purchase creatures. Getting a triple star rating in some levels is also dependent on multiplier squares randomly appearing in the right places as well.
It should also be noted that getting a triple star rating on every level in the game gets you nothing, not even a text blurb of congrats. There is no point to completion. There is also no point to getting a high score in survival mode, as the top two scores are clearly hacked. Even at the end of my 3rd place run with a score of a quarter million points, there was such an incredible deluge of enemy creatures placed every other turn that it would be impossible for anyone to survive 4 times (2nd place) or 16 times (1st place) as long.
I don't recommend this game. I felt annoyed and cheated during most of my playtime, and for a puzzle game, the developers sure tried their best to eliminate strategy and planning.

As you can see, I've played a LOT of this game.  Given the amount of content in its current state (as of October 2014), the game is worth buying if you accept it AS IS.  $15 or less for over 150 hours of gameplay is more than fair.   The team does post regular beta updates that are unsafe and can damage save files and cause crashes etc..., but there hasn't been an update posted to the main branch of the game for a VERY long time.  It's Chucklefish's response to people complaining that their more frequent updates to the main branch in the past weren't good enough... which they weren't in all honesty.  Daily and weekly bug fixes don't equate to content and playability.  I wish I could refuse to recommend this game since Chucklefish has been nasty to those providing negative criticism in their forums etc... but the truth is that I enjoyed it until there was nothing left to do in the current state with my circle of friends.  The game will remain uninstalled until the day the full release comes out (which I'm not crossing my fingers for).
Pros:
Decent detail to gameplay
Interesting weapons and drops
Interesting planets, biomes, and enemies
Cons:
Limited content (It's an Alpha)
Lack of many core features that would give this game significant bulk and replay value
Limited enemy AI, making many enemies act the same way leading to identical battles
No true goal or purpose at this point
Doesn't stack up to minecraft or terraria AT ALL
Again, if you take it at face value and enjoy games like Terraria and Minecraft, you'll likely enjoy this.  If you're looking for a promising early access game with hopes of a final product, don't hold your breath.

A remake of a first person adventure game that originally looked a bit like an RPG.
An enjoyable and (if you ignore the fact that it's set in a fantasy world full of magic etc.) so far pretty straight forward, first-person adventure game. No nonsensical (il)logic puzzles, although having said that, it was (save for Starship Titanic) generally always the 3rd person point'n'click variety that had that type of thing...
...Shadowgate has just the kind of stuff that's typical to first-person adventure games, but most definitely at the easier end of that continuum (nothing like Schizm or Rhem here (at least not so far)).
Reminds me a little of Zork Inquisitor (just without the overt humour) although having said that it does seem that much of its text could be read as being very subtly toungue-in-cheek (I'm not a fan of obnoxious, flip and glib commentary in video games and thankfully there's none of that here).
Altogether a very enjoyable game (if you're into 1st person adventures and aren't looking for something that's going to play like a graphically enhanced mensa test, as so many of the 1st person adventure games of the past have tended to do).
The biggest (and for me really the only) potential problem I've encountered so far is the possibility of overlooking relevant objects and actions (if you don't want to pixel hunt every node and be subjected to skimming the same descriptive text over and over again, which you would almost certainly have to do on the higher difficulty setting (and why anyone would want to play like that is beyond me. For me (outside of the crazy logic typical of the 3rd person point'n'click adventrures) that's the biggest flaw in the adventure game format.)).
Thankfully there is a hint system and a button to reveal the hotspots and on the easier difficulty, all possible actions appear in the context menu when you click on each hotspot (one cavaet to that is that I have to say that (apart from Telltale's adventures) I don't think I've played a single adventure game that isn't incompletable due to broken design or glitchy programming. One can only hope that Shadowgate can be updated should that be the case here).
One criticism I do have, is the relatively poor quality of the sound-files. I've got an Asus Xonar Essence STX driving a mid-range 3-point speaker setup that staggered the reviewers for their quality within their price range. One common criticisms of my speaker setup was the quality of the trebble, and while, for the most part, it's more or less unnoticable, the sound that Shadowgate's pushing out of my speakers is sharp to the point of discomfort. It's the first time I've experienced this with my speakers and it almost sent me -- thinking there might be a fault somewhere in my setup -- reaching over to check my hardware.

I'm not sure why Shadowgate's sound should be as it is, unless for file-size convenience but I can only imagine that on cheaper speaker setups, or worse still, the kind of speakers that are built into monitors, Shadowgate's sound may very well, rather than just failing to enhance the game, be tinny enough to actually mar the experience.
My sound set up is capable of creating sound that envelopes and absorbs the player into it but Shadowgate's sound almost seems like it's doing its best to be impenetrable, to the point of almost feeling kind of repellent, and it's a shame. I wanted to turn the volume up and have Shadowgate's audioscape unfold around me, but unfortunately the quality was just not there. It would seem that with no size-restrictions in terms of limited CD or DVD space, games these days could have very full, very clear audio but unfortunately that just doesn't seem to be the case with Shadowgate. Maybe they just didn't want the sound to upstage the graphics, who knows...)

An Undead Lazer Review of...
STARBOUND!
Starbound is a 2D platformer-crafting-tech-adventure-creativity-sci-fi RPG of sorts. It is currently available to all as a beta of sorts with nightly (albeit unstable) builds upon which they add or change certain features of the game. At surface level, this game seems to be "Terraria... IN SPACEEEEE!" However, it is MUCH more than that.
~~~~~OVERVIEW/GAMEPLAY~~~~~
At the moment, with a bit of progress already made in development, the game boasts 7 different races with different (and inherently ironic) backgrounds and slightly varying questing lines. This, however, is something that has changed since the initial closed release and will most likely change even more as the game's developed. I would love to see the game developed with BOTH the sandbox elements as well as the RPG questing elements in mind, because it gives users who need a wee bit of structure (like me) a bit of a jumping off point, which, I will concede, the game has somewhat done since the initial closed beta. The gameplay is, well, a lot like Terraria in a few ways and very much UNLIKE Terraria in many more ways. The basics, such as the 2D platforming, similar building mechanics and somewhat similar crafting system make Starbound something similar to Terraria in a couple of ways. However, the tech aspects as well as the boss battles and procedural generation of the environment of the game are what distinguish the two. Unlike Terraria and a certain other game with procedural generation *cough* *cough*, Starbound contains a virtually endless (like 13 QUADRILLION - 13,000,000,000,000,000 - planets or something) universe with different tiers of difficulty and different environments. The planetary differences ACTUALLY have an effect on the way you play the game, which makes it refreshing and more difficult (which is always a good thing in my opinion). These differences range from the heat (or lack thereof) of a planet as well as the tier of the monsters and resources, etc. Overall, as a beta game, the games has solid gameplay and should hold up well or even improve even more upon the final release of the game (to come of course).
(8.5/10 for a beta game)
~~~~~ART/SOUND~~~~~
Oh goodness, the sound. Let me just be frank with everyone. This game has a PHENOMENAL sound track. Seriously, it's great. I emailed the composer, Curtis Schweitzer, upon first hearing the game's soundtrack (after pre ordering the game of course) and let him know just how great this soundtrack was. Of course, without playing the game, I could not truly get a feel for how it attributed to the ambiance. What a game soundtrack it is, one of my new favorites (and I've played a LOT of games with some soundtracks that would make top movie score writers blush). The art of the game is simplistic yet beautiful. The animations are well done but not too flashy. Even with a few graphical bugs here and there being acceptable for the game as a beta release, I think that the art was done very well for the game's type. Not too flashy, because it doesn't need to be.
(Music is like a 14/10 for me, and the art is a 8/10, soooooo.... a 9/10 because nothing's perfect)
~~~~~FINAL THOUGHTS~~~~~
I like this game. It's a lot of fun to play, it's exciting to see what the awesome dev team does each and every day in the nightly builds and it has a TON of potential to pass Terraria as the best 2D sandbox platformer around. That is, once it's finished. I will say, there are some issues that need to be worked out. Multiplayer is a bit of a mess, but from a dev standpoint I can understand why it may not be the top of priorities with core mechanics still being developed. All the work that needs to be done actually gives me hope for the future. I CANNOT WAIT to see what this game becomes once it is fully fleshed out in its final release. Being a programmer and amateur game dev myself, I have a lot of respect for what this dev team has done and am really excited to see what comes next for Starbound. Along with the recommendations I have given to my friends for this game, I invite everyone out there who hasn't experienced Starbound to do so, if only for the great music or the modest price. Give it a shot. I don't think you'll be disappointed.
A 9 out of 10 and a recommendation to buy it, because for the price and all it has going for it, it is definitely worth the try. Who knows, you might even stay a while.

Genre says RPG but it fallout 4's case I'd say "RPG". Right from the get go the main characters origins and morals are so clearly defined that you are instantly stripped of any resemblence of a true role playing game.
The most annoying part about calling this a role playing game is actual character interaction with npcs. You can either ask questions, be rude, be neutral some times, or be nice some times. Unlike other fallout games there are no skill checks in conversations, just Charisma checks. The higher your charisma the higher chance of passing the check.
Even with that there isn't a hard line you need your stat to be in order to pass one of these speech checks and because you can quick save and quickload while speaking to someone, you can just re-load over and over and regardless of your charisma you will eventually pass the stat check.
There is no perk that changes or adds extra possible lines of dialogue, and because skills don't exist there obviously can't be any skill checks.
So it isn't really a role-playing game, it's more of an open world action adventure game with a little bit of choice only really on which faction you side with and that's it. Your character is far to defined, no matter what you always cry for your son or wife and husband, and seeing how your character is literally frozen in time he doesn't even have a character arc where the wasteland breaks him and makes him more of a survivalist or soldier or whatever.
If that had happened then that is where you could have customized your character more to your liking and how you were going to roleplay. Instead your characters morals are very clear and when acting certain ways in game it just comes off as strange as you already know your character right from the start.
Oh also they flat out lie calling creation clubs mini dlcs and it is just a shady workaround to add paid mods, none of the content is original, it doesn't feel like there actually was quality control. There is clipping on the hellfire armor, and the means in which you obtain some of the gear from the creation club makes zero sense.
While there is already a mod that enables achievements the creation club mods keep them enabled by default. Meaning you can buy the hellfire power armor, start a new game, go kill Pyro because a forged has it for some reason stupid joke slapped together in five seconds, the X-03 mod is more tasteful and lore friendly, anyways you get the power armor right away and you already have the best power amor in the game since it comes fully upgraded and can start kicking♥♥♥♥♥

, the basic gameplay is this: Pac-Man roams around the maze, typically an asymmetrical grid, eat dots.  When he eats enough dots, a fruit appears that will change that half of the maze into a different layout.  Eating dots builds up Pac-Man’s speed, and the overall goal is to rack up a high score in X amount of time.
expanded on this formula by introducing the ghost train.  With sleeping ghosts scattered throughout the map, any time Pac-Man rushes by, the ghosts wake up and form a massive conga line behind him.  Eat a power pellet, and they’re yours for the taking.  Get caught in a bind?  Hit any button to through a bomb, and all ghosts return to the cage in the middle of the screen.
While
has these concepts, it takes them in a whole different direction.  The maze changes, high speed, bombs, and ghost trains all still exist, but their functionality has changed drastically.  To start, there really isn’t a build of speed anymore; Pac-Man jettisons off right from the get-go, so there isn’t a need to build up to anything.  Ghost trains now roam the map, attaching themselves to the four main ghosts.  Bombs serve to move
back to the starting point, and no longer affect the ghosts at all.  And, most of all, instead of changing half of the maze to something else, fruit now throws Pac-Man and the ghosts on a completely new grid.
The action is quick, the score flies, and the game is constantly making you feel on edge.  The core gameplay of
is something that can stand on its own, and doesn’t really relate, functionality-wise, to the previous titles in the genre, and this is where I’m having trouble enjoying the game.  See,
is probably one of my most played games, starting with it on the Xbox 360 when it came out originally.
built on CE in a natural progression; you still had to build up your speed, be cautious about your route, and aim for that highscore once the blood starts pumping a few minutes in.  But, in
, you’re already starting out at lightning speed, and now the ghosts aren’t even very threatening anymore.
One of the major changes to the Pac-Man formula in
is that hitting ghosts
no longer kills you.  Instead, the ghosts have a threshold for the amount of times you can bump into them.   When you bump into them enough in a short period, they’ll get angry,
will you lose a life.  On top of that, ghost trains, despite being however large they are, scatter across set paths when you eat the power pellet.  While you can easily see these set paths,  it’s a literal game of cat and mouse, and you have to be quick to catch them, as they’ll always move opposite direction you’re headed.
What unfortunately irks me about this game is how it doesn’t feel like there’s a buildup anymore.  While, yes, the action does culminate to ghost-train-power-pellet-fest once you reach a certain iteration of level jumps, that’s the only signifier that you’re near the end of the time limit.
had, in my opinion, much better pacing to give you that satisfaction when you reach max speed, and you were zooming by because
built that all yourself.  Screwing up your plan by missing a turn or hitting a ghost meant that you had to rebuild a chunk of what you’ve done.  In this, well, it feels like nothing really happened.
However, despite all that, the game is still solid fun.  And at the $13 price point, it’s a no brainer if you enjoy arcade games.  My only issue is that I still feel that
is the superior game of the two, and that isn’t a bad thing.  Both
and
are great games.
My only real complaints against the game are:
•	It feels like Pac-Man floats in his movement.  Turning corners preemptively takes practice, as there is much more leeway for if you screw up.  Say you passed an intersection, and are just riding on the edge of the next wall, pressing up to preemptively turn at the next intersection at this point may throw you upwards at the intersection you just passed.
•	The graphics look like they clash in many places.  It feels like everything was placed in here, rather than everything was created here.

The idea of having to hunt ghost chains also adds fun via variability.  Except when you're forced to nab them with surgical precision to extend a very short mission timer in certain modes...that can be the antithesis of fun.
Also liking the fact that bombs can (and should) be used tactically and actually critical to attaining high scores.  Quite a change of mindset!

I am so happy with how this game turned out. My biggest fear after the announcement of this game was that it would basically be a map pack for CE DX. However instead we got a game with a very different scoring system and play style while still being as engaging and fun as the original.
It seems that every new mechanic has been designed to make the game much more aggresive. You can now bump into ghosts a few times before they get angry and become lethal. This allows you to forcefully push yourself where you need to go with the added risk of more deadly ghosts. Making ghosts angry will also cause them to jump into the air which allows you to manipulate their position to your advantage. Further in order to destroy a chain of ghosts you need to collide with the front making the ability to manipulate and chase down ghosts key to succces. This mechanic takes a while to get used to however is very satisfying when you come up with setups to preform quick kills.
The cost of these aggressive changes means that the game is less threatening, however I don't feel that this is a bad thing. Scoring optimization plays a much bigger role here as a result and the game includes a 1 life extreme difficulty if you want a more threatening experience.
Pac Man Championship Edition 2 has not succeeded the previous games, rather it created something new which shares similar themes but a different and equal gameplay experience. I highly recommend checking the game out.

This game is simply incredible. The controls are simple and gameplay requires heavy teamwork and tactical planning. The graphics are also quite good, and the game should be able to run on older or less powerful machines, though on low graphics. My GTX 960 runs the game on ultra at well over 70fps, so some newer iGPUs can probably get 30-40 on low, maybe even higher. However, the game has some issues with balance, but it's only in Alpha so you can cut it some slack. I'll go into detail about some of the features available right now:
Crew customization - you can customize what crew members are working on your ship to give your ship special buffs, that really can make a difference in battle
Ship customization - there are various skins available for each ship, although they cost a large amount of a currency you must pay for
Variety of ships and ship classes - There are 3 different manufacturers each with a decent number of ships. In these catagories you can find stealth ships, attack ships, support ships and more. However, each ship has its own weapons that can't be changed.
Again, the game is in Alpha, so it has a long way to go. But, it's definitely playable and super fun as it is. I recommend that you check it out!!
