Honestly, I wanted to like this game.  It looked like it was introducing new ideas, plus French Revolution seemed like an awesome place to run around in to do cool assassiny things.  But, it was a let down for $60.  The launch issues with the framerates and performce were bad.  Arno constantly STILL gets stuck on things or jumps to objects you don't want to go to, which makes escapes and chases a pain in the butt.  The story is mediocre at best and has a ton of holes in it.  The map, while quite large, is splattered with collectibles, some of which you can't even get without using the mobile app.
It seems like this game is trying to do too much at once without focusing on story or character development.  Arno is a weak character, and doesn't hold together well.  Even Connor from AC3 was a better character development.
That being said, the game itself is gorgeous to the eyes.  However, since the framerate stutters constantly, it's hard to appreciate it.  Ubisoft should have pushed this out a while, and now they're trying to scramble to patch it and apologize for screwing up to save face with the community.  Too late on that front for several people.  I regret pre-ordering the game, and honestly can't recommend this to anyone.  While some ideas are great, such as the new movement, both up and down buildings, or going inside of buildings, or the murder mysteries; the overall feel of the game is lackluster.
Wait for a year for them to fix it and pick it up on a steam sale.  Can't recommend it until then.

Anticipating at least a modicum of a poor man's Dark Souls, this was a great disappointment.
Your character is a slow-as-syrup-moving 60 year old guy with emphysema. While he's rolling you can make yourself a cup of coffee and watch the news before he's back up. Striking a few times with a weapon leaves our hero gasping for air like a 400 pound chain-smoking runner. It's super off-putting and becomes annoying within a few minutes. Attacking takes forever and makes the combat dull as yeast-infected dishwater.
Inventory is unnecessary confusing, greeting you with the warmth of a Calculus 3 exam, menus splattered on the screen with no order to it whatsoever. You're also stuck with a camera that is all over the place, even failing to adjust correctly as your character moves up and down simple stairs, or effectively zooming out when enemies press you into a wall and you can't see sh|t.
Hit-detection is reminiscent of a drunken, back alley-circus knife throwing act; results vary from horrifying to laughable. Will this swing hit you/the enemy? Place your bets, gentlemen.
There's no poise or stagger like you're used to from the Soul's games it tries to copy, not even a plunge attack is present, and it's obvious that a poor man's Dark Souls isn't even fitting this title; it's just a turd dressed up in pretty colors.
Many times you can't cue for example a roll action when you are getting massacred, even when you still have enough stamina to do a roll - which would often save you and make the fighting and dodging so fun in Soul's games. Nope, game doesn't register the button press until your character comes to a complete £vcking standstill. Which means you'll see over and over again that "I am going to be hit now, I have stamina left to do a roll, but the game won't let me and....I died again". Bvllsh|t like that would leave anyone p|ssed because it hampers your actions instead of actually letting you act upon your skill and observations during the fight. Instead you can't but stare helplessly at your character dying, while the stamina bar shows that you should be able to continue the fighting and then some.
I ended up beating the first boss and I felt...irritated and aggravated. Like I'd had a gruesome day at work, been stuck in traffic for an hour, only to come home to someone b|tching at me for not having taken out the trash and having dinner ready. There was absolutely no sense of joy, accomplishment, or challenge. Just spite and resentment.
And that's when I quit.

The Old Tree is a strange, unsettling point & click adventure game, which runs only about 10 minutes and has little-to-no gameplay. The atmosphere is this game's strong point: it creates a very unsettling and bizarre world in no time at all, and makes you almost believe it as you follow and help your abnormal four-legged apple-like creature traverse the maze that is the "Old Tree".
It's lacking in gameplay, which consists of clicking every now and then. There is no story present whatsoever, though with a little imagination I suppose you could pretend there was, and the puzzles are usually fairly simple, though there are a couple that are pretty clever. The imagination put into this game is also a strong point, alongside the atmosphere & art. It's definitely nothing I've seen before which makes it unique, though there are just too many flaws to give The Old Tree a higher score than this.
Perhaps if the game were longer, the puzzles more complex, the gameplay more engaging, some sort of a story, a point to the game, or a tad of explanation, The Old Tree could receive better marks. In a weird way it reminds me of Botanicula, which is an awesome game I recommend as I personally think it's kind of similar to The Old Tree and if you liked this game I'm sure you'll enjoy Botanicula.
Though to be fair, The Old Tree is a free game, and it takes barely any of your time, so honestly what do you have to lose? Try it out and see if you like it, in the very least it will be a brief breath of fresh air; a break from the normal mainstream games, even a break from most indie games. So this may be the first time I've ever recommended a game I've rated this low, simply because it's free and only takes 10 minutes of your day, and there's a chance you'll love it. Check it out!

Okay, so apparently Pajama Sam 4 has a mostly negative reception here on Steam, which is kind of a shock to me since all the other Humongous Entertainment games have mostly positive reviews (and why shouldn't they? after all, Humongous Entertainment is pretty much the Dr. Seuss of computer games)
I decided to check it out anyway, after revisiting the first three... and... despite the fact that I never got to play through this one until I was 22... I actually liked this one. I'd even call this a legitimate entry for the Pajama Sam series.
The environments were cool. Pajama Sam games usually have a theme to the worlds that Sam runs around in, and in this case, the world is based on a messy room. I liked some of the dialogue (as well as that twist towards the end) it's not as clever as in the first three games, but it was still pretty fun. And I was able to figure out the puzzles on my own. (and they don't look TOO difficult for a kid to solve)
That being said, I will admit this game is not without its problems:
-The Esc key doesn't skip cutscenes. I had to go to the manual to find out that the ENTER key is used for that. I'm glad I can still skip cutscenes at all, but this change is a little hard to get used to.
-Sam's voice was always noticably different in each game, but here it seem that the voice actor/actress wasn't even TRYING to sound like the character. Once again, this is hard to get used to.
-The game is pretty linear. In earlier Pajama Sam games, there was usually more than one solution for finding specific items. Here, the only thing that changes is the location of the cape at the beginning, and the location of the jar that you will use later.
-From what I've heard, other people have had trouble running this game on steam which is AN ACTUALLY LEGITIMATE REASON to not like it. It worked Perfectly Fine for ME though (and I use Windows 10) but I notice that the frame rate is very choppy. Don't know if this is just for the Steam version, or if this was always a thing, but it's kinda distracting.
But regardless, the good seems to outweigh the bad for me. And you're probably gonna end up with this game anyway if you get the Pajama Sam pack or the Humongous Entertainment COMPLETE PACK (which  for the record is far less expensive than purchasing all the other games in the pack even excluding the ones you probably don't want) So you might as well try it out.
And once again, this is coming from a 22-Year-Old who considers all the other Pajama Sam games nostalgic EXCEPT this one.

Well, we're finally here at the end of the road. I've gone back and played the original HE Pajama Sam trilogy from my childhood, and now it's finally time to see how Atari finished off the series with the conclusive Pajama Sam 4!
And, I've gotta say, at the end of this long road... the destination sucks!
I've played all of the Pajama Sam original three games, so all it took for me to review them was to just simply play them as a fully-grown adult, and compare them to the sandard I now hold to video games. But I never knew there was a Pajama Sam 4. It just silently exists. Like a foul turd at the bottom of a toilet from your friend failing to remember how to flush.
Pajama Sam 4 continues the story of Pajama Sam learning important values as a child, when he's about to go see Pajama Man at the mall, and loses his comic in his messy closet. He then enters a world of lost objects and assorted trash to find his comic and... ugh... I don't care. I really don't care.
I've never been so apathetic about Sam in a plot before. Even with my least favorite game in the original trilogy, Pajama Sam 2, there was still some drive. You had to fix the weather machine and save the world! How cool is that? And Pajama Sam 1 and 3 had the drive of you overcoming greediness and the fear of the dark. Both of which were subtly laid out and never preached to you.
I don't care about getting the comic book mainly because it's too tied up in Sam's mundane child life. The first three games felt like you were solving problems within Sam's massive imagination, and while that feeling is still here in Pajama Sam 4, the goal is too close to something so dull and uninteresting, that I legitimately don't care about it.
It also doesn't help that the world you travel in is one of the most vapid, boring worlds in the HE games library. Everything is just various shades of turquois and purple. with no variety thrown in. The first three games had some fantastic color palettes that didn't just stick to two colors. They used different shades of all the colors that complemented blue and purple. This world feels disgusting, bland, and ultimately unimaginative.
And I do mean disgusting. There are some gross animations, like watching a sponge eat mold off a horn, seeing a pizza turn black and sink into a sidewalk, and watching a pig greedily chew on a meal in a greasy diner. It's just an unpleasant world, as well as bland.
The plot in Pajama Sam 4 is incredibly stupid, and relies to heavily on a gag to give you any drive to succeed. You need to get a shirt, some socks, and some shoes in order to enter the garbage mall, see Dr. Grime (who you never actually meet), and get your comic book back. Yes, it follows that Humongous formula, but the mystery of seeing Dr. Grime is spoiled, when the garbage children mistaker Sam for Dr. Grime because he's so dirty. He looks nothing like Dr. Grime! Can you be that stupid?
And at the end, Sam cleans up the garbage mall and makes a speech about how he should take care of his stuff and make sure to stay clean. I would've been fine with this if there were no speech, since everything you did already contributed to the message (kind of like the last three games. Huh.), and you didn't have the point of the story spelled out for you. That and most of the characters are too incompetent and lazy to take care of their problems and rely on a 7-10 year old to fix it for them. That was very irritating. I think only two characters go out of their way to help you: the scuba diver and the sponge. That's it.
Technically speaking, there are some things that are just okay in the game and things I abominate. I like the music. It's actually pretty decent. There's some singers that'll hum or snap their fingers while you traverse the world, giving it a more charming feel than it actually is. I like the character animation and graphics now. They look actually hand-drawn and animate the same way, too. It looks nice.
However, these features are blown out of the water by the terrible voice dubbing. The characters don't even match what they're actually saying half the time! I also hate how little animation there is in the world. It doesn't feel living. And that could be because I played Spy Fox 3 not too long ago, and a lot of the backgrounds were fully animated, but that game was made 2 whole years before Pajama Sam 4! Shame on you, Atari.
While the animation is fine, there's a constant framerate lag for each screen. On a cartoon point-and-click game made in 2003. It's not enough to be a massive problem, but it's incredibly annoying when you have to wait for the game to catch up with where you are. Pajama Sam will walk from one side of the screen to the next, but will stop halfway for about five seconds, and then pop into the new area halfway into it already. Every time. I thought this was just my copy, but on the walkthroughts I watched, it seems to be the same case. This game runs like thick sh**.
Along with that, once you've played the game once, that's it. There aren't anymore variations. I attempted a second playthrough, but everything was exactly the same. I think the only thing that changes locations are the trading cards you can find (which is expected), and... wait for it.... are you ready?... this is gonna blow your mind!... a jar. A motherf***ing jar. That's it. There are arcade games you can play, but they perform just as laggy as everything else that I have no motivation whatsoever to coninue playing them.
Of course the final nail in the coffin is the horrendous voice acting. Sam has a totally new voice, and I wouldn't mind it so much, if she didn't emote like a wacky kid from the 90's. "Whoooaaah!", "Yippee!", and "Alllllright!" come out so many times, that it makes me physically cringe to hear her force those uncomfortable phrases. Most of the other voice actors are so stiff and dry, that it sounds like they're reading off their script in front of the mic, and only slightly adding an accent to it. Terrible all around.
Pajama Sam 4, while it is the final Pajama Sam game, is by far the worst. It's clear that Atari didn't know how to make a Pajama Sam game and just feebly attempted to do what they thought make a good kids game from the established formula, but they failed so horribly on every level, that I can consider this one of the worst games I've played on my library. I'm giving Pajama Sam a 1/10. Despite the nice new animation and music, this game is one of the worst Humongous titles, as well as one of the worst games I've had to suffer through. My advice: just play the first three. I may not have enjoyed Pajama Sam 2 that much, but it's better than this hunking pile of sh**.

I recommend this game, but that's because I love the series a lot. As other players have noted, the original voice actress  does not voice Sam, so he has a noticeably difference voice. It's a bit of a jarring change. I can ignore it, but I understand it may bother others. Additionally, the art style and music are different (which kind of makes sense given the time gap between this game and the third); this isn't necessarily bad, but both seem less zany than previous games. Upsettingly, the dialogue isn't as fun or quirky either, and the voice delivery is as flat as the dialogue.
On a technical level, this Steam version, for me, has very laggy cutscenes where the audio would occasionally cut out for some lines. I own this on the original CD too, and I nevwr had such problems. Regardless, the gameplay is also terribly taggy, even on aforementioned CD. When moving from A to B, the screen pauses with an image of Sam exiting before popping over to the new screen instead of a smooth transition as seen in other Humongous Entertainment games. Even the speaking in non-cutscenes is laggy. Another example is the overly laggy Bejeweled-like game, and, possibly lag-related, the stupid drawer game is stupidly easy.
Plotwise, the plot still fits with the general feel of the Pajama Sam series (the end progression is weird, though), and I like the trading card system (because I'm also a giant nerd for cards). Thus, overall, the different execution makes the game feel very, very different from its predecessors and not in the best way.
TL;DR: I recommend the game because I like the series and the game itself is not bad, but it is flatter, more lackluster, and laggier.

Pajama Sam was one of Humongous Entertainment's big franchises from my childhood, managing to be very entertaining, thoughtful, and funny. This installment, helmed by Atari after their purchase of the company, sometimes manages to have dialogue that can be funny, but fails in every other aspect.
I don't need to be one of the many people who has blasted the voice-acting of this game, however, after playing this game and attempting to play it again for the sake of review, I would fell empty to not mention how horrible this voice acting is. Sam sounds far too young, and barely has much power behind his voice. He is far from the only one with bad vocie acting, among a slew of obnoxious characters even small children could easily find annoying.
The plot for Pajama Sam games where usually easy accuses that make sense, yet this one somehow messes that up. It makes no sense and feels rushed, and the game itself is littered with not just confusing choices, but bugs. My second try end only ten minutes in after a bug broke the mouse. I do not understand how a point-and-click adventure game can make the mouse stop working, and yet that's exactly what happened with this game.
Life Is Rough When You Lose Your Stuff is a buggy and annoying mess that should not be played. Do not buy this game for your children, and do not believe that it is good simply because of the previous installments, which thankfully hold up incredibly well.

Bastion is a critically-acclaimed steampunk/fantasy-themed action RPG, and the acclaim is very justified. The story is very intriguing and well-executed, told in an amusingly sardonic fashion by an NPC/main character who serves as a narrator. The narrator even goes so far as to narrate the player's actions, but the narration isn't overdone and manages to avoid being annoying.
Combat is fun, yet challenging. The player gets to use some melee weapons (a hammer, a knife, etc.) and also some firearm/projectile weapons (bow, musket, rocket launcher, etc.). The challenge is customizable in that you can give yourself certain perks, or you can give the enemies their own perks. So, combat can be as challenging as you want it to be.
The game is relatively short, but it has a New Game+ mode, during which you can find an easter egg that allows you to summon Portal turrets straight from Aperture Labs (and even get one to interact with at the Bastion).
Anyway, don't hesitate if it's on sale.

=== TL:DR ===
For anyone that's a fan of the competitive team-based games, who also happens to love enormous capital-class spaceships, I'm sure you could find something to enjoy here.
At first, piloting the ships seems like it's going to be slow-going, and initially I had the feeling that things weren't going to ever really get "intense" - honestly, that's just plain wrong.
=== ABOUT GAMEPLAY ===
The space you fight in is a lot like an "arena" - there are 3 sectors of space that you have to FTL-jump to (leaving your ship vulnerable while spooling the drives) - two of the sectors are for capturing and holding mining stations that allow your team to slowly upgrade their ship's capabilities. On either "end" of each of these sectors is a forward base that must be captured to enable your team to FTL into the opposing team's home base, destroying their turret control systems and ultimately capturing it.
While this sounds like it might be an exercise in a commonly used mechanic - the developers have done a fantastic job of making teamwork a pivotal part of the experience and leveraging each of the captial ships' abilities in a finely-balanced ballet of death. I'm honestly shocked at how well each of the ships has a distinct "feel" to it, each one having specific play-styles it is best suited for.
Different weapon systems have different effective ranges, behaviors, and cooldowns associated with their uses - learning to utilize your ships abilities to their maximum potential is a part of the learning curve. This can be a little daunting at times, and requires some thought on the players' part for figuring out where things might've gone wrong.
However - when the ships meet in a contested sector, the firefights are intense and satisfying. VFX make each weapon system feel unique and gives it "heft" in the battle and the sound effects are fantastic.
Personally I was skeptical going into the game - but now that I've played it for a while, I can honestly say this is one of those titles that'll sit in my "currently playing" category in Steam for quite some time.

In Lords of the Fallen, you play as Gruff McGrufferson, the gruffest, toughest dude around. But under that gruff exterior, he is actually a wobbling mound of jelly. Our pal Gruff the jelly man must wobble his way around a castle and a demonic realm, fighting a bunch of angry demons and their sickly looking pals.
Unfortunately for our chum Gruff McJellyman, his wibbly legs make him less manouverable than an asthmatic sloth, and his wobbly arms mean that swinging anything bigger than a toothpick is a real struggle for our intrepid hero. Even more unfortunate for our dashing dispatcher of ne'er do wells, the villainous villains he encounters have some deviously diabolical tricks up their muscular sleeves.
Every one of these no good rascals comes equipped with an invisible record player, which they stand upon. What this means for mighty Jellyman is that all these cads he encounters can swivel on the spot... without moving their feet! The KNAVES! The SCOUNDRELS! The UTTER CHEEK! Our poor hero must face large, brutish enemies, who hide behind mighty shields, have vast qauntities of health, and who only give miniscule openings in their defence. These dastardly fiends laugh at our delicious Jelly hero, for they know that further down the corridor, two more of their identical brethren lie in wait - and our gruff protagonist must face them all, lest he be overwhelmed! Oh the horror...
Although, it's not all bad news for our gelatinous champion.
On his quest, he is accompanied by his best pal, Jam, the friendly invisible cameraman! Jam eagerly follows Jelly Goat Gruff on his delectable adventures. Unfortunately, Jam gets a little giddy whenever his pal Jellyman charges into battle, and can't keep a firm grip on his camera.
Also accompanying our damn tasty chum is Karlo...Kaslo?...Carlos? Whatever. Our ABSOLUTELY memorable pal Karlos freed the magnificent Jellygruff from his horrible jelly prison, where our hero was placed after attempting a coup against the Ice Cream king, to supplant him from the delicious dessert throne. Mage-o Kazooie brings Gruff McJellyjelly to Keystone to fight the nasty demons, because only he, with his superior reflexes, nimble footwork, and masterful weapon-handling, can save the day from EVIL!
Our gastronomical hero also gains assistance from an amiable demon blacksmith!
"I can inscribe your weapons with runes to make them worthy of Gods!", he proudly claims.
Lo and behold!, Jellyman was overjoyed to find that his now godly weapon turned a monster that previously took 12 hits to kill, into a monster that now takes a measly 11 hits to vanquish.
Oh yeah, there's also this woman, Yetka or something. She definitely wasn't as memorable as Kazoozle, the COMPLETELY memorable wizard dude. Also, there was some bad dude who's name began with A. But who cares, he was just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Dare you join the mighty Jellyman on his quest?
Dare you battle these fearsome record player equipped demons?
Dare you slog through dozens and dozens of said demons, over and over again?
Dare you wrestle with the dreadful beast known as the inventory?

After completing the game just now, I cannot refrain from writing anything but a positive review when there are so many negative ones here bringing the rating of this game down which is real injustice and a shame. Sure the game lacks Dark souls level of polish and there is the issue of crashes when the fighting gets a little too intense during certain boss fights and especially when magic spells are used too often in such scenarios but this in my opinion does not take away all the goodness this game offers overall. Being a carbon copy of Dark Souls in most aspects, Lords of the Fallen starts feeling like an entirely different game after a few hours. With a decent story, great graphics with spectacular lighting and particle effects, clever use of magic, tricky side-quests, hidden secrets and npc interactions, it creates an experience which is different from the Souls series which actually is a good thing in my opinion. LOTF is an easier version of Dark Souls with a merrier environment - much for the pleasure of a casual gamer though still only a Souls fan would connect to. First timers with no prior induction to Dark Souls kind of gameplay might find this game tough enough for few bouts of frustration.
The graphics and lighting are really good and almost all armors are intricate in design. The music is satisying, voice acting good but the animations that support it look stiff most of the time. Combat feels strikingly similar to Dark Souls with identical button mapping on the gamepad which is a good thing for a Souls player. The loot is diverse and a few of the weapons and shields are awesome. For example, a shield called 'Twisted Ways' (DLC content) has a rotating map on it. How cool is that? Talking about map, the overall size of the game world known as Keystone is quite big and most of the time would leave you scratching your head as to how to get to a particular spot which had a locked chest that you now found a key to. With twisted dungeons hiding secrets, a castle holding plenty of hidden areas and a portal to a whole new dimension, the whole process of exploring every nook and corner can be daunting.
Enemies and Bosses aren't that tough compared to Dark Souls and what I like most about them in LOTF is there is a knack in taking them down. Ofcourse, Dark Souls has it written all over it but in some areas in LOTF, especially in one or two boss fights you might want to think out-of-the box to avoid taking damage which is something spectacular when you discover it yourself. However, some boss fights are crash-riddled if you do not own a beefy PC and the DLC boss is such a pain to beat. End of the day, bad optimization is where the game loses at and If it weren't for this it would've received rave reviews for sure.
Simply put, this game might fall short on optimizations but it is a very good game if your PC can power it. Following the footsteps of Dark Souls and yet bringing a whole new feel within is purely refreshing. LOTF is best played with keeping Dark Souls' gameplay in mind and might do enough to frustrate newcomers. But to those who are well acquainted with the Souls series, LOTF is yet another epic journey.

This is just a little post I'd like to make about The Walking Dead game made by telltale, I must say they have done an absolutely phenomenal job on it so far and really captured that apocalyptic, real and gritty feel akin to the tv series and comics, its the real world and it definitely likes to remind you that it is no fairytale!
The game puts you in control of a man called Lee Everett, the game plays out sort of like one of those old point and click games where you wander around examining things, collecting items and talking to people. The biggest part of the game is based around a little girl under your protection called Clementine, an 8 year old with no apparent parents to be seen. She's just so damn adorable!
With Clementine under your wing, the biggest part of the game is the decision making and conversational based gameplay, everything you contribute to situations and conversations will affect the story or characters in some way, will you play as the nice hero or will you only be out for yourself, maybe you even want to just ruin someone as much as possible, the choice is literally yours!
Your choices do not come without consequences however, as I said before, almost everything you contribute will affect something in some way, maybe x may remember what you said about them back in episode 1, well now you've got yourself into a pickle of a situation with some walkers in episode 2, they don't feel the need to help you since you pee'd them off! Those sort of shenanigans!
Clementine will also pick up on the things you say to her and your actions, so based on how you want to play you can try to raise her well and be careful what you do around her, strengthening your bond or perhaps be careless and cold, ruining her poor little mind with the things she is exposed to. Again, the choice is yours.
Nurture her or neglect her, Clementine is your responsibility now.
You really are placed into some tough situations throughout the episode, even to the point of who lives and who dies, who to save first and things such as who you feed the last of the limited rations to, they'll all be taking note!
Throughout the game, you'll make friends, you'll make enemies and the moments where you have no idea what your stance is on an argument between two people you want to get along with are inevitable, sometimes no matter what you do it still wont be good enough. You aren't superman and the game definitely reminds you often that no matter what you do, people will die and people will do what they want.
The rules of the living are in tatters now, you just have to hope people stick by them, the walkers are no problem compared to the living.
You'll meet all sorts of people throughout your story. Crazies, friendlies and people from all backgrounds and each with some sort of story to come with them.
Many conflicts leave you with very hard calls to make. All have consequences.
Now onto the technical aspects of the game. I'll start with the graphics first, the visuals of the game come across very cleanly. They are easy on the eyes in their cartoony manner and look great in action, being smooth and fitting to the comic book inspiration the game came from, don't let them put you off they suit the game down to a tee! They only fall short in the texture department at times on far objects but other than that they are pretty solid, facial expressions are excellent and the overall look of characters is great, Lee and Clementine for example, Clementine is absolutely adorable whilst Lee actually looks like he has a personality unlike in some games. I'll give the graphics an 8/10.
The sound next, the game has some great sound work in it I must admit. For a game based around a lot of voice acting they pulled it off well. The voice actors sound professional, fit their characters in game and portray their emotions really, really well. Its almost like a movie/tv show trapped in a game. Sound effects again, are great, a lot of effort has gone into the overall sound effects of the game, from ambient sounds right down to the footsteps of a person. Not to mention the great soundtrack that goes with the game, adding that extra bit of atmosphere and emotion to vital moments. 9/10 for the sound.
Lastly the Gameplay. The gameplay is very solid and works well for the purpose of the game. When you are not involved in conversations and decision making to progress the story, you take control of Lee, walking around able to point and click to examine things, talk to people and solve any obstructions/puzzles there may be. There are also very tense moments involving things such as walkers coming at you and you having to frantically try to click on a moving target or mash a few keys before you become lunch!
It may sound silly but it is actually pulled off very well and is great for moments when you get caught off guard. I grew up with the Age of Empires saga. I delved into the Age of Mythology and its expansions. I do miss the Wololo and Rogan, but they do tribute these sounds in the pre-programmed multiplayer taunts. The soundtrack isn't bad; could have used a little more variety.
As always, take this review as an opinion. I'd recommend it.

TLDR;
------
They should have named it "XCOM 2: Terror from the deep"
Pros
-----
- Nice Graphics
- Hacking is a neat addition
Bad
----
- Aggressive timers on every mission force you to make hasty and poor tactical decisions

- You don't really feel like you're making strategic decisions in the world view: it's just there to pass time
HUGE XCOM fan. I used to play the old XCOM games as a kid, and loved the XCOM remake. The DLC for the XCOM remake was also really great! I'm also the type that doesn't like to load from saves: if I lose all but one guy, it happens. That's what makes XCOM so fun.
I had a hard time getting into XCOM 2. The first time I tried it once and got bored with it after a couple of hours. I figured I'd come back to it after some patches and updates. On my second run, all three of my first missions I had to load from save because the timer ran out and I failed the mission. Now I'm no novice: I've played XCOM since forever, and I'm not timid about putting my squad in danger. I get it: they don't want you taking time to set up "perfect" positioning every for every encounter, but you literally have to send your squaddies out without cover fire, out of cover, or without ammo if you want to complete these missions. The timer isn't just a component of the strategy: it literally forces you to make stupid and hasty decisions.
There are so many situations that can run the timer down that have nothing to do with making poor decisions....
Your squad misses every shot one round thanks to the RNG. That's one timer turn down! Time to reload! >:(
The last alien is "on the run" and retreats two turn distances away? Time to reload!
You're two blocks away from the extraction point on the last turn? Time to reload!
You positioned your sniper on the roof and put your assaults ahead? Yeah, he's not making it out in time. Time to reload!
What I don't understand is that they took the most annoying aspect from XCOM 1 and made it a staple of gameplay in XCOM 2.
Now I often complain that "games nowadays are too easy," but this is just NOT FUN. I never liked the timed missions in XCOM 1, but the timers weren't all that aggressive. You had to be a little more careful about reloading and overwatch, but overall it wasn't bad and it wasn't EVERY mission. And if you killed all the aliens, you didn't have to then run everyone to an extraction point. -_-
The fact that EVERY mission is timed makes this a really high stress game. I want to play a game that is fun: if I want to stress out, I'll work and get paid for it. I don't want to have to reload from saves to stand a chance of succeeding, nor do I want to mod the timer so it's gone, nor do I want to develop a habit of recklessly sending my troops into danger. I enjoy setting up tactical positioning. I enjoy designing my squad. I enjoy the rush of taking the shot or getting shot and watching to see if it connected. I enjoy strategically setting up my base and choosing which techs to develop based on things that change.
I didn't like how they "dumbed down" XCOM 1 from the DOS versions, but I understand that they needed a design that was simple enough for console gamers and to attract a modern audience. I was really hoping that with XCOM 2, they'd re-add some more of the tactical and strategic complexities of the originals. I feel like XCOM 2 is a new skin on XCOM 1 with the addition of hacking, timers every mission, and a simplified overworld strategy.  TFTD anyone? Let's just make it harder and put a new skin on it!
Playing this game just makes me frustrated and want to play the older XCOM games. I do not recommend this. If you really want it, pick it up on sale.

This has brought something completely new and unique to the action rpg world. Bastion has a way of making you feel just that bit overwhelmed. The best way I could describe it is like a bright colourful Diablo with a much greater emphasis on tactics and reflexes and less focus on loot. Bastion is much more demanding game than its competitors, requiring good timing and situational awareness, instead of the simplistic click fest most action rpgs call for. Bastion also has a unique story telling element. As you play through the game, particular actions and interactions are narrated - constantly reminding you of how you are driving the story forward. In all, this is one of the most impressive indie titles I've played in recent time - providing not just a fun game, but also a new experience. If you like Diablo or other action RPGs, you must play this.

Basically, it's a very good game that's plagued by some framerate issues. I've had no game-breaking bugs but I've fallen through the floor a few times pre-patch but it seems to be fixed now. The normally overpowered Assassins Creed "kill-counter-instakill-repeat" combat has been changed that it now feels like you, as only a single man, are now at a disadvantage agains the massive hordes of Frenchmen. There are 5 categories of weapons, One-Handed, Heavy, Long, Rifles, and Guillotine Guns. They each have their own advantages and disadvantages, but can all be compensated for very well. Coop mode is fun, but players can leave the mission at anytime and they are quite difficult, but possible, to do on your own. The signature freerunning of AC has been improved so that you can choose whether you want to go up, down, or flat with a button press. The story as far as I've played it is decent, and a little predictable. The world has an amazing atmosphere depending on which district you waltz into and the graphics are state of the art. Money is a little hard to come by but for good reason, the highest level of items are massively overpowered. People complaining about microtransactions have no reason to, everything in the game can be bought with in-game currency. Overall, Assassin's Creed Unity is a very good game, an improvement over the regular AC title, but plagued by a lagging framerate.

This is often cited as the weakest of the Pajama Sam quadrilogy. But I completely disagree on that remark as this game is just as enjoyable as the previous three installments. In the fourth and final game, Sam (who isn't voiced by Pamela Adlon) learns that Pajama Man(which is actually a guy in a mascot costume) is giving out autographs at the local mall. Sam knows that his first issue of Pajama Man comic series is the prefect item to get signed. Only problem is that his room is a mess and couldn't find it. So once again he imagines that he "visits" a ficitional land. In this case it's a junk land where Sam encounters all sorts of characters and creatures. The thing I love about this game is that it explores the Pajama Man series more with the info of the characters on the trading cards you collect throughout the game. A lot of the cards reference characters and items mentioned by Sam in the previous installments. Which gives the Pajama Man character a sense of history to him. Overrall this game isn't as bad as people claim it to be, plus it be a bit hard to come up with newer ideas had this series went on longer. So the idea of exploring the Pajama Man universe and backstories is a logical choice to conclude this franchise. If you loved the first three games, give this one a chance cause it's far from being bad or boring.

This game is free, so why are you reading this review instead of playing it? Anyway, for those that want a little bit more information here we go:-
This is an odd little 'on rails' 'puzzle' game. Do not get overly excited though, as the whole game is completable in about 10 minutes (well what do expect for free?).
You play as a weird little 4 limbed octopus type alien creature in a surreal world, well I say 'play as', but really it just moves along when it stops you use your mouse to complete a puzzle to get the alien to move again. The game world consists of a few dark tunnels, a kitchen, a lobby and couple of outside bits mostly in hand drawn looking blacks and greys with the odd little smudge of faded colour here and there. Overall the visuals are fairly unique and have an 'indie' look to them which you will either like (a bit) or hate.
There is a simple yet eerie ambient sound track in the background which helps add to the limited atmosphere and is not unpleasant to listen to. Game play wise you progress along a predetermined course and solve simple puzzles to reach your goal, which is just freedom I guess.
The puzzles are as straight forward as clicking a glowing red dot in the dark to switch on a light, to working out how to get into a flood-able section of tunnel and then re-flood it to get onto the ceiling amongst other stuff. It's certainly not going to strain your brain although there are often no clues as to what you have to do, so sometimes it's just a case of trail and error or just click on everything you can see and see if it reacts. It's not as frustrating as it sounds as you'll work out how to solve each puzzle within an attempt or two.
If they were charging say £0.70 for the game I'd say it was over priced and only worth about £0.10. But as it is free I think you should add it to your collection, even if it's just so you can complete it and increase your (probably) horrifically low 'Avg. Game Completion Rate' found in your profile.
(*spoiler - In the lobby there is a switch behind the plant on the left, you need to switch off the light, then click the red switch and repeat a few times to call the elevator. This is probably the hardest puzzle in the game)

Usually I find games with turn-based combat uninteresting, but this a special exception. Most of the negative reviews of this game are ♥♥♥♥♥ing about the RNG in it, but don't let that turn you off. There are ways to manage the RNG, and you can come back from even the heaviest of setbacks (unless if you're playing on the highest difficulty where there's a limit on how many heroes can die, and that playthough's over). The RNG also works both ways. Yeah, it's possible for the enemy to hit your party with four crits in a row, but it's also possible for your team to dodge every attack that's thrown at you (these are both unlikely scenarios though).
TL;DR: Even if you're not a fan of turn-based games and RNG, you shouldn't pass this one up.

I had Fallout 4 since the release date. I was stopping myself from writing this review for a long time. I was hoping I will discover something that would make me appreciate this game and see it in a positive light. Unfortunately I didn’t find anything that could allow me to recommend this game. Beside this I shouldn't need to look for positives with some much effort.
Fallout 4 is the most shallow game of this franchise. In my opinion even Fallout: Tactics had more to offer when it comes to story and this literally was a tactical turn base game.
Pros of Fallout 4:
- Thought me to not pre-order stuff.
- If you never played any Fallout game you might enjoy this one. However you would be better off if you get one of the previous games.
- You can mod it. Make sure to do it through Nexus, not Creative Club’s microtransactions.
Cons of Fallout 4:
- Dialogue choices are almost not existence. In the previous games you could choose exact line that your characters would say. Now you have vague short descriptions to cover the fact that your four choices are: “Yes”, “Of course yes”, “F*** you, but yes” and “No. I will come back later to say yes”.
- In theory there is this epic quest that’s about war for humanity and your family. In practise non of the characters that the quest revolve around feel real. You can’t feel the importance of this quest at any stage. Therefore the quest feel like a To Do list of house chores.
- Most of the quests are based on “Go there, kill that, bring this back”. This minimise the meaning of a word ‘quest’ to a walk and shoot experience.
- Downgraded character levelling (perks and SP.E.C.I.AL.)
- Graphics for the time of release were below average even for an open world game and even for Bethesda standards. I know Bethesda never was famous for great graphics, but the engine was not up to the task anymore. You can get some nice screenshots if you position camera right, but in general it’s very basic.
- Settlement feature was under developed. You could have put enough turrets to kill a small army, but you still need to come to help settlers if four raiders try to attack.
Bethesda dumbed down Fallout game to bare minimum while adding as much crafting as possible and ended up with a Fallout Minecraft. This will work for some people, but a Fallout fan will not find a real Fallout experience here.
Fallout 4 wins an award for most boooring Fallout game.
On the top of that Bethesda added micro-transactions by introducing paid mods. They cost way more than what they offer.

I hate to do this, because I grew up with the classic Shadowgate on the NES and loved it, but this game just isn't as "good" as the classic.
When I first saw this in the store, I thought that it was going to be a remastery with better graphics and some of the more obtuse puzzles refined to the point where they make more sense.
What they actually did was re-imagine most of the entire game, changed a ton of the puzzles, changed how a bunch of them worked and put in a LOT of back tracking into the game.
The classic game already had a standard "timer" with the torches that didn't allow you drag your feet all day, but it was spaced out enough to the point where the system was "fair". Not only does this game still have that timer, but worse, they enforce a mandatory curse that will end your game every time unless you can solve it. I don't know what they were thinking, but it was not an intelligent design decision.
Let me tell you something, when your biggest selling point is the nostalgia your game generates, the last thing you want to do is change the game so much it is no longer recognizable.
This isn't Shadowgate and frankly I am offended by what the developers did here. They ruined this game. I hope they NEVER get around to working on any of the other classic titles or they'll most likely just ruin that as well.

In my review for DOOM, I said that the history of first person shooters could be divided into "Before DOOM" and "After DOOM". Whilst that is true, if I had to pick another game that changed things so much, it would be this one.
1998 was a great year for FPS games. We got both Unreal, and this. Both games set new standards for immersiveness - Unreal giving us collectable items which filled in back story, and amazing dynamic lighting, along with a fully dynamic soundtrack. Half-Life set a new example for story telling.
The game never leaves the first-person view. There are no cut scenes, and no points at which control is taken away from the player (well, besides one scene which you'd know about once you played), and as such it's far more immersive than many games of it's nature. The game isn't divided into levels, each section flowing on straight from the previous, making things seem far more natural and realistic than before.
It was the first game I had which took advantage of my 3D graphics card, and I'd frequently use the opening train ride to show it off to my friends. Yes, it doesn't look so great nowadays, but that was 16 years ago!
It's also worth checking out the fan game "Black Mesa" which requires any Source game to play, but try the original first.
The sections with Xen are still awful though. Sorry.

TLDR;
------
They should have named it "XCOM 2: Terror from the deep"
Pros
-----
- Nice Graphics
- Hacking is a neat addition
Bad
----
- Aggressive timers on every mission force you to make hasty and poor tactical decisions
- Too many recycled game play components from XCOM 1 (Tactical Missions, Base Design, Squad Loadout, Stupid AI)
- You don't really feel like you're making strategic decisions in the world view: it's just there to pass time
HUGE XCOM fan. I used to play the old XCOM games as a kid, and loved the XCOM remake. The DLC for the XCOM remake was also really great! I'm also the type that doesn't like to load from saves: if I lose all but one guy, it happens. That's what makes XCOM so fun.
I had a hard time getting into XCOM 2. The first time I tried it once and got bored with it after a couple of hours. I figured I'd come back to it after some patches and updates. On my second run, all three of my first missions I had to load from save because the timer ran out and I failed the mission. Now I'm no novice: I've played XCOM since forever, and I'm not timid about putting my squad in danger. I get it: they don't want you taking time to set up "perfect" positioning every for every encounter, but you literally have to send your squaddies out without cover fire, out of cover, or without ammo if you want to complete these missions. The timer isn't just a component of the strategy: it literally forces you to make stupid and hasty decisions.
There are so many situations that can run the timer down that have nothing to do with making poor decisions....
Your squad misses every shot one round thanks to the RNG. That's one timer turn down! Time to reload! >:(
The last alien is "on the run" and retreats two turn distances away? Time to reload!
You're two blocks away from the extraction point on the last turn? Time to reload!
You positioned your sniper on the roof and put your assaults ahead? Yeah, he's not making it out in time. Time to reload!
What I don't understand is that they took the most annoying aspect from XCOM 1 and made it a staple of gameplay in XCOM 2.
Now I often complain that "games nowadays are too easy," but this is just NOT FUN. I never liked the timed missions in XCOM 1, but the timers weren't all that aggressive. You had to be a little more careful about reloading and overwatch, but overall it wasn't bad and it wasn't EVERY mission. And if you killed all the aliens, you didn't have to then run everyone to an extraction point. -_-
The fact that EVERY mission is timed makes this a really high stress game. I want to play a game that is fun: if I want to stress out, I'll work and get paid for it. I don't want to have to reload from saves to stand a chance of succeeding, nor do I want to mod the timer so it's gone, nor do I want to develop a habit of recklessly sending my troops into danger. I enjoy setting up tactical positioning. I enjoy designing my squad. I enjoy the rush of taking the shot or getting shot and watching to see if it connected. I enjoy strategically setting up my base and choosing which techs to develop based on things that change.
I didn't like how they "dumbed down" XCOM 1 from the DOS versions, but I understand that they needed a design that was simple enough for console gamers and to attract a modern audience. I was really hoping that with XCOM 2, they'd re-add some more of the tactical and strategic complexities of the originals. I feel like XCOM 2 is a new skin on XCOM 1 with the addition of hacking, timers every mission, and a simplified overworld strategy.  TFTD anyone? Let's just make it harder and put a new skin on it!
Playing this game just makes me frustrated and want to play the older XCOM games. I do not recommend this. If you really want it, pick it up on sale.

I love the xcom games, and I expect a lot from new additions to the franchise. I've been playing them since xcom began in 1994. Xcom 2 provides hours of entertainment as you take on the alien menace across the globe. It follows directly from xcom, which I would implore you to play first.
Visually stunning on high settings. Great storyline and lore. Fluid, cinematic action turn-based combat. Interesting dlc that adds depth and variety to gameplay. Interesting spread of in-game systems to manage strategy (supplies, Intel, resistance communications). Highly customisable characters, weapons and base building. Controller support. Mod and workshop support.
A few people suffer from technical problems resulting in game crashing (minority, but still...). No co-op or multiplayer (a co-op mod exists).
*Minor gameplay spoilers below, read with caution.*
I'd like to be able to zoom out a bit further on the base screen (avenger). I'd like more reasons to visit certain rooms on the avenger, notably the commanders quarters and the bar/memorial. More map variety. More customisation options, specifically controlling amount of enemies per group/map, speed of avatar project and so on (yes I know there's mods). I feel like the game should last longer, and there should be another weapon tier, perhaps between magnetic and plasma.

I did not enjoy the adventure/puzzle aspect of the game I just did not find it interesting or fun, it's not as hard as it is obtuse its more about exploration than anything else. I didn't like that there is just a ton of going back and forth and the game has 100+ rooms if you think about it the game is just a corridor of rooms you go up and down over and over. Then with the pick-ups the vast majority of them do nothing and are just there for flavor. Surprisingly there are not a lot of items needed to beat the game. I suppose the difficulty is primarily based on your time limit more than puzzles but I find that just makes the game more annoying because then you have to restart completely if you run out of time.
What I do consider good about this game is that they built a world because there is just so much stuff that has nothing to do with the solution there are even side-quests and many things that you will not see if you only stick to the path. There is still a problem with that though because its a time limited game I don't feel that the exploration aspect really fits though I do applaud the fact that it is there.
The extra difficulties are nice as well, especially since they made the puzzles different, so playing on higher difficulties changes the game slightly. Unfortunately I don't find the lower difficulties to be necessary. They are too easy and master difficulty is not any harder just "longer" by a few steps here and there. I think there's a stigma that this game is super hard and they tried to reinforce this with the difficulty levels but starting at anything below master is really just a waste of time.
In closing I also want to say I was a bit disappointed in that there were not as many deaths as I thought there would be because I thought that was a big part of the game. I might have fallen from a few things or gotten shanked by some goblins but nothing I didn't see coming. From what I understand most of the deaths, or at least the good ones, you have to actually try to find. If you stick to solving the game though you will not die very often or at all which is the opposite of what I was expecting.

I have played more than 50 hours on Unity, so I have my fair share of experience of this game.
7.5/10
Pros-
Excellent time, the idea of fighting during the French Revoulution is a great idea, wish the main story focused more on the revoulution than Arno's love life, but I understand that it was necessary to show the flavor to Arno's personality. I also wish you got to spend more time with Napoleon.
Personality, Best likeable assassin since Ezio. Excellent Personality, not the brick wall, emoitionless Connor; not the scallywag, total d-bag pirate of Edward Kenway. Not the badass OG Altair. But still a pretty awesome assassin.
Story, not as good as a story as black flag (AC4 is still my favorite), but still good, probably my third favorite storyline.
Customization: finally customization in an AC game, dont have to be Assassin white
Co-op: When it works, it's awesome, the combat is not OP like in the other games (just counter and win) and it is actually a challenge.
Faffing about, most fun faffing about in this game than any AC game besides black flag. When it comes to doing random, non-story stuff, this game had it nailed down.
Cons-
Frame rate: Yes, sometimes it drops below 40 fps
Glitches:
- Sometimes the AI in a mission (co-op) doesn't move so you can't complete it.
- Rarely you fall through the world.
- Sometimes you can see random AI that aren't walking normally, but are walking straight up
- you can fall into a building that you aren't suppose to access that has no doors or windows that you can access.
- you can randomly jump into the carts of hay- no, not into the HAY, but in the cart, Arno is standing up, walking in the cart of hay. Sometimes
Save corruption: heard of people getting it, never had it happen to me
Overall: 7.5/10, love the game, love the story, love the assassin personality, love the customization.
But I HATE the glitches.

4. Story: In the past ubisoft sucess as been their storytelling by tying in their story within significant historical moments in time. The new main lead Arno suffers from the same problem of previous games being poorly fleshed out with no real personality of their own. Terratech is a game which I have never played the likes of before. That's not to say that they aren't out there, but I've never played something like this before.  It was enjoyable.  I had fun.  However, that hit the wall pretty damn hard after a certain point.
You see, the game doesn't ever stop unless you're paused.  Even when you're building your vehicle.  If you find that you need to do some major restructuring, then all it takes is one enemy to completely ruin your day.  This happened many times over the amount of time that I have played, which either says something about me or about the game.  In addition, there is absolutely no concept of taking a breather.  Anything you build is doomed to a slow destruction.  You just got through with a boss?  Invasion on your base before you can repair.  Dealt with that invasion?  Swarm of little guys.  Barely finish them off and in the middle of completely restructuring your tech because of damage?  Missed one that pegs your cab before you can do anything even remotely similar to fighting back.
It's a novel concept, and it has a lot of potential.  Think it needs a bit of a break between fights.  Maybe enemy techs leave you alone while the build beam is active, and actively run from you after you finish a boss or an invasion.  Maybe a co-op mode, so someone can at least watch your back while you're doing your thing.  Until then, I can't recommend it.

I'm always surprised when a solid game gets really awful reviews on steam, but I think in this case, it's mostly souls fans who aren't too pleased with this game taking elements from souls wholeheartedly without shame. Is it as good as Souls? No, but that doesn't mean I didn't have fun with it.
+Great visuals
+Good music
+Combat is a watered down souls experience. Diluted souls is still excellent. If you're going to steal, steal from the best.
+I actually liked the story, but I have a thing for janky euro stuff. The detailed ending was really cool, either way.
-Game doesn't explain stats well at all. Took me a while to realize items I don't meet the requirements for? Yeah, it shows them as being trash. Then suddenly they're better. Bad system. It doesn't explain poise, it's hard to compare items, the rune system is awful, etc... A lot of the stat scaling is off, too.
-Magic isn't explained well either. Prayer is actually "decoy". I'm still not sure what the point of stab is.
-Enemies aren't explained well - By this I mean, enemies can be higher or lower level, or have totally different skills, but all use the same model. Wut? Seriously, you can think 'oh this combo will take this guy down' and it takes off 25% of his health instead. Because it's actually an elite.
-Game world is very small and poorly laid out.
Basically: It's a decent game direly missing a better translation and more polish.
As an aside, the first boss is so poorly done in this game. He has a long combat string that you don't have enough stamina to handle if you're at all off balance, and you're supposed to wait for an opening - an opening that can be 30 seconds apart, and one shots you if you're too close to it. Derp. It's pretty miserable, but all the other bosses feel way more fair and less tedious. Also, if you do buy it, don't get the DLC unless it's in a good bundle.

This is just a little post I'd like to make about The Walking Dead game made by telltale, I must say they have done an absolutely phenomenal job on it so far and really captured that apocalyptic, real and gritty feel akin to the tv series and comics, its the real world and it definitely likes to remind you that it is no fairytale!
The game puts you in control of a man called Lee Everett, the game plays out sort of like one of those old point and click games where you wander around examining things, collecting items and talking to people. The biggest part of the game is based around a little girl under your protection called Clementine, an 8 year old with no apparent parents to be seen. She's just so damn adorable!
With Clementine under your wing, the biggest part of the game is the decision making and conversational based gameplay, everything you contribute to situations and conversations will affect the story or characters in some way, will you play as the nice hero or will you only be out for yourself, maybe you even want to just ruin someone as much as possible, the choice is literally yours!
Your choices do not come without consequences however, as I said before, almost everything you contribute will affect something in some way, maybe x may remember what you said about them back in episode 1, well now you've got yourself into a pickle of a situation with some walkers in episode 2, they don't feel the need to help you since you pee'd them off! Those sort of shenanigans!
Clementine will also pick up on the things you say to her and your actions, so based on how you want to play you can try to raise her well and be careful what you do around her, strengthening your bond or perhaps be careless and cold, ruining her poor little mind with the things she is exposed to. Again, the choice is yours.
Nurture her or neglect her, Clementine is your responsibility now.
You really are placed into some tough situations throughout the episode, even to the point of who lives and who dies, who to save first and things such as who you feed the last of the limited rations to, they'll all be taking note!
Throughout the game, you'll make friends, you'll make enemies and the moments where you have no idea what your stance is on an argument between two people you want to get along with are inevitable, sometimes no matter what you do it still wont be good enough. You aren't superman and the game definitely reminds you often that no matter what you do, people will die and people will do what they want.
The rules of the living are in tatters now, you just have to hope people stick by them, the walkers are no problem compared to the living.
You'll meet all sorts of people throughout your story. Crazies, friendlies and people from all backgrounds and each with some sort of story to come with them.
Many conflicts leave you with very hard calls to make. All have consequences.
Now onto the technical aspects of the game. I'll start with the graphics first, the visuals of the game come across very cleanly. They are easy on the eyes in their cartoony manner and look great in action, being smooth and fitting to the comic book inspiration the game came from, don't let them put you off they suit the game down to a tee! They only fall short in the texture department at times on far objects but other than that they are pretty solid, facial expressions are excellent and the overall look of characters is great, Lee and Clementine for example, Clementine is absolutely adorable whilst Lee actually looks like he has a personality unlike in some games. I'll give the graphics an 8/10.
The sound next, the game has some great sound work in it I must admit. For a game based around a lot of voice acting they pulled it off well. The voice actors sound professional, fit their characters in game and portray their emotions really, really well. Its almost like a movie/tv show trapped in a game. Sound effects again, are great, a lot of effort has gone into the overall sound effects of the game, from ambient sounds right down to the footsteps of a person. Not to mention the great soundtrack that goes with the game, adding that extra bit of atmosphere and emotion to vital moments. 9/10 for the sound.
Lastly the Gameplay. The gameplay is very solid and works well for the purpose of the game. When you are not involved in conversations and decision making to progress the story, you take control of Lee, walking around able to point and click to examine things, talk to people and solve any obstructions/puzzles there may be. There are also very tense moments involving things such as walkers coming at you and you having to frantically try to click on a moving target or mash a few keys before you become lunch!
It may sound silly but it is actually pulled off very well and is great for moments when you get caught off guard. In the conversation/decision making department you really are forced to make some tough decisions along the road and the freedom of choice is great, being able to respond to things how you see fit and shape your own character for Lee, even influence others to a certain degree. Just remember, nothing comes without consequences. The gameplay gets a 10/10.
The game gets a solid 10 overall from me, I am absolutely in love with it and it has definitely justified its price tag. It did that even just on the first episode in fact. I have never quite played a game like it, telltale really have pulled off the world of the walking dead incredibly well, basically this is me telling you to buy the game...Now. Why are you still here? Go get it!
Overall Ratings:
Graphics - 8/10
Sound - 9/10
Gameplay - 10/10
The game overall - 10/10!

Probably the best F2P shooter I've played in my life. If you're any bit curious about this game and you enjoy twitch shooters, then just try the game out. If you played AVA, Cross Fire or Combat Arms, this is essentially those games but better and newer, and less clunky. The mechanics in this game feel very smooth much like Cross Fire.
It has TDM so you can get a quick feel for the game and decide whether or not you like it realtively quick.
As always, there are a few minor issues that may deter you from joining in or playing for long periods of time.
All the weapons are balanced and the paid weapons are only skins and do not effect the stats of the weapons themselves. That alone is great!
Leaving the game clear of the P2W factor that haunts every other F2P game out there. Let's hope it stays that way.
So what is the bad then? Well, sometimes lag gets into play and it can be very noticeable from time to time. The game allows you to hop onto any region you wish so the chances of playing against 150+ ping players is really high. At first you may not really feel the lag since you're just getting used to the game but after a while, you'll realize that there's some split-second shots that don't seem to line up with what actually happened on your screen. Lag is always going to be in the game but I do believe that Black Squad does its best to keep things as close as possible. At least, it seems like it does a decent job of not having the lag be overly obvious like in other games.
In regards to overall content, the game is pretty light but it does have a fair number of maps for the different game modes so I can't complain. The weapon variety is claimed to be light but if you're just starting, there'll be enough weapons to keep you busy for a while.
So there's 2 stores 1 that uses "gold" which is the in-game currency you get while playing the game.
And the other store uses "medal" which is the in-game currency you get while playing the game, only not as much as gold.
If you keep playing and leveling up, you'll obtain enough medal to buy 1 gun within the first 10 - 15 hours in my experience. I joined in at a time where there were exp+ and gold+ bonuses so it may take a little longer depending on how well you play and how often you play.
That being said, Gold currency weapons are typically easier to obtain but they do have a drawback. None of the assault rifles are 1 hit headshots. This is insanely crucial in twitch shooters like this, but most of these weapons have controllable recoil so it shouldn't take too much to land 2 headshots one after the other.
The medal currency weapons are where you get your 1-shot headshots. The SR47, AK47 and AK12 being the more popular of the rifles. Their drawback is that they have an insane recoil that can be difficult to control. Which forces you to tap-fire and burst-fire most of your shots. The medal weapons aren't just exclusively high recoil/high damage weapons. There's also the MDR and the M4 which have low recoil but lesser damage. It depends entirely on your play style but if you do miss getting those 1 hit headshots, you will have to devote a little bit of time, or money to get the medal currency weapon you want.

Blaming RNG is for people who suck (I was one once). Here's a list of things you need to master:
-Enemy types/attacks
-Prioritizing enemies
-Party configurations and attack types
-Stuns
-Stress Management
-Inventory Management
-Camping
-Disease/ Negative Quirk Management
-Positive Quirk Preservation
-Roster Management (i.e. being able to dump♥♥♥♥♥♥heroes)
-Curios drops and interactions
-Dungeon navigation (i.e. scouting so you can avoid uncessary fights)
-Town management
-Money allocation
If there's something on the list you haven't mastered, then that's why you're dying. Endgame DPS is too hard and healing doesn't keep pace with damage? Did you get the Tome of Holy Healing and Vestal's Scroll? Too many battles? Are you scouting and avoiding unecessary battles that can be walked around? Stress healing costs too much? Are you killing stress dealers first and then using Crusader or Jester to stress heal on the fly?
Are you using stuns effectively to manage stress dealers? Do you have at least one antiquarian on the roster that you send on long missions to grind money? Do you have a Grave Robber or Plague Doctor to remove diseases for free while camping? Are you taking secondary heals like the Crusader's/Arbalest's/Plague Doctor's or self heals of the Leper/Abomination/Houndmaster/Hellion so you can magic pixel if need be until your Vestal/Occulist goes after you've been put on Death's Door? Do you have a secondary heal if your Occultist rolls a 0 or a 1? Etc.
Once you understand how the systems interlock you should lose next to nobody. The game is hard, the difficulty spikes can be a little much, and the time it takes you to grind up heroes and money (especially after a hard loss) can be infuriating.
But it can be done. It's not just a slot machine.

To put it simply, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you like difficult rogue-like RPGs, if you like cosmic horror, if you like absolutely phenominal sound and music design, if you like one of the most bone chilling narrators I've ever had the pleasure of listening to: Then by all means, buy this game now, and play it to your heart's content.
This is one of my absolute favorite games of all time-without a doubt-and as angry as it can make me sometimes, I find myself coming back time and again to try my hand at it all over again. Certainly, this game isn't for everyone, and if you're the type of person who is easily put off by harsh consequences, and sometimes just bad luck ruining a well thought out run (as in Xcom series), then this may not be the game for you; and that's entirely okay.
I feel like a good way to think is to not think of this game as a simple strategy RPG, where you're hunting numbers, or what have you. You're simply incharge of a bunch of human beings, all pretending to be heroes, and (many times) failing when the time calls. Once you accept that, a lot of the failures the game throws at you are a lot easier to take, in my opinion.
I could go on and on, but I will simply leave with: the warning the game gives you at the start of the game is true:Darkest Dungeon is about making the best of a bad situation. Learn to take your small victories where you can manage them, and you will be able to weather the more crushing failures and stand back up to try again: Like the heroes your men and women are all trying to be.

In my review for DOOM, I said that the history of first person shooters could be divided into "Before DOOM" and "After DOOM". Whilst that is true, if I had to pick another game that changed things so much, it would be this one.
1998 was a great year for FPS games. We got both Unreal, and this. Both games set new standards for immersiveness - Unreal giving us collectable items which filled in back story, and amazing dynamic lighting, along with a fully dynamic soundtrack. Half-Life set a new example for story telling.
The game never leaves the first-person view. There are no cut scenes, and no points at which control is taken away from the player (well, besides one scene which you'd know about once you played), and as such it's far more immersive than many games of it's nature. The game isn't divided into levels, each section flowing on straight from the previous, making things seem far more natural and realistic than before.
It was the first game I had which took advantage of my 3D graphics card, and I'd frequently use the opening train ride to show it off to my friends. Yes, it doesn't look so great nowadays, but that was 16 years ago!
It's also worth checking out the fan game "Black Mesa" which requires any Source game to play, but try the original first.

Shadowgate may or may not be a thing that you remember from the past. If you do remember it, there are several possible versions across different platforms that you may remember. The version of Shadowgate that I remember is the NES version. I never owned the game, but I rented it a few times and enjoyed it. When I saw that someone was remaking it, I had to check it out.
For the most part, the 2014 remake of Shadowgate is faithful, while also being respectful in its adaptation. This isn't a 100% translation. While some things you may remember from the past are still present in this version of the game, others may be absent or changed, while new puzzles and features have been added. The spirit of what made Shadowgate great is intact however and that's what's most important.
It would be easy to quibble over the changes and additions made to this version of the game, but ultimately they are no better or worse than what was in the game to begin with. Certain puzzles still require odd leaps of logic and certain connections sometimes feel a bit stretched, but I've experienced worse and in the context of the game world it's forgivable. Ultimately I enjoyed Shadowgate and the addition of difficulty levels (with differing puzzles and win conditions) and achievements for time and turn limits, mean that there's decent replayability here. It's a classic game remade well and worth checking out. I'm looking forward to the next offering from this team.

TLDR;
------
They should have named it "XCOM 2: Terror from the deep"
Pros
-----
- Nice Graphics
- Hacking is a neat addition
Bad
----
- Aggressive timers on every mission force you to make hasty and poor tactical decisions
- Too many recycled game play components from XCOM 1 (Tactical Missions, Base Design, Squad Loadout, Stupid AI)
- You don't really feel like you're making strategic decisions in the world view: it's just there to pass time
HUGE XCOM fan. I used to play the old XCOM games as a kid, and loved the XCOM remake. The DLC for the XCOM remake was also really great! I'm also the type that doesn't like to load from saves: if I lose all but one guy, it happens. That's what makes XCOM so fun.
I had a hard time getting into XCOM 2. The first time I tried it once and got bored with it after a couple of hours. I figured I'd come back to it after some patches and updates. On my second run, all three of my first missions I had to load from save because the timer ran out and I failed the mission. Now I'm no novice: I've played XCOM since forever, and I'm not timid about putting my squad in danger. I get it: they don't want you taking time to set up "perfect" positioning every for every encounter, but you literally have to send your squaddies out without cover fire, out of cover, or without ammo if you want to complete these missions. The timer isn't just a component of the strategy: it literally forces you to make stupid and hasty decisions.
There are so many situations that can run the timer down that have nothing to do with making poor decisions....
Your squad misses every shot one round thanks to the RNG. That's one timer turn down! Time to reload! >:(
The last alien is "on the run" and retreats two turn distances away? Time to reload!
You're two blocks away from the extraction point on the last turn? Time to reload!
You positioned your sniper on the roof and put your assaults ahead? Yeah, he's not making it out in time. Time to reload!
What I don't understand is that they took the most annoying aspect from XCOM 1 and made it a staple of gameplay in XCOM 2.
Now I often complain that "games nowadays are too easy," but this is just NOT FUN. I never liked the timed missions in XCOM 1, but the timers weren't all that aggressive. You had to be a little more careful about reloading and overwatch, but overall it wasn't bad and it wasn't EVERY mission. And if you killed all the aliens, you didn't have to then run everyone to an extraction point. -_-
The fact that EVERY mission is timed makes this a really high stress game. I want to play a game that is fun: if I want to stress out, I'll work and get paid for it. I don't want to have to reload from saves to stand a chance of succeeding, nor do I want to mod the timer so it's gone, nor do I want to develop a habit of recklessly sending my troops into danger. I enjoy setting up tactical positioning. I enjoy designing my squad. I enjoy the rush of taking the shot or getting shot and watching to see if it connected. I enjoy strategically setting up my base and choosing which techs to develop based on things that change.
I didn't like how they "dumbed down" XCOM 1 from the DOS versions, but I understand that they needed a design that was simple enough for console gamers and to attract a modern audience. I was really hoping that with XCOM 2, they'd re-add some more of the tactical and strategic complexities of the originals. I feel like XCOM 2 is a new skin on XCOM 1 with the addition of hacking, timers every mission, and a simplified overworld strategy.  TFTD anyone? Let's just make it harder and put a new skin on it!
Playing this game just makes me frustrated and want to play the older XCOM games. I do not recommend this. If you really want it, pick it up on sale.
