I really liked this game, though it has one major downside that might drive some people crazy.  I've just finished my first run through of it on "Normal" mode (which has to be considered easy mode by the looks of it - possibly even in comparison to the easiest of the retro modes), and I completed it in one session.
I was only stuck once or twice, and sure enough it was largely down to me not noticing things I should have noticed.  I will say that in 2 areas this was not the case though;  one scene involving mirrors did not work correctly until I saved and re-opened the game, the other major issue there was a pumpkin based puzzle (a side mission) I could not complete.  I even watched a playthrough of that section to make sure I had done everything correctly, and it simply wouldn't work.
The main gripe I had though, and the one major warning I'll give anyone reading this, is that the controls are horribly old fashioned.  I ended up using the keyboard as all the clicking to do simple tasks was doing my head in.  An example with the keyboard would be as follows (same thing with clicks but you need to keep moving the mouse to different icons as you go):
Task - use an item on an object in the scene
1 - Press I to open inventory
2 - Press U for Use
3 - Press I to close inventory
4 - Click on object you wish to use it on
If you wish to use the object on multiple items, you need to do this every single time.  Sometimes it doesn't register properly either.  This was a major frustration for me, seeing as this is a point and click adventure game.  I know they were going full retro, but they could have implemented something in there to cut out a hell of a lot of clicking.
With that said I still recommend this game, if you can get it on sale.  It is a fun adventure, with a so-so story, pretty images, and some puzzles that will make you scratch your head.  I'm guessing the harder modes are an awful lot harder.
The issues I've mentioned keep it from being a full price recommendation.  Only get it if you think the controls wont drive you mad.

Whew... I held off writing a review for this game for a small while, even though I have actually spent a good amount of time playing the game. Tonight, I bought a game-pad controller, and I did find the gameplay much more pleasant. So, I am going to try writing my thoughts, because I have had some fun times. Would I recommend this game? I am going to say yes - but do your research first, simply because the game does a good job at what it says it is going to do. And it does it very well but not much more.
Folks, this is a what-you-see is-what-you-get type situation. The nes-zelda gameplay feels right out of nes-zelda, but that is all the gameplay you will see. In fact, there is not even any story. And are there items and skill upgrades? Yes, but they are stripped down to just numbers on the screen. Even me - who loves the minimalistic approach - is a bit taken back by the lack of flourish here. But if you want nes-zelda type gameplay, and you want to jump right in and have lots of control with your upgrades, then maybe you will be right at home here. I know that Legends of Pixelia will remain on my recently-played list, because it is just so easy to pickup and to get back into playing. I can see myself playing this years into the future, because the gameplay is - of course - timeless.
Now, there is also a multi-player mode. I imagine that is a pretty good time, but I did not get to experience it. Might be another plus for you.

The story is awesome, it stays away from the (annoying - to me) first civilization stuff and focuses on the struggle between the Assassins and Templars - with some character driven conflict thown in there. In this way the game "stays true to the creed".
In most other ways though this game is a complete failure. It is very buggy. There is a game killing QT event (I had to use cheat engine to slow the game to .1 speed). It freezes in random places. I can be in the middle of a crowd fighting 15 enemies, with all kinds of particle effects going on and run at near ultra settings (despite the fact that my pc is officially "below specs"), but then walk into an enclosed space with nothing moving and no complex geometry and everything comes to a standstill (even if I drop everything to the lowest setting - windowed - with horrible resolution). Then there is the issue that at least half of the equipment/missions are unavailable to me because they fall behind some Uplay setting that does not work for me - no co-op, no multi etc. Then they try to sell you things using microtransactions.
Oh well.. so mixed review, but I'm most likely going to get a free copy of Far Cry4 out of the deal so I am happy. Maybe after a few months - when everything is ironed out - I'd recommend getting this game. Until then do yourself a favor and wait.

What can I say about this game. The best way to surmise it is, it's like being in a relationship with an abusive partner, that requires you to abide by very strict rules but doesn't abide by the same ones.
Did I finish the game? Yes.
Did I have fun at points? Definitely.
Did I continue to play after that? Yes. Mostly out of spite.
Here is an example of what I am talking about:
Me: Enemy, why didin't you die? I have fought you many times before and you have always died with one hit?
Enemy: *shrug* Suck it nerd.
Me: Why the hell did I just die? I jumped and landed on the platform!
Platform: Your pinky toe was kind of hanging off a little bit, @sshole.
Me: I AM HITTING THE ROLL BUTTON! ROLL FOR THE LOVE OF ALL THAT IS GOOD!
Game: Meh. I didn't feel like it.
Me: I swung my weapon but it didn't cause any damage? What is going on, this doesn't make any sense.
Enemy: Oh we're supposed to make sense now? LULZ
Me: OH MY GOD I AM GOING TO BREAK MY KEYBOARD INTO LITTLE PIECES AND BURN THOSE PIECES! I WAS DOING A COMBO, WHERE IS MY COMBO?!?!?!?!
Game: Hahaha. Go ♥♥♥♥ yourself.
Now, these things wouldn't normally be a big issue, as no game works 100% perfectly. The problem is this game expects you to play absolutely perfectly but doesn't offer a perfect platform to do it on.
Ultimately, this game does have a lot of cool things to offer, great graphics, somewhat interesting story (very short though) and actually pretty good replayability with the Game+ feature. I just cannot bring myself to recommend it as it will probably cause you many hours of suffering and possibly a broken keyboard or gamepad.

I beat the game on Stygian with one death that wasn't mandatory, and he wasn't killed in combat. He was killed because I sent an ill-conceived party into DD3 and had to retreat.
Blaming RNG is for people who suck (I was one once). Here's a list of things you need to master:
-Enemy types/attacks
-Prioritizing enemies
-Party configurations and attack types
-Stuns
-Stress Management
-Inventory Management
-Camping
-Disease/ Negative Quirk Management
-Positive Quirk Preservation
-Roster Management (i.e. being able to dump♥♥♥♥♥♥heroes)
-Curios drops and interactions
-Dungeon navigation (i.e. scouting so you can avoid uncessary fights)
-Town management
-Money allocation
If there's something on the list you haven't mastered, then that's why you're dying. Endgame DPS is too hard and healing doesn't keep pace with damage? Did you get the Tome of Holy Healing and Vestal's Scroll? Too many battles? Are you scouting and avoiding unecessary battles that can be walked around? Stress healing costs too much? Are you killing stress dealers first and then using Crusader or Jester to stress heal on the fly?
Are you using stuns effectively to manage stress dealers? Do you have at least one antiquarian on the roster that you send on long missions to grind money? Do you have a Grave Robber or Plague Doctor to remove diseases for free while camping? Are you taking secondary heals like the Crusader's/Arbalest's/Plague Doctor's or self heals of the Leper/Abomination/Houndmaster/Hellion so you can magic pixel if need be until your Vestal/Occulist goes after you've been put on Death's Door? Do you have a secondary heal if your Occultist rolls a 0 or a 1? Etc.
Once you understand how the systems interlock you should lose next to nobody. The game is hard, the difficulty spikes can be a little much, and the time it takes you to grind up heroes and money (especially after a hard loss) can be infuriating.
But it can be done. It's not just a slot machine.

To put it simply, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you like difficult rogue-like RPGs, if you like cosmic horror, if you like absolutely phenominal sound and music design, if you like one of the most bone chilling narrators I've ever had the pleasure of listening to: Then by all means, buy this game now, and play it to your heart's content.
This is one of my absolute favorite games of all time-without a doubt-and as angry as it can make me sometimes, I find myself coming back time and again to try my hand at it all over again. Certainly, this game isn't for everyone, and if you're the type of person who is easily put off by harsh consequences, and sometimes just bad luck ruining a well thought out run (as in Xcom series), then this may not be the game for you; and that's entirely okay.
I feel like a good way to think is to not think of this game as a simple strategy RPG, where you're hunting numbers, or what have you. You're simply incharge of a bunch of human beings, all pretending to be heroes, and (many times) failing when the time calls. Once you accept that, a lot of the failures the game throws at you are a lot easier to take, in my opinion.
I could go on and on, but I will simply leave with: the warning the game gives you at the start of the game is true:Darkest Dungeon is about making the best of a bad situation. Learn to take your small victories where you can manage them, and you will be able to weather the more crushing failures and stand back up to try again: Like the heroes your men and women are all trying to be.

This game is not too shabby, good even.
Pajama Man's show just ended. Sam is about to turn of the television until he sees the credits - an autograph from Pajama Man himself at the mall! Joyous, Sam asks his mom if he can go, and she says yes, telling him to bring something to sign for his favorite hero. He finds a special edition comic book after a brief search. As Sam reaches for the comic book, it is sucked down in a pile. Pajama Sam dives in to retrieve back his possession. That's where the adventure begins.
As the fourth installment in the series, people expect the game to live up to its reputation. Does it? Not quite.
-The voice actor for Pajama Sam contrasts its predecessors. Once you hear a voice that sticks out, it's memorable. Fortunately for us, we all loved the original voice actor. Although this one shows satisfactory, it's just not up to par.
-I don't know about anyone else, but the game is choppy when I move from map to map. This diminishes the overall fluidity of the game.
-Collecting items. In Pajama Sam One, you collected socks. Pajama Sam Two, puzzle pieces. Three, box tops. Here, you collect these trading cards. These aren't bad. I actually like them. It's just the AMOUNT you have to collect. Essentially every place you go to has a card lying around. Like with the mini glitches stated in the previous statement, the collection of trading card simply reduces the flow of movement.
-There aren't many objects you can click on anymore, and if you do, it's passable. One of the things I clicked on was some kind of poster in the first map of the main game. When I did, it just changed. No movement. No animation. Nothing. As a child, I loved looking at everything popping out of the screen. Don't get me wrong, there are some good ones out there. Just not as much.
-This is a little detail, but saving the game bugs me. With the other Pajama Sam adventures, you saved and went about with your business. Now, we have Sam telling us what to do. At first, it was charming. Then, it turned annoying real soon.
-The game in general doesn't make sense. In the previous three games, they all had a theme, and they all logically made sense. In No Need to Hide When It's Dark Outside, it was about darkness. In Thunder and Lightning Aren't so Frightening, it was about weather. In You Are What You Eat From Your Head to Your Feet, it was about food. In Life Is Rough When You Lose Your Stuff, it was about...well, stuff. Why do we need a shirt, some socks, and some shoes to meet Pajama Man?
-Back to the previous thought, a lot of the characters contribute little to the theme. I felt they were placed there just for show instead of adding value. They did little to push the game in the right direction.
Okay, so aside from all the substandard effort put forth, some good came out.
-The different pathways continued in this game. This is a point-and-click adventure, and I welcomed exploring the various routes.
-I liked the "Part Two" side of this game. It's in the Freddi Fish and SPY Fox series. In the Freddi Fish and SPY Fox games, once you were done with your main objective, there was a little more you needed to do in order to fix the problem. In this Pajama Sam game, you experienced a little of that magic in this game.
-Probably the idea I liked most was you can try more items to other items. Before, in the other games, if something didn't work, Sam would say "That's not going to help" or "I don't think that's going to do me any good." Now, you can do some trial and error. I won't try to spoil too much, but there's one part with fireflies. I tried catching them with a jar, but they wouldn't be able to breathe. I tried catching them with a net, but they were too small. The options available allowed me to think, and I enjoyed the puzzle-solving.
As a whole, Life Is Rough When You Lose Your Stuff is not a bad game. It's a charming, fun game with interesting characters, designs, and effects. With that being said, its performance compared to its older installments puts the Pajama Sam series to shame. This is a fantastic game for those who never received a chance to play with any of the Humongous Entertainment games, but for veteran players such as myself, this game will dust in my Steam library.

Creation Club is part two of paid mods. I bought Fallout 4 for $60 when it came out, and the fact that the singleplayer game I bought has now been retrofitted with microtransactions is insulting.
I'll never use Creation Club because I'm not going to pay money for a backpack or a pipboy skin. If Bethesda wants to add content to their game, they should create something more substantial. I loved Far Harbor and everything in it, because it's something that only a developer studio with time and resources could do. Making one-off armor sets or guns is better left to the realm of the community.

Fallout 4 is a Fallout game in name and setting alone, it abandons all aspects of the past games which made them great. It has neither the memorable atmosphere of Fallout 3 nor the freedom and interactivity of Fallout 1, 2, and New Vegas. The writing quality ranges from aceptable to cringe worthy, and while the shooting has improved drasatically from the previous games and I do enjoy the more open, elevated areas around the map, it isn't fantastic enough to cary the whole ordeal. Fallout 4 isn't a terrible game, and in the scheme of  things it's probably not even a bad game, but no matter how I slice it Fallout 4 never appears to be anything beyond average. In short, this a mediocre shooter with some addicting gimics like base building set in the Fallout universe, and unless the modding community becomes on-par with New Vegas and you can grab it way on the cheap, don't buy this game.

This game enthralled me long enough to finish it on normal mode and I purchased it at a discount, so I'll be fair and give it a "thumbs up". There are quiet a few things you should consider if you plan to buy this, though:
- It's not an RPG in any way regarding skilling, equipping or upgrading your character. You don't have skills, attributes or whatsoever you could manage or upgrade. You can't buy or sell items and all items you find in the game are basically "use item x for adventure element y (e.g. use the only arrow you'll find in the whole game against precisely one specific enemy).
- There are no fights in the classical sense. You don't aim or use skills or the like against enemies. You use item x, which is specifically designed to be used in this "fight" on the enemy or another item to win the fight.
- There are some clues about what to do, but like in most adventures, you'll end up several times with spamming item x or ability y on everything you can to see if it has any effect. I felt really lost during the late game when I was just running around and trying to figure out where's the chance to progress with the game.
- There are NO, I repeat, NO possibilities for alternative ways to get around a challenge. You either stick to the scripted plan of using item a on element b in situation c after you've accomplished event d or you are srewed. That's actually the reason why adventures died out some time ago.
- I needed 6 hours to finish the game. That's a pretty short time to play through a game. You can choose to play the game on different difficulties, and I've read that some puzzles are different then. Nonetheless, I consider the replay value of this game to be like the reeat value of a pizza.
If you've played the original Shadowgate (and liked it) or if you're a huge fan of fantasy adventures, you may give this game a try. All others should really think about if they really want to play this game.

It starts out tough, just like you'd imagine it would be to start a resistance movement, but once you've gained momentum, you really get the sensation you have them on the run. You put them on their heels, you're at their rear nagging, and just waiting for them to shout out the all familiar "E.T. phone home" in dispair.

A major disappointment, after Black Flag. They added a few things, but then made everything else worse in the process. Added crouching for stealth, but removed whistling, hiding underwater and moving bodies. Added the ability to quickly move downwards, but give you areas with so much clutter that you're constantly getting stuck to them. Made combat take a bit more thought than just constant countering, but then removed the ability to shield yourself against gunfire.
The character advancement is a mess, with little indication of what, exactly, the stats on your equipment do. You'll get equipment rewards from the main plot that are garbage compared to things you can buy from doing just a few sidequests. The map is littered with chests that you can't open until you max out the Lockpicking skill, but you can't tell that you can't open them until you actually get close. The less said about the Nomad stuff, the better, and Initiates has been ridicuously buggy. It still hasn't given me credit for other games in the series, even though elsewhere in the same system it notes that I've beaten them.
The setting is irrelevant for more than half of the main plotline, as is Arno's membership in the Assassins. The plot does nothing to advance the overall plot of the series. I didn't run into the craziest of the bugs (missing faces, etc.), but I've had multiple crashes, and could not get the unique assassination on one of the missions because an NPC kept walking into a wall, breaking his script.
I'd recommend avoiding this. Even if you're a big fan of the series, you won't actually miss any plot development.

It’s like Legend of Dungeon meets Binding of Isaac, but with retro 2D pixel graphics.
First, you must choose a class - Knight, Barbarian, or Paladin. Then, you beat procedurally generated dungeons and like any RPG, you pick up loot that lets you equip better items. You also level up and spend some stat points unlocking your character’s passives.
But grinding will only take you so far. This is all about skill. To beat some enemies you need to attack in a specific way, which gets pretty hard when you have to kill a ton of pixelated ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Playing solo or as a party is cool, but PVP is awesome - you won’t even notice the hours shed away until you realize you’ve spent your whole day being a monochromatic stack of blocks. Test your proficiency against a skilled AI or just go with local co-op. Either is challenging and fun.
Not being able to attack in all directions seems weird at first, but you learn to embrace it pretty fast. It’s a very addictive dungeon adventure that is still being developed by only one dude. And that’s awesome, but… it shows.

offers, oldschool beatem up set in roguelike dungeons. Minimalistic by appearance and game design which isn't a bad thing at all.
Initially given 3 class options all having different skills and base stats, Knight, Barbarian and Paladin. Clear enough levels and be rewarded with alternate options such as the sentinel. Progress involves clearing each room which has procedurally generated item and enemy placements. While mouse was playable I would suggest a gamepad as class skills were set to each button and block on the triggers. Felt much more responsive and can be quite challenging playing solo.
No loot drops in levels, just gold coins and health potions. On each floor was a treasure room which contained gold coins and a large chest with your choice of 1 of 3 items. Gold coins collected can be spent between levels at the blacksmith on upgrading items you have obtained. Can also take this opportunity to raise stat points that were received from characters leveling up. No complex skill trees involved but enough to be interesting. On character death you have the option of restarting on same floor or returning to the start of the dungeon, between sessions all items obtained and stat points invested were retained.
Great soundtrack but could use a little more variation and I thought the levels were maybe a little repetitive too early. Perhaps mix in the fresh tile colours earlier and would suggest possibly adding some secret rooms that require bashing on cracked walls, just for something extra to find. Only supports local multiplayer (4players) so I didn't have a chance to test multiplayer unfortunately. Would make a fun couch co-op game without a doubt.
First impressions = Decent and worth checking out if you're a fan of roguelikes or even just older sidescrollers. As mentioned it's a little difficult solo and probably more directed toward mp, but far from being impossible and rather rewarding. Not just about button mashing either, plenty of timing involved. Cheers folks. :)

Relying on 90% hit chances to save your day (or night) won't work, what it'll do is give you an actual headache instead. When things come together though it's beautiful, Once you manage to sort that out, your beefy operatives will slice through aliens as there was nothing to it, and this is one of the true joys of this game:
It starts out tough, just like you'd imagine it would be to start a resistance movement, but once you've gained momentum, you really get the sensation you have them on the run. You put them on their heels, you're at their rear nagging, and just waiting for them to shout out the all familiar "E.T. phone home" in dispair.
On top of that, it's very nicely made, a beauty to watch. I strongly recommend this game, and urge you to give it some time. Don't worry, it won't mind you having other games on the side.

This game just kind of felt off... It had all the things that made the last game great for the most part, so why was it so off putting?
One of the main reasons I can think of is the dififculty. I'm not one to shy away from a difficult game, but this one seemed so unfair a lot of the times.

Especially in the first few missions you play. Sectoids instead of having a little health with few psionic powers became an engine of destruction. The sectoid is able to mind control your soldiers, disorent them and even reanimate dead enemies you've already killed.
This is only a taste of what makes the enemies so unbearable throughout the campaign. The game also suffers from serious problems with "hang ups". Basically your soldier shoots at an enemy, then the game sits there looking at your soldier for around 10 seconds before finally deciding to move onto the enemy turn.
XCOM 2 looks like the previous installment, which isn't bad or anything. It just is kind of... the same really. I wished they included a lot of the features from the Enemy Unknown expansion into this one. Plus a lot more balancing fixes which would've helped a lot.
Overall, I would say this game is really disappointing and could've been something great. If you're a hardcore fan of the XCOM games, then you should probably pick it up. If you're interested, then pickup XCOM with the Enemy Unknown expansion to really have a great time.

In light of the ongoing flood of negative reviews, I'll take a shot of writing a review of my own given my 800+ hours; with a little more detail than "paid mods." I would like to give a mixed review if I could instead of yes or no. Fallout 4 had a massive hype building for years and it did much more harm than good, just like with half life 3 there could be nothing that would live up to the expectations of gamers. The biggest difference between Fallout 4 and the rest of the Fallout games is the addition of a voiced player character. While this make Fallout 4 more at home with more modern video game titles, it severly limits dialogue options witch made the previous Fallout games extraordinary. If you want to see what Fallout is like, get Fallout New Vegas and/or Fallout 3. The graphics havent aged well, but modders have made various fixes and improvements over the years. The cause of the recent review bombings is the addition of paid mods. Normally I would just recommend to ignore something if you disagree with the product/service or the vendor. The problem with Fallout 4 however is the mods were added in an ~2 gigabyte update, with the content hidden behind a paywall. Since this was in a developer update there is no (legal) way of removing the content. This was the last straw for me personally since I have severly limited hard drive space to use for everything.
Pros:
unique base building mechanic
no level cap
ability to increase all special (base stats) to 10 (max)
weapon and armor customization
fairly good fps/third person shooter (depending on whay you set camera to)
good storyline for 1~4 playthroughs
lore for the fallout universe pre bombs
voiced protagonist
easier for primarly shooter game players to get into fallout
modding community second only to Skyrim (still a long way to surpass though)
legendary weapons are rng based with a few uniques
post apocalyptic 40~50's setting
Cons:
overall bad Fallout game
voiced protagonist (not good for roleplaying)
limited dialogue options (compared to FNV and F3)
bugs (it is still a Bethesda game after all)
2 gigabytes of content locked behind a paywall in a $60 + DLC game (launch day price)
weapon and armor customization can get old quick
main quest has 4 paths
Preston Garvey: endless "There's another settlement that needs your help, I'll mark it on your map."
TL;DR Fallout 4 is a good game (if you have the space for it) but a bad Fallout. If you want to get into Fallout, get Fallout New Vegas and/or Fallout 3

So most of this review is to counter the people saying assassin's creed unity is bad.
seriously, running a i7-860 (a 2009 processor) only 8gb of ram and a radeon R9 280x I have had the best experience playing a video game since either skyrim or borderlands 2 (i can't decide).  Yeah, sure, i get framerate drop every now and then, and on release date I fell through the floor once or twice, but it's a HUGE ♥♥♥♥ING GAME.  I've played a good 40 hours of this game and am only half done with it.  Sure I get low frames around the cafe heater, sure i get lag every now and then, but for the other 90% of my gameplay I am the king of the world.  This game is fun as♥♥♥♥♥♥ The combat is super satisfying (most of the time), the parkour is almost always perfect, and the story makes me happy.  Granted, my introduction to long term gaming was fallout 3, so i'm forgiving, if not even laughing at the occasional bug.  This is a massive game released to a massive variety of platforms, and of course there will be problems on some configurations (especially if you're a dumbass and don't update your drivers first), but that's to be expected.  Ubisoft can't test every configuration! They can only test "x" number of "common" configurations and hope it works, then release patches for systems and situations they couldn't anticipate.  Granted the micro-transactions/pay to win are pretty annoying, but the game itself is ♥♥♥♥ing great.  ♥♥♥♥ing update your system and actually play it before writing it off.
All of that said, the universe (paris) is gorgeosus, it feels real and populated, and the crowd events make you feel like you're really esperiencing the time period..  The story is satisfying, and the pletheral of side quests leaves you never feeling like you're without something to do.  You cans spend hours exploring, getting in the occasional fight, and feel like they were hours well spent.  The new mechanics like murder mysteries, parkour down, and the re-vamped combat system are absolutely excellent, on top of the already fantastic system.  The world is rich and beautiful, and there is always something to do.
In short, play the ♥♥♥♥ing game before you make your judgement.  Everyone criticizing it is a perfectionist expecting a massive game, that is the first of its scope, to be perfect on release.   Of course some things may need to be patched, but even with them still in the game, Assassin's Creed Unity is a top 5 must play of 2014

And if F♥♥♥face is telling the truth, why is he allowed to broadcast to you? Why would an organization kidnap you and wipe your memory to perform an experiment that they could pay an undergrad $15 to do? Why would they set up such an elaborate facility and damage it so much just for the experiment?

This is an excellent expansion to the original game. The artwork, mechanics and flavor of the new content are all gorgeously creepy and on point, but one thing you should take into consideration before buying this expansion is that it adds another layer of strategy, depth and difficulty to the core game play once you choose to open up the new dungeon.
The added difficulty and new layer of strategy is the reason you see a lot of people screeching about the crimson curse. The new character class and trinket sets are incredibly powerful as are the amazing new buildings you can add to the hamlet, so to balance all this new power they have added what is essentially an eldritch twist on the classic curse of vampirism. The curse does have some up side to it, but for the most part it is a dread plague that will spread through your ranks turning your heroes into blood addicted maniacs.
The other issue compounding the misery of the curse for some people is that the new dungeon is a very challenging area, and once you open up the can of worms that is the crimson curse by questing there the only effective way to treat or cure it is to go back and visit the area again.
So people were taking low level starting heroes into this place assuming that it was going to be a normal apprentice level cake walk and they just got wrecked leaving them in the painful position of having unleashed the curse and  powerful new enemies on their hamlet without out properly preparing for it. Now they are forced to quest in this new brutal dungeon in order to harvest blood for their cursed heroes and to seek more permanent solutions and some folks are just not up to this extra challenge even with all the powerful new tools they have at their disposal. I personally love the expansion and the challenges that come with it, but more casual player might not appreciate the added difficulty.
So if you are looking for an amazing but challenging expansion to the core game play of Darkest Dungeon then I highly recommend the new expansion, but if you are a more casual player who doesn't want to deal with the added difficulty and complexity that comes along side the powerful new tools and content then you might want to stick to the vanilla game.

Cheap game, so I bought it and did a video for it. Check out the video to get a sense of the gameplay or read my quick review below.
Tinboy is a puzzle-platform game in the 8bit style.  Players must make their way through various levels of an AI Testing Arena, starting at one door and navigating various platforms and obstacles to reach an exit.  They are aided in this by the use of a multi-purpose bow which can fire ordinary arrows, rope arrows or exploding arrows. Each arrow type enables the player to affect different game mechanics.
Pros:
+puzzles have a basic structure but could be solved a number of ways
+mechanics are simple but allow for depth of level design
+puzzles appear to be well thought out
+challenging enough to maintain interest
+difficulty scales in a reasonable way
Cons:
-some controls are not intuitive (double jump to release rope, finicky bow aiming method)
-UI is a little unintuitive (surely an ESC menu for quitting isn't too much to ask)
-No options menu (for turning down/off game audio, for example or rebinding keys)
-Graphics get a bit fuzzy when upscaled.
-Doesn't fully support a controller (it would play better with a controller, imho)
It's a pretty fun, little puzzle-platformer and, for the price they're asking, it's worth it. So, I'll give it a thumbs up.

Having bought this recently, nine months after launch, I am stunned by the amount of glitches. XCOM2 does not feel like a finished game. At this point whenever I load it up, I expect to find a new bug or two.
From a carried VIP not registering as alive on EVAC (there is a mod to fix this because the devs apparently could not be bothered?) to graphics glitches like the Make Weapons Available button disappearing, or a soldier's arms disappearing, to a save-breaking bug where the keyboard did nothing after reloading, to line of sight bugs (soldier could not see snake, snake tongue pulled him through solid walls), to getting two mind controlled enemies via lamp post hack instead of one, to Psi Zombies from a Dominated Gatekeeper showing up as lost soldiers on mission end screen. And so on and so forth.
Only one of the above has been save-breaking so far, but I will not give a thumbs up to something that just doesn't work right half the time.
Having said all that, the premise of the game is still good old XCOM.
Good:
- Concept of customising soldiers is great.
- The guerrilla approach is novel and the turn counters make for good fun, though perhaps are a bit too common.
- The gameplay is XCOM when it works. Great stuff.
- Lots of nifty weapons and special skills. The skills seem to be better balanced than the original (2012) XCOM, in that you often have to consider your two options at the levelup instead of going for the clearly stronger one.
- AWC perks are very cool, though they should be retroactive from the get go, or unlock at the final level if the right one has been passed, or something. 2012 XCOM had the same problem where you had to throw away your original A team because their will ended up inferior to new soldiers.
- Shen's Last Gift is a good mission. I have not used the SPARK enough to do it justice, but the concept fits in.
Bad:
- Bugs. Lots and lots of bugs, glitches and annoying things that aren't working right.
- Changing armors resets some customisation options, and sometimes they just bug out and change the props around.
- Very slow loading times, slow animations and pauses between turns. Why do I need to press caps lock on a loading screen? Why doesn't the damn thing press it for me?
Personal preference:
- I found the character models and armors from the 2012 game to look better, more human.
- Anarchy's children customisation options (For Digital Deluxe) are mostly glam rock and horror movie props that make no sense in the context of the game. There are a select few exceptions.
- The strategy screen has no pause or fast forward buttons and the constant interruptions and holo-globe transitions are very jarring.
- I would like to say something about Alien Hunters, but I did the scanning part and the Nest never showed up. Going to go ahead and guess this is another bug.
- Swords are inferior to the shotgun, except in very rare and specific conditions.
The bottom line in all this is - if you do not own XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within, go buy that instead. If you own that and want more, this is a beta version of a good sequel. I wouldn't pay full price for it.

Starbound: We are all binded to the stars! We are star matter!
Starbound is similar to Terraria meets No Man's Sky. A 2D space/planet exploration game. There aren't as many items as in Terraria, updates are far and scarce sometimes, though they do add interesting content, and the planets aren't that detailed for a 2D game. But to me, this game has some more value, than just face value.
The story is simple. A big bad Universe deadly being exists, you need to unite all races (except Novakids) and get items to open a portal to kill this big bad being. The missions are, in my opinion, actually fun. It's a custom made map, where you explore, find interesting loot, kill enemies, and fight a boss. But the buildup to those missions are boring af.
Before you get a main mission, you are tasked to gather info about a certain species items, trying to promote you to go out and explore the universe.
>Species A items are located in A planet. Explore A like planets to hopefully find one that has species A colony.
>Species B items are located in B planet. Explore B like planets to hopefully find one that has species B colony.
>Species C items are located in C planet. Explore C like planets to hopefully find one that has species C colony.
And so on. For that, I would recomend a workshop mod that removes this more tedius tasks from the game, because they are just really poorly implemented.
Now, if you do want to explore these planets, you are free to do so. Like Terraria, this is a sandbox open-world like game. You are free to say "fukk it" to the quests and explore, build, harvest, colonize, get rent from NPC's, make an underwater base, make a space station, and more. I have found joy in taking hold of a whole solar system, each planet being a different thing. One is a big science lab, another a military compound, asteroid field is the prison, space station is the main base, and the underwater base is my personal home.
I would Roleplay my way around this solar system, and just have fun messing around and creating my little "Galactic Conquest" like story, in my mind. If you have friends that are into this sort of things, roleplaying and messing around in your own universe with your own lore, then by all means, this game is amazing at that. If you have imagination, this game is good to try and expand it.
To help with the "Roleplaying" side of things, and gameplay too, there are several species you can play as.
>Boring Human
>Plant People
>Bird People
>Donald Trump (Ape People)
>Star People
>Robot People
>Fish People
And with the Frackin Universe workshop mod, each species is unique, with their own skills and abilites, to make each different. The Bird People will jump higher, whereas the Fish People can swim faster and stay underwater longer.
Workshop is a really big feature for this game. It adds a lot to it. Makes it more fun sometimes. If you do get this game, take some time to explore the workshop. There are a lot of fun mods there that are almost a must-have for Starbound.

Pros:
+A remake of the classic 1987 Shadowgate, but doesn't feel phoned in or a simple cash grab. The game is faithful to the original, but expands greatly upon it.
+Fans of the original (and later re-releases, including the popular NES version) will absolutely love the option to choose either the new transitions and music or the original 1987 music and transitions.
+The new music pieces are not simply remixes of the original pieces, but rather hauntingly-beautiful retellings.
+Game difficulty determines how hard and how long the game is. A puzzle that requires backtracking or multiple steps on Hard will either be simplified or outright removed on Easy.
+The game's many causes of death reinforces the idea that you don't need your hand held to have fun.
Cons:
-Whoever thought of the idea for retro graphics mode needs to be fired. The "retro" option simply places a filter over the screen, pixelating everything. Imagine playing a game that runs at a native 1920x1080, then changing the resolution to 320x200. That's how bad it is. Unlike the transitions and the music, it is in no way faithful to the original game.
-Unlike the original, the game gives you no indication that your torch is about to go out, leading to an untimely and unexpected death. The NES version had its own music piece to warn you when your torch was about to go out.
-Newcomers to the game may be put off by all the trial-and-error they will have to do, as many of the puzzle solutions seem counter-intuitive.
Full disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter.

The most horrifying thing about this game is the fact that it is neither as bad as its infamous reputation suggests, nor is it the single worst horror game available on Steam. It is, however, pretty darned close on both accounts...
First bad sign: Opens in a small window which, when maximised, simply transforms the game from a small screen overlaying your Steam page to a small screen surrounded by whiteness. Spif-fy. Second bad sign: The only way I found to exit the game after achieving this extraordinary display option was to shut down my computer by force. Third bad sign: The, ahem, "game" itself...

It's a point-and-click game with static images, first person POV. So even when you look out a window to observe that your neighbour's house is on fire, you don't get even the slightest hint of animated flames writhing; just a static image of, well, your neighbour's house on fire.

None of this would be an especially huge minus, if the story itself were interesting enough. Spoiler: It's not. Nor would it be worthy of enormous criticism if the gameplay was compelling enough. Second spoiler: It sure as ♥♥♥♥ isn't. Heck, even the presence of some cool jump-scares, or moments of split-second kill-the-zombie-before-it-kills-you action might have saved this from being one of the biggest♥♥♥♥♥♥sandwiches you could ever opt to eat, and I've read reviews which claim you can use the shotgun you pick up to quickly shoot zombies as they pop up on-screen, but...I either had zombies fill the screen, munch the crap out of me, then unceremoniously disappear, or I had zombies fill the screen, take one bite out of me, and give me an instant Game Over. Neither event seemed to occur with any semblance of rhyme or reason, and the lack of any save system means that you'll be going back to the beginning over and over and over again, despite reports that the game can be completed in something like four minutes (a first-time feat which would require much more luck than skill, I suspect).

Add to this the hardest-to-find items in a video game EVER - I seriously challenge anyone to find that axe in the park without witnessing a walkthrough first, or simply spamming every inch of the screen just to see what happens - and basically what you have is an unplayable mess. It's a shame, too, because for all of two minutes the opening cut scene gave me some small semblance of hope that this WASN'T the crap-croissant which everyone claims it to be (i.e. said opening is actually quite good). Then the game proper begins, and it's all swiftly downhill from there.

The semi-competence of small aspects of this game - i.e. the moderately decent graphics and sound - unfortunately prevent this from even being one of those "so-bad-it's-good" propositions...so perhaps the only true saving grace of this product is the fact that it's almost eternally on sale for under a dollar. Given that the devs should probably PAY people to play it, that's still not much of a bargain, I'm afraid.

Lords of the fallen is supposed to be a more clunky and slow souls-like game. I had heard it was possible, and almost encoureged to soak damage with heavy armour and trade blows with weak enemies. This however is not the case. I started the game as a warrior with the intent on using thick heavy armour and heavy strength weapons and going through the game as a tanky soldier. But unfortuntly the combat system does not support this. Even in the thickest armour i could find i was getting staggered by every enemy that hit me, even archers who poke me with their crossbow stagger and stunlock me while im wearing full platemail.
Later in the game there are enemies who look identical to normal mobs, are in the same area (And even coridor sometimes) as other mobs of the same time and yet they are inexplicably waaay harder. They have 5-10x the health and can either one hit you or stunlock you and one combo you (Which is basically the same thing) And because of the sluggish and slow nature of the game it is extremeley difficult to hit them before they hit you because of the huge wind up time.
Speaking of slow and sluggish the combat is clunky in a bad way. Every attack has at least 1-2 seconds of wind up time and none of the weapons i have found so far have a long range or a lunging attack to compensate for the sluggish nature of them. Furthermore very few of the enemies i have fought have been staggerable. And I am using a greatsword. The bosses are unimaginative and dull, all three i have faced so far have been big guys in armour, 2 of which had greatshields, 2 of which summon adds. All of which feel lackluster and mundane.
I would not recommend this game to anyone really. It feels harder than any of the bloodsouls series (But not faily hard, more punishing and cheap hard) So i can't recommend it to a newcommer to the genre and as a lover of bloodsouls who hated this game i can't recommend it to others who like the genre either.

I recommend buying this, but only at a sale. It's basically Dark Souls, but worse. Way worse.
The combat is unresponsive and slow. Some attacks will hit you when they shouldn't. Rolling is unreliable. The developers clearly built the game with a Strength build in mind, disregarding the Agility build. Enemies with a shield will be a pain for you if you're an Agility character, unless you use Magic. You will get hit and it's gonna hurt, because you can't use heavy armor because of the roll speed. The fact that most enemies don't stagger at all if you use an Agility weapon will not help you. Despite all that, the game is pretty easy, but you'll use magic a lot. And using magic is even more boring than Melee combat. You get used to the enemy attacks quite quickly because there are not many enemy types.
The bosses are uncreative. They all feel the same. None of them felt threatening at all. They're all slow and they choreograph their attacks like they're in slow motion. They repeat their 3 or 4 attack types over and over again until you kill them.
One thing they got right, I believe, is the map design. It's all interconnected, and you open up shortcuts as you progress; just like Dark Souls. I give them props for that. We need more of these map designs.
The soundtrack and the story are terrible. Skip every cinematic whenever possible. Nothing else to say about it.
Now, my biggest gripe about the game. This game has crashed my PC at least 6 times. It consumes my CPU and GPU completely, at 100% capacity. When I first started the game, it ran like CRAP. Stuttering, low FPS, and inconsistent FPS at random points of the game. I had to spend hours trying to solve it. Testing out different graphic configurations, playing around with the driver settings, modifying .ini files. And to this day, I'm still not sure if I solved the crashes. I had to run the game at the lowest possible settings, except for Texture quality; when it shouldn't be that way, because I can even run Battlefield 1 at medium settings at over 60 FPS. Note that I'm writing this on 09/02/16, so they had PLENTY of time to solve these issues. Make sure to save everything in your computer before you start playing, and be mindful of your CPU and GPU temperatures, because this game might melt them.
I am aware that this review was very negative, but the game did manage to entertain me enough to beat it and play it for 18 hours. I can't take that away from them. If you like Dark Souls, there's a good chance that spending $15 or so in this is worth it.

This is an excellent game, but I imagine it appeals to a pretty narrow audience. It's a hardcore, turn-based RPG that features permadeath for your characters and prevents you from saving before battles and retrying them. That being said, the monsters, characters, mechanics, and items are carefully designed to provide an extremely challenging but rewarding experience.
Characters will die, you will fail some missions, and progress will be lost at times. But if you take the time to learn the mechanics, think about your strategy, and carefully plan for missions, you will find that it feels great when you figure out the game and become successful. It also features some unique elements that I've not seen in RPGs before.
I'd consider this a must-play for any fan of old-school or tactical RPGs.

Have you ever played classic first person point and click adventures but wanted them set in a zombie apocalypse with a cheap, gritty feel? Well here comes Paradigm Shift crawling on the floor covered in its own vomit missing legs and both of its arms. Its a hastily thrown together game devoid of interesting puzzles. The game excels at startling you if you take too long on a screen. Horrifying zombies pop in screaming when you least expect them.
There are a few death traps such as gas leaks that you'll need to simply back out of. You need to be hasty though, sticking around in one area too long will kill you in one way or another. Like the zombie apocalypse, you need to get from point A to point B as quick as possible and you do that through trial and error. The game plays out quick and it feels like there's a small amount here to keep it interesting. You can be done with everything in less than ten minutes. Its ultimately a death trap. A price for a horrifying jack-in-the box. You never know when its coming, but it'll jump out.
You are packing a shotgun, but it feels useless. Even when you have the time to pull it out and shoot a zombie, it does nothing, but it could be out of ammunition when you first get it. The game needs to specify such things or at least have a click. The game's instructions say that a blast can take out most enemies. What's even stranger is facing off against a girl crying in a corner removes the shotgun from the inventory time and time again. I would say its to prevent from hurting her, but you still have a screwdriver.
You can find a few descriptions of flavor text, but the game feels empty and vacant. Your mouse cursor never changes, it just stays as an arrow forcing me to click like mad. The toughest part about the game is finding little doors, nooks and crannies. Clicking around to find everything even if it looks like nothing.
Its obvious that its someone's first game. There's the cheap price and the Click Fusion icon still on the game. When you start up Paradigm Shift you're greeted with more external links than anything else. There are no options or settings, you play the game in a window rather than having a choice. Its bare bones.
The environments look good, gritty and downright cheap, but it fits for a horror game. There's no animation, just static photos. Even when zombies pop in they're just pasted on your screen and in a way that adds more drama. Their eyes are cut out, mouths pasted on their lips. The editing of real people is disturbing and does add a unique flair to the game. The real problem with the atmosphere is that its all ruined when the game forces you to stay in a window rather than full screen. Its scary seeing my kitten wallpaper on my desktop among still frames of burning buildings.
As for the puzzles, you have things like a simple keypad and you need to find the combination that's somewhere close at hand. You have a door lock that you need to pick. When you do so it returns you to the hallway you were already in. Its all so quick between game overs that it never gets a chance to be dull. I kept up a rapid pace through memorizing what to do and where to go.
To the game's credit there is tense music that adds something to a dirt cheap game. It hastens your pace and adds intensity to a bare bones game. There's budget and then there's cheap. It still feels gritty, but its nothing I can ever recommend.
If you're big into jump scares and little more than pictures and clicking, Paradigm Shift is a cheap enough game to be worth your time. To the other majority of people, avoid this game, because you never know when a horrifying zombie with all the animation of a cardboard cutout will burst into the area and start blood staining your screen.
It's a simple game to veg out on. The play time is enjoyable and I love to play this game when things are hectic in my life.

The gameplay introduces a steady stream of mechanics to the player, starting with simple coloured blocks that only perform one action like the yellow ones that form a 3 block stair set or the single blue block that acts as a launchpad. Eventually mixing new concepts with the old will have you doing something like rolling a grey blank ball down a slope while using the aforementioned coloured blocks to guide the ball away from pitfalls and through a transparent cube that transfers its colour to the ball and allows it to pass a similarly coloured gate.
The story is explained through a radio voice-over and right up until the very end there is some doubt to what you're being told by the voices in your head. The writing is more on the scale of a good creepypasta than the New York times best selling list, it's schlocky but enjoyable.

This is short game. Like 15 minutes short kind of short. But brilliant nevertheless. It is from the simple perspective of a seed like thing that is travelling to a far away land in search of another soul to germinate with. Or maybe it's just a weird shaped bacteria in a human world. Whatever it is - one thing is for certain, that this game can be interpreted in multiple ways. Some might say it is nothing more than an attempt to recreate the mundane - but for me it was more like a metaphor for the simplicity of an uncomplicated life with purpose. It was as though the ease of play, and the short duration of the game was what aided it's primary theme and the message it was trying to propagate.
All in all - a fun experiement, and since it's so short, totally worth playing it.

How you proceed in the remake has changed greatly from the original and infact what were solutions to problems in the original now kill you in somewhat humorous ways and even offer secret death endings which I greatly enjoyed.
"point and click adventure" is a name that has been slightly tarnished with games that have you find 10 objects on a still screen while a timer ticks down (you know what I am talking about) but shadowgate tells a story and makes you think. Also if you want to just want to enjoy a story theres always guides, so you never feel stuck if you want to just enjoy a tale. I hope to see more of these classic games revived like Deja Vu.

There was a time in my life where the original Shadowgate on NES consumed all of my attention.  Friends and I would sit in Biology class drawing maps and comparing notes, then spending the evenings on the phone doing the same.  This lasted until the end of the game; it was pretty great.
Naturally, when I heard that there was a remake of Shadowgate coming to Steam, my curiosity was piqued immediately.  It was easy to worry though that my fondness of the game only existed in the rose colored glasses of nostalgia.  Thankfully, once I got my hands on the remake, I discovered that Shadowgate was in fact a great game and the remake was pretty great in its own right.
I've never been one much for modern adventure games, but Shadowgate seems to be a shining example of the genre.  Its packed with some great graphics updates and a great score.  The game play proves to be fun too.  I was worried that a point and click style adventure game wouldn't hold my attention.  Since this game has a good story that gets unveiled the further you journey with hints and clues scattered about the castle, it manages to be pretty engrossing.  It's common finding myself coming back to the game sooner than expected just to find out more story.  This is a strong trait for a strong adventure game!
If my words don't convince you, check out my ongoing Let's Play series of the game over on my youtube channel!

Believe it or not, I got Fractured Space for free during its release and first free weekend way back in April 2015. Here is a screenshot of my account licenses for proof:
[
]
I really enjoyed Fractured Space when it first came out. And honestly I really enjoyed it back then but I had to stop because of inevitable bugs. The particular bug that struck my account was related to the database. It couldn't register my earnings in a match so I was not earning any credits/manufacturer exp no matter what I did. I had to wait for a long long time for an update that would reset the database or at least fix it. That update was the one made in preparation for the second Free Weekend. When I came back, several improvements were made, a lot of new ships too, and the best part was that FS had become so polished and it was SO MUCH BETTER than it was way before.
Note: I had to stop recently because my internet service is really terrible right now and FS’ servers don't really show love for Asia and Australia yet lol.
Fractured Space is a 5v5 MOBA where capturing objectives is key to winning a game. You have to capture Forward Stations to allow you to jump (hyperspace) to the enemy’s base to capture it, Mining Stations to collect resources for upgrades, and Gamma sector when it activates for temporary but helpful buffs. Capital ships are used in the game. There are three manufacturers to choose from, each with their own tech trees. Each ship also has its own role and is specifically designed for that role only. Knowing every ships strengths (eg: weapon range) and weaknesses is a MUST if you are to win a battle. There are also crew members who provide bonuses to your ship so choose the best crew according to your ship and playstyle.
If you should wonder about how FS looks; the graphics, sound effects, and animations are really well done! Attention to detail is magnificent, sound effects are great just as how important they are in battle, and animations are there for eye candy =D.
Now of course, a MOBA is never complete without matchmaking and MMR right? Sadly in FS, matchmaking is a bit flawed. MMR is based on your completed to quit matches ratio. Disconnecting from a match without returning, even if it was through ping, counts as a quit and severely punishes your MMR. Matchmaking also doesn’t take into consideration your arsenal and how good you are with your ships. This could mean newbies without quit matches can end up in experienced players’ matches with the same completed to quit matches ratio.
HECK NO. There are Premium Ships and exp boosts in the game yes, but Premium Ships are nothing more than shinier targets whose arsenal CAN’T be upgraded. You can choose to grind to buy a ship, or you could spend real cash to buy a new ship quickly. I must point out that ship’s place in the tech tree doesn’t define how powerful it is. It all comes down to the player’s skill. So might I request that nobody whine “P2W” in a match please?
Matchmaking should be renewed to not just look at how many matches you have completed. It should also look at your arsenal, K/D ratio with your ships, and unlocked upgrades. We also need better Asia and Oceania servers. Not all places on Earth can achieve 80 ping you know(not to mention how sensitive FS’ servers are to rise in ping).
I must also express my concerns about removing the Manufacturer Exp from the game altogether. Who wants to hear that a rich P2W newbie chucks on a lot of money and gets high tier ships that need skill, is totally inexperienced, and enters his first match and has the most crucial role of the team?!
Please IMPROVE and FIX these issues at least BEFORE making new ways to get players’ money *cough* skins *cough*?
Fractured Space is a game I would highly recommend to other people. It is polished but not without flaws. Terrible newb-noob playerbase and bad matchmaking are the only notable flaws in Fractured Space. You can expect the devs to do a good job as they always listen to the community. So what are you waiting for? JUMP IN!

All around solid game. Relatively short campaign, but there are extra challenge puzzles and time trials to keep those kinds of people interested for more than just a few hours.
Lots of reviews make the Portal comparison. Indeed, both are very short first-person physics platformer puzzle games. What really makes the two feel similar, though, is how all the puzzle chambers have a futuristic white and tiled aesthetic, and how throughout the course of the game, you are radio contacted by one-way voice communication by story characters. I feel Q.U.B.E., though extremely similar to Portal in this respect, still manages to stand on its own with its unique aesthetic of everything being composed of cubes, allowing for lots of appealing tesselations in the rooms and hallways that are satisfying to watch.
The puzzles felt very straightforward and the rooms tended to feel rather empty, but all the puzzles were a treat to solve. The game is a good brain tickler; it's nothing obscenely challenging, but it will make you think a couple times.
There's no deaths or any failure conditions. Aside from some instances where you might jam yourself on some strange collision geometry for a minute or two, you will never get into a situation where you are punished or stuck for trying to solve a puzzle the wrong way. Most rooms with complex solutions or puzzles that involve free-roaming objects will have reset buttons that completely reset the state of the puzzle to how it was originally introduced.
My only complaint is the shallowness of the primary campaign. I was hoping to see more ways that cubes could be manipulated, and more intricate puzzles as the game progressed, but it ended before I was completely satisfied. Hopefully the recently announced sequel will add more to this fantastic base.

I'm glad I only got this game for ten bucks, and I can see why it is so cheap. Played too much of it so now I can't return it, but believe me I would. I get that there is a market for ridiculously difficult games like this and Dark Souls (which I hear is even harder), but I have no time for that. The controls are at times unresponsive. I go to attack, and instead do this little kick move that does nothing. By the time I come back from that, the enemy has already swung up his next move which takes like half of my health. There is no sense of direction. You just slog around a castle and fight monsters, and occasionally take on bosses. A lot of the game you have to figure out on your own (like how to consume potions). You carry two potions at the start. This dumb monk got his arm chopped off (by me), and I gave him a potion, thinking I still kept my two vials and I'd just have to fill one up at the checkpoint. Nope. Gave the monk a friggin' vial, meaning I have can one potion at a time, which made the game that much harder. The combat is definitely visceral and real (slow), which is refreshing at times (the first boss fight was pretty cool), but most of the time you're locking on to an enemy and circling around them, which is repetitive. With the unresponsive controls, glitches (like when my guy just disappears or gets stuck in the ground), camera angles moving away from the fight and behind a wall so you can't see the enemy delivering his final blow, and terrible physics (like when the enemies change direction in mid attack or jump, making the dodge obsolete), I honestly can't recommend this game. I hear Dark Souls is awesome though, get that instead.

Solid game in the same vein as another popular first person puzzler (ehem, portal) .
For the gameplay,  you basically manipulate the world around you in order to traverse from sector to sector. Each contraption have their own set of rules depending on their color ( red squares can be elevated to give you height, blue can give you propulsion, yellow can make stairs and so on). Sometimes you  will also need to guide a ball using these mechanics,  leading to some Rune Goldberg moments that are very fun. It aslso keeps on introducing new mechanics for each sector allowing you to rotate rooms, guide lasers and manually select a color for your tile.
The story is "good enough" to be there  but it basically never progresses from the initial plot of "Is she telling the truth, or all of it is a lie?" right up until the end. I had to read a coment from a steam discussion about the ending in order to really appreciate the context the devs proabably intended. It is also something to note that this game was originally released without the plot, so maybe it will be more refined in the upcoming recently announced sequel. Voice acting was good, but not really anything that engages you.
The game is really short and quite easy for fans of the genre, though the last few were really challenging. I was hoping there was quite a bit more of those in terms of spike in difficulty. There were also instances where a ball can get stuck and you must restart the level from the menu, but its not really gamebreaking.  Overall it feels like a game with massive potential and it certainly got me pumped up for what Q.U.B.E. 2 has to offer. Just from watching the teaser,  this game felt like it was just a prototype of its puzzle mechanics as much like portal 1 was to portal 2.

Only 1,5% of those who own this game has finished it.
Darkest Dungeon has undeniably great setting, art and narration but wonky, repetative and frustrating gameplay which  heavily relies on RNG. Yes, forums are full of people saying "git gut", but can one git gut in luck? Sometimes you can get destroyed in the first few dungeon rooms only to restart with the same party and steam roll through with no sweat on the next attempt.
The basic summary for the game tactics: you cannot outheal the flat dmg done by enemies and therefore you want to kill the enemy before they have any chance to hit or stress your heroes at all. Few combos and buffs that you can set up are rarely worth it timewise. The venerated stress system with its afflictions is just a bunch of debuffs on top of the chance for your heroes to act randomly, which can end your dungeon run pretty fast by itself if you are unlucky to get afflicted early.
Well indeed with the right setup and knowledge of the game you can negate most of the damage, but from time to time the RNG just rolls the dice and decides to kill your hero before you get the chance to act, focusing your champs down with crits. And that wouldn't be a problem, except for the fact that the game lacks any sort of good recovery mechanism: you have to grind all the gold and time you invested in the char back, which artificially prolongs the game even more. It could be 3 times shorter to be honest, since higher difficulty lvls reuse enemies and bosses from lower difficulty by simply giving them better stats (those can get ridicululous in champion lvl dungeons), so the tactic of beating baddies down with the largest stick available doesn't change much in the process.
This is just a rough summary of what's wrong with the game. I myself bought the game when it was still in early access, played it for hundreds of hours during multiple attempts, I "got gud" and I did well until the RNG decided that I didn't. Unprevantable deathes, horrible quirks which had to be removed immediately for the hefty sum of gold, grinding said gold...
Once again, only 1.5% overcame the hours of staleness and frustration of the later parts of the game, managing to finish it. If you think you got what it takes, or actually don't ever intend to finish the Darkest Dungeon -- well you are welcomed to buy it. Otherwise, I don't recommend it.

Sorry... Half-Life is boring by 2015 standards.
I got this game so excited to play it and was so disappointed. It's just outdated not for somebody who hasn't ever played it before. My friends who played it when it came out love it to death, but I just can't get into it. My bar is set higher, I guess. The action is really slow and the weapons are clunky.
It also never ends. Given, I was a bit bored, but I thought it was almost over and was excited to be done, finally. Then I discovered there were many more levels still to go! Parts were very good, but I found myself really bored playing it, and really hating that I was making myself play it just because of the fact that it was the legendary Half-Life. I think I have two or three more levels still to go... I'm not even sure. And I took a step back and asked myself: what is this? The things I'm doing aren't fun. They were not fun.
Some specific complaints: There's a lot of tedious wandering around the confusing levels. The assault rifle seems to do no damage. There are many weapons, but I only used a few. There is not a lot of variation. The enemies take a lot of rounds to go down. Your vitals and energy being recharged is weird. There is not a whole lot of plot. The human soldiers are all played by the same voice actor, which is actually pretty funny. Dialogue is really cheesy in a game with such high standards. I got stuck a lot, making me very frustrated and upset and usually made me quit or look up the solution online, which is never fun. Big shoutout to my man, Big Mac Davis on youtube, for his level walkthroughs, I couldn't have done it without you.
This review is not meant to be an attack on Half-Life fans, it's just a perspective from someone that is probably shared by most of the people who have never played it before.
If you still want to play Half-Life, consider Black Mesa, expecially if you already have an application it'll work with. Look up Black Mesa! It is basically a redux of HL with enhanced visuals and gameplay. The story is identical.

I was excited to see yet another old game I played on NES had been remade and released on Steam (the other being Gauntlet)!  The original was released in 1989 on the NES, and was a lot of fun (though very difficult) when I played it as a kid.
The new one is just as tough, and has a new and very beautiful art style.  A nice soundtrack was made for this as well, though after exploring the options menu I saw there were options to make this game feel more like the original, "retro" Shadowgate.  One of those options was to have the old soundtrack play instead!  There's other options as well to make it feel more like the old version.  They did good there.
So what is this game...well it's an old school point-and-click adventure game.  Extremely heavy puzzle elements that will get you killed and/or confused.  A lot.  There are ways for you to fail this game, without you even knowing it right away too.  You'll be unlocking new areas, as well as a fair amount of backtracking.  There are also a lot of items to be had, you'll want to get most of them because you never know when they might be of use.
They've introduced some different difficulty settings, and the ability to either play the game with no saves or with the ability to save.  Unless you have the hints option on, there's really not much in the way of handholding.  And even with the hints, it doesn't really tell you much.
Great game, and worth checking out if you like games that really make you think and pay attention to details.

Starbound: We are all binded to the stars! We are star matter!
Starbound is similar to Terraria meets No Man's Sky. A 2D space/planet exploration game. There aren't as many items as in Terraria, updates are far and scarce sometimes, though they do add interesting content, and the planets aren't that detailed for a 2D game. But to me, this game has some more value, than just face value.
The story is simple. A big bad Universe deadly being exists, you need to unite all races (except Novakids) and get items to open a portal to kill this big bad being. The missions are, in my opinion, actually fun. It's a custom made map, where you explore, find interesting loot, kill enemies, and fight a boss. But the buildup to those missions are boring af.
Before you get a main mission, you are tasked to gather info about a certain species items, trying to promote you to go out and explore the universe.
>Species A items are located in A planet. Explore A like planets to hopefully find one that has species A colony.
>Species B items are located in B planet. Explore B like planets to hopefully find one that has species B colony.
>Species C items are located in C planet. Explore C like planets to hopefully find one that has species C colony.
And so on. For that, I would recomend a workshop mod that removes this more tedius tasks from the game, because they are just really poorly implemented.
Now, if you do want to explore these planets, you are free to do so. Like Terraria, this is a sandbox open-world like game. You are free to say "fukk it" to the quests and explore, build, harvest, colonize, get rent from NPC's, make an underwater base, make a space station, and more. I have found joy in taking hold of a whole solar system, each planet being a different thing. One is a big science lab, another a military compound, asteroid field is the prison, space station is the main base, and the underwater base is my personal home.
I would Roleplay my way around this solar system, and just have fun messing around and creating my little "Galactic Conquest" like story, in my mind. If you have friends that are into this sort of things, roleplaying and messing around in your own universe with your own lore, then by all means, this game is amazing at that. If you have imagination, this game is good to try and expand it.
To help with the "Roleplaying" side of things, and gameplay too, there are several species you can play as.
>Boring Human
>Plant People
>Bird People
>Donald Trump (Ape People)
>Star People
>Robot People
>Fish People
And with the Frackin Universe workshop mod, each species is unique, with their own skills and abilites, to make each different. The Bird People will jump higher, whereas the Fish People can swim faster and stay underwater longer.
Workshop is a really big feature for this game. It adds a lot to it. Makes it more fun sometimes. If you do get this game, take some time to explore the workshop. There are a lot of fun mods there that are almost a must-have for Starbound.
Paid mods? Seriously this needs to stop. Don't support companies like this.

I really hate to give this a NO because I am a fan of the IP, but alas, it can't be avoided.  Here comes the breakdown:
Graphics: Not too bad at all, but any time there is an intense animation on my screen, I get a very noticable framerate drop in the animation itself. The good looking scenery is actually a little bit of a hindrance, because the environment doesn't offer a lot of context clues on items to be picked up or alternate rooms to go into. Everything blends together a little too well.
Sound: AMAZING. Orchestral arrangements of the classic music, decent sound effects.
Controls: The UI is clunky beyond belief. SCUMM worked back in the day, but In the modern era, not so much. Not tweaking the interface (and actually making it worse at times with what changes were made) for the sake of nostalgia is a bad design choice. The inventory system is horrible. Click command. Open inventory. Click on item. Close inventory. Click on environment.
Gameplay: I  remember the old NES version well enough to remember most of the puzzles, but when the devs added in their new content, everything falls apart. They provide little to no context as to what you need to do, and the in-game hint system is a joke. They also put in a "banshee curse" in the beginning section which will eventually kill you, and if you take too long getting through the game and can't complete it in time, you will have to start over from the very beginning. These two elements together ruin it for me.
A good adventure game should make you have an "Ah-HA!" moment when you get to the next section, not cause you to punch a hole through your monitor out of frustration when you hit the next barrier of progression.
Overall score: 5/10

Shard of Mystery didn’t overthink its plot too much, but it also uses its simple premise to deliver a plethora of hidden object gameplay elements to lure the player forward.
Lost Grimoires 2: Shards of Mystery reaches back to the roots of story-oriented modern hidden object games. It doesn’t sacrifice most of its gameplay elements and play time to tell a tale, it rather uses its simple plot as nothing more but a small incentive to drive the player forward, by offering the next snippet of the story as a small reward for completing a batch of puzzles.
Compared to the more abundant point ‘n’ click nature of the first game, Shard of Mystery likes its hidden object scenes and alchemy mixing minigame a lot more; which, considering this is the hidden object genre, makes it all the better.
There was a price though: Lost Kingdom’s moral shades of grey are gone, replaced by a generic evil witch, who kidnaps the now adult son of the king we saved in the first game. Although our returning alchemist protagonist does everything to keep this cliché interesting, in the end it is the puzzles that will move the player onwards, and not the story itself.
