After playing for almost a year here, i finally got to make a Review about Fractured Space. So here goes:
Fractured Space is a space-MOBA game where you are given command of captial ships, some of which measure more than 2 kilometers in length. In a team of 5 players, you have to defend your home base and your mining stations from the 5 enemy ships in the ensuing massive and sometimes quite frame-costy skirmishes. Teamplay is everything here, unlike your average shooter you can't just say: "Oh, i got killed there, let's go into the other sector.". This might cost you a match, so if you are looking for a lone wolf style of gameplay, i have to warn you that Fractured Space will not often allow you to play like that. On the other side, if you like to have a team around you that you can (most of the time) count on, this is a game for you.
For a while, Fractured Space included 2 different game modes, a "Conquest" mode with a map divided into 2 Sectors, your base, the enemy base and the famous Gamma Sector, which will activate in intervalls, granting the team that conquers it a massive boost, and, with the 4th Gamma, access to the opponent's Home Base. Such access can also be gained by opening one of the enemy's froward stations, one in each sector. When the Home Base is fully capped, you win. Or lose depending on which base it was. Your average Conquest game takes about 30 minutes, so be sure to calculate a bit of time for it.
The other game mode that is currently locked was called "Frontline". It dropped the idea of a Gamma Station and different lanes, and instead went for a more FPS-style approach. An open map with lots of asteroids as cover, 3 mines to cap, jump points distributed all around the map allowing for quick surprise attacks, and a permanent death after 12 minutes of game time. The mode is locked right now and there is no info on when it will be reintroduced, if ever, we will have to wait for a longer time. The Devs are working on it though.
Not long ago, the game became free to play, which will hopefully increase the playerbase quite a bit. Although there are lots of buyable assets, it is not necessarily a pay to win game. In the coming updates, the game will move to Unreal Engine 4.1.1, which will drastically increase the stability of the game. Crashes are currently quite common for me, but there is an option to reconnect to the server. Also, expect lengthy waiting times while Matchmaking is looking for a server for you, but you have a small 2D game called "Fracturoid Extreme" that will help you make time pass. Or show you how horrible reflexes you have. Sounds hilarious? Maybe...But it is currently the only possible solution, as the playerbase is just too small, and it is just temporary I think.
So, what else to say? I would recommend the game to any fan of Battlestar Galactica instantly. The depth of the gameplay and big picture thinking is something unique, and the only comparable game named "Dreadnought" doesn't offer you this.

Anyone who complains that this game is "too hard" or "too RNG reliant" is a ♥♥♥♥ing idiot. It's not sadistic, it's just classically difficult. And damn fun as well. Yes, there are RNG elements, but if there weren't this would be a solved game; the randomness is what adds challenge and stress to the experience. And your ability to deal with the randomness and adapt to bad situations is a gauge of how good you've become at the game. It's a well designed game in that it's fairly forgiving of failure (there's no game over; you could party wipe multiple times and just keep trying again).
The art style is gorgeous, the narration provides just enough flavor to add atmosphere without being annoying, and the dungeon crawling is in the purest, most distilled form I've seen in a while. This is a game in which reaching the end really does not matter, because every dungeon you enter provides a challenge and sucks you in. Nevertheless, the promise of more horrors urges you onward, and the game does build up to a satisfying ending.
Buy this game, you won't regret it. The game is not unfairly hard; it just asks you to use your brain.

A good game, plauge by an unforgiving difficulty curve and some extraordinarily tedious grind.
What's good? Basically the whole game, for the first few hours. The atmosphere and character design are outstanding. The mechanics are solid and straightforward. The challange, at first, is just about right.
What bad? As I stated, the difficulty ramps up quite fast, often before you are read. This might not be a negative, depending on your preferences. Personally, it got a little too hard, a little too quickly.
The real nail in the coffin, however, is the grind. Every mission is essentially the same: navigate the dungeon, kill the monsters, loot the chests, hope that some freak with a wine glass doesn't spill too much wine on your party. The first few hours, no problem. You're still figuring out the game. The golden hours (5-10), the game is fantastic. After about 12 hours, the game starts to grate. There are some town events and random encounters designed to spice things up, but ultimately it comes down to the same formula.
The bottom line is Darkest Dungeon is a dark, Lovecraftian RPG, with excellent atmosphere and design, that gets old sooner than your average RPG. Personally, I'm unconvinced that the game is really meant to be beaten. It's possible, but you will probably get bored before you do.

It's inevitable that Q.U.B.E. is going to be compared to Portal with its sterile testing environment and insidious motivations in the plot. But where Portal uses humor to keep the player engaged, Q.U.B.E.'s story is much darker. You are a silent amnesiac with a sweet pair of glowing gloves trapped in an environment made of moving, glowing cubes.
You are contacted by a woman named Commander Nowak who is aboard the ISS and tells you the bad news: you're in some sort of ship that is heading for Earth and you're the only hope to stop it. The plot seems generic enough until a mysterious unnamed man contacts you separately telling you nothing is what it seems. The two voices become more in conflict as you progress and the ending truly surprised me.
Gameplay in Q.U.B.E. revolves around the various colored cubes you find in ther environment. Red cubes can extend to make platforms, blue cubes act like spring pads, and yellow cubes rise up in sections of three. These elements are then mixed with rotating rooms, light beam reflecting, rolling balls, magnets and moving puzzle elements. Puzzles increase in complexity and mechanics are combined routinely throughout, but the final sector amps things up even further by presenting blank puzzles where you must choose the mechanics to best complete them.
The puzzles are challenging but give a great feeling when you complete them. Only one puzzle near the game's turning point felt like it was the result of luck. The campaign isn't too long, I finished it in just under 2 hours, but Director's Cut includes an Against the Qlock mode for timed puzzles.
Story - 4/5 Excellent narration and a sinister vibe mixes well with the claustrophobic environments.
Graphics - 5/5 Not the most graphically intensive game given the setting, but the design is clean and lighting is great.
Audio - 5/5 Ambient score is nicely done, voice actors are great.
Gameplay - 5/5 Simple puzzle elements are multiplied throughout with unique modifiers.
Replay - 2/5 Time trial mode but story presents no additional content once beaten.
Overall - 5/5 The perfect puzzle alternative to Portal that does enough to distance itself from the Valve classic. It's short and sweet, but Q.U.B.E.2. has been announced and it looks to expand on every aspect of the formula.

You wouldn't be alone in looking at the marketing for this game and thinking it looks like a knock-off Portal. The truth is that's more or less correct, but Q.U.B.E. is just unique enough and the idea itself is good enough for that to not really matter.
The game's puzzles were, I thought, actually kind of exciting. They rely more on straightforward logic than trial and error and finding the solutions was quite satisfying.
The narrative which accompanies them was also quite strong (due in large part to some excellent voice acting), though somewhat farfetched. If you can put your sense of disbelief to one side, it's an enjoyable, more-serious-than-portal-whilst-nodding-at-it-in-passing yarn.
Overall, it's short and sweet. If you can get it for cheap and like a puzzle game then I definitely recommend spending a couple hours with it.

I had Fallout 4 since the release date. I was stopping myself from writing this review for a long time. I was hoping I will discover something that would make me appreciate this game and see it in a positive light. Unfortunately I didn’t find anything that could allow me to recommend this game. Beside this I shouldn't need to look for positives with some much effort.
Fallout 4 is the most shallow game of this franchise. In my opinion even Fallout: Tactics had more to offer when it comes to story and this literally was a tactical turn base game.
Pros of Fallout 4:
- Thought me to not pre-order stuff.
- If you never played any Fallout game you might enjoy this one. However you would be better off if you get one of the previous games.
- You can mod it. Make sure to do it through Nexus, not Creative Club’s microtransactions.
Cons of Fallout 4:
- Dialogue choices are almost not existence. In the previous games you could choose exact line that your characters would say. Now you have vague short descriptions to cover the fact that your four choices are: “Yes”, “Of course yes”, “F*** you, but yes” and “No. I will come back later to say yes”.
- In theory there is this epic quest that’s about war for humanity and your family. In practise non of the characters that the quest revolve around feel real. You can’t feel the importance of this quest at any stage. Therefore the quest feel like a To Do list of house chores.
- Most of the quests are based on “Go there, kill that, bring this back”. This minimise the meaning of a word ‘quest’ to a walk and shoot experience.
- Downgraded character levelling (perks and SP.E.C.I.AL.)
- Graphics for the time of release were below average even for an open world game and even for Bethesda standards. I know Bethesda never was famous for great graphics, but the engine was not up to the task anymore. You can get some nice screenshots if you position camera right, but in general it’s very basic.
- Settlement feature was under developed. You could have put enough turrets to kill a small army, but you still need to come to help settlers if four raiders try to attack.
Bethesda dumbed down Fallout game to bare minimum while adding as much crafting as possible and ended up with a Fallout Minecraft. This will work for some people, but a Fallout fan will not find a real Fallout experience here.
Fallout 4 wins an award for most boooring Fallout game.
On the top of that Bethesda added micro-transactions by introducing paid mods. They cost way more than what they offer.

On first glance, Super Sanctum TD seems like a very nice addition to the genre, but beware as the game is unbelievably hard even at normal difficulty forcing you to grind the same levels over and over until you get enough points to unlock new abilities/equipment. The 16-bit graphics look nice and serve their purpose, but the sound design is weak and rudimentary.
Generally speaking, the game is way too hard and demands a far bigger commitment than I'm willing to make for what is basically a 2D flash TD game. Could've been much better if the devs weren't so hard-core. But I guess even the TD genre has to have its masochistic version of IWBTG.

General bugs:
This game was moderately interesting, though buggy, for the first hour or so.  The keyboard didn't always work, so I couldn't type commands at a rate I was used to.  Every once in a while, the keyboard would completely break (you type in a few characters of a command, and the game backspaces them out).  However, you could always save, quit the game, and restart to fix it (although the keyboard was always buggy).  This was on Mac.  I decided to switch to a Windows machine, and the keyboard worked perfectly.
Annoyances:
Commands don't work like you'd think.  Many of them are close to real commands (e.g. scp).  However, you can't download a file to a different filename, like real scp.  AFAICT, there is no way to create a directory.  For someone who likes organization, being only able to put dozens of random files from different missions into one big directory (or move them into one of two subdirectories already created) was frustrating.
Game-breaking bug:
Before I switched platforms, I hit a game-breaking bug on a certain mission where I had to decrypt a file.  My research told me what the password should be, but the command didn't accept the password.  The problem persisted on Windows once I switched.  I spent hours trying to figure out my issue, but failed.  I even did cryptanalysis and found the 'passcode' that was used in encryption, but that did me no good since you cannot type in a passcode.  You must enter the password, which gets converted into the passcode.  With the passcode, I could literally decrypt the file by hand, if only I had a text editor.  A hacker without a text editor?
Ultimately, to my shame, I had to look in the forums, guides, etc.  To my surprise, I found at least 3 different ways that other players solved this mission.  One solved it without a password at all.  Another used the password that I was trying all along.  The third used a misspelling of the name (with a 'd' instead of a 't'), and for some reason it worked.  None of those worked for me.
I have a feeling if I started a new game on Windows, the problem would go away, but I'm not sure if this game is interesting enough to start it all over again.
Review:
The game is interesting, and there are plenty of fun tidbits, such as IRC logs with humorous situations.  They are repetitive, but worth a laugh.  I'm not sure why the executive at KFC spends time on IRC, but whatever. ;)  The missions, though, are very repetitive.  Hack these ports, download a file.  Can't hack a port?  Download some command to do it.  There is no hacking so much as using tools.  You are a script kiddie.  I'm not sure I'd play it again, given the possibility of another game-breaking bug, but I was entertained before that happened (even with the other bugs).
Edit:  I ended up restarting the game on Windows, and all of the bugs described above were fixed, including the game-ender.  I ended up having fun, since I was able to get past the previously completed missions very quickly, and didn't need to nose around the IRC logs, etc. as much as the first play.

Journey once more into the castle Shadowgate
Do you remember having a favorite video game that it seemed not many other people fully appreciated? One that you were completely obsessed with, spent tons of time with played over and over again, gathered every bit of information on it that you could? For some people, the games that they find themselves so devoted to end up becoming big series, with numerous sequels. For others, those games get periodic sequels and live on. And for yet others those games just sort of fade away, becoming forgotten in time.
For a while, it seemed that Shadowgate would be one of those games in that last group. Certainly, it was much-loved by a number of people who experienced the original adventure on NES, Macintosh, and PC. And, the series did get some sequels - a side-scrolling adventure game for the TurboDuo, and a 3D exploration game for N64, as well as a port of the original game to the Gameboy Color. But, the series never seemed to receive quite the appreciation that it deserved, and, after those N64 and GBC versions in 1999, the series seemed to slip away. While the series, or mentions of the series, would pop up occasionally, it was never anything significant. And, after a while, it seemed all hope was gone, and the legend of Shadowgate would be lost to the passage of time.
Sometimes, however, all it takes is a few dedicated people to make something happen. And fortunately for the Shadowgate series, it had two extremely dedicated people - Dave Marsh and Karl Roelofs - who had been with the series since the beginning, who still maintained that love for the series after all those years, who wanted to see the series live and thrive again. They surrounded themselves with a great group of talented people at Zojoi, acquired the rights to the Shadowgate franchise, and set out to find if there was still a desire to see Shadowgate live again. And, through the relatively new (especially at the time in 2012) format of Kickstarter, soon found out that there were nearly 3500 people were still passionate about Shadowgate, and wanted to see it brought back to life. And, after over a year and a half of work, that dream finally become a reality, with the new Shadowgate game!
The first thing that should be clarified/emphasized with regards to the new Shadowgate game is that it is not simply a port/remake of the original Shadowgate. While it is based off of the original Shadowgate, and shares similarities with it, there is a significant amount of new content - rooms, items, descriptions, everything that goes into making the game. So, anyone who has played the original who is expecting to simply blow through this game in short order is in for a big surprise.
That said, the new Shadowgate shares much in common with the original, where it is a near certainty that anyone who enjoyed the original will enjoy the new Shadowgate as well. All of the core aspects of a good Adventure game are here. In your journey through the castle Shadowgate and surrounding areas, you will be exploring through a wide variety of locations, gathering hints, clues and information, discovering items and putting them to use, solving puzzles, uncovering mysteries, all while working toward your end goal. The challenge and adventure of Shadowgate is alive and well, and fans of the series will be thrilled to see all of this brought into a new game so well.
For people who are new to the series, or to the genre entirely, the new Shadowgate also provides as an excellent entry point. There are three different difficulties - allowing one to experience the adventure while working through different amounts of puzzles, different challenges, and more forgiving circumstances. There is also an optional hint system in place, where one can make use of a companion to receive information about situations and guidance toward solutions. So, one can start on a level where one is comfortable, and work up through the difficulties and help with those difficulties, until one is a master of the castle.
In bringing Shadowgate to a new generation, new expectations, and new groups of fans, Zojoi have brought the game up-to-speed not only with regards to the puzzles and adventure, but in the graphics and music as well. Each area - old and new - is beautifully illustrated, to make each room come alive. In addition, a wonderful soundtrack has been created for this game, each piece of which which perfectly fits and sets the mood for the rooms and the entire game.
For those with a fondness for the original soundtrack and style of the original game, however, there are a set of options - for audio, text, and transitions - which can be toggled on or off individually, to provide for a more "retro" style of play. The audio allows one to experience either the new soundtrack, or the NES one. The text option causes text to appear letter by letter, drawn by a quill. And, the transition option causes the more blocky style of moving from room to room, as opposed to more blurred option of the newer version. Each of these, depending on one's preference, can either provide for a more "retro" feel on a newer adventure, or allow one to experience an entirely new adventure altogether.
Between the different difficulties, different challenges, new things to explore and discover and overcome on each difficulty, new details to notice, and an intricate story to uncover, as well as the various options for display and experience of the game, there are many reasons to play through Shadowgate multiple times. While it's easy enough to do a quick playthrough of the game on the easiest difficulty with hints, it's a very rewarding experience to play through at the hardest difficulty without any hints. That may be a bit much to tackle the first time through the game, however, even for seasoned Shadowgate veterans, and so going through the game multiple times on different difficulties to uncover increasingly more of the game is highly recommended. Even beyond that, however, the world of Shadowgate is so rich and rewarding that it will continually draw one back into its world, to explore and experience it time and again.
The new Shadowgate game takes as a starting point the original Shadowgate, and builds off of it to bring forth a game which is similar in style, while still modern and up-to-date; a game which has a similar feel, yet doesn't feel archaic; a game which stays true to the roots of the original, while providing a significantly new experience; and which takes a franchise that at one time, and for so long, had seemed lost to the ages and tales of the past, and brings it once more to the forefront of gaming. The new Shadowgate is not meant to merely be a one-off thing either. Having seen the passion and love that still exist for the franchise, Zojoi have plans to bring Shadowgate as a franchise back to life, continuing to combine old and new as old adventures are revived, forgotten tales are brought to the fore, hidden information is revealed, and bright future is once more in sight.
It's not very often that a game like the new Shadowgate comes along. A beautiful blend of old and new, a game which will appeal to fans of the series, fans of the genre, and people new to both of them. A game in a series which for so long had seemed lost and without hope, brought back to life, not in just a simple port or in a cheap use of the name, but in a lovingly-crafted game, both a tribute to what has come before, and a promise of what is to come. Dave Marsh, Karl Roelofs, and everyone at Zojoi, have created a masterpiece with Shadowgate. The series is once more in good hands, and the future is brighter than it has ever been.

This game has a lot of potential for an early release. There have been some complaints about Twitter integration, however that is optional. I have played several hours and have never linked my Twitter account to the game. The sandbox aspect of the game is very nicely put together and reasonably intuitive. The ability to make aircraft for in-air dogfights is downright spectacular.
Pros: Easy to learn, with the advanced stuff still being complex enough to be entertaining. Nice variation of AI opponents, which scale nicely with your advancement level. Lastly: PLANES!
Cons: At this point there is no multiplayer beyond basic sharing of vehicle designs through Twitter. Unless they add some PvP this game will get boring once you've played with most of the pieces. Also, the turning controls are a little counterintuitive, as instead of the realistic turning while backing up (where it switches which direction is which) we have where it turns in the same direction regardless of which direction you're travelling.
Would I recommend? At this point unless you want to get involved with the development side of things (feedback on blocks and such) or the game is on sale, I would say wait until there's more content and/or multiplayer. I don't regret buying it, but I doubt I will play much more until the game is better developed. However, the direction development is going leads me to believe that this will be one of the better sandbox games out there once it is finished, and I will update this review when I start playing again.

This is less of a remake and more of a reconstruction from the ground up. For old fans wondering if it recaptures the old shadowgate experience, yes it does, but don't expect to be faced with the same old puzzles we've seen again and again in the previous shadowgate ports. The essence of what makes shadowgate what it once was is still there, but puzzles, map even the story have been rewritten and expanded to make this revival a grander new experience to recapture the attention of old fans and delight the new.
Old fans, as you can see from the screen shots, many iconic rooms from the original are back touched up and modernised in a striking art style. Don't expect them to serve the same purpose they once did though or you will probably get stuck. While the new puzzles are quite challenging the game now has many new modes to curb the difficulty for new players and still provide the hardcore experience for old fans. Achievements unique to different modes and the new unlockable hidden deaths mode which will have you searching for old a new creative ways to kill your character (a homage to old adventure games like kings quest and the original shadowgate) provide an modicum of replayability this genre usually lacks.
Race against the clock as each mode gives you only a limited amount of time and resources to reach the end before the world ends or your life is snuffed out, also note the attention given to the new narrative. The plot is much the same as the original but now told in much more detail with written lore, voice acting and stylised cutscenes to give a sense of epicness to your quest to save the world from the dark wizard.
Whether you are a fan of the original or just point and click adventure games in general you owe it to yourself to experience this lovingly crafted remake of this much adored classic. The industry needs more remakes like this and the monkey island special editions to offset the influx of shovel ware hidden object games polluting the genre.

Lost Grimoires 2: Shard of Mystery is a fantasy themed hidden object game from World-Loom and it manages to live up to the standards of the magnificent first game in almost every aspect. The game's main trademark is the alchemy, we have to concoct different potions from various recipes requiring many ingredients and use them to achieve our goal.
Unfortunately the game doesn't have much to do the with the original, altough apparently we are the same female alchemist and we serve the same king from the first part. The king decides to step back and entrusts his only son with his crown. We, as the king's most trusted alchemist and also the aunt of the heir, have to keep the prince - now the new king - out of harm's way, as an old adversary of the old king reappears: an evil witch who once almost managed to destroy the entire kingdom by raising an army of crystal soldiers. She had been banished and locked inside a magic mirror, from which she has now escaped. This time it will be our (the prince and a mysterious young girl will also provide aid) job to defeat her, once and for all.
The use of alchemy is quite similar to the method we've seen in Lost Grimoires: Stolen Kingdom. First we have to acquire the necessary recipe, then gather the 3 ingredients it requires. Once all 3 have been placed, there's a minigame, in which we have to connect the required amounts (a minimum of 3 must be connected in 1 move) of runes of the 4 basic elements, which are adjacent to each other within a limited number of moves. It might sound a bit complicated, but it's actually pretty simple, not as good as it was in the previous part though. The useful item we receive through the alchemy is usually a once usable magic potion or another consumable object, that'll  always be the key to progression.
Another important part of our repertoire is going to be a shard, a piece of the magic mirror, in which the witch was imprisoned. It is going to be invaluable for solving some minigames.
The minigames are refreshing and most of them are really good, but again they don't reach the level of the puzzles (I'm thinking of those fine text riddles primarily) from the first game, Lost Grimoires: Stolen Kingdom. Some of them have been encountered in other HOGs, not that it's a problem, while some are quite original. There are very few hidden object games, instead we get to solve many creative minigames. They are generally fairly easy, I could have used more hints with some of them though, as the instructions were quite vague about solving these. There was one, in which we have to reassemble a totem representing forest animals and it wasn't clear for me that we actually have to place the animals on top of each other (I was looking for a missing piece instead). Also, some minigames, like the one preceding the final showdown, where we have to steer a ship and dodge the crystal obstacles, don't seem to be making much sense (there's no time limit and no palpable penalty upon failure).
The collectibles come in the form of roses (1 can be found at each location) and some of them are really well hidden. Their general shape and size may vary, so good luck finding them! :)
The graphics is amazing for a hidden object game: we get to visit a wide variety of many beautiful locations, the ones I liked the most were the lush backgrounds from the forest area, in which we have to track down Rose, the mysterious girl.
The music is simply enchanting, some of the best I've heard in a HOG recently, I especially loved the ones in which flute was involved. I had the feeling that at some places music was missing (in the introduction for example), while at some parts the voiceover was way too quiet and hardly audible.
Lost Grimoires 2: Shard of Mystery is a great sequel to the excellent first part and a very good hidden obejct game on its own. Along the splendid minigames and the pleasant plot, there's a great deal of cutscenes that make the story more immersive and movie-like. I also loved how many elements of the prelude was introduced through mingames as we played.
Since the game is barely connected to the first, you can start playing this right away, even if you haven't played that one (altough you should, since the prequel is even better). For me, World-Loom has become one of the best hidden object game developer with this title.
PROS
+ alchemy and a wide variety of minigames
+ fairytale setting with a good little story
+ nice graphics accompanied by enchanting music
+ plenty of cutscenes
CONS
- altough comes close, isn't as good as the first part upon comparison
- a bit more informative hints at some puzzles would have been nice
RATING
7.5/10

If you have ever played World of Tanks or Armored Warfare than I'm sure you are comfortable with this type of playstyle that Fracture Space offers. Currently there is only one gamemode and that is conquest, which is a long and drawn out command and capture 5v5 gamemode. I've only played a few games, but I will say that the action is something to behold. It is very intense and very rewarding. However, team work is with out a doubt required for victory... sorry World of Tanks players. In the few games I've played I've lost all of them, not because we sucked, but because we never stuck together while the enemy team stuck together. I'm sure this only the case in low tier battles because I cant imagine players not sticking together in a high tier, or what they call an expert, game. The tech trees for the three manufactuers are limited but they do have diversity. The U.S.R is the medium attack line for the basic support player. Zarek is for the tankish player who wants to do massive damage, take massive damage, and also play a large roll in the team. And then there is Titan which is the best of both worlds as they have the most interesting weapons in the game, like plasma guns and smart cannons. I prefer the Titan as the starting ship is the best of the bunch in my opinion.
But of course every game has their downside. The loading time is very long I noticed, and in addition to that matchmaking takes around 3-10 minutes! Another thing that bugs me a lot is that players can choose what ship they want to use in the game as it's loading. So there is an increased chance that the teams will be imbalanced because of one team picking the heavy defence ships and the other team picking the light support ships. Also, it is a 5v5, and nothing is worse than a 4v5. If a player disconnects then you are are at a serious disadvantage. I have played two games where one team had 4 players and my team had 5, and the enemy team although outnumbered still won, while in another game my team had 4 players and the enemy team had 5... that game was just a slaughter as I died 8 times and we just couldn't secure points fast enough with 4 players.

Competent little tower defense game. Classic TD with various abilities you can fire off to affect the enemies directly, and some skills which you can raise to improve certain types of towers and such.
If you've played a few TD games there's nothing much here you haven't seen before, but what there is works well and it's also pleasant with this kind of pure gameplay from time to time.
The only issues I've had is that the difficulty is a bit uneven (the very last mission is far easier than the next-to-last, for example), and I don't much like the way the Survival mode (endless waves) is done; enemy types just get more health as you progress and it's not very evenly done, so an enemy that was easy to kill in one wave can be next to impossible the next.
I've also had some crashes which I suspect are due to a memory leak. At least, if I restart the game after playing a number of missions (~10), there are no problems.
More campaign missions would have been nice too, but considering the price I paid (less than one Euro in a sale), that's not really a fair criticism.

Like others I've found memories of the NES port of Shadowgate. The music, the atmosphere, everything on that game smelled like adventure.
This game is a reimagining of the original NES version. I say reimagine insteado of remake because it's obvious to me that while they have strong roots on the NES version, this version isn't held by those roots.
Many rooms are similar but almost all puzzles are completely different and even the ones that look like a puzzle found on the NES version will have twists to them.
The visuals are gourgeous. They use a handpainted style with very few animations and the whole experience is like playing a painting. They also vastly improved the delivery of puzzles in the sense that this game isn't a pixel hunt at all. Everything you can interact with will glow when you just click it to indicate that. That doesn't mean you SHOULD interact to everything but there is never a moment where you have to interact with some hidden object that you'll only discover by clicking everything on the screen.
Some flaws that I did find are for example the interface. Many times you have to use an item you have on the inventory and use it on the scene. The inventory screen takes the whole screen so you have to open the inventory screen, go to the page the item is at, click the item, click "use", close the inventory screen and click where you want to use the item. This becomes a little tedious when you're trying some combinations to solve a puzzle. The NES version kept the inventory open at all times at your side so you could quickly try many items. They could fix this by having a closeable inventory panel that doesn't obstruct the screen so you could keep it open while you try using items.
I'm having a blast. The game have three dificulty settings that actually change the puzzles. I went and selected the Master dificulty directly because that's how the NES version where - ruthless. I recomend you do the same.

Some time back in elementary school, my dad brought home a DVD version of the lighthearted quick time event and snuff film that is Dragon’s Lair II. Thanks in part to my relative inexperience with games at that point, but mostly thanks to the fact that a remote control is a lousy way to play a game, I only ever made it to the second world before getting frustrated from dying over and over again. However, despite my decision to not actually play any more of the game, the fact that each failure cued an elaborate animation of Dirk the Daring’s dorky demise was fascinating enough that I watched the whole death reel. Unlike in other games I had played by that point, death in Dragon’s Lair II wasn’t just a penalty for your mistakes; it was a morbid merit badge.
It was at some other point in elementary school that I was again introduced to a game that had a multitude of ways to die, albeit not so comical: Shadowgate 64. I had rented the game from a Power Video because it was featured in Nintendo Power, and that’s just how I did things. Plus, the cover art of a staff with an eyeball on it looked cool. I didn’t know what to expect going in, and I couldn’t have told you that it was an adventure game once I did play it, even though I had played point-and-clicks such as Pajama Sam by that point. All I knew was that I hadn’t played anything exactly like it before, and that there were an awful lot of ways to die for a game without combat.
I never made it far in the game because I didn’t have a controller pack to save with, and I would always reach a starry-ceilinged room in some tower, get stuck, and inevitably kill myself with an item called Forest Nectar no matter how I tried to use it. I didn’t fare well on the save files of other people who had rented the game and managed to accomplish more, either. But my inability to progress in this game that was all puzzles and no combat and plentiful deaths didn’t keep it from occupying a part of my brain reserved for only the warmest and fuzziest of nostalgia.
And only recently we got a remake of the original Shadowgate, and I finally had a convenient method of seeing what made it so special to its fans as opposed to the sequel for the Nintendo 64, which I later heard wasn’t received all that well. Now, having played through the remake’s three difficulty levels, I realize that what I like best about this Shadowgate is what impressed me so much in Shadowgate 64 and Dragon’s Lair II and the Souls games: the sense of fragility and disempowerment that makes every moment and every decision matter. And, for me, the variety of deaths is what drives that helplessness home.
In the Shadowgate remake, you play as Jair, some hapless knight whose physical prowess makes even Dirk the Daring look good. As such, the only way young Jair can hope to overcome the trials he has been tasked with facing at the legendary living Castle of Shadowgate is by using his wits and whatever he can find that isn’t magically attached to the floor. Whereas death in Dragon’s Lair II results from the failure to respond quickly and accurately to a prompt, death in Shadowgate usually results from the failure to scour the environment for clues about potential dangers, or perhaps just because you decide to
Use a lit torch on Thyself a few times in a row.
You explore Shadowgate using a series of commands that you would find in text-based adventure games, only they’re mapped to buttons at the top of the screen. Your most-used commands will be Look, Use and Go, and puzzles will often require you to use the Look command on everything you can click to fill the dialog box at the bottom of the screen with narrative text that just might include cryptic hints in the form of riddles or keywords. Except for Look, commands will add to your turn counter, and in most situations, the deaths you have to worry about are directly related to your turn counter. The most common scenarios involve making the right decision within a turn or two of encountering a monster. If you fail to use the proper action or proper item, or perhaps even just do things out of sequence, you’ll experience just how easy it is for everything to kill Jair.
It is the less immediate deaths in Shadowgate, however, that have the potential to be both the most frustrating aspects of the game and the most important to its replayability. Each of the torches you use to navigate the castle has a limited number of turns before it burns out, leaving Jair to promptly connect his skull with the hardest object in the room should he not have any further torches. There is also an overall turn limit for beating the game, which I never ran up against. The timed death that is the source of the frustration I mentioned is a curse young Jair has inflicted on him by a banshee early on in the game. If you don’t find a cure roughly 600 turns after being cursed, you die.
When you’re still getting used to the game, it’s easy to run up your turn counter and prevent yourself from being able to find a cure in time. So, it’s a good idea to create multiple saves and be prepared to load from an earlier point once you know how to more efficiently solve certain puzzles. Assuming you don’t start the game on Master difficulty, whose puzzles’ solutions have the most steps involved, the banshee’s curse becomes a constant and compelling reminder to carefully consider your every move through the castle as opposed to the vague promise of death that gets pushed to the back of your mind when trying to solve the game’s major puzzles for the first time.
Other than the banshee’s curse, the game’s logic behind why certain items are useful in certain situations and not others can occasionally be frustrating. But, for the most part, as long as you’re as thorough and attentive as possible, there’s no solution in the game that just comes completely out of the blue or requires an extensive amount of trial and error. And, even if you don’t pick up on the most helpful clues for certain puzzles, there are often other hints to help you.
Shadowgate isn’t for everybody. Plenty of people will find its hints too vague and its interface too involved. But it also isn’t a game that can only be appreciated by fans of the original or of the adventure game genre, or even by a guy who has an odd amount of nostalgia for the franchise, given that he had barely even played part of a possibly ill-regarded sequel. Shadowgate puts you in control of an unlikely hero and leaves success to your own powers of observation and abstract thinking, not to any amazing abilities possessed by the character. And, for those who appreciate the sense of peril and empowerment that comes from having that much agency over the fate of a particularly vulnerable protagonist, Shadowgate is an experience that is far more fascinating than frustrating.

Hacknet is a terminal based hacking simulator- Think something along the lines of uplink, but a little more realistic. The game uses UI's similar to that of UNIX and LINUX based interfaces, with the command line being one of your biggest friends in this game. You start the game off small, breaking into weak computers and advancing the story. As time progresses, you become part of a Hacker group and get access to stronger tools. You have to build up stronger resources, hack into firewalls, work fast against traces on your machine, and in the end work towards finding out the death of the mysterious hacker "Bit", and foil the intentions of his killers. The game is short, but does have some community members who are piecing apart the game to make mods. I have like 800 hours of play between Dark Souls 1, 2 and 3. I have never played Demon Souls or Bloodborne as I have never had a console and will never own one. Period.
I have just installed Lords of The Fallen as I finished DS3 three times and got enough of it.
And…
So far so good...
It is not Dark Souls game. In some aspects it is familiar to DS, but it is more fantasih with a touch of D&D. The plot/story feels more significant and clear than in DS with a touch of mystery.
I also do not understand all the hate towards this game. I do feel it is hugely underrated on Steam.
Pros:
-	Beautiful graphics – I find the graphics way better than in Dark Souls 3. The game is simply gorgeous.
-	Performance/Optimization – again better than in DS3 – On full QHD and everything maxed out (all details on very high and antis on x16) I can run it 50-60 fps on my laptop. Whereas DS is only 40-45 on just full HD with occasional drops to as low as 30.
-	Apart from occasional Memory leaks I have not encountered any bugs yet
-	Lore – I like the logs you find throughout the game
-	Atmosphere – proper Dark Fantasy Game with more stress on Fantasy than in Dark Souls
-	NPCs  - so far I encountered like 5 of them and I found every one convincing and interesting
-	Plot – so far so good – mysterious and stimulating
-	Character development – very intuitive
-	Equipment – armours and weapons – well developed – imo better than in DS
-	Portals to the other worlds – I like the idea
Hard to say
-	Fighting system – it is okay but comparing to DS it feels much slower and clunky; I can still enjoy it though. Especially with some final hits that feel so powerful
-	Levels design – I am still in two minds about it; levels seemed well connected but in the same time felt too small and shorts; I need to play more.
-	Voiced Protagonist  – he feels like a really badass criminal – maybe not my type but I am able to impersonate while playing so its good and he has a good voice… but still I prefer the solution like in DS where you can shape your protagonist the way you like.
Cons:
-	You can’t hit a wall with your weapon like it is always too far. That feels really unreal
-	Enemies – so far I have not seen anything special, just humanoids with shield, few assasins with daggers or crossbows and mutes – I will change this if I encounter more interesting enemies
-	Bosses – so far I beat two and they were very easy + very similar – I will change this if I encounter more interesting bosses
-	Rolling – it just does not feel right, even when not almost overcumbered it is slow and has short range. I barely use it
-	Enemies that are covered behind their shields at all time – I find them really frustrating especially when using heavy slower weapon
-	Memory leaks – it kicked me out like 2 times during 3 hours of play to the desktop with a message to close apps in order to free some RAM. I have 16GB of RAM and it is just not right; I am not sure if that is the game’s problem or Windows 10. Same thing happened to me with Fallout 4, but not in DS3
-	Move set – only light and heavy attack + roll attack – is that right or am I missing something
-	No multiplayer – that is too bad; I like the DS multiplayer and I think same thing could have been implemented here
My Ratings:
DS 1: 9/10
DS 2: 8/10
DS 3: 9/10
Lords of the Fallen: 7/10

Fractured Space is pretty unique in its own way, but the gameplay can be compared to a select few. The choice of gameplay that they chose is slightly entertaining, but not for anybody hoping for a quick break. Average games should take the normal amount of time of about thirty to forty five minutes. The main objective of the single gamemode that they have right now is something alike to a conquest match. You are given five control points on both ends, each of which has a fair amount of time to capture. Alongside  that the more players that control it, the faster it captures. This will add another piece of teamwork in the game that adds more challenge. Speaking of teamwork, you only work in teams of five, which will limit your abilities to call for help.
One piece of the single gamemode that is extremely to deal with is the health of characters, and the damage you deal to them. Most starships take a long time to destroy a single ship and vice versa for yourself, even including when you hit them directly. There are two things that will assist you in destroying ships; a group of allies, or when they jump. Whenever a character begins to use their jump drive to escape, all of their shields deactivate, while their health decreases, making a single shot very lethal to them, leaving you the choices to deal as much damage as you can and have the very rare chance of destroying them, or die while your at it. The respawn times dont increase by the time you die, but as the time increases. One of the games I played I died only once, but had the respawn time of a boring and painstaking time of a minute and a half. And if your not careful, or very inexperienced, you will die a lot and will not have a lot of game time.
Another one of the functions of the game that can turn the tables is the gamma outpost. About every seven or ten minutes, an outpost in the dead center will activate, and is possible to take. What it does, is that it places a temporary damage buff which reduces the time to destroy starships. This can also add another aspect of strategy. What I most typically do, is while everybody is posted at the gamma, fighting for their lives, I take as many points as I can. The one downside to that plan is that it is very likely that the point can be taken swiftly. The next thing I know, i'm ambushed and lose another minute and a half of my game.
They have a large variety in starships that can adapt to anybodys needs. There are three companies in the game that are available for use. There is government class (thats what I call it, it has a different name) which focuses in exploses and slower characters, but have heavier armor. Then, there is the Zarek industries which focuses in the laser technology, which can be useful for consecutive damage. they have a well balanced armor and speed, which is decently alright for sniping, but more focused  for medium range or up close. In my opinion, i recommend it the least, because I never really achieve anything with it. But the ships I do recommend in it are the more advanced ones, where the laser duration gets longer and more deadly. But takes longer to recharge. Finally, there is the TITAN class. These take a little longer to first get, you have to complete the whole tutorial (yes, even the advanced ones.) once you do, you get the TITAN class. What they focus on, is smart cannons but using weaker armor. That makes them faster, and able to still fight from a safe distance. The one problem is, is that it is very easy to destroy. That is something that you should be very aware about. That fact means that you should stay away from combat, and if you want to escape, you must have a smart place to hide.
One problem I have though, is the currency system. There is the main currency option, where you can buy weapons and ships, but the biggest problem is that, each class uses their own individual currency that you can only achieve by playing on that one class, that takes a while to reach enough credit for it. But then, once you reach enough credits, then you have to pay more, this time works universally with all classes and characters. And then, MORE CURRENCY MUST BE USED. This is another universal currency, but known as DNA. You use it to create staff for you ship that takes even more time for a prepared ship. Aside from that, (even though it takes a while) there are plenty of ships that you are free to sample. With all the ships that there are, they are all very entertaining and fun to use.
And now, the graphics. The starships are very detailed and realistic, which makes me always feel like im straight out of an episode of star trek. They are all so unique, making them easy to classify. The emitters that they use for the engines could use improvement, considering that all they change is hue an alpha, not adding any new textures or size. However, the fire emitter is realistic and good looking. The placement of all the parts is done so well, they make it seem so reasonable as if they were actually built.
My total rating for the game, is about 6.5/10, because of its gameplay, graphics, and ship selection, mut it has the lower score because of the wait times, and the amount of time it takes to complete a game. The one thing that prevents me from giving this a thumbs down, is that it is in early access and its free. If it wasnt, then I wouldn't enjoy it very much. But since it is early access, I expect that there will be lots of potential, i'm expecting good potential, but it is still very possible for a bad future.
A good gamemode that would be cool, is a 1v9 game, where the nine are basic characters, while the 1 is very strong, kind of like a gamemode from Evolve.
And maybe a newer class which focuses on rapid attacks instead of the ones that they currently have.
I hope that the developers will take note of this and probably fix the problems that I have stated, and keep all the greats that are here, and if not, make them better.

You'll get 10ish hours of gameplay, pretty limited replayability (even though there is a NG+), and if you choose not to use any of the "statues" (which give you some minor currency / exp bonuses while potentially making the game much more difficult) the game was not particularly challenging to me.
I actually got distracted after a couple hours, and lost interest in picking it back up. I ended up coming back to it months later and vowing not to use any statues just so I could power through and see the end of the game and get it off of my list of games to play.
I'd say it's worth the money, and worth supporting indie artists to put out such a well polished game. I definitely expect you'll have fun messing with the various weapons and fighting strategies, and while a little abstract, the story was certainly palatable.

Right Half Life, the game that has had worldwide acclaim at being one of the best games ever made. There is no denying that it had left a huge impact in gaming culture but does it still hold up to this day?
The answer is: Mostly
The game is great, a real blast to play. The story is menacing and top notch, the atmosphere is just fantastic and the pacing is really good. Now here is where I think the game is a little outdated. The combat I will admit is fun but I found it sometimes a bit jittery compared to something like Return to Caslte Wolfenstein which I played beforehand. It is still good combat but I was just spoiled with RtCW to fully enjoy it.
The puzzles I am honestly a bit mixed about. On the one hand they can be fun, I do remember some cool puzzles but other times it can get fustrating like with the platforming. There was this one puzzle where I had to activate a fan and use the fan to lift myself to get to the chute in the ceiling. I had to look at that one up. Am I stupid or is that just flawed game design? Please reply whether that kind of logic is viable?
Visually it's nice whether you're using the HD texture pack or not. The music for what little there is pretty good and odd at the same time. I also encountered a couple of glitches such as missing sound and this one time I would just die by pressing this button.
Okay so overall it is still great and I would recommend it dearly but there are just a couple of certain aspects I think people these days seem to sort of forget or forgive which is not a bad thing but I think we have to at least acknowledge their existence. Sorry for sounding so negative. Consider this as a modern perspective of a classic. I give it an 8/10

Many of the puzzles require precise timing, something which is hard to achieve due to a cooldown lockout on the gloves, meaning that you must wait almost an entire second before using it again. I did not complete this game due to mounting frustration from multiple puzzles in a row that reset entirely if you messed up. It's not exactly the difficulty in figuring out the puzzles themselves, its more that the setup and timing have to be precise enough that the solution is executed, something that is hard to do because of bad gravity and physics simulation, poor controls, and unintuitive mechanics. Maybe it's just me, but multiple times when I tried to flip a purple switch, I meant to flip the other direction. Just as well, the left and right gloves have the same appearance and animations, making it easy to confuse what they do, of which I'm still not entirely sure. This game feels half-baked, poorly coded, and has an uncompelling story.

The game isn't quite as polished as Portal 1/2, but it has it's own blocky style and unique atmosphere, especially in the darker sectors. Be warned that some twisting of the walls while riding some of the elevators might give you motion sickness, but you can easily look away when riding those.
Given its low price, it's worth every cent, especially if you get it at 75% off like I did.

Fallout 4 by itself is a pretty good game. Shooting mechanics are nice, the settlement building is very fun for those into that sort of system, and the major DLCs are for the most part stellar additions.
However, recent events mean I can no longer recommend this game. Bethesda has shown themselves to be a hostile force to their community with Creation Club. Not only are the current selection of 'curated mini-DLCs' completely laughable at the prices they charge, the big name items even go against the supposed rules Bethesda themselves laid out. In addition, this system has disrupted loading orders, which can be a serious stability issue for heavy modders.
PRO
-Enjoyable, responsive shooting mechanics
-Settlement system offers an alternative game style
-DLCs are worthwhile additions
-Environments can be interesting to explore and discover their stories
-Offers the incredible modding base Bethesda games are known for
CON
-Main story is less than interesting
-Conversation options are distilled down to 'Good, Evil, Smarmy Smartass Good, Maybe Later'
-Play areas outside constructed set pieces are largely uninteresting
-Settlement system can be a required distraction for those who do not care for it
NEUTRAL
-Simplification of SPECIAL and stat system is a pro or con depending on the player
-Some game mechanics are never explained (did you know there's a cover system?)
DEAL BREAKER
-Bethesda is increasingly a hostile force to the modding scene, arguably the biggest draw of their games

Super Sanctum TD looks like it was made 20 years ago in some kid's basement. Sound effects, UI & graphics are basic, but behind the mediocre fascade is a challenging & balanced tower defense game. Strategy is important along with your selection of towers & skills you choose to arm yourself with.
Small tactical mistakes can be unforgiving often resulting in restarting the level with a new defense plan. Hard mode is HARD! There is also a reasonable number of levels - they are not too complex or big for that matter, but they do generally allow for some mazing.
I would have liked to see some better high resolution support though; but it runs & looks ok in fullscreen windowed mode. There is probably around 10hrs of gameplay to complete everything & an infinite wave survival mode to add some replayability.
This was a surprisingly fun & addictive casual TD game.

XCOM 2 is a good turn-based game -  I recommend it!
You race around a map in a very massive aircraft, collecting resources, and taking on missions.  These missions involve shooting aliens.  A large number of missions have timers (which adds a level of difficulty).  If your dudes and dudettes survive, they get more beastly.  You spend lots of time researching and building gear for your soldiers and watching them mend in the hospital after they got shot up in the last mission.  In said missions, Sometimes your soldiers really suck and you get so incredibly furious.  Other times, they totally rock and you well with pride.  There is also a big timer that works against you all game, but I found it pretty lax.  The Proving Ground (a buildable facility) throws an element of randomness into the game by never knowing what the heck those engineers will actually come up with for you (special ammo, grenades, body armour, etc).
I really got attached to the squad members in this game. I loved customizing them, changing voice sets, nationality, gender's, etc, to make the right set of killer dolls.  The number of reloads due to key team members biting the bullet was high.  I like the classes available for squad members, of which there are five, each with two skill options to decide between on level up.
I have played all the XCOM's to date and feel that perhaps XCOM UFO Defense (the oldest) was harder, but not by much (and my memory may be failing me, that was a while ago).  I played it through on normal, but had to turn it down to easy on two missions (which felt like cheating, but it was easier!).  Good on ya if you can play it on harder modes, although I didn't try them.
It certainly has a few bugs, but none prevented me from accomplishing anything and at worst made me reload a save.  Mostly, they ocurred in the form of odd misclicks with the UI, a team member not getting off the dropship at mission start, terrain issues, squad members looking but not acting alive when they had been nuked by an alien, etc.  Nothing too important.
I took my time, but it was around 35 hours or so from start to finish.

Darkest Dungeon provides an engaging (if occasionally frustrating) mix of dungeon crawling, team management sim and city-builder, with the last two components playing a supporting role for the first one. It comes wrapped in a decent-enough narrative and enough visual flair to keep you playing through the occasional walloping. That is good.
You play the unnamed distant relative of a much-debauched and newly-dead nobleman. Said nobleman set the plot in motion when he got bored with non-stop drinking binges and orgies and figured that the pursuit of blasphemous occulted knowledge would be a way funner use of his fabulous wealth. He read some books in dead and terrible languages, arranged for a bit of digging in the basement and woke up something with way too many tentacles and teeth. Then he ate a bullet, after calling you in to clean up the mess. Fighting your way through boss dungeons will enlighten you further on just how gigantic an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your ancestor was. You hire adventurers, arm them, train them, send them to clear out dungeons, level them up, treat the psychoses they inevitably develop and provide them with entertainment to keep them semi-sane, until you (hopefully) send your best troops to kill whatever's in the... Darkest Dungeon.
The game has well-illustrated 2d visuals, drawing on gothic and Lovecraftian imagery. Settings include the wreckage of a ruined manor house, an encroaching hostile forest, dim-lit coastal caverns and an underground pig-man slum, populated with a reasonably wide range of distinct monsters. You get vaguely medieval-looking (except for the guns) human bandits, fish-people a la Innsmouth (though more closely resembling actual fish than the froglike mutants from Lovecraft), icky-looking boar-human blends and the mandatory walking skeletons, among others. Each region has a distinct look and the monsters in each one tend to have somewhat different tactics, which helps keep the game fresh.
Dungeon crawling is the heart of the game. You have to make exactly one dungeon run each in-game week, which you choose from several randomly-generated offerings. Four adventurers maximum in a party; never take less. Once you've picked your guys you have to buy their gear: food, torches for light, consumables like bandages for curing status effects and other consumables like shovels and skeleton keys for interacting with objects you come across. Inventory space is limited, and it takes a bit of trial-and-error to figure out the proper mix of gear for a particular region, dungeon length, challenge level etc. Adventurers also have non-combat skills they can use during rest periods on longer missions, while some are better at spotting traps and secrets than others, giving you additional variables to consider. A well-equipped party with the right skills will find a lot more loot and hit fewer snags than a random one. Sanity is also a consideration; both attacks and the environment itself can inflict stress, and if an adventurer's stress level gets too high they develop a neurosis that causes them to do things like refuse healing, freeze up in combat, throw temper tantrums at their teammates and other fun things to increase the odds of a party wipe. You can quit a dungeon at the cost of stressing out your adventurers and forfeiting the rewards for completion
The combat system is solid, which is fortunate since you're going to do quite a lot of fighting. Combat is turn-based, with each character and enemy going on their own initiative. Positioning works somewhat like Disciples II, with each character occupying a slot on their side of the battlefield which determines what powers they can use and who they can and can't hit. Different classes and builds are optimized for occupying particular spaces on their side and targeting certain enemy ones; you have to pick and arrange your goons so that they all have as many possible targets for their most situationally useful abilities as possible. Character abilities are straightforward; you have melee attacks for hitting the front rows, ranged attacks and area attacks for the back rows, healing, buffing and debuffing spells, and tricks for moving your own and your enemy's people. Each character class has 7 combat abilities, out of which you can have 4 active at any one time, so each class has some variety in how you can play it. Critically, combat damage does not automatically heal after a fight ends and healing powers can only be used in combat or while camping. Winning a fight with everyone standing isn't enough; you have to limit the health and sanity damage your adventurers take in each one so that they don't get TPK'd through attrition. The game provides you with enough tactical options and threats to keep the fights from getting tedious, and individual dungeon crawls are generally short enough that you can play one or two and then put the game down for a while if you don't feel like binging.
You manage your home base and roster when you're not out murderhoboing. You have buildings for upgrading weapons and armour, training combat and non-combat skills, recruiting and housing adventurers (there's a hard cap on how many you can have at one time), reducing stress and curing illnesses. Upgrades make their effects more potent, reduce the cost or increase the number of people they can handle. These upgrades require special resources that you collect during dungeon crawls and as reward for victories, with the cost going up as the facility gets more advanced. Equipment and skills also get more expensive to upgrade as they advance. All this adds a profit/loss calculation to each dungeon you select. A short, low-tier dungeon poses little danger to your characters and requires fewer supplies, but offers far less loot and experience than a large and/or high-tier one, while the costs of equipping your heroes and treating their battle damage will change depending on what facilities you've upgraded. It helps if you can think a few dungeons ahead. Having a plan for the development of your town also helps. Both of these things will also require some trial-and-error and/or a visit to the forums.
In sum: a collection of fairly straightforward mechanics that work well together. Meaningful strategic and tactical choices, decent story, evocative art and a sense of hard-won progress as your side gets stronger and you approach the final battle. Just don't smash your monitor when your Champions get slaughtered and their Very Rare items fall into oblivion.

Like we haven't had enough Minecraft-Inspired FPS, and it got old after the 10th clone.
This clone however, is one of the worst offenders, so far. It suffers from some awful issues that anybody who developed a frontal lobe could notice. Which is why a portion of the community hasn't.
Balancing Issues:
The M14 practically dominates the field. It's a one shot kill if you aim for the head, which isn't hard because the heads are freaking huge and way too easy to aim at in this game. It's a two-three shot kill with bodyshots. It would be fine if the other guns wouldn't be utter crap compared to the M14. The M3 shotgun is a one shot kill, yes, but only if you're up at the enemy's face. He would probably pop an M14 round into your skull before you even get close, especially when the only GOOD maps are the expansive ones. The MP5 is garbage, it takes way too long to kill someone, about half a mag. No one ever uses it. The pistol is the exact same thing as the MP5 with a smaller magazine. Pretty much use the M14 and be average at aiming and you'll be good. Which is the problem. Just look at the kill counter on the top and you'll see it's nothing but "LittleBoy123 Killed BrazilianGuy098 with a headshot and M14!".
Lag. A Whole lot of it:
It's crazy how much lag there can be. The US servers couldn't be worse. I keep seeing my character jump back a few steps, and my connection is fine. Say RIP to your connection, because no matter how good, the servers will always mess with you.
Griefers:
Because it's a good idea to allow others on your team to break your stuff freely, and then restrict us to 35 blocks a life. Yeah, good one, devs.
The Modes Are Just Crap:
Zombies- Wait 30 minutes for a match to be over, then be allowed to play as a human/zombie. Yeah, I'm not joking. Unlike other games, that let you join as a zombie if you jump in the middle of the match, they make you look at a horrendous spectator camera for more than 30 minutes. Uninspiring, tedious, and really boring. This mode overstays it welcome. Not worth any of your time.
Survival- God awful A.I. They just act brain-dead and walk right towards you, must faster then they should. The tip of their fingers touch you, and you're pretty much half-dead. Boring.
Tank- Good idea, I'll give you that. Although, the tanks control like crap and glitch out like crazy. Hopefully that'll be fixed with patches. The tank sounds are terrible, the engine revving is just a 2 second sound-loop. Going up a hill slows that same sound into a 4 second sound-loop. Pretty much every sound the tank makes is just a clip looped over and over. The Tanks are way too OVERPOWERED. They're often not enough tanks to go around, so when you go on foot, you're done in a single hit. There is NO WAY for infintry to take out a tank either. That's total bullocks.
Battle- The only mode worth playing. That's all I'll say.
Carnage- It's garbage. You just flick your shovel at enemies and it's... Oh so boring and tedious.
The rest of the modes I've yet to try out, I'll edit the review when I try them out soon.
Render Distance:
The render distance is attrocious. Apparently "Far" means a couple of feet in front of you. Come on, render distance shouldn't be a thing that can be altered. People with slower PCs won't be able to see very far and faster PCs will see an enemy across the world, and that is why the "Far" setting isn't far at all.
Pay Model:
It doesn't annoy me that you pretty much have no additional weapons past the ones you start off with and the only way to buy anything is to use real money. What bothers me is that the terrible balance of the free weapons aren't fixed with the premium weapons. This game generally has horrible balance.
BLOCKADE 3D is an unbalanced, uninspired, ugly, buggy, laggy, mess of a game. I'd say this game has some good ideas if it weren't that 10 games and mods haven't done this before it. This whole "Minecraft as an FPS" has been done to death and it's getting old. It's a blatent cash-grab towards the Minecraft fan-kids and nothing more. Is it worth your time? No.

As a HUGE fan of the NES port, THIS REMAKE IS AMAZING. Puzzles have changed, so don't think that having the original or NES games memorized will help you. If you liked the feel of the original, there's so much more. New things just everywhere. New places to explore. New ways to solve old puzzles, some that still harken back to their original solutions while managing to be different. (You'll see what I mean when you have to freeze the lake.) For those interested in the lore, MAN has that EVER been expanded. You will interact with Lakmir. You will learn about the Circle Of Twelve. There is so much more depth and richness to this reimagining.
If you don't like point-and-click, exploration-type games, well, this isn't for you. For those of us with fond memories of the original and want more depth to it, then it's a grand thing that your adventures have begun here. ;)

Gameplay: Shadowgate is not reinventing any wheels here - it plays exactly like its predecessor and exactly like any other point-and-click adventure game, a set of pre-defined commands used to interact with the world and solve hella puzzles. The game deftly avoids making you actually pixel-hunt, most interactable items fairly easy to spot.
The game is an adventure of the old-school, with red herrings everywhere and huge amount of items you can grab that you will never actually use. Nearly every puzzle has good, if sometimes somewhat obtuse hints, with very little♥♥♥♥♥pull adventure logic. The difficulty levels are also very serious, massively simplifying things on the easiest level as compared to the hardest. You /can/, on all difficulties, screw yourself into an unwinnable position - the game will allow you to destroy necessary items (though not casually) and it's extremely possible to just run out of time (though not very likely).
The biggest flaw in the gameplay is some UI related clumsiness, as using items on the environment can get very clunky very quickly when you're experimenting on a puzzle. Items can be bound to number keys for things you use a lot, but I don't think that ended up particularly useful near the end.
Story: Shadowgate has never, on its own, had a particularly deep mythology. The Shadowgate remake drops a lot more lore on you, completely resetting the world and freely changing some very major details. It does some interesting things once you get to the end.
I did personally find it to largely suffer from being written by 50-year old men whose greatest influences are clearly in the Lord of the Rings vein, naming conventions clearly suffering from a lack of... I want to say modern creativity. It's all a bit out of date.
Art: Here's where Shadowgate really shines - which is important, since the game is little more than a series of paintings you flail at with a mouse. Shadowgate is not a colorful place, with most scenes generally only having two or three different colors at any time, and Chris Cold does an excellent job making a dreary Shadowgate that seriously looks like it wants to kill you.
Jair in particular is excellently rendered - the classic portrayal of the game's protagonist was a standard square-jawed manly hero in full armor and a beautiful head of hair. New Shadowgate portrays Jair as a man dragged out of his life and sent on a journey without ever really being allowed to understand why - his hair is long and filthy, his cloak is tattered, and his shadowed face imparts the idea that Shadowgate is destroying him even as he triumphs over it.
Perhaps most importantly, the art is /clear./ Despite everything being dirty, dull, and cracked, mostly in greys and browns, nothing looks maddeningly ambiguous. An item on the ground is clearly an item on the ground, a doorway is clearly a doorway, and if you at any point get fooled it's because the game is actively trying to fool you.
Music: I have a clear bias here - New Shadowgate's score is an orchestral treatment of the original music, the old songs appearing as almost etherial strains inside some deeply atmospheric stuff. Compared to the original, this score is much darker, much more ominous, and much more effective (which shouldn't be too difficult, considering the original was on an 8-bit system). There is an appreciated option to set the music to the classic beeply bops.
Shadowgate: Yeah, it's Shadowgate. You can die on almost every screen, you watch your torches steadily dwindle down, and the Warlock Lord pops in from time to time just to talk♥♥♥♥♥♥ Most sadistically, the game is explicitly /not/ the previous Shadowgate. Very few puzzles are solved the same way, and the game will often directly punish you for having the unmitigated gall to underestimate it in this fashion. Much like the original, the game (on Master difficulty) is not here to be your friend. It is here to laugh at you as you stare blankly at its legitimately hard puzzles and then brutally kill you for blinking.
--
All told, I give the game high marks. The UI's clunkiness just takes a little getting used to, and if you enjoy adventure games that kind of slap you around, you can't get much more slappy than this. If you're a fan of the original and you haven't picked this up yet, you should absolutely do so.
