I think I must be the only reviewer who never even heard of Shadowgate and thus was not motivated to pick it up out of a sense of nostalgia, but because I thought the art was pretty and I heard that you could actually die a whole bunch. I've played plenty of point-and-click adventure games in the past and, with few exceptions, you're never really in any danger at all.
The basic setup is that you are a guy named Jair and you are the Seed of Prophecy, you're contacted by a mage named Lakmir who tells you to go to a castle called Shadowgate armed with only a torch, a dirk, and courage and defeat the evil Warlock Lord. It's not the most original premise in the world but it's a remake of a game that came out in the 80s, so I'll forgive the lack of originality.
As Lord Jair, your job is to navigate through the castle, room by room, grabbing items and stuffing them into your satchel  You explore the castle by using various menu commands: look, hit, use, eat, etc. At first I found it a bit clunky, having to "use" myself (or "hit") when pulling a lever when other games would just let me use the lever by clicking on it, but I think the clunky interface is part of the charm. While you're exploring, you need to keep an eye on your torch and keep picking up new ones that you come across. If your torch burns out, well, let's just say the game warns you that bad things happen....
Besides exploring, the other thing you'll do in Shadowgate is die a lot. Taking the wrong item, using the wrong item, not wearing certain equipment (via using them on your portrait), and a myriad other things can prove fatal. There's even an achievement for uncovering all the hidden ways that you can die in the game. The funny thing is that as frustrating as dying is, in Shadowgate it's actually fun provided you save often. I found the autosave feature saved pretty frequently but I always saved as soon as I entered a room, just in case.
Graphically, Shadowgate mostly has static pictures and some animations, but I can honestly say that I don't think I've ever played a prettier adventure game. The artwork could have come straight out of a D&D manual. Shadowgate definitely has the look and feel of an RPG but it's an adventure game, through and through. The music is also great. The main theme is my favourite but the tense track that plays when your torch is running low had me frantically scrambling to light a new one every time, even though I knew I had plenty of them.
One aspect of adventure games that I often have trouble with is the puzzles, particularly puzzles that require something I call Adventure Game Logic, that is, puzzle solutions that involve combining items in a way that makes absolutely no sense. Shadowgate takes a subtle approach to puzzles, dropping hints here and there and letting the player figure things out on their own. If you get stuck, you can always ask Yorick the skull for help. Since this was my first time playing Shadowgate, I decided to play on Apprentice (the lowest difficulty setting) and oftentimes Yorick would pretty much tell me the answer to a puzzle. However, sometimes he seemed to be jumping the gun a bit, like when he told me I needed to cross a certain bridge when I actually had to do a few more things to get the means to get across. Other times I was simply stuck with a bunch of items and no idea where to go next. This is one of those games that requires a ton of trial and error (or a walkthrough at the ready) which is compounded by the fact that the inventory is very disorganized. I lost track of how many times I remembered a passage in a book that was hinting about the puzzle I was working on and then not being able to find it in the archives. At times it seemed as if some information that would have been useful in other difficulties (the game closes off certain areas and puzzles are much easier on Apprentice, giving you some incentive to play again on harder difficulty levels) was just a bit confusing.
If you like point and click adventure games and you're willing to put up with a lot of trial and error (and dying a lot). I wouldn't recommend Shadowgate as someone's first experience with the genre but it is an interesting look at a piece of adventure gaming history. I will definitely be going back and playing it again on a harder difficulty level and I can't wait to see if they come out with more games in this series.

Hacknet is a semi-realistic terminal-based hacking simulator with scintallating entertainment potential.
You play as an individual who carries out requests that were given to him/her by a recently deceased hacker that went by the psuedonym of "Bit", as well as many other individuals and organizations. These requests typically include breaching servers in order to collect information, deleting logs, rendering services unusable, and various other unscrupulous activities.
Gameplay - 8/10 - When I first began playing Hacknet, I was genuinely surprised at just how realistic and immersive it was. You don't start the game as an omnipotent l337 haxx0r. Your skillset grows over time, and so does your toolset. Tools such as "SSHcrack.exe", "FTPBounce.exe" and others are all realistic in that these could easily be batch files and scripts that a person with malicious intent could use. New tools and gameplay elements are introduced incrementally over time, but even then, it becomes repetitive, and to an extent, stale.
Soundtrack - 9/10 - The soundtrack primarily consists of electronic music, with a focus on tech house and ambient/chillout. A new song plays for every single stage of the game that you enter, and a new tune plays when you begin a mission. The production value is excellent, and consistent throughout every single track.
Storyline - ??? - The quality of the storyline is completely subjective and dependent upon the outlook of the player. It may be cringy and cliché to some, yet tantalizing and immersive to others. I can't say much in the way of it without risk of spoiling plot details, but it's Russian Roulette in terms of enjoyability.
Replay Value - 0/10 - No. Stop. No. Stop this right now.

Old school gaming lovers rejoice! Shadowgate is back! I am a HUGE fan of the NES version. I have logged dozens of hours into this new version and I think it is pretty awesome! I'm excited to see what Zojoi's has in store next! (I know, but no spoilers for you!)

+   Nostalgia trip back to the castle that I got so many nightmares from when I was young
+   Lots of 'Hidden Death' cut scenes that are really fun to discover and watch
-   The puzzle structure is firmly rooted in old school style gaming-- (for good or bad) so that means some puzzles can be confusing at times-- even on easy, Puzzles can get very confusing on hard! -   So many items! Not everything has a use either. First time though you will have a massive amount of things to pick up and keep track of. I've seen people get stuck on Hard mode and then try using everything, on everything trying to brute force their way through.
Final verdict : 7.5 / 10

Anyone that knows me knows I loved the original Shadowgate. When the kickstarter for this one went up, I immediately dropped a large sum of money into seeing a remake in my list of steam games. Was it worth it?
Absolutely!
This edition of Shadowgate improves in just about every way from the original. The artwork is amazing, the new music hits the same emotions as the original, and the puzzles as as difficult as ever.
Even better is if you don't care for the new music, you can turn on the original NES soundtrack, as well as the original NES screen transition effect and sound. Great for a retro feel.
I only find myself with two dislikes and they are indeed minor. First, the game lessens the difficulty by providing Yorrik, a skull who will give you advice if you want. He also likes to talk way more than he should and since you must click through his dialog it slows the game down and throws off the rhythm you build as you progress, especially on replays. Secondly, when you try to use an action, it isn't clear if you have already selected something at times, and again will throw you off. Having a dagger selected and wanting to look at a wall will confuse you when a detail of a dagger is talked about.
Neither of these at all ruin the game, but are things to watch for as you progress through this wonderful title.

Darkest Dungeon provides an engaging (if occasionally frustrating) mix of dungeon crawling, team management sim and city-builder, with the last two components playing a supporting role for the first one. It comes wrapped in a decent-enough narrative and enough visual flair to keep you playing through the occasional walloping. That is good.
You play the unnamed distant relative of a much-debauched and newly-dead nobleman. Said nobleman set the plot in motion when he got bored with non-stop drinking binges and orgies and figured that the pursuit of blasphemous occulted knowledge would be a way funner use of his fabulous wealth. He read some books in dead and terrible languages, arranged for a bit of digging in the basement and woke up something with way too many tentacles and teeth. Then he ate a bullet, after calling you in to clean up the mess. Fighting your way through boss dungeons will enlighten you further on just how gigantic an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your ancestor was. You hire adventurers, arm them, train them, send them to clear out dungeons, level them up, treat the psychoses they inevitably develop and provide them with entertainment to keep them semi-sane, until you (hopefully) send your best troops to kill whatever's in the... Darkest Dungeon.
The game has well-illustrated 2d visuals, drawing on gothic and Lovecraftian imagery. Settings include the wreckage of a ruined manor house, an encroaching hostile forest, dim-lit coastal caverns and an underground pig-man slum, populated with a reasonably wide range of distinct monsters. You get vaguely medieval-looking (except for the guns) human bandits, fish-people a la Innsmouth (though more closely resembling actual fish than the froglike mutants from Lovecraft), icky-looking boar-human blends and the mandatory walking skeletons, among others. Each region has a distinct look and the monsters in each one tend to have somewhat different tactics, which helps keep the game fresh.
Dungeon crawling is the heart of the game. You have to make exactly one dungeon run each in-game week, which you choose from several randomly-generated offerings. Four adventurers maximum in a party; never take less. Once you've picked your guys you have to buy their gear: food, torches for light, consumables like bandages for curing status effects and other consumables like shovels and skeleton keys for interacting with objects you come across. Inventory space is limited, and it takes a bit of trial-and-error to figure out the proper mix of gear for a particular region, dungeon length, challenge level etc. Adventurers also have non-combat skills they can use during rest periods on longer missions, while some are better at spotting traps and secrets than others, giving you additional variables to consider. A well-equipped party with the right skills will find a lot more loot and hit fewer snags than a random one. Sanity is also a consideration; both attacks and the environment itself can inflict stress, and if an adventurer's stress level gets too high they develop a neurosis that causes them to do things like refuse healing, freeze up in combat, throw temper tantrums at their teammates and other fun things to increase the odds of a party wipe. You can quit a dungeon at the cost of stressing out your adventurers and forfeiting the rewards for completion
The combat system is solid, which is fortunate since you're going to do quite a lot of fighting. Combat is turn-based, with each character and enemy going on their own initiative. Positioning works somewhat like Disciples II, with each character occupying a slot on their side of the battlefield which determines what powers they can use and who they can and can't hit. Different classes and builds are optimized for occupying particular spaces on their side and targeting certain enemy ones; you have to pick and arrange your goons so that they all have as many possible targets for their most situationally useful abilities as possible. Character abilities are straightforward; you have melee attacks for hitting the front rows, ranged attacks and area attacks for the back rows, healing, buffing and debuffing spells, and tricks for moving your own and your enemy's people. Each character class has 7 combat abilities, out of which you can have 4 active at any one time, so each class has some variety in how you can play it. Critically, combat damage does not automatically heal after a fight ends and healing powers can only be used in combat or while camping. Winning a fight with everyone standing isn't enough; you have to limit the health and sanity damage your adventurers take in each one so that they don't get TPK'd through attrition. The game provides you with enough tactical options and threats to keep the fights from getting tedious, and individual dungeon crawls are generally short enough that you can play one or two and then put the game down for a while if you don't feel like binging.
You manage your home base and roster when you're not out murderhoboing. You have buildings for upgrading weapons and armour, training combat and non-combat skills, recruiting and housing adventurers (there's a hard cap on how many you can have at one time), reducing stress and curing illnesses. Upgrades make their effects more potent, reduce the cost or increase the number of people they can handle. These upgrades require special resources that you collect during dungeon crawls and as reward for victories, with the cost going up as the facility gets more advanced. Equipment and skills also get more expensive to upgrade as they advance. All this adds a profit/loss calculation to each dungeon you select. A short, low-tier dungeon poses little danger to your characters and requires fewer supplies, but offers far less loot and experience than a large and/or high-tier one, while the costs of equipping your heroes and treating their battle damage will change depending on what facilities you've upgraded. It helps if you can think a few dungeons ahead. Having a plan for the development of your town also helps. Both of these things will also require some trial-and-error and/or a visit to the forums.
In sum: a collection of fairly straightforward mechanics that work well together. Meaningful strategic and tactical choices, decent story, evocative art and a sense of hard-won progress as your side gets stronger and you approach the final battle. Just don't smash your monitor when your Champions get slaughtered and their Very Rare items fall into oblivion.

Few games are capable of telling such a compelling story, and Walking Dead is one of them. Few stories can pull at you heartstrings like this one. You are Lee Everett, a convicted killer who is given a second chance at life when he comes across a little girl named Clementine, and decides to protect her. The game plays a strong emphasis on choices, and you will be faced with some very difficult ones too.
While the choices you make in the game does not overall change much of the outcome, it does affect the people's opinion about you, how they see you and how they will remember you. Depending on these choices whether you will grow to like the main character and the people around him, or whether they will leave you with a bitter feeling at the end. And that's where the Walking Dead's greatest strength lies. In it's characters. And the choices you make regarding them.
Overall, this game is an adventure that remains with you and you will never forget it. Easily the best game of 2012, worth every single penny. It would be a shame to miss on it.

Wow what a gem this game is.  You play as Lee a man with a questionable past thrown in at the deep end at the start of a zombie apocalypse, at the start of the game you meet Clementine, a little girl alone.  Throughout the game Lee and Clem meet all sorts of characters and together try and survive in a world gone mad.
The Storyline is dark in places and full of twists and turns but i felt myself constantly wanting more, it was like a book i couldnt put down chapter after chapter.
There are lots of great things i can say about this game, the character development is some of the best i've seen in any game.  The dialogue is perfect, it really gives each character a personality and you get the feeling these people really exist.
With every conversation i found myself not just trying to say the right thing but voicing my own opinion as if i was the main character i was playing (Lee).  From dilemma's to arguements to simple discussions and decisions this is a game that will make you wonder a second later if you did or said the right thing.  The fact that almost everything you say or do has a lasting effect and moulds the game to your decisions amazes me.
The quicktime events are quite simple at times but then it really catches you off guard at other times where you near enough need lightning reflex's.
I've never been a fan of cell shaded games but this is just something else, graphically it looks fantastic.
By the end of chapter five i didnt want it to end, i felt a real deep connection to each of the characters, even more so with Lee and Clementine.
Telltale did a fantastic job with this game and really can't wait for future installments of this series.

Quick and Dirty:
***DO NOT BELIEVE THE FLAMERS WHO HAVE RAGE BOMBED THIS GAME DOWN TO AN UNDERSERVING SCORE***
***YOU NEED A FAIRLY POWERFUL GPU TO PROPERLY ENJOY THIS GAME WITH LITTLE TO NO ISSUES***
Assassin's Creed Unity is the best game yet to come out of the AC franchise. With two hundred + hours of total play time between the previous two AC games, I can easily say that Unity beats both AC3 and Black Flag in any measurable contest. If you like the style of game, you should love this one.
I have seen very little issues as far as glitches. The only exception is the ocassional ragdoll effect on a downed enemy gets a little excited. It seems that this game is guilty of only one thing: It is poorly optimised. So if you have a slower/older rig or are trying to play it on a console (*sigh), you may have problems running it at a reasonable frame rate and/or glitch free.
Long and Boring:
1) The graphics!...oh god the graphics!! They're absolutely gorgeous maxed out... but it's always the little things that make it truly great:
Amazing PhysX application
- Makes for a lot of great enemy/NPC dynamics in fights and death scenes.
- Awesome light play off particles in the air gives the atmosphere a real life quality
- Motion of clothing looks incredible. It really looks like the characters are wearing the clothes (not just skins that flap around when you move).
2) The volume of people that move around and gather together in huge crowds will amaze you. Seeing several hundred fully rendered and independant civilians all in the same place is one of the coolest parts of this game. Lots of games do crowds, I get that, but it's a sight to see how these masses of people are done in AC Unity.
3) The "RPG" element that Ubisoft put into this game is essentially BS. It's largely a super nerfed and vanilla form of an RPG concept. However, it's a welcome development coming from a franchise that had essentially no prior character development (besides weapons and gear). The reality is that you will eventually have every skill you want and in fairly little time. The only real decision ends up being which skills you want first. There is no personel development to the character, just skill unlocks. This makes for a very minor overall impact to your play style and ultimately goes unoticed as a feature in this game. It's a fun little perk, but largely useless. At least it doesn't make the game worse?
AC has never been about the RPG style of play, so this is hardly a fair criticism. To me, it really seems like this is the kind of game that could do very well if given more depth. It would definitly be more satisfying to spend time playing (or replaying for that matter). So although it was a bit of a cheeseball effort, I give Ubisoft a big thumbs up for even trying to move AC in the right direction.
4) The fighting is defenitly harder in AC Unity than in previous games, so that's a plus. However, with no difficulty adjustment, it can become too easy as you progress in power and skill throughout the game.
- Weapons have a parry skill that gets better as they increase in cost, meaning you can't necessarily parry every attack when you first begin. Dodging/rolling becomes necessary to stay alive.
- Heavy weapons and long weapons have been introduced into AC Unity and both provide a fun change in fighting style that can keep battles fresh after you've mastered one style.
5) THE BEST PART: The absolutely rediculous, cluncky, and completely unnecessary "Abstergo" storyline gets the back shelf for this title. Even Ubisoft has aknowledged how stupid this story line is; they poke fun in-game at the fact that the Abstergo story line is disorienting and distracting to the immersion of the game. Luckily for all of us, this goofy concept is minimized in AC Unity.
Conclusion:
1) 9/10 for the AC line up
2) You need a good GPU to run it with no glitches (I have a GTX 780 3GB).
3) Haters gonna hate, especially console kids.

Q.U.B.E is a first person puzzle platformer where you have the power to manipulate special colored cubes. There's a background story of sorts involving an astronaut inside a massive alien structure, but in practice you are simply solving lots of puzzles involving said cubes.
The visuals are fairly simple but work well enough for a game of this type. Quite fittingly almost everything inside the alien structure is built of smaller cubes.
The voice acting, music and sound effects are all rather average but get the job done.
The game has a nice variety of different puzzle types and it does a great job of introducing new puzzles elements during the campaign. There's some basic platforming and precision jumping too, but the focus is definitely on the puzzles themselves. Luckily the puzzles are generally well designed and interesting.
The cubes of different colors all work in different ways, and combining these effects is usually crucial in solving the puzzles. For example blue cubes act as springboards, red cubes act as extendable platforms and purple cubes let you rotate parts of the level.
Overall the game was fairly easy with only a few trickier puzzles mixed in.
The controls are somewhat unresponsive and this can lead to frustration, especially with the more time-sensitive puzzles.
The writing is not particularly good and the story is frankly forgottable rubbish with some bad science thrown in.
The physics engine is not particularly good and suffers from occasional glitches. At least you usually have the option the reset the puzzle if necessary.
Q.U.B.E certainly has some issues. The story is rather weak, the physics engine has some issues and the controls are not great. I still enjoyed the actual puzzles quite a bit and would recommend the game, especially to fans of first person puzzle games.

Let's start with the bad points. The game has a lot of flaws, but you can overlook those flaws and have a pretty fun time.  For starters, it's a MMORPG with a real money item shop that gives you major advantages over other players, at least in PvE areas.  The classes you can choose from are limited initially, so you will have to level again if you want one of the classes not listed to start with.  You have to spend money in order to unlock all the classes on a single account, but you could potentially start more accounts and alternate between them to access specific classes.  The game sometimes updates just to create major game-ending bugs and server instability.  I had not been able to even play the game today.  Otherwise, I would not have made time for this review.
Now, the good points. It has so much to do!  It's like Minecraft had a baby with Guild Wars 2.  You get raid dungeons, too!  The grinding required to do various activities is tremendous, which is fun in its own way.  You also get to build player-owned houses, club worlds, and a variety of both useful and not-so-useful items.  Crafting is fun and rewards players for collecting vast quantities of various items.  Building a house means making your own personal playground, complete with vents and bouncy blocks.  It's also easy to get others to your base or wherever you are.  Playing with friends in a MMOG has never been this easy before.  The game's performance is also pretty good.  It looks crisp, offers a decent amount of settings, and has a high framerate, even on my very old budget rig.
Overall, the game's good points outweigh its bad points.  It's a fun Minecraft-like MMORPG that offers both official content and player-generated content in a way that is mostly satisfying but not overly so.  It's worth your time and costs no money to play.

Probably unlike most people who picked up the remake of Shadowgate, I never played the original or any of its ports. I'm also not a veteran of point-and-click adventure games. I gave this game a shot because I enjoyed Shadowgate 64 and I'm a sucker for the great artwork of Shadowgate.
What makes Shadowgate feel unique from the few adventure games I've played is the persistent threat of time. You become cursed very early in the game. If uncured, this blight will kill you after a certain number of actions. At first I felt that this discouraged exploration. Indeed it does, but it fits perfectly with the tone of this game, which is one of urgency. From a gameplay perspective, this is somewhat similar to the constant deaths faced in rogue-likes. With each death, the player gains more knowledge to progress through the game with greater efficiency, so the curse no longer becomes a threat after a few playthroughs. But even when the curse is cured, there is always the threat of darkness in the form of your torch. Each turn dims the torch until it is eventually snuffed, resulting in a quick death. I found that on the medium difficulty, there were plenty of torches, but there aren't an infinite supply. Thus, even when one becomes adept at the game, there is still the lingering pressure to move ever onward.
The puzzles in this game cover a range of difficulty from "modern" easy to logic-defyingly challenging. In some regard, the harder puzzles may feel like trial and error, especially if the hint is located in a scroll that you missed but cannot waste the turns to find. Perhaps in these situations, it is best to restart. There are a few situations in which it would be nearly impossible to know what item to use on what object to move forward, but a quick glance at a walkthrough can help.
The three difficulty settings and many achievements add a great degree of replayability to this game. The biggest difference between the difficulty settings is in the difficulty and the number of puzzles. I played on the medium difficulty at first, but I look forward to trying the game on the hardest difficulty to experience all of the puzzles the game has to offer. The achievements also encourage the player to try different play styles, such as being extremely efficient or avoiding killing any goblins. Of course, it helps that the sound, music, and graphics are all good enough to keep the player interested through multiple playthroughs.
After completing the game, I went back and read reviews of the original Shadowgate ports, especially the NES version. Most of the reviews were lukewarm at best and I'm not sure why. Shadowgate has few glaring weaknesses compared to other adventure games (it seems all adventure games have a few puzzles that require strange logic). I'm also seeing mostly lukewarm professional reviews of this remake. My opinion is that anyone interested in a challenging puzzle game with great graphics, music, and lore ought to give Shadowgate a try.

But, if you spend some of your 'supplies' (surprise!!!), you can make a new first aid kit.  Again.
Once again you're kicked out of Dr. Shen's workshop and not allowed to go back in.  But remember, YOU'RE the commander.  You're in command.  Next, you're ordered by the almighty loudspeaker to report to the lab where they ripped a chip out of your brain.  It seems they've discovered something new - they've been running Wargames through your head faster than the WOPR for the past 20 years straight while you floated in a tank.  Hopefully we'll find out why later.  Maybe.
After picking a research project (I finally got to make a choice!!! YESSSSS!!!), you exit the menu and FINALLY you don't get kicked out of the lab.  The doc orders you to report to the 'bridge', but at least he doesn't eject you from the premesis.
I head to the armory, customize my only unwounded joe, and go to customize my first 'new' joe.  He's from England.  So, NATURALLY, he reports for duty wearing a 1800's STYLE TOP HAT.  How do I assign him to Assassin's Creed: Syndicate???
So I proceed to go through the rest of my troops to make sure they aren't wearing anything else too ridiculous for words...I confiscated an X-COM bandana off somebody's face, a pair of mutton chops that would make General Ulysses S. Grant turn green with envy, and A SUIT OF PINK ARMOR.
SERIOUSLY.
Now, the next part is pretty informative - I finally report to the 'bridge' and find out why it's called a bridge.  This base isn't a base at all.  It's a gigantic roving UFO.  Good idea, but they launch it right away.  Seems like a secret worth keeping...but okay.  Let's run with this and see where it goes.

This game, is a piece of memory. A childhood, consumed by puzzle solving, thought provoking death.
Shadowgate is- and is always will be a wonderful game. The original has always been challenging for me, it took me nearly 7 YEARS to beat the original.  I had given up many times, but in the end, I persisted, and succeeded. When I first started, I was young, the complex approaches, or even the most simplest thoughts, hadn't occurred. Getting stuck is the part of the game that will destroy you.
Even today the game on Master mode is a challenge, it stresses to the finest detail, that every aspect is important. For a veteran, every solution is the same, perhaps some have been changed. But the problem is different. The answer is the same, but you still need to solve the problem, understand the question.
You may need to backtrack, and  play much more cautiously. You may find torches to be limited on supply. The game will continue to challenge you, and make you question things, and answers. They're there, sometimes puzzles have more than one sollution. Which often ends to be a pleasant surprise, and quite gratifying, when you learn of it.
I've only managed to get past  the room of mirrors, and into the courtyard on Master Mode.
But the game is .. a good challenge, for a mind, a veteran. The game remains refreshing, and enjoyable just like the original, for the newcomer, it offers multiple difficulties, to help you warm up to the game. The game is unforgiving at times, my only reccomendation is, look at the game's controls. Master hotkeying, and using the controls.
l to look
i for inventory
o for open
u to use
h to hit
g to go
c to close
And so on, this will save a lot of mouse movement, and pains in such developments. F5 is quicksave, etc. You'll find the experience more modern, while maintaining to it's roots.
The music is still wonderful, and amazing, I was worried about the game, concerned that it was ruined, but I caved, and acquired the game, It- is most satisfying, and I don't.. regret it at all.

Cheap.  If I had only one word to describe this game, that's it.  Not naturally difficult, just cheap.  On my first play-through (lasted only a few missions), I was completely caught off guard by some of the "rules" of the game, such as reinforcements that drop off of a helicopter and get a free move before you even have a chance to seek cover, enemy soldiers who run twice the distance you can and still get to stun you, and the need to do the "sneak and throw grenade" tactic all the time.  Oh, I can't forget to mention how annoying the countdown is for many levels.  I loathe that mechanic.
Furthering the cheapness is the need to keep leveling characters without them dying in battle.  Thus, if your best soldiers die, most players will want to reload the game rather than march on.  This mechanic means that if you don't play near perfectly early on, you'll need to start over and make sure that your veteran soldiers live each time.  I even ran into a mission where all 5 of my veteran soldiers were too injured to fight, leaving me with a squad full of rookies.  And 4 rookies vs. about 9 enemies that are all better marksmen equals frustration.
My only remedy would have been playing on "Easy," but as a gamer that always feels like cheating.  Plus, I played XCom on Xbox 360 without nearly this amount of frustration, and even at higher difficulties.
I'm a fan of deep, challenging gameplay, but not when it feels more cheap than organic.  I wish I could get my money back on this one, and I'm really disappointed after enjoying the last XCom so much.
And yes, I'm still playing, since I can't get my money back, and now starting a 3rd playthough on normal.  I'm guessing this will be my last effort to actually enjoy this game, but the same ol' tactics all the time make it somewhat boring, on top of the frustration.

I honestly have no idea why this game has such a negative image. As you can see from my played time I have experienced this game to the fullest and I loved every seccond.
-The game is beautiful on max settings, I have a very powerful rig and have played a lot of games to their highest capability and I struggle to think of many games that are better looking.
-Runs very smooth as well, has the odd crash to desktop but that happens once in maybe 8 hours. When its running it runs great.
-The asthetic of the game is great as well, the world is a little small and you repeat a couple areas with enemies just moved around but to be fair it does fit into the story. They do a fantastic job of making a dark and gritty world. Theres bodies strewn around blood all over the place and building burning. The enemies fit in with the asthetic well, they have dark demonic armor with brutal looking weapons witrh hints of fire and brimstone. They look amazing. The first boss really is a testament to this. The charactger you played (Harken) has great character design, theres lots of little touches that make him a very good character (except his voice acting, some of that is terrible) but he dosent do much talking.
-The armor and the weapons, I have been gaming for 26 years and have never seen more badass armor designs in a game, I seriously mean that. Just look at this
The capes flow and move perfectly as well. Have a quick google and look through the sets you will be impressed by most of them. Some are generic and look crap though but they are very few and far between. I love the weapon designs, they just fit the world perfectly, they have such tiny details on them that add to them so well. Nice variety as well.
-The main issue I have seen from other peoples reviews is the combat system. If you expect to go into this game and roll about like you can in the Dark souls series you are going to be disapointed. If you understand that this game is methodical, you plan your blocks and your rolls. If you manage your tallents and skills along with your inventory well you will be fine. Weapons are very acurate to how you would swing them in real life. A longsword you can swing several times  so you can get away with spamming and a huge Greathammer is a long slow devastating attack. You have to take into account the enemies range, the enemies abilities and if they have a shield etc. If they do use a heavy attack and guard break them, or kick them or use a spell etc. I absolutely adore the combat system.
-The leveling system is actually very robust, you gain xp and can choose to put the xp into skill points or spell points. Skill points increase your main atributes such as strength agility endurance faith etc. Spell points are invested into various abilities in the spell tree you picked at the start of the game along with your armor. Which brings me to another point, it may look like you only have 3 skill trees but the armopr you pick at the start changes things as well. For example you can have Warrior with light medium and heavy armor same with Rogue and Guardian.
Theres many more pros but I dont want to bore you too much!
-The voice acting, every character sounds like they are speaking the words phonetically and dont actually understand the words, it takes you out of the world a little but theres very little talking which leads me to my next point.
-There is very little story, its there just not very well explained. I could probably sum it up in one sentence. So I will SPOILER
-There are a few bugs, nothing massive though. For example if you lock onto a certain bosses head during a certain phase the camera clips through the floor and you can see nothing. Theres a couple sound bugs where a sound stays stuck on and audiologs sometimes have no audio but saving and restarting the game solves these issues and if you want a bity of world building you can acess the audio logs through a menu.
-New game + and ++ are very limited, in NG+ theres a few new trinkets and 1 set of armor for a light armor user but not medium and heavy. That really iritated me at first but the final armors for medium and heavy look so good I stopped caring. But this is important to a lot of people and I totally understand that so be prepared for enemies to scale, a few more audio logs but no new weapons. All you unlock is a 2nd spell tree by entering NG+ and the 3rd and final one on NG++
-The DLC is pretty rubbish, the main one is unlocked later into the game and gives maybe an hour of content your first playthrough but soon as you know the puzzles thats dropped down to 20mins max. The rest are weapon and armor which all look great (especially the armor) but they are starting gear and give you a tiny edge at the begining but thats it since they are soon replaced. The heavy armor is obsolete in about 10mins for example.
-This is a tiny issue but I will put it anyway. The jumping is a bit crap. Theres an element of playforming in the game to reach chests with armor or hidden places etc and when you land you always do this long exagerated roll which more often than not causes you to roll off the other side of where you were jumping. But you dont need to do it often.
This game really is a diamond in the rough, it was plagued by bugs at the start which ruined its reputation. 99% of those have been fixed. I pre ordered this game and stuck it out for 1 playthrough and loved it. I decided to reinstall it a week ago and havent put it down since. This game is, in my eyes, a masterpiece. This is obviously my opinion but hopefully thats an indication of how good this game really is.
There are a lot of people that expected this game to be something different when they picked it up, hack n slash or a standard rpg etc. They were disapointed with that and gave the game a bad review because they didnt do the research or were terrible at the combat system because they were used to a fast paced Dark souls style. This game was marketed as being very similar to Dark souls, which it isnt. The game can be hard but not as hard as higher NG+ cycles in Dark souls games.
All in all this game is an incredibly rewarding experience, and for £15 its a bargin. One full playthrough of full exporation will be a solid 40 hours of enjoyment.
Thanks for reading guys and I hope you decide to give this gem a try. Any questions leave a comment etc il be happy to answer them.

I highly recommend this game. To me it has one of the best plots of all video games i ever played.
The Story and the plot are .. just great.  Never saw something this sad and yet, you want to get going and going. Death always lies right around the corner and you really have to fear that something bad could happen and you still want to know what will happen next. The developers made a really good job. I think this game could be something even for people that despise the zombie genre in general, because it isn't so much about the Zombies but more about the charactrs and the drama.
The characters are all great. The story itself is about Clementine a 8 year old girl that is alone in a world full of Zombies. You play as Lee. A guy who was about to go to jail for murder, but doesn't get there..... Don#t want to spoil that much, but in the end you meet Clementine and Lee tries to protect her. Especially that is what makes the plot and story so great. At least to me, it made me really want to protect that little girl. You really start to care for her and so does lee. The dynamics between these two are awesome.
The other characters are very well written as well. Evey character you meet has a unique personality and yet, it isn't easy to figure them all completely out.
The graphics are "unique". It is more a comic look. Not the preference of everybody, but it fits this dark plot quite well. Of course they are a bit outdated, but the comic style makes it look younger than it really is.
The mechanics are rudmentary. You actually use 4 keys and the mouse. That its about it. In the end it is more like a tv show than a game. Which isn't really bad, because of the story and the characters. You actually just walk around and solve some puzzles. You talk to people and this way keep the plot going. Here and there you have to shoot zombies or have to click something in a short period of time. Those "minigames" felt not overdone and mixed the game a bit up. Yes the game could give you more controls over Lee, but in the end it is about the characters and story and not the game mechanics.
There aren't any bugs i noticed. Isn't that hard to create bugs anyway. Since every scene and possible outcome is scripted anyway.
If i would have one wish, i would like to see that your choices do matter a bit more. Yes your coices matter quite a lot for the ongoing plot. Who do you side with, who do you distrust, but a bit more impact wouldn't have hurt.
Anyway, i recommend this game to anyone who has the money and seeks a sad, but yet powerful story with great characters and, of course, zombies :)

If you answered "Yes" to any of the above questions, then
Not convinced? Well here is why:
1.
It has been in development for years, and very little has been accomplished. Most notably in the past 12 months. So little progress in fact that many players believe the game is dead. It hasn't recieved even a minor official update in the last 9 months and counting.
2.
The creators made a public announcement a while back meant to sooth supporters in which they stated "Chucklefish could fund Starbound for another 9 years at least.” They also explained that "even if Starbound and Chucklefish never make another dime, the company has enough money in the bank to pay for office costs, employee salaries, and other expenditures." That would be reassuring if any tangible progress has been made since then. They post update blogs on the official website weekly, detailing what they're supposedly working on, but since none of it has been added to a stable release we can only go on faith that they're not just sitting on our money.
3.
When accused of slacking the Developers tell players to download the "nightly build". This is an incredibly unstable version which they themselves describe as "more beta than the beta". Unfortunately, it's so broken it's not easily playable. The starter missions are incomplete and impossible to finish, requiring console commands to progress and all the while avoiding obscure/mudane actions to prevent crashes. This could almost be tolerable if these same major issues haven't existed since the very first "nightly" builds. None have been fixed.  Remember those update blogs I mentioned before? They are all about minor cosmetic improvements, or about some new items they've mocked up. The game's basic progression and structure sits ignored and unfinished as they post screenshots of a gun shaped like a crayola crayon (seriously). It speaks volumes about their priorities.
Combine all these issues, and it becomes apparent that the Starbound team cares very little about their fan base. If you are still on the fence, I urge you hold off and keep an eye out for when (or if) this game comes out of early access. Make your decision then.

Shadowgate is a re-imagining of the point-and-click adventure game released almost three decades ago, under the same name, on NES and Mac. Given these origins, your motivations for venturing into Castle Shadowgate are about what you would expect: you are a hero who must defeat an evil warlock. The graphics, music and the majority of puzzles have been reworked; new, voice-acted cutscenes and story elements have been peppered throughout; while the mysterious atmosphere and memorable locations of the original remain intact, along with the option to use the retro soundtrack.
While most of the information needed to reach puzzle solutions does lie somewhere within the game, it is not explicit in its detail: clues are often cryptic, making experimentation necessary—experimentation that results in death just as often as a satisfying solution. Shadowgate is a game in which the reaper is literally waiting around every corner for you to make your next mistake. The only difference is that, this time, it’s almost as if you’re collecting the various deaths since you’re rewarded with achievements for experiencing them and special cutscenes for discovering the hidden ones.
On Master difficulty, the puzzles are as challenging as the name implies but often in a manner just as obtuse as in the original Shadowgate; fortunately, the developers included two lesser difficulties that make the game more approachable and groom you for your playthrough of Master—if you’re still interested by then. An optional tutorial and a talking skull companion that gives hints upon request, the equivalent of the “hint” command from the original, also help to alleviate the difficulty.
Dependent upon how you like your point-and-clicks, Shadowgate is potentially flawed: Turns are limited because the torches that keep you alive are limited in both number and duration, complicated by the fact that you’re unavoidably afflicted with a curse very early on, which will kill you if not cured in time. This is fairly forgiving on lower difficulty settings but, on Master, it’s very easy to waste enough time searching for the cure that you damn yourself in the process and must either go back to an earlier save or restart the entire game. The facts that many items aren’t necessary to progress and anything that isn’t a simple inspection of your surroundings will consume a turn, combined with the experimentation-based puzzle solving, where items must frequently be combined with each other or the environment, could make this adventure an exercise in frustration for some.
If you enjoyed the original Shadowgate, this is a no-brainer. If you hated the original Shadowgate, this isn’t likely to change your mind, though the lesser difficulties will undoubtedly be less offensive. For those who haven’t played the game, nostalgia aside and despite its difficulty, it is a very memorable game that is full of mystery and your enjoyment will largely depend on how much trial and error you are willing to endure in an adventure game.

I honestly have no idea why this game has such a negative image. As you can see from my played time I have experienced this game to the fullest and I loved every seccond.
-The game is beautiful on max settings, I have a very powerful rig and have played a lot of games to their highest capability and I struggle to think of many games that are better looking.
-Runs very smooth as well, has the odd crash to desktop but that happens once in maybe 8 hours. When its running it runs great.
-The asthetic of the game is great as well, the world is a little small and you repeat a couple areas with enemies just moved around but to be fair it does fit into the story. They do a fantastic job of making a dark and gritty world. Theres bodies strewn around blood all over the place and building burning. The enemies fit in with the asthetic well, they have dark demonic armor with brutal looking weapons witrh hints of fire and brimstone. They look amazing. The first boss really is a testament to this. The charactger you played (Harken) has great character design, theres lots of little touches that make him a very good character (except his voice acting, some of that is terrible) but he dosent do much talking.
-The armor and the weapons, I have been gaming for 26 years and have never seen more badass armor designs in a game, I seriously mean that. Just look at this
The capes flow and move perfectly as well. Have a quick google and look through the sets you will be impressed by most of them. Some are generic and look crap though but they are very few and far between. I love the weapon designs, they just fit the world perfectly, they have such tiny details on them that add to them so well. Nice variety as well.
-The main issue I have seen from other peoples reviews is the combat system. If you expect to go into this game and roll about like you can in the Dark souls series you are going to be disapointed. If you understand that this game is methodical, you plan your blocks and your rolls. If you manage your tallents and skills along with your inventory well you will be fine. Weapons are very acurate to how you would swing them in real life. A longsword you can swing several times  so you can get away with spamming and a huge Greathammer is a long slow devastating attack. You have to take into account the enemies range, the enemies abilities and if they have a shield etc. If they do use a heavy attack and guard break them, or kick them or use a spell etc. I absolutely adore the combat system.
-The leveling system is actually very robust, you gain xp and can choose to put the xp into skill points or spell points. Skill points increase your main atributes such as strength agility endurance faith etc. Spell points are invested into various abilities in the spell tree you picked at the start of the game along with your armor. Which brings me to another point, it may look like you only have 3 skill trees but the armopr you pick at the start changes things as well. For example you can have Warrior with light medium and heavy armor same with Rogue and Guardian.
Theres many more pros but I dont want to bore you too much!
-The voice acting, every character sounds like they are speaking the words phonetically and dont actually understand the words, it takes you out of the world a little but theres very little talking which leads me to my next point.
-There is very little story, its there just not very well explained. I could probably sum it up in one sentence. So I will SPOILER
-There are a few bugs, nothing massive though. For example if you lock onto a certain bosses head during a certain phase the camera clips through the floor and you can see nothing. Theres a couple sound bugs where a sound stays stuck on and audiologs sometimes have no audio but saving and restarting the game solves these issues and if you want a bity of world building you can acess the audio logs through a menu.
-New game + and ++ are very limited, in NG+ theres a few new trinkets and 1 set of armor for a light armor user but not medium and heavy. That really iritated me at first but the final armors for medium and heavy look so good I stopped caring. But this is important to a lot of people and I totally understand that so be prepared for enemies to scale, a few more audio logs but no new weapons. All you unlock is a 2nd spell tree by entering NG+ and the 3rd and final one on NG++
-The DLC is pretty rubbish, the main one is unlocked later into the game and gives maybe an hour of content your first playthrough but soon as you know the puzzles thats dropped down to 20mins max. The rest are weapon and armor which all look great (especially the armor) but they are starting gear and give you a tiny edge at the begining but thats it since they are soon replaced. The heavy armor is obsolete in about 10mins for example.
-This is a tiny issue but I will put it anyway. The jumping is a bit crap. Theres an element of playforming in the game to reach chests with armor or hidden places etc and when you land you always do this long exagerated roll which more often than not causes you to roll off the other side of where you were jumping. But you dont need to do it often.
This game really is a diamond in the rough, it was plagued by bugs at the start which ruined its reputation. 99% of those have been fixed. I pre ordered this game and stuck it out for 1 playthrough and loved it. I decided to reinstall it a week ago and havent put it down since. This game is, in my eyes, a masterpiece. This is obviously my opinion but hopefully thats an indication of how good this game really is.
There are a lot of people that expected this game to be something different when they picked it up, hack n slash or a standard rpg etc. They were disapointed with that and gave the game a bad review because they didnt do the research or were terrible at the combat system because they were used to a fast paced Dark souls style. This game was marketed as being very similar to Dark souls, which it isnt. The game can be hard but not as hard as higher NG+ cycles in Dark souls games.
All in all this game is an incredibly rewarding experience, and for £15 its a bargin. One full playthrough of full exporation will be a solid 40 hours of enjoyment.
Thanks for reading guys and I hope you decide to give this gem a try. Any questions leave a comment etc il be happy to answer them.

I've been dreading playing this after what a phenomenal clusterfućk the first game was, and how much time IGN spent sucking on their nutz...
But I'm finally playing this.  And I'll give it a chance.
_____________________________________________________________
Mission 1:  The Sacrifice of Ana
Well, giving this game a chance was obviously a mistake.  So mission one...the game tells you precisely where to go.  You can't take cover in ANY spot other than where the game tells you.  Even if you know that the right move is to advance on the outer flanks and catch the enemy in a crossfire - NO!  You WILL march your troops right up the middle of an alleyway and attack them from dead center.
And so, Ana Martinez is dead.  Whomever that was.  And apparently, I'm not allowed to review this game until I've played it for 5 minutes.  On Steam only.
The entire opening 'mission' basically consists of the game telling you exactly where to go and when.  It's basically a cutscene that the game pretends is offering some kind of choice.  You must shoot who the game tells you.  You must take the cover the game says to.  Even if you know you're marching your people right into a crossfire.
The dweeb in the green X-COM cardigan from the first game shows up and drags a corpse out.  Since the 2nd trooper you started the mission with is no longer important, the game forces you to leave him with his♥♥♥♥♥♥swinging in the wind.  He could take cover in the doorway of the building you're occupying, but that would never work because he might actually surivive.  Godforbid.
The dweeb [pbuh] drags a corpse out of the building (oh wait...I mean *YOU* do...because you totally have control over the mission...now bring the corpse to the skyranger)
_____________________________________________________________
Base 1:  Obey us, 'Commander'
So it turns out you're the corpse that dweeb carried out of the building.  Everybody calls you 'Commander', with heavy emphasis on the word.  This is apparently sarcasm because you don't seem to be in charge of anything.  You go to the lab, the game tells you what to research.  You go to the armory, the game tells you who to promote.  You aren't allowed to even LEAVE until you follow the game's orders.  But, of course, you're in *ahem* COMMAND...
Once you promote your sole suriviving trooper, you are immediately kicked out of the armory and not allowed to go back in.  But you're in command.  A voice on a loudspeaker tells you to report to the 'bridge'.  The 'bridge' of a stationary 'base' in the middle of the 'desert'.  Again, you cannot go ANYWHERE else but the 'bridge'.  But you're in command.
You enter the bridge, which immediately sets off an alarm, and dweeb tells the computer something about an echelon.  The computer says it's transferring command.  Maybe THIS explains why you haven't even been in charge of your own taking of a♥♥♥♥♥♥
Dweeb tells you about a mission to snatch some kind of power converter, and the game immediately has all the base's equipment start malfunctioning.  Sort of like an employee calling in sick, immediately following the word 'sick' with *cough* *cough*.  Apparently these people have never heard of plutonium.
This brings you to a screen where you equip 4 troopers.  That's right, FOUR.  Apparently, the five troopers you had in missions from the first game were too much.  Humanity has advanced so much that now, all wars can be won by FOUR dudes.  Boy, warfare sure has advanced a lot since King Leonidas and the Battle of Thermopylae.  Back then, it took a whopping 300 dudes to win a war.  Now, we've advanced so much that it only takes 4.
_____________________________________________________________
Mission 2:  I Got the Powah!!!
Now THIS looks like you're in charge.  You're presented with your mighty 4, and 3 options appear at the bottom of the screen.  Apparently, you can make 'utility items', weapons, and armor available from other troopers.  FINALLY some flexibility in inventor...oh.  Wait.  Nevermind.  Same bullshìt as the previous game - only certain types of troops can pick up an assault rifle, autocannon, etc.  If you're a rookie, it's impossible for you to even PICK UP another type of weapon.
Also, it's impossible for any X-COM trooper to wear a helmet, apparently.  This one actually makes sense - why bother?  Nothing important there to protect...fortunately, some of them can wear durags (white troops only, so far).  Others can wear baseball caps, as long as they have a ponytail that can fit through the sizing adjuster to keep the cap on.
Upon landing, you'll note that all the research you did into plasma weaponry and Elerium-115 (if they even bothered including that in the original X-COM) has been put to excellent use.  You'll quickly disembark the Skyranger and everybody quickly draws their...solid-propellant ammunition assault rifles...because...reasons.  How realistic.  At least Terror From The Deep had the excuse that the war was being fought underwater.  What excuse do these idiots have for not remembering or saving ANYTHING from the first game???  Not so much as a god damn plasma Derringer?
WHAT THE HELL???  I KNEW they were gonna screw this game up.  And once again IGN just dropped to their knees to lick the nutsacks of the losers who ruined the X-COM franchise for the sake of a bunch of X-BOX players who are too stupid to figure out how to use a mouse.  Why couldn't they just name this piece of crap 'X-BOX/Playstation Panderer 2'?
_____________________________________________________________
Base 2:  All Your Save Game Are Belong To Us
After a fierce battle of the 'saved-games' you return to your base to meet your chief engineer, named Chen.  Because Asian chicks always like tinkering with machines.  Don't you remember Fallout 4: Far Harbor?  Nuff said...
Remember all that research you did on medical kits and stun guns in X-COM 1?  Well, apparently somebody ate all that research, then squatted down over the deepest part of the ocean and took a big, fat, hairy, moldy, crusty, nasty♥♥♥♥♥dump.  Poof.  Gone.  But, if you spend some of your 'supplies' (surprise!!!), you can make a new first aid kit.  Again.
Once again you're kicked out of Dr. Shen's workshop and not allowed to go back in.  But remember, YOU'RE the commander.  You're in command.  Next, you're ordered by the almighty loudspeaker to report to the lab where they ripped a chip out of your brain.  It seems they've discovered something new - they've been running Wargames through your head faster than the WOPR for the past 20 years straight while you floated in a tank.  Hopefully we'll find out why later.  Maybe.
After picking a research project (I finally got to make a choice!!! YESSSSS!!!), you exit the menu and FINALLY you don't get kicked out of the lab.  The doc orders you to report to the 'bridge', but at least he doesn't eject you from the premesis.
I head to the armory, customize my only unwounded joe, and go to customize my first 'new' joe.  He's from England.  So, NATURALLY, he reports for duty wearing a 1800's STYLE TOP HAT.  How do I assign him to Assassin's Creed: Syndicate???
So I proceed to go through the rest of my troops to make sure they aren't wearing anything else too ridiculous for words...I confiscated an X-COM bandana off somebody's face, a pair of mutton chops that would make General Ulysses S. Grant turn green with envy, and A SUIT OF PINK ARMOR.
SERIOUSLY.
Now, the next part is pretty informative - I finally report to the 'bridge' and find out why it's called a bridge.  This base isn't a base at all.  It's a gigantic roving UFO.  Good idea, but they launch it right away.  Seems like a secret worth keeping...but okay.  Let's run with this and see where it goes.

Cheap.  If I had only one word to describe this game, that's it.  Not naturally difficult, just cheap.  On my first play-through (lasted only a few missions), I was completely caught off guard by some of the "rules" of the game, such as reinforcements that drop off of a helicopter and get a free move before you even have a chance to seek cover, enemy soldiers who run twice the distance you can and still get to stun you, and the need to do the "sneak and throw grenade" tactic all the time.  Oh, I can't forget to mention how annoying the countdown is for many levels.  I loathe that mechanic.
Furthering the cheapness is the need to keep leveling characters without them dying in battle.  Thus, if your best soldiers die, most players will want to reload the game rather than march on.  This mechanic means that if you don't play near perfectly early on, you'll need to start over and make sure that your veteran soldiers live each time.  I even ran into a mission where all 5 of my veteran soldiers were too injured to fight, leaving me with a squad full of rookies.  And 4 rookies vs. about 9 enemies that are all better marksmen equals frustration.
My only remedy would have been playing on "Easy," but as a gamer that always feels like cheating.  Plus, I played XCom on Xbox 360 without nearly this amount of frustration, and even at higher difficulties.
I'm a fan of deep, challenging gameplay, but not when it feels more cheap than organic.  I wish I could get my money back on this one, and I'm really disappointed after enjoying the last XCom so much.
And yes, I'm still playing, since I can't get my money back, and now starting a 3rd playthough on normal.  I'm guessing this will be my last effort to actually enjoy this game, but the same ol' tactics all the time make it somewhat boring, on top of the frustration.

So something that's been on my mind recently regarding XCOM 2...
There are a lot of ladies in it. And by "a lot," I actually mean equal.
Of the main characters, your lead engineer and pilot are women (traditionally masculine roles).
Your gender as the Commander is not assumed, and you are never reference by a gender-specific pronoun. (In the intro video, the medical readouts display a male and female body, with a question mark between them.)
In the tutorial, you have four soldiers, two of which are women (one Irish, one Latina).
Your new engineers, scientists, and soldiers are randomly assigned male or female genders and random nationalities (different ethnicities, voices, appearances). The VIPs you get assigned to rescue (or subdue) are randomly male or female.
As far as I can tell, when the characters are created, it literally feels like somebody flipped a coin and selected the gender—and I cannot express how fully I am 100% okay with that.
If a turn-based strategy military tactics video game can do this, there is zero reason that you can't do the same in your creative works.
This is not to say that it's a flawless game as far as representation or diversity goes, of course (body diversity and non-binary genders immediately come to mind). But goddamn it, I am pleased to see steps being made, and game studios doing better. Keep at it.

I wasn't sure I would like this, because I'm not really into horror or Cthulhu. I prefer my RPGs to be more standard fantasy or sci-fi.
I purchased purely on the strength of the reviews, and I'm glad I did. The game sports a fantastic turn-based engine and AAA attention to detail in all respects; I especially liked upgrading my town and the idea that heroes were expendable, though you do invest large sums of gold into a set few. The puzzle-like boss battles were also great fun -- I wiped on the pig boss on my first try, and laughed the whole time.  Oops...better not do THAT again (you'll understand what I mean if you make the same mistake).
Learning to master the mechanics was a joy, but once I felt I'd conquered them, the game started to drag a bit. Although it has tons of atmosphere, its one weakness is its fairly barebones story, and I stopped playing before I'd finished because I wasn't all that interested in seeing the plot to the end. Still, I got 30+ hours of pure joy from the game and I expect I'll finish it some day.
I'm hoping to see more from these devs, and to see this engine used for RPGs in other genres.

+ High difficulty videogame with roguelike elements
+ Fair duration: expect at least 30-40++ hours of gameplay
 
- RNG will capitalize on your mistakes

- Demoralizing if you are not well prepared

 this game features which is one of the best, the most satisfying and the most deep combat system I have ever seen in a turn based combat videogame. Not only the four skills you have to select from each one of your four heroes is unique, but also each of them can reach different enemy positions and must be used from a different place too. So positioning matters a lot and if your party is surprised or shuffled out, you will be screwed. You have to carefully select your party each week and combine their skills. Remember there are 4 heroes and usually the enemies appear in groups of four too. Ah, and the corpses of the defeated enemies remain in the very same position where they die, so you need to remove them with some specific skills or waste some time. Each turn the initiative is determined with a random roll plus the speed stat of each hero, so it’s not a fixed order and you will be forced to carefully plan each turn in advance and improvise.
 
not only your heroes can die if they lose their health but also they can get afflicted if they suffer enough stress. Once a threshold is reached they can get afflicted and start to generate more stress to their fellow party members, insulting them when they act, acting on their own, etc. If they keep receiving stress they will finally die by a heart attack.
 
each hero will start with some random positive and negative quirks and during your adventures they can acquire more. Some of them make your character better, but the bad ones do the opposite and may also make your character touch blindly every curio he finds with catastrophic results. You can treat them while in town, but that involves a big waste of valuable gold…
 
 during your exploring in dungeons you will find many different interactive curios. Some of them provide treasures or heal stress if you interact with them with the correct item, but others could hide a lethal trap or add a negative quirk to your adventurer, so choose wisely.
 
 There is a light meter that provides bonuses or penalties to your party depending on the amount of light. You have to buy torches each week and use them if you wish… or you can take risks and fight in complete darkness, which gives you more loot, but make you more vulnerable to monsters and ambushes.
 
 Darkest Dungeon forces you to decide carefully where to invest. Would you prefer more recruits to choose from each week, better stress healing and medical treatment buildings, or more skillful heroes? Everything costs heirlooms and gold, and if you try to upgrade all at once you will be lacking on both soon. Use your resources in the buildings you need and improve and heal the characters you prefer to get ready and sane.
 
 The savefile is automatically overwritten by your progression. This means that you can’t save the game manually. If one of your heroes die not only he is done forever, but also you lose all the investment made on him. The dungeons are also randomly generated each time whith some exceptions. Oh, and there are some random Town Events which can give you an advantage or disadvantage for the upcoming week.
 
Darkest Dungeon is a hardcore, roguelike difficult dungeon crawler videogame requiring skill, but with a huge amount of RNG involved.
But because of that, even with three difficulty levels, some players not used to turn based games, RNG or both, can be overwhelmed. If you read some other reviews proclaiming this is ALL about RNG, an unbalanced mesh, etc., please don’t trust them: they are wrong. They just don’t understand the mechanics well enough or they don’t know how to play the game properly, and thus got demoralized soon before learning how to deal with the RNG, which exists indeed, but it’s not as determining as they say in absolutely any way.
Even if you are an experimented turn based gamer you will be punished sometimes too. That means that you can have a perfect geared party but sooner or later you will miss a couple of attacks. You will be hit by some critical blows in a row, all landing on the same high-level, well developed character, and he will die just in the blink of an eye before you can heal it or retreat. Lost. Forever. So deal with it and don’t get salty. Learn from it. That’s called RNG and that happens.
The difference between a good and a bad player is that the bad player not only cannot accept a bit of RNG, but also he is not aware of his minor mistakes. He is not as bad as an ugly player —which makes big mistakes—, but he makes “invisible” mistakes from time to time. Once he commits a couple of them, he is fully exposed to the RNG and he will get salty because he thinks the game is always cheating him and he lacks the knowledge to blame himself for his minor mistakes. Sometimes of course you can’t do anything to prevent a disaster in Darkest Dungeon —and that is what makes this game good—, but in most situations you can. Losing a hero because of RNG is not a big deal, but if this happens very frequently to you and not to other better players, you are doing something wrong, hands down. You have to ask yourself:
Didn’t you use a bandage to remove that bleeding?
Did you buy enough provisions?
Did you push too much when you should have retreated?
Are you using the correct trinkets and party combinations? Are you selecting their skills well?
Did you hit for 3 in spite of stunning that dangerous enemy?
Did you lose your first turn healing a minor wound despite killing a guy?
Did you spread your first hits when you should have focus on one enemy?
Did you get ambushed because you had a low scouting chance during your low torch run?
Did you equip that luring “+damage” trinket thinking it was OP and didn’t realize about the “-ACC” and “–SPEED” lines, forcing your character to miss and act the last every turn?
Did your character really get mad because of the last RNG hit he received? Or because you didn’t remove this quirk and that made him touch a stress curio 5 minutes before?
 
So think very carefully about everything I have said. Ask yourself what kind of person you really are —if you are patient to learn, mature enough and capable of self-criticism; or if you always find someone to blame—, and decide for yourself if this game is for you. I recommend this game not only based on your tastes as usually, but also on which kind of person you are in real life.

Super Sanctum TD is a low budget Sanctum series spin-off that lets you play a “retro” style 2D tower defense game instead of the usual Sanctum mix of tactical tower defense and engaging first-person shooting. If you’ve played either of the full-fledged Sanctum titles, you’ll immediately be familiar with the towers, the enemies, setting and soundtrack. However, Coffee Stain Studios may have pushed the “retro” thing too far. While the graphics and the soundtrack are pleasing, there’s no widescreen support and the sound effects are not only atrocious, but after a while they get pretty irritating. There’s really no reason for this game to be this low budget.
The game plays like a typical 2D tower defense game with a few twists. There’s a decent number of towers although less than in the main series. The usual staples are here: gatling gun, laser towers, etc. You even get the slow and amp fields from the original Sanctum which for some reason didn’t appear in last year’s sequel. The aliens are back as well and there’s less of them as well. They range from big brutes, fast chargers, annoying flying ones and big bosses. The objective is to build mazes and place your towers in a way that’s most efficient in destroying as much aliens as quickly as possible before they get to the core.
Keeping in line with the hands on approach from the main series, you also have a number of skills at your disposal which you can use during the alien onslaught. For example, you can set up mines, freeze a group of aliens, make them hover in the air for a limited amount of time, strike them with lightning, send them backwards for a bit and so on. All of these skills have varying cooldowns so you need to use them at the most opportune time.
There’s not much content here. The single-player campaign spans 15 missions that you’ll be able to finish in under 10 hours on the normal setting. After that you can play each level on hard or in survival, but as far as game modes go, that’s about it. This is a low budget spin-off that never pretends to be anything else which is reflected in its price as well. The full price is only 3,99 euros, but it’s not unusual to see it slashed by 90%. And if you sell the trading cards, it’s likely that you’ll break even.
In the end, Super Sanctum TD is a solid tower defense game that’s worth playing as it manages to deliver that tactical and addictive experience that such games aspire to offer. And even though it’s too low budget and extremely light on content, at that price you really can’t go wrong with this one.

TL;DR: Buy Lords of the Fallen if you have a decent PC to run it on
A lot of people bash this game, as you can probably see up there under the user reviews percentages.
Most of those people are folks that live, breathe, eat and sleep Dark Souls or one of the other souls games in general (or bought it on launch day, more on that in a minute ) and as a result they spew bad reviews at it simply because its a similar game/competition, not harcore enough or simply "Not the same!", Its rather unfortunate really.
Lords of the Fallen was really buggy on launch, like game destroying buggy, but now all of those bugs have been fixed and now the game works flawlessly. Having put 20+ hours into it I havent encountered a single bug or issue since it was patched up, like this "animation lag" or "crash" people falsely throw at this game nowadays ( once again, to make it less appealing than a Souls game because of blatant bias )
Having a high end of average rig, I get a super stable 60fps when playing, and not only does it run smoothly the game looks amazing, so amazing on ultra, especially with its later armour designs  that frankly Im disapointed that Dark Souls 3 didnt end up looking this good. Animation quality with the exception of one or two characters is great and frankly its one of the few games wearing a cape actually looks cool as opposed to it looking like a sack of buggy Gmod crap.
Gameplay and combat are pretty much what you expect, its a souls style game, a big open-ish area to area world. Combat consists of the usual light attack, heavy attack, block and then a parry/special shield move, also with a block-breaker, spriting, rolling and jump/lunge attacks. Dodging works just fine but heavier armour makes your dodge less viable etc etc, less emphasis on range, though you do get a ranged weapon eventually.
Kill bad guys and fight a boss, if you die you lose all your experience until you can go visit the spot where you died to get said experience back, die again and its all gone. Stats n' the like work a little differently, but the idea behind them is the same, use gained EXP to level up, but if you hold onto your experience without visiting and saving your progress at a checkpoint you gain a multiplier to your EXP, which is good when you need to farm for levels and cuts out on some that needless busy-work time.
While Lords doesnt have any multiplayer components, it places more emphasis on the story, and while the narrative is 'okay' thats where it all falls short. The main characters themselves with the exception of your main guy Harken, are sort've shoddily done. But there is dialogue choices and lil' sidequests where you have to make a decision that affects the reward you gain at the end. If you dont care so much about narrative as you do gameplay, you wont mind how bad the story is that much.
Bosses are fun, each one with a little secret 'extra' way to beat them to gain a boss-item/weapon from them, the secrets can be fun to find even if some of them are somewhat missable or hard to figure out. Quest-lines, hidden secret weapons and armour, runes to upgrade you weapons and armours with, its all just filled with really good stuff.
If you have a decent rig/desktop PC to run it on, and you want something new and fresh from the Dark Souls monotony, then just buy Lords of the Fallen,

Warcube is a simple game based off of popular systems found in other games, like Shadow of Mordor and Mount and Blade. It includes top down camera that provides a nice view of your character, the "Warcube", as he slo-mo kills his way around levels that can be entered from an overworld.

The best part is that there isn't any true meta to the game, any combination can work.
Not only is the game itself a blast to play, but the developer is also trying his best to communitcate with the public to fix and improve the game. Each update brings more fun gameplay and hotfixes are commonly released to fix any issue that might arrise from the new patch.
