Finally, an adventure game that lives up to the difficulty of the old point and click adventure games.
Once in a while you see a game advertised as "old school adventure puzzle," and what do you find? The game is too easy. The puzzles are straightforward, too easily solved, and there's never enough death to punish the player. Sometimes the game won't even kill the player at all. So when a remake of the original Shadowgate was announced, my one fear was that it was now going to be too easy. Little did I know the game would be every bit as difficult as the original.
It's as difficult as the original, but not quite as brutal. The original Shadowgate sometimes had passages you could move into that existed only to kill you the moment you went into them. Or it had traps that came out of nowhere with no hint you were walking into a trap. In this manner, Shadowgate has done away with the cheap kills, doing away with the need to constantly save in every room.
Some gamers may not be able to embrace this style of gaming anymore. Its point and click and the gameplay revolves entirely on selecting verbs to interact with the objects, like "use sword on goblin." But for me, this is pure good nostalgia. Shadowgate is a game I grew up with and this is a great return to form. It's close enough to the original to push all the nostalgia buttons, but it has its own new cool style as well. The puzzles are familiar, but never quite the same as the original game. In my own subjective opinion I couldn't have asked for a better remake. I only hope they give Deja Vu and Uninvited the same treatment.

From the constant narrator, to the story, to the endgame choices, I felt myself drawn to it's characters and style. You get to know more about a world you only experience through the narrator's account, and even then, it sounds like the most amazing civilization ever created.
It's gameplay is also very good, although it may suffer from control problems sometimes. It's a kind of cross between Diablo and Zelda. It's upgrades keep things ever fresh, and the game is constantly challenging you with every new map.
Bastion really desevers to be played. It's a masterpiece.

This video isn't in your face gay.
As a straight white male I can find that offputting and exclusionary, but I was prepared based on the information at hand.
As it turns out it's just a documentary about people who would like to be able to play games that are representative of their thoughts and desires, and are maybe just a bit sick of 90% of games being about male power fantasies or saving a damsel in distress.
There seems to be a backlash from straight male gamers who also don't want their games to be filled with a whole lot of gay stuff being forced down their throat.
In essence, both groups want the same thing.
They both want a safe place without things that make them uncomfortable.
As more and more games offer freedom of choice and restrictions of typical games disappear, I think both groups can be satisfied at being able to play games how they want to play.
As a straight gamer moving into game design, I'll definitely try to make games as open and accessible as possible, and give people the option to turn off features that make them feel uncomfortable, regardless of their background.
Also, I have a general problem with authority so I don't like games that force me down a narrow path.
This doco helped me understand one of many minorities that exist in western media, and hopefully in future we can be more inclusive of people from all walks of life, sexual/gender/personal/physical orientation, race, size, religion, whatever, without needing to force it at people, but instead to let them experience what they wish to experience at their own pace.
Including straight white western males like myself.

Gaming in Color is a documentary about the gay gaming culture. I donated to the kickstarter of it a couple of years ago, looking forward to a documentary that covers an aspect of who I identify as, and I'm glad it got made.
The documentary discusses aspects of the gayming community, and in particular some of the difficulties (and successes) it has had.  It interviews a number of gaymers - I agreed with much of it, though not all of it, and there were some insightful things said (not just about the gayming community and the problems it faces, but occasionally about gaming in general.
It addressed a number of issues, most of those that I would have wanted addressed, although some not in as much depth as I would have liked, but given that it's only an hour long, that's not suprising - this serves as more of a springboard for discussion.  It discusses the (lack of) representation in games, the harrasment of gamers online, the struggles of feeling accepted, the creation of safe spaces, reasons why some gamers gravitated to gaming, peoples experiences, and so on.
I would have liked to hear about more people's personal experiences (this could have been an excellent space to make people who aren't LGBT gain empathy in the issues faced), some more discussion about the history of the issue (eg, those rare LGBT characters in gaming that were almost exclusively negatively portrayed, EA's LGBT conference, more coverage about GaymerX (since the documentary clearly was made during it)), the proposing of more LGBT people being involved in the creation of gaming to try to address the problem of representation, etc.   The documentary also focused on video games (thankfully also including some PC games), but overlooked tabletop gaming - while it doesn't face as many of the issues that video gaming does (probably in part because it's played face-to-face), it still should have deserved a mention.
Overall, this is a good documentary to give you some insight into the gayming community and the issues it faces.

I highly recommend this game. To me it has one of the best plots of all video games i ever played.
The Story and the plot are .. just great.  Never saw something this sad and yet, you want to get going and going. Death always lies right around the corner and you really have to fear that something bad could happen and you still want to know what will happen next. The developers made a really good job. I think this game could be something even for people that despise the zombie genre in general, because it isn't so much about the Zombies but more about the charactrs and the drama.
The characters are all great. The story itself is about Clementine a 8 year old girl that is alone in a world full of Zombies. You play as Lee. A guy who was about to go to jail for murder, but doesn't get there..... Don#t want to spoil that much, but in the end you meet Clementine and Lee tries to protect her. Especially that is what makes the plot and story so great. At least to me, it made me really want to protect that little girl. You really start to care for her and so does lee. The dynamics between these two are awesome.
The other characters are very well written as well. Evey character you meet has a unique personality and yet, it isn't easy to figure them all completely out.
The graphics are "unique". It is more a comic look. Not the preference of everybody, but it fits this dark plot quite well. Of course they are a bit outdated, but the comic style makes it look younger than it really is.
The mechanics are rudmentary. You actually use 4 keys and the mouse. That its about it. In the end it is more like a tv show than a game. Which isn't really bad, because of the story and the characters. You actually just walk around and solve some puzzles. You talk to people and this way keep the plot going. Here and there you have to shoot zombies or have to click something in a short period of time. Those "minigames" felt not overdone and mixed the game a bit up. Yes the game could give you more controls over Lee, but in the end it is about the characters and story and not the game mechanics.
There aren't any bugs i noticed. Isn't that hard to create bugs anyway. Since every scene and possible outcome is scripted anyway.
If i would have one wish, i would like to see that your choices do matter a bit more. Yes your coices matter quite a lot for the ongoing plot. Who do you side with, who do you distrust, but a bit more impact wouldn't have hurt.
Anyway, i recommend this game to anyone who has the money and seeks a sad, but yet powerful story with great characters and, of course, zombies :)

However, recent events mean I can no longer recommend this game. Bethesda has shown themselves to be a hostile force to their community with Creation Club. Not only are the current selection of 'curated mini-DLCs' completely laughable at the prices they charge, the big name items even go against the supposed rules Bethesda themselves laid out. In addition, this system has disrupted loading orders, which can be a serious stability issue for heavy modders.
PRO
-Enjoyable, responsive shooting mechanics
-Settlement system offers an alternative game style
-DLCs are worthwhile additions
-Environments can be interesting to explore and discover their stories
-Offers the incredible modding base Bethesda games are known for
CON
-Main story is less than interesting
-Conversation options are distilled down to 'Good, Evil, Smarmy Smartass Good, Maybe Later'
-Play areas outside constructed set pieces are largely uninteresting
-Settlement system can be a required distraction for those who do not care for it
NEUTRAL
-Simplification of SPECIAL and stat system is a pro or con depending on the player
-Some game mechanics are never explained (did you know there's a cover system?)
DEAL BREAKER
-Bethesda is increasingly a hostile force to the modding scene, arguably the biggest draw of their games

I'll preface this by telling you I am one of the fortunate few who has had no issues with this game, no ACU.exe has stopped working, no co op issues, no real fps issues. I play with a 970 and an i3-4150, every setting the highest it can go, and on street level I get 26-35 fps, in crowds I get 20-25, and rooftops I get 40-50. I really should be getting higher fps, but 30 fps is playable I suppose, and the game looks REALLY nice on high settings.
Now to the review
I'm really enjoying the bustling city feel that has been missing from then last 2 games, I think it really pulls you into the wonderful atmosphere. Ubisoft was not kidding when they boasted their npc count, cause that really is an impressive feature. The fact that they're all doing something is really cool. For example, after unlocking the blend ability (like sitting on a bench, this does not affect crowd blending) I walked over to a few people who we're trying to move a cart, and Arno moved under the cart to try and lift it. Not incredibly amazing, but I thought it was really neat. 9.5/10
Now in terms of actual plot, it's somewhat disappointing, but it holds up. The events seem kind of independent and don't have much of an impact on the rest of the story, you kind of just go back to stabbing people? I did however like Arno as a character, it was clear that Ubi was trying to recreate AC2 Ezio, but I think Arno is different enough to be an entertaining character. I also quite liked Elise, she was a nice complement to Arno's personality. If you're a modern day story fan you will ♥♥♥♥ing /hate/ this plot, because NOTHING HAPPENS. The time anomalies were weak as ♥♥♥♥ too, I mean they were nice to look at but I thought they were lame. 6.5/10
Now onto gameplay, Ubisoft did a phenomenal job on the new movement system, (when it doesn't bug out) running up a wall has never been more satisfying, especially the addition of starting a climb from an angle oh god I think about that when I'm not playing. Arno is quite agile, and overall free running is sexy as ♥♥♥♥. Honestly this is what keeps me playing. 9/10
Combat is quite weird, it seems to be hard at first but then it turns into AC3/4 minus the actual countering, you kind of just mash X and B (IMHO this is a controller game) till everyone dies, and if you stop giving ♥♥♥♥s just keep tapping that shoot button till everyone is dead. The animations for finishers and parrying are gorgeous though, and parrying actually is affected by what your hands are doing, but overall combat feels more of a chore. 6/10
Stealth was actually really hard, as taking cover never seemed to work when you want it to. The best way to stealth something is to throw a smoke bomb in and kill everyone before the smoke dissipates. A good idea but poorly executed. 5.5/10
I won't give customization a point value but it's really cool, you have a lot of different options for clothing, but unfortunately your color options are quite garbage. Something that would have been cool was. Halo: Reach sequel where you picked primary, secondary and tertiary colors. Maybe in the next game.
Overall this is a really cool game that was quite honestly ruined by how Ubisoft conducted their launch day, I mean I really want to defend their decisions because I like this game so much but I really can't. Ubi dug their grave this year. There is hope though as now EA is starting to shape up nicely [good job EA! :)] so maybe Ubi will follow their footsteps. Sooner rather than later let's hope. With any luck, AC Unity will be like AC1 and AC3, new ideas and mechanics that don't quite work very well, but are very well polished in the next installment. Let's hope next year we see the best assassins creed yet :)

Darkest Dungeon is a game about reclaiming the once majestic manor of your ancestor who frequently describes it as "Opulent and Imperial", So as our ancestor who got bored of living the life of debauchery, he found some ancient texts about great power lying beneath the surface. Spending all of the family's fortune on working hands and shovels to reach the gates that will bring ruin to your family. This isn't your usual hero of destiny fights evil with the greatest of ease with his band of merry men who act as a supporting cast to your adventure, in fact your task is the hiring of mercenaries and scholars who seek redemption, knowledge or riches to cleanse the land from evil. Along the way you'll uncover what happened to your ancestor and the monsters that dwell within.
"Luck favours the prepared"
The game lets you bring a team of 4 individuals each with their own set of skills and personality in the dungeon, some quests involve simply scouting 90 % of the ruins or finding 3 artifacts for the abbey. The game has a Lovecraftian atmosphere with pigmen, fishmen, eldritch creatures and insane flesh monsters. As you fight these beings, you will understand that the RNG will not always be in your favor which some people will complain about, but my suggestion would be to also realize that luck will also be at your side in times of need; An Occultist performing a critical heal that gives your party a second chance to fight or one of your Jester's resolve was tested and helped rally the team from despair. Sometimes, you have a fight where you should have won but got stomped from the insane dodges from a fishman with a toothpick and deals heavy blows from lucky rolls that make you look like a scrub or you needed just 1 more battle to finish the mission with all the party intact but the game just gave you the middle finger and killed your favored Plage Doctor and then shoving a Quest complete in the next empty room.
Overall that is what I think lovecraft all about, we can delay the inevitable and have small victories today but in the end we are still mortal. Cherish those lucky rolls but do not rely on it until it spoils, Weep from your losses to the unfair advantage but return with a vengance that will turn you into the most manliest being who delivered your family from the ravenous clutching shadows ...of the darkest dungeon.
Shoutout to Wayne June for giving a stellar performance in giving this game the atmosphere of dread. Don't let my game time which are just rookie numbers compared to other reviews fool you, I just started to return after hearing that they are still continuing with more DLCs about the Crimson Court and wanted to start learning the ropes. The developers know how to make an indie game and continue to work on it even after delivering the final release.

I think this game is well done and well polished, but i cannot recommend this game.
Art is amazing, narration is great, story is intriguing, class variety is very good compared to most games out there. However.
Everything is set up for you to lose. Absolutely everything in this game is against you at every single moment, and i'm not even talking about RNG. It's not a game that you can dump 10 hrs in and say it got any easier. It's just stressful at every turn. Some people like it, some do not. Those that do enjoy getting tied up/gagged during sex too but I don't judge.
The difficulty covers up it's painfully short campaign. Actual game should only take about 25-30 weeks if you can actually progress at a reasonable pace. Character progression is meaningless because higher level characters can't do lower dungeons. The only way the game get slightly easier is if you get a lot of resources and upgrade items. Which brings me to the next point.
Resources collection. Inventory is painfully small. For a medium mission you're not gonna have a lot of space to pick anything up, and even then, stack size is ♥♥♥♥ing tiny. So you're stuck grinding away on the same missions for hours on end for almost nothing each time, all while rotating through your shrinking roster. "But inventory management is part of the game". Yeah it's ♥♥♥♥ing bad.
But not as bad as the fact that this game is a terrible turn-based game. Turn order is completely random, so you can't even reliably set up anything. Worst part is it's hidden from you for no other reason than to make it more difficult. WHich brings me to the final point.
Difficulty. Is this game like Dark Souls where if you actually take the time to "git gud", you will stop suffering like a casual? Abso♥♥♥♥inglutely not. This game isn't traditionally difficult. Good and experienced players will suffer less, but suffer nonetheless. New and inexperienced players will eat a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥for no gain whatsoever.
All in all, if you're the type that don't respect yourself/enjoys rough kinky sex be done unto you, then this is the game for you. But if you're just looking for a team turn based game to enjoy, this is not the game for you.

Qube is a surprising good game, it is very much a portal clone in that is a first person puzzler where you enter rooms and must use several typical mechanics to advance to the next room where a new puzzle awaits. Ofcourse Qube doesn’t use portals but qubes which can be manipulated depending on their colour. It’s either a jump qube, or one that can extend or form a staircase and so on.
The similarities with portal don’t end there, you start the game not knowing what is going on or how you got there. It becomes more clear as you advance through the game. There is also a voice talking to you, and as you progress the rooms tend to fall apart/malfunction. I’m sure you get the picture on how much this game takes from Portal, however it doesn’t mean it is a bad game or a boring story. It’s all different enough to keep you interested, even the story keeps you wondering what is going on until the end. Though I must say the ending felt like a rushed job.
I can’t say a bad thing about the graphics, they are just fine, but ofcourse nothing special either, just executed well within the set premise. The sound effects and music are minimal, but fitting and do their job well enough to emerge you into the qube-world.
If you want a very decent Portal clone, this is the game to get.

Fractured space takes the standard MOBA model and adds a 2 notable features
1). 3 dimensions. I know it may not seem like a large deal, and it is still pretty limited, but it forces you to think about your ship, where it's going, and how to use cover most effectively.
2). Objective based gameplay. Destroying another ship in FS doesn't give you credits for levels or somehow "upgrade" your ship. It just clears the way in order to capture mining stations, which do upgrade your ships.
While these are nice, the real advantage to FS is it's community. Compared to other more popular MOBA, Fractured Space has an accepting, laid back attitude. When playing this game it's a lot less stressful and for me, more enjoyable to be able to just try hard and savor the game. The devs are active in the Discord, and routinely send out mail notices and streams.
Finally, the free-to-play model, as it stands, is reasonable. There isn't a great amount of incentive for premium currency, and after only 50 hours I've unlocked around half of the ships that I'd like to. I would highly recommend this game if you're looking for a game to enjoy, and not a massive timesink.

Don't expect it to be exactly like dark souls, just because it uses similar gameplay ideas. It admirably tries to make a game that isn't a straight up clone, but turns the souls games into a genre that this also sits in.
It provides interesting new twists of familiar mechanics. For instance attacks can be timed with perfect intervals for lower stamina usage and performing combos that otherwise don't get triggered. As you kill enemies, you build up a multiplier for xp and loot and using a bonfire-equivalent resets it. That makes for an interesting choice where even for a new area, you might not want to refresh yourself but keep your multiplier instead.
The fighting style of this game is slower than souls games and it's not as widely varied in how many different types of playstyles are fully supported. You'll find some options that are offered to be inconvenient and not totally viable, but plenty are, and all the common options like big-sword-guy or shield-guy or daggers-guy are all perfectly doable, with the game being easier or harder by player choice by wearing heavy armor or light gear.
For full price I can see how it could have disappointed some people in the obvious comparison against dark souls. But especially at it's current price point, it's worth the time and money investment for sure.

Starbound is a 2d sandbox game, but not in the conventional sense.  Instead of having one world that randomly spawns, a la Terraria or Minecraft, you have MANY (many many many many) worlds that randomly spawn, each split up into different sectors of the universe.  The amount of exploration is about as limitless as I could think a game could get.  On top of that, there's crafting, hunting, dungeon traipsing, epic boss fights, and gorgeous 2d vistas.
:
+  Limitless.  No two worlds are the same in terms of layout and what type of dungeon (as well as the size of said dungeon) will spawn on the planets are always different.  I personally find this perfect for long term play, as well as just jumping into the game and flying to the next planet in small chunks.
+  Very approachable.  What do you want to do- travel the planets and leave your mark on the worlds your visit, via a monument you've built or maybe even just graffiti?  Or just dungeon dive, seeking out the next labyrinth to spelunk and claim the rewards within?  Add friends to this mix, and you can approach the game similairly or individually.
+  Quaint 2d graphics.  In terms of "pixel art", this game (to me) is the Mona Lisa of the 2d plain.  And, thankfully being 2d makes the game EASY as all get out to mod.  Between custom races to custom ships, to custom ships for custom races with custom armors/weapons, I see a lot of potential here for a solid modding community (which, of course, there already is one).
+  Co-op.  Joining up with friends is about as easy as I can think they can make it, and depending who goes into who's universe, said universe will be forever changed.  Your friends could be in a completely different sector than yours, and beam to your ship with ease to join you on the fly.  I was worried this game would have co-op limitations, but in my opinion, co-op only reinforces the ideals of the limitless that is space- that is Starbound.
+  Music.  The music is pretty good, and cycles between ambiance to classic combat music.
+  Cycles.  Every planet has a day/night cycle (save for some moons and asteroid belts), and each planet has it's own weather system, as well as it's own gravity.  Weather in Starbound includes soft rain, very heavy rain, snow, sand storms, star showers (gorgeous!)- there is a vast amount that furthers making each planet feel different than the last.
+  Community don't play.  Be rude to someone, either in favor of the devs or against them, and you're liable to get blocked.  There is a downside to this, though, and I will dig into that below.

:
-I am at a loss here.  I do have some problems with the game, but so far it has been things like EA bugs, so I don't really want to list them, as they may have been fixed since the last time I encountered them.  Mostly inane things like descriptions still needing to be set, false icons.  More annoying bugs include losing pixels inexplicably (pixels is the games currency).
-I could say lack of updates, but I'm not someone that plays an EA game as if it were a final product.  My 130 hrs have been spurts, spanning weeks or months with many longer breaks in between.  Each time I have come back to this game, either through devs or modders, my experience has always been enhanced from the last time.  This is a sign of progress.
-Community don't play #2.  That being said, it has been mentioned on both the Starbound forums, as well as here in the Steam discussions, that being an♥♥♥♥♥♥will get you cut off.
:
All in all, this review cannot be complete until the game is.  What is described on the Store page is offered in this game, and as long as you come into Starbound with the understanding that it is still under development, and can walk away from time to time when you feel it's gone stale, then you will greatly enjoy this game.
Bring a friend or go alone- either way, Starbound will be a digital masterpiece once it is complete.  That doesn't stop the game from being fun in it's current incarnation.  I feel most are just impatient.  The ones this game is made for are the people that are always in game, not taking to Steam forums trashing it (and anyone who doesn't agree with them).
*  It's like the honeymoon phase is over.  For a while, Starbound was getting all thumbs up, now it's getting all thumbs down.  I have followed the thoughts of the community, and am still at a loss as to why this is.  I have heard the claims of "game's dead" and "devs don't work on it", with very little to no insight as to why
of people believe this.  The claims do not seem logical if you have a clear grasp on what EA is (from my perspective).  Development for every individual EA game is different, so saying one has had more frequent updates than Starbound is like comparing Oranges to some other fruit you don't know.

Positive review:
I have to confess I did not play this game new.  I missed out.  Because this game is atmospheric and engaging, which is unusual for an FPS.  Compared to the FPS games of the era, this game stands out for many reasons.
One obvious one is the continuous levels.  Other games loaded different levels with cut screens, usually changing the entire environment.  Unreal used the end of one level as the beginning of the next.  But Half-Life is one, seamless world.  There are still loading pauses, but you never leave the screen.  It feels like a single game.
This game is scary.  It's hard to explain when you hear certain sounds, and don't know where they are coming from, and you have to anticipate sudden attacks.  There were lots of scary, violent games in this era, of course.  This game, however, is just the right kind of creepy.  It's what you don't see, or what you partially see, that make it work.
The game itself is well made, with great level design.  I don't find the levels to be much of headscratchers, but they do require some original thinking in spots.  There are parts that are very demanding of strategy, and quite frustrating.  A few areas (like a certain lift going down) are designed to inspire nightmares with frustration.
And another standout in this game is the storyline.  It has a strong narrative, except unlike most story-based FPS games (like Jedi Knight), the game never relies on cutscenes to propel the plot.  The plot is told visually, through actions, and through things being said around your character.  You never speak, never directly converse, and the game never leaves your point of view for any reason.  From the moment the game loads, you are Gordon Freeman.
The story is not entirely original, not unique to the FPS genre.  Chasm: The Rift and Doom 2 explored similar concepts already, in a less articulate way.  It also owes heavily to some Stephen King stories, particularly The Mist.  Gordon Freeman is a physicist working on a top secret government project, when an accident occurs, what becomes known in gaming history as The Black Mesa Incident.  Now Gordon has to get out alive and try to undo what was done, before the military cover-up.
This game has one of the highest metacritic ratings of all time, and is generally considered the best FPS game by many.
-----
Negative review:
I hate writing a negative review, because this is an excellent game.  Really is.  Unfortunately, in the current state it's in, there are two kinds of computer it is not completely compatible with:  New computers, and old computers.
This is an old game, designed to run well on 166 MHz pentiums, I believe.  Even with patching an improvements, it should be excellent on any computer made in the last decade or so.  It is not.  Audio quality is horrible, with a frequent stutter and crackling.  Sometimes audio affects the framerate.  Which is especially bad when the framerate is unacceptable on any decent settings.  The game can run in HD, but on many computers does so poorly.
For reasons that baffle me, the game chokes on recent computers, in framerate and audio.  The game chokes worse on older computers.  I tried playing it with a late 2006 computer using XP, running a 2 GHz processor and dedicated graphics.  On native resolution, the game ran 8 FPS.  On a Core i7 with Intel HD, the game runs 45-60 unless there is heavy gunfire, in which it drops to crawl.  In short, neither computer can handle the game in OpenGL mode.
Doing some reading, there are reports of the same choking on AMD and NVIDIA cards.
None of the problems exist in Half-Life 2, interestingly.
More frustrating and baffling is the removal of a number of features somewhat recently, that affect older computers.  EAX and surround sound are no longer possible, even when playing on an XP computer with a decent sound blaster or a modern one with Alchemy.  Direct3D support has also been removed, making the game impossible for people who have trouble with OpenGL for some reason.
And along with all of the problems with the current Windows version, I found the Linux version to be entirely unplayable.
The game also has strange behavior when changing graphics options. A common bug is changing to software rendering causes the game to run at an unbearably small resolution.  You cannot even see the menu with it, and have to do some command-line trickery to fix it.  I've had the menu screen corrupted with rainbow tiles that seem to get worse and worse.  The game also can start crashing in the menu if graphics options are changed frequently.
I have also had a problem with the game deleting my cloud saves, making me start over.
So what this means is a classic game, one of the highest rated games ever made, runs at a crawl with choppy sound, and no means to fix it, and rather than seeing maintenance, patching now amounts to removing features that made the game work.
It's still enjoyable.  Just turn the graphics way down, put up with the choppy sound, and expect the frame drops.  They mar an excellent game.

At its core, Assassin's Creed Unity is a very good game. It does have some faults, but I think it is worth it in spite of them.

It makes it incredible difficult to tell how many people are really experiencing actual issues with the game, because the majority of the comments are "lololol this game is so broken and terrible, ubisoft is the devil." These people watch glitch videos and think this is what it's like playing the game, without realizing these are compilations of several seconds of video captured over hours of gameplay, and also that there are glitch videos for EVERY GAME IN THE WORLD.
I'm sure there are some legitimate technical issues for some people, which is unfortunate. I experienced a couple crashes in the first few days, but none since then. I got stuck in a hay cart once. A once nice game ruined by corporate greed. perhaps I should put some detail into Trion's unforgivable actions concerning the class system.
In the game, you can get "cubits," an ingame currancy attainable by beating the various dungeons in the worlds ranked from "novice" to "U6" filling the bar once daily would get you 500 Cubits a day. These cubits could be used to progress- buying a few mounts, potion flasks, emblems (buffs for potions), and perhaps most importantly, CLASSES! which are needed to progress in the game and have a good time for about what? 7500 Cubits at most? but then, Trion being the moneybags they are, decided to REMOVE THAT OPTION entirely! Yes, they do claim it is still possible to unlock classes without paying them a cent, and that IS technically true, BUUUUUT that would require you to go to the marketplace to buy what is called a "Class Coin", which is, you guessed it, only available for real money. So, someone out there has to put one on sale in exchange for an exorbitant amount of "flux" the most common ingame currancy used by players, and as such, results in an even greater Pay2win advantage, and even more time required for free players.
If this is what is required for Trion to pay it's bills... to avoid getting bankrupt, dont you think that something is wrong here? If this is the case, someone is not doing thier job. Either that, or the "Free2Play /w microtransactions" is a much worse buisness model than anyone could ever guess. Players are able to use the companies rescorces (like server space, which needs money to run, I can only imagine), racking up thier bills and not pay a cent for it, but in turn, have content stripped away from them if the company says so, for possibly good reason. I'm pretty sure it says so in the "terms and conditions" Ultimately, this is a bad deal for everyone involved: unhappy players, and a buisness  that effectively runs on tips.
On the other hand, lets say Trion has alot more funds than assumed above, (which I have no doubt as to the possiblity) and that the company is actually doing just fine... that would make it's actions entirely inexcusable, a mere bid to milk more and more money from it's players or else suffer a brutal grind. and that gets real boring, real quick.
I may have been rather brutal in this review, but that is for good reason. I'm angry that things had to turn out this way, as another decent game was ruined by a failing buisness model... or company, not sure which. I am unlikely to return to trove, ever, and will probably think twice if I take interest in a game made by it's developers in the future.
But, thats just my two cents.

Well, I purchased this game earlier this week for 30p and honestly, I can say its one of the best 30p purchase's I've ever made, the only others being game purchase's from second hand stores where they didn't know what they where selling.
The game is a retrovised version of the game 'Sanctum' that plays much like an older tower defence game, keeping a fixed top down view through out. You are given a selection of boards to play on for the various missions and unlock new towers and powers as you go, between each wave you're given build time which also acts as time where you're able to plot out the pathway on the boards, though the earlier levels are very linear.
The game has a good selection of towers and powers that can catter to varying play styles, though using the shock tower pretty much gaurantee's a win on levels which only use ground targets, making the later game somewhat dissapointingly easy compared to how it should feel.
Once the game is completed, you can tackle the levels on hard if you hadn't already done so, or try survival and see how long you can last for against wave after wave on enemies.
The soundtrack and audio is quite simple and enjoyable, nothing majorly memorable but pleasent non the less.
For a 30p purchase, I would say to buy this game even if you're not that much of a tower defence game fan, its only 30p after all, you wont even notice the change is gone and I've managed to sink about 9 hours into it thus far. At full price, I would say to only buy if you enjoy retro tower defence games, though it may feel a bit short at full price.

Warcube is a fast-paced combat game. Obviously, because if you are the intelligent individual you are, you read the description before reading reviews. Now on to the actual review. I am going to be doing a 10/10 review on Graphics, sound, etc.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Graphics
The graphics in this game are cartoony and I can see how that might make some people look the other way but hang in there. The graphics are not at all realistic in any way, meaning they are minimalistic, simplistic, and cartooney as mentioned previously. I personally like the simplistic graphics but I still think they could use some work.
Overall I would rate the graphics a 6/10
Obviously, graphics are not the main selling point in most indie games so if you have bought indie games previously with simplistic graphics this should be fine. Even if you haven't you will be fine.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Sound
There are some decent sounds in Warcube. The sounds overall are not revolutionary, however, they are still good and are probably better than what you will find in a lot of indie games, but still not revolutionary.
Overall I would rate the sounds a 7/10
Same with graphics sounds are not the main selling point of indie action games so that is why I give it the rating I did.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Gameplay
The gameplay in Warcube is about the most unique and fun things I have played in a LONG time. You use a variety of weapons found throughout the game including, dynamite, crossbows, and the legendary sword in the stone! There are some problems with the aiming reticle when you try to charge a melee attack or shoot a bow. But don't let that hinder your feelings for the game because for me it doesn't happen that often and in the heat of combat even if it does mess up you will still hit someone so it is fine.
Overall I will rate the Gameplay a 9/10
This is the main selling point of the game and I believe that the game does deserve this rating based on its current status.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Gif Capture
Generally, this would not be a section in a review but this little indie game is an exception. The game has a built-in gif capture system allowing you to make gifs of the last few seconds of gameplay. Then the gif is placed in a file that is convenient menu if you hit escape during the game.
Overall I rate it a 10/10
I give it this only because of how rare this is to see in a game and I think that it works well.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Settings
For those hardcore gamers that have the best computer money can buy, you will be disappointed with the graphical settings because there are only two settings low and high, These not changing much but still a welcome addition. The audio settings are probably what you would expect from this type of game, master volume slider, music slider, and SFX volume slider. The third and final section of settings are the game settings including key remapping, cursor visibility, and a few others mentioned below.
Graphics settings (in order of appearance)
Quality - Low or high
Ambient occlusion (AO) - On or off
Toggle fullscreen - On or off
Antialiasing - None, 2x, or 4x
Map shadows - On or off
Audio
Master volume slider
Music volume slider
Sound effects (SFX) volume slider
Game
Key Remapping - which allows you to change any of the keys to any button
Epic Gif Capture - Which allows you to capture "epic gifs" applying a filter to the gif
Cursor visible - allows you to turn the cursor on or off
Reset game - which by its name resets your progress
Isometric movement - This turns off fluent movement basically only allowing you to move in the cardinal directions
Frames Per Second (FPS) display - Shows your frames in the top right corner
Overall I will consider the settings a 7/10
I give it this score not because the settings don't work but because I think there could be more of them, especially for graphics.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Easter Eggs
There are a good number of easter eggs in the game waiting for you to find. I am not going to list them here because they are easter eggs you are supposed to find them yourself.
Overall I rate this a 9/10
I rate it this because the easter eggs in it are good and make sense but there could be more.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Content
The game has A LOT more content since it launched back at the beginning of 2017, however, this game is still VERY, VERY MUCH in development. Right now there are 14 complete maps, a map that is still under construction but is available to play, and two maps you can see but can't play. Each map consists of probably 20 minutes of game time for completionist route and about 10 minutes for casual play. There are, however, a lot of weapons and armor already in the game and readily available each with different looks and slightly different stats. also. there are some cosmetics that you can apply to yourself to look different but that is all they do. Finally, there is a special ability which is not going to be the only one but for now, it is.
Overall I give this a 7/10
Hear me out as to why. Right now I know there is not all that much content but Craigz (The developer) is very good at getting content out is really working hard so I believe we will see this game go a long way.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Devs and Communication
Craigz works on everything in the game, except for sound which Blake works on, but Blake doesn't really respond to anyone because he is not full-time on the game. Craigz, as I said before, is very hard working and is working on the game full-time resulting in a lot of communication and soon to be content. Also, Craigz and the mods (myself included) will almost certainly address any problems, concerns, questions, or anything of the sort relatively quickly.
Overall I give this a 9/10
I give it this because with the combination of a lot of communication from the mods and the dev along with the dev working full-time on the game it is well worth a 9/10.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This concludes the review, I will be updating this as I see fit and feel free to leave me or any other of the mods and or dev a question in the forums, discord or twitter and we will respond to you as soon as possible.

As a longtime CASUAL player, I would rate this game 5/7. If you guys don't understand Reddit jokes, think of that as a 10/10.
I would first like to address a few common points.
1. This is not Pay to Win. The grind is on par with other MMOs, like LoL, Wot, World of Warships, etc. There is literally no way a player can skip their way to a ship late in the tech tree. Everyting has to be unlocked with XP, and usually when you unlock a ship with XP, you have close to the amount of credits required.
2. The tech tree is not like WoT or WoWs. Ships later in the tree are not simply better than the early ships. There is a reason why you see a lot of Reapers, Hunters, Colossi, Protectors, etc. They are good ships. Very rarely will you see a high end ship, like a Guardian, a Watchman, a Persecutor, etc. Thet take much more skill to operate, which is why they are at the end or near the end of a tech tree.
3. Premium ships are not better. They are identical the their stock counterpart, just with a flashy skin, and they are all easily unlocked. The Reaper and hunter are fairly eay to get.
Now for the god parts. It's basically all the other positive reviews, teanwork, great visuals, etc.
But one thing that most of them don't mention is the great devs. They listen to the community. For example, there was massive backlash over a new crew system, and so the devs have changes in progress.

A game inspired in mechanics by the Souls-series, a couple of nice features and a more mainstream approach to story and exposition.
LotF mostly plays like Dark Souls.
You've got classes of melee weapons that you can either one-hand with a shield or two-hand for more damage. You can parry enemy attacks, block them or dodge out of the way. It also has a couple of features that ended up in DS3, like paired weapons, where you wield one in each hand when two-handing, and charged heavy attacks.
You explore dark fantasy locations like castles, tombs and hellish realms, mowing down enemies, looting treasure and killing bosses. Although progression is mostly linear you'll soon find that most environments interconnect and you'll end up reaching blocked out areas of the early game and opening shortcuts.
The story is somewhat short, taking around ~20 hours if you go about it at your leisure. Once you beat the game you can start new game plus which offers harder enemies and better loot.
There is no multiplayer like in the Souls-series.
It has an intersting spin on "currency". Like DS you earn XP that you can either use to level up and upgrade weapons or you can keep on yourself to boost your item find, with the risk of losing it upon death.
Overall the game is a good attempt at a Souls-like. It wears its inspiration at its sleeve.
You may feel it is easier than the Souls-games. Combat-wise it's not, though I personally don't find DS hard either, both games require patience to progress but you never feel lost in LotF, you always have a sense of direction and there are almost no points where you need to wiki it.
As I said at the start of the review, it's has a mainstream approach to story telling, exposition and pacing, done through dialogs with NPCs and recovered audio logs, with Souls-like combat and exploring in between.
On the other hand said story is cookie-cutter dark phantasy writing, men fighting against demons, sent by a vengeful god and the expected twist near the end. You won't cringe but won't be search Youtube for lore videos either.
Surely worth the asking price on a sale. I got it for ~12.5€ and don't regret it.

It's hard to talk about Lords of the Fallen with out immediately comparing it to Dark Souls, both are 3rd person ARPGs in medieval settings with stamina driven combat; at a quick glance LotF seems like little more than your standard Souls-like, but there are multiple things that seperate it from DkS both good and bad.
First I'd like to talk about what LotF does right, and that's its interesting take on risk/reward; while playing you will notice that every kill increases an experience multiplier, this multiplier lasts until you either die or activate one of the games checkpoints. This incourages you to be a bit reckless and make decisions on whether you want to play it safe or push on and reap more rewards. This system is made even more risky by the fact that when you die you have a limited ammount of time to recover your experience before it starts to decrease, meaning that skipping checkpoints not only makes survival riskier since you won't be  replenish your consumables it makes recovering your experience a bit of a risk since you might spawn several multiple checkpoints from where you died and will need to fight your way back as fast as you can.
When the system works it's incredibly satisfying, and if LotF was fast paced and fluid as it's inspiration it could have made the game an instant classic. Unfortunately LotF feels incredibly slow and clunky, which in turn makes every encounter feel like a labored effort; but I will come back to that later.
In order to understand what exactly keeps LotF from being a great game I think you need to look at what makes DkS a great game. Souls games are known for being difficult and throwing a variety of challenges at you; what it is also known for is giving you an incredible array of tools and choices to deal with these challenges. It's this freedom to face challenges any way you'd like with any number of possible strategies that keeps DkS feeling fresh and appealing to such a wide base. LotF however doesn't do this at all... Instead from the very beginning of the game LotF feels like it is constantly bottlenecking you into using specific strategies and character builds.
Between it's unchangable class choices, its stong emphasis on balanced upgrades over min-maxing just so you can use your class abilities, and it's lack of weapon upgrades and minimal stat scaling forcing you into using heavy weapons just to deal enough damage to keep up with enemy health levels and healing LotF constantly feels like it is forcing you to play in a pretty specific ways; and unfortunately those ways aren't really all that fun.
You are left between min-maxing to make the most of your damage and survival odds or dropping all your experience into spells/faith to make use of your class; you are given the choice of using fast weapons that do very little damage against enemies, some of which can heal faster than you can deal damage, or use high damage weapons that can take out enemies but are insanely slow and leave you open to be staggered constantly. The end result is a slow and clunky process that never really manages to make you feel like you are making meaningful choices instead of simply putting experience where the game wants you to, and that's ultimately what makes LotF feel so unfulfilling.
Did you enjoy the first game? If yes is oyur answer then but this game, if not then do not buy this. While it makes improvents it is still very similar so keep that in mind.

The puzzles are good I geuss, or at least some of the ones near the end are good and the progression of how it introduces new stuff is handled well. But the game's also terribly short. First impressions review:
This game is better than the other reviews lead me to believe and I have to say re-reading them now makes it clear that the people who are railing on the game aren't playing this game, they're trying to play Dark Souls after they launched this game.
The similarities this has with Dark Souls are the lack of direction in side quests, a somewhat similar death system where accrued and unspent (or unbanked in this case) experience is lost.
That's pretty much it. There's no real dodging invulnerability I've seen, your character has to be physically out of the way of the attacks in order to avoid damage. The weapons and attacks have a good deal of weight to them, but even the fast ones are a bit slower than the usual rapier or dagger spam from Dark Souls. You have this trade-off where if you want to use the highest damage weapons in the game, you're going to give up your shield and you're going to have to start timing your attacks a lot more precisely since you can't do hit-and-run wielding a greataxe.
With regards to stats, the benefit from a single stat point isn't very apparent, but after you spend your attribute shards and bank experience after a boss fight, that 5+ point collection truly makes a difference in unlocking new spells, giving you a lot of strength or agility to make the most of your weapons, and even gives your magic or endurance a visible boost to the meter and usage.
The boss fights are all unique in their attack patterns and animations, and proper use of your chosen setup is key to getting a fast victory, or even fulfilling the hidden conditions to earn yourself a special version of the boss weapons.
My chosen loadout was a heavy-armor, medium-weight, 2 handed fighter with enough faith to cast all 4 spells available to the Paladin class. Small enemies I usually just run and kill in one hit with an overhand swing of the greataxe, while the larger enemies I have to distract or slow with my spells in order to get good hits in.
The enemies themselves are quite varied and your strategy has to be tailored to each of them. People keep comparing this game to Dark Souls but seem to forget that no matter what enemy you face, you're pretty much just going to dodge and critical, or you're going to melt it with pumped up stats or spells.
One part of the game that's been a failure from the start for me was the gauntlet system. It's supposed to be this great multi-functional and customizable arm cannon that just doesn't serve any purpose for me but to spend too much mana that I would rather be using on spells. If this had some sort of ammo that replenished at each checkpoint, I'd be MUCH happier about it and would use it frequently.
Simply put, this game is INSPIRED by Dark Souls, but it's objectively not another company trying to steal the design from.

Shadowgate hearkens back to the classic point and click adventures from the days of early computer gaming.  You start off with just a nudge out the door, a torch and a dirk and are charged with the quest of vanquishing evil in the living castle of Shadowgate.
The game is loaded with puzzles, traps, and head-scratching moments depending on your chosen difficulty.  Having said that, I distinctly remember the NES version being far easier.  Perhaps the hardest difficulty wasn't the best idea...
The menu options are pretty much the same as they were, but the full-screen approach to the UI is a nice change away from the classic version.  You get to see far more of the environment and the amount of detail that went into the hand-painted imagery.
As I delve further and further into the game, I find some of the puzzles famliar but often with new twists (also thanks to the difficulty).  It's tough, at times, and potentiallly frustrating as all good puzzle games should be.
The music is atmospheric and adaptive, laced with familiar nostalgic themes from the classic. The artwork is nice and crisp and the added storyline so far makes it far more immersive than its original form.
For exta nostalgia, they have options to utilize some of the classic NES features such as the music and room transitions.
I would recommend it to fans of the original and fans of point-and-click adventures (like Myst and its ilk).  Beyond that, if you don't like this genre of game, Shadowgate doesn't really offer anything outside of what's safely within the niche of the genre.

This is the weakest portal-like game I've played.
It 's ugly, controls feel sluggish and the story is garbage. I have to give some credit for music though, which fits in well for a puzzle game. I could forgive the shortcomings if gameplay was any good. Which wasn't, but let me say why.
The game's basic mechanics are simple and lackluster. They don't offer much creative space for interesting levels. You see the three interactions there are and you've seen it all.
The game seems to realize that because it follows with a long phase of physics-based puzzles. The solutions are obvious, you just need to time your button presses correctly to progress. Annoyingly, to press the buttons you have to turn away from the action as they are on walls behind you. Makes you appreciate how elegantly this was solved in Portal.
After winning your battle with physics you proceed to the next area with lasers. These "puzzles" are extremely easy. You just choose which of the two way the laser should face, left or right. If the solution wasn't obvious enough it's very easy to brute-force your way through.
This is followed by a story-intensive with more physics-based puzzles. After this you enter a giant room with another huge physics puzzle. I looked at it played with it a little, randomly found a solution, but then one of the cubes pushed the other away and I would have to reset. This is where I stopped playing. (stage 6 out of 9)
You can disregard my opinion thinking that maybe the devs saved the best puzzles for the end However, I doubt that. I can tell you, I don't like this game. I don't recommend it to anyone. It's over-reliance on physics-based puzzles and lacking complexity make it an unrewarding and frustrating experience. You'd be better off playing Portal, Witness or AnteChamber if you haven't yet.

A remake of the original game from the Nes, Shadowgate is a  click and point adventures that follows the original retro style redone  with voice acting, animated graphics, and the complicated puzzles changed up to blow your mind in fustration but full of satisfactory when solved. Fans of the original Shadowgate will love the remake of this game and the feeling of retro nostalgia.
The game starts with an animated opening accompanied by a  great soundtrack and voice narration that will give you the immersion and overhwelming feeling of  epicness to your adventure to conquer the castle and stop an evil warlock.
Though not everything is voiced in the game except for major plotline cutscenes for the story. The game still does a great job with the  text dialogue. The graphics will remind you of a really well done animated  graphic novel if you've ever experienced any of those. The gameplay itself a click adventure puzzle game and might not be everyone's cup of tea.
Upon playing the game and starting off your adventure you'll be greeted with 3 different difficulty mode to the game, each of which changes up the solution to the puzzles to the game and stop players from thinking they know the puzzles after playing the first time. Along with starting the adventure you'll be given a well detailed tutorial that explains how the mechanics, and how the game works. This isn't your usual point and click adventure but a retro gameplay style with the player having to use hotkeys and clicking on top for buttons to execute commands such as use, speak, or even to open doors and move forward etc. So an example is  in order to get in through a door to the next area  to progress you'll have to first open the door or you'll run headlfirst into it.
The game will feature puzzles that are pretty complex and feels VERY satisfying when you actually solve it. The game does give you hints hidden in well written riddles and text on spells, items, and scroll you find in order to progress.  Upon being stuck however, players  do have the ability to talk to your only sidekick skull partner Yorick who at times talk alot but does give you hints also in riddles  but unless you paid attention to certain surrondings and the riddles, you'll be stuck at certain areas for quite a bit.
The way to solve certain situations sometimes is trial and error sometimes and  be warned however that making a mistake at certain locations and it's death for you in many ways. There are creatures in this castle to stop you along the way such as krakens and dragons.  Luckily the game does offer saving and  quicksave to keep on playing. To add on to this the game has a mechanic that everything you do is considered a move except for looking. So each time you are using a move your torch is slowly diminishing. If you run out of torches you'll have no choice but to restart a previous save becuase leaving  will make you fall in the dark and break your neck. Along with the torch there will be another element later in the game that will be more brutal on you forcing you to quicken your pace a bit.
The one thing about the game is when you do die you'll die in a gruesome way. Along with death flying along and giving you a speech about your misery sometimes in a humorous manner. So try not to die and do your best at the puzzles, Read, look, and tread carefully in this castle of doom.

This is truly an excellent callback to the original Shadowgate from 1987 for the NES (which I owned).  The art is fantastic first and foremost, with the UI being relatively easy to navigate.  While the rooms have a similar look to their 1987 counterparts, the puzzles have been changed slightly.  To top that off, there are three difficulties that change how quickly the torches run out, the frequency/difficulty of puzzles, and etc.  There's also a retro mode, allowing you to listen to the old music and experience the transitions we've come to know and love.  A hint system exists to help you somewhat, though it won't give you the answer flat out like BTTF: The Game did.
Bottom line: if you're a retro-gamer like myself, you owe it to yourself to pick this up.  Well done, devs!

There are a couple hidden extra puzzles which are mildly fun and were a nice distraction from the rest of the game, but if you need a distraction while you're playing a game there's most likely something wrong with that game.

I want to like this game. I played a good chunk of it and it was fun. I want to like this game so much. I am incredibly upset that I have to recommend against buying it. I got this game before it even came to steam. I bought the four pack straight from Chucklefish's main site. Played around in it, did all there was to do- I even have some hilarious screenshots of bugs that were fixed very early on. It was fun but eventually doing the same basic things over and over got very boring. The progression was basically broken past tier 2 (and there are 10 tiers) and if you wanted to make a nice base you had to luck out and find the right building materials on some planet. Which is fine, it was an alpha, I accepted it.
Fast forward to now. Almost nothing has changed. There is a little bit of tweaking here, some touch-ups there, but nowhere NEAR the amount of progress you'd expect from this amount of time. So I went back to their website and a wave of dread washed over me as I saw what I knew was the death knell of this game:
Several of the key developers advertising their personal pet project.
I heavily suspect they are using Starbound as a financial springboard for these projects. There is literally no other reason to do them besides ignorance. A studio as small as chucklefish can't AFFORD side projects like that, because all they do is take away from their primary project. Either they know this, and we're all being swindled so they can fund their pet projects (which, by the way, will likely be DOA, if not DNF, as most one-man projects turn out to be) or they do not realize this and they need to get their act together and put their personal projects on hold until Starbound is ready for release.
I am upset that I have to give this game a no-go. I wanted it to turn out good so much. The concept is here but the staff keeps side-tracking and delaying so they can work on petty dead-end distractions.

All the nostalgia you'd expect -- All the new trials and challenge you wouldn't.
For the fence sitters of this reimagining of Shadowgate:  To shrug this offering of the Shadowgate franchise as simply a remake does the efforts of the development team no justice.
For those who have played any of the previous versions of the game across its many iterations, you will indeed feel as though you have returned to the same castle, and the same aura of the game remains surprisingly intact and pervades each and every room.
But be warned, the familiarity is both friend and foe as you begin to traverse the new puzzles and challenges.  Old riddles may not always be what they seem and familiarity can lend itself to misdirection.  It will take a fresh perspective from the player to prepare for the fresh traps, trials, and tribulations of this new castle shaped the guise of the old.
I must admit I had a skeptical approach to the title myself before being part of its testing; but have been pleasantly surprised by the respect to the original and the careful balance of nostalgia vs new content paid by the development team.
If you enjoyed the previous generations of the Living Castle, Shadowgate, then you will most certainly find quite a lot to love about its newest incarnation.  And if you are new to this genre of gameplay or this franchise, then Shadowgate is an apt place to start.

Having purchased Hacknet after a recent sale, I'd like to give a solid recommendation for this game. Despite reports of crashes on some systems (installing the XNA branch seems to fix it for many), it ran perfectly for me and was a solid 7 hours of fun to 100%, or 4 hours for my first playthrough.
The hacking systems in this game are reasonably simple, which opens the game up to a larger audience than just programmers. However, the command line interface is there, faster, and even required for parts of the game. It's definitely intuitive and simple, but it's got widespread appeal too. As a programmer myself, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. However, the timings of the programs are a little too slow, a lot of the hacking portions are sitting and waiting.
Rather than just focusing on one storyline, the developers have created multiple tracks, and added various "contracts" that you can take from some of the major groups in the game. You have to take a certain number to continue, but the choice is there. On subsequent playthroughs, it's very possible to find another route through the game with an entirely new faction, which definitely adds replay value.
There's also a little satiric minigame called "Point Clicker" (which you can hack!) with two steam achievments with it. Fun?
There are also many irc logs and funny files dotted around foreign systems. I spent much of my time in the game looking around these systems for more cheap laughs. However, I'm not a fan of some of the random binary files dotted around the game. They definitely seem to flesh out the filesystems but they do seem kind of irritating.
Failures in the game (in the form of being traced, which is a countdown from 100) are very well balanced. Without going into too much detail, if you can pass a hacking challenge you continue as you are, otherwise the game shuts down and you are forced to continue from your last save point.
Pros:
-Simple and intuitive UI with a useful and functional command line interface
-Engaging storyline with added laughs in the form of irc logs
-Branching gameplay
Cons:
-Reported stability issues
-Slow hacking experience with a little too much waiting
Verdict: 87/100!
10/10 would play again

If you liked the first one, this is an improvement in basically every way. There's new classes so it doesn't feel redundant and the main map format is much better done imo. I wish there had been a little more depth to it and I felt like I hit the max on all my upgrades pretty quick. This has some of the same... quirks, we'll call them, as the original; 75% or less on shots means you will rarely hit, the mechanics of cover can be a bit baffling at times, there are some issues with the Psi class. This game adds some frustration in the hacking department (although Specialist was by far my favorite class) and you will regularly fail hacks of 70%+ and even with the greatest possible hack stat in the game you'll have some hack rewards <20%. None of that should stop you from loving this game. The default difficulty is probably not challenging enough if you like these games but it can get quite brutal depending on the setting and circumstance. They added an autosave feature that anyone who remembers the original will be very appreciative of (no more 5-6 missions with no save only to wipe and lose your mind). The story is very well done and it's good to see (hear) all your old allies back again (with the exception of one). The Resistance role of your squad is a great narrative touch and the stakes seem bigger and your victories seem more significant (I do miss arc thrower captures). The maps are a lot more fun and feature a ton more elevation than the original. If you haven't played the first one, this one makes it irrelevant (even the ending from the first one is invalidated) and on sale it's about the same price. Very much reccomended!

Alright so this game has recieved a lot of bad reviews for being derivitive of the DS series, however I believe firmly that this game is very much on par with the souls games for a number of reasons. If  you don't want to read the whole review let me sum it up for you: if you enjoyed the souls games and were looking for something similarly difficult and fun then you will most likely enjoy this game. Here are the reasons why you will enjoy this:
1. Visuals. This game has stunning visuals, much better than DS 1 & 2. The bosses, the textures, the armors and weapons all look ♥♥♥♥ing sweet. Very ambient lighting as well also sets a great mood for the game.
2. Difficulty. Similar to the souls series, this game is extremely difficult and is paced much the same as the souls series (ie. kill enemies to gain something similar to souls, which you use to level up and if you die you lose your souls and can retrieve them on your next life and if you die again before getting them they are lost).
3. Bosses. The bosses in this game look awesome and are extremely hard. If you beat one on the first try then kudos to you, but it's taken me at least 2 or 3 for most bosses and sometimes more. This difficulty leaves you with an extremely satisfying feeling when you finally understand the patterns of the boss, and their attacks and kick their asses and take their loot.
4. Story. So in the souls games, the story is very vague. You hardly ever understand what you're killing and for what purpose, as well as your character because it is created by you, has no back story that you know of. Sure you get a general idea at the beginning as to what you're doing, but no real explaination or plot thickening occurs and you basically walk around killing♥♥♥♥♥♥ LotF however has a nice little back story to the game, as well as much more interactable NPC's within the game that really give it a better, more complete RPG feel.
So basically that's it. This game is thoroughly enjoyable and I would highly recommend buying it ESPECIALLY if it is on sale as it is well worth  you time. This is an criminely underrated title and if you have any love for the format of DS's games then you should give this a shot.

I don't do many reviews but this game warrants one.
Even though this is early release alpha the game is quite a bit more finished than you would expect giving way to some reviews which may be more critical than they should be. I've been playing since Jan 2016 during a free weekend and have played almost daily since.
Coming from a faster pewpew game my initial thoughts were that this may be a bit slow paced for me, but the graphics and feel were great so figured I would give it a fair shake. I'm glad I did. And it's not slow.
Some things:
1. The Ship tree/Progression tree really should probably not be called that because the ships are balanced to play with and against each other. The "starter ships" are really just free well rounded ships. They are able to fit in and fight with all ships. Progressing up the tree you will find ships with different specialties. Not better. They do however, require much more knowledge of the game to fly and contribute to the team.
2. Speed. Game pacing is actually just about right. FS is not a twitch game, but I find that as you learn the game and pay more attention to your team, strategy, timer, enemy team you are always moving. Always doing something and almost always fighting over something.
3.The movement is more like space submarines than spaceships but I've gotten use to that. This was changed a while back and this was the consensus.
4. Progression. It's not really progression since each ship can hold it's own when flown properly. But you will progress in gaining skill and fighting tougher more organized opponents.
5. The community is, for the overwhelming part, quite helpful and welcoming
Seeing the progression of the game since I started I'm encouraged to keep playing. More maps and more ships coming and beta stage looming FS is in a good spot.

Q.U.B.E. is a minimalist first-person puzzle game. You wake up in a sterile environment consisting entirely of white cubes. There are a small number of colored blocks – when you point at them and press your mouse, you can cause them to extrude from the walls or retract back into them. There are four kinds of blocks – purple blocks, which rotate the environment (either 90 degrees or, in a small number of puzzles, 45 degrees. There are red blocks, which extrude a line up to three blocks long. There’s yellow blocks, which always come in threes; clicking on either end causes them to extrude 1 block on the opposite end, 2 blocks in the middle, and 3 blocks on the clicked block. And there’s blue blocks, which slingshot you (or any other object) when you touch them.
There’s a couple other mechanics – there are some round marbles which must be navigated through environments by use of the block mechanics, as well as some autonomous robots which always turn left which must be navigated through the environment using block mechanics. Later on, there are some wires (which, when they contact pads, light them up – these are only used for a very small number of puzzles, as they are pretty limited) and a few laser light puzzles, where you must reflect a laser using mirrors to get to the final point.
A few puzzles make use of tinting blocks – either to change the color of lasers or to change the color of marbles – which adds an additional element to some puzzles.
While the game tries to do a lot with its mechanics, I have to say that a lot of the puzzles weren’t actually all that much fun to solve. The game was very fond of the marble puzzles, but I have to say these were my least favorite part of the game; some of them involved fairly exact timing, particularly on some blocks with some amount of delay to them (the yellow ones), and on at least one puzzle that involved rotation, I’m fairly certain I “cheated” the game and didn’t solve it the “right way”. It was also common to face several marble puzzles in a row, which made them feel a bit more repetitive than they might have otherwise.
However, the game as a whole doesn’t have all that many tricks to show the player; it clocks in around four hours in length for the main game, plus maybe another couple hours for the various side challenges if you’re intent on getting a lot of medals. But the game simply doesn’t have all that many puzzle elements to it, and so after a while it feels like the game is just remixing stuff you’ve seen a bunch without doing anything particularly clever with it. The fifth zone – doing puzzles in the dark – was particularly notable in this regard, as the main mechanic was that you couldn’t see all of what you were doing at the same time. This wasn’t a particularly fun mechanic, but it didn’t really do anything new with the puzzles, just made it more inconvenient to solve them. The first couple zones of the game were basically a tutorial in the games’ mechanics as well, with a lot of very simple puzzles which weren’t all that interesting to solve.
And unfortunately, this game doesn’t boast much else other than puzzles; whereas Portal boasted GlaDOS, Wheatly, and Cave Johnson constantly chattering at you, Q.U.B.E.’s “mission control” voices are somewhat more limited in their appearances. Worse, however, is the fact that they just aren’t all that interesting; one of them says you’re saving the Earth, the other one says that the first voice is lying and you’re imprisoned in the Earth solving puzzles for their sadistic satisfaction. The second voice introduces a fair bit of fridge logic to the game, but neither scenario being presented to the player ultimately feels like it makes much sense – the second voice points out the ridiculousness of the game’s premise, but the game never really to justify why someone would be doing what they were doing. And unfortunately, in a non-comedy game that seems to be taking itself seriously, that’s a bit of a problem; why am I supposedly in some sort of alien spaceship solving puzzles to destroy it? How does that make sense? How does the player character solving these puzzles have any relation to stopping the ship? And, assuming that mission control really is telling the truth, how do they know that there is an escape shuttle waiting at the end of the ship for you?
There isn’t even any real attempt at explaining all this made by the game, which seemed to be trying to be cleverly ambiguous but instead simply undermined itself.
The one thing that I can say that the game did well was its graphics; Q.U.B.E. is an indie game, but by making use of the extremely minimalist environment composed almost entirely of white cubes, the producers managed to make a game that looks very good – I don’t think anyone would immediately identify it as an indie game just by looking at it, at least not at the start. The environments were very clean and were visually appealing, though unfortunately by the end of the four-hour long game the white cube walls had begun to get a bit samey looking, and mixing it up with ruined areas didn’t really work, instead making it just look kind of dingy.
Ultimately, like a number of similar minimalist puzzle games (such as Quantum Conundrum, Antichamber, and The Talos Principle), Q.U.B.E. feels like it was emulating Portal, but failed to recognize that Portal worked so well in part because the new mechanic, the portal gun, was virgin territory. Nothing in Q.U.B.E. felt like virgin territory. And while the Talos Principle managed to carry itself with a clever story and worldbuilding, Q.U.B.E.’s attempt at a serious story didn’t feel like it ultimately made much sense or was particularly well-written. The voice actors did a decent job with their lines; the problem was that the plot itself made no real sense, and indeed, the game undermined itself by questioning its own nature and then not really resolving all the inconsistencies it brought up
If there was one mercy to this game, it was that it was short, clocking in at only around 4 hours to beat the main story, including all the side content therein. But without a really interesting central mechanic or plot, there’s not much here worth experiencing. My advice? Play the Portal games or The Talos Principle instead.
