Before you see my rating and go, "Ermeh Gerdness, Merst Therms Down Rerview Becerse it's not nergative!" Just hear me out on what I have to say.
The game is, undeniably, plagued with performance issues. Issues reported have prevented people from launching the game, progressing the story, finishing missions, or even running a decent framerate, etc. The list goes on. For this alone, I am deeply dissapointed with Ubisoft, as these issues actively try to ruin what is otherwise a very fun game.
Assassin's Creed Unity is the 7th (Or 8th, Or 9th, Or, screw it no one counts these things anymore) game in the yearly franchise. Unity follows the adventures of Arno Dorian amidst a French Revolution setting in a faithfully recreated and very beautiful Paris. If Ezio is the Italian Batman, then Arno is the French Batman. However, I wouldn't say he's like Ezio as much as he reminded me of Edward from the previous games. He's cunning, deceitful, self-centered, and witty. He's a great character overall.
The story is alright. The game starts off with possibly the greatest first act in the series that eventually leads Arno into becoming an Assassin. However, after you have dawned the Assassin robes, the story begins going downhill. It's a mesh of random events and action sequences that the writers at Ubisoft probably thought up, but had no way to connect them together in a very interesting way. As a result, the story comes off as unimpressive, and sadly, it's greatest weakness is the Assassin vs. Templar feud that is in every game of the series now. If I were Ubisoft, I'd take a page out of Black Flag's book and go for something completely irrelevant.
Aside from the story, the gameplay is very fun. Parkour is faster and fun(er?) than ever, as you'll be ascending up buildings with speed and, courtesy of a new feature, descending from them easily without having to jump 5 stories and hope you'll survive. However, it's still difficult to navigate (you still act like spiderman) though it's the best it's ever been.
The game puts a much larger emphasis on stealth than in previous games, however, cover-binding can be problametic and there's a lot of 'how did you see me?' moments.  Though it's still a victory for the series to have the first ever crouch button and an assortment of abilties that make stealth fun and challenging at the same time. Combat is no longer a counter-kill fest, thank god. Taking on multiple enemies is quite challenging, but satisfying when done correctly. It's very fun to engage in large fights and test the limits.
As far as Open-World content goes, Paris is littered with activities to do. You have Murder Mystery invstigations, Club Assassinations, Notradamus Puzzles, Paris Stories, lots of loot chests, cockades, etc. However, sorta like Watch Dogs, the game suffers from having almost too much to do. It's very overwhelming.
One of my favorite new features to be added to the series is the ability to customize your Assassin. There's lots of different hoods, robes, and other gear pieces spread throughout the game to fully optimize the look you want. Better yet, the gear pieces you earn improve various stats, such as Health, Melee, or Stealth.
So how about co-op? I've done a few games with my friends so far and have had a lot of fun. Sure, killing guards is a button mash fest, but for heist missions, you have to be stealthy to reap the most rewards, which is not just a challenge for your ability to stealth, but your ability to coordinate with your team. There's several co-op missions spread throughout the game so there's plenty of content for you and your friends to enjoy. Not only this, but you can free-roam the open world at anytime just to goof off.
Overall, Unity is a very good game with several minor flaws. The game in its current state is not very playable for most, so I highly recommend you wait for Ubisoft to release a patch (which they have been hard at work on apparently). I feel like Unity has restored a lot of the core components of the series, but has not done so in the best way possible. Hopefully the next game (which I SERIOUSLY hope Ubisoft plans to release in a finished state) is the one to do that.

I was searching around on the Steam Store for some free to play games to pass the time and I stumbled upon 'Realm of the Mad God'. I read the description and it said RPG, Bullet-Hell, Multiplayer. I thought "Awesome"! Then I played it... I am sorry but I cannot recomend a game that has so much stuff behind a paywall. Seriously! Everything in this game costs gold. Which has to be bought with real life cash. The only way to get gold otherwise is to trade which is impossible if you are at a low level. It costs gold for extra character slots, the rest of the other nine classes (you only start out with six). Hell, it even costs gold to wear the alternative costumes which you have already unlocked! It cost gold to get the real good loot, otherwise you are stuck with a minimal amount of good items. I played the archer class and I only found 5 weapons, 3 armor pieces, 1 arrow quiver and 3 rings, after 2 hours! Not to mention the repeating loot drops. But thats the economy side. I can forgive it if the gameplay is solid and the classes are diverse. Are they? NO. Since this is a bullet hell game every class has ranged attacks which renders the warrior and rogue classes worthless because of their short range! The extra classes might as well be just different visual effects with differing range. What about enemy variety. There is some enemy variety but they spawn so frequently and have so many similar attacks that most of them feel like reskins of the same 10 enemies. How about bosses? The same boss can appear multiple times and they do so little damage  they feel like they are just bigger versions of their minions (which for most of them, this is actualy true). Also did I mention that if you die (because the game spawned a load of enemies on you when you were trying to kill the same boss for the 50th time), you lose eveything!? I am a fan of roguelikes (read my FTL review for proof) but losing EVERYTHING EACH AND EVERY TIME YOU DIE IN THIS MULTIPLAYER ONLINE ONLY RPG was the last straw for me. This game is essentialy everything bad about an MMO. Do not play this game.

-Positives-

Arkaia is a game made by one man as an homage to the puzzle adventure games of yore alike Myst, Zork, and most of the games by The Adventure Company, among many others. It is also as it appears the first chapter for what seems to be an entire series.
Personally speaking with the developer, it would seem that it is intended as more of a proof of concept rather than a full-fledged game, and in that, it definitely succeds, All the elements are there, puzzles, scenery, Myst-style point-and-click movement, and beautiful scenery.
On the other hand, it is a proof-of-concept indeed, with all what that entails; outdated generation visuals, finicky puzzle controls, and hastily put together UI elements, along with one track for the entire game, which takes about 20-30 mins to complete.
Why do I recommend it? The developer is upfront about it being a game in design, he is alone in development, and the price is very reasonible. A cause I can get behind. Maybe this is the start of his success story and I'll get to play a much better second chapter.

Darkest Dungeon is one of the better new games I've played in awhile, and it's scratching an itch that I've had for a long time.
The game is difficult, punishing, and from start to finish is a tense experience. The game is not for the faint of heart for sure, if you're not a fan of challenging games, or don't enjoy dealing with the negative consequences of failure, this is definitely not the game for you. This is a game for people who want to constantly be at edge, biting their nails at the worst of times and feeling sweet relief wash over them at the best of times.
It also has an amazing art style, one of the best I've seen in ages, and as a result I can see this game aging like a fine wine in the long term.

Do you like building and grinding to build more to grind more? No? Good, because you're not doing either of those things here. Warcube is an action adventure RPG that takes inspiration from a few well received and critically acclaimed games, and and
while at the same time not feeling like a bunch of 'cool' features tacked on at random; the developer did a good job of making sure things fit well into the game.
The combat is great, you could compare it to Shadow of Mordor because of the combo potential with the slow motion of the 300 movie remake, but quite a bit harder as attacks are aimed 100% manually and your mistakes are easily punished by your opponents; if you rush into a group of enemies and miss one of your combo hits, your melee attack will go into a cooldown, the length of which depends on the weapon you're currently using, and you'll be stuck in amongst a large crowd of enemies with your ranged weapon and parry. If you die, the enemy that struck the killing blow will grow into a larger, tougher and more powerful enemy, and will do so again should you lose another fight to it. The videos and gifs on the storefront do a great job of showing how the combat functions, so go look at those.
The game is "open world" in that the world is open, but the levels aren't. In the world map, you move around to points of interests, like camps, castles, towns, and other stuff, which all act as levels which you enter. Some of these points of interest send enemy soldiers out into the world which if you happen to run into, it can cause an ambush encounter where you fight a wave of 20 or so enemies. You can capture these locations, at which point they'll start sending troops of your own to
. You can move near them and click on them to have them follow you into levels and encounters, where despite seeming to be half baked, they will fight the enemy until they die.
Levels aren't all that complex, the objectives are pretty simple actually. Kill enemies, capture the flags and open chests for gold, sometimes doing these things aren't all that simple, sometimes the location of things isn't really obvious, sometimes what you have to do to get to the next area in the level can be hard to discover and sometimes it's just a challenge to actually get there.
Something else about combat is that there's a stealth element, if you haven't been spotted by the nearby enemies, you can sneak around in the often copious amount of bushes to either get into a good position to start the encounter or
sneak past them entirely
Another thing is there's some very well implemented easter eggs and references that are there, you know they're there, but they're not in-your-face obnoxious, or in your way, screaming "LOOK AT ME!". I really hope the developer does more stuff like this.
There isn't too much story yet, so far we know that you're a godlike being that has been gone from their land for almost 4,000 years, and it seems said land is in the hands of your enemy. Even though there isn't really much story so far, what's there has a nice and enjoyable charm to it, and the narrator / floaty head guy is quite a funny character. Some 4th wall breaking, but it certainly enhances the experience as it's done well.
As far as Early Access goes, I have very high hopes for this one. I played the very first Early Access version, which had quite a few crashes and bugs, as well as some things I was concerned about, and I contacted the developer (now this can be done through the Steam forums for the game on the bug report thread), and he not only fixed the bugs and (I think) all of the crashes, but he thanked me for reporting them and said that he's currently working on addressing the things I was concerned about. The game is very much playable in the current state and I'm confident that if something big or game breaking were to pop up in the future, the developer would be jumping all over it asap.
Worth is always subjective, but I can give you facts and my personal opinions to work with. I obtained the game elsewhere for my first playthrough, and bought it the next day despite $9 USD ($12 AUD) being a lot for me to spend on a game right now. Right now the game has 3 to 4 hours of playthrough content, depending on if you rush it or not, but it has plenty of potential for making your own fun by trying to pull of awesome combos or neat tricks with the current arsenal of weapons at your disposal as some hit harder and some combo faster and have very little cooldown when you miss, which can lead to some pretty amazing looking stuff.
If the currently small playthrough time doesn't bother you, then I'd seriously suggest either getting this game, following and wishlisting it and looking back every week or so, or looking up gameplay on YouTube to see if it can change your mind.
Sorry for the very long wall of text, but I've really tried to cover everything, though if I haven't you can reply to this review to ask questions and I'll try my best to answer them. Also, this is my first serious written review, so any feedback or advice would really be appreciated.
I'll attempt to keep this updated within reason, although there may be a time when there's just so much more stuff that I have to entirely rewrite it.

Really amazing game. I bought it a few days ago and I am hooked. The game runs very smooth, and the gameplay is quite fun and engaging. In addition, at least playing in pubbie lobbies, ships seem to be fairly balanced, and it feels like every ship plays quite different from the others.
This game plays a lot like world of tanks or world of warships, but with spaceships and with a 3D range of movement. However, it also has MOBA-esque qualities of having multiple "lanes" and having to push defensive structures to kill your enemy's main base.
What makes this very enjoyable is the fact that you have to position, shoot and maneuver your ship on a micro level to defeat your enemy - but you also have to make sure that your overall map positioning and timing is good on a team level as well (i.e. making sure your team arrives at gamma together and on-time, making sure you are defending base when the enemy has access, etc). It can be a little daunting at first, but the learning curve isn't too steep, especially if you've played MOBAs and understand positioning, timing, etc.
TLDR: Great game, plays like a mixture of world of tanks/warships combined with a MOBA-esque style.

XCOM 2 is an amazing game and probably my game of the year for 2016 but... It isn't perfect and I'm going to talk about Cons before I get to the pros.
The biggest complaint I saw about this game was that almost every mission is timed.
(X turns to secure and rescue the VP)
(X turns to stop them from destroying Y)
(X turns to capture supplies)
(X turns to eliminate this guy)
etc. etc.
Now along with the the timer being really annoying the lack of mission variety is also upsetting but it didn't bother me THAT much.
The amount of new enemies is also a little lacking. Yeah you're fighting Advent which is mostly made of humanoid aliens with normal guns and robots but this is XCOM, a game about fighting aliens and the aliens aren't even fought that often.
I mean don't get me wrong XCOM 2 introduces 13 new enemies in the base game as opposed to Enemy Unknown's 11. This means XCOM 2 has a total of 18 enemy types and that sounds all fine and dandy until you realize that at least 7 of those are Advent enemy types and only 6 of those are brand new aliens. That means only 5 enemies from EU came back for XCOM 2. The new aliens are kind of cool to fight but for the most part you're fighting Advent forces which means you'll be fighting Soldier after Officer after Lancer after Mech after Heavy Mechs after Turrets after Shieldbearer and so on...
However the positives do outscale the negatives by a lot.
The story and the concept of a resistance movement fighting an evil leadership is nothing new but there is something unique about XCOM 2 that makes it fresh and exciting.
You might be thinking well why is there a sequel if I beat the first game? Well if you beat the game and got every achievement... I have some bad news.
In Enemy Unknown you were a super beefed up organization funded by the governments of the world and now you find out you lost
and have to rejoin the fight with little to no equipment
This is definitely the best part about XCOM 2 and the gameplay revolves around you being the underdog. In Enemy Unknown you were the one hunting the aliens and in this game it's vice versa. THEY are the hunter and YOU are the prey. You can't go guns blazing and expect to not lose someone (this is XCOM after all). The Concealed mechanic is amazing for getting the drop on the enemy and really sets up some killer ambushes. In addition you actually have to scavenge for supplies and get items from enemy drops or fly the Avenger to a scavenging site. The black market in this game actually makes a little more sense because of the scenario you're put in.
Overall I would highly recommend this game. It is much harder than Enemy Unknown and I can guarantee you that you will lose some of your best men, but hey that's what having lots and lots and
of saves are for.
Good luck out there Commander.

I'm glad I gave this game a chance. It looks like a low budget Mega Man, and it is, but it's also very fun. I can honestly say I had more fun with this than any official Mega Mans I've played in the last 10 years.
The level designs are tuned to perfection with amazing attention to detail. The boss patterns are all unique and interesting. It's very minimalist, more in the vein of Mega Man 1 & 2 (no sliding, no megabuster), but the pacing is just right. It's a little on the easy side and has an XP system which makes the game a little easier as you progress. I also played on Easy mode which gives infinite lives.
Yes, the sprites are awful (with the exception of a few backgrounds). I think they made an honest effort, but the art is bad in so many ways. If they got a sprite artist to redo everything it would make a huge difference in how the game is perceived. Level themes are super weird... I'm not even sure how to interpret them, but at least they aren't cliche! The soundtrack has some kickin' chip tunes and fits great with the style. The story is a little too wordy, but it's easy to skip through it. It ends on an unwelcome cliff hanger that caught me by surprise.
But most of this is nitpicks. It all adds up to one of the best Mega Man type games I've played in a very long time. Short and sweet with just enough of it's own identity.

I still really enjoy this game. There's no sugarcoating it. This is one of my favorite games of all time and it probably had an influence in my life choices.
Looking at the game closer, everything about it appeals to me. I love the character design, the music is above fantastic, and the scripting is amazing. The game mechanics are pretty smooth too, but that wasn't the thing that made this game one of my favorites of all time.
The characters became a part of my life while I was playing this game, and not to sound like a crazy person here, but I connected with them all on an emotional level. Every single protagonist made me wonder about my life choices. I'm including Zulf in the pool cause I believe that he is in fact a protagonist, but that's an argument for another day.
The Kid is the character that really makes this game. You befriend him as the player. The Kid isn't some faceless hero that you can imprint your own desires on to. The Kid, is The Kid, and everyone in the game recognizes that. The Kid has a personality, yet he's quiet the entire game. Again, I could rant about the similarities and differences that The Kid has to Link from LoZ, but that's an argument for another day. The kid, different from Link, existed before you started to control him. He had a mother and a life of his own. The Kid had feelings and dreams that the player can experience through dream snippets that make a separation possible between character and player. Rucks' narration also helps separate The Kid from the player, but when it comes down to it, this game is beautifully written and I can't stress it enough that this game is worth your money and time.

Week 48.  Radiant ("easy") difficulty.
Things are progressing well at the 1st Game Estate (I realized later your save title is also your mansion name).  I've learned the basics and some of the advanced tactics of combat.  I plan.  I synergize.  I consider the foes that are likely to appear in a given region before sending in the team.  I strap my heroes down in the sanitarium and condition their more malignant personality quirks out of them.  I buy trinkets with dubious magical properties from nomads.  Every now and then a hero falls in action, but it's a dangerous world, and the Caretaker has been calling them "corpses" since they stepped off the stage coach.  I have a strong team of experienced heroes.  Surely it's just a matter of time now before total victory is mine.
I arrange a routine sortie for some of my moderately-experienced adventurers.  All have survived trials before, and none are suffering from any (severe) psychological conditions.  They are well-trained.  They are well-equipped.  They are well-provisioned.  The mission is a level lower than their experience.  Their task is to destroy a hag terrorizing the Weald with her cookpot and giant meat tenderizer (she also seasons her prey with frogs and eyeballs).
The mission goes well.  Bandits, cultists, and even the undead fall easily before the team.  Our arbalest provides fire support from the back lines while the crusader and grave robber mix it up in melee with knives, swords, and the occasional Pickaxe to the Face.  The team's medic, a plague doctor with a variety of offensive and defensive potions and vials, develops a case of paranoia after a series of run-ins with black-magic-wielding cultists and occasionally attempts to stab her compatriots, but all is otherwise going smoothly.  The group camps for the night before facing the hag, to ensure maximum preparedness.
Five minutes later, the crusader stands alone, unable to reach the hag, whaling sensely on the indescructable cauldron with his sword, the stewed and beaten bodies of his fallen allies scattered around him.  The hag drinks from the cauldron, healing herself, before smashing the crusader with her tenderizer.  No one from the 1st Game Estate ever sees any of them again.
10/10 would abandon all hope again.

If you like round based games where your heroes die permanently, this could be the game for you.
You are charged with cleansing the surroundings of an estate of evil and madness. The estate consists of several buildings, which can be upgraded through ressources gathered in dungeons. Some buildings serve to heal your heroes of stress, maladies and mental illnesses. Others to upgrade equipment and skills. You can also increase the size of your hero roster and of the daily available heroes to recruit. A large roster is important, as your heroes will regularly require a time-out from their adventures. Sometimes... a permanent one.
Through special loot you find in dungeons you will be able to upgrade your buildings. Valuables such as gems will be turned into gold, which is required for equipment or skill purchases and upgrades for heroes.
There are six hero levels and dungeon difficulties. Every dungeon has a different theme, enemies and multiple quests with varying difficulty level, which rotate randomly. Once you pick the quest and dungeon of your choice, you are tasked to chose four heroes and then select the provisions you want to bring. They can consist of torches, food, bandages, antivenom, medical herbs and more items. Depending on the type of dungeon and quest you might want to bring different items with you. Looted valuabes will also take up inventory space, and you will have to balance greed against survivability in the dungeon.
Once entering a dungeon you will get assigned a procedurally generated map, consisting of several rooms and corridors connecting them. Moving through corridors will slowly consume your torch, but you can always light another one. IF you have any left. Darkness brings more loot, but also more stress and increases the power of your enemies. There are many objects (curios) to interact with, and usually require an item to cleanse them, for a good result. Otherwise you might regret your actions instantly.
You will move in real time through the dungeon until combat is initiated. Fighting will take place in turn-based mode between your four heroes and a maximum of four enemies. Heroes and enemies can be controlled from a side view, much like a platformer, and stand one behind another, effectively occupying four positions on each side. Some enemies can shuffle your hero positions (or simlpy getting surprised by enemies will do that), and can be hard to deal with. There's also heroes which change positions through abilities, which somewhat counters these enemies. Every combatant has four available skills, which either target one or multiple heroes or enemies. Many can only be used from certain positions, and also on enemies in particular positions.
There's also bosses and different, more powerful enemies through the dungeon on the higher difficulties. In most cases you can retreat from combat and the dungeons entirely. Sometimes an afflicted hero will simply refuse to retreat, even if it kills him.
A particular mechanic, similarly important to health, is stress. Some enemy abilities or the lack of light will raise your heroes stress level. Once it reaches 100, they will most likely become afflicted. They have a small chance to gain a virtue instead, but chance is small. It's only temporary until stress is reduced back to 0 in town. Until then they will sometimes skip turns, hit each other, attack randomly and most importantly increase the stress level of the other compations. Once stress level reaches 200 a hero will suffer a heart attack.
Heroes also gain many permanent positive and negative traits, which will become more severe over time, if not cured. Some of them can be really annoying and problematic. The thought behind it is to treat only really problematic quirks in the sanatorium.
The goal of the game is to get enough heroes to level 6, then well equipped and skilled, in order to succeed in assaulting the Darkest Dungeon three times.
The DLC Crimson Court consists of an additional dungeon based on vampires and a formidable tank class - the Flagellant.
There's more mechanics and more to say about the game, but I'll leave that up to you to find out. The game offers many complex and interesting mechanics and nice challenges without actually being unfair and random. The risk is very calculable and can be reduced by a great amount by being well prepared.
A large amount of workshop items is also available for download, offering changes to gameplay and even more hero classes.
Tl,dr: Turn-based RPG with basebuilding, permadeath and procedurally generated dungeons.

Side scrolling turn based RPG crawler with dark gothic graphics and sound to match.
Several different dungeon areas to explore with different dungeon levels and different lengths, all with different rewards to boot.
Autosave feature means you can stop anytime and pick up right where you left off, but you can't go back to your last good save to try something again.
Random number generator (RNG) determines outcomes on hits and misses etc.
Some of the negative reviews cry about RNG, it is a double edged bittersweet blade. Some of my best characters have died because they received a 0 point heal while knocking on death's door. Dead forever, (well they may come back someday but it's very rare). There are also times I've gotten 32 point heals when I thought I was a goner, or landed a crit on a slimy Eldritch right when I needed it. Is like playing Dungeons and Dragons with HP Lovecraft as the Dungeon Master.
Some of the best battles I have ever had in any game have been playing this. Not even boss fights, just ambushes when I am low on everything, and bleeding profusely from every orifice. No strategy seems to work, but I somehow pull through and win the fight. Sometimes with the whole party intact, sometimes with 1 guy left standing. Real pulse pounding stuff.
So yes this game rules all. Lots of classes with skills, armor and weapons to upgrade. Lots of class combinations to round out different groups for different dungeons. Trinkets from common to rare to help with this and that. There is a Psych ward in the hamlet for treating mental quirks that bring out the worst in you when you get stressed, and a hospital for treating ailments like the plague that slow you down or make you hit like crap. There is also an abbey in town for stress relief through meditation, a tavern for stress relief through drink, and a brothel for stress relief through the old nudge nudge wink wink.
Or you can let your character build up so much stress he has a heart attack and dies. Stress in this game can be a real killer. Make sure you have plenty of food and torches!
My graveyard keeps filling up, but I love this game and can't stop playing it. Have not gotten the DLC yet, but I will.

TLDR;
Hacknet comes down to running a few exploits, DDoS the proxy server, bypassing the firewall, and grats your in.
*  Asthetically pleasing interface
*  Marginally authentic hacking process
*  Well developed and compelling story line
*  Casual game play
----------
Pros:
I really enjoy the fact that the interface authentically portrays a Linux or Unix environment.  The interface is very authentic.  Especially if you use window managers rather than a full desktop environment.  The requirement to use the terminal instead of clicking everything makes the game feel more like real world hacking.  The Hacknet story line is more developed than other hacking simulators.  There is a sense of freedom to pick diversified contracts and to complete them however fit.  All of this supports casual game play.
Cons:
(More of a preference than a con.)
Breaking the security of a real world network devices requires time, caution, ability, and patience.  People with InfoSec experience will feel like they are rolling their face on the keyboard.  It would be nice if the game was a bit more difficult and more accurately portrayed real world hacking.

A really unique game. It's by far not a common dungeon crawler and it deserves a very own genre.
You return to your hamlet and have to "clean up" what went terribly wrong in the past. Therefor you will have to visit every week (week = one dungeon run) a dungeon to get rid of the enemies, sometimes bosses, collect treasure for buying provisions, pay for recovery and so on.
It takes some time to get used to all the game mechanics, but it's not a big deal. Many things are random generated, so it will need some experience to face them properly. Darkest Dungeon is difficult, but not unfair.
Really good is
* the awesome 2D-graphics
* the sound / sound effects
* many different hero classes
* many trinkets (=accessories with benefits/maybe also handicaps)
* many possibilities for preparation, recovery
* different dungeons with many different enemies
* all the game mechanics that make this game unique, and also realistic in a way
* Developer updates, patches
* the Narrator, oh gawd, the Narrator <3
* ..and for sure much more
might be difficult for
* people with thin skin, the game demands a lot from the player
Important is
* Always prepare for the worst case (preparation can and will save your heroes lifes more than once)
* The game punishes mistakes very savagely
* You will make mistakes
* You might lose a hero or more of them, and they will stay dead
* the heroes are human, they're not overpowered, besides taking damage they get stressed, hungry, get quirks and so on

Type of Game: Hidden Object Game/Casual Adventure
Review in short: A good Hidden Object game, with a sympathetic story. A must buy for Fans of Fairy Tales, and Hidden Object afficinados.
Rating: 7.5 out of 10.
The story is a freeform of the Grimm Fairy Tale "The six swans". But instead of keeping too close to the story, which is quite familiar and actually exists in different versions (The twelve brothers, the seven ravens etc) it also uses freedom from the original, making it very interesting.
Artifex Mundi actually managed to catch the charm and the enchantment of the old fairy tale. The game is for younger people, and it's also aimed to a younger female audience. The game mechanics are, as with Hidden Object Games common easy to explain, and the tutorial could be easily put aside. The graphics are, again - as most of the time with Artifex Mundi - beautiful and enchanting. The riddles aren't always logical and more on a medium challenge level, yet they are perfectly integrated into the game and the story. The soundtrack also creates a good atmosphere.
Recommendation: For Fans of Fairy Tales, Hidden-Object-Game, for younger audiences.
Given the presentation and the game in general, it's a nice game to play - albeit it's short (all HOGs are short) it's worth the time invested into it.

First off, I do actually like the game. I really do. It is quite pleasing aesthetically, and has a great system in place that lets you play the game how you want.
Problem is, how you want to play the game might not be very successful.
It is of this gamer's opinion that a tower defense game should not be a puzzle game. There should not be a narrow band of builds that will actually grant victory among an immense number of combinations that could be played. With 15 different towers and 17 skills, picking just four of each can be difficult, yes, but it affords the player the ability to define how they want to go about defending their cores, and that's not even counting the perk points, which add another layer of depth and customization. This system by itself is fantastic, but the execution that makes use of it is rather poor.
There is progression; not everything is available from the start. This progression, however, cuts off quite fast. Everything is unlocked at the point of hitting level 12, but the levels keep going, rather pointlessly. Perk points are gained differently, at a rate of 1 per completed map, and when you feel like you're not powerful enough to get past a particular map, there's a problem.
Now, I can understand a TD needing some strategy; if one doesn't make you think about what you're doing, then it's probably not very good. SSTD, though, feels like it asks too much of strategy, putting the player on a very fine line between perfection and failure. I was doing fine with this game through the first few levels. I made a blunder here and there, and learned from what were clear mistakes (setting all Violators to attack the highest HP targets was a bad idea, for the record). There were some tougher levels that took me a couple attempts to figure out, but it felt okay. The challenge was fair. Then along came Works.
Works is the map that I feel enforces an unfair level of difficulty and shows that the game really wants you to use a very specific setup to get through it. I have taken numerous attempts at it with different builds and have yet to even see the boss wave. I have beat my head against it long enough that I don't really care to continue. Maybe it's a fluke, maybe the rest aren't so bad after it, but I'm not going to put myself through the torture of trying to figure out the exact combination of towers and skills it takes to get through this map that seems to have too much of everything.
Sure, I could just use the magic of Youtube and look for a setup that gets through it so I could continue, but that's not how I play; I would get no sense of accomplishment and may as well have used Cheat Engine to bypass the level in terms of enjoyment. When a game completely shuts down a player's ability to progress, without giving them an opportunity to either adequately learn what they're doing wrong or power up to overcome the challenge, then there is a significant problem that needs to be addressed.
The game doesn't need to be easy; it just needs to cater to more than an elite 1% of builds. Don't tell the gamers how to play their game.

How should I put it in the simplest of terms...? X-COM 2 really likes to slap the player over his stupid face. If you are a little confused by what I mean, please understand that these words are not to be taken as a complaint or a sign of dissapproval from my part. I actually thoroughly enjoyed X-COM 2. It is – without exaggeration – one of the best, if not THE best turn-based strategy I played in this decade. It is thematically refreshing, cinematic where it needs to be and tactically demanding. And by 'tactically demanding', I mean hard as ♥♥♥♥. Yes, you heard me correctly; so if you consider yourself to be a rather casual player of strategy games, you should sit this one out. This game is cruel and unforgiving; I had to restart my campaign after 14 hours of gameplay just because I had made so many tiny mistakes along the way that, when accumulated, they created a scenario that was unwinnable. Nevertheless, if you take your time, learn from your past mistakes and never cease to improve your tactics, you will, eventually, experience one of the greatest feelings – beating the game for the first time. And for a while, you shall feel truly unvincible... I mean, until you try the Ironman mode and get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you all over again.
TO SUM UP: If you love great strategy games with brilliant micro-management, complex systemics and you don't mind turn-based combat and a difficulty setting that will never give you a break, don't you dare waste another minute and go buy this master piece of modern gaming.

I didn't think I would like this one as much as I did. The early praise for the game came mostly from the more art-afficionado sectors of the indie games journalism movement, so as a so-called "hardcore gamer" I thought I could safely ignore it. Not so. I was generously gifted the game, and went into it not expecting much, and for me it hit a good balance between "art" and gameplay. It plays like a more action-oriented Diablo, or a tiny bit like Boktai/Lunar Knights if you are familiar with that, and the combat has a very quick but unfrustrated pace. While you can gain levels and upgrades, they're generally more interesting than straight stat bonuses: new levels give you new "drinks" to consume which add special effects, like increasing blocking speed, and weapon upgrades can change how a weapon works at its fundamental level, such as having it cause damage over time.
As for the "art" portion, the game is composed of absolutely stunning watercolors, and has great...narration?

This is the same length as Call of Duty (about 7 hours) and introduces sprinting, a flamethrower, scripted sections in which you mark targets for artillery strikes, and equippable machine guns which you can deploy (but only when prone).  Otherwise it plays just like Call of Duty; a mechanically simple WWII shooter with multiple protagonists to show different sides of the war (American, British, and Russian protagonists), some emphasis on vague historical accuracy, diverse gameplay with some stealth missions and vehicle gameplay, and some obvious synthetic limitations like invisible walls and relative lack of physics.  Enjoyable, but far from excellence.
United Offensive stands out for having larger scale missions, gameplay within an aircraft (no piloting), and featuring Italy.  It takes place parallel with the original game.
The larger scale missions showcase AI limitations more than the original game, so expect them to struggle and act more stupidly than the base game (like in CoD 2).  United Offensive installs on top of the base game, so both along with CoD 2 use DirectSound3D and EAX 3 to offer superior sound quality to the rest of the franchise (better positional audio and dynamic environmental effects).  A Creative sound card is needed to take advantage of this, preferably X-Fi which allows for hardware acceleration rather than software which improves sound further.
Be sure to use marcomix's Real Weapons mod, as it adds more guns to the game and improves their models.

Most definitely recommended.

I must admit, I was initially put off by the 'simplistic' art style, but it turns out much much depth lies beneath.
Between the art DIRECTION, game design, mechanics, and sound design it all comes together beautifully.
First mention really must go the to the sound design, it's super tense, including that superb narration, it geniuely adds to the experience. so much so that if I've had a stressful day I can't listen for too long!
There's alot of 'under-the-hood' elements which aren't explained, especially if you've never played an old dungeon&dragons game before, and I've seen many players complain about cruel rng, but you actually do have a choice on how to play;
- You can put it on easy and run through it as a trial and error run while you find things out for your self which will be harsh, but that can be fun for certain typs of players.
- However if your like me and need to know stuff (not lore, I mean rules) you can have a quick read of the wiki ( I only read the curios section) and that will help you make choices that balance the risks so it doesn't feel so out of your control.
Play mechanics are deceptively deep, but ultimately fun and not confusing, you grasp more as you grow with your characters.
regaring the random elements, I think they are very fairly done, and it's ultimately what keeps you coming back.
The dungeons are tastefuly random, as inthe shape and contents vary, but within a theme for each area, so you can expect and prepare. They are also leveled, like your characters, which stops the size and challenge becoming truely unfair. The combat effectly involves 'dice rolls' based on percentages, which again adds to tension, as you can never truely know the outcome of a battle other than an educated guess. Another thing that keeps you both on edge and coming back for more.
Now all the above would be just basically sado masicsm if it wasn't for a worthwhile reward system and again this is really well done.
There is a guranteed reward per quest to aim towards, plus the promise of all the unknown loot from random curios and battles whilst exploring. The sense of progression and upgrading/managing your characters and facilites is great and ties the whole cyle together nicely. It's equally enjoyable leveling up and equiping your new loot as it exploring and fighting.
Overall the game direction is intended to be harsh, but totally to it's strength. The unified direction of horror and stress are both purposeful and unique, and it will stay with you.

Well, to start, the game is very poorly optimized and suffers from various glitches and bugs. All that nonsense can be patched out and likely will and I'm pretty sure we all know what a glitchy game looks like. As such, I won't be mentioning that sort of thing past this point since I wouldn't recommend this game even if it ran at 120 FPS  while looking better than Crysis 3. What can't be patched out are the numerous and inescapable design flaws that have utterly destroyed this game. Let's dive into them. (Note that I may ramble a short while here, but the ramblings will have a point.)
*Uninteresting main characters who make irrational and erratic decisions. For the first time, I did not like the protagonist of an AC game. During a specific fight with an old friend of Arno's, I found myself wishing the old man would kill Arno so maybe I would be able to play as one of the three interesting characters in the game, the other two being the new King of Rats and good ol' Shawn.
*Enough plot holes to give this game the nickname Assassin's Creed: Swiss Cheese. (For example, Arno's status within the Brotherhood at the end of the main story.)
*It is devoid of rewarding gameplay. One of the many things I loved from previous AC games is the series of puzzles (almost all of them fun and well-designed, this game included) you can solve to gain access to an INTERESTING LOOKING and FUNCTIONALLY USEFUL set of armour. In this game, the reward is literally a recoloured version of Altair's robes that is purely cosmetic. Talk about a slap to the face after solving puzzles for an hour.
*A crushing amount of immersion-breaking - including, but not limited to, asking you to create/link accounts in the middle of gameplay, (these next two are closely linked) being able to "hack" equipment to obtain it, and a series of missions known as "Rifts" that I found patently ridiculous. So, these last two have the same basic mind-numblingy outrageous problem. They both give Arno items/money through means that he did not have. You may hack items to gain access to them without Arno buying them and when you play the Rift missions which take place in a sort of purgatory-like simulation in a time period Arno was not alive during, you are rewarded with in-game currency that Arno can use to buy weapons and items. This is supposed to be a MEMORY SIMULATION. You are reliving MEMORIES that you can only participate in, not influence the outcome of. I don't think Arno had a person from the future controlling him and magically giving him money and equipment when he did this in his actual life, did he?
*Due to in part by the uninteresting main cast, the story falls  apart more and more as it progresses, with the high point being in Sequence 4. This is when you meet one of the three interesting characters; the man who  will become the next King of Rats. Well, I hope you don't like interesting characters because he'll only be shown twice more after this in the entire game, one of the other interesting characters is killed by Arno for what I consider to be a very bad reason, and the last one standing is Shawn, who you never actually see and only hear from on a few occasions. His witty humour is still visible in the Database, if you're feeling nostalgic and want to forget what game you're playing for a few blissful moments. (Yes, I realize I put two points about characters, but it's honestly bad enough to deserve two points.)
*The combat is unpolished, unfun, and - until you get a very powerful heavy weapon - almost always unfair. (Last- minute note I wanted to add: Want to know what was the most unfair and actually the worst-designed fight I've ever played? The final boss! Arguably the most important moment in the game, where everything you've been working towards comes to a head! It's almost beautiful in its horridness.)
*The game suffers from serious issues recognizing and reacting to input, and as such the lockpicking system is torn asunder and blocking in the combat is made even more difficult.
*A disturbing amount of missions have ridiculous "full synch" objectives, some of these objectives even require equipment you likely won't have purchased. That majority, though, are simply very poorly thought out. For instance, in other AC games, you would get full synch for doing common sense things or just doing the mission properly, but in this game the full synch objectives virtually never make sense. Some are outright impossible to fulfill (such as in a certain side mission where you must slide over/under 5 objects but there's not 5 to slide over/under and you're in a confined space).
*The game is very random in its equipment unlock system. You can not get a single high-level full outfit because most pieces of every outfit are locked until you win it in a "Club Competition" or a seemingly unrelated co-op mission or main mission. I just want to look like a musketeer, Ubisoft. Let me have more than a bracer and some pants.
*The game is essentially pay-to-win. You "hack" the most powerful items in the game right off the bat (with the power of real money, of course) and Ubisoft's Uplay rewards for this game are horribly, horribly unbalanced. The full soundtrack for the game costs 20 Uplay points, while 2000 of the game's currency can be purchased for 30 Uplay points. That same 2000 currency can be gained from a SINGLE medium-skill locked chest in the game.
*Lastly - and this is a very subjective opinion that I hold that does not necessarily reflect negatively on the game - I am quite disappointed that there weren't more references to popular writers of the time, though there were a mild amount. Particularly Voltaire. I mean, you show absolutely none of the wittiest man of the century's writings, but you send the player to his tomb? Positively cruel.
I'm sure I'm forgetting a few negative things, but there are a few positives, as well. These will be shorter as I'm a tad burnt out from all that ranting and raving (and also because they don't make up for the flaws).
*The art team for this game was phenomenal. Just what I'd expect from a group of skilled artists with a beautiful universe to create in.
*The mocap team was, as always, spot on. There's even a kissing scene about 30 minutes into the game that is the most realistic kiss I've seen in a video game to date.
*Remember earlier when I said the "main cast" was bad? That's true, but most (maybe all) of the side characters I've seen were interesting, fleshed-out, and well-written.
*The puzzle missions, murder mystery missions, Paris Stories (aka side missions), and Crowd Events (random events where you can help people) were for the most part very good. Puzzles and murder mysteries were engaging and sometimes challenging, and the Paris Stories were well-designed and really helped to flesh out the world.

This is Artifex Mundi at their absolute most glorious. Lovers of lesser-known fairy tales will recognize the homage to "The Wild Swans" as the base of this, albeit with a chillingly dark turn. The villain is a bit predictable, but that's easy to forgive with all the effort, love and breathtaking artistry on display. The art style especially - for both the surroundings and the hidden object scenes is breathtaking. In former titles, character animation was a bit lackluster, but they really put all their heartsblood into it this time. Another plus: here is less confusing backtracking than with Artifex Mundi's other titles (that tended to drag them down) The mechanic of letting forest animals help you on your journey is a delight. Special mention also for the music, which is beautiful, calming and really puts you into a fairy tale mindset.
Bravo, Artifex Mundi. Bravo, bravo, bravo. You show us how HOGs are done. For any fan of HOGs, this is an absolute must. And if you're new to HOGs, this is a shining diamond of the genre.

Realm of the Mad God is certainly a game worth taking the time to experience.

Super Sanctum TD is a refreshing call-back to the TDs of the Starcraft / Warcraft 3 era. It's a TD stripped down to its most basic. You get a handful of towers and a handful of active skills. You kill waves of mobs for money and you build and upgrade towers. That's it.
SSTD is long enough that you'll get your money's worth and short enough that you won't get bored. The difficulty curve is forgiving (perhaps too much) and, unlike most TDs these days, SSTD lets you maze (within limits).
It's a fun TD.
Note for completionists: the achievements are both attainable and generally enjoyable.

This is a very good game with a few exceptions. First of all, i absolutely love the game, it is one of my favorite games i have . There are a few problems though, when you get pretty far into the game, say 10 plus hours on one save, the block number gets really high, especially if you decide to make a base. This in turn causes some lag, and under extreme conditions, freezing. While this type of problem makes sense, it limits the ammount that can be done in "end game". Another problem is that occasionally any base that you set up can sometimes teleport pieces of it a couple feet, this can cause different pieces to mesh together and making you spend the next half hour fixing it. Free to play MOBA in space with no goons.
If you want a MOBA style capital ship combat game, this is it.
Combat is frantic, skin of your teeth, heart pounding stuff when things go well.
Recent improvements in matchmaking have made these knife-edge battles uncommon but not rare.
The learning curve is steep:
- 3D manuevering in an asteroid field
- long range combat with mostly non-hitscan weapons
- Complex ability interactions
- Split second decision timing where small errors or victories can be decisive
- Information is spread out and communication is still difficult
- Situational awareness requires you to eye the screen corners
- minimap is hard to read and doesn't identify the dots
Co-OP vs AI (5v5) at higher levels can beat disorganized or drunk player teams.
Like so many MOBA:
- ridiculous death penalty that increases with level to about 60 seconds
- Disconnects inactive players, replaces them with AI control until the reconnect.
- Finding a game takes a couple minutes, sometimes much longer.
Ships, Crew, Weapons are all obtainable through free play, and the 3 starting ships are very good.
Technical difficulties - Keybinding:
Keybinding is ... very troublesome.  If you have problems you'll have to delete files in
%LOCALAPPDATA%\spacegame\Saved\Config
like:
%LOCALAPPDATA%\spacegame\Saved\Config\WindowsNoEditor\Input.ini
In fact it's best to edit that file directly instead of using the In-Game UI.
Keep a backup of this file and updates will be less painful.
Recent improvements to the UI help players realize that the mechanics exist, and matter - but it's still a forum hunt to understand how it all works.
- Capping requires your team to have more ships in the area than the enemy.
- 'Armor' - a pool of directional HP, when it runs out you take over double damage (2.6 times) from that direction
- Situational Awareness
- How to earn points (points get you credits)
- Weapons / abilities, effective use vs ineffective use
- Crew bonuses are misleading
- in game tooltips are often wrong
- Match making uses a win/loss point system to gauge player skill, which is very crude.
Enjoyable - yes, but not late at night (nobody is online and matchmaking has difficulty)

I didn't think I would like this one as much as I did. I was generously gifted the game, and went into it not expecting much, and for me it hit a good balance between "art" and gameplay. While you can gain levels and upgrades, they're generally more interesting than straight stat bonuses: new levels give you new "drinks" to consume which add special effects, like increasing blocking speed, and weapon upgrades can change how a weapon works at its fundamental level, such as having it cause damage over time.
As for the "art" portion, the game is composed of absolutely stunning watercolors, and has great...narration?

Half-Life is one of the greatest pc games of all time. Prior to HL, most games required roaming around corridors in predetermined paths shooting monsters and grabbing keycards. People loved it (and still do). But then HL came out and totally took things to a whole new direction. FPS were not just simple gimmicky shooters, they had puzzles, platforming sections, multiple paths and smart enemies. HL did all of this when nobody else did and it was a step forward in gaming. That was then.
Today, Half-Life has shown it's age quite a bit. The AI is less smart, and more just frustrating. The enemy respawns, which were once terrifying, are now just a grind. The graphics, which were years ahead at it's dawn, are definitely aged. Then there are bugs. Bugs galore now. You can get by without ever playing half-life and just go straight to it's sequel, (which is arguably more frustrating in areas). But doing so you would miss out. Because despite all of Half Life's frustrations, it still remains a fun and challenging experience.
You should play Half-Life. More so, you should have played it 15 years ago.

"Is darkest dungeon a good game?"
Most definitly. A turn based rpg has never put me on the edge of my seat more than this.
"Then why don't you recommend it?"
Well, this is gonna be a hard one. And i'm probably gonna be called out for being wrong and♥♥♥♥♥♥but honestly i still felt like sharing my mind about what i think is this game's biggest issue: Progression.
Disclaimer: There might be some hidden mechanics that i am not aware of but concidering how many of these there is in this game, including character perks i would have never known until a friend told me, this game has so many of these.
So what's wrong with the progression then? Well, back then i used to think the game's strenght was mixing rogue lite elements to a turn based rpg so you still have the perma-deaths and difficulty but at the very least you have the convenience of not having your overall progress destroyed when you die. Recently however i found out this is the game's greatest weakness (at least in my perspective).
So here's how things work, you hire a bunch of heroes (mind that while you have a pool of choices(which can be increased at the cost of special quest "heirlooms"), they are purely RNG and the pool only resets once you've been through (or atleast tried to accomplish) a quest. And when a hero die, its permanent. And as heroes go through dungeon, they develop stress, phobias, insanity and etc, and it costs you some money if you want to calm them the ♥♥♥♥ down to keep em sane for later uses. At times you might have to simply get rid of a character cause not only he is not that useful but he went batshit crazy beyond redemption, and the gold might not be worth saving the character.
So at first i liked the concept as it encouraged not getting attached too much to specific characters unless you are willing to pay gold for them, and hire as many different heroes as possible for all situations, allowing the player the try new things.
But the game itself seems to have missed that because, as you keep going through the same dungeon types, the dungeons permanently evolves, grows stronger and gets harder and harder quests. And note that certain dungeon types have very specific enemies that can require some quite specific setups and on your first run might cost you some adventurers on your first shot with them.
The problem is creates is that when you are used to level up newer adventurers on a certain dungeon, because of dungeon evolution, it becomes at somepoint quite impossible to do so as the dungeon will absolutely destroy a party of new adventurers, or even 1-2 heroes with some stronger ones won't be spared. And then what remains are the other dungeons that have some quite specific enemy types that might beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of newer adventurers. So you got permanently evolving dungeons that gets harder and harder as if this was an rpg where you can rez your characters at any time in town and just level them up over and over, but in a game with perma-death where keeping stronger heroes tends to be more expensive than just hiring and training new ones, which becomes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and straight impossible at a certain point.
Tell me "git gud" as much as you want but while i really like darkest dungeon and its unique approach to classic turn based rpg, it really has some counter-productive design flaws.

I don't really have many problems with this game. It's got a good art style, it seems like it'd be a lengthy experience which is good for the price, it has some interesting concepts that seem to be executed pretty damn well and the game is stable with zero performance issues BUT...I just don't find it fun for one reason and one reason only, the RNG.
Now I'm no stranger to RNG. I play a lot of Dark Souls using the randomizer mod (Which makes items RNG dependant), I play MMO's and they have a lot of RNG and I play dice games which are literally dependant on RNG for everything so I don't have a problem with RNG I just have a problem with RNG in this game specifically.
With the RNG in this game I don't feel like Positive vs Negative is what is being rolled for. For those of you who don't know how RNG generally works, a number value is rolled where you have an equal chance of something good happening vs something bad happening (this is RNG in its base form)
It doesn't feel like that in this game though, it feels like It's not something good vs something bad, it feels like it's something bad vs something worse and that just isn't fun to me. I love a challenge, I hate easy games but I love a well designed challenge, a challenge that is a bi product of good game design not♥♥♥♥♥♥just thrown in to a game because "Hurrduur diffcurt!" which is what this game seems to suffer from.
Only thing that I think needs changing is the punishing RNG, the game would be difficult enough without something bad vs something worse RNG which I would be 100% fine with.

I love AC. I've loved the series ever since the first installment. There has always been a good mix of storytelling, game mechanics, and lore to keep me interested. As far as that goes, Unity is no different. It offers a good (though not groundbreaking in any way) addition to the overall story, updated control system and animations, and it sits well in the series' continuity. There are a few gripes I have with it on this front, but those are entirely creative differences, and I am totally willing to accept the developer's right to tell the story they want to tell.
The things I can't forgive are entirely technical. Admittedly, my rig is under the minimum requirements, but this is a boat shared by almost everyone, because the minimum system requirements are a farce. It is ridiculous to release a multiplatform game and expect that players on one platform will have to provide horsepower orders of magnitude higher than those on other platforms. I could have accepted the performance that I get with my system, if the game showed any regard for the graphical settings I chose to run.
For example:
On Low graphics preset, with antialiasing off; I average 20 fps in most situations. (Whatever, I'm below the minimum as recommended by the publishers, if I have to live with that so be it).
On UltraHigh graphics preset, with fxaa on; I average about 19 fps in most situations, with no real difference in playability when compared to low.
(Admittedly a higher setting of AA does bring down the fps. Just putting this here for compleness' sake)
This is ridiculous. If the game had tanked to 5 fps on ultra, I could call it a day and have fun with 20 fps, knowing that my equipment is really being pushed to its limit and delivering the best experience it can. This is obviously not the case, and for that I am disappointed.
The game is gorgeous, the controls feel natural and for-the-most-part fluid, and the co-op is super fun. But this game is in beta, at best. At this point in time, it is not worth any money. I very highly recommend all of the previous AC games; I, II, Brotherhood, Revelations, III, and IV, are all fantastic games. I would really love to recommend this game for the story, but there is a very, very small demographic that would find the price tag worth it for the story alone. If Ubi patches this game to where it runs smoothly, AC:U would probably be my top game of the year; but as it stands, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game for anyone.

More stuff, fixes, but still bland. Read on.
First I want to say I really want to like this game, but honestly, I can no longer stand the poor design choices and the incompetence of the people behind this company. They also like to delete posts created by people with legitiment complaints.
The patch didn't change the core problem with this game. It has a incredibly large star map that does nothing to add to the gameplay. There is so little incentive to explore this massive universe, because each system has very little to offer. You seen one desert planet, you have seen them all. None of them feel unique. They are only different at a glance.
The progression is also borked beyond all recognition. Progression is only artificial. Its just another color of ore to make a slight variant on the armor you just had. The weapons end up being the same, just diferent colors and graphics.
Gameplay consists of landing on a planet, digging for the next ore, and then going to the next planet. Thats it. There are some minor adjustments to your equipment. For example, a tech that allows you to breathe on a planet without an atmosphere. Exciting as this all may sound, the "yippee factor" then dies off when you meet the next form of alien life that is pretty much the same as the last boring group of aliens you shot on the previous world.
The inexplicable change to the star map baffles me on why this change was implimented. Sure, you want progression. But now, it made each star system bland. Why? Because there are few planet types in each system now. Why someone thought this was a wonderful idea seriously should question his own ability to make good decisions when it comes to game design.
You can now have a "Frozen" star with eight "Frozen" planets in the system. There is also "Eccentric" stars, which is a new one on me that makes little sense. "Radioactive" stars are now present, which, well, is what stars are. Almost forgot the "Firey" star type. Gee. Imagine that...a star that is on fire. Did it really take a whole year to come up with these names and overall silly idea?
The new food system is also a joke. Its got a ton of recipes, but they are all the same. This is the central theme to Starbound. That theme is "mindless variety of tiny variations." The buffs the food gives you are minor, and they don't last long. What makes it worse is that you can't even eat more food to replace the short buff because of a poorly implemented timer.
I could go on and on about how poor and disappointing this title is for as long is it would take to discover every unremarkable planet in this botched attempt to create a universe.
The "Winter Update" is just a mish mash of stuff thrown together in an attempt to possibly bring in more unearned income. Believe what you want, but this game is lacking quality design people.
I will add on this this review when the next update comes along, which will probably be next winter.

I enjoy this game and the sandbox space travel idea immensely, but...
This game has been "out" as a pre-release for roughly a year.  The lack of stable updates has been dissapointing, considering how much money Chucklefish has managed to make off the pre-order alone.  The "Nightly" updates are interesting, but extremely unplayable.  It feels as if the developers are more concerned with concept art and new biomes than actually finishing the game.  I understand why they stopped announcing update deadlines, but it's frustrating that they haven't released a stable, playable update since March which is still very much unfinished.
I get that it's an early release game, but I do think that it would help if they actually focused on implementing a stable update every once in a while instead of putting it off and losing their customer base.
This game has a ton of potential- if it ever gets finished.  I stopped playing for a long time period hoping that a new stable update would happen, but still waiting.
That all being said.  The positives.
There are many paralells with Terraria, but Starbound still manages to have a feel of it's own.  It has an interesting multiplayer dynamic, allowing PVP and cooperative play.
The hours I can pour into building the perfect space base is impressive.  Though there is very little incentive to actually get off your ship with the current stable branch, it's still fun to try and design your own personal center of operation.
TL;DR.  This game has a ton of potential, and I do recommend it to friends to try.  BUT.  Until this game is finished and a new update is released, don't spend the money.

Although this is the second
game, the story is not a sequel to
and can stand alone. The story is a retelling of a fairy tale with many variants where a sister must rescue her brothers from swan form by making shirts of nettles. Since I'm a sucker for fairy tale retellings, this automatically gave it plenty of credit in my eyes despite the overly expository intro.
As far as game mechanics are concerned, I really liked that they had a bottle that glowed if you hadn't found the collectible on that screen yet. I only wish that was a feature they had continued using in successive games. Instead of just one animal helper like in the first game, you had three helpers depending on location who make a noise to indicate when there's a task they can help with.
The music wasn't quite as good as the first game, but I did like how they used feathers instead of just sparkling to indicate hidden object scenes. Little details like that can really make a game.
There are several cute and unique minor characters that are surprisingly well-developed for such a short game. Some of these characters make appearances in both the main adventure as well as in the prequel bonus adventure.
Despite a couple of inevitable idiosyncratic moments, this is a quality hidden object puzzle adventure game that is well worth adding to your inventory.

Super Sanctum TD is a competently-designed, retro-flavored tower defense game that takes few risks and offers an appropriate degree of Fun. An endless horde of horrible space monstroids is pouring out of a weird invasion portal cabbage and it's up to you to place a variety of defensive turrets in the way to stop 'em! Along with your chain guns and flamethrowers and gauss rifles, you also have access to a variety of special abilities you can activate to blast those determined jerkfaces who manage to scrape their way past your gauntlet. As you play, you earn experience, unlocking new turrets and abilities. Level layout and wave composition are well-balanced, keeping up the challenge and often requiring multiple level attempts to achieve any sort of victory. And when all is said and done, you can go back for further challenges by attempting earlier levels on Hard Mode or Survival Mode.
Unfortunately, this game comes from the same people who made Sanctum, which was a delightfully innovative tower defense / FPS hybrid. Dropping all the innovative aspects of the game just makes this seems like an attempt at cashing in on the franchise's name, which, y'know, isn't terribly exciting to the fans; the lore was never terribly compelling to begin with, and this entry contributes nothing new on that front. If you're an avid tower defense enthusiast, sure, the game isn't bad, but you'd be better off playing the other games in the series or trying out a more polished, well-developed tower defense game like Sol Survivor.

This "Director's Cut" version should have been acquired for free if you have the original Q.U.B.E. prior to this one's announcement that this was being given out in that manner.
Using minimalistic graphics, most everything looks smooth & clean. That said the levels will probably start to look stale since all you'll see wherever you look are squares. Later on you'll come across a couple of slightly different shapes or so but there are always going to be the same looking squares around.
The single player campaign probably won't take even more than a few hours to beat and the puzzles themselves, while they can be pretty clever, aren't very hard on their own.
The idea of this game is to manipulate colored blocks to solve a puzzle to reach the next room. Each specific color has a different function for that block which have to be used for a small variety of reasons depending on the situation whether it be as a means of adding a platform for jumping on or pushing something aside.
There's no how-to-play kind of tutorials here aside from the simplistic first levels where you're to learn on your own how to manipulate the blocks. The controls are in the options menu and everything else is pretty much self-taught.
There are a total of 7 sectors to go through with each sector being lengthier than the last either from the amount of levels in each one or because the levels are just larger. Could be the puzzles themselves just take longer to solve, which isn't necessarily a bad thing.
Each sector has a different theme to it though you'll usually be using the same assets and what you've learned from previous levels.
I've experienced some bugs on a couple of levels where cubes are clipping through other objects and their sliding mechanics suddenly don't work as intended. If you've got the puzzle figured out or you're just experimenting with the objects given to you, the bugs can be a serious hindrance when trying to progress through the current area. You can keep screwing around until you eventually get whatever you need to to work but I'm pretty sure such problems shouldn't be there to begin with.
In this version of the game they added a narrative storyline to the single player campaign, which I thought was absolutely unnecessary. Right at the ending there's a heavy implication within the narration of there being decision making, which turns out there wasn't. The entire game's linear, which is fine, but again I don't believe this added story was really needed.
The silence & mystery I thought was a novelty of its own in the original. Here, it seems like they forced the story in given how there are a lot of details mentioned with not a whole lot of connection with what you see & experience. You can't even turn off the narration since the only audio slider in the game is "MASTER". It doesn't help a whole lot that there aren't any subtitle options either in case you actually got into the added story.
The "Director's Cut" also features the previously released DLC. They're just 10 extra levels that are more focused on speedrunning than puzzles, which aren't actually bad. If you're achievement hunting you'll be spending more time with the DLC than the campaign due to how grindy they can be.
So the gameplay of this isn't bad as far as puzzle games go but really it's just too short, there's a shoved in storyline you can't turn off unless you mute the entire game, and physics bugs can be potentinally gamebreaking.

Lords of the Fallen has a somewhat dented learning curve: unless you're a veteran of the Dark Souls franchise—which I'm told LotF emulates—you'll probably find the combat pretty challenging in the beginning, to say nothing of taking down the first boss or two. But once you develop certain magical skills, the difficulty drops almost to the point of tedium (for me, the skill that did it was "Stab" on a rogue, and to a certain extent, "Shift"). Most common opponents suddenly pop like soap bubbles, and as soon as you learn to evade the most damaging boss attacks, the big guys no longer pose nearly as much of a threat as they're probably meant to do. And since the story is dark fantasy boilerplate with ciphers for characters, even the admittedly gorgeous visuals can no longer make up for the fact that your sole incentive for plodding through the game is the prospect of finding shinier toys in the next chest. That ain't much. I'm by no means saying LotF is a bad game, especially if you can get it during a sale, which is why I'm still recommending it. You may well get a few hours worth of fun out of this title. Just not enough fun—or challenge—to last to the very end of it.

Half-Life is one of the greatest pc games of all time. Prior to HL, most games required roaming around corridors in predetermined paths shooting monsters and grabbing keycards. People loved it (and still do). But then HL came out and totally took things to a whole new direction. FPS were not just simple gimmicky shooters, they had puzzles, platforming sections, multiple paths and smart enemies. HL did all of this when nobody else did and it was a step forward in gaming. That was then.
Today, Half-Life has shown it's age quite a bit. The AI is less smart, and more just frustrating. The enemy respawns, which were once terrifying, are now just a grind. The graphics, which were years ahead at it's dawn, are definitely aged. Then there are bugs. Bugs galore now. You can get by without ever playing half-life and just go straight to it's sequel, (which is arguably more frustrating in areas). But doing so you would miss out. Because despite all of Half Life's frustrations, it still remains a fun and challenging experience.
You should play Half-Life. More so, you should have played it 15 years ago.

Honestly one of the best games I have ever played.  Assumed it was just a typical RPG/Dungeon Crawler with a few Roguelike elements but I had no idea what I was in store for.  For a Min/Maxing style gamer with a penchant for dark yet comic game atmosphere this game is a godssend (that would be the unspeakable elder gods).  There are many aspects of this game that are enjoyable and I'll list a few in no particular order.
-Min/Maxing Opportunities:  I surmise that this is likey a barrier to casual gamers, given that this game is very challenging in it's standard design and you need to really strategize both your party design in each expedition as well as the long term planning for your Estate.  Once you get the hang of it (and there are some truly amazing community guides here on Steam), this trulu taps into the enjoyment potential of the game.  RNG still allows for some epicly amazing mishaps at all stages (at least from my own limited experience and what I have taken away from various guides), but you can get a real sense of thrill at making 'the right party' to shred through a particular region.
-Turn Based Play: Got kids or other regular attention nabbing responsibilities like me?  Love the fact that Civilization was a game you could play in short spurts yet draws you into 5 hour late night gaming sessions?  Play this game and be reminded of how terrific well paced turn based games can be.
-Comic yet Horribly Dark Atmosphere:  If H.P. Lovecraft and Robert Kincaid decided to do some sort of bizarre joint artistic project with help from Stan Lee, well that would just be bloody amazing.  This game, while not quite that insanely beatiful/horrifying is pretty damn good all the same.  The art and models are amazing and so far I haven't met a Klei produced or supported game that I haven't thought did some amazing things with lighting.
-Lengthy Play Experience:  Again, this isn't a selling point for people that just want to reach the end in a timely matter, but this game's pacing is such that you spend a lot of time grinding to improve your Estate/Adventurers, and it is a lovely experience.  If you don't map it out a little, it will definitely feel like you are failing by inches, but with a few adjustments to game play you will progressively move forward even while your favourite adventurers are dissolved in acid, shredded by unnameable horrors, felled by heart attacks or just simply made so idioscyratic by a host of poor habits that you have no recourse but to kick them out of your Estate to make room for more damned souls.
So far I have not found any cons to this game.  Every time I return from an expedition I discover some new joy in a skill advancement or party combination that compels me to return again and again.  My limited frustrations from this game came from lack of understanding of the basic mechanics and strategies.  As soon as I invested some time to read on those I was able to unlock the full potential of fun in this game (or at least head well on down that road).  Most certainly in my top 10 pc games of all time.
