United Offensive was released in 2004, 11 months after Call of Duty. Developed by Gray Matter, who is known for creating Escape from Castle Wolfenstein, which from what i heard is considered a good game by both wolfenstein and fps fans.
The addon perfectly captures what made the original so good. For those that haven't read my COD1 review, it's about having cinematic setpieces every now and then. COD and other shooters are not very different, but what makes COD stand apart is that aside from all the shooting levels, it has the cinematic levels mixed in, and in general, all levels are highly inspired by war films.
The campaign features americans in ardennes (heavily inspired by band of brothers). British campaign features a fully modelled B-17 plane, which you can traverse as the level goes on, and you will have to, because as the level will go on, crewmen will be dying and somebody will have to take up their machine gun. The rest of the british campaign is about working with the resistance (in Holand) and the SAS (in Sicily). The soviet campaign in the original was about Stalingrad, Poland and Berlin. UO is about the events after Stalingrad - Kursk.
The campaign is not as lengthy as the original though, but that is to be expected from an expansion.
UO added many new mechanics into the game. Like the sprint ability (which is also featured in their wolfenstein game). They added machine guns for every side (DP-28, MG34, M1919). The original game also only had Colt and Luger pistols, so they added missing ones for the british and soviets. They added semi-auto rifles - G43 and SVT40. They added rocket launchers - Panzerschreck and Bazooka. In the eastern front, they also added flamethrowers to the germans.
All of them are great (sounds and reloading animations are much more superior), though the machine guns mechanic is slightly underworked. You have to place down the bipod before shooting, but usually the only place you can place it is on the ground. You cannot place it on a crate or a sandbag for example, except for a few specific locations.
The multiplayer is dead (about 10 servers, some of which have "bots" in their title), but just for the record i will tell you a few things i managed to dig up. First of all, original COD was about infantry warfare. UO added jeeps and tanks to the game for each side (US, USSR, Germany). Other than the 3 normal tanks: Sherman, T-34 and Panzer IV, there are also tank destroyers that are present on some maps - Elefant and ISU-152. Google up the elefant tank if you don't know what that is.
They also added a ranking system into the game that resets during every match. It works sort of like killstreaks of today. As you play you gain points and you get extra stuff, like more grenades or ability to call an artillery strike.
Since the game came out almost a year after COD1, and a year later, COD2 was released, majority of the improvements on COD1 were not added to COD2, which i feel was a big step backward.
Finally, i want to add that Grey Matter Interactive was merged with Treyarch in 2005. Treyarch at the time was doing the old gen version of COD2 (for PS2 and xbox), The Big Red One.
If you ever lose access to your email/password, you are basically screwed because there is no support anymore for online play.

Every once in a while you come across a game that is more than the sum of its parts yet defies traditional definition. Such is the case with The Old Tree, a minimal and simplistic point and click adventure that takes less than a minute to download, less than twenty minutes to complete, and leaves a lasting impression.
The gameplay has you clicking on interactive objects while the camera follows a small squid like alien through several unsettling and atmospheric scenes. You could say this is more interactive art than actual gameplay – it is a little creepy, and the game’s experimental nature is clear from its opening.
Yet this doesn’t detract from the experience. The art is clearly the major draw for this game – and the minimal design aesthetic works well in its favour. There are several small puzzles that work on a light versus darkness factor, and this is usually very easily discovered. There really is no frustration. It feels familiar and yet different.
The sound is also minimal and simplistic, with an unnerving background drone-like soundtrack. It repeats often, but I think this also is to The Old Tree’s benefit. I’m not sure what it’s trying to accomplish, but I feel urged on to completion and at the same time just slightly rattled.
While there really isn’t anything to say for the game’s replayability or even for the game’s controls – The Old Tree is an easy recommend. Being available for free helps – but I feel it’s important to recommend games that are just a little different than the norm. And in that – The Old Tree really works.

I love this game. Plain and simple. The combat feels amazing, the animations are fantastic and the voice acting is just as astounding. I've come to love all of the characters i've been introduced to and I haven't had one bad experience with the game itself.
Bear in mind, the bad experiences I have had were entirely graphical. I have not run into bugs, although supposedly they've fixed them anyway. The game is not optimized well. I'm running a Nvidia 760 2GB with an AMD 8320 8-core 3.50GHz processor and I can only get ~30 FPS on High/Medium with FXAA.
BUT. It has not ruined the experience of the game for me. It's one of the most solid-gameplay titles i've played in quite some time. Don't let the bad reviews get in the way, the game is absolutely fantastic. The customization is MASSIVE with tons of weapons and gear, although I found myself sticking to one chest/hood/legs and such once I got to that point, I find myself constantly changing weapons. All of them (and their AMAZING finishers, specifically the spears) feel totally badass.
Co-op is a really fun experience regardless of cooperation among the members, although I found it to be even better when everyone is trying to stealth rather than go in swinging. 2-man missions seem to be the most fun and easiest to coordinate.
Keep in mind that combat is challenging this time around, it's not like the other ACs which (from what i've seen) you just counter which = a kill. You actually have to plan engagements, try to stealth, or if you ARE going to go head-on, take them in strides. Don't try to 1v8. You WILL lose.
If you were on the fence before, i'd say give the game another week or two, wait for the optimization patches Ubisoft announced they're working on to come out, then pick it up. It's definitely worth a buy.

Okay, there are way too many negative reviews, and I know for a fact, this game isn't bad.
The game has only crashed on me once so far, and as far as performance issue, I occasionally dip under 60 FPS, but only occasionally, and there was one moment when it hung up, freeze for about 20-40 seconds, but in unfroze itself. I'm running the game on High settings, and my computer can "handle" Ultra, but the FPS tanks too low to tolerate for me, but I pretty much don't tolerate if it can't stay above 50 FPS.
As far as microtransactions and bugs, there are occasional MINOR bugs, but they aren't too distracting and are not game breaking. The ones I've noticed so far are NPCs standing in weird places (on a table, etc.) which is quickly self-rectified, Arno having trouble with the navigation a bit (which is also quickly rectified by simply altering movement direction slightly), and enemies who are dead start squirming on ground as if still alive (it's slight though so it's not THAT big of a deal).
As far as people complaining about navigation, it is NOT buggy or bad. It's actually quite fun. There is still some challenge for climbing some areas, and in my opinion a MAJOR improvement. It IS meant for gamepads though, and will take some time getting used to, and even then, sometimes it'll not do what you want it to do, but that's been present in nearly every AC game so far to a certain degree.
Keep in mind, that I played this game with a beefier setup than probably most using 8 GB of RAM, a NVidia GeForce GTX 660 Ti w/ 3 GB of vRAM, a dual quad-core i7 processor at 3.4 gHz, and used a gamepad and not a keyboard. You need more than just the right video card to run this game, you need RAM, and a processor that can handle it.

is the second installment in the
game series, it has no connection to the first title however. In this game you play a world famous healer brought to the Eagle Kingdom to tend to the beautiful queen. What starts off as a simple visit turns into an epic adventure battling dark magic and an evil curse. The fate of two kingdoms -and the lives of their denizens- lay in your hands. This game is filled with interesting twists and turns as well great gameplay, making a very enjoyable experience for fans of hidden object games.
You take the role of the famous healer brought to a majestic castle, you begin your job tending to the queen and everything is going well until the young prince is kidnapped and the queen is accused of practicing black magic. This offense is punishable by death and she is taken to jail. Her king is distraught and tasks you with the job of proving her innocence. Soon you’re dragged into a world of magic, curses and death as you race to find the prince and save his mother. Despite the title mentioning a “dark swan” this doesn’t play too big of a role in the story, mainly confined to the first half, which I found disappointing. The story is also rather predictable and not very interesting. I found the story of the Swan Kingdom, where the queen is from, to be the most alluring. It’s told via flashbacks and explains why the kingdom fell under a curse.
To play the game you use your mouse to interact with people and objects as well as move around. You also collect useful items and tools that you need to progress in the game.The main crux of the game are hidden object scenes where you are given a written list of items to find in the scene. There also some scenes where the list is presented as pictures of items to find. I felt that the game could have used more hidden object scenes, I also felt that the scenes could have been a bit more complex- such as requiring you to perform a few different steps to find an item, like move a piece of paper aside or paint a feather red. There are also puzzles in the game, they’re not too difficult but some do offer a challenge. One note, you play a healer in the game so I expected potion-making to be a larger part of the gameplay. While it did factor in more than usual hidden object titles I felt it was under-utilized.
Graphics-wise the game is beautiful. Lovely colors and artwork help keep the feel of the fairy tale land you’re exploring. The hidden object scenes are very well done with the items not being too small that it would hurt your eyes. The character models are very well done though movements can be a bit stiff. The game has full voice acting which is well done, though some of the younger characters can sound a bit annoying and their acting is off, but this is a minor issue. Music in the game is lovely and fits the tone of the story and all of the sound effects are also spot on.
Overall I do recommend
as an addition to your library. While not as stand out as the first title in the series, it’s still a solid gaming experience. There are Steam cards and achievements as well as collectable items to find during your playthrough. There is also a bonus chapter which is very adorable and also gives a nice side story about the queen. You have three cute sidekicks to help on your adventure which adds a bit of levity to the story, however, I did find the ending anticlimactic. All complaints aside, this is a good game, it’s fun to play and I recommend grabbing it when you can.

XCOM 2 is a turn-based strategy game where you control a squad of soldiers fighting alien invaders. An old alien ship is used as your base of operation which you have to renovate. You have missions on the map you can choose to which to do for various rewards, including special ones where you have to stop the aliens end-game. This contrasts the original game where you have multiple bases, use landing ships to start missions and have to shoot down spaceships.
You have 2 moves per soldier, f ex move + attack.. You have classes and levels while in XCOM 1 your attributes increase as you use them. XCOM 1 combat is similar to Fallout 2; using action points which are dependent on a soldier attribute.
There are other games in the genre worth checking out; namely UFO:AI (free and open source). The game is casual-friendly since you can play losing 1 or 2 soldiers each mission and still win the game.
Verdict:
XCOM 2 is a huge letdown for me as a fan of the original. If your platform is PC, I recommend getting UFO:AI instead.

Grim Legends 2: Song og the Dark Swan is much like the first one a cute point and click adventure game. And I will recommend them for anyone that want to experience the old kind of folk narratives, as that is what the story reminds me of the most. (Fairy Tales, Moral stories, legends.) While the game plays and feel mostly the same, I think it is an improvement from the first one.
The game is in first person, but unlike the first game it doesn't really bother me so much here. Since the protagonist is known as the "healer" and doesn't have a preexisting relationship with any of the characters, so while her profession is given she is pretty much a blank slate. (Personally still prefer most games in third person, but unlike the first game, I think the first person works here.)
The story is easy to follow and the puzzles are mostly enjoyable. This time the story fits the slower puzzle solving gameplay better than the first one, as the threats to the characters aren't presented to be as immediate as they were in the first game. So it makes sense that you work slowly to uncover the story. It is more the: “We need this done as soon as possible!” As opposed to some moments of the first one: “We need to do this NOW or we will die!”
The characters are easily identifiable and not very complex, but that fits well with the genre of story that is told in the game. As it is more about telling an enchanting tale, rather than how the characters experience the events. So you will be most likely able to guess who the evil one is before it is revealed just from clichés in old stories, but the story is still cute and charming. I won’t replay it, but I don’t regret buying or playing it.

I just bought this game for the fourth time via the warchest bundle while it was on sale. All my previous copies were physical since I still remember playing this shortly after it came out at the end of 2004. My current hours logged on via steam does not reflect the hours I sunk into this game for 6 years. I will admit the moment I got into a server and started playing base assault again for the first time since 2010 it made me remember why I loved the series at one point and brought back a lot of nostalgia. While by modern standards this game is dated in multiplayer gameplay for lacking health regen, classes, killstreaks, attachments, etc that is to be expected considering this is from 2004 before those became "core" to modern fps games. For me personally i find the lack of those things to be a giant pro. It feels like it provides a bit of an actual challenge, and nice change from modern shooters
Pro:
Mods for multiplayer. Besides the original I don't think any other Call of Duty is mod friendly. I will check out 2. But most of my experience with Call of Duty after 4 was limited to console.
Vehicles. Multiple stock tanks both light, heavy and jeeps available for multiplayer. Mods add even more vehicles not included in the game. I recall at one point there was a mod that added stuka dive bombers that you could fly. I will have to look for that mod.
Crazy amount of maps, all of which are free(see settings to enable downloads)
Cons:
Multiplayer is as much as I hate to say it more or less dead but still hanging in there with half a dozen servers that I can find via steam that are populated by actual people rather than bots like the zombies server. Also doesn't help the community is a tad split, there a few servers that wont show up but can be conenected to if you know the IP mainly with people that have pirated versions. Then for some odd reason there are still servers active on older version prior to 1.51 patch. Then theres still a few people on the original base game that this is the expansion to.
Requires that you have Call of Duty (2003) installed. This is understandable since expansions at the time worked this way, since this was the pre DLC days so this is only a con in that you need to buy the first game.
Price. For christ sake steam or Activision. I don't know who still controls the price. I would've bought this game soo much sooner if it was fairly priced. On sale 20$ for Cod, CodUO, and Cod2. Considering how old these games are 20$ is what the bundle should cost as it is  before being on sale and Im being generous given my love for the game. More copies might actually move. Others would say 15 a more fair price for the bundle.  The standard 20$ just standalone on steam when its not on sale would have been fair like 5 years ago but a little excessive now. I honestly think Activision could get something outta ressurecting this and the base game by mking it free to play and mking money off it somehow.
Visually, the game shows its age quite badly. Again though this is from 2004 so its forgivable. If activision is gonna start going down the remastering Call of Duty's businesss route then they should remaster the this and the base game together as they would benefit the most from a remaster.

If you play without saves on the highest difficulty, you will find yourself frustrated and ultimately unable to play the game.
From a multiplayer perspective, this beats what you got on CoD1. I will admit that the older CoDs offer a relatively simple layout of weapons, maps, and general combat mechanics, but it's a hard and precise go to kill someone. That's what makes it all the more challenging and exciting for the nostalgics. But because FPS games have now been more about attachments, perks, and these types of accolades, you might find yourself getting bored after a few rounds.
That being said, this expansion is rife with bugs and does not play well with current technology. This is far from worth the price of retail let alone a 50% off sale price, and I'm gobsmacked that IW is being this greedy.
I cannot recommend it on price and bugginess alone.

Visually it's beautiful but that really is its biggest plus, along with some good voice acting. The camera is another big problem, I died a few times because I completely lost sight of the enemy while using the lock on feature which is really poorly implemented, you will often lose your target entirely and for some reason the game will pick a target on the other side of the room instead of the mob right next to, switching locked targets is also cumbersome, it's not a simple flick of the right stick that we're all used to by now. The gameplay itself is what I'd call "clunky", and not just because it's very slow (which it is), but because it just feels very unrefined. A big part of these types of games are the boss fights and once again Lords of the Fallen falls short, every boss has a very simple gimmick/mechanic and once you know it the fight just becomes a war of attrition as all bosses have very high HP so I found the fights tended to drag on which made them feel less epic and more tedious.

This is one of the defining early first person shooters. Dated now in terms of graphics and sheer complexity. You can, however, adjust the difficulty. It can also regularly scare you to death, and it has a nice blend of exploration, light puzzles, and action. It is also quite a long game with large environments to explore. You will die many times and will spend many hours playing this masterpiece. Sometimes you need stealth. Sometimes you need to run. Fast. Really fast. Sometimes you need to go very slowly. Sometimes going in guns blazing is the right move. Sometimes you need to pick off your enemies one at a time. Sometimes you need to figure things out and solve problems. These changes in gameplay along with the sheer length and story will make you want to play it again and again. This is the first game. There are many more set in this same world after it. If you want to play them, play this first.

It starts off with an accident at a top secret lab and throws you into a sci-fi world of monsters, secrets, and other dimensions. You need to keep on your toes and fight your way out. Piece by piece you uncover a massive secret and conspiracy bound to destroy every person's reality down to their core.
Everybody who likes video games and everyone who especially likes FPS needs to have this game. Outstanding story for an FPS.

Visually, Starbound is amazing. The animation is smooth, the lighting engine is GODLY.
The problem is that Starbound is shallow and empty. Combat is awkward, the UI clumsy.
For all its worth, Starbound feels like it was made by graphics designers. There's randomly 'made' moster sprites, lots of weapons and tilesets, but none of it does anything special. Starbound is COD. A looker, but it leaves you empty.
If you want a deep, amazing adventure with excitement and action, play Terraria, or try Crea. Crea's also in Early Access, but the polar opposite of Starbound. It looks a lot less (but still pretty great) but has a lot more mechanical depth in it.
EDIT:
Let me add something else. Starbound doesn't change over time. Terraria gave you potions and weird weapons, but Starbound keeps being obsessed with mining and crafting. Crafting, however, is clumsy, and mining very boring (other than the pretty tileset).
The worst part is that, despite its focus on cool monsters, being underground makes the floaty movement choke on itself. And unless you're hunting for dungeons, there's no reason to be surface-side.
Starbound is a sightseeing tour (like I mentioned with COD). Once you've seen the sights, you lose a lot of luster. Destiny is better, because at LEAST Destiny's combat and core gameplay is enjoyable(?).

The controls are awkward the least to say. Can't explain how, but it just doesn't feel smooth enough.
And the gameplay itself? Get's old in 5 minutes. Even if it didn't, the fighting mechanics are horrible.
You have an attack and a shield to defend yourself with. The shield doesn't block enemy attacks, instead just reduces damage taken from one. This mechanic is completely fine.
But the bad mechanics come out when you attack an enemy. There are 3 types of enemies: Skeletons, bats and slugs. Slugs die from jumping on them. Combining the awkward controls and the small hitbox of the slugs, it can get difficult to jump on them, although you'll get used to this.
Bats die from a single hit, self explanitory.
The skeletons are the problem. You need to knock them out of the map, because they have unlimited HP. Once again, a great idea. But the problem is that if you hit them, they might get knocked on to the next platform, but they don't get stunned. So you can hit them 10 times and during that 10 times, they can shoot you so many times they feel like.
When you learn to play the game, it can be fun to beat through the hardest possible stage setup. I consider myself pretty good or at least decent at the game, but seriously, the fighting mechanics are horrible, at least with a mouse and keyboard.

This game isn't bad. I'm not a big puzzle game fan, and never played the portal games. This game is literally only puzzles, theres really not even much in the way of platforming. You spend the entire game solving puzzles with cubes. You can manipulate different colored cubes in their specified ways. You spend the entire game in white cube levels made of a bunch of cubes (get it?). The game does a good job introducing new mechanics and ramping up difficulty. Later harder puzzles may require a walkthrough, but most won't. The story doesn't really make sense, the mystery is interesting, but for how dramatic it is, its pretty stupid how the world supposedly rests on you solving some cube puzzles for no reason, so it makes it all unbelievebale. The game is super short, around 2-3 hours. The problem is its quite repetitive. There are some cool visuals with the cubes in certain rooms spinning, but for the most part every area looks the exact same. You manipulate the 4-5 same color cube shapes every level. Theres not multiple solutions, just the one allowed by the game. It all just starts to feel monotenous. It would have been nice if more platforming were in the game, or if other puzzles didn't only just feature the same 4 colored cubes. The stuff with wires was pretty interesting, more fresh ideas like that would be appreciated.
This game is close to a recommendation, but the lack of variety, boring level and world design, and ridiculous story, make it a puzzle game that just doesn't quite cut it.

There's two parts to Q.U.B.E.  Like most games, there's the story and then there's the gameplay.
The gameplay in Q. U. B. E. Director's Cut is actually quite good.  You start the game in a weird space built out of cubes, with a pair of gloves that allows you to interact with a small amount of the world, namely colored bricks.
From this, the game is based on manipulating those bricks, traversing the levels, and exploring the world.
And that's what Q.U.B.E. does exceedingly well.  I played this game back before the Director's Cut and remember one or two puzzles I had trouble with.  This time around, I only had a single problem with a puzzle (an annoying puzzle, but it's also the last one in the game I believe).    However the puzzles are a highlight of the game, and will make most fans of puzzle games or games where the goal is to merely traverse a level (like Portal) enjoy themselves.
On the other hand there's a story, and to be honest, that's where the game falls apart.  The original Q.U.B.E. didn't have a story and I remember thinking "Man I'd love to have some reasoning for me to do this."  Hell I'm sure I suggested a portal-esque story.
Unfortunately I got what I requested, and worse... well it's just bad.   The story itself feels disjointed, as if it was placed in the middle of an already complete game (which it was) and sadly the game isn't better for it.  The story, tries to be this deep probing or even contemplative thing.  But comes across as just manipulative and forgettable.  Even the ending is just there.  I like the puzzles, not the part where the game tries to talk to and interact with the player.
I actually wish there was a way to not play the story (I still have Q.U.B.E. so I can just play the old version).  It's just not a good addition to the original game, luckily they have made it a free upgrade otherwise I would have been unable to recommend this version of the game.
However with that being said, the gameplay is above average, there's some time attack maps that you can play that are actually quite difficult, there's a lot of enjoyment to be had on the first playthrough of the game.  Just don't expect an amazing story, or even a game you can play through more than once.   You'll spend a couple hours playing the game, and get a fun experience, but it's not going to blow any minds, and since it came out in the same year as Portal 2, it didn't win any awards.   That all being said, it's still a solid experience and quite enjoyable for fans of the puzzle genre.

As usual for this publisher: lovely music, graphics, and locales. The voice-overs and story coherence were above par, IMO (though it's clear from the beginning who the villain is). The puzzles seemed to get more annoying later in the game, but i'm not really a puzzle person, and that's what the Skip button is for :-D. i found myself needing a Hint on how to continue now and then, unfortunately, but that's my problem, not the game's.
Down-side: other than being short (finished it in under 4 hours), none. There were a few "what the HELL just happened?" moments for me (specifically, the tree with the acorn in its mouth, the arrow stuck in a tree, and collecting the evil snail's slime).
HO scenes: they are overall quite easy, but many of them follow the pattern which is seemingly more common in games from Big Fish: the items collected in such scene combine to build up the item you end up getting after the scene. (i prefer this approach over searching for many random items and keeping one of them afterwards.) Some reviewers complain about the abstract shapes of some of the HO items, but that's clearly a matter of taste. Yes, they DO make the HO scenes more difficult, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Ambiguous search terms in HO scenes are relatively common (e.g. looking for a "face" when there are at least 3 faces in the scene), but i've seen much worse.
Good pacing, though, combined with nice voices and lovely scenery, make this a nice casual HOPA.

I think I both pirated and ruined my own experience of Walking Dead, yet I still was so deeply impacted by the story and the characters that I will be buying and playing blind through all the subsequent seasons.
To explain what I mean, I originally watched the entirety of season 1 including the 400 days DLC on Zemalf’s YouTube channel. Because this game is essentially an interactive narrative, watching the game through a let’s play spoils all major plot points of the game. This is not to say I did not enjoy it -just watching the game on YouTube was an emotional rollercoaster and I loved every minute of it- but I already knew exactly what would happen and when. Now fast forward to about a week ago and I decided to do an experiment: what happens if you let the game play itself. Basically there are only a finite number of open areas where you have to take control or do a QTE to stay alive, aside from those I left the game muted and did other things.
This is where the weight of the story and connection with the characters absolutely blew my mind. You see, even though I was essentially ignoring the majority of the game, I found myself glancing over and then sprinting to my controller when I saw someone I really connected with about to be hurt by something Lee said or didn’t say. Even while trying to completely disconnect from the game and let it play itself, I felt this weight and sense of responsibility for my group of survivors. This amount of investment is hard enough for a game to earn while I’m deep into a gaming session, and here Walking Dead is pulling it off while I’m trying to watch House of Cards across the room.
The Walking Dead is a crowning achievement in game narrative as a mechanic and connecting players to characters in a deep emotional way. This game is spectacular and I honestly believe that everyone should play it at some point.

I bought this game when it was in one of the January sales. I am a big fan of The Walking Dead, both the comics and the tv show. I've heard poor reviews for the other walking dead game which was released 'Walking Dead: Survival Instinct' so I decided to give this one a try as it was a mere £5 at the time.  I enjoyed this game because It was like being welcomed into a new chapter of Robert Kirkman's Walking Dead Universe.
I will admit then when I first started playing Episode 1, the gaming format threw me a little, the character's movements are restricted and slow with minimal maneuverability. The game is all about making decisions and the way you select your dialogue between each character. Each decision has a limited amount of time and options to choose from.
I will say this for the game, as you play through each episode you grow attached to the character's around you and feel a sense of personal investment in your own character as all of your in-game decisions effect the outcome of what is happening around you. A few limited parts of the game have a faster pace to them and some moments can get quite tense and gripping. Overall this is a little slow and 'rigid' if you are used to action based games. I enjoyed this from the perspective of being a huge fan of TWD and all things 'Zombie'. As I previously stated it was great to be able to take another bite from the walking dead universe and to feel slightly included in the plot in a 'semi' interactive way.
This game was frustrating at times purely based on how slow and restricted certains parts felt, but overlooking that I did enjoy playing it. It's not the kind of game I would recommend playing all at once though... unless you have more patience for the format than me... In which case go ahead!
I've not played 'Survival Instinct' but from what I've heard of that game and my own experiences with this one I would say this is probably better... but in the end that all depends on your preferred gaming format.
P.S: IF YOU PLAY THROUGH TO THE END... AHH THE FEELS! (you will understand)

Overall, a great FPS. Here are the pros in my opinion :
- Truly F2p, no P2w implementation so far.
- Good optimization, it runs very well.
- A good choice of guns.
- All primary and most secondary guns can have a silencer attached, simply by pressing "F" in-game.
- All weapons seem pretty balanced, nothing is OP.
- There are many in-game settings to play around with.
- Guns aren't expensive, nor hard to obtain.
- Multiple game modes.
- It's free.
A few cons, again, in my opinion :
- UI could be a little better, but it probably will be when officially launched.
- Many primary weapons have grenade launchers attached, I don't like this.
- In-game items that have an expiry date. You can obtain an item that lasts for a limited amount of time, for as little as 24 hours.
- While the maps look nice, they aren't very unique and feel uninspired.
- RNG loot boxes. These are, and always will be a negative. No matter how you implement them.
Even with these cons, the game is still enjoyable and most importantly free. Give it a try.

The game (w/o Ancient Labyrinth DLC) took me about 15 hours to beat. Having freshly beat it and played about 30 minutes into my New Game +, here is what I have to say.
Lords of the Fallen got a bad rep on release for being a Souls rip-off. This is, to some extent, true. However, the formula has been boiled down to its most basic components and new usability features added, resulting in a much more accessible game.
The game has a story. It's not brilliant, and on the first playthrough it's not actually possible to get all of the lore, but it was interesting enough to keep me hooked and playing the game.
The game also has a dialogue system. You won't use it a whole lot and npc interactions are fairly scarce, but it exists and contributes to some of the game's more poignant moments.
The game is bloody beautiful. Apart from lacking character customization, the weapons and armor are well designed and detailed, the enemies and environments are detailed, and the particle effects are well done. Props to the developers on that.
The game is responsive. People complaining about long lag times between input and action are *probably* running a sword and board strength build. Dual-wielding while wearing light armor is much faster, but an unpopular choice because of the inability to block. Don't listen to people wielding greathammers with one hand and a tower shield with the other.
Quests are vague af. I only barely registered the planetarium quest's existence despite clearing almost all the other ones, and by the time I had the items I went into the room and couldn't find anything to activate due to how far I was in the story, but the ending told me that yes it was possible and I was a dumb.
Occasional steam controller sync bugs, and the quest prompt occasionally would reset for no reason or display the incorrect objective.
The game is $20. The DLC is $8... Buy the game. If you like it and care about achievements get the DLC, otherwise ignore it as it's not brilliant. Even if you're a souls fan, buy the game. It's shorter and easier than most of the souls titles, but still an engaging experience that doesn't deserve to be maligned by people who haven't bothered to try it. I loved every minute of my first playthrough, and will definitely be back for more.

Lords Of The Fallen is obviously inspired by the souls series. Really obvious,but the fact is that it does a very good job in creating a world and using the souls gameplay in a very good way. It is to be expected then, that you will be drawing parallels between the two. First of all is it worth the money? I would say even though there is no pvp as far as my knowledge goes (it might change latter) that it is worth the money and time to play this game. It really has been a long time since I spend 30 hours in a few days not even a week in a game such as this, the combat system is fun and challenging (not as much as the souls series) and there are enemies that will require you to really figth hard to beat them (or use magic but we'll get to that) the leveling system is also nice, one small critisism I have is that faith weapons become really weak later on, but over all it's a really well made game polished with fun staged and bosses. At this point I have to say that it is rather easier that what dark souls, demos souls or bloodborne are to the point that an experienced souls player can beat bosses on a first run without a guide (which is wild fantasy in a souls game) and thats because of what I refered to previously as "magic".
Magic in this game or spells are really overpowered, to the point that you 3 shot a boss with a fully upgraded quake, now that doesn't hold true for the NG+ but you have to remember that unless you want a specific item for the aestherics of it and a few achivements, there is absolutely no reason to replay the game in NG+, NG++ and so on. Unless you really love the game. But appart from the no PVP problem other than that this game packs a really nice storyline with some plot twists some nice secrets, interesting gameplay especially stealthy gameplay at some points since there are enemies who can not hear you and has a few choices that matter in terms of story and gameplay (not too many and no where near as much as they do in the souls games but your choices matter non the less).
So in all honesty if you really like the souls series but you are not an easily buthurt fan boy, in which case you should avoid the game and the review all together, then I can not recomment this game enough, it has really been a long time since a game had such nice aestherics in regards to the enemies the weapons the armours the effects in pretty much everything it incorporates, the gameplay is polished and works very nice the bosses have specific patters which if you don't want to abuse with spells then they make for a really nice challenge, also a thing I really like is the fact that you can use any weapon you happen to come by and by that I mean there are no useless weapons, you still need the appropriate skill to use them (dex stg etc) but I haven't found a single weapon that was legitimately useless. So over all it's an awesome under rated game that has been hated a lot mostly for the lack of PVP and really deserves your time if you are into this kind of games like I am.

This game can be best summarized as potential. Slowly dieing potential. I've played off and on since the "Play for free for the Weekend, keep the game forever!" a year or so ago, while they've added a lot more ships and crew then, the fact they where willing to give away a 20 USD game for free should have been a bigger omen to me at that point in time then I took it to be, allow me to explain;
The game has gone from a 20 USD game to a Free to Play model in little over a year, it averages a 200 people at low population hours and rarely peaks more then 400 at peak weekend hours,
you are lucky. This was before and after it went Free to Play, it had a minor boost in people playing, ala 600 or so but that lasted all of a few days.
While there is no hardcore Pay to Win at play, all weapons and having to be purchased with in-game currency, and ships and other weapons them being side-grades as opposed to straight upgrades, the things they do ask money for, skins, boosters, crew packs, ect. are all grossly overpriced, a sure sign of deep finical desperation.
Redeeming qualities, like the interesting crew who have detailed art and colorful, deep back stories and great voice acting (including a guest appearance from The Mighty Jingle and Boo the Chihuahua), and very detailed, beautifully rendered ships, stations and effects, that's about all it has going for it.
Early Alpha status aside the balancing is poor, with no signs of intended improvement, they seem to express deliver more ships, skins and "value packs" then they do spending the time balancing what they already have, they even have the audacity to say in the Hanger interface that "All ships are balanced to play against one another..." Something you
say to players, let it stay unspoken and debated but don't outright say, even less advisable to do when you know they aren't.
Getting behind in a match makes coming back nearly impossible, loosing out on the Gamma bonuses more then once just deepens the divide. I've had off and on good matches, I've had some fun, but it doesn't outweigh by any greater margin the amount of frustration I've felt playing this game. I
to love it, I just can't.
My final verdict is if you seen this game still alive a year after this then it's probably worth playing at last, though I doubt it will live to see the end of the year if it stays the course it's on now. But stranger things have happened I suppose, enjoy the few good memories and try to forget about the bad ones.

I bought this, like many people of my (relatively young) generation, on the heels of the utter joy I derived from Half-Life 2 and its Episodes.  I knew that the original would be different, but I was still struck by surprise.  This isn't a bad thing; kinda like expecting something to taste delicious, and it
--but in a different way than you expected.  Where playing HL2 felt like a cool, robust, rich and yet pleasantly mild drink of milk or the like, this original is like a super-carbonated beverage, constantly assaulting your senses with little bubbles and bursts of stimulation, maintaining a certain overall heat and intensity.  It's also got a pretty good deal of caffeine or sugar or something like that, because it is
.  It's got the feel that instantly lets you know it's still somewhere among the ranks of those classic, balls-to-the-walls, pure-twitch-reflex heart-pumpers that pioneered the FPS genre: there are headcrabs (much faster and deadlier than their fat, sluggish regular counterparts from Half-Life 2) around
corner, in every vent and crevice, behind and atop many boxes; WAVES of deadly alien creatures teleport/spawn in around most areas--if, that is, these areas haven't already been hard-claimed by incredibly aggressive (AI-wise; no waiting it out behind a door frame like the Combine) Marines cleaning up the evidence of the catastrophe using mounted .50-cal and rocket-launching turrets, laser-tripmines and laser-activated robo-turrets, oh, MY!!  Not quite as much time to stop and smell the atmosphere as the sequel, ladies and gentlemen!
However, those happily familiar with Half-Life 2 can enjoy noticing a lot of the subtleties in this first game that point in the direction the second went: elements of immersive storytelling, atmosphere, background, answers to continuity nods you didn't even know were
in Half-Life 2, and the evolution of the whole universe between the events of this and 2.  Inside jokes, origin stor(y/ies), and little things that would become elements of the next installment abound; Barney's beer-debt to Gordon, the strange speech of the G-Man, the original noises the vortigaunts made that helps the player put together
they have that weird, hypnotic accent and cadence in the second game, and some illuminating facts that make their cryptic fortune-teller-ominous-type dialogue lines in HL2 a bit clearer.  There are some familiar monsters, like barnacles, headcrabs and zombies and vortigaunts, but
different from those
, Half-Life 2-only newcomers to the series, have known.  Plus, a whole
of others that are at most only
at in the sequel: Bullsquids, Houndeyes, Ichthyosaurs, and Gargantua, just off the top of my head.  Also, where HL2 only has 11 weapons at most, you get an arsenal of 14, with 5 pretty crazy weapons never encountered in the second game--plus one more that you only get to use on a vehicle (the buggy) for a few levels (Highway 17 and the next few).
Overall, a
more intense, even

in its own right, and certainly MORE than worth its current price.  Need I say any more?  Pick up Half-Life today!  Heck, pick up the whole 15-buck original pack!

The Old Tree is a short puzzle-based animation game of watching a baby alien explore its environment, which you can finish in around 15 minutes. I went in with a low expectations of the game, and I could only say that I'm glad I did. I don't have many complaints about the premise of the game and its puzzle mechanics, but as for the entire game itself... it leaves many things to be desired.
The main problem with the game is that it lacks any form of development, i.e. the baby alien you're playing as stays a baby until the end, and after going through a simple series of puzzles, you finish the game without any form of conclusion or ending. For me, playing through this game did not leave me with any sense of satisfaction or accomplishment.
I think the game has potential, but that potential was wasted with the game's lack of content. If you have time to spare and want to see a very basic indie game with good puzzle mechanics, then by all means try it out. Otherwise, move on and spend your 15 minutes playing some other game that's more worthwhile.

This is one of the defining early first person shooters. Dated now in terms of graphics and sheer complexity. You can, however, adjust the difficulty. It can also regularly scare you to death, and it has a nice blend of exploration, light puzzles, and action. It is also quite a long game with large environments to explore. You will die many times and will spend many hours playing this masterpiece. Sometimes you need stealth. Sometimes you need to run. Fast. Really fast. Sometimes you need to go very slowly. Sometimes going in guns blazing is the right move. Sometimes you need to pick off your enemies one at a time. Sometimes you need to figure things out and solve problems. These changes in gameplay along with the sheer length and story will make you want to play it again and again. This is the first game. There are many more set in this same world after it. If you want to play them, play this first.
Some might think the story is cliched or been overdone, but it was not so back when it was originally released almost 20 years ago. It starts off with an accident at a top secret lab and throws you into a sci-fi world of monsters, secrets, and other dimensions. You need to keep on your toes and fight your way out. Piece by piece you uncover a massive secret and conspiracy bound to destroy every person's reality down to their core.
Everybody who likes video games and everyone who especially likes FPS needs to have this game. Outstanding story for an FPS.

A bold departure from what we've come to know as Assassin's Creed in the last 4 years, and it's in the right direction!
I will preface my review with acknowledgement that the game (at launch) has quite a few bugs, some more devastating than others. To be completely frank, it didn't sour my experience-- and I was victim to the bug that erased my save file (I was 25 hours in, at sequence 10 by that point). People are bashing the game left and right across the internet, claiming its an unfinished game and that Ubisoft has betrayed their playerbase by serving them unpolished garbage. Here's the thing:
Since the debut of Assassin's Creed 2, Ubisoft has consistently added feature upon feature to the series to the point that it leaves the player overwhelmed, confused, and claustrophobic. In this way, they've all but ignored what made Assassin's Creed about assassinating templars. It became focused on action, combat, sailing, being a pirate, being a soldier.
This is what makes Assassin's Creed Unity so special; it's back to basics. You assume the persona of Arno Dorian as he rises through the ranks of the Assassin Brotherhood in Paris, where the core gameplay and storyline revolve around giving you a specific templar target, the building he or she can be found, and saying 'have at it'. You'll find no hand-holding or linear gameplay options forced upon you, in fact, the game can become legitimately difficult and frustratingly unforgiving-- and I love that.
Now, the story is a bit short. Most people clock it at about 15 hours, but if you speed through it, I reckon you could beat it in under 10 (little-to-no side missions or co-op missions included). Not only is it short, it's a bit underdeveloped. The characters go through so much change without proper build up and pacing which devalues their stories and dilemmas, leaving you mostly uncaring for nearly all of them. I'd say the best element to the story is the fact you rise up in the brotherood with actual mentors as guides, giving you tasks and missions. It gives you something to strive for, and makes you feel like a part of something more.
Gameplay in this game brings the series to an all-time high. Everything has been reworked and overhauled to make a fresh experience to both newcomers and veterans of the series. Combat is tough as nails as the killstreaks and counter-attacks have been completely stripped from the game, forcing you to juggle enemies with dodges, well-timed parries, and sneaking in a hit or two. For at leas the first half of the game before you unlock / purchase good armor and weapons, if you attempt to face off against more than 3 enemies you can consider yourself dead. This is a much needed change of pace that I think we've all wanted for years now (I know I have). Parkour has seen a large facelift as well! The game mixes the functionality of AC3 and AC2's parkour, while introducing its own new feature: High Profile + A = Parkour Up; High Profile by itself keeps you level but still jumps from object to object; High Profile + B = Parkour Down. This is a gigantic game changer, and takes a while to get used to. Once you've mastered its nuances and understand how to navigate the city with this new and vastly improved parkour system, you'll have a sincere blast as you traverse Paris with style and speed. Lastly, there's stealth. This is an interesting subject, as it is a literal tennant of the Creed: Hide in plain sight. Thus, you'll find all your social stealth options have returned, but now with a couple of new features: active cover that allows Arno to hide around corners and behind waist-high objects such as boxes and carts, and a fancy new stealth mode that is activated with the left trigger / L2. To be honest, it's a little clunky and needs some tweaking. I'd say the biggest problem with the cover / stealth is the lack of corner switching, meaning you have to press A to back out of cover, move around the corner of the wall you want to take cover of, and press A against it to resume cover. It's not a HUGE deal, as it doesn't force you to stand up and break stealth or anything, but it prevents the stealth from feeling consistently fluid and intuitive.
There's much, much more to this game-- a plethora of side content, the modern day segments (where YOU, literal you in front of the screen holding the controller, are the character being referenced as unnamed characters inform you of the assassin's plight against the templars, and convince you to help them and do some things for them), co-op missions (these mostly funciton the same as single-player missions, but are usually a bit larger in scale to accomodate more players.
To cut to the chase: should you buy Assassin's Creed Unity? Yes. If you were ever a fan of the series before it became Warrior's Creed, you should absolutely get the game. It's laid the foundation for a beautiful future, where we play an actual Assassin set in large, sprawling cities full of activities and distractions.
I'd rate the game 9.5 / 10. An amazing game with a story that's just a bit too short and suffers from some sub-par character development.

You may think like me that "Grim Legends 2: Song of the Dark Swan" can be the sequel of the first game Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride. But the story is really independent, the only link between them is that each of them relate a grim legend.
The story is very good and graphics are awesome. The puzzles and hidden objects scenes are fairly shared.
The game features an inventory where you can store items to combine with the environment to go deeper in the story. In the game you will also find several animal fellows and one spirit that will help you through your adventure.
The game have several difficulties and have a guest feature : all the family can play the game and resume it where they left. There is also a map which is useful to fast travel through the different places and that can have some hints if you play in an easier mode. Also you can use the Hint/Skip hourglass whenever you want and wait until its refill to use it again. But be warned that you may not skip or use a hint in any puzzle or hidden objects scene if you wish to have some achievements. It's also the case for not skipping the first ten cut scenes while playing the story.
There is a wide choice of puzzles and there are two kind of Hidden objects scenes. The first Hidden objects scene features the name of the objects to find some are found easily (normal one) and some others need you to interact with the environment or to combine two items to found them. The second Hidden objects scene let you find the shape of the objects in the scene and sometimes ask you to use them in order to obtain the others.
(*) :
The game has some achievements that can be missed even some collectibles related achievements and also some challenging achievements including finishing the game on hard mode. There is a guide on steam that will help you to not miss any of these achievements. The challenging achievements require you to finish a puzzle or an hidden objects scene or a domino game under a minute. And two achievements require you to find 3 objects in 3 seconds or find all objects without any misclick in the hidden object scenes.

has easily become one of my favorite Artifex Mundi series, with a theme centering around Brothers Grimm Fairytale collection. Each new game is an original and beautiful interpretation of one of their collected European fairytales. Thus, there is no story consistency between games in the series. You can pick and enjoy them as stand-alones. Being a lovely interpretation of
story,
is no different.
Here, we take the role of a healer, brought in to the Eagle Kingdom to find a solution to the young and beautiful Queen's unknown ailment. She has never spoken a word for the years that she has passed with her beloved King; not even after the birth of their son. According to Queen Mother - the Peacock Lady - all she ever does is weaving shirts out of nettle without ever resting. As we just start to examine the young Queen, a sinister green smoke breaks into her chamber, engulfing her and the heir. When the smoke is gone, so is the heir. The Peacock Lady steadily accuses the Young Queen with witchcraft - punishable by burning at the stake as the laws of the land dictate. Suspicious of this accusation, the King pleads with us to find a way to prove her innocence. So, our journey towards the Swan Kingdom - the homeland of the Queen - in hopes of finding proof of her innocence begins. We are to learn of an old tragedy, unmask the real villain and break a curse while we are at it.
Maybe not as dramatic or impressive as the first game,
is still a beautiful interpretation of the original tale and a well-made addition to the series. Artworks are trademark Artifex Mundi at this point: vibrant, appealing and picturesque. Character designs themselves are quite fitting for the tale, with thriving animations, mimics and color choices. Voice acting is not spectacular, but still well above average. Whenever I write about one of these HOGs hailing from Artifex Mundi, I feel like working on a paying advertisement; but I swear that's not the case. Their work in these silly casual games is nearly always that good, that's all.
Gameplay though, is a bit sterile in this one compared to other Artifex Mundi games. We don't have as many HOG scenes as we'd expect. The game is dominated by FROG - Fragmented Object Games - where you are expected to collect pieces of a certain item to make a whole, then use as a part of another item combination. Puzzles are fine - nothing shallow or suicidal, just the right amount of brain scratching, if not a bit basic. Compared to other titles, there is a fair amount of backtracking too, so be ready to recall details from past environments if you are playing in expert difficulty. There is domino or mahjong alternative gameplay here, since there isn't much HOG scenes to alternate between anyhow so one playthrough would be suffice for collecting all achievements.
By the end, this second instalment in the series, is a beautiful game appropriate for a lazy midweek afternoon. Grab it on sale and admire some beautiful artwork accompanied by a neat selection of puzzles and an enchanting retelling of a Grimm Brothers story.

So I've almost completed this and these are my honest thoughts.
QUBE is a first person puzzle game, where you have several different kinds of colored cubes you can manipulate which are usually atached to the walls. Every color is sort of a different mechanic. It starts off in a chamber where you wake up with no memory of yourself and a lady kind of explains the situation. At certain places in each chapter some narrative takes place in the form of people speaking to you through a com link and that's generally how the game tells its story.
The Good
The narrative is surprisingly enjoyable and the voice actors do a good job for most of the time. The story is a bit simple, but kind of interesting. Unfortunately the pros end there.
The Bad
For a puzzle game I went in expecting something that would make me think, QUBE didn't. The puzzles were simple and easy throughout the whole game. Most of them were actually frustrating and not because they were hard, but because of the clunky gameplay and overall design. The whole game feels sluggish. Usually when you look at a puzzle you see the solution rather quick, but it will take some time and frustration to successfully solve it because of how the whole thing is designed. The concept is good, but the execution is bad. There are gamebraking glitches every now and then too. When a certain part of a puzzle bugs ut it just forces you to restart the whole thing. Last but not least, it's really short, I'm on the final chapter and you can see how much time it took me.
I wish I enjoyed this, but I didn't. I cannot write a positive review in good conscious. To sum it up: QUBE is slow, frustrating, clunky and easy.

This game is pretty straight-forward, which is a good thing.  The game was overall refreshing, and it played well (meaning, no performance issues or serious glitches).  Most of the puzzles were modestly challenging, though few were exceptionally difficult.  But unlike games such as Portal, the puzzles can only be so complicated before they're totally overwhelming. I would like to point out that there were a couple puzzles that were a bit clumsy to solve, where I "solved" them by exploiting inconsistencies in the physics engine.  Though the level design may be clever, the physics engine can sometimes make the puzzles seem a lot less elegant.
My biggest gripe with the game is the overall effort put into it, particularly toward the end.  The ending was very sudden.  It felt incomplete, rushed, and as though the developers lost interest.  I liked the psychological dichotomy in the story, but it felt like the entire concept of that was completely thrown away at the very end.  It would have been nice to have at least been given a choice to how the game ends.
TL;DR:
Decent game to get on sale and play during a weekend.  But the physics need refinement, it's visually boring, and the story is anticlimactic.

The Walking Dead is an interesting visual novel/point and click type of game. When I first went into it I thought it was about  talking to my group and trying to change their fates through our interactions. I was horribly disappointing to realize no matter what you do or what you say, the outcome is always the same.
There is a huge amount of "illusion of choice" There is one point in the game where you have to choose between saving this guy or saving this girl. When you save one, the other dies and the story goes in a different direction and encourages replaying the game! Right? Wrong. Not twenty minutes later, the person you save dies anyways. In the end no matter your choice, both end up dead. There was no choice! This pattern continued through the whole game, I'd be promoted with a choice and the inevitable would eventually happen. I finished the game with a bad taste in my mouth.
That is until I saw a discussion online about Kenny, one of the characters. The thread started off with someone saying how awesome Kenny was.He always had your back, was friendly, sacrificed himself, he was cool. I agreed. However most people in the thread said he was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! I was completely in disagreement! They were even listing quotes he NEVER said in the game! That was when it hit me. The events of the game are unchangeable but the characters and the way they interact with you is completely different for each player depending on your choices. Kenny was a nice guy in my game but a jerk in many other people's games. It made discussion about the game a ton of fun since everyone's experience with each character was completely different. Some characters tell some players things other players will never hear them say.
Sure the events were out of your control but that kind of game would be a little high budget for Telltale, so I think what they pulled off was pretty well done all things considered. My advice is do NOT go into the game with the thought that you can change the outcome of certain character's gruesome fates, but you can change their personalities, and compare the differences and similarities between your characters and your friend's characters' personalities. Darkest Dungeon is a game to both love and hate.
You will party wipe. You will lose heroes, and you can't do anything about it, yes. But the point is trying to manage what is going to happen. It's a game about playing the numbers. People say that there's no skill in this game, only luck. That's not true; the skill is the ability to predict and adapt, the ability to make the best of a bad situation. It's a hard game. By design.
Thematically, Darkest is wonderful, combining Lovecraftian elements to provide a dark world of the occult, with great visuals, music, and narration.
The only other thing to say is this: when you open the game, you get this screen. It DIRECTLY addresses many of the things that other people say about Darkest Dungeon:
"Darkest Dungeon is about making the most of a bad situation. Quests will fail or must be abandoned. Heroes will die. And when they die, they stay dead. Progress autosaves constantly, so actions are permament.
The game expects a lot out of you. How far will you push your adventurers? How much are you willing to risk in your quest to restore the Hamlet? What will you sacrifice to save the life of your favorite hero?
Thankfully, there are always fresh souls arriving on the stage coach seeking both adventure and fame in the shadow of the...
Darkest Dungeon"

A great classic and yet another must for all FPS lovers!
This game pretty much pioneered with many things later found in a lot of FPS: "mute" protagonist, lots of weapons (classic and futuristic/alien), big variety of enemies/bosses and levels (even for today's standards), a bit of mystery/horror and an engaging story, left open for a sequel.
After all those years and despite having been outdated by many modern games, it still holds up well today, you can see what made it great at the time!
The game's "man with a gun" (or crowbar), the scientist Gordon Freeman, also became quite an iconic protagonist, boosting the belief that "nerds can be cool too"!
Some influences seem to have been taken from Wolfenstein 3D/Original Doom, though in their turn the latter games's sequels seem to have taken influences from Half-Life, showing how important all those games were for the FPS genre.
The whole "protagonist in a robotic suit, fighting a variety of aliens and marines" plot, makes me think that Halo probably also got some influences from here.
The addition of G-man as an antagonist, who watches your progress as you march further and further in the game and only those who pay attention will notice, was also great!
Finally, if I had to name just a minor flaw that would be that I didn't find the music addictive enough, it seemed almost non-existent to me (Return to Castle Wolfenstein for example had a great soundtrack and totally immersed you in the game), but don't let this small factor drive you away from this gem of a game, you can't be considered a true FPS fan until you have played this!

I have played quite few HOGs and Artifex Mundi is still one of the best HOG developers. They can make any basic story sound interesting with good storytelling, having few plot twists, good puzzles and with really amazing background art. The pros of their games is making the most simple stories interesting and memorable but always having a high quality in their games. The cons are that these games are like Undertale; you get the most fun and delight when you don't know anything about it. Later on it's nice to replay it few times but it doesn't have the same charm anymore. But this game has something that just makes it better when you replay it few times. I played this game twice and the story made lots of more sense.
This game isn't sequel to earlier Grim Legends-game, the Forsaken bride; it's just an another tale and another story in distant country far away.
The story is quite decent for HOG game; something bad happens and player has to solve the problem and also seek the truth which lead to horrific events. Basic day. But Artifex Mundi gives live to this story with intriguing backstory which in my opinion sounded realistic.
The puzzles are not hard but they might take time depending, how accustomed HOG player you're.
The voice acting is good too, quite good for HOG game. The voices have personality and I have to admit that I still remember clearly the nasal voice of the Peacock queen
.
The art has personality and looks nicely rough and the background looks slightly twisted in my opinion, contrast to the bright colors and prettiness. It makes the game more memorable but also gives the feeling that the world is alive and breathing when our protagonist is on the adventure.The music also is really pretty but not something that really stays in mind.
There's a main game but also a bonus game but the main games story is much more well thought than the bonus. It just gave me the feeling that Artifex Mundi had to add some kind of bonus story so the CE wouldn't feel waste for the buyers. But it is still enjoyable if you don't think it too much.

It's good game with basic story where you solve the mystery of mysterious events. It's one of the best Artifex Mundi games they have made for awhile and for it's high quality in art, story and possible the collectibles you can say that you haven't wasted you money in vain. If you're still thinking should you buy this use your extra money to it when you wan't to just sit down and have fun or buy it when it's on sale. This game is a good introduction on the Hidden object genre and on the Artifex Mundi games.
The pros:
- gorgeous art
- basic story with an twist
- memorable voice acting
- realistic characters
- replay possibility
The cons:
- needs more than one play through to enjoy properly
- slightly linear story
- predictable

Short (3-4 hours) but enjoyable experience despite the very poor story line (or lack of story at all really).  The game revolves around a guy in a cube spaceship who must solve challenges using different coloured cubes to progress through the levels to try and escape the spaceship.  The story is extremely disappointing and really doesnt add anything to the game in my opinion.  I was left confused by it at the end and because its so random i felt no urge to even look up what it was about.  It had zero lasting effect on me in this sense.
The puzzle elements of the game however are really well done and although not massively challenging they are also not frustrating either.  The game has some hidden puzzles which are a little harder but again nothing to hard.  The game revolves around using some special gloves that allow you to manipulate cubes to progress to the next area/level. Each cube is a different colour and they all act differently, you need to use a combination of the cubes to progress through the level with some timing needed also.
The directors cut includes speed runs which i personally am not interested in but it might appeal to others.
Overall i enjoyed the game from a puzzle aspect and if you are a fan of puzzle games i would recommend it especially when its on sale for less than £2.  However dont expect any gripping story line from this title.

Menu navigation was a little different but i blame the game rather than the controller for this as it was created for mouse navigation.

This is going to be a hard one to review. It's a stroke of genius that I would wholly recommend to get and play, and I mean NOW. Still...it's vastly different than most games out there. In fact, one could argue whether this is a game at all.
Let's start what this game is NOT: it is not
-fun
-engaging as far as gameplay is concerned (it has clunky controls to say the least)
-fast paced
-great on visuals or sounds (in fact, it's even below average)
-casual
-competitive (yes, I know this seems at odd with the previous)
If you're now scratching your head about what this thing is about...good. Because I rather have people not buy it than buy it expecting it to be something else than it is.
So...what kind of game is this? Well...if I had to classify this, I'd say it is somewhat of a mix of a point 'n click game with those text-based adventure games/books where the next piece of story depends on the choices you make. And TWD leans strongly toward that last part.
The absolute strong point is the story. For those unfamiliar with the comic books or the TV serie (btw: how's life under your rock?)...there is this disease thing that turns people into zombies. These roam the land and bite, infect and turn the living into them. So far, so cliché...but like most great horror tales, this focuses not so much on these 'walkers' but on the people attempting to overcome the total downfall of civilization. You are Lee Everett. You start the game on the day the whole outbreak starts, not knowing what's going on. Pretty soon, you'll find a little girl named Clementine, whom you'll take under your wing. From there on, giving details would end up in spoilers. Well...maybe. That's where the choices come in. In particular parts (usually dialogue), you can choose what to do. And the story will unfold from there on out. In other words: the actions you take directly influence the result.
This choicetree may not sound much to you when reading it, but believe me: immersion couldn't be implemented better. Not all choices matter or have direct influence, but you usually won't know about this until (sometimes much) later.
It's somewhat funny if you think about it. I played diablo 3 and skipped through whole conversations and even pretty expensive cutscènes because I didn't care about the whole apocalypse-story...and here I am, honestly wanting to know what Clementine thinks while she's on the swing.
As said, visuals or sounds aren't interesting. For the most part, it's just filler that is only there to get the job done. The exception is where it matters: in voices and facial expression. These are top-notch and believable for everyone. And speaking of characters: as in the TWD franchise, there are no clichés here. Everyone has their own personality, their own agenda, mental bagage, fears and motivations. That easily helps forget about the cartoony outlook of the game.
Speaking of 'cartoony'...don't make the assumption that this game is kiddy in any way (if you've read the comic books, you'd already know that). It's actually the direct opposite: some of the choices you'll have to make are very hard. Will you give water to someone's dying, knowing that the rest of the group is starving? When forced to choose, whom will you be saved and who will die? The game certainly doesn't censor itself, which makes things even worse at times. Especially if Clementine's involved.
Lee isn't Clementine's father, but the game nonetheless plays into some dilemma's parents have to tackle. It plays into the difference to what's just and what's right. What we want versus what needs to be done.
That's a good thing. It doesn't make the game fun, but it doesn't have to be. Schindler's list wasn't a fun movie, but that doesn't make its existence any less important. The same can be said here. And yes, that comparison's valid: this game is that good.
This is the sort of game that really needs to be played by critics. Despite the zombies and it being a game, this isn't entertainment. It's an experience, and one that may teach you more about yourself and your behaviour than you might like. Or humanity, for that matter (though that might be a bit too much).
All in all: absolutely recommended.

I was very pleasantly surprised by Q.U.B.E: Director’s Cut. I had heard nothing and seen nothing of it before playing it (Humble Bundle syndrome) so I really didn’t know what to expect. I don’t generally consider myself to be a fan of first-person puzzle games because I do not consider myself to be very smart or very patient; whenever I pick up a puzzle game I expect to be bored while I figure out how to play, and as soon as I understand how to play I expect to be frustrated once the puzzles move beyond the easiest of the easy. Because of that I have abandoned many puzzles games soon after starting. Q.U.B.E seems to anticipate that mentality and provides an excellent learning experience to ease you in to every mechanic of the puzzles as they appear, without ever making you feel overwhelmed. Accomplishing that in the early part of any puzzle game is worthy of praise, but Q.U.B.E never stops accomplishing that as new mechanics and variations on old ones continue to be introduced throughout the game right up until the end, and never once did I feel like I was playing a tutorial. The puzzles themselves are mostly very well balanced in difficulty (for my personal skill lever). When a series of one type of puzzle starts to feel like a chore, the developers smartly introduce a new mechanic soon thereafter, which almost always managed to relieve my frustration by invigorating my curiosity. There were several times when I got incredibly frustrated with a particular puzzle and was feeling very prepared to call out the developers for cheap/unfair puzzle design, when eventually I “got it” and realized that the problem was me, not the puzzle. This happens most often on puzzles involving the physics engine, which did a few times “spaz out” and make objects bounce around in obviously unintended ways. But I realized later that this only happened because I was approaching a puzzle the wrong way, and I thought I needed to force my way through using some bizarre and implausible manipulation of the physics objects. The puzzles are thankfully not designed to rely on the physics engine nearly as much as it might appear they are, and once the right solution is found it becomes obvious that no “forcing” of the physics is necessary. It reminds me of a challenging jigsaw puzzle; sometime you really, honestly think you need to “trim a piece to make it fit” but that’s just because you haven’t found where it actually fits yet.
The story is understated but excellent. Being told almost exclusively through voiceovers, it utilizes mystery, excellent voice acting, and simple but effective themes of faith that I found to be surprisingly compelling, and kept me motivated to complete the game in a just a few days. Considering the game’s style I was beginning to dread that the game would have a cop-out “ambiguous” ending with no answers, but thankfully that’s not the case. The ending does have answers for the player, but whether you find them to be satisfying or not is going to be a matter of opinion. I appreciated that I was given answers, but I personally didn’t like the answers very much. Whether you like the ending or not is going to depend much more on your personally held beliefs than on your opinion of the quality of the ending cinematic. But the very fact that the story manages personal involvement on that level at all is very impressive.
Overall, for excellent quality and accessibility of puzzles paired with a very engaging story, I highly recommend  Q.U.B.E: Director’s Cut.
MUST PLAY
