Short version:
Fractured space brings something unique to space combat games.  Although it doesn't currently offer a great deal of variety in it's objectives or modes,the devil is in the details and mastering your ships and developing your teamwork is the most rewarding element.
It's well worth the hour or so it takes to go through the trainer and your first live match, and if you ever enjoyed a space opera, this is going to get your attention in a unique way.
Long version:
Fractured space is in an alpha release state, so a lot of things are likely to change.  This review is a work in progress as I push through the early game and get to know Fractured Space better, and reflects a relatively new player's experience.
Fractured Space is a game focused on commanding massive spaceships in space combat.
The game attempts to deliver a massive sense of scale, with the primary player controlled asset being very large space ships.  Three manufacturers are currently available, with very different looks and feels, each of which offering it's own unique role.  Like other MOBA style games, the depth comes from the interaction between differently composed teams, and emphasizes teamwork, strategy, tactics and skill over anything else.
Starter ships tend toward flexibility, with every other ship being unlockable through gameplay, and offering more niche speciality roles.
So far there are no real pay to win elements, no timers, no exclusive modules or gear.  Cash items currently offered are cosmetic, with the sole advantage of the few premium ships being a full team boost to cash and exp (up to 5%).  The ships themselves perform exactly the same as their vanilla counterparts, while being unable to have their custom skins replaced by any other skins availabe through the market.
Fractured Space offers a crew system, with a crew being made up of 5 crew.  Potential crew members each belong to a crew role, like captian, CAG, tactical officer, engineering, jump specialist, and so on.  Crew currently can not be doubled up on a specific role; only one captain, only one CAG.
The current recruitment system for crew is the only randomized element of the game I've seen so far, and is probably the weakest element.  The current system is a lot like a one armed bandit, spitting out a random crew member in exchange for currency earned in game, or credits purchased with cash.  There is also a drop system from playing a set number of games during any given day, with 3 tiered rewards at 2, 4, and 6 games played.
The randomness of the system, and the fact that you may continue to get crew you already have, feel oddly out of tune with an otherwise very accessible game.
Gameplay:
Currently the game contains a short basic tutorial (really an actual game match with AI opponents, a UI introduction and some additional standard trainer content added).  Additional tutorials are planned.
Gameplay has one released mode, a complex 5 on 5 capture the control point battlefield, split up into 5 distinct arenas.  You will travel between them using a warp drive system, warping from point to point, capturing nodes, fighting enemy craft, all with the ultimate goal of capturing the opposing team's home base.
I haven't yet seen the second mode, which is currently disabled in the U.I. and called "Frontlines Mode".
In addition, there is a custom game option that lets you pack just your friends into a game, and a firing range mode that gives you the opportunity to test fly any ship in the game.
Each ship has it's own set of unique weapons and modules, speed, vulnerabilites and strengths.  The variety feels pretty deep so far as I've played into, although it looks like it takes dedication to significantly open up the ship options.
The visuals and the handling of the ships do a good job conveying the size and majesty of thousand meter spaceships, and the handling end is very important, positioning plays a vital role in combat, and gets complex very quickly.
Shields in Fractured Space are a utility module for certain support ships only, with armor being the acme of defense.  This for me adds to the space opera feel of the combat, where any hit on an enemy hull is meaningful.
Teamwork is the key to gameplay, with no ship being particularly good at lone wolfing it.  I havent explored any voice options yet, but players seem to quickly grasp basics, and the game is flexible enough to lay traps, temp enemy groups into walking into ambushes, pound ships out of cover, expoit support craft to defend nodes, and so on.
Audio:
Music does a good job without standing out too much or getting in the way.
Crew voice overs are fantastic fun, however.  Each crew member available in the game has their own deep backstory and motivations, and will chime in with frequent reports whenever something relevant to their sphere of expertise is going on.
Just drilled an enemy vessel with a crippling debuff?  Your tactical officer will jump on the bridge comm, popping up a static visual of the crew member, to let you know.
Warping in?  That natty nav-droid you've got at the nav station might remind you of the dangers in jumping under fire (try not to).
And on and on.  With upwards of 40 crew available, the personalities you pick really change the feel of your command, and add a tremendously fun element to the game.
Weapons fire are also extremely impressive to listen to, from the shudder of the ship when you fire off your missile racks, to the droning energy discharge of certain heavy energy weapons.
Fracture Space is not a game you will want to play with the sound turned off.
Visuals / Performance:
Game performance is very good on my Area 51 Alienware rig.  The ships are stunning, from attitude jets to very slick warp animations.
The feel of the game is a little down to earth, compared to many sci-fi ship games. Thrusters don't leave impossibly long visual contrails ala EVE, energy weapons are common, but most of them will not wear out your eyes with pop and flash and screen shaking.  That said, there are some that do have extremely flashy effects.  Overall I think it works for the feel of the game, but ymmv.
User Interface:
The main UIs do not feel particularly good or intuitive to navigate.  If you've played Star Conflict or Hawken, you are going know where to go.  Otherwise it will be mildly frustrating but a short learning curve.
The in game UIs are a different story.  Somewhat customizable, these are extremely functional, interesting and enjoyable.
Round-up:
Fractured Space feels something like a MOBA, with a stately, tactical pace, but manages to also offer frantic firefights.
For an alpha title, the depth of ship variety and balance is surprisingly good, the audio is generally outstanding, and the in-game ui and controls feel very good.
The game elements outside of the actual gameplay generally do not yet feel very polished, and that extends to the crew system, unfortunately.
For space sim fans, Fracture Space offers a unique and very promising experience, and the existing gameplay is rewarding enough that I'd recommend investing the hour or so it takes to learn the gameplay and go through your first match.

"Darkest Dungeon is about making the most of a bad situation", says the game's intro. To put it differently, it's possible to say that the aesthetics (audiovisual content and gameplay) of DD is designed mainly to cause some kind of affliction.
As you play and pay a closer attention to the visual details (every wrinkle, every dirt, every vestige of decay, the everywhere shading); as you read the heroes constant laments and provisory hopes; as you watch their stress grow; as you presence the process of a negative subjective condition arousal; as you hope for a positive "resolve"; as you, at the edge (of HP, food, torch, money etc.), are obliged to make irreversible decisions (because there's no save and load available); as you need to chose among heroes that already have enough pathologic sequellae from last runs which one can make the most (often the "less worse") of the next run; you may feel the pain of each of these details, you may feel some affliction.
At the game menu, we are welcomed by a music that sounds like a warning, an alarm, an inflamation, a sound that reminds us of an iminent or present distress. The menu music isn't atmospheric dark (like the usual ones from games tagged as "horror"), it's more afflictive.

Darkest Dungeon is a very liked game and I feel like any attempt to criticize it is met with disdain from people calling you a crybaby for not being able to handle randomness and difficulty. So let me explain why I believe this game fails on several critical elements.
It pains me a lot to give Darkest Dungeon a negative rating, but there comes a point where a game crosses the line between difficult and infuriatingly frustrating. Darkest Dungeon is not actually a difficult game, like Invisible Inc., Super Meat Boy or Dark Souls are. These games give you a challenge and expect you to get good enough to overcome it. And everytime you fail it's because of a mistake you made. Everytime.
What Darkest Dungeon does is something quite different than that. It only expects you to give it time. Its difficulty is nothing but a facade. Most of your failures will come from random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that you can't do anything about. And believe me when I say I tried to convince myself of the contrary for as long as possible, but I can't anymore. Can you play the game better ? Can you find smarter strategies ? Yes, of course, but even by playing well your skill only contributes to like 5% of the result. You can succeed over and over again by playing terribly, or fail even when making no mistake. Trying to improve gets extremely demotivating when you realize your improvements barely matter. Moreover it's not even satisfying to succeed because you know you had nothing to do with it...
Aesthetically, it is brilliant. The tone, narration and the general feel of the game are astounding, and only for that I can't say the game is worthless. But if you value your time in the slightest, I would encourage you to stay far away from Darkest Dungeon. A few years ago I would probably have been fine with losing dozens of gameplay hours to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but with limited free time in my week I can't imagine wasting it like that.
Let me explain what the game does wrong in my opinion :
- Randomness is a very powerful design tool that allows for diversity and longevity, but it's a double-edged sword. If you are not careful enough with it you can end up sabotaging everything. And that's exactly what happened with DD : a lack of control. Randomness affects absolutely every aspect in the game, and because of the enormous variance of the results strategic decisions are almost inconsequential. Why try to increase your damage by 1 or 2 points when the dice roll goes from 0 to 30 (between a miss and a critical hit)? THAT is really the main problem of this game : the random variance is way too important to allow for any kind of meaningful decisions.
- It seems like a lot of elements in the game are solely designed to induce frustation for the sake of it. The inventory system is way too contrived, and often forces you to drop loot before being able to activate a curio in the VERY SAME room. It's like objects instantly vanish when you drop them, making it impossible to pick them up again. That would be fine if the inventory wasn't WAY TOO small for the later missions, in which you have to leave thousands of gold coins and numerous useful objects behind. Why not have less loot in the dungeons instead ? The result would be the same but players would be way less frustated.
- Another annoying element is the hunger system. Beside not having any control over it, it also makes absolutely no sense. Your characters may not ask for a meal during an entire dungeon, or need to eat every two rooms. This makes buying an appropriate amount of food extremely difficult, if not plainly random.

- Without spoiling, there comes a point in the game where some event happens that you have to respond to. It is interesting narratively, but it also occurs WAY TOO early, meaning that you will not be able to deal with it. That failure sets you back around 15 hours, basically erasing everything you have done during that time. This is easily the most frustating moment I have ever experienced in a game. Once again, there is nothing difficult about it : it's simply an annoying time waster.
In my opinion Darkest Dungeon is very close to being a masterpiece, and I completely understand that many people would call it that. If you are able to deal with the frustration, or even convince yourself that you are always the one to blame, it's probably a hell of a good time. But losing 30 hours of gameplay or more when it represents all the free time you have in three weeks is a bit too much, especially when it relies on a coin flip...
A difficult game should never be frustating. I played through all the Souls games and not once was I frustated. Demotivated, yes, against some particularily tough bosses. But I knew the only thing I had to do was to improve. On the other hand Darkest Dungeon only requires time from you. Time that it then decides to waste at random intervals. Every once in a while it will give you progress. But very rarely will you feel like you are the one to blame or to congratulate. Maybe I'm looking for something else in games than playing dice...

Fallout 4 is a wide expansive world that can be filled with rich backstory and replayable side quests - if you decide to mod that in, same with very high res textures, over the lesser quality and more storage intensive the 58GB free pack you get. Fallout 4 can be fun to play even without DLC, and for a first play-through, even without mods (which is a good thing, if you want to get achievments from this game). And well... talking about the mods, there is an extremely large selection of them on the internet, completely free of charge, including some which expand the bredth of the game beyond some of the DLCs which you can buy, however, there is one recent point of contention in the Fallout 4 community, and that is to say "paid mods" from the creation club. Bethesda claims that these mods (or "mini DLCs" as they want us to think of them as) are not paid for, as you utilise an ingame currency, called "Creation Club Credits" of which, you have to buy, in clunky packages which almost guarantee that you will over pay for the mods. Along with said mods being lackluster - what with free alternatives that are superior to the paid ones, you often have to go on a quest that dictates a very similar quest line of "go here, kill the things, get the item, leave" or just drops the item in your inventory - at whateveer time in the playthrough you are at, which can result in unbalanced gameplay, what with the player coming out of the vault at level two with a shotgun ready to kill everything in the wasteland. Of course, the paid mods would not be such a large sore spot if Bethesda hadn't already attempted to roll out paid mods and had them fail catastrophically, and with them attempting to edge their way into that market again, you can expect that the fallout and maybe even the elder scrolls series will fall under the drudgery of constant, endless micro-transactions to get that gun a bit earlier, a bit more mana to take down that boss or even just more carry weight, so you can fast travel back to your mountain of hoarded items which start to lag you out if you stare at it for too long.
all in all, I would have recommended this game before the 28th august, but now I have to sadly let it die in infamy, as the way bethesda is going, if we don't shut down their money grab now, well.. the next few games may be the ridiculous parodies that we laugh about, such as "the start menu DLC - £5.99".

Beater Spirit was developed by Airwolt and published by Atriagames	. Generally, the game is a grindy platformer that has no real objective, no story and no real reason to do what your actually doing in the game. I feel like this game is just a quick cash grabber and wasn't really designed very well.
This game seems very far fetched and not designed well what so ever. I will explain why I think this in the game, and generally why I think you SHOULDN'T even give this game a chance. At the end of the day it's your choice whether you buy this game or not, but here are a few reasons you should consider before purchasing this game (even if it's on sale).
First of all, the gameplay itself is extremely boring, repetitive and just generally not fun after a hour or so of gameplay (if you can even tolerate that much). All this game is, is basically setting up a arena being able to choose the amount of platforms, enemy types, the number of enemies and how difficult the enemies are. The difficulty of the enemies will increase its health, attack & exp that you will receive. So the entire game is you just making these arenas, killing these enemies and collecting money. You can then use this money to gamble for new weapons and equipment to increase your characters defence and attack. That's it, as you progressively level up your character you will be able to gamble for more higher tier items and keep grinding for money.
I feel like the game is extremely repetitive and dull because it is basically the same thing over and over again. I found a simple way of getting money easily, just putting the max amount of enemies and platforms on the hardest difficult. You then just hit the enemies off the edge of the platform to kill them and then collect your gold and exp. Despite that, I feel like if the game was made into some sort of platformer with a story to it with levels and so on that this game wouldn't be half as bad but because the gameplay is so repetitive and dull it really is bad.
As well as the game not being very fun and extremely repetitive there are very few enemies to choose from when you create your own arena in the game. The art style I guess is interesting and alright for the most part, but then again the maps only really change the background and not the actually platforms which just makes it look really dull with all the same colours.
+ Cards (I guess)
- Dull & repetitive gameplay
- No story to the game
- Very grindy to get gold
- Limited number of enemies
- Dull different maps
- Overpriced (In my opinion)
Overall, I feel like the game itself is very dull, boring and extremely grindy because there is different style to the game. It's just the same gameplay over and over again, with limited enemies (3 enemies to make with your arena), repetitive gameplay and generally boring graphics after a hour or so. In conclusion, I WOULDN'T recommend this game to anyone because of lack of gameplay.

Got this game about a month ago, as I've been waiting for a good discount on it.  I have played it obsessively since then and can honestly say I've enjoyed myself every step of the way through a normal playthrough and currently pretty deep into my second character in  'survival difficulty'.
- Its not a very good Fallout RPG.  If you compare this to the earlier games in the series expecting more of the same you will be disappointed.  There are very few meaningful choices to make that impact the story outside of choosing which of the major factions you will have to wipe out to finish the story.  I like the writing better than Fallout 3's, but it is still far behind the quality of 1/2 and New Vegas in my opinion.
-  Skills and perks are dumbed down and fairly standard fare compared to the pros and cons perks of the first games, or the 'wild wasteland' perk from New Vegas.
-  The recently added Creation Club.  This thing is an abomination.  Advertised as 'more like mini DLC than paid mods', this  thing lets you purchase overpriced basic mods such as backpacks, new colors on your pip boy or a new power armor suit.  Or the cringy Giddyup Buttercup Horse Armor.  What is even more egregious is that the service downloads and installs all the mods for sale even if you don't care about using any of them.  Even with the pitiful choice of mods for sale on CC so far, the install size of the game went up by over 2GB, and will only go up as more content is added to it.  This is such pathetically poor design it is almost physically painful to even think about how stupid the people in charge of thumbing this feature up are in the head.
-  Performance problems, in the busier downtown areas of the game.  My PC isn't great so I'm okay with this, but it seems to be affecting the vast majority of other players as well.  Sustaining stable 60 FPS in the busiest downtown places is but a pipe (gun) dream for most players, even on very expensive hardware.  Similarily, playing with highest quality shadows and godrays on also has a completely unreasonable performance hit.
-  As usual, as hefty injection of mods to fix bugs and improve various aspects of the game is required.  You will want mods for letting you know what your character will say during dialog instead of just seeing options for what kind of mood you want to reply with.  You will want mods for deconsolifying various aspects of the UI.  You want mods for disabling companion fall damage so they dont fall off highrises becoming 'downed' and and requiring a stimpack within a short time limit (literally impossible to reach in time, if you have to go through an interior or take run a ways to take a lift or such to get down to them) before they return to wherever they were recruited from.  You want mods for removing object limits in settlements.  You want a sorting mod, so you can actually look at a piece of gear and compare things in a practical way.
-  Mechanically, it is a FAR better action shooty game than FO3/NV.
-  The most interesting game world to explore yet in the Fallout series.  The Commonwealth is a big and exciting playground.  You also learn more about Boston and its history in this game than you did of the places visited in the older games, props for that.
-  Settlement building, while optional and ultimately a giant waste of time, are to me a very fun way to waste my time.
-  While this is not a great Fallout RPG, it is
.  I've had a great time getting sucked into the many stories of tragedy and morbidity, of the delicious alternate history post apocalypse Fallout world, yet again.
-  Weapon and Gear modification is a blast.  Any excuse to rationalize my compulsive hoarding disorder in Bethesda games gets a thumbs up in my book.
I considered not recommending Fallout 4, because of the fairly big downers that are 1. Creation Club and 2. Not much RPG going on in this thing.
In the end I decided it would be unfair to the game, because I really love playing this game as a action shooter survival exploration buildy crafty game, thinking of it as a better Borderlands game.  Fallout 4 does that exceptionally well, and because of that this review lands with a thumbs up from me.
I would definitely recommend picking this game up during a discount.

I love tower defence games but Super Sanctum TD failed to keep my interest.
Before the update that happened sometime this December, I was having decent fun with the game in the earlier levels - even though I thought they were a little too difficult for players who just started the game. All enemies had a little too much health but it was still managable, given that the player was able to use the right combination/positioning of towers and mazes. I found myself patiently restarting levels over and over again just to finish them perfectly before moving on to the next. I played this casually to let off some steam from schoolwork and studying. Despite the slight problems in balancing, I was actually enjoying myself.
Fast forward to Dec 23 when I decided to play it again after exams.
I opened up the game and was surprised to see all the changes: the UI had an all new look, the pricing of towers/blocks increased, monsters had even more health now and numerous other things changed as well. I already thought the game was hard enough as it is, but for some reason the developers thought it would be a good idea to make the game even more unforgiving. I am now unable to go past a really early level in the game because of this.
Super Sanctum TD has a great concept, with a variety of towers and powers you can utilize. I also liked being able to set up a maze for the monsters. Unfortunately, the balancing is currently out of whack so players will be struggling and wasting time trying to get past even the easiest of levels. If you think you have the patience, feel free to try it out but I doubt you'll go very far with the current version.

The overall experience is solid - but.
I understand it's not easy to live up to the kind of success the 2012 XCOM inarguably was, but there is a way it shouldn't be done, and that is making a major part of the sequel consist of a slightly different retelling of the original. It's not that I mind the retcon, and the dystopian society certainly has an appeal, and XCOM2 is nowhere near the lazy reskin that was the 1995 TFTD.
Still, once the initial freedom fighting and customization high tapers off, you start to realize the storyline is seriously underwhelming, and the way the game has you running around the clock both in the tactical mode and on the geoscape mostly serves to distract you from how barebones everything is compared to EU+EW.
It's another step down in complexity compared to the originals (which weren't overly complex to begin with, despite what many people claim), and this time it hits harder. There's a line between streamlining and truncating. I believe XCOM 2 has crossed it, and not even the constant ticking of the clock can conceal the fact. Sure, you can still choose a plethora of approaches in the tactical mode (mostly thanks to the skill trees, this time bordering on magic even more heavily), but other than that the game is reduced to something akin Pac-man. Unfortunately, the DLCs that could have been the game's saving grace are also very hit-or-miss, trending on the miss with the exception of Shen's Last Gift. Comparing any of them to EW is just out of the question.
I enjoyed the game a great deal, so I can't but recommend it, and I look forward to any major DLCs that might expand the gameplay further, but as it is now it just isn't worth it for the full price.

The Walking Dead is an interesting visual novel/point and click type of game. When I first went into it I thought it was about  talking to my group and trying to change their fates through our interactions. I was horribly disappointing to realize no matter what you do or what you say, the outcome is always the same.
There is a huge amount of "illusion of choice" There is one point in the game where you have to choose between saving this guy or saving this girl. When you save one, the other dies and the story goes in a different direction and encourages replaying the game! Right? Wrong. Not twenty minutes later, the person you save dies anyways. In the end no matter your choice, both end up dead. There was no choice! This pattern continued through the whole game, I'd be promoted with a choice and the inevitable would eventually happen. I finished the game with a bad taste in my mouth.
That is until I saw a discussion online about Kenny, one of the characters. The thread started off with someone saying how awesome Kenny was.He always had your back, was friendly, sacrificed himself, he was cool. I agreed. However most people in the thread said he was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! I was completely in disagreement! They were even listing quotes he NEVER said in the game! That was when it hit me. The events of the game are unchangeable but the characters and the way they interact with you is completely different for each player depending on your choices. Kenny was a nice guy in my game but a jerk in many other people's games. It made discussion about the game a ton of fun since everyone's experience with each character was completely different. Some characters tell some players things other players will never hear them say.
Sure the events were out of your control but that kind of game would be a little high budget for Telltale, so I think what they pulled off was pretty well done all things considered. My advice is do NOT go into the game with the thought that you can change the outcome of certain character's gruesome fates, but you can change their personalities, and compare the differences and similarities between your characters and your friend's characters' personalities. Your "best bro" in your game could be your friend's biggest rival or worst enemy!

What an absolutley wonderful game. With a few modded classes added, even more wonderful.
The sound design is superb, and the music is nice and fitting. The voice-acting is amazing -- I haven't felt so enthralled by a video-game narrator since the likes of Arcanum. 5/5 Sound Design.
The visuals are pretty great as well. My low-end, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ computer can run everything (except for the opening cutscene) perfectly. The artistic direction perfectly fits the whole middle-ages/lovecraftian tone. And all the little details -- from meticulous little items hanging off each the characters' belts -- really make it special. 5/5 Visuals.
The gameplay itself is, while having a steep difficulty curve, pretty fair. Though, it can feel a BIT unfair at times, it's never so overwhelmingly so that it ruins the game. A few of the classes feel a bit lacking compared to others (for example, I find that the Man-at-Arms is really only good for guarding the weaker characters, and most everything else about him is done much more efficiently by other melee- or strongman-type classes). But, in the end, the positive FAR outweighs the negative. 4/5 Gameplay Mechanics.
The storyline, I honestly haven't given much thought to. And while it may seem trite to some to have the storyline revealed, bits by bits, via journal entires and ghostly narrations, it's important to keep in mind the theme. For a lovecraftian heavy game, having things revelaed through the mad scribblings of a madman warning others about the 'eldritch' and 'grotesque' monsters that have driven him mad GREATLY compliment the whole tone. So, while I haven't paid too close of attention to the story itself, I love the way in which it is told. 4/5 Storyline.
Now, I did get this game on sale just a few days ago, so as for value for the money I paid, $10 almost feels like a steal. This feels, to me, like a $30 game, so I feel $25 is definitely a fair price. 5/5 Value.
And, lastly, I don't think I could think of another game -- besides maybe the Civilization titles -- that compete to the amount of replayability this game has. Though, it heavily relies on how you view it. If you're looking for countless new characters and monsters, then you're probably not going to play it more than once. But if you're looking to mix-and-match the heroes, and try new combinations, and perfect your strategies, then you're going to fall into a bottomless pit of replayability. With the few mods I've added (from Actionjack), it's definitely added to the replayability by exponets. 3/5 Replayability.
Overall: Superb visuals, sound, and a great value at this price. Pretty great storyline and gameplay mechanics. And replayability if you're one that's into perfecting strategies and team-combinations. 4/5 Game.

As someone who's played and enjoyed many other games in similar genres, I was excited to play Darkest Dungeon, but found that it didn't hold up in comparison to the others I'd played.
The most obvious game to compare this to is Monster's Den: Book of Dread. Monster's Den is a free turn based game from 2008 where you explore a dungeon and fight enemies for rewards. There's no town, but the combat is incredibly nuanced and rewarding. Compared to this, Darkest Dungeon combat felt repetitive and clunky. The equip system was also not nearly as harrowing. There's generally only one or two characters where their equips will even *work*, so you don't need to worry about who gets the rare shoes and who gets cloth stockings.
Still, there's something to be said for simplicity. The modern XCOM games abstract a lot of your choices, leaving you with a 2D movement system and a few variations on 'fire', and are still formidable chance-based strategy. Darkest Dungeons is essentially the same thing, only with 1D movement. The problem is that 1D movement is a lot more constrained than 2D. There are only 4 positions in every battle, and players mostly stand in the same place to keep their attacks effective. This leaves just management (torches, looting, town) and attacks as the deep mechanics.
One of the most powerful draws of Darkest Dungeon is the 'roguelike progress', which invites you to feel like you're moving forward, even as heroes crumple at your feet. Adding story-style progress to a roguelike is a difficult yet emotionally powerful mechanic that's difficult to do right. Darkest Dungeon uses a RPG-style checklist as well as town management mechanics to motivate this. It's effective, but not an elegant solution, and you're prone to feeling sometimes that you're just slogging through dark halls, as opposed to participating in a story.
Another draw is the art style. Even if the mechanics of a game aren't as well oiled as they could be, that can all be made up for by a slick visual style. I have to admit that I don't know anything quite as striking as the stress and victory halos the heroes get as they fail and succeed.
Still, it's not as if this game is unique in that right either. As a top-down shooter, Our Darker Purpose is a bit different gameplaywise, but it still does far better at motivating 'roguelike progress', and equally good at putting out a visual style to make you question the dark nature of humanity.
In conclusion, if you look at Darkest Dungeon and say "a Cthulian-style roguelike management game? That's just what I've *needed*", purchase it, you won't be disappointed. If you're like me and say "Darkest Dungeon? I've heard good things about it, so it must be really great", then I'd recommend you think twice. There's not much here that hasn't been done better elsewhere.

I wasn't sure what to expect from Team Arena. It never caught on back when it released, or at least no one I played with bothered with it. Turns out it's a pretty full package, with new game modes, new powerups, and new bot systems to spar with. It's enough that it probably would have caught on, in fact, if it hadn't committed one of the cardinal sins of multiplayer games.
Team Arena continues with the same "story" as Quake III Arena, that the yet-unseen Vadrigar have a hard-on for gladiatorial combat, and the Quake veterans they've nabbed for it have had enough and are teaming up. The new game modes are all team-based, including classics like Capture the Flag and Team Deathmatch but also new inventions like One Flag CTF, Overload, and Harvester. One Flag CTF is just that, CTF with a neutral flag to claim. Overload places a destructible node in each base and awards victory to the team that destroys the opposing node. Harvester is like Team Deathmatch except kills produce skulls you can collect, which then must be dunked in the opposing base to score points.
There's more than just new modes (and associated maps) to see here, of course. A handful of new weapons are included, mostly throwbacks to older Quakes like the chaingun and nailgun (which is more flechette shotgun than the Q1 version) but nothing that will usurp the basic Q3 arsenal. A new class of powerup that persists until death seeks to imitate class-based multiplayer by giving the holder double health or insane movespeed, but only spawn in your base on long cooldowns. You'll find a few other odds and ends like a suicide bomber power and an invulnerability shield as well.
It is exceedingly likely that none of this content sounds new to you, and that's not just on account of the intervening 15+ years. The big knock against Team Arena at its release was that it was content that had already been added to Quake III Arena via modding. And it's true, even now you can find all of these modes and far, far more in the Q3A modding scene. This is doubly important if you want to play any of them with humans, too, because Team Arena has zero servers running last I checked. Zero. The cardinal sin of multiplayer that I mentioned before is splitting the player base with paid content, and that's exactly what Team Arena threatened to do. Instead of migrating to the new title, however, everyone just stuck with what they knew and loved.
If you're determined to give Team Arena a fair shake, the bot matches are bound to entertain you at least as much as they did in Q3A. You can give orders to bot teammates, and supposedly they will pick up habits from your orders and playstyle. The presentation is lacking compared to the clean interface of Q3A though, with overly-busy menus and a chunky HUD that you'll need to learn the parts of. Graphics and sounds in matches are still the same as ever, along with the frenetic firefights and high-velocity movement. But when all that's offered by the base game, along with actual people to enjoy it with, there's not much reason to bother with this.

Still, once the initial freedom fighting and customization high tapers off, you start to realize the storyline is seriously underwhelming, and the way the game has you running around the clock both in the tactical mode and on the geoscape mostly serves to distract you from how barebones everything is compared to EU+EW.
It's another step down in complexity compared to the originals (which weren't overly complex to begin with, despite what many people claim), and this time it hits harder. There's a line between streamlining and truncating. I believe XCOM 2 has crossed it, and not even the constant ticking of the clock can conceal the fact. Sure, you can still choose a plethora of approaches in the tactical mode (mostly thanks to the skill trees, this time bordering on magic even more heavily), but other than that the game is reduced to something akin Pac-man. Unfortunately, the DLCs that could have been the game's saving grace are also very hit-or-miss, trending on the miss with the exception of Shen's Last Gift. Comparing any of them to EW is just out of the question.
I enjoyed the game a great deal, so I can't but recommend it, and I look forward to any major DLCs that might expand the gameplay further, but as it is now it just isn't worth it for the full price.

I have been waiting for this game for quite some time now. Not a long time, but I was one of those who upvoted it on  greenlight. Since then the developer has been very active in the fledgling community, being very positive and open to new ideas. So now that I have had a chance to play this game, I am very happy to say it was well worth the wait.
First impressions were very good, as the game opens with some somewhat of a dialogue after you press a strange button, the mysterious voice says you have been asleep for a few thousand years, and implies that you used to be someone of great importance. The voice acting was very good, it was very professional and believable, and does a good job giving some context to the setting.
Although there are not too many levels fully completed, the ones that are there show off the gameplay quite nicely. The combat seems entirely skill based, as melee weapons seem to do the same damage. In combat, each melee attack is a lunge, if you miss there will be a short cooldown and you will have to wait before attacking again and thus will leave you open to attack. However, if you land a hit, you can immediatley attack again, thus encouraging players to be more deliberate while striking. When you hold down the attack button, the game goes in slow motion and an arrow appears showing where you will go, thus making it a bit easier not to miss. Don't get me wrong, its still very easy to whif, as your movement keys are factored in during the lunge. However, in a large crowd, if you are able to keep the hits going you can almost bowl right through the crowd, this is very satisfying when you manage to pull this off as a miss will lead to certain death, as a few hits will kill you.
When killed, the enemy dealing the killing blow will grow in size and pwer. If one enemy kills you enough, they basically turn into a boss fight all on their own. While most enemies die in one to two hits, the big boys can tank enormous amounts of damgae and deal just as much with every swing. The only problem is that eventually, the enemy will get so large he won't be able to hit you, though this is probably just a glitch.
Ranged attacks are both satisfying and frustrating. It is very nice to land a shot and see the enemy fly off screen, especially when leaping through the air. It takes a bit of getting used to but its still fun.
The look of this game is very nice, its simplistic with bright popping colors that suit the cube theme nicely. Environments are fun to explore and move around.
All in all this is a fun game, combat is solid, the asthetic is nice, I like the character personlization in this game as you can buy new outfits or find them as well as other cosmetics. I look forward to seeing nerw content come out, as there are only a few levels available at this point, but I can see there is much more to come. Definetly recommend pickling it up.

A great improvement to the original, Keeping the tactical forward planning mind-set required but allowing greater customisation and adding a layer of gritty despair to the setting makes this a fun world to inhabit.
Building further on the story which seems to have an approach to “cannon” as convoluted as the DC universe, XCOM 2 confusingly picks up 20 years after the start of XCOM : Enemy Unknown in a world where that game wasn’t played and humanity did not unite and successfully defend an alien threat.  Or perhaps (in this continuity) you installed the game and left it Idle while Alien forces infiltrated and replaced governments with their own international system of control. ‘Advent’, As the enemy forces in this alternative sequel are now called, have you on the back foot, and unlike the previous game seem a little more comfortable in power while small pockets of resistance around the world wait to be united, Can you guess your role yet?
Perhaps it might be more useful to discuss the sequence of this game in terms of the mechanics which build on those of Enemy Unknown more directly. You once again take control of 3 elements of the resistance: Globally, Starting with only a single region and expanding out to gain more resources and uncovering the story line as you continue. Secondly the development of your base, a recommissioned alien craft that can spend the gathered resources and allow a high level of customisation to your final responsibility. Your turn based combat, the real meat and potatoes of the game.
This is also where the Sid Meier pedigree is most apparent, turn based micromanagement of your small squad of hardened XCOM Fighters each with a different commission giving the generated maps a decidedly unique feel, Combining this depth of choice and a very balanced difficulty gradient you can quite quickly find yourself very  frustrated about a single miss step, proper preparation however can lead to some very satisfying traps being sprung and pay back for the long re-loads when you’ve cocked up and it’s taken 3 turns for it to become apparent that you won’t be able to dig out of this one.
The frustration I mentioned does feed well into the satisfaction of completing a mission with no injury to the completely cusomtisable team you’ve grown attached to, and it is worth saying that the mechanic is a numbers game that can effectively be played with very little random element.
When standing out from its predecessor XCOM 2 pays us in its aforementioned extra options on the field of battle but also in its look, this is a game that demands your emersion through its gritty characterisations and its detailed and fully destructible landscape.
Once again its story is set to a ticking clock that doesn’t give that much time to appreciate these finer points of the game but if you’re new to this genre of  turnbased combat action then it may take a few starts to get you to a place where you can truly appreciate its latter game anyway. x

So, I'm seeing a lot of "received this product for free" reviews which is awesome! Glad people are reviewing this game. But, as someone who personally always is a little leery of those, I wanted to post a "I paid $10 for this" review.
And it was definitely worth the money.
There are glitches, it's pretty brief from what I can tell, and for the love of god the movement needs to be tweaked.
But it is REALLY. DAMN. FUN. (If you want to see gameplay details, I did a video of the beginning of the game here
)
There is a lot of potential here: the way the overworld is set up is really clever, there's a lot of room for cool kingdom building and exploration mechanics, and the combat is stupidly fun. I haven't been this jolly about attacking hordes of enemies since my Dynasty Warriors childhood. The slowmo action is great, I actually really like how floaty the physics are, and even the rudimentary stealth mechanics are enjoyable. My biggest complaints are a few interface weirdnesses (the character screen was very unclear and buggy for me, the overworld map moves really slow but also teleports you) and the movement. It uses grid movement, so W is always up, A is always left, etc rather than AD rotating and WS being forward back...but the game isn't on a grid, and you dash/shoot in any direction. Dashing actually feels better as a movement method than walking, which is baffling.
I was originally going to just try this out since it was just released today, say "its cool" and then wait for future versions, but I'm actually going to go finish the Early Access.

Other notes: The game looks great - dark atmosphere, good enemy/boss design, weapons / armour look suitably fantasy, so you get that extra bit of satisfaction from new gear. Where a Call of Duty/CS:GO crossover could've done so well, this game fails. I do play it frequently, but what they've done here is meshed parts of games that just don't work. Weapons can scope - but only with the scope that comes attached. Not that scoping is genuinely important, as it's plausible to get headshots by accident unzoomed from across a map. Speaking of maps, they're cluttered and small. While in a small setting one would expect close quarters, active combat; this is not at all what is delivered. The clutter makes it hard to get around - except for in a situation that requires sniping. More often then not, people will sit in their own spawn zoomed in on an area that a player from the other team would emerge right after invincibility runs out. Ah yes, spawn invincibility. While this isn't present in game modes that offer 1 life (duh), it is obviously active in others. I understand the concept of invulnerability, its the same in every game - prevent spawn killing on teams already being wiped. Sure, but this lasts too long on such small maps. When a map already has no room for movement, the moment someone emerges from the spawn you're in their view - and you guessed it - he or she is still fully invincible. Grenade launchers are rampant and don't really work properly(functioning essentially as just extra thrown grenades). While it most certainly isn't P2W (which is the biggest UP this game can get), the idea of having a nice knife/gun skin is more farfetched than on CS:GO. Chests offer a 1% chance at recieving an item, and the paid chests offer no better luck than chests bought with in-game currency. That's my biggest gripe - for this reason - The company will lose revenue in every aspect or have to go paid subcription if they keep the store the way it is. Nobody will pay for the ability to open chests if the chests offer no reward. The game also offers no real competitive side to alleviate the ridiculousness of playing with confused people who have no real grasp of aiming. There are clan wars, but it isn't taken seriously nor should it be. The small assortment of maps, broken shop, nonexistent competitive play, and lack of players with any real understanding are just a few of the things that make this game fall flat overall.

It was in fact the recent slew of negative reviews that first brought this product to my attention while exploring my que and got me curious as to what the hubbub was all about, then later on that same day a Twitch/Youtube streamer that I frequent started streaming the game and got me REALLY curious once I actually saw the gameplay.
I think this game is a blasty blast.  It brings thoughtfully strategic AND tactical gameplay in a 3 dimensional environment to a broad genre of games that are very similar to each other.  Longtime RTS, MOBA, and shooter fans alike could all find different reasons to like this game.  The ships are gorgeous and remind me of cover art for sci fi novels out of the 80's and 90's.  (i.e. Larry Niven, Steve Webber, Isaac Asimov and the like)
If you were ever that guy that liked the idea of MOBA/arena style gameplay like LoL, Dota 2, Heroes of the Storm, Paragon, Smite, etc etc but were looking for something that slowed things down a little bit (not the length of match but the pace of gameplay) then this could be the game for you.  Add in the fact that you are piloting massive warships with kilometers long engagements ranges instead of a wee widdle Hero/Champion trudging down the same dirt path and it gets even better!
Fans of games like X2/X3/X4 that thought the world was a little lonely without other people, or the strategy gem Sins of a Solar Empire that wanted some more fast paced (and shorter game time) matches but still want to get their blowy up the space ships on should give this a try.  People who like the concept of EVE Online and enjoyed the basic pvp gameplay but got turned off by the way super hardcore community, world, etc may also want to try this out.  Hell, even Starcraft fans might find something to like in this game.
The community is dangerously small, (I hope this game makes it to full release) and the overall level of content has a long way to go before this game is ready for the masses but it has that magic spark that could could develop into something awesome.
If you want more on the negative aspects of the game go find another review, if you want to figure out what makes this game awesome just install it and give it a try.  And be patient, this isn't Call of Duty in space.

THIS IS A REVIEW FOR AN EARLY ACCESS GAME, WRITTEN AS OF 8/4/2015. SOME OR ALL OF THESE PROBLEMS MAY HAVE BEEN FIXED ALREADY.
Fun, but with serious problems. Crafting is physically painful to attempt, there are no recipes, tutorial is annoying and difficult, you're completely screwed if any of your starter blocks or the plane you start with gets blown up during the tutorial, commonly used crafting materials are almost impossible to find, AI drones are completely useless(harvesters go and fill up their storage, then sit there doing nothing, even though the patch notes state they should go back to base and dump it, follower drones dont know how to turn around obstacles, idle drones dont STAY IDLE AND BREAKDANCE AROUND WHILE IM TRYING TO STICK WHEELS ON THEM), and you have to experiment to find recipes(yes, minecraft did it, no, nobody likes it), automation is abysmally dumb, and the game runs far too poorly for how basic the graphics are.
Other than the glaring problems, I attribute most of this to early access and enjoy the game very much.
My recommendations:
1. Make storage units actually store things, instead of floating them above it. It's annoying when you fit one to a vehicle and you have an antenna of blocks waving around.
2. Allow conveyors to allow or deny specific blocks.
3. Research system to find recipes or unlock buying blocks, instead of having to guess, look on the wiki like a cheater, or get lucky and find a guy with the block you're looking for.
4. Allow item crafters to only accept certain recipes, instead of just throwing whatever goes past into it.
5. Skip tutorial button.
6. Fixing AI should be a priority. It's a major part of the game.
7. Enemies shouldnt attack your home base when you're an hour away.
8. Add an ore radar or something similar, so you can find the materials you're looking for, instead of praying you find the right things just by roaming.
9. Quicksave.
10. Add an info window for vehicle center of mass, weight, and how much weight the wheels can support before they become overloaded.

I have played Quake III Arena for a very long time. When I was a kid, I enjoyed it to death. Then I had found that there was a Team Arena expansion pack. Since I was really obsessed with the Quake franchise as a whole, I immediately flipped out and needed this in my Quake library. Unfortunately, I wouldn't get to play this for a long while. Like..."when I bought this on Steam" long while. So as a very curious Quake fan, I checked it out.
Okay so IF you don't know what Quake III Arena is, it's a fast-paced shooter that has a huge following and great multiplayer. I wrote a review on here so if you want more details just go ahead and check that out. As for Team Arena, it's all in the name. It's literally an expansion that revolves around teamplay. Team Arena adds some new maps and some new weapons. It's pretty cool.
One big addition to the game that I really like is the team communication. Yes it was in Quake III Arena, but the problem with that was the fact that it was all text and if you didn't look up in time, you wouldn't be able to see it. With Team Arena, however, when you used a team order, your character would speak. THAT is the big reason I am recommending this. It is super useful for team games like CTF.
So I already said that I recommend it, but if it was still 1999 and Steam hadn't existed yet, I'd say I WOULDN'T recommend it. There really isn't enough new things to make this a real expansion. The weapons aren't even added to Quake III, so they're pointless. The new maps aren't added to Quake III, so they're pointless. And even though the new communication tool is nice, nobody really plays this game enough for even that to be worth it.
But thankfully, id Software must have realized this since now EVERY copy of Quake III Arena seems to come with Team Arena, so it's a nice bonus for all us Quake fans. Thanks, id!

Quake 3 Team Arena is an Expansion Pack for Quake 3, coming out in 2000, one year later. It's supposed to buff up team modes of Quake 3, probably in order to compete with other games at that time in this area. Still multiplayer arena FPS, yep.
Now, for technical side. Yep, same problems as Quake 3 on Steam.
Widescreen is not supported by default but you can edit resolution and FOV in config like in Q3.
Steam overlay conflicts with game and would result in graphical glitches by default. You have to disable "GL Extension" in game's system options. If you will encounter random crashes, then you should just disable Steam Community for this game.
Quake 3 Arena and Team Arena can break each others saves. After trying Team Arena I found that my Quake 3 campaign progress and options were wiped out, so watch out.
As far multiplayer community, it's completely empty. If you go to server browser and filter it to Team Arena only servers, then you will see void, unlike original Q3.
So, what it leaves us with is single-player portion of a game. There is no more campaign with whatever progress feel, just a bunch of matches to choose to play. Pretty much Skirmish. You can either play duel against 4 new bots in 4 new maps, not much to say about it, like a bonus. Or you can play in small teams in team based modes, therea re four of them. All of them involve you getting into enemy base to score, so defence is important. Classic CTF, One flag one (grab middle flag and bring to enemy), The one where you have to destroy skull thing at enemy base and where you have to kill people and bring skull they may drop to enemy. All four use same set of maps.
Bots were improved too. At least because you can give commands individually. And because they behave better, you can relay on them not to be dumb running around cluelessly with machine gun. They feel improved in general.
And well, when it comes to bots team matches in most FPS, there is a problem that player may feel like he can't impact battle overall. Whcih is important, as he is the only real player. Youw ill feel somewhat disconnect from teambots in this game too, but at least with usual team size being 3v3 or so you will feel that you can take it on yourself. Maps are designed for such team sizes too. You can also give orders individually, though I didn't feel like these will be useful. Some matches cases can be won just by ordering all bots to go after enemy base, seriously.
It also introduces new weapons, powerups and runes. New weapons aer your everyday proximity mines, Nailgun that is like shotgun but shoots slow nails and Chaingun. I feel that chaingun is too powerful, being hitscan and packing a punch.
As for usable-at-anytime powerups you got only two and they both are fun: Kamikaze that lets you blow yourself and enemies and push back teammates. Really good. And thing that makes you stop in one spot, even in air, creating a timed shield around you, while you are free to shoot around.
And then game attempts calsses in a really strange way. You see, one team's side of arena there are four runes. Runes can be picked only by member of it's own side and give him bonuses until he dies. It means that only four members can be classed too. Oh well, maps aren't designed for more than 4 on each side or so. Everys ingle of these runes is powerful:
Guard - Gets 200 health and 200 armor. Health slowly regenerates.
Scout - Double speed and double speed of fire. Can't pick armor though.
Double - Double damage.
Ammo-Regen - Double fire speed and slowly regenerated ammo.
In all honesty, I don't like them. They don't really make you play differently, it doesn't feel like each class requries it's own approach. More like, each class is powerful in their own way. But overall good, no big weaknesses. And well, some may get too powerful at times, it feels.
I mean, if Ammo-Regen gets Chaingun, making already powerful hitscan shoot two times faster, it will not be pretty.
And well. I can't really recommend this game. It feels more like a mod, I think that it was seen as redutant even when it was released. There is no online part due to lack of community and it's not much fun with bots either, having no campaign to progress too, sadly. Not sure of overall balance either. You can skip it.

is a casual point and click adventure game set in a fantasy/fairy tale world. For adventure gamers who aren't particularly fond of hidden object scenes, I have pleasant news, as hidden object scenes in Grim Legends 2 occur very occasionally. The bulk of the gameplay consists of exploration, inventory-based puzzles, and a large variety of puzzle mini-games, and I found myself being constantly impressed by how refreshing the mini-game selection was. I play a LOT of point and click adventure games (or HOPAs) and consider myself to be very picky within this genre, however, I never felt like I had a dull moment exploring the beautiful and immersive world of Grim Legends 2. The storyline is a bit cheesy, but that's OK, as some characters were memorable and lovable, and the artwork and music was of a very high-quality. I think what stood out most to me in this game was how beautiful the scenery was.
Keep in mind that this is a Collector's Edition (this fact isn't mentioned on the Steam store page). This means that aside from the main game/story, there's also a (much smaller) bonus game/story, as well as goodies to include wallpapers, concept art and re-playable hidden object mini-games. The main game as well as the bonus game took me about 4 hours to complete on Expert mode, so you can expect a similar amount of gameplay hours if you're familiar with point and click games.
I would recommend it (on sale) to anyone who enjoys point and click adventure games, particularly those who enjoy fantasy settings. It's an excellent game for young children who have demonstrated interest in fairy tales, too.

Gameplay for those just interested in that:
Simple yet incredibly fun. Warcube is a twist on what you would expect a cube-based game to be thanks to the popularity of Minecraft. In this game, you focus on combat instead of building. The combat is fairly simple, but very well done and responsive. The slow-motion effect is also a nice touch since it adds a "cinematic feel" to the game when you're attempting to do a combo or perform a trickshot.
There is also a nice built-in feature that allows you to create a gif or take a screenshot from inside the game itself and uploads it to imgur. Although I don't find myself using it often, I can see where it may be useful for when others may do a move that they would like to share.
That being said, my main issue is the small amount of content currently in the game. However, I expected it going into the game so I'm not that disappointed. It is an early access game after all, and I still had a LOT of fun playing the content that is currently available (I should probably mention that - at the time of this review - I have not finished all the content currently in the game).
Overall, I really do like this game and hope it does very well, and I can't wait to see where it ends up!

3 minutes of gameplay & full review commentary, if you want more details:
Warcube is an action/adventure game, where you control, that’s right, a cube of war. You’ve returned to claim back your kingdom (and to fight red cubes). The game consists of one world map split into regions, you can “zoom in” and conquer them as you travel, which adds additional dimension to the game. The combat system is quite simple: click on the enemies to charge and damage them, but there’s a twist: after you hit an enemy, the slow mo turns on and there’s a chance to start a new attack, making you “combo” through your enemies and chain kill them. One thing that deserves extra notice is the developer’s character built into the game: there’s a small cube that you are going to meet as you progress. It gives the game personal approach and makes you feel welcome while playing.
•	The battle system is simple, yet entertaining. Chaining combos is really fun and I feel that this mechanic is not represented enough in video games. Luckily, this game fixes that.
•	Enemy gets stronger when he kills you: It’s a pretty cool mechanic that prevents mindless rushing.
•	Interesting approach to early access: “developer’s character” makes you feel welcome
•	Different maps that don’t feel repetitive
•	Neat, minimalistic style
•	Great soundtrack
•	Movement seems clumsy: especially when you’re going up the slope and trying to jump. Jumping is complicated: not because of challenging terrain, but simply because the jumping mechanics are not implemented well enough yet. Overall, control responsiveness could be a bit better.
•	Not much weapon/equipment variety so far
Summary
You can see that developer puts his soul into the game: even though there is not too much content yet, there’s a good attention to detail and his „personal” character presence in the game makes you feel very welcome. Overall, I’d say get it if you want to influence how the game is developed. Otherwise – wait for full release to experience the game completely.

These days, thanks to the likes of popular games like Minecraft or Roblox, we've come to associate blocks and cubes with building and creation. Sure, cubes can be used to make stuff, but they're also excellent at destroying things!
In Warcube you assume the role of a little cube, whose sole responsibility is to reclaim the land from the red bandit cubes. It's clearly evident that the developer has drawn inspiration from the games mentioned in Warcube's description (Shadow of Mordor, Assassin's Creed, Mount & Blade etc) which is excellent for me personally, as I LOVE the free-flow combat mechanic that SoM had, but even more so that the Batman franchise had as well. To find similar mechanics in a game that's clearly as different as Warcube is, is exciting.
Warcube is obviously an early access title and still has a long way to go before it develops into the game that Craigz (dev) envisions it to become, but I have high hopes for the future of Warcube. With the addition of the Arena mode that's coming very shortly, the game is going to have even more to offer than it has now, and whilst I don't yet know what the Arena mode will be like, I can only hope that it's going to be something as addictive as the Endless Mode in Clone Drone in the Dangerzone (RIP 30+ hours).
One thing that I feel I really need to mention here is that I have never in my life spoken to a developer that has so obviously been so heavily invested in his creation like the developer of Warcube is. Craigz lives, breathes and dreams Warcube and this is exactly the type of developer that I believe will see his product all the way through and out of early access to full release (unlike many others who abandon their games and remain in EA forever). Every bug that I've reported to him and suggestion that I've made on improving the game, he has actioned immediately. He understands and realizes that the input of his community is essential in the development of a successful game, and this is what we as consumers value most (personal opinion).
The one thing about Warcube that I personally feel needs to be changed, is the soundtrack. I've mentioned this to the developer and he is currently searching for something that's both thematically appropriate but significantly more energetic than the music that the game currently has. Music is very important to me, particularly in a game, and Warcube's music is definitely lacking in energy and inspiration. An upbeat chiptune track would make the game considerably more enjoyable than it is now.
TL:DR The time that I've spent with Warcube so far (almost 3 hours) has been great, and I very much look forward to see where the developer takes it in the future.

Warcube looks very nice, and even with the limited scope of it's character designs, it all gives a certain level of charm and unique immersion. With diverse landscapes en scenes being available, and excellent level design creating enjoyable gameplay. And the gameplay is mostly solid - Cool slow-motion and active combat with movement and timing at the fore-front, accompanied with fitting sound and music and set with a good bunch of interactive elements to facilitate gameplay.
Where the game starts to show its gaps, is quite literally - in the gaps of content. There is just so very little of it. The early access build only has about 2 hours of content available, with limited replay value. The content that is here - is very fun, but there is very little of it available
Another issue, but very minimal comperativly, is the physics. They feel and act very floatly and "heavy" at, seemingly, random. Very sad.
Overal a very solid build in terms of quality and design, with a solid set of core mechanics that mostly need expanding and MORE of everything. More levels, more enemies, more dificulty options, more items, more combat mechanics, etc... A cool and interesting game that deserves your attention, but might also need a bit more content to be worth the money.
